A derailment between Bala and Goudiry on 13 May 2009 killed five and injured thirty-seven, and passenger service was halted in May 2010. In 2015 the governments ended Transrail's concession in favour of Dakar-Bamako Ferroviaire, but freight service was suspended in 2018. A scheduled passenger service between Kayes and Bamako restarted in 2023.
dakodonou: Dakodonou is also written Dakodonu, Dako Donu or Dako Danzo. Oral tradition makes him the son, or grandson, of Do-Aklin, the founder of the royal dynasty of Dahomey. According to that tradition a succession struggle in Allada led Do-Aklin to move a large population onto the Abomey plateau, which the Gedevi people had settled. When Do-Aklin died, or in some versions was deposed, Dakodonou became leader of the group, and the Gedevi chiefs allowed it to settle on the plateau. One legend says his name was first Dako and that he took the name Dakodonou after killing a man called Donou, either a farmer or an indigo painter, in a pot of indigo.

Tradition holds that Dakodonou asked a prominent Gedevi chief named Dan, or Da, for more land, and that the chief answered by asking whether he should open his belly and build him a house in it. Dakodonou is said to have killed Dan on the spot and built his palace on the site, and the kingdom's name was derived from the incident: Dan, xo, belly, me, inside of. He is reported to have conquered two more villages. His reign coincided with the start of the Royal Palaces of Abomey, whose first structures were probably replaced by Houegbadja, and of the Agongointo-Zoungoudo Underground Town.

The historian Edna Bay argues that Dakodonou was himself a Gedevi, one of the local people, and that Agaja added him to the royal line to establish the kingdom's rule over them. She points out that the head priest of the kingdom, the agasunon, always came from Dakodonou's lineage, and that traditions of lineages outside the ruling group call Houegbadja his adopted son. Monroe holds that the story of Dan's killing is unlikely to rest on a single incident, and Bay considers the meaning In the belly of Dan a false etymology.
dakovo: Đakovo is a town in Slavonia in Croatia, 37 km south-west of Osijek and 34 km south-east of Našice, at an elevation of 111 m, and it is the centre of the fertile Đakovo region. The name comes from the Greek diákos, in Slavic form đak, 'pupil'; it is uncertain whether it came directly from Greek, from Hungarian diák or from the local Slavic form. In Roman antiquity the settlement of Certissia stood on the same spot until it disappeared in the Migration Period.

The settlement is first mentioned in 1239, when Béla IV of Hungary granted it to the Diocese of Bosnia, and the bishop moved his seat there in 1246. A predecessor of the present St Peter's Cathedral was built in 1355. In 1374 the place is recorded as Dyacou, and on 25 July 1386 Croatian rebels captured Queen Mary of Hungary and her mother Elizabeth near it. Ottoman rule began after the Battle of Gorjani in 1537 and lasted nearly 150 years, during which Đakovo, then called Yakova, was the centre of a kaza in the Sanjak of Pojega.

In 1805 a herd of Lipizzan horses was evacuated to Đakovo when Napoleon invaded Austria and Hungary, and part of it stayed. In 1910 the population of 6,304 comprised 4,894 Croatians, 890 Germans, 249 Hungarians and 164 Serbs. Around then the town was a district capital in Virovitica County in the Kingdom of Croatia-Slavonia. From 1 December 1941 until 7 July 1942 the Ustaše operated the Đakovo internment camp, mostly for Jewish, Roma and Serb women and children.

Đakovo has 19,491 inhabitants in the town itself, and its economy rests on farming, livestock, leather and wool processing, wood processing and food production. The Cathedral basilica of St Peter, built in 1866–1882 under Josip Juraj Strossmayer, then Catholic bishop of Đakovo and Srijem, is the most important sacral building in Slavonia. A park of the 19th century near the bishop's palace is a protected horticultural monument. The folklore festival Đakovački vezovi is held every year at the beginning of July, with traditional costumes, dances and a horse and wedding wagon show, and white Lipizzaner horses from the breeding centre at Ivandvor, active since 1506, can be seen on the racecourse. The region is also known for its Slavonian cooking and wines.
dakshina-kosala: Inscriptions recording grants of villages in the Kosala country, issued by rulers with titles such as Kosaladhisha, Kosaladhipati and Kosala-narendra, show that the lands of the present Raipur, Bilaspur and Sambalpur districts belonged to it, and at its widest it may have taken in part of Vidarbha. The 7th-century Chinese traveller Xuanzang put the kingdom at 6,000 li in circuit. To the north lay Mekala, which the Puranas and the Balaghat inscription of the Vakataka king Prithvishena II treat as a distinct region.

Its capitals at different times included Bhadravati, Sirpur (ancient Shripura), Tuman (Tummana) and Ratanpur (Ratnapura). In the 19th century Alexander Cunningham, the founder of the Archaeological Survey of India, treated it as a synonym of Mahakoshal, but no ancient text or inscription supports this.

The Ramayana tradition gives South Kosala to Kusha, son of Rama, who founded a capital at Kushasthalipura, identified with a place near Malhar in Bilaspur district. In the 1st century BCE Mahameghavahana, a king of Chedi, conquered Kosala; early in the 2nd century CE it fell to Gautamiputra Satakarni of the Satavahana dynasty, and the Megha dynasty later regained it. Samudragupta defeated Mahendra of Kosala, bringing the region under the overlordship of the Gupta Empire in the 4th century.

After the Gupta decline small dynasties ruled, their chronology unclear because their inscriptions count regnal years. The Sharabhapuriyas, at first Gupta vassals, laid the foundation of the distinct Dakshina Kosala style of art and architecture; the Panduvamshis of Shripura began as their feudatories. Xuanzang visited under the Panduvamshi king Mahāśivagupta Bālārjuna, a devotee of Shiva who patronised the Buddhists, and counted about one hundred monasteries with somewhat less than 10,000 monks of the Great Vehicle. Centuries later Tummana was founded by Kalingaraja, a descendant of the Tripuri Kalachuri king Kokalla I, and Ratnapura by Ratnadeva.
dakshinapatha: The name joins two Sanskrit words, dakshina, south, and patha, road. The later Vedic texts divide the Indian subcontinent into three parts: Aryavarta in the north, Madhya Desha in the centre and Dakshinapatha in the south. The Aitareya Brahmana, of the first half of the first millennium BCE, names peoples of the south of Vindhyan and north Deccan origin, among them the Satvants, Vidarbha, Andhra, Nishadas and Kuntis. The grammarian Panini, about 500 BCE, mentions the Asmaka Kingdom in connection with the south and with Kalinga.

The term has carried three meanings. It can denote the ancient south of the subcontinent below Uttarapatha, usually the Deccan and sometimes Tamilakam and Ceylon as well. It can mean the great southern highway, running from Magadha to Pratishthana. It has also been used for a kingdom on the Godavari River. The Junagarh rock inscription of 150 CE, set up by an Indo-Scythian king, records that he twice defeated Satakarni, the lord of Dakshinapatha, in fair fight and did not destroy him because of the nearness of their connection.

The southern road was one of two great highways that have linked the parts of the subcontinent since the Iron Age. The other, the Uttarapatha or great northern road, ran from Taxila through the Punjab to the Yamuna and followed that river south to Mathura; from there a route went on to Ujjain in Malwa and to Broach on the western coast. According to the writer Sanjeev Sanyal, the course of the northern road has stayed roughly the same since before the Mauryas, while the southern road appears to have drifted.

The route of Rama into exile in the epic may reflect an early version of it. By the time of the Buddha it started at Varanasi and ran through Vidisha in central India to Pratishthana, now Paithan, and it probably extended to the Chola, Chera and Pandya kingdoms of the far south. By the Mauryan period there would have been a branch from Ujjain to the ports of Gujarat, which made Ujjain a major city by the Gupta era. The modern highway that roughly corresponds to it runs much further east than the old road but still meets the northern road at Varanasi.
dal-cais: The Dál gCais traced their line to an ancestor, Cormac Cas, said to have lived in the 2nd or 3rd century and made in their genealogies a younger brother of Eógan, founder of the rival Eóganachta. Later scholars came to regard this as a politically motivated fabrication, since kinship with their rivals strengthened their claim to Munster. Present scholarship holds that they were a northern branch of the Déisi Muman, part of whom moved north-west towards the River Shannon between the 5th and early 8th centuries. The name Dál gCais is first recorded in the Annals of Inisfallen for 934, at the death of their king Rebachán mac Mothlai.

After 934 leadership passed from the Uí Aengusa kindred to the junior Uí Thairdelbaig. Cennétig, who styled himself King of Thomond, began to challenge the Eóganachta, and his son Mahon defeated the Norse under Ivar of Limerick at the Battle of Sulcoit in 968 and seized the Rock of Cashel. After Mahon was murdered in 976, his brother Brian Bóruma avenged him, took Munster back and, after a 15-year war, received the high kingship from Malachy II in 1002. He died at the Battle of Clontarf in 1014.

Three more high kings came from the dynasty, Donnchad mac Briain, Toirdelbach Ua Briain and Muirchertach Ua Briain, the last reigning from 1101. The Treaty of Glanmire of 1118 split Munster, granting Thomond to the sons of Diarmait Ua Briain and Desmond to the Mac Cárthaigh dynasty. The Norman de Clares, granted Thomond in 1276, were defeated at the Battle of Dysert O'Dea in 1318, and Thomond stayed outside foreign control for another two centuries.

In 1543 Murchadh Carrach Ó Briain surrendered his Gaelic kingship to Henry VIII and became Earl of Thomond and Baron Inchiquin, and the kingdom became County Clare. After the O'Brien kings of Thomond the most powerful Dalcassian families were MacNamara, O'Kennedy, MacMahon, O'Grady and O'Dea; the Clancy sept were the hereditary Brehons of Thomond, the MacBrody sept its poets and historians. Two election pamphlets of Éamon de Valera's Fianna Fáil party later addressed voters as Dalcassians, by then a romantic name for the Irish as a whole.
dal-riata: The name Dál Riata comes from Old Irish and means the portion of Riata. Bede wrote that the kingdom was named after its founder, a man called Reuda, while the 11th-century Duan Albanach says that the three sons of Erc, Fergus Mór, Loarn and Óengus, conquered Scotland. Tradition has seen Gaelic in Scotland as the result of migration or takeover from Ireland. The archaeologist Ewan Campbell argues that there is no archaeological or place-name evidence for either. He suggests that Argyll and Antrim formed a maritime province united by the sea, and that the medieval accounts were dynastic propaganda. His theory has been challenged.

The kingdom reached its largest extent under Áedán mac Gabráin, who died about 608. In 575 Columba negotiated an alliance with the Cenél Conaill at the Convention of Druim Cett. Áedán campaigned as far as Orkney but was defeated by Æthelfrith of Bernicia at Degsastan about 603. Under Domnall Brecc the kingdom suffered defeat at the Battle of Magh Rath in 637, and Domnall was killed in 642; Dál Riata then became tributary to Northumbria.

In the 730s the Pictish king Óengus mac Fergusa conquered Dál Riata, and Alex Woolf concludes that he effectively destroyed it, though some scholars see a revival under Áed Find, who died in 778. Viking raids began in 795. Tradition attributes a merger of the Dál Riatan and Pictish crowns to Cináed mac Ailpín, who became king of the Picts about 843, and the two peoples formed the Kingdom of Alba.

In Argyll there were four main kindreds: the Cenél nGabráin in Kintyre, the Cenél nÓengusa on Islay and Jura, the Cenél Loairn in Lorne and the later Cenél Comgaill in Cowal and Bute. Dunadd was the most important royal site; excavation found weapons, quern-stones, jewellery moulds, and glassware and wine amphorae from Gaul.

Most people lived by subsistence farming, with oats and barley as the main crops, and herding was especially important. Travel by sea was the easiest way to move any distance, and houses were grouped into twenties, each group providing 28 oarsmen for the war fleet. The monastery of Iona did much to spread Christianity in northern Britain and insular art.
dala-hill: Dala Hill stands in the city of Kano in Kano State, Nigeria, and a stairway of 101 steps leads from its foot to its top. The city itself was originally known as Dala, after the hill. In the 7th century the hill was the site of a community that worked iron, and from about 700 CE it held the shrine of Tsumburbura, which lasted until the cult collapsed under the growing dominance of Islam in the 13th century.

Kano tradition tells of Barbushe, a man of great size and strength who hunted elephants with his stick and carried them back to the hill on his back. There he built a shrine to Tsumburbura, a deity the Hausa are believed to have worshipped before Islam. Only Barbushe could enter it, and anyone who went in without his leave was said to have died. He came down from the hill only on the two days of Idi, when people from all around brought animals to sacrifice in the hope of Tsumburbura's favour.

The hill is also tied to the Hausa legend of Bayajidda, a stranger believed to have come from Baghdad, who married into a ruling family and fathered the rulers of the seven city-states of the Hausa Bakwai. In tradition Dala was the centre of power around which all rituals revolved: the place where the ancestor figure first lived with his wives and seven children, and to which his descendants had to return. The hill kept its standing after Islam arrived. As late as 1819 the second Fulani Muslim ruler made forty days of prayer on its summit to gain assurance of victory in war.
dalai-lama: Dalai Lama is part of the full title Holiness Knowing Everything Vajradhara Dalai Lama, which Altan Khan gave to Sonam Gyatso, the leader of the Gelug school, in 1578 at Yanghua Monastery. Dalai combines the Mongolic word for ocean with the Tibetan bla-ma, master. Sonam Gyatso had just given teachings to the Khan, and the title was extended to the whole tulku lineage, so he became the 3rd Dalai Lama, while the first two were awarded it after their deaths. The 1st, Gendun Drup (1391 to 1474), was a disciple of Tsongkhapa and abbot of Drepung, and the 2nd established the method of finding later incarnations through visions at the oracle lake, Lhamo Lhatso.

The 4th Dalai Lama, Yonten Gyatso (1589 to 1617), was a Mongol, a great-grandson of Altan Khan, and his connection led the Mongols to support the Gelug zealously. The Gelug were the newest school and lacked an established network of Tibetan clan patronage, so they relied more on foreign patrons. After his death the Tsangpa rulers of Central Tibet forbade a search for his incarnation, but in 1618 the child was secretly identified and later recognised as the 5th Dalai Lama, Lobsang Gyatso.

From 1642 to 1951 the Dalai Lama led the secular government of Tibet, directly or through regents, in the government known as the Ganden Phodrang, which governed the Tibetan Plateau with varying degrees of autonomy. The Qing dynasty established control over Tibet in 1720, and Chinese authorities have asserted the right to oversee the selection of spiritual leaders since the 18th century, a practice formalised in 1793. The 6th Dalai Lama, Tsangyang Gyatso, gave up his monk's robes in 1702 and chose a layman's life.

Since the time of the 5th Dalai Lama in the 17th century the Dalai Lama has been a symbol of the unification of the state of Tibet. His religious authority goes beyond the Gelug tradition and represents Buddhist values not tied to a single school. The extent and nature of the Dalai Lama's secular and religious power remains contested. One interpretation is the mchod yon, usually translated as priest and patron relationship, an alliance between Tibetan Buddhist leaders and secular rulers such as the Mongols, Manchus and Chinese authorities. Critics, including Sam van Schaik, hold that the theory oversimplifies the situation, and historians such as Melvyn Goldstein have called Tibet a vassal state or tributary.
dali-kingdom: Nanzhao was overthrown in 902, and three short-lived dynasties ruled its successor kingdoms in quick succession: Great Changhe, Great Tianxing and Great Yining. In 934 Duan Siping, an official in the Tonghai Area Command, organised a coalition of Nanzhao sympathisers and overthrew the Yang regime, and in 937 he seized power and established himself at Dali. The Duan clan professed Han ancestry, and Yuan records say they came from Wuwei in Gansu, which neither Song nor Dali sources confirm. The kingdom took its name from Dali, which means marble in Chinese.

Relations with the Song dynasty were cordial, though Dali was essentially independent. The founder of the Song, Taizu, declared the Dadu River the border and refused further claims, so as to avoid the costly wars the Tang had fought against Nanzhao. Dali established tribute relations in 982, but Song officials allowed it to offer tribute at court only three times. Its horses were prized as military assets. In 1094 the former prime minister Gao Shengtai forced King Duan Zhengming to give up the throne and renamed the realm the Dazhong Kingdom; when he died in 1096 the Duan family regained it, but the Gao clan stayed in power at court and later fought among themselves.

Möngke Khan sent envoys demanding surrender, and the king of Dali had them killed. Möngke put his brother Kublai in charge of the invasion. Kublai's army crossed the Jinsha River at night and routed the Dali army, and in late 1253 three Mongol columns converged on the city of Dali. King Duan Xingzhi fled to Shanchan and it took two more years of fighting to capture both cities. In 1256 he surrendered, and the Duan family continued to govern Yunnan as vassals of the Mongols under the title Maharaja. The Ming conquered Yunnan in 1382.

The administration of Dali has been characterised as a mandala state similar to Southeast Asian kingdoms, with some Chinese influence. The Duan rulers gave Sinitic-style appointments and hereditary fiefs to clans such as the Gao, Yang and Dong, and allied with the leaders of peripheral peoples. The kings styled themselves Buddha-kings, and ten of the 22 kings retired to become monks. The ruling elite wrote in Chinese script, supplemented by Bai characters, so most sources are in Classical Chinese. Most Bai people trace their ancestry to Nanzhao and Dali, though the records of those kingdoms do not mention them.
dalian: Dalian is a prefecture-level, sub-provincial port city in Liaoning province, on the southern tip of the Liaodong peninsula. It is the southernmost city in Liaoning and in Northeast China as a whole, and shares maritime boundaries with cities across Liaodong Bay and the Bohai Strait and with North Korea across the Korea Bay. Its climate is humid continental, with warm, wet summers under the East Asian monsoon and cold, dry winters. The municipal area consists of Dalian proper and Lüshunkou, formerly the city of Lüshun, known in Western and Russian sources as Port Arthur, about 40 kilometres away.

The Qin and Han empires annexed the Dalian peninsula from a Korean state, and in the Sixteen Kingdoms era the Korean state of Goguryeo controlled the region. In the 1880s the Qing government built bridges and heavily fortified the peninsula. Mining camps on the northern coast of Dalian Bay grew into the small town of Qingniwa, from which modern Dalian originated. The British briefly occupied Qingniwa in the Second Opium War in 1858 and returned it in 1860. Japan overcame the Chinese defences in the First Sino-Japanese War, and in the Treaty of Shimonoseki of 17 April 1895 China ceded the Liaodong Peninsula, Taiwan and Penghu.

The Russian Empire coerced a lease of the area from the Qing dynasty in 1898 and built a commercial town called Dalny, a name meaning far-away. After the Russo-Japanese War of 1904-1905 Japan occupied the area as the Kwantung Leased Territory and renamed the city Dairen, the Japanese reading of the Chinese name of Dalian Bay. Shipbuilding and locomotive works were already located in the city before and during the Second Sino-Japanese War. Many farmers and fishers from Shandong settled in the area during the Chuang Guandong migration, and the Dalian dialect, a Jiaoliao Mandarin speech, has a few loanwords from Japanese and Russian.

After Japan's surrender, the Soviet Manchurian offensive took the city on 22 August 1945. Unlike many cities of the northeast, it never reverted to Nationalist authority. The Soviets and the Chinese Communists cooperated to develop its industry and port, which had been relatively undamaged in the war, and in 1945 the first Communist mayor of the Lüda Administrative Office was appointed.

Dalian is Liaoning's second largest city after the provincial capital Shenyang, with 7,450,785 inhabitants at the 2020 census. It is a shipping, financial and logistics centre of East Asia. Zhongshan Square, laid out by the Russians, is surrounded by classical buildings that the Japanese built in the first half of the 20th century. Dalian University of Technology and Dalian Maritime University, founded in 1909, are among its universities.
dalit: The Sanskrit word dalit is rendered as broken or scattered; the same people were also called Harijans. They were excluded from the fourfold varna of the caste hierarchy in Hinduism. Their status was tied to hereditary occupations that caste Hindus considered polluting or debased, such as working with leather, disposing of dead animals, manual scavenging and sanitation work. The economist and reformer B. R. Ambedkar said that untouchability entered Indian society around 400 CE, through the struggle for supremacy between Buddhism and Brahmanism. Several scholars have drawn parallels with the Burakumin of Japan and the Baekjeong of Korea.

Gopal Baba Walangkar (c. 1840–1900) is generally considered the pioneer of the Dalit movement, and Ambedkar himself held him to be its progenitor. Harichand Thakur (c. 1812–1878) led the Matua organisation among the Namasudra community in the Bengal Presidency, and Jyotirao Phule (1827–1890) worked to improve conditions for Dalits; his Gulamgiri of 1873 is regarded as a seminal moment in Dalit literature. In the nineteenth century the Brahmo Samaj, Arya Samaj and Ramakrishna Mission took part in the cause.

The Laxminarayan Temple in Wardha was the first upper-caste temple to welcome Dalits openly, in 1928, and the last King of Travancore issued a Temple Entry Proclamation in 1936. After independence in 1947 Article 17 of the Constitution outlawed untouchability. The Untouchability (Offences) Act of 1955 was amended in the same year into the Protection of Civil Rights Act, and when neither proved effective the Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe (Prevention of Atrocities) Act of 1989 followed.

Most Dalits in India are Hindu, with significant populations following Buddhism, Sikhism, Christianity and Islam. In 1956 Ambedkar launched the Dalit Buddhist movement, and about half a million Dalits joined him in rejecting Hinduism. Mass conversions to Christianity involved groups such as the Chuhras of Punjab, the Chamars of North India, the Vankars of Gujarat and the Pulayas of Kerala. Among Sikhs the two Dalit castes of Punjab are the Mazhabis and the Ramdasias.

The 2011 census counted Scheduled Caste communities at 16.6 per cent of India's population. A study found more than 900 Dalit sub-castes, with divisions between them. Dalit literature has formed an identity across languages including Marathi, Bangla, Hindi, Kannada, Punjabi, Tamil and Odia; its earliest identifiable writers include Madara Chennaiah, an 11th-century cobbler-saint, and Dohara Kakkaiah. Dalit communities also settled in the Caribbean, where about a third of the immigrants arriving in 1883 are estimated to have been Dalits, and later in Britain and the United States.
dalmatia: Dalmatia is a narrow belt of land on the eastern shore of the Adriatic Sea, stretching from the island of Rab in the north to the Bay of Kotor in the south. The Dalmatian Hinterland ranges in width from about 50 kilometres in the north to a few kilometres in the south and is mostly covered by the rugged Dinaric Alps. Seventy-nine islands and about 500 islets run parallel to the coast, the largest being Brač, Pag and Hvar. The coast has a Mediterranean climate, and olives and grapes grow there. The name comes from the Dalmatae, an Illyrian tribe that lived in the area in the 1st millennium BCE.

The area was part of an Illyrian kingdom between the 4th century BCE and the Illyrian Wars, when the Roman Republic established a protectorate south of the river Neretva. The province of Illyricum was formally established around 32-27 BCE. In 9 CE the Dalmatians rose in the last of a series of revolts, together with the Pannonians; after it was crushed, Illyricum was split in 10 CE into Pannonia and Dalmatia. Urban centres were almost completely romanised, while in the countryside the Illyrians kept their language, gods and tribal organisation.

From the middle of the 6th century Slavic migrations pushed the Romance-speaking population to the coast and islands. By 619 the Slavs and Avars had ruined the capital Salona, which allowed settlement in the nearby palace of Diocletian, and the Croats and other Slavs founded their own territories. The Kingdom of Croatia was founded in 925. The Republic of Venice held parts of Dalmatia from 1000 to 1358 and from 1420 to 1797, while the Republic of Ragusa existed from 1358 to 1808. Most of the hinterland fell to the Ottoman Empire in the early 16th century, and Venice later reconquered it.

At the Congress of Vienna in 1815 Dalmatia was granted to the Emperor of Austria as the Kingdom of Dalmatia. In 1848 Croatian demands for union with Croatia, supported above all by Dubrovnik, were blocked by the March Constitution. Until 1909 Italian and Croatian were both official languages; by 1910 all but one of the 82 urban communities had a Slav majority. After the First World War Dalmatia became part of the State of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs.

Dalmatia is a historical region only and has no formal status in Croatian law, so its extent rests largely on the borders of the Austrian kingdom. It roughly corresponds to the four southernmost Croatian counties, with seats at Zadar, Šibenik, Split and Dubrovnik. Split is the largest city, followed by Zadar, Šibenik and Dubrovnik. The major rivers are the Zrmanja, Krka, Cetina and Neretva.
dama-dam-mast-qalandar: Legends at the shrine of Lal Shahbaz Qalandar in Sehwan hold that the poem was first written by the 13th-century Sufi poet Amir Khusrow and modified in the 18th century by Bulleh Shah, who added verses in praise of the saint and gave it a strong colouring of Sindhi culture. The poem names the town of Sehwan and venerates Ali, the cousin and son-in-law of Muhammad. The word Lal may refer to the saint as a young man, to the ruby glow attributed to him or to his red dress.

The song is performed with dhamaal, a devotional Sufi whirling for spiritual ecstasy, across the northern Indian subcontinent, above all in Punjab and Sindh, and in Iran. The historian and anthropologist Michel Boivin writes that the term Jhulelal in the song was used historically by Sindhi Hindus for Jhulelal, an avatar of the god Varuna; after the song became popular, Lal Shahbaz Qalandar himself was often called Jhulelal.

The best-known modern melody was composed by Master Ashiq Hussain for the 1956 Pakistani film Jabroo, where the song, then called Lal Meri Pat, was sung by Inayat Hussain Bhatti, Fazal Hussain and A.R. Bismil. Hussain said he set an edited version of the poem brought to him by Saghar Siddiqui. He spent his later life in poverty in Lahore, and when he died in 2017 most Pakistanis did not know he had composed the tune. Modified by Nazir Ali and sung by Noor Jehan in the 1969 film Dillan Dey Soudey, it became the most popular modern rendition.

Many singers have performed it since, among them Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan, Abida Parveen, the Sabri Brothers, Runa Laila and the Wadali brothers. Khan and M. Arshad composed a new song inspired by it, released as Dam Mast Mast in 1991, and the Bollywood music director Viju Shah used Khan's version for Tu Cheez Badi Hai Mast Mast in the film Mohra (1994).
damaji-rao-gaekwad: Damaji was the third son of Pilaji Rao Gaekwad, himself the adopted son of Damaji I, who had received the hereditary title Shamsher Bahadur from Chhatrapati Shahu. The Gaekwads were at first lieutenants of the Dabhade family, the Maratha chiefs of Gujarat and holders of the title of senapati. After Trimbak Rao Dabhade was killed in 1731 for rebelling against Peshwa Baji Rao, his young brother Yashwant Rao became senapati, and Pilaji, then from 1732 Damaji, held the real military power.

When Peshwa Balaji Rao refused to release the Dabhades from sharing their revenues, Umabai Dabhade joined Tarabai's rebellion and sent Damaji with 15,000 men. He defeated a larger force of Trimbakrao Purandare at Nimb, north of Satara, but was beaten on the Venna River, trapped in the Krishna valley and forced to surrender. In May 1751 the Peshwa arrested him and his relatives and held him at Pune and then at Lohagad, at one point in chains, while he refused to cede half of Gujarat.

In March 1752 Damaji gave up the cause of the Dabhade family and was made the Maratha chief of Gujarat, promising the Peshwa an annual tribute and a force of 20,000 cavalry. His troops joined Raghunathrao's army in a siege of Ahmedabad, which the Mughal governor Jawan Mard Khan Babi surrendered in March 1753, and part of the city was given to Damaji. In 1756 he helped retake it after Momin Khan, Nawab of Cambay, had seized it.

Damaji also kept a fleet of his own, based at Billimora, which attacked English and Dutch shipping off Surat. In 1757 his forces captured an English boat and the galbat Shark, and the English and Dutch planned a joint attack on the fleet. Though nominally loyal to the Peshwa, the Gaekwad fleet was not under his control. Damaji died at Patan on 18 August 1768. His son Fateh Singh Rao Gaekwad received Ahmedabad from the British after the Treaty of Salbai in 1782.
damascus: Damascus stands in south-western Syria on a plateau 680 metres above sea level, about 80 kilometres inland from the Mediterranean and sheltered by the Anti-Lebanon Mountains, which block rain from the sea. The Barada River, fed by mountain streams of melting snow, supplies the city with water, and the Ghouta, an irrigated belt of farmland, has produced vegetables, cereals and fruit since ancient times. The site lay at a crossroads of the north–south route linking Egypt with Asia Minor and the east–west desert route linking Lebanon with the Euphrates valley.

The name first appears as tjmsqw in a list of places of the Egyptian king Thutmose III, in the 15th century BCE, and as Dimašqa in the Amarna letters; its origin is uncertain. Greek myths gave three explanations of the Greek form Damaskós, among them a founder named Damaskos, a son of Hermes.

Radiocarbon dating at Tell Ramad, on the outskirts, suggests occupation possibly from around 6300 BCE, and settlement in the wider Barada basin goes back to 9000 BCE, though no large settlement stood within the city's later walls until the second millennium BCE. The Amarna letters of about 1350 BCE name Biryawaza as its ruler. Around 1260 BCE the region was a battleground between the Hittites and the Egyptians, and under a treaty between Hattusili III and Ramesses II control of the Damascus area passed to Egypt in 1259 BCE. After the Sea Peoples arrived around 1200 BCE, Damascus emerged as an influential centre, and from the 11th to the 7th century BCE it was the hub of an Aramaic kingdom.

Damascus was the capital of the Umayyad Caliphate from 661 to 750. When the Abbasid dynasty won, the seat of Islamic power moved to Baghdad and the city's importance declined. It regained significance in the Ayyubid, Mamluk and Ottoman periods.

Damascus is the capital of Syria and the seat of its central government, with a metropolitan area that includes Douma, Harasta, Darayya and Jaramana. The Ancient City of Damascus was inscribed on the World Heritage List in 1979 and holds over 125 cultural heritage sites from the Hellenistic, Roman, Byzantine, Islamic and Ottoman periods; the best known of its more than 200 mosques is the Umayyad Mosque. Damascus University is the oldest and largest university in Syria.
damel: The office began as that of the Great Lamane of Cayor, chosen by the other lamanes from the Fall family of Palene Ded, who claimed descent from Ousmane Boune Afal, a companion of Mohammed, by way of Wagadou. The word Damel may come from the Wolof verb damma, to break, recalling how Cayor broke its vassalage to the Jolof Empire at the battle of Danki in 1549.

The Damel stood at the top of the social hierarchy of Cayor and was traditionally seen as a great magician. Royal blood passed through female relatives, and every descendant of a Damel in the maternal line became a garmi, a noble. Lat Jor was the only Damel elected who was not of the Fall paternal line.

Some holders reigned for decades: Amary Ngone Sobel Fall from 1549 to 1593, Lat Sukabe from 1697 to 1719 and Isa-Tende from 1719 to 1748. Others held the title for a year or less, and some more than once: Maissa Bigué Ngoné Fall reigned from 1748 to 1749 and again from 1758 to 1759, and in the 1860s Ma-Jojo Jegeñ Kodu Fal and Lat Jor each reigned twice, the one giving way to the other in 1864.

Lat Dior Diop, who held the title from 1862 to 1864 and again from 1871 to 1882, resisted French encroachment on Wolof territory for decades and was killed by the French in 1886; he is a Senegalese national hero. Amari Ngone Fal reigned only from January to August 1883. The 30th and last Damel, Samba Laobé Fall, who succeeded him on 28 August 1883, was killed at Tivaouane by Captain Spitzer, the leader of a French delegation, and his reign ended in 1886.
damghan: Damghan lies 342 km east of Tehran on the high road to Mashhad, at an elevation of 1,250 m, and serves as capital of Damghan County and its Central District. The historical town was called Qumis, after a province of the same name stretching from Sabzevar to Garmsar, and up to the first century CE Damghan was the capital of that province. The name is derived from deh, village, and moghan, Magi, a name given by Zoroastrians. Tradition ascribes the founding of the town to Hooshang, the great-grandson of Keyumars and founder of the Pishdadi dynasty. Its climate is cold semi-arid. The city is known for pistachios and for paper almonds with very thin shells.

Excavation at Tepe Hissar, in the village of Heydarabad southeast of the city, shows that the area was inhabited in the Chalcolithic period, in the fifth millennium BCE, with metal production in its earliest layers. Its layers belong to several periods, including the Median, Achaemenid, Seleucid, Parthian and Sasanian, and it reached its peak in the Seleucid and Parthian periods. Ernst Herzfeld and Erich Schmidt were the first archaeologists to explore it. After the conquest of Persia by Alexander the Great, the nearby city of Hecatompylos, meaning hundred gates, was the main population centre.

Damghan was half destroyed in the earthquake of 856 and was an important city in the Middle Ages, though few remains of that time survive. It was capital of the province of Qumis until it was destroyed by the Afghan Hotak dynasty in 1723. Fath-Ali Shah Qajar was born in a citadel in the western part of the city in 1772, and later Qajar rulers built palaces at the spring of Cheshmeh-Ali, 30 km to the north.

Damghan is known for its monuments. The Tarikhaneh Mosque was built over a Sasanian fire temple and is one of the oldest mosques in Iran, with massive columns, wood carvings and two minarets of the 11th century. Many Seljuk buildings survive, including the Gunbad-i Chihil Dukhtaran mausoleum, built in AH 466 (1087 CE) and 14.8 m high, the shrine of Imamzade Ja'far and the tomb of Pir-i Alamdar. North of the city stand the Ismaili fortresses of Gerdkuh, said to have been used by Hassan Sabah and conquered by the Ilkhanate under Hulagu Khan, and Mehrnegar on Mansourkuh. Sections of the old walls, some from the Sasanian era, remain.
damkina: The name Damgalnuna can be translated as the great wife of the prince, the prince being Enki. Its writing with the cuneiform sign NUN, used for the name of Eridu, reflects her tie to that city. The form Damkina developed later, late sources spell it Damkianna, and the Hurrian form was Tapkina. Beyond her marriage her character was poorly defined. Believers held that she interceded with Enki for human supplicants, and like him she was linked with purification and exorcism and invoked against demons. In astronomy she was identified with the Wagon of Heaven, Ursa Minor, and lions may have been her animals.

Nanshe, Asalluhi, Marduk and Enbilulu were counted among the children of Enki and Damgalnuna, and the deities Ḫasīsu and Uznu, wisdom and ear, were her attendants. The myth Enki and Ninhursag treats her as the same goddess as Ninhursag, though the two were usually separate.

Her worship is attested in every period of Mesopotamian history, though it gradually narrowed. The Early Dynastic Zame Hymns name Eridu as her cult centre. At Malgium, south of Eshnunna, the Code of Hammurabi lists her among the city's deities, and its rulers Takil-ilišu and Ipiq-Ishtar called themselves appointed by her and Ea. Shulgi built her a temple at Nippur. On Old Babylonian seals from Sippar she and Enki are among the three divine couples most often invoked, and an inscription of Ashurnasirpal II shows that the pair shared a temple at Kalhu.

She entered Hurrian religion as the wife of Ea, perhaps as early as the third millennium BCE according to Piotr Taracha. She is named among the divine witnesses of the treaty between Šattiwaza and Šuppiluliuma I and appears in the procession of goddesses at Yazılıkaya.

The only known myth centred on her, which Wilfred G. Lambert titled Damkina's Bond, tells of a conflict between the gods of Babylon under Marduk and those of Nippur under Enlil, ended by her intervention after a messenger brought her word of the battle. Lambert dated it to the Kassite or Isin II dynasty and thought it came from Malgium; Takayoshi Oshima holds it is no earlier than Nebuchadnezzar I. In the Enūma Eliš she appears as Marduk's mother under the name Damkina, without a genealogy of her own.
dammam: Dammam is the seat and largest city of the Eastern Province of Saudi Arabia, an industrial port on the Persian Gulf coast. It forms the core of Greater Dammam, which includes the neighbouring governorates of Khobar and Qatif. The climate is hot desert, with extremely hot summers, sparse rainfall mostly in winter, and dust storms called shamals that generally come from the north in summer. Water comes from desalination plants, and large stretches of the shallow Gulf have been reclaimed.

The area that became Dammam was settled by the Dawasir tribe around 1923 with the permission of King Ibn Saud, and it was originally a fishing hamlet. In 1866 the United Kingdom attacked the fort at Dammam, then held by the Second Saudi state, and was repelled. After the unification of Saudi Arabia Dammam was made capital of the newly formed Eastern Province.

An oil concession agreement was signed in Jeddah in spring 1933 between the government of King Abdulaziz and the Standard Oil Company of California. Drilling of the first well began on 30 April 1935, and Dammam No. 1 was abandoned in January 1936 after poor results. Most of the next wells disappointed. Work on Dammam No. 7 began on 7 December 1936, and by 4 March 1938 it was producing a promising amount of oil. The well, later called the Prosperity Well, showed that the kingdom held very large reserves of hydrocarbons.

In 1950 Dammam had 22,000 inhabitants, and by 2000 759,000. The area was planned from the start on modern principles, with residential and commercial districts separated and broad, straight roads. Dhahran International Airport opened in 1961, and in 1999 commercial flights moved to the larger King Fahd International Airport. King Abdulaziz Port, founded in the late 1940s, is the largest port on the Persian Gulf, and the King Fahd Causeway, 28 kilometres long, links the region to Bahrain. Saudi Aramco dominates the oil sector, with its headquarters in nearby Dhahran, and industrial cities were built to encourage other industries.
damrong-rajanubhab: Born Prince Tisavarakumara on 21 June 1862, the son of King Mongkut and Consort Chum, a lesser royal wife, Damrong learned Thai and Pali from private tutors and English at the Royal School. At 14 he entered a palace school created by his half-brother King Chulalongkorn. He commanded the Royal Guards Regiment from 1880, built army schools and helped modernise the army, and in 1887 became commander-in-chief of the army and Minister of Education in the king's provisional cabinet. In December 1891, on a journey to Europe, he recruited Gustave Rolin-Jaequemyns as general adviser to the king.

Chulalongkorn promoted him over his older half-brothers to head the Ministry of the North in 1892; with the southern and western provinces added in 1894, it became the Ministry of the Interior. Damrong retired older officials in favour of men loyal to him and opened promotion to clerks on merit. His ministry also took over provincial revenue, irrigation, forestry, mines and a provincial gendarmerie. A tour of the northern provinces in 1892 had convinced him that they were almost cut off from the centre.

Under the thesaphiban system each monthon had commissioners for judicial, financial and administrative affairs. Provincial nobles lost revenues such as judicial fees and transit duties, were paid salaries from them and were often transferred, which cut their local ties. The Ministry of Interior regulations of 1899 made the changes countrywide, and state revenue doubled. Relations with King Vajiravudh after 1910 were less close, and Damrong resigned in 1915, officially for his health.

Under King Prajadhipok he proposed the Royal Institute and became its first president; the National Library and the National Museum grew out of his work. The historian Nithi Aeusrivongse described the Damrong school as joining the royal chronicle to nineteenth-century Western history, and his work is now often seen as overly nationalistic. A defender of absolute monarchy, he was exiled to Penang after the Siamese revolution of 1932, returned to Bangkok in 1942 and died on 1 December 1943, a day now kept as Damrong Rajanupab Day.
dance-of-zalongo: In December 1803, during the Souliote War, the Souliotes began to leave Souli after their defeat by the forces of Ali Pasha, the local Ottoman-Albanian ruler. Some of the refugees made for Parga, while others sought shelter at the convent of Zalongo. Approximately 60 women, with their children, were trapped on Mount Zalongo. The war gave rise to many legends, and the events are told differently depending on the version.

Versions that rely on the History of Suli and Parga by Christoforos Perraivos present Ali as a cruel tyrant who broke a promise of protection to the Souliotes who had withdrawn to Zalongo and ordered his men to attack; the men prepared to fight to the death, while the women, to avoid enslavement, formed a circle dance and went over the cliff. The Alipashiad, which does not hide that many Souliotes were enslaved, stresses instead Ali's honourable dealings with the Souliote chief Fotos Tzavelas, whose wife he released and whom he allowed safe passage to Parga with a number of families.

William Plate of the Royal Geographical Society suggested that Ali was angered by the monk known as Last Judgement Samuel, who with five others blew up the Souliote arsenal with Ali's soldiers inside, and that he took revenge on the fugitives. In this account the convent of Zalongo was stormed and its defenders killed, and those who escaped climbed to the top of the mountain, where, according to legend, they went down the precipice one after the other, singing and dancing.

The story became known across Europe and reached the English-speaking world in the 1820s, when it was used in England and the United States to win sympathy for the Greek War of Independence. Ary Scheffer showed The Women of Souli at the Paris Salon of 1827, and Constance Blanchard exhibited her painting of the scene there in 1838. During that war, after the siege of Naoussa, thirteen women and their children leapt to their deaths into the Arapitsa in the same way. A popular kalamatianos dance-song comes from a drama by Spyridon Peresiadis, published in 1903, and the Monument of Zalongo now stands on the mountain.
danebury: Danebury stands on Danebury Hill, which rises to 143 metres above country that rarely exceeds 100 metres, about 19 kilometres north-west of Winchester. The fort covers 5 hectares, and its territory took in forest, upland pasture and the waters of the River Test. The nearby hillforts of Figsbury Ring, Quarley Hill and Bury Hill were probably founded at about the same time, at similar sizes and spacing. The name appears as Dunnebury Hill in a grant of 1491 and is read as a hill fort.

The first defences, from around 550 BCE, were a ditch and a timber-faced box rampart, with gateways to the east and south-west. Around 400 BCE the rampart was heightened above a ditch 6 metres deep, and outer earthworks added 5.3 hectares, probably for livestock. Danebury then became a developed hillfort, perhaps the seat of a chieftain with his retinue and craftsmen and a population of 200 to 350, with shrines at its centre and granaries supplied by surrounding farmsteads.

The gates were burnt more than once, probably in attacks. Around 100 BCE the east gate was burnt and not replaced, most people left, and charnel pits received about 100 bodies, many with weapon injuries. By the start of the 1st century CE the site was probably a single farm. Barry Cunliffe's excavation uncovered 57 per cent of the interior, the longest investigation of any hillfort in western Europe, after a first dig by Augustus Wollaston Franks in 1859.

Danebury is a Scheduled Monument and a Local Nature Reserve, surrounded by a Site of Special Scientific Interest. A meteorite found in a grain pit in 1974, first taken for slag, is now held by the Hampshire County Council Arts and Museums Service.
danegeld: Danegeld, literally Dane yield, was a tax raised to pay tribute or protection money to Viking raiders so that a land would not be ravaged. It was characteristic of royal policy in England and Francia from the ninth to the eleventh century, collected either as tribute, to buy off attackers, or as a stipend, to pay defensive forces. The term itself did not appear until the late eleventh century. In Anglo-Saxon England the payments to the Danes were called gafol, and the levy that supported a standing army was called heregeld. The Norman administration was the first to call the tax Danegeld.
In England the basis of assessment was the hide, a unit notionally sufficient to support one family, though hides varied greatly in size and value. Kent used the sulung and the north the carucate.

The first English payment, of 10,000 Roman pounds of silver, was made in 991 after the Viking victory at the Battle of Maldon, on the advice of Sigeric, Archbishop of Canterbury. In 994 the Danes under Swein Forkbeard and Olav Tryggvason besieged London unsuccessfully, then ravaged the south-east until they received 16,000 pounds. In 1007 Æthelred the Unready bought two years of peace for 36,000 troy pounds, and in 1012, after the sack of Canterbury, a further 48,000 troy pounds was paid. That year he also introduced an annual land tax to pay Scandinavian mercenaries led by Thorkell the Tall. After Canute became king in 1016 he paid off most of his fleet with 72,000 troy pounds collected nationally and 10,500 pounds from London.

Elsewhere payments were often local. In 845 a Viking army under Ragnar Lothbrok was bought off from destroying Paris with nearly six tons of silver and gold. In Kievan Rus the Rus Vikings exacted an annual tribute called the dan from the Slavic and Finnic peoples.

After the Norman Conquest William the Conqueror used the geld mainly to fund continental wars and the costs of conquest, and he and his successors levied it more often and at higher rates than the Anglo-Saxon kings. By 1130 Henry I was taxing it annually at two shillings on the hide, and in 1129 to 1130 it brought in about £2,400, roughly ten per cent of the year's revenue. The last year it appears on a pipe roll is 1161 to 1162, and a levy on moveables, requiring the consent of parliament, later replaced it.

The word survived as a name for any coercive payment. Rudyard Kipling's poem Dane-geld contains the lines: once you have paid him the Danegeld, you never get rid of the Dane. In Britain the term has come to mean a warning against any such payment.
danelaw: The Danelaw approximately covered Yorkshire, the central and eastern Midlands and the East of England. The name is first recorded in the early 11th century as Dena lage, and only then was it used for a geographic area. Five fortified towns became particularly important: Leicester, Nottingham, Derby, Stamford and Lincoln. Known as the Five Boroughs, they broadly delineate the area now called the East Midlands. Borough derives from the Old English burh, a fortified enclosure containing several households.

The term can also describe the legal arrangements made in the treaties between Alfred the Great, king of Wessex, and the Danish warlord Guthrum after Guthrum's defeat at the Battle of Edington in 878. They allowed the Danes to govern themselves in exchange for loyalty to the English crown and set equivalences for matters such as the wergild payable in reparation. The wapentake, the standard land division in the Danelaw, was effectively interchangeable with the hundred.

The Great Heathen Army landed in East Anglia in 865 under a combined leadership that included Halfdan Ragnarsson and Ivar the Boneless. In 867 it captured Northumbria and its capital York. Mercia fell in a campaign lasting until 874, after which Guthrum led the army. Only Wessex still resisted. After Edington, Alfred demanded as a term of surrender that Guthrum be baptised, and Alfred acted as his godfather.

In the 910s Edward the Elder and his sister Æthelflæd, the Lady of the Mercians, conquered Danish territories in the Midlands and East Anglia, and some Danish jarls who submitted were allowed to keep their lands. Viking rule ended in Northumbria when Eric Bloodaxe was driven out in 954. Cnut the Great later ruled a unified English kingdom from 1016 to 1035 as part of his North Sea Empire. The Danelaw still appeared in legislation in the early 12th century, in the Leges Henrici Primi, as one of the laws into which England was divided.

Scandinavian settlement can still be seen in the North of England and the East Midlands, above all in place-names with Old Norse endings such as -by, meaning village, and -thorp, meaning hamlet. Contact between Old East Norse and Old English brought many Norse words into English, including law itself, sky, window, and the pronouns they, them and their. Four of the five boroughs became county towns, of Leicestershire, Lincolnshire, Nottinghamshire and Derbyshire; Stamford did not.
danes: Denmark has been inhabited since ancient times by Germanic peoples including the Angles, Cimbri, Jutes, Herules and Teutones. The first mention of Danes within Denmark is on the Jelling Rune Stone, which records the conversion of the Danes to Christianity by Harald Bluetooth in the 10th century. Between about 960 and the early 980s Harald established a kingdom stretching from Jutland to Scania.

Danish Viking expansion brought Norway and England into the Danish North Sea Empire, though England broke away after the death of Canute the Great in 1035. The Danish realm later spread along the southern Baltic coast. In the 14th century King Olaf II acquired Norway, with Iceland and the Faroe Islands, and his mother Margrethe I united Norway, Sweden and Denmark in the Kalmar Union.

Sweden won its independence in 1523, which ended the union and created Denmark–Norway. The kingdom grew wealthy in the 16th century from tolls on traffic through the Øresund, since it controlled both shores. In 1524 Hans Mikkelsen and Christiern Pedersen translated the New Testament into Danish, which became an immediate best-seller. Denmark–Norway colonised Greenland in the 17th century. After a failed war with the Swedish Empire, the Treaty of Roskilde of 1658 removed the Scandinavian Peninsula areas from Danish control and set the borders between Denmark, Norway and Sweden that exist today. The people of Scania came to be fully integrated as Swedes.

Defeat in the Napoleonic Wars cost Denmark Norway and territory in what is now northern Germany. That loss, the Danish Golden Age that followed and the liberal and national movements of the 1830s helped form a Danish national identity. After the revolutions of 1848 Denmark became a constitutional monarchy on 5 June 1849, when Frederick VII accepted a constitution that separated powers and gave the vote to all adult men.

Danishness, the basis of modern Danish identity, stresses the connection of the people to the territory, the thousand-year-old monarchy and the 19th-century national romantic idea of the people. It has not been tied to a racial or biological heritage. N. F. S. Grundtvig named the Danish language and attachment to Denmark as its defining marks, and Danish identity was built on peasant culture and Lutheran theology. About fifty thousand Danish-identifying German citizens live in Southern Schleswig, and Danish emigrants settled notably in the United States, Canada, Argentina and Peru.
danevirke: The Danevirke consists of several walls, trenches and the Schlei Barrier. The walls stretch for 30 kilometres, from Hedeby on the Baltic coast in the east to the marshlands in the west of the peninsula, and stand between 3.6 and 6 metres high. Excavations of 1969 to 1975 used tree-ring dating to show that the main structure was built in three phases between 737 and 968, at about the same time as Offa's Dyke on the border of Wales and England. Later carbon dating showed that some parts are older still.

Written sources say that King Godfred began work in 808, fearing an invasion by the Franks, who had conquered Frisia and Old Saxony. Legend credits Queen Thyra, wife of Gorm the Old, with ordering the wall built, and most of the work in the tenth century is attributed to Harald Bluetooth.

The early ramparts were of soil, followed by a timber palisade built in 737, later wrapped in a stone wall. The Danevirke was strengthened in the early twelfth century, when the moats were deepened and the ramparts raised. King Valdemar the Great then built the brick wall known as Valdemarsmuren, a wall of stone in mortar about 7 metres high on a granite base. It was the last true reinforcement. Danish kings used the structure as a gathering point for expeditions, including raids on the Slavs of the southern Baltic. It lost its purpose from the fourteenth century, because of the cost of manning it and the development of siege engines.

In the nineteenth century the Danevirke became a symbol of Denmark in its struggle with Germany over Schleswig. It was strengthened with cannon emplacements and entrenchments in 1850 and 1861. In the Second Schleswig War of 1864 no battle took place at it: General de Meza withdrew his army to Dybbøl after the frozen Schlei and marshes made a flanking attack possible, a decision that shocked Danish opinion and cost him his command.

The site has stayed in German possession since 1864. After the Allied invasion of Normandy in the Second World War, the Wehrmacht considered turning the wall into an anti-tank trench, and the Danish archaeologist Søren Telling persuaded Heinrich Himmler to forbid it. The Danevirke and the nearby Viking town of Hedeby were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2018.
dang-district: The Dang district lies in the south-eastern part of the state of Gujarat in India, with its administrative headquarters at Ahwa. It has an area of 1,764 square kilometres. The meaning of its name is uncertain: in common speech dang means a hilly village, and it can also mean bamboo. The name is also tied to the Dandakaranya of the Ramayana, and tradition says that Rama passed through the area on his way to Nashik during his exile. In ancient Indian scriptures it is known as Danda Aranyaka, the bamboo forest.

Before Independence the five tribal kings of Dang fought several wars with the East India Company. According to the history of the Dangs, the largest was at Lashkaria Amba, where the kings of all five states joined to defend the region and the British were beaten and agreed to a compromise. By the treaty signed in 1842 the Company was allowed to use the forests and their natural products, in return for about 3,000 silver coins paid to the five kings. Historically there were 14 Dang states, and the five kingdoms that remained are Daher-Amala, Linga, Gadhvi, Vasurna and Pimpri.

The five kings still receive a yearly political pension under the agreement of 1842, which continued after the privy purses of the princely states were ended in 1970 because the agreement was between the monarchy of Dang and the Government of India, not the Crown. At Holi they gather in Ahwa for a royal ceremony, in decorated buggies with bands and tribal dancers, to receive it. 65 percent of them belonged to scheduled tribes. 53 percent. Part of the Purna Wildlife Sanctuary lies in the district, and Saputara is a hill station.
dang-hyang-nirartha: Dang Hyang Nirartha, also known as Ida Pedanda Sakti Wawu Rauh, Mpu Nirartha and Dang Hyang Dwijendra, was born in Java during the final period of the Majapahit Kingdom and spent most of his life in Bali. He came from an elite social milieu and was a disciple of Syekh Siti Jenar, a Javanese member of the Wali Sanga, the revered Muslim saints of Java, who taught a mystical, pantheist form of Sufism opposed to the shariatic Sufism of Sunan Kudus. Balinese texts call him a poet, intellectual, wonderworker and advisor to rulers.

He was sent to Bali by the Javanese royal court of Majapahit and became Bagawanta, the royal priest, of the Gelgel Kingdom. His coming brought the support of the spiritual world (niskala) and the sanction of Java's earthly powers to King Dalem Waturenggong's rule over Pasuruan, Blambangan, Puger, Bali, Nusa Penida, Sasak and Sumbawa, and he was to choose a local priest to lead the rajasurya or aswameda ceremony the king held for the occasion.

His travels in Bali, Lombok and Sumbawa are recounted in a lontara called Dwijendra Tatwa. He was still alive in Bali in 1537: a colophon he wrote on a copy of the kakavin Sumanasāntaka records that the copy was completed on 14 July 1537. According to the Dwijendratattwa and the Babad Brāhmaṇa, he had completed a work called Mahiṣa Mĕgat Kūng the year before.

Nirartha refashioned Balinese Hinduism and promoted in Indonesia the idea of moksha, freedom from the cycle of death and rebirth. He founded the Shaivite priesthood now found throughout Bali and is regarded as the ancestor of all Shaivite pedandas. The padmasana shrine he introduced, an empty throne serving as an altar to the supreme god Acintya or Shiva, was added by the dozen to the coastal temples of Bali during his travels.

A tradition among the brahmana of Bali holds that wetu telu Islam, a mix of Islam and animism, was brought to the Sasaks as his teaching, and that he took the name Pangèran Sangupati in Lombok and Tuan Seméru in Sumbawa; another version makes Pangèran Sangupati a different person, perhaps a Sasak pupil of his. Legend says he crossed from Java on a pumpkin, the origin of a taboo on eating pumpkins among some Balinese Brahmins, and that a hair he gave the king to end a plague was placed in a temple that became a Shaivite pilgrimage site.
dangun: In the legend, Tan'gun's grandfather was Hwanin, the Lord of Heaven. Hwanin's son Hwanung yearned to live on the earth among the valleys and mountains, and with 3,000 followers he descended onto Taebaeksan, now believed to be Paektu Mountain, where he founded Sinsi, the City of God. With his ministers of clouds, rain and wind he instituted laws and moral codes and taught humans the arts, medicine and agriculture. A tiger and a bear prayed to become human. Hwanung gave them twenty cloves of garlic and a bundle of mugwort and told them to eat only this and stay out of the sunlight for 100 days. The tiger left after about twenty days, but the bear persevered and became a woman, Ungnyeo.

Ungnyeo made offerings to Hwanung but had no husband, and she prayed beneath a divine birch tree for a child. Hwanung took her as his wife, and she bore a son, Tan'gun Wang'gŏm. He ascended the throne, built the walled city of Asadal near Pyongyang, though its location is disputed, and called his kingdom Joseon, now called Gojoseon to distinguish it from the later Joseon kingdom. The bear and the tiger are said to represent two tribes that sought the favour of the heavenly prince.
His reign is usually reckoned from 2333 BCE, following the Tongguk t'onggam of 1485, and sources place it in the reign of the Chinese emperor Yao, though they differ on the year.

The earliest recorded version of the legend is in the 13th-century Samguk yusa, which cites the lost Gogi and China's Book of Wei, though the surviving Book of Wei holds nothing about Tan'gun. Similar versions appear in the Jewang Un-gi of Yi Seunghyu and in early Joseon records.

Tan'gun drew attention in the late Goryeo dynasty, when Koreans fought the Mongol Yuan dynasty, and the Joseon dynasty built shrines to him. At the end of the 19th century he became a figure of resistance to imperialism, and he was central to nationalism and the independence movement under Japanese rule. Until 1961 the official South Korean era, the Dangi, counted years from 2333 BCE. National Foundation Day on 3 October was begun as a religious anniversary by Daejongism, which worships him, as do the followers of Cheondoism.
daniel-coxe: Daniel Coxe was born in London, the oldest of thirteen children of a father also called Daniel Coxe, who came from Stoke Newington and died in 1686. The family traced its line to a Daniel Coxe of Somersetshire in the 13th century who had taken a doctorate of medicine at Salerno University. The younger Daniel was educated at Jesus College, Cambridge, where he became a doctor of medicine in 1669. On 12 May 1671 he married Rebecca Coldham, the only surviving child and heiress of John Coldham of Tooting Graveney, an alderman of London.
He was a Fellow of the Royal Society and a member of the Royal College of Physicians. Samuel Pepys's diary entry of 3 May 1665 describes him poisoning a cat with tobacco oil at Gresham College.

Coxe began buying land in West Jersey in the mid-1680s and served nominally as its governor from 1687 to 1688 and from 1689 to 1692, without ever leaving England. He opened the earliest commercial-scale pottery in New Jersey. He also bought land in the Mississippi Valley and tried, without success, to settle a colony of Huguenots in Virginia.

In 1698 he acquired Carolana, a grant first made by Charles I to Sir Robert Heath, buying it from Sir James Shaen or his son Arthur; Shaen had obtained the rights from Henry Howard, 6th Duke of Norfolk. The Carolana holding stayed with the Coxe family until 1769, when it was exchanged for land in the Mohawk valley of what is now New York state.

Coxe died in 1730 and was buried in London; his portrait is held by the Royal College of Physicians. His son, Colonel Daniel Coxe (1673–1739), lived in the American colonies from 1702 to 1716 and in 1722 published A Description of the English Province of Carolana. In 1731 the son claimed a title superior to that of the West Jersey Society through a deed his father had recorded years earlier, and the courts upheld it. Hundreds of families had to buy their own property again or be evicted; there were lawsuits and riots, and many residents of Hopewell left New Jersey, some founding the Jersey Settlement on the Yadkin River in what was then Rowan County.
daniel-defoe: Daniel Foe was probably born in the parish of St Giles Cripplegate, London, and his birth date is uncertain, with sources offering dates from 1659 to 1662. The summer or early autumn of 1660 is considered the most likely. He later added the aristocratic-sounding De to his name. His father, James Foe, was a prosperous tallow chandler of probable Flemish descent. His parents were Presbyterian dissenters, and around the age of 14 he was sent to Charles Morton's dissenting academy at Newington Green.

Defoe entered business as a general merchant, dealing in hosiery, woollen goods and wine, and he was rarely out of debt. On 1 January 1684 he married Mary Tuffley, and the marriage lasted 47 years and produced eight children. In 1685 he joined the Monmouth Rebellion but gained a pardon, and after William III was crowned in 1689 he became one of the king's close allies and a secret agent. In 1692 he was arrested for debts of £700 and declared bankruptcy.

His first notable publication was An Essay Upon Projects, a series of proposals for social and economic improvement, in 1697. His poem The True-Born Englishman of 1701 defended William against xenophobic attacks. While imprisoned in a case of seditious libel he wrote to William Paterson, and Robert Harley, the leading minister, accepted his services and released him in 1703. Defoe then published the weekly Review, which was the main mouthpiece of the government in promoting the Act of Union of 1707. By September 1706 Harley had ordered him to Edinburgh as a secret agent.

As many as 545 titles have been attributed to Defoe. He used at least 198 pen names, and since most of his works were published anonymously, scholars have had difficulty crediting them all. Moll Flanders and Roxana were published anonymously for over fifty years, until Francis Noble named him on their title pages in 1774 and 1775.

Robinson Crusoe, published in 1719 when he was in his late fifties, tells of a man shipwrecked on a desert island for twenty-eight years. Crusoe's struggles with faith run through the narrative. The book had run through four editions before the end of 1719, and its imitations gave rise to a genre called the Robinsonade. Defoe died on 24 April 1731, probably while in hiding from his creditors, and was buried at Bunhill Fields.
daniel-oconnell: Daniel O'Connell was born at Carhan House, near Cahersiveen, County Kerry, to the O'Connells of Derrynane, a wealthy Roman Catholic family that, under the Penal Laws, had retained its land only through Protestant trustees. His parents were Morgan O'Connell and Catherine O'Mullane. He grew up at Derrynane House in the household of his childless uncle Maurice O'Connell, who made him his heir presumptive. After legal studies in London, including a pupillage at Lincoln's Inn, he returned to Ireland in 1795.

In 1802 he married his third cousin Mary O'Connell, in defiance of his uncle, who thought he should have sought an heiress. They had four daughters and four sons, and each of the sons later sat in Parliament. O'Connell's principles drew on the Enlightenment and on William Godwin's Enquiry Concerning Political Justice; for a period Thomas Paine's The Age of Reason made him a deist, but by 1809 he had returned to the Church.

In 1823 O'Connell established the Catholic Association. For a Catholic rent of a penny a month, typically paid through the local priest, it drew the labouring poor into a national movement. It mounted monster rallies of over 100,000 people and emboldened enfranchised tenants to vote for pro-emancipation candidates in defiance of their landlords. His enemies derided him as the King of Beggars. Disavowing revolutionary violence, he held that no political change was worth the shedding of a single drop of human blood.

Emancipation passed in 1829, but the Parliamentary Elections (Ireland) Act of the same year raised the county franchise threshold five-fold to ten pounds and cut the Irish electorate from 216,000 voters to 37,000. At Westminster O'Connell championed reform causes and was known internationally as an abolitionist. He relaunched the Repeal Association in April 1840, and on 15 August 1843 he gathered a crowd at the Hill of Tara estimated by The Times at close to one million.

In 1845 O'Connell condemned the proposed non-denominational Queen's Colleges, which dismayed the Young Irelanders grouped around The Nation. Weakened by this split and by criticism of his political compromises, he made a pilgrimage to Rome and died in Genoa in May 1847, aged 71. In accord with his wishes, his heart was buried in Rome and the rest of his body in Glasnevin Cemetery in Dublin. The Repeal Association was dissolved in June 1848.

Honoré de Balzac called him an incarnation of a people. In the German states he became a folk hero among Catholics, and his Catholic Association was a model for the Katholischer Verein Deutschland. Dublin's Sackville Street was renamed O'Connell Street in 1922.
daniel-salamanca: Daniel Domingo Salamanca Urey was born in Cochabamba on 8 July 1869 into a wealthy landed family and studied law at the Higher University of San Simón. He married the poet Sara Ugarte de Salamanca, with whom he had five children. Elected to the Chamber of Deputies for the Liberal Party in 1899, he was made Finance Minister by President José Manuel Pando two years later. In 1907, as a leading opposition figure, he attacked the Pinilla-Soler Treaty, which had divided the Chaco between Bolivia and Paraguay.

He later left the Liberals, helped found the Republican Party and ran unsuccessfully for vice-president in 1917. Opposed to the ambitions of the Republican leader Bautista Saavedra, he founded the Genuine Republican Party with Juan Maria Escalier and others, and lost the presidential election of 1925 to Saavedra's chosen successor, Hernando Siles. He then withdrew to teach law.

After the military overthrow of Siles in 1930, Salamanca led a coalition with the Liberals, with José Luis Tejada Sorzano as his running mate, and took office in March 1931. He introduced an unpopular austerity programme and clamped down on the opposition. A long-standing hawk on the Chaco, he took as his motto We must stand firm in the Chaco. The discovery of oil in the foothills of the Andes raised hopes of oil in the Chaco, and he ordered more small garrisons, fortines, to be set up. In 1932 a Bolivian unit attacked the Paraguayan post at the lake the Paraguayans called Pitiantutá, which in effect began the war.

Relations with the high command were poor from the start: he placed the German Hans Kundt at the head of the army, and after defeats on the southern front Kundt was replaced by General Enrique Peñaranda at the end of 1933. Salamanca blamed his generals for the setbacks and decided to replace Peñaranda and several commanders.

The generals, among them Colonel David Toro and Major Germán Busch, put Tejada in his place; it has been alleged that Tejada was part of the plot. Salamanca retired to Cochabamba and died of stomach cancer on 17 July 1935, days after the ceasefire. Many blamed him for the war, while others saw him as betrayed by his officers. Bolivian historians call him El Hombre Símbolo, the symbolic man.
daniel-webster: Webster was born on 18 January 1782 in Salisbury, New Hampshire, in what is now the city of Franklin. His father, Ebenezer Webster, was a farmer and local official who had served in the French and Indian War and the American Revolutionary War. Webster was the second-youngest of eight siblings and was close to his older brother Ezekiel. After admission to the bar he practised at Boscawen, and after his father's death in 1806 he handed the practice to Ezekiel and moved to Portsmouth, where he handled over 1,700 cases in a decade.

Elected to the House of Representatives in 1813, Webster criticised the War of 1812 and opposed conscription, wartime taxes and a new embargo. He then moved to Boston and became a leading attorney before the Supreme Court, winning Dartmouth College v. Woodward, McCulloch v. Maryland and Gibbons v. Ogden. Back in the House from 1823, he chaired the Judiciary Committee under Speaker Henry Clay. In 1827 the Massachusetts legislature elected him to the Senate, where he worked with Clay to build the National Republican Party.

After Andrew Jackson defeated John Quincy Adams in 1828, Webster led the opposition to Jackson's domestic policies. His Second Reply to Hayne of 1830 answered the theory of nullification of John C. Calhoun. He supported Jackson against the nullification crisis but broke with him over the Second Bank of the United States, joined in forming the Whig Party and ran unsuccessfully for president in 1836.

Webster became secretary of state under William Henry Harrison in 1841. He negotiated the Webster–Ashburton Treaty, which settled border disputes with Britain. Returning to the Senate in 1845, he led the Cotton Whigs, who stressed good relations with the South over anti-slavery policy. He had called slavery a great moral, social and political evil in 1837 but did not think Congress should interfere with it in the states. As Millard Fillmore's secretary of state from 1850 he helped pass the Compromise of 1850, which included a new fugitive slave law and was unpopular in much of the North.

Webster suffered from cirrhosis of the liver. He died at his Marshfield estate in Massachusetts on 24 October 1852, aged 70, his last words being 'I still live', and was buried in Winslow Cemetery. Historians have offered mixed opinions on his moral qualities and his ability as a national leader. Stephen Vincent Benét made him the main character of the story The Devil and Daniel Webster.
daniele-manin: Manin was born Daniele Fonseca in Ramo Astori, Venice, on 13 May 1804. His mother, Anna Maria Bellotto, came from Padua, and his father's family from Verona. His grandfather Samuele Medina was Jewish and converted to Christianity in 1759, taking the name Manin because Ludovico Manin, the last Doge of Venice, sponsored his conversion. Daniele studied law at the University of Padua and from an early age hated Austria, which then ruled Venice.

In 1847 he presented a petition to the Venetian congregation, a consultative assembly tolerated by Austria, setting out the wants of the nation, and he was arrested for high treason on 18 January 1848. The crowds forced the Austrian governor, Count Pallfy, to release him on 17 March, revolutionaries seized the Venetian Arsenal, and the Austrians withdrew on 26 March.

Manin handed his powers to Piedmontese commissioners on 7 August 1848, but after King Charles Albert's defeat at Custoza and the armistice that abandoned Venetia to Austria, he saved the commissioners from a lynching crowd and headed a triumvirate. Chosen president again early in 1849, he directed the defence with the Neapolitan general Guglielmo Pepe. Fort Marghera was abandoned on 26 May, the powder magazine blew up on 19 June, and Austrian batteries bombarded the city. On 24 August 1849 Manin negotiated an amnesty under which he, Pepe and others went into exile, and he left on a French ship on 27 August.

His wife died in Marseille on the way to Paris, where Manin became a leader of the Italian exiles. Turning from republicanism to monarchy, he founded the Società Nazionale Italiana with Giorgio Pallavicini and Giuseppe La Farina to spread the idea of unity under King Victor Emmanuel. His daughter died in 1854. Manin died on 22 September 1857 and was buried in Ary Scheffer's family tomb. In 1868, two years after the Austrians left Venice, his remains were brought home for a public funeral and placed in a sarcophagus in the Piazzetta dei Leoncini beside the Basilica San Marco.
danilo-i-metropolitan-of-cetinje: Danilo Šćepčević was born in Njeguši, the son of Stepan or Šćepan Kaluđerović, a merchant, and Ana, who later became a nun; his paternal family belonged to the Heraković brotherhood. He was 13 when the Great Turkish War began in 1683. After the death of Metropolitan Sava Očinić in 1697 the election of a successor caused riots, and the Montenegrin tribal assembly chose the monk Danilo. Refusing consecration by Kalinik I, whom the Ottomans had appointed Patriarch of Peć, he went in 1700 to Dunaszekcső in Habsburg Hungary, where the exiled Patriarch Arsenije III Crnojević consecrated him.

Danilo coordinated defence against the Ottomans and settled some tribal disputes. In the 1712 Battle of Carev Laz against Ahmet Pasha he commanded the Montenegrins and was wounded; the Ottomans entered Cetinje but withdrew with heavy losses. In 1714 Numan Pasha Ćuprilić burned the monastery at Cetinje, took captives into slavery and burned many houses, a campaign considered the worst in Montenegro's history. Danilo fled to Venetian territory and on to Russia, returning with letters from Tsar Peter the Great that granted the Cetinje Monastery 500 rubles a year.

In 1715 he visited Peter I at St Petersburg, a journey that became traditional among his successors. He restored the monastery at Cetinje and fortified Podmaine Monastery near Budva. In 1718 the Republic of Venice recognised his spiritual authority over the Orthodox of Paštrovići and the Bay of Kotor, with the right to build and repair churches there.

To keep the succession out of the tribes' hands, Danilo had his nephew Sava ordained in 1719 by Patriarch Mojsije of Peć and made him coadjutor. After Danilo's death in 1735 Sava II succeeded him, but another nephew, Vasilije Petrović Njegoš, became for more than two decades the effective authority in Montenegro. Tradition links Danilo to the forced reconversion or expulsion of Montenegrins who had converted to Islam, dated by folklore to Christmas Eve 1709 and taken by Petar II Petrović-Njegoš as the subject of The Mountain Wreath; some hold that it never happened.
danilo-i-prince-of-montenegro: Danilo I Petrović-Njegoš was born on 25 May 1826. When Petar II Petrović-Njegoš died, the Senate, under the influence of Đorđije Petrović, the wealthiest Montenegrin of the time, proclaimed Petar's elder brother Pero Tomov prince rather than bishop. In a brief struggle Pero lost to the much younger Danilo, who had more support among the people.

Danilo made peace between the Crmnica and Katunjani tribes, was recognised by all the clans except the Bjelopavlići, and travelled to Vienna and then to Russia, supposedly to be ordained as bishop. He returned in 1852 with the endorsement of Nicholas I of Russia to be prince, taking Pero and his supporters by surprise.
