darul-islam-indonesia: During the Indonesian National Revolution, Kartosoewirjo, a Muslim politician, raised his own fighters in West Java, known as Hizbullah and Sabilillah. In protest against the Renville Agreement of 1948, under which Indonesian leaders ceded West Java to the Dutch, he created the Majelis Islam Pusat, the Central Islamic Council, around Tasikmalaya in May 1948. The Islamic State of Indonesia was proclaimed on 7 August 1949, under Islamic law and with Kartosoewirjo as its imam. The movement did not disband after the transfer of sovereignty later that year and so came into conflict with the government of the Indonesian Republic.

Rebels in South Sulawesi under the army deserter Abdul Kahar Muzakkar joined in 1951, and on 20 September 1953 Daud Beureu'eh declared Aceh part of the Islamic State. The movement grew in the 1950s amid the instability of the central government in the era of Liberal Democracy. In 1957 it was estimated to control a third of West Java and more than 90% of South Sulawesi and Aceh outside the towns, with 15,000 armed guerrillas of the Tentara Islam Indonesia, and that year its agents threw grenades at Sukarno at a school function in Cikini, Jakarta, but failed to kill him.

Martial law in 1957 and Guided Democracy from 1959 turned the tide. Colonel Ahmad Yani's Banteng Raiders crushed the bands of Amir Fatah in Central Java, and the forces of Ibnu Hadjar in South Kalimantan surrendered in 1959. Negotiations from 1959 to 1962 ended the revolt in Aceh, which became an autonomous province with special rights for Islamic law. In West Java the fence-of-legs method of encircling mountain hideouts broke the rebels' hold; Kartosoewirjo was captured on Mount Geber near Garut on 4 June 1962 and ordered his followers to surrender, and the last band there gave up in August.

Underground networks persisted. Leaders arrested from the group known as Komando Jihad, blamed for terrorism in the 1970s and 1980s, were Darul Islam veterans, and the movement's offshoots range from Jemaah Islamiyah to non-violent religious groups. By May 2022 the police unit Detachment 88 had arrested more than 20 members, though observers held that the threat was exaggerated.
darwin-northern-territory: Darwin lies on the western shoreline of the Northern Territory, where the Beagle Gulf opens into the Timor Sea. The central business district occupies a low bluff overlooking Darwin Harbour. The Stuart Highway begins in the city and runs south through Tennant Creek and Alice Springs to Port Augusta in South Australia. The climate is tropical, with a wet season that usually arrives in late November or early December.

The Larrakia people are the traditional custodians of the area, which they call Garramilla, 'white stone', after its rock and sea cliffs. They had trading routes with Southeast Asia and imported goods from as far as South and Western Australia. Dutch ships visited the northern coast in the 1600s. On 9 September 1839 HMS Beagle sailed into the harbour, and John Clements Wickham named it Port Darwin in honour of Charles Darwin, who had sailed on the ship's earlier voyage.

The settlement became the town of Palmerston in 1869. South Australia administered the Northern Territory until its transfer to the Commonwealth in 1911, when the town was renamed Darwin. On 10 December 1919 Captain Ross Smith landed there in a Vickers Vimy and won a prize of 10,000 pounds for the first flight from London to Australia in under 30 days. Darwin has been almost entirely rebuilt four times, after cyclones in 1897 and 1937, Japanese air raids in the Second World War and Cyclone Tracy.

Cyclone Tracy struck on 25 December 1974, killed 71 people and destroyed over 70% of the city's buildings. Some 30,000 of the 46,000 inhabitants were evacuated in the largest airlift in Australian history. The Darwin Reconstruction Commission, led by Clem Jones, rebuilt the city in the late 1970s.

Darwin is the capital and largest city of the Northern Territory and had 139,902 inhabitants at the 2021 census, nearly 63% of the territory's population. Few historic buildings survive; the Administrator's Office of 1883 was rebuilt after 1974. Charles Darwin University is the main provider of higher education, and the Alice Springs to Darwin railway, completed in 2003, links the city with Adelaide.
darya-i-noor: The Daria-i-Noor, whose name means sea of light, is a pale pink diamond. Pink is one of the rarest diamond colours. Like the Koh-i-Noor, it is presumed to have been mined at the Kollur Mine in the Golconda region of Andhra Pradesh, India. Its early origins are shrouded in mystery, but it is believed to have been one of the eyes of the Mughal Peacock Throne.

In 1739 Nader Shah of Iran invaded northern India and occupied Delhi. As payment for returning the crown of India to the Mughal emperor Muhammad Shah, he took the whole Mughal treasury, including the Daria-i-Noor, the Koh-i-Noor and the Peacock Throne. After his death in 1747 the diamond was inherited by his grandson Shahrokh Shah, and then passed to Lotf Ali Khan. When Agha Mohammad Khan Qajar, who founded the Qajar dynasty, defeated Lotf Ali Khan, it entered the Qajar treasury.

The Daria-i-Noor is one of the largest cut diamonds in the world, weighing an estimated 182 carats, or 36 grams. It measures 41.40 by 29.50 by 12.15 millimetres and is the largest known pink diamond. It may originally have been cut from an even larger stone. During the reign of Naser al-Din Shah Qajar an elaborate frame was made for it, set with 457 smaller diamonds and four rubies and crowned by Iran's imperial insignia. The shah was said to be very fond of the diamond and often wore it as an armband, an aigrette or a brooch, and its care was an honour given to high-ranking people. It is kept in the Iranian National Jewels collection of the Central Bank of Iran in Tehran.

In 1965 a Canadian team researching the Iranian Crown Jewels concluded that the Daria-i-Noor may well have been part of a large pink diamond set in the throne of the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan. The French jeweller Jean-Baptiste Tavernier described such a stone in his journal in 1642 and called it the Great Table diamond. It may have been cut into two pieces, the larger being the Daria-i-Noor and the smaller the 60-carat Noor-ul-Ain diamond, which is set in a tiara in the Iranian imperial collection. A much smaller diamond has occasionally been called the Daria-i-Noor in Bangladeshi reporting.
darzalas: Darzalas, also called Derzelas and Derzis, was a Thracian or Dacian chthonic god of abundance, the underworld, health and the vitality of the human spirit. Scholars debate whether he was an indigenous Thracian god, of Greek origin or the product of religious syncretism. His name is Thracian, while Theos Megas, the Great God, is a Roman term usually given to Pluto. He was linked with Pluto, with the Orphic Dionysus, with the Graeco-Egyptian Sarapis, and with the Thracian Horseman.

At Odessos he became identified with the city's Great God and was called Theos Megas Darzalas, though his worship never fully displaced the older cult of Apollo there. He was also addressed as the god who listens to prayers. Odessos had a temple to him with a cult statue, and the Darzaleia games were held every five years, possibly attended by the emperor Gordian III in 238 CE. Another temple to him was built at Histria, a Greek colony on the Black Sea, in the third century BCE.

Darzalas appears often on the coins of Odessos from the third century BCE to the third century CE, usually in a himation and holding a cornucopia, with altars beside him, and on three of the city's four countermarks of 281 to 250 BCE. Under emperors from Caracalla and Elagabalus to Severus Alexander and Gordian III he was shown on the reverse, at times between Heracles and Athena; he also appears on the coins of Tomis, the modern Constanța, and in terracotta figurines and a rare lead figure of the 4th century BCE. A relief from Metodievo names the Thracian Horseman Derzis, and some scholars hold that this link gave the Horseman a role as guide of souls. Darzalas Peak in Antarctica is named after him.
das-kapital: Karl Marx began intensive economic studies in the 1840s and, after the revolutions of 1848 and his exile, resumed systematic research in London in 1850. The writing of Capital then stretched over several decades. The work engages three traditions: classical political economy, including Adam Smith and David Ricardo, German idealist philosophy, especially Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel, and French socialist thought. Marx said his aim was to lay bare the economic law of motion of modern society, looking for the historical laws of capitalism's origins, development and decline. He delivered the manuscript of Volume I to the Hamburg publisher Otto Meissner in April 1867, and it appeared in September.

Volume I treats the process of production. It begins with the commodity, which has a use-value and an exchange-value, and argues that value is congealed abstract labour, measured by socially necessary labour time. Surplus value comes from the labourer working longer than is needed to reproduce the value of their labour power; Marx distinguishes absolute surplus value, gained by lengthening the working day, from relative surplus value, gained by cheapening wage goods.

Volume II, published by Friedrich Engels in 1885, examines the circulation of capital. Volume III, published by Engels in 1894, considers capitalist production as a whole, including how surplus value divides into profit, interest and rent, and the tendency of the rate of profit to fall. Running through the work are commodity fetishism, in which relations between people appear as relations between things, and the accumulation of capital, which Marx argues creates a reserve army of unemployed labour.

The first volume was received quietly in Germany. Engels sent hostile pseudonymous reviews to newspapers to draw attention, and the first edition of 1,000 copies took four years to sell out. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries the book, often in simplified form, became a foundational text of workers' movements and socialist parties. George Bernard Shaw studied it in 1883 and called it a revelation. It has also shaped sociology, political science and philosophy, and Marxian economics grew from it. Its labour theory of value, its predictions about capitalism and its association with 20th-century communist states have been criticised.
dasa: Dāsa first appears in Vedic texts of the second millennium BCE, and there is no consensus on its origin. In 1806 Karl Heinrich Tzschucke noted parallels with the name of the Dahae, a people of the south-eastern shores of the Caspian Sea. Michael Witzel compares the root with Avestan, Latin and Greek words implying enemy or foreigner, and takes the Vedic dasa to be a North Iranian tribe hostile to the Vedic Aryans.

Asko Parpola links the word to an Iranian and proto-Saka daha, meaning man, and identifies the dasa with the people of the Bactria–Margiana Archaeological Complex, whose circular forts recall the enemy forts of Indra in the early Rigveda; his theory is controversial. Max Müller had held that the dasa were peoples living in South Asia before the Aryans arrived.

In the Rigveda the word often stands for disorder and darkness set against order and light, and some dasas are plainly mythical, such as Urana with 99 arms or the six-eyed, three-headed dasa overcome by Indra in hymn 10.99.6. Sri Aurobindo read such passages spiritually, as demons hindering the mystic. R. S. Sharma found the sense of slave traceable in only four of the Rigveda's 10,600 verses, and H. H. Wilson translated even these as servant.

Kautilya's Arthashastra gives the thirteenth chapter of its third book to dasas. A person who was bankrupt or guilty of a minor crime could mortgage himself as a dasa to whoever paid his bail. A dasa kept what he earned without prejudice to his master's work, and his father's inheritance; a master who made him carry the dead or sweep ordure, or violated a female dasa, forfeited the price paid. Early Buddhist texts bar a slave from becoming a monk, and their narratives show slaves donated to monasteries as property.

Edmund Leach saw the word move from indigenous inhabitant to serf, tied servant and finally chattel slave, and proposed unfreedom as a term to cover all these senses. In devotional use dasa came to mean a servant of god. In Tamil it is commonly used for devotees of Vishnu or Krishna, in Gaudiya Vaishnavism devotees take it into names such as Hari Dasa, and many saints of the Bhakti movement added it to their names. As Das it is a surname among Hindus and Sikhs, mainly in northern India; Mohandas Gandhi's first name means slave of Mohan, or Krishna.
datames: Datames was born around 407 BCE, the son of Camisares, an Iranian satrap of Cilicia under Artaxerxes II who was most likely from a Persian noble family settled in Caria, and of Scythissa, a Paphlagonian princess. His name is the Hellenized form of an Old Iranian name, from either Dātamiθra, gift of Mithra, or Data-ama, to whom force is given; in Aramaic it appears as Tadanmu. He was also known as Tarkamuwa, a name of Luwian origin.

Datames became one of the king's bodyguards and distinguished himself in the war against the Cadusii, in which his father fell, and he was appointed to succeed him in the government of his province. He brought back under the king two officials who had revolted, Thyus, governor of Paphlagonia, and Aspis of Cataonia. Artaxerxes then gave him the chief command of a force to recover Egypt after the failure of Pharnabazus II, but the intrigues of his enemies at court and the risks they brought led him to throw off his allegiance around 370 BCE. He withdrew to Cappadocia and joined the Satraps' Revolt.

Artabazos, satrap of Hellespontine Phrygia, advanced against him from Pisidia and was entirely defeated, and Autophradates, sent with a large army, had to retreat with heavy losses. After evading many plots, Datames was assassinated at a conference by Mithridates, son of Ariobarzanes, who had won his confidence by pretending to be hostile to the king. His son Ariamnes I succeeded him as satrap of Cappadocia.

Cornelius Nepos, whose sketch is the only connected narrative of his life, ranked him the bravest and ablest of all non-Greek and non-Roman generals except Hamilcar and Hannibal. The accounts are confused, however, the anecdotes recorded by Polyaenus are hard to place, and the chronology is obscure.
date-masamune: Date Masamune was born Bontenmaru, later Tojiro, the eldest son of Date Terumune, probably at Yonezawa Castle. He led his first campaign at 14 in 1581, helping his father against the Soma clan, and in 1584, aged 17, succeeded Terumune, who retired. A childhood smallpox left him blind in his right eye, and accounts differ on how the eye was lost altogether: one says he plucked it out himself, another that his retainer Katakura Kojuro removed it. He was known for his crescent-moon helmet, and his army for black armour and golden headgear.

After the Date retainer Ouchi Sadatsuna defected to the Ashina clan, Masamune campaigned against the Ashina and the allies of Sadatsuna, even kin. In 1585 Nihonmatsu Yoshitsugu offered to surrender; when Masamune demanded most of his territory, Yoshitsugu seized Terumune at Miyamori Castle, and Terumune and Yoshitsugu both died as the party fled. Masamune took revenge at the Battle of Hitotoribashi in January 1586, attacked Nihonmatsu again in 1588, and by the end of 1589 held southern Mutsu Province.

In 1590 he delayed joining Toyotomi Hideyoshi's campaign against Odawara. Expecting execution, he appeared in his finest clothes, and Hideyoshi spared him, saying he could be of some use, but reduced his lands. His men served in the Imjin War of 1592-1598. After Hideyoshi's death in 1598 Masamune supported Tokugawa Ieyasu, fought on the eastern side in the Sekigahara campaign of 1600 and received the Sendai Domain. Promised a million koku, it produced only 640,000. In 1604 he moved there with 52,000 vassals and their families, and fought in the Osaka campaigns of 1614 and 1615.

Ieyasu and Hidetada regarded him with caution, but he gained the trust of Iemitsu, who liked to hear the stories of warlords of the Warring States period. He died in 1636, aged 68, of esophageal cancer and peritonitis, and the shogunate approved his eldest legitimate son, Date Tadamune, as heir.

Masamune sheltered Christian missionaries, released the missionary Sotelo from Ieyasu's custody, and funded the embassy of Hasekura Tsunenaga to Rome, sailing in the ship San Juan Bautista built with European techniques. At least five members stayed in Spain, and about 600 descendants carry the surname Japon. Once Ieyasu outlawed Christianity, Masamune obeyed and let Christians be persecuted in his domain. The nickname One-Eyed Dragon is first found in a poem by Rai San'yo in 1830, and no record shows him wearing an eyepatch; his portrait shows both eyes open, as his will directed.
date-munenari: Date Munenari was born in Edo on 1 September 1818, the fourth son of the hatamoto Yamaguchi Naokatsu, and was then known as Kamesaburō. Because Naokatsu's father was Date Muratoki, the fifth lord of Uwajima, the boy was a candidate for adoption by the heirless seventh lord, Date Munetada. He succeeded to the headship of the domain in 1844 as its eighth lord.

In 1858 the tairō Ii Naosuke ordered his retirement and placed him under house arrest. He returned to prominence in the political manoeuvring of the following years in Kyoto as a member of the conciliatory kōbu gattai party, which sought a union of court and bakufu, and late in 1863 he was made a member of the imperial advisory council, the sanyō-kaigi, together with Matsudaira Katamori and other like-minded lords.

After the fall of the shogunate in 1868 Munenari took an active part in the new imperial government, and Uwajima was deeply involved in the campaigns of the Boshin War of 1868–1869. He was a central figure in Japan's foreign relations in the early Meiji era: in 1871, representing the Japanese government, he signed the Sino-Japanese Friendship and Trade Treaty with Li Hongzhang, a viceroy of Qing China. The abolition of the han system that year allowed him to cut his political ties to Uwajima entirely.

In 1881 Munenari entertained King Kalākaua of the Kingdom of Hawaiʻi, on the first state visit to Japan by an actual head of state in its recorded history. His stepson Mune'e was first created a count in the new peerage system and was later promoted to marquess. Munenari died at Imado in Tokyo on 20 December 1892, at the age of 75.
datong: Datong lies in the Datong Basin of northern Shanxi, at an elevation of 1,040 metres, bordering Inner Mongolia to the north and west and Hebei to the east. It is the northernmost city of Shanxi and about 250 kilometres west of Beijing. Mountains surround the urban area on three sides, with passes only to the east and southwest. Its climate is continental and dry, with long, cold winters and very warm summers. The area was a frontier between agricultural China and the nomads of the Great Steppe, and was known for its trade in horses.

The area lay near the state of Dai, which the Zhao clan of Jin conquered in 457 BCE. Under the Qin it was Pingcheng County, part of the commandery of Yanmen. The Han founded a site within present-day Datong in 200 BCE, after their victory over the Xiongnu at the Battle of Baideng. Near a pass to Inner Mongolia along the Great Wall, Pingcheng prospered as a stop for camel caravans moving from China into Mongolia, and it was sacked at the end of the Eastern Han.

Pingcheng was the capital of the Xianbei-founded Northern Wei dynasty from 398 to 494, and the Yungang Grottoes were carved in the later part of that period, between 460 and 494. Under the Tang it was the seat of the prefecture of Yunzhou, and the first Guandi temple was built. It was renamed Datong in 1048 and was the Xijing, the Western Capital, of the Jurchen Jin dynasty before the Mongols sacked it.

Under the Ming, Datong was an important military stronghold against the Mongols to the north, and many of its notable structures, among them the Drum Tower and the Nine-Dragon Wall, date from that time. It was sacked again at the end of the Ming in 1649 and rebuilt by 1652. In the Second Sino-Japanese War the Japanese included the region in the puppet state of Mengjiang, and it returned to Shanxi after the war. In 1982, with part of its city walls still standing, it was listed among China's national historical and cultural cities.

Datong is a prefecture-level city of about three million people. Coal mining has long been its dominant industry, and a locomotive works opened in 1954 made almost all of the QJ class of steam locomotive, built as late as 1988. The Yungang Grottoes, 16 kilometres west of the city, hold over 50,000 carved images of Buddhas and bodhisattvas, most about 1,500 years old, and are a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Hanging Temple, built into a cliff face near Mount Heng, dates to the Northern Wei.
datu-uto: Datu Uto, also called Sultan Anwarud-din Utto, was the son of Sultan Bangon Marajanun Sa Didagen of Buayan and Tuan Bai Sa Buayan. In 1864 his father sent him with 500 men to help the Spaniards under Colonel La Hoz, Governor of Cotabato, against the Talayan rebels, but Uto went against his father's orders and sided with the Talayan datu. The Spaniards, who had artillery, won the fight. Uto lost an eye in the battle, which earned him the name one-eyed man, but it also made him a recognised leader in Buayan. His uncle Bayao succeeded Bangon in 1872, and Uto followed as ruler in 1875.

Uto ruled from the inland town of Sapakan and married Rajah Putri Bai-labi, daughter of Sultan Qudratullah Untong of Maguindanao. In 1874 he joined Sultan Jamal ul-Azam of Sulu against the Spanish, supplying the slaves Sulu needed; at his height he held as many as 5,000 slaves. When the Spanish took his stronghold of Bakat, he won it back and forced them to sign a peace accord in May 1875. He bound the leaders of the Pulangi basin to him through debts, friendships and some 60 marriages, and his domain reached from Lake Buluan to Sarangani Bay. To confuse the Spanish he kept the title of datu and had his cousin Tambilawan installed as titular sultan.

The Tausug and Chinese traders sold him Enfield and Spencer rifles in exchange for slaves. Fearing he would become a new Muhammad Kudarat, Governor-General Emilio Terrero y Perinat launched an offensive in 1885, and in 1886 two Spanish corps razed Bakat. Uto's forces harassed the builders and turned the metal of their works into krises, but as his allies submitted he signed a peace treaty imposed by the Spanish on 10 March 1887.

By 1888 many of his allies had defected, yet Uto remained strong in local politics. When Maguindanao had no sultan from 1888 to 1896 he backed his brother-in-law, Datu Mamaku, for the post, though Mangigin took it in 1896. Uto remained a powerful figure until 1899 and had left the political scene by 1900. Among those who carried on resistance, now against the Americans, were his former companions Datu Ali and Datu Djimbangan, while Datu Piang, once his minister, chose to cooperate with them.
daud-khan-karrani: Daud Khan was a son of Sulaiman Khan Karrani, during whose reign he commanded an army of 40,000 cavalry, 3,600 elephants, 140,000 infantry and 200 cannons. After the assassination of Bayazid Khan Karrani the nobles raised Daud to the throne. Like Bayazid, he shook off his allegiance to the Mughal emperor Akbar and issued coins in his own name, but his hot temper caused disruption among the Karrani nobles.

The war with the Mughals began when Daud's army invaded Zamania, near Ghazipur, razed the town and captured its fort. Akbar ordered Munim Khan, the governor of Jaunpur, to move against him, but Munim Khan met his friend Ludi Khan, Daud's prime minister, at Patna and agreed a truce. The agreement pleased neither ruler, and Daud had Ludi Khan put to death.

Munim Khan then attacked Bihar and forced Daud to take shelter in Patna. Daud sent Katlu Lohani, Gujar Khan Karrani and Sri Hari against the Mughal army, led by Munim Khan with Todar Mal and Man Singh. The Bengali and Afghan forces came close to victory, but the Mughals took the nearby fort of Hajipur, the source of their rations, and they fell back to Bengal. Akbar left Munim Khan as governor of Bihar and Bengal, with Todar Mal to assist him.

On 3 March 1575 the two sides fought at Tukaroi. The battle ended in a draw; the Afghans withdrew to Katak in Orissa, and the Mughals took Tanda, after which Munim Khan moved the capital of Bengal from Tanda to Gaur. By the treaty of Katak Daud gave up Bengal and Bihar and kept only Orissa. Six months later plague broke out, and Munim Khan died in October 1575. Kalapahar and Isa Khan drove the Mughal army out of eastern Bengal, and Daud marched from Orissa and recaptured Gaur.

Akbar sent a new army under Khan Jahan Quli, who captured Teliagarhi and advanced on Rajmahal. The battle there lasted many days; Akbar called on Muzaffar Khan Turbati, the governor of Bihar, and other generals to join it, while Daud was supported by the Afghan leaders Junaid, Qutlu Khan and Ismail Khan Lodhi. After the fighting of 12 July 1576 Daud was defeated and executed. He was the last ruler of the Karrani dynasty and the last Sultan of Bengal.
daugavpils: The town's history began in 1273, when the Livonian Order under Ernst von Ratzeburg built Dünaburg Castle on the site of a Lithuanian settlement, Naujinis, about 18 km from the present city. Lithuania ruled the area between 1281 and 1313. In 1577 Ivan the Terrible captured and destroyed the castle, and in the same year Stephen Báthory built a new castle and town 20 km downriver. It received Magdeburg town rights in 1582. In 1621 Dyneburg became the capital of the Inflanty Voivodeship of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. Russian troops held it, as Borisoglebov, from 1656 to 1667, until the Treaty of Andrusovo returned it to the Commonwealth. After the First Partition of Poland in 1772 it passed to the Russian Empire.

Under Russian rule the fortress was built between 1810 and 1878, and the city was connected to the Saint Petersburg-Warsaw railway in 1860. It was called Dvinsk from 1893 to 1920. A large Jewish community lived there from the 1780s onwards, and the census of 1897 counted 32,400 Jews among 69,700 inhabitants. Two prominent rabbis lived in the city: Joseph Rosen, the Rogatchover Gaon, and Meir Simcha of Dvinsk. The painter Mark Rothko was born there in 1903. The newly independent Latvian state renamed the city Daugavpils in 1920, after fighting there from 1919 to 1920 among Latvians, Poles and Soviet troops.

Soviet rule lasted from 1940 to 1941 and again from 1944 to 1991, with German occupation between 1941 and 1944. After the German invasion of 26 June 1941 the Germans and Latvian collaborators carried out mass executions of Jews, and the survivors were forced into a ghetto. Only about 100 survivors remained of a community of 16,000 when the town was liberated in 1944.

Daugavpils is a state city in southeastern Latvia on the Daugava River, the second largest in the country after Riga, which lies some 230 kilometres to the northwest. Its parts north of the river belong to the historical region of Latgale and those to the south to Selonia. It is a major railway junction and industrial centre. The population has long been multicultural: the 1935 census counted Latvians, Jews, Poles, Russians and Belarusians, and since the Second World War the city has had an overwhelmingly Russian-speaking population. Church Hill holds Lutheran, Catholic, Orthodox and Old Believer churches side by side, and the fortress houses the Mark Rothko Art Centre.
daulat-khan-lodi: Daulat Khan Lodi was the son of Tatar Khan, the previous Nizam of Lahore, who had asserted his independence from the Lodi dynasty under Bahlul Khan Lodi. Daulat Khan was first governor of the Jalandhar Doab and was promoted to the governorship of Lahore between 1500 and 1504, serving under Sikandar Khan Lodi and then Ibrahim Lodi. He was loyal to the dynasty but turned against Ibrahim, whose nature was rigid, proud and suspicious.

In Sikh tradition he is remembered as an employer of Guru Nanak. One of his officials, Jai Ram, was married to Nanak's sister Nanaki and found him work as keeper of Daulat Khan's store and granaries. When complaints were made that Nanak was wasting the stocks, two audits found them full and correctly accounted for, and when a Qazi called Nanak to court over his teachings, Daulat Khan defended him.

In 1523 Ibrahim Lodi was locked in a power struggle with his relatives and ministers, and Daulat Khan was one of his chief opponents, together with the sultan's uncle Alam Khan, then living under the protection of Sultan Muzaffar II of Gujarat. Daulat Khan sent his son Ghazi Khan Lodi to Delhi, who returned with the warning that Ibrahim meant to remove him. He then sent messengers to Babur in Kabul, offering allegiance in return for help.

Babur's army captured Lahore and Dipalpur. Daulat Khan and his sons Ghazi and Dilawar Khan Lodi joined him at Dipalpur, but Babur gave Daulat Jalandhar and Sultanpur instead of Lahore. Daulat and Ghazi went into hiding, while Dilawar accepted Sultanpur and the title of Khan Khanan.

When Babur left India to fight the Uzbeks at Balkh, leaving forces to help Alam Khan besiege Delhi, Daulat Khan offered his help in the hope of recovering Lahore, but was refused and left in charge of the Punjab with Ghazi. The attack on Delhi failed. Hearing that Babur was returning, Daulat and Ghazi fled to the fortress of Milwat, north of Lahore. Babur besieged it, Daulat Khan surrendered, and he died on the way to Bhera, where he was to be imprisoned. The invasion he had begun ended at the Battle of Panipat in 1526, where Ibrahim Lodi was killed and Babur went on to found the Mughal Empire.
daulat-rao-scindia: Daulat Rao was a grandson of Tukoji Rao Scindia, elder brother of Mahadji Scindia, who was killed at the Third Battle of Panipat on 7 January 1761. When Mahadji died without an heir he took the Gwalior throne on 12 February 1794, aged 15; the Satara Chhatrapati and the Peshwa installed him on 3 March, and Shah Alam II gave him the titles Naib Vakil-i-Mutlaq and Amir-al-Umara on 10 May. He inherited the modern army Mahadji had built under Benoît de Boigne, and saw himself less as a member of the Maratha Empire than as the chief sovereign in India.

The death of Peshwa Madhavrao II in 1795, the rise of Yashwantrao Holkar and the intrigues of Nana Farnavis let him gain the ascendancy in the confederacy. Under the influence of Sarjerao Ghatge, whose daughter he married in 1798, he seized lands from the Ponwars of Dhar and Dewas. In July 1801 Yashwantrao extorted a large sum from Ujjain; in October Ghatge sacked Indore with every form of atrocity; and in 1802 at Hadapsar, near Pune, Yashwantrao defeated the armies of Scindia and Peshwa Bajirao II, opening the gardi-ka-wakt, a period of unrest in which armies and Pindari bands overran central India.

By the Treaty of Bassein of 31 December 1802 the Peshwa recognised the East India Company as the paramount power, and Scindia's evasions brought him into war with the British and defeats at Ahmadnagar, Assaye, Argaon, Asirgarh and Laswari. He lost his lands between the Yamuna and the Ganges, South Haryana and Bharuch, and the fortresses of Gwalior and Gohad, which were restored in 1805 with the Chambal as his northern boundary. He conquered Chanderi in 1811 and signed the Treaty of Gwalior in 1817, promising help against the Pindaris, and in 1818 ceded Ajmer and other lands.

Daulat Rao, who also bore the title the defender of Delhi, ruled Gwalior until his death on 21 March 1827. His kingdom kept its independence longer than most Indian states: in 1832 a British parliamentary committee reported that within the Peninsula Sindhia was the only prince who preserved the semblance of independence.
daumantas-of-pskov: Until 1265 Daumantas was duke of Nalšia, a northern province of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania. He married the sister of Queen Morta, the second wife of King Mindaugas, and is first mentioned around 1252 defending the king's castle at Voruta. When Morta died in 1262, Mindaugas kept Daumantas's wife as his own, allegedly at Morta's request so that she could raise his young children. Daumantas conspired with the king's kinsmen Treniota and Tautvilas, and in the autumn of 1263 he killed Mindaugas and his sons Ruklys and Repeikis. When Mindaugas's son Vaišelga returned in 1264 to take the throne, Daumantas fled to Pskov with his family and 300 men.

Baptised by Prince Sviatoslav, he married a daughter of Dmitry of Pereslavl, son of Alexander Nevsky, and led raids into north-eastern Lithuania in 1266 and 1267 against the new duke of Nalšia, Gerdenis. His success persuaded the Pskovians to elect him their knyaz, or military leader. In 1268 he joined the Novgorodians in invading Danish Estonia and fought at the Battle of Rakvere on 18 February. The following year Otto von Lutterberg, master of the Livonian Order, burned Izborsk and besieged Pskov, but Daumantas held out with Novgorodian help and made a truce.

He beat the Livonians near Pskov on 8 June 1272 and again in 1278, and in 1282 he seized the treasury of the ousted Prince Dmitry from the Novgorodians at Ladoga and freed Dmitry's daughters, one of whom, Maria, he married. In 1285 he was defeated and briefly taken prisoner in a campaign against the Principality of Tver. When the Livonian Order besieged Pskov in March 1299, he defeated it on the banks of the Velikaya River.

Daumantas died during a plague outbreak and was buried in the Trinity Cathedral, where his sword and belongings were shown until the 20th century. The Pskovian Chronicles praise him above every other ruler of the city, and in 1460 his sword was placed in the hand of the new prince Yury. Under him Pskov gained de facto independence from Novgorod. The fortifications he built became known as the Daumantas Walls, a church dedicated to him was built in 1567, and he is venerated as patron saint of Pskov and of the Russian army, with a feast on 20 May.
dauphin-of-france: The word dauphin is French for dolphin. Count Guigues IV of Albon, who died in 1142, ruled in Viennois within the Kingdom of Burgundy, under the suzerainty of the Holy Roman Empire. He bore a dolphin on his coat of arms and was nicknamed le Dauphin, and in time the nickname became a title. From about 1285 the counts of Albon used the title Dauphin de Viennois officially, and their domains came to be known as the Dauphiné.

In 1343 Humbert II of Viennois, who had no heirs, began negotiations with King Philippe VI of France over the future of the Dauphiné. By 1349 he decided to give up his rule, and the final agreement named the king's grandson Charles as his successor, on condition that the Dauphiné remain a separate polity and not be absorbed into the French realm. In the summer of 1349 Charles became the first Dauphin de Viennois of the House of Valois. In 1350 his father ascended the French throne as John II, and for the first time the same person was both heir to the throne and Dauphin.

Originally the Dauphin ruled the Dauphiné personally. It was legally part of the Empire, whose emperors had stipulated that it must never be united with France. Because Dauphins were often minors or occupied elsewhere, the Dauphiné suffered from anarchy in the 14th and 15th centuries. Louis, the son of Charles VII, defied his father by staying in the province longer than the king allowed, and married Charlotte of Savoy against his wishes. Charles VII's soldiers drove him out in 1456. After he succeeded as Louis XI in 1461, he united the Dauphiné with France under royal control.

From then on the title was held by the next heir in the direct line, automatically at birth, at the parent's accession or at the previous Dauphin's death, whereas the British title Prince of Wales is in the monarch's gift. A Dauphin combined the arms of the Dauphiné with the French fleurs-de-lis. The sons and grandsons of a Dauphin ranked above their cousins.

The Constitution of 1791 abolished the title, and the heir was restyled Prince Royal. It was revived on the accession of Charles X in 1824, when his son Louis-Antoine, Duke of Angoulême, became Dauphin, and it fell into disuse after the removal of the Bourbons in 1830.
daura: Daura is a city and local government area in Katsina State, in north-western Nigeria, about 79 km east of Katsina and 117 km north of Kano. It is regarded as the spiritual home of the Hausa people, and its emirate is counted among the seven true Hausa states, the Hausa Bakwai, with Biram, Kano, Katsina, Zazzau, Gobir and Rano. Its Hausa and Fulani inhabitants trade in sorghum, millet, onions, groundnuts, cotton, hides and skins, and keep cattle, goats, sheep, horses and donkeys.

In the legend, set in about the 9th century, Bayajidda reached Daura after crossing the Sahara and killed the snake named Sarki, meaning king, that kept the people from drawing water from the well. The queen, Magajiya Daurama, married him in gratitude, and one of their seven children was named Daura. The Kusugu Well, where he is said to have slain the snake, stands under a wooden shelter and draws visitors. The town became a caravan centre for salt and potash from the Sahara and for cloth, slaves, leather and farm produce from the south, though it never gained the political or military weight of Katsina or Kano.

In 1805, during the Fulani War, the Fulani warrior Malam Ishaku took Daura and set up an emirate. The Hausa founded rival states nearby, of which Zango, founded in 1825, was the most prominent, while Fulani emirs also ruled at Baure. After the British and French divided the three Daura polities, the British installed Zango's ruler, Malam Musa, as emir of Daura. The emirate was part of North-Central State after 1967, joined Kaduna State in 1976 and became part of the new Katsina State in 1987.

The Emir of Daura reigns as a ceremonial hereditary monarch in the Kangiwa palace complex at the centre of the old city; the 60th emir took the throne on 28 February 2007. The emir hosts a durbar at Eid al-Fitr, Eid al-Adha and the Durbar of Gani, when groups of horsemen from the surrounding villages charge towards him in salute.
davi-canabarro: He was born David José Martins on 22 August 1796, the son of José Martins Coelho of Porto Alegre and Mariana de Jesus Ignacia of Santa Catarina. The surname Canabarro came from his grandfather, Manuel Teodósio Ferreira, who had received it as a nickname from Luís Teles da Silva Caminha e Meneses, 5th Marquis of Alegrete. He took the name himself by 1836, at the insistence of his uncle Antonio Ferreira Canabarro.

At fifteen he asked his father's leave to go to war in his brother's place and served in the first campaign in the Banda Oriental of 1811 and 1812, under Dom Diogo de Sousa, Count of Rio Pardo. He fought again in the second campaign, from 1816 to 1820, which ended in the annexation of the region as the province of Cisplatina.

In the Cisplatine War of 1825 to 1828 he was a lieutenant under Bento Gonçalves, played an important part at the Battle of Rincón de las Gallinas on 24 September 1825 and fought at the Battle of Ituzaingó. Neutral at first in the Ragamuffin War, he later joined the rebels and rose quickly, taking command in June 1843, when Bento Gonçalves stepped aside to avoid a split among the republicans and served under him.

His only defeat came at the Battle of Porongos, where he was surprised by imperial troops despite having the Black Lancers with him. When Juan Manuel de Rosas, ruler of the Argentine Confederation, offered help against the empire in return for the rebels' cooperation, Canabarro replied with a letter declaring his loyalty to the country. He accepted the amnesty offered by the Baron of Caxias on 18 December 1844, and the terms agreed on 25 February 1845 let the republicans choose the next provincial president, made the imperial government answerable for their debts and pardoned the prisoners. He later fought in the Platine and Uruguayan wars and, with the honorary title of general, in the Paraguayan War. He died on 12 April 1867.
david: The First Book of Samuel and the First Book of Chronicles identify David as the son of Jesse of Bethlehem, the youngest of eight sons. He had at least two sisters, Zeruiah, whose sons all served in his army, and Abigail. The Bible does not name his mother, though the Talmud calls her Nitzevet, and the Book of Ruth makes him the great-grandson of Ruth the Moabite and Boaz. In the biblical narrative God, angered by the disobedience of King Saul, sends the prophet Samuel to anoint the shepherd David as king in his place. David then enters Saul's service as an armour-bearer and plays the lyre to soothe the king.

According to the Book of Samuel, David becomes a hero by killing the Philistine Goliath and then falls out with Saul and goes into hiding. After the deaths of Saul and Jonathan he becomes king first of Judah and eventually of all Israel. He conquers Jerusalem, makes it his capital and brings the Ark there. After committing adultery with Bathsheba and arranging the death of her husband Uriah, he survives the rebellion of his son Absalom. Denied permission to build the temple because of his bloodshed, he dies at 70 and names Solomon, his son with Bathsheba, as successor. Almost half the Psalms are headed as his, but the headings are late additions.

In the last two centuries BCE the son of David became an apocalyptic and heavenly figure who would deliver Israel, the background for early Christian ideas of the Messiah, and the Gospel of Matthew and the Gospel of Luke describe Jesus as descended from him. In the Quran he is a prophet and king who killed Goliath and was given the Psalms.

The only sources directly attesting David's life are biblical. Some scholars believe the Books of Samuel were substantially composed in the time of Josiah at the end of the 7th century BCE. The Tel Dan stele, found in 1993 and erected by Hazael of Damascus, contains a phrase most scholars read as House of David, taken as evidence that outsiders saw a Judahite dynasty descended from a founder named David. Richard Nelson holds that David was certainly historical but was more like a chief than a king.
david-alfaro-siqueiros: David Alfaro Siqueiros was born José de Jesús Alfaro Siqueiros, the second of three children. His mother died when he was four, and he was raised largely by his paternal grandparents. In 1911, at fifteen, he took part in a student strike at the Academy of San Carlos, and at eighteen he joined Venustiano Carranza's Constitutional Army against President Victoriano Huerta, an experience that exposed him to the lives of the working and rural poor. In 1919 he went to Europe, where he absorbed cubism in Paris, met Diego Rivera and studied Renaissance fresco painters in Italy.

In 1922 he returned to Mexico City to paint murals under José Vasconcelos, alongside Rivera and José Clemente Orozco, and in 1923 he helped found the Syndicate of Revolutionary Mexican Painters, Sculptors and Engravers. In Los Angeles in 1932 he led a team using airbrushes, spray guns and projectors. His América Tropical, depicting American imperialism in Latin America, was whitewashed by 1938. On 24 May 1940 he led an attack on Leon Trotsky's house in Coyoacán. Trotsky was unhurt, but his 14-year-old grandson was shot and survived, and the bodyguard Robert Sheldon Harte was found executed.

Siqueiros went into hiding, was arrested in Jalisco and held at Lecumberri prison, but never stood trial and left to paint a mural in Chile. In 1952 he made The People to the University, the University to the People in Mexico City, and in 1960 he was arrested after criticising President Adolfo López Mateos, remaining in prison until the spring of 1964.

His last major work, the Polyforum Siqueiros, was completed in 1971 and combines architecture, mural painting and polychromed sculpture. He believed that art should be public, educational and ideological, and he painted the struggle of working people, stressing the angles of the body and the strength of hands. He died in Cuernavaca on 6 January 1974 and was interred in the Rotunda of Illustrious Persons. A few days earlier he had donated his house in Polanco to the Mexican state.
david-ben-gurion: David Grün was born on 16 October 1886 in Płońsk, in Congress Poland, then part of the Russian Empire. His father, Avigdor Grün, was a court scribe and unofficial legal adviser who co-founded a Zionist group, Beni Zion, after the publication of Theodor Herzl's Der Judenstaat in 1896. His mother died in 1897. His formal education ended after his bar mitzvah, and at fourteen he and two friends formed a youth club, Ezra, which promoted Hebrew studies and emigration to the Holy Land.

He landed at Jaffa on 7 September 1906 and worked as a day labourer at Petah Tikva, where he caught malaria. He adopted the name Ben-Gurion in 1909. Deported to Egypt by the Ottoman authorities in March 1915, he travelled to the United States, where a speaking tour to raise a Jewish pioneer force produced few recruits.

In 1919 Ben-Gurion led the centrist faction of the Labor Zionist movement in forming Ahdut HaAvoda. He helped found the Histadrut, the Zionist labour federation, in 1920 and was its general secretary from 1921 to 1935. After the British White Paper of 1939 limited Jewish immigration to Palestine, he changed his policy towards the British and began preparing the Yishuv for war, while also urging support for the British war effort. He became executive head of the World Zionist Organization in 1946.

On 14 May 1948, the last day of the British Mandate, he proclaimed the State of Israel and was the first to sign its Declaration of Independence. During the 1948 war he ordered the militias merged into the Israel Defense Forces; in the Altalena Affair he had the Irgun's arms ship shelled, and sixteen Irgun fighters and three soldiers died. The war involved the expulsion and flight of most of the Palestinian Arab population, and historians disagree about his part in it. Benny Morris holds that he created an atmosphere of transfer without written orders.

Elected prime minister after the election of 14 February 1949, he held office until 1963 except for 1954 and 1955, when Moshe Sharett led the government. He oversaw the airlift of Jews from Arab countries, the National Water Carrier and settlement of the Negev, and he backed Israel's invasion of the Sinai in the Suez Crisis of 1956. He also pursued a reparations agreement with West Germany.

Ben-Gurion retired from politics in 1970 and lived in a modest hut at the kibbutz of Sde Boker, writing an eleven-volume history of Israel's early years. He suffered a cerebral haemorrhage on 18 November 1973 and died on 1 December. He is buried beside his wife Paula at Midreshet Ben-Gurion. Israel's main airport and Ben-Gurion University of the Negev bear his name, and his hut is now a visitors' centre.
david-friedrich-strauss: Strauss was born in Ludwigsburg, near Stuttgart, on 27 January 1808. At twelve he was sent to the evangelical seminary at Blaubeuren, where his masters Friedrich Heinrich Kern and Ferdinand Christian Baur taught their pupils to appreciate the ancient classics and the principles of textual criticism, which could be applied to sacred texts as to classical ones. In 1825 he entered the Tübinger Stift. He later taught Latin, history and Hebrew at Maulbronn and Blaubeuren, and in October 1831 went to Berlin to study under Schleiermacher and Hegel, though Hegel died just as he arrived. In the autumn of 1833 he resigned a Tübingen post to finish his book on Jesus.

Das Leben Jesu, kritisch bearbeitet appeared in 1835 and 1836, when he was 27, and was a sensation. Without denying that Jesus existed, Strauss argued that the miracles of the New Testament were mythical additions with little basis in fact. By myth he meant not mere falsity but the imaginative expression of religious truth. He held that the early church developed the stories to present Jesus as the Messiah of Jewish prophecy. This was a third way between rationalism, which explained miracles as misread natural events, and the supernaturalist view that the accounts were entirely accurate.

The book brought fierce controversy. When Strauss was elected to a chair of theology at the University of Zurich, the storm was so great that the authorities pensioned him before he began, and effigies of him were burnt at the Shrove Tuesday festival. He gave the pension of 1000 Swiss francs a year to the poor. In 1840 and 1841 he published Christliche Glaubenslehre, which argued that the history of Christian doctrines was the history of their disintegration. He then left theology for over twenty years and wrote biographies. His last work, Der alte und der neue Glaube (1872), caused almost as great a sensation, since friends saw in it a one-sided view of Christianity and a turn from spiritual philosophy to materialism.

Strauss died in Ludwigsburg on 8 February 1874. George Eliot translated his Life of Jesus into English in 1846. Albert Schweitzer wrote in The Quest of the Historical Jesus that research fell into two periods, before and after David Strauss. Marcus Borg has suggested that the details of Strauss's argument have not had a long-lasting effect, but that his basic claims, that many gospel narratives are mythical in character and that myth is not the same as falsehood, have become part of mainstream scholarship.
david-hume: David Hume was born David Home on 7 May 1711 in a tenement on the north side of Edinburgh's Lawnmarket, the second of two sons. His father Joseph, an advocate of Ninewells, died just after David's second birthday, and his mother Catherine raised the family on her own. By the age of 25 he had no income and no learned profession, and he worked as a merchant's assistant before travelling to La Flèche in Anjou, where he had frequent discussions with the Jesuits of the college there and probably used its library.

Hume published A Treatise of Human Nature in 1739 and 1740, aiming to introduce the experimental method of reasoning into the study of human nature. By his own account it fell dead-born from the press. His main teaching was that the mind consists of perceptions, divided into impressions and fainter ideas, and that every idea is copied from some impression. He argued that reasoning from past experience to the future cannot be justified, because it presupposes that nature is uniform, which cannot itself be shown. Belief in causes therefore rests on custom and habit. He held that the self is only a bundle of perceptions, that morals rest on sentiment, not reason, and that free will is compatible with causal determinism.

He was chiefly known in his lifetime as a historian and essayist. From 1754 to 1762 he published the six-volume History of England, which runs from the invasion of Julius Caesar to the Revolution in 1688 and widened its subject beyond kings, parliaments and armies to literature and science.

From 1763 to 1765 Hume was attached to Lord Hertford in Paris, serving as secretary to the British embassy and in 1765 as chargé d'affaires. In January 1766 he took Jean-Jacques Rousseau to England, where the two quarrelled, and Hume published an account of the dispute. He died of an abdominal cancer in Edinburgh on 25 August 1776. James Boswell saw him a few weeks earlier, and Hume told him that he thought the idea of life after death a most unreasonable fancy. He asked for a simple Roman tomb, which stands on Calton Hill. Immanuel Kant credited Hume with waking him from his dogmatic slumber, and his influence runs through utilitarianism, logical positivism and cognitive science.
david-ii-of-imereti: David was born in 1755 into the Bagrationi dynasty, the son of George VII of Imereti, who had briefly ruled in 1741, and of Princess Mzekhatun Lipartiani, daughter of Prince Giorgi Lipartiani. On the death of his cousin King Solomon I he became regent, and he kept the rival princes David, the future Solomon II, and George from being crowned. With the support of Katsia II Dadiani, prince of Mingrelia, he seized the throne and proclaimed himself king on 4 May 1784.

As king, David tried to establish contact with Imperial Russia and to restrict the powers of the great nobles. In 1787 he sent the poet Besiki, ostensibly to negotiate with the Russians; Besiki, rumoured to be the lover of David's queen, lingered in Ukraine until 1789, was never allowed to go on to St Petersburg, and died at Iaşi. David's policies drove many leading aristocrats, including the Mingrelian prince Grigol Dadiani, into opposition. In 1789 King Heraclius II of Georgia sent his army into Imereti and helped David-Solomon drive David II out to Akhaltsikhe, in the Ottoman-held Georgian province.

In 1790 David returned with a Turkish force and deposed Solomon II, but he was eventually defeated and fled Imereti. Through the mediation of Heraclius he was later allowed back and granted a fiefdom. Between 1792 and 1794 he tried again, with mercenaries from Dagestan, to reclaim the crown, was defeated and withdrew from Imereti. He died of smallpox in exile at Akhaltsikhe in January 1795.

He was married to Ana Orbeliani (1765–1832), daughter of Prince Mamuka Orbeliani. Their son Prince Constantine (1789–1844), heir to the throne of Imereti, later became a major-general in the Russian service, and their daughters Tamar and Mzekhatun married into the Eristavi-Sharvashidze and Tsereteli families. A natural son, Prince Rostom, died in 1820; his son Vakhtang rose in revolt against Russian rule that year.
david-ii-of-scotland: David was born on 5 March 1324 at Dunfermline Abbey, one of twin sons of Robert the Bruce and Elizabeth de Burgh. His mother died in 1327. Under the Treaty of Edinburgh-Northampton he was married on 17 July 1328, aged four, to the seven-year-old Joan, daughter of Edward II of England and Isabella of France. Robert the Bruce died on 7 June 1329, and David became king at the age of five. He and Joan were crowned at Scone Abbey on 24 November 1331, and he was the first Scottish monarch to be anointed at his coronation.

During his minority the kingdom was governed by guardians, several of whom fell in battle, among them Donald, Earl of Mar, at Dupplin Moor in August 1332 and Archibald Douglas at Halidon Hill in July 1333. After Dupplin, Edward Balliol, a protégé of Edward III of England, was crowned by the English, and the Second War of Scottish Independence began. After the English victory at Halidon Hill, David and Joan were sent to France, reaching Boulogne on 14 May 1334. He returned to Scotland on 2 June 1341, landing at Inverbervie, and took government into his own hands at the age of 17.

In 1346, under the Auld Alliance, David invaded England to draw Edward III away from France. His army was defeated at the Battle of Neville's Cross on 17 October 1346, and he was wounded by two arrows to the face and taken prisoner. He remained in captivity in England for eleven years. By the Treaty of Berwick of 3 October 1357 the Scots agreed to pay 100,000 marks at 10,000 marks a year. When the instalment of 1363 could not be raised, David offered to bequeath the throne to Edward III or one of his sons, and in 1364 the Scottish parliament rejected a proposal to make Lionel of Antwerp the next king. From 1364 David governed actively and dealt firmly with defiant nobles.

Queen Joan died on 7 September 1362. David married Margaret Drummond in about February 1364 and tried to divorce her in 1370 because she had borne no children; Pope Urban V reversed the divorce. David died unexpectedly of natural causes at Edinburgh Castle on 22 February 1371, aged 46, and was buried before the high altar of Holyrood Abbey. As the last male of the House of Bruce, he was succeeded by his nephew Robert II. Despite long periods in exile and captivity, he had ensured the survival of his kingdom and left the monarchy in a strong position.
david-iii-kuropalates: David was the younger son of Adarnase Kouropalates, a representative of the Second House of Tao, a branch of the Bagratid dynasty that held Tao, a province on the historic Georgian-Armenian border known to the Armenians as Tayk, from the 940s. He inherited the principality jointly with his brother Bagrat in 961, when their father died, and became sole ruler after Bagrat's death. He earned wide renown for martial valour and skill, and was given the epithet the Great. His realm was administered from the towns of Olti and Narivan.

A revolt led by Bardas Skleros broke out in 976 and threatened Constantinople. The young emperor Basil II asked David for help, and David sent 12,000 cavalry under Tornikios and Jojik to reinforce the general Bardas Phokas. The loyalists won the Battle of Pankalia on 24 March 979. As reward David received, for his lifetime, large territories in eastern Asia Minor, including Theodosiopolis (modern Erzurum), and the court title of kouropalates. Basil also funded the Georgian monastery of Iviron on Mount Athos for Tornikios. The grant was on terms unfavourable to David, since the lands were to revert to the empire at his death.

Between 987 and 989 David joined Bardas Phokas in a rebellion against Basil. After the rebels were defeated, an imperial force under John of Chaldea compelled David to submit, and he bequeathed his domains to the emperor. He then campaigned against Muslim emirs, recapturing Manzikert from the Marwanids and defeating Mamlan, the Rawadid emir of Azarbaijan, in 998, though his forces suffered heavy casualties near Khlat on 17 April 998. His revenues from the trade routes of the south-western Caucasus paid for towns, forts and churches, including Oshki, and for Georgian monastic communities and translations by Euthymius the Athonite.

David had no children and adopted his kinsman Bagrat, heir to the Bagratid throne of Kartli and, through his mother Gurandukht, a potential heir to Abkhazia. David occupied Kartli for him in 976 and helped secure the crown of Abkhazia for him in 978. Sources differ on the manner of David's death. Aristakes Lastivertsi says nobles poisoned the communion chalice and strangled him, while Matthew of Edessa names the Georgian archbishop Hilarion as the main culprit.

Basil II marched to claim David's lands, and the local nobility submitted without serious resistance. Bagrat recognised the new borders and received the title of kouropalates, and went on to become the first king of a unified Georgian monarchy. Georgian and Armenian sources describe David as just, peace-loving and generous, and modern scholars rank him high in Georgian history.
david-iv-of-georgia: David IV was the only son of King George II of Georgia and Queen Helen, born in Kutaisi. He grew up in a time of war and devastation caused by the Seljuks. Opposition to George II led to a transfer of power to the young David, who came to the throne at sixteen. He inherited a kingdom much reduced from its early eleventh-century extent, now consisting largely of Abkhazia and Kartli. Since 1080, when the emir Ahmed captured Kutaisi, Georgia had accepted Seljuk suzerainty and paid annual tribute, yet seasonal raids continued.

David reorganised an army whose morale had been shattered, forming small detachments of minor nobles and peasants from royal estates and developing a strategy of surprise attacks on Muslim encampments. He stopped the Seljuk incursions and then launched counterattacks. The duke Liparit V of Kldekari conspired against him in 1093 and was imprisoned; after a second conspiracy he was exiled to Constantinople. David then campaigned against Kvirike IV of Kakheti-Hereti and captured the fortress of Zedazeni in 1101 or 1103.

Around 1103 to 1105 he convened the Council of Ruisi-Urbnisi, which addressed corruption in the Church. From 1110 he fought the Turks, and on 14 February he destroyed Turkish forces at Botora. At the Battle of Didgori in August 1121 he defeated the Seljuks, with a Latin battalion of 200 to 1,000 men among his forces, and went on to take the Emirate of Tbilisi.

David died in Tbilisi on 24 January 1125, after a reign of thirty-four years, having named his eldest son Demetrius as successor. At his request he was buried at the main entrance of Gelati Monastery, so that all who came to its academy would step on his tomb. Around 1120 he composed Hymns of Repentance, a sequence of eight free-verse psalms. The epithet the Builder first appears in a charter of 1452. Georgian historiography regards his reign as the beginning of the Golden Age of the Kingdom of Georgia.
david-komnenos: David was the son of Manuel Komnenos. His life is poorly documented: Michael Panaretos, the main historian of the Empire of Trebizond, never mentions him. Exactly how he and his brother Alexios were related to Queen Tamar of Georgia is unclear. Cyril Toumanoff argued that their grandfather Andronikos had married a sister of King George III while in Georgia, while Michel Kuršanskis has argued that their mother or grandmother came from the Palaiologos or Doukas families. After the deaths of Andronikos and Manuel, Tamar gave the boys refuge at the Georgian court, where they were presumably raised. Two lead seals and an inscription at Heraclea Pontica show that David was the first of his family to use the style Megas Komnenos.

After the seizure of Trebizond, Oinaion and Sinope declared for the brothers. With Georgian troops and local mercenaries David made himself master of Pontus and Paphlagonia, including Kastamonou, said to be the ancestral castle of the Komnenoi, and advanced from Sinope to the Sangarios River, welcomed by Amastris, Tios and Heraclea Pontica. There he met Theodore Laskaris of the Empire of Nicaea, who surprised and defeated David's general Synadenos when he tried to occupy Nicomedia.

David then sought the protection of the Latin Empire, sending it grain and hams and asking to be treated as its subject; in the words of William Miller, it was his interest to prefer a nominal Latin suzerainty to annexation by Nicaea. A raid across the Sangarios ended when Andronikos Gidos, a general of Laskaris, destroyed about 300 Frankish auxiliaries. In 1208 Laskaris besieged Heraclea Pontica, but the Latin emperor Henry of Flanders occupied Nicomedia and forced him to withdraw.

Allied with the Seljuk sultan Kaykaus I, Laskaris later took Heraclea Pontica and Amastris, and David disappears from the record. Earlier scholars from Jakob Philipp Fallmerayer onward placed his death at the siege of Sinope in 1214, but a marginal note from Mount Athos records that he died as a monk of Vatopedi on 13 December 1212. The historian Shukurov takes Panaretos's silence as deliberate and suggests that Alexios confined him there after his submission to the Latins.
david-lange: David Russell Lange was born on 4 August 1942 in Ōtāhuhu, then a small industrial borough since absorbed into Auckland. He was the oldest of four children of Eric Roy Lange, a general practitioner and obstetrician, and Phoebe Fysh Lange, who had trained as a nurse in her native Tasmania. He graduated in law from the University of Auckland in 1966, and worked at the Westfield Freezing Works to pay his way. He became a lawyer who represented poor and struggling people in the Auckland of the 1970s.

Lange joined the Labour Party in 1963. He won the Mangere by-election of 1977, and in Parliament he made his name as a debater and wit, the scourge of Prime Minister Robert Muldoon. He succeeded Bill Rowling as leader of the Labour Party and of the Opposition on 3 February 1983.

Muldoon called a snap election for July 1984, and Lange led Labour to a landslide. Before he was sworn in on 26 July 1984, a foreign exchange crisis arose, because traders expected Labour to devalue the New Zealand dollar. Muldoon refused Lange's instruction to devalue until 19 July. At 41, Lange was the youngest prime minister of the 20th century. He made Roger Douglas minister of finance, and the free-market reforms became known as Rogernomics. The government held an Economic Summit on 14 September 1984.

Lange kept a campaign promise to deny port facilities to nuclear-armed and nuclear-powered vessels, making New Zealand a nuclear-free zone. Labour was re-elected in August 1987, and Lange made himself minister of education to draw a line in the sand against what he called the Treasury troika of Douglas, Richard Prebble and David Caygill. The stock market crash of October 1987 was followed by a recession, and he introduced Tomorrow's Schools, which replaced education boards with elected boards of trustees. Geoffrey Palmer succeeded him as prime minister in 1989.

Lange served as attorney-general from 1989 to 1990 and retired from Parliament before the 1996 election, in failing health. In his valedictory speech he thanked those whose lives were wrecked by his government's reforms. He was diagnosed with amyloidosis in 2002, and he died on 13 August 2005 in Middlemore Hospital in Auckland, five days after the publication of his memoir My Life. He received the Right Livelihood Award in 2003 for his fight against nuclear weapons, and Prime Minister Helen Clark described the nuclear-free legislation as his legacy.
david-livingstone: David Livingstone was born on 19 March 1813 in the mill town of Blantyre, Scotland, the second of seven children of Neil Livingstone and Agnes Hunter. At the age of 10 he began work in a cotton mill, where he and his brother John worked 14-hour days tying broken threads. At 21 he was excited by a pamphlet setting out Gützlaff's call for missionaries to China, who should be trained as medical doctors. He joined Anderson's University in Glasgow in 1836 to study medicine and chemistry, paying his way by working at the mill from Easter to October.

Livingstone left London on 17 November 1840 for the Cape of Good Hope. To improve his Tswana and find sites for mission stations, he journeyed far north of Kolobeng with William Cotton Oswell, and in 1849 they crossed the Kalahari Desert and reached Lake Ngami. In August 1851 they reached the Zambezi. In 1852 he travelled to Linyanti, where the Kololo chief Sekeletu gave him authority to investigate trade routes to the coast. They reached the Portuguese city of Luanda in May 1854, after great difficulties and Livingstone's near death from fever. He returned to Britain in December 1856, and his Missionary Travels of 1857 was a bestselling travelogue.

In 1858 he agreed to lead a second Zambezi expedition. The river proved impassable past the Cahora Bassa rapids, which he had failed to explore earlier. From January 1866 he sought the source of the Nile from Zanzibar, believing it lay farther south than Lake Albert or Lake Victoria. He was wrong about the Nile, but he identified for European science Lake Ngami, Lake Malawi, Lake Bangweulu and Victoria Falls.

Livingstone lost contact with the outside world for six years and was ill for most of his last four. He died on 1 May 1873 at Chief Chitambo's village at Chipundu, southeast of Lake Bangweulu, from malaria and internal bleeding caused by dysentery. His attendants Chuma and Susi buried his heart under a tree near the spot. By the late 1860s his reputation had suffered from the failure of his missions and of the Zambezi expedition, but it was restored by Henry Morton Stanley and by the loyalty of his servants. The Universities' Mission to Central Africa was founded at his request in 1860. He is recorded as having converted only one African, the Kwena chief Sechele.
david-lloyd-george: David Lloyd George was born on 17 January 1863 in Chorlton-on-Medlock, Manchester, to Welsh parents, Elizabeth Lloyd and William George. His father died of pneumonia in June 1864, and his mother took the children to her native Llanystumdwy in Carnarvonshire, where they lived with her brother Richard Lloyd, a shoemaker, lay minister and strong Liberal, who became a towering influence on his nephew. He qualified as a solicitor in 1884 and set up his own practice in 1885.

He won the by-election for Caernarfon Boroughs on 10 April 1890, narrowly, and held the seat until 1945. As a radical Liberal he supported Welsh devolution, the disestablishment of the Church in Wales and land reform. His fierce opposition to the Second Boer War brought him national fame, though he insisted that the British Empire should rest on freedom rather than racial arrogance.

Lloyd George became President of the Board of Trade in 1905 and Chancellor of the Exchequer in 1908. His 1909 People's Budget imposed a 20 per cent tax on the unearned increase in land values, higher death duties and income tax, and a Supertax on incomes over £3,000, to pay for welfare programmes and battleships. He also helped to secure the disestablishment of the Anglican Church in Wales, in force from 1920.

As Minister of Munitions from 1915 he took arms production from the generals and made it an industrial department. He became Secretary of State for War in June 1916 and prime minister in December 1916, the first Welshman in the post, replacing Asquith. He created a smaller war cabinet and, against U-boat food shortages, introduced the convoy system and rationing.

After the war he negotiated independence for the Irish Free State in 1921. In 1922 he was embroiled in a scandal over the sale of honours, and the Carlton Club meeting decided that the Conservatives should end the coalition, and he resigned. He led the Liberal Party from 1926 to 1931, and in May 1940 his speech in the Norway Debate helped undermine Chamberlain as prime minister.

Lloyd George died of cancer on 26 March 1945, aged 82, and was buried four days later beside the river Dwyfor at Llanystumdwy, under a boulder with no inscription. The Lloyd George Museum nearby, designed by Clough Williams-Ellis, opened in 1963. Scholars have praised his welfare reforms and his leadership to victory in the First World War, and criticised his presidential style and his scandals.
david-malo: Malo's father was named Aoʻao and his mother Heone. Early in life he married Aʻalailoa, a widow much older than he, who died in 1822 without children. In Lahaina he took the baptismal name David, which he spelled Davida after the open syllables of his language. His second wife, Pahia, who took the Christian name Bathsheba, died childless in 1845. With his third wife, Lepeka, or Rebecca, he had one daughter, named Aʻalailoa after his first wife and given the Christian name Emma; she later married John M. Kapena.

Malo was Richards's teacher of Hawaiian and worked with him on a translation of the book of Matthew. All his writing, from genealogies (moʻokūʻauhau) and laments (kanikau) to letters, was in Hawaiian. His kanikau for Kaʻahumanu, who died in June 1832, is regarded as one of the most beautiful and complex of the 19th century and was printed several times in Hawaiian-language newspapers; he wrote laments for other women in his life as well. A history of Kamehameha I that he wrote was lost.

From about 1835 he worked with members of the Lahainaluna School and the instructor Sheldon Dibble on notes on Hawaiian religion and cultural history, and the class published its findings as Ka Mooolelo Hawaii in 1838. In 1841 he helped Samuel Kamakau form the first Hawaiian Historical Society. His own Ka Moʻolelo Hawaiʻi gained further stories in a second Hawaiian edition of 1858, and Nathaniel Bright Emerson's English translation of 1898 was reissued in 1951 and 1987.

Ordained at Kēōkea on Maui in 1852, Malo supervised the building of Kilolani Church that year and settled in the seaside village of Kalepolepo, where he died on 25 October 1853. He is buried above the Lahainaluna School, which named its boys' dormitory after him and celebrates his work each April. In 2017 Jeffrey Lyon found an anonymous unfinished translation of his history in the Bishop Museum archives; it became the basis of a bilingual edition with Charles Langlas, The Moʻolelo Hawaii of Davida Malo, published in 2020.
david-moore-robinson: David Moore Robinson was born on 21 September 1880 in Auburn, New York, and earned his A.B. in 1898 and his Ph.D. in 1904 at the University of Chicago, with a dissertation titled Ancient Sinopea. He taught at Johns Hopkins University from 1905 to 1947. Besides Olynthus, the ancient city whose discovery is credited to him, he took part in excavations at Corinth in 1902, Sardis in 1910 and Pisidian Antioch in 1924.

He is credited with training 75 Ph.D. and 41 M.A. recipients, among them George M. A. Hanfmann, George E. Mylonas, James Walter Graham, Helen Henrietta Tanzer, William Andrew McDonald and Mary Ross Ellingson. He was elected to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences in 1934 and the American Philosophical Society in 1936, and King Paul of Greece awarded him the Cross of the Royal Order of the Phoenix in 1957.

Robinson published the finds from Olynthus in the 14-volume series Excavations at Olynthus, which appeared from 1929 to 1952 in the Johns Hopkins University studies in archaeology, partly with George E. Mylonas, and most of which he wrote himself. It has since been proved that he plagiarised the work of his student Mary Ross Ellingson, whose master's thesis and doctoral dissertation he published as his own in volumes VII and XIV, and he has been accused of plagiarising at least three other students. His other books include Sappho and Her Influence on Ancient and Modern Literature (1924) and catalogues of Greek vases in the Royal Ontario Museum and in his own collection.

His retirement from Johns Hopkins came with a falling out with the university, and he moved to the Department of Classics at the University of Mississippi in Oxford, where he died on 2 January 1958. Many of the ancient objects he had collected were given to that university and form the David M. Robinson Memorial Collection of Greek and Roman Antiquities, while his papyri and manuscripts went by his will to his colleague William Hailey Willis.
david-ochterlony: David Ochterlony was born in Boston, Massachusetts, on 12 February 1758, the eldest son of Captain David Ochterlony, of an old Forfarshire family, and Katherine Tyler, a niece of Sir William Pepperrell. He attended the Boston Latin School and Dummer Charity School. After his father died on Saint Vincent in the West Indies in 1765, his mother moved to England and married Sir Isaac Heard, Garter King-of-Arms. In 1777, aged 18, Ochterlony went to India as a cadet.

Commissioned into the Bengal Native Infantry in 1778, he was wounded and captured by the forces of Haidar Ali in the Second Anglo-Mysore War in June 1782 and held until peace in 1784. In the Second Anglo-Maratha War he served under Lord Lake at Koil, Aligarh and Delhi, and after the battle of Delhi became Resident there. In 1804 he defended the city with a very inadequate force against Yashwantrao Holkar, and he was made major-general in 1814.

In the Anglo-Nepalese War his column was regarded as the only truly successful one, and his flank march through the Kourea Ghat Pass outmanoeuvred the Gurkhas. He was made a baronet in November 1815 and Knight Grand Cross of the Bath in December 1816. In the Pindari War of 1818-1819 he detached Amir Khan from the Pindaris and then, placing his force between the enemy's two main divisions, brought the war to an end without an engagement. As Resident in Rajpootana and then in Malwa he came to oversee the affairs of central India.

In 1825 Ochterlony, on his own authority, backed the infant Raja Balwant Singh of Bharatpur against Durjan Sal and sent troops. Lord Amherst repudiated the move, and Ochterlony resigned in bitterness and died at Meerut in July 1825; he was buried in St. John's Church there. At Delhi he had embraced Mughal culture and was reputed to have thirteen Indian wives or concubines. The best known, Mubarak Begum, inherited the garden tomb of Mubarak Bagh that he had built in the north of Old Delhi.
david-of-burgundy: David was bishop of Thérouanne from 1451. Through a joint effort of the Cod faction and Burgundy, the pope appointed him bishop of Utrecht, although the Utrecht chapters had elected the provost Gijsbrecht van Brederode, favoured by the Hook party. Philip the Good forced the Nedersticht to accept David by the treaty of IJsselstein on 3 August 1456, and the Oversticht also had to be compelled: Deventer held out for five weeks of siege before it surrendered. As bishop he was also the sovereign ruler of the Prince-Bishopric of Utrecht.

Facing continued opposition, David left Utrecht in 1459 for the newly acquired Wijk bij Duurstede, where he lived from then on. With Burgundian backing his authority grew, helped by the creation of the Schive, a central court of appeal standing above city law. The capture of Gijsbrecht van Brederode and his brother Reinoud in 1470 led to the First Utrecht Civil War of 1470-74, which David won. He then appointed the schout, took criminal jurisdiction from the city council, controlled the tolls and reduced the city's influence over the countryside.

The death of his half-brother Charles the Bold in 1477 changed his position. In 1481 supporters of the Hook party rose against him and he was captured, and Maximilian I had to intervene to free him. David retook Utrecht at the Battle of Westbroek but was driven out again, and the revolt ended with the Siege of Utrecht in 1483.

His last years were spent restoring finances ruined by the civil war and balancing the influence of the Habsburgs, who by then held Holland and Guelders. A lover of art, he drew artists to his court, gave a strong impulse to the building of the Dom Church in Utrecht, modernised Duurstede Castle and built the large church at Wijk bij Duurstede, where he was buried. His cope is kept in the Museum Catharijneconvent. He is the third longest-serving bishop of Utrecht, after Balderic and Willibrord.
david-of-trebizond: David Megas Komnenos, sometimes numbered David II, was the third son of Emperor Alexios IV of Trebizond and Theodora Kantakouzene. Throughout the reign of his older brother John IV he held the courtly title of despotes, which in Trebizond marked the heir to the throne. He took part in John's expeditions against the Genoese and carried out diplomatic tasks. In 1458 he ratified his brother's treaty with the Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II at Adrianople.

David took the throne shortly after John's death. John had named his nephew Alexios V as heir, but Alexios was a minor, and according to Laonikos Chalkokondyles David, backed by the Kabasitanoi archontes, pushed him aside. John had spent his last years building alliances with the Georgian princes and Uzun Hassan, and David seems to have counted on them. Michael Alighieri, who said he was David's envoy, negotiated a treaty with Florence that gave the city a consulate and a 2% levy on exports, as the Genoese and Venetians enjoyed.

Before Western support was firm, David asked Mehmed to remit the tribute paid by his predecessor, using the envoys of Uzun Hassan, who made arrogant demands of their own. Mehmed sent a fleet along the Black Sea coast and led an army east, taking Sinope. When Uzun Hassan's mother, Sara Khatun, made peace with the Sultan, Trebizond lost its strongest ally. The fleet reached the city in early July 1461 and besieged it for over a month.
