His protovestiarios George Amiroutzes advised David to sue for peace, and David surrendered on 15 August 1461, on condition that he keep his family, household and wealth, with the promise of a profitable retirement in Thrace.

David was settled at Adrianople with estates in the Struma valley, but Mehmed saw him as a possible rallying point for Greek resistance. Letters said to be from his niece Theodora, asking that one of his sons or his nephew Alexios be sent to her, gave the excuse; Theodore Spandounes claims they were forged on the Sultan's orders. David, his three sons and Alexios were imprisoned on 26 March 1463 and executed with the sword on 1 November 1463 in Constantinople. His surrender marks the end of the Empire of Trebizond and of the Byzantine imperial tradition. In July 2013 David, his sons and his nephew were canonised by the Holy Synod of the Patriarchate of Constantinople, with a feast day on 1 November.
david-ricardo: David Ricardo was born in London on 18 April 1772, the third surviving of the 17 children of the stockbroker Abraham Israel Ricardo. The family were Sephardic Jews of Portuguese origin who had recently moved from the Dutch Republic. He began working with his father at 14. At 21 he eloped with a Quaker, Priscilla Anne Wilkinson, and converted to Unitarianism against his father's wishes, and his father disowned him.

He made his fortune financing government borrowing. A popular story that he profited from the Battle of Waterloo is not supported: he was already very rich, and in June 1815 he sold his government stock before the result was known in London. He later bought Gatcombe Park in Gloucestershire.

Ricardo wrote his first economics article at 37 and published The High Price of Bullion in 1810. His Principles of Political Economy and Taxation (1817) concluded that land rent grows as population increases. He tried to repair what he saw as problems in Adam Smith's labour theory of value, holding that with three factors of production, land, labour and capital, no single one could determine value alone. In his theory of profit, rising real wages lower real profits.

Against mercantilism, which treated trade as a way to gain gold or silver, he argued that industry specialisation and free trade always produce positive results, even when one country is more efficient in every product. The term comparative advantage was introduced later by John Stuart Mill and his contemporaries. In 1821 Ricardo also wrote that machinery was often injurious to the labouring class.

In 1818 Ricardo bought a seat in Parliament for £4,000 as part of a loan, and as member for Portarlington voted for free trade, parliamentary reform and criminal law reform. He opposed the Corn Laws, which he thought raised rents and directed profits to landlords. He died on 11 September 1823, aged 51, of an ear infection that spread to the brain.

Early socialists such as Thomas Hodgskin drew radical conclusions from his value theory, Henry George drew on his concept of rent, and Piero Sraffa edited his works. Parliament repealed the Corn Laws in 1846.
david-roentgen: David Roentgen was born at Herrnhaag in 1743. In 1753 his father, Abraham Roentgen, who had trained in London in the workshop of William Gomm, moved to the Moravian settlement at Neuwied near Coblenz and set up a furniture factory there. David learned the trade in his father's workshop, inherited the business in 1772 and went into partnership with the clockmaker Kintzing; by then the firm was known even in France.

Paris was the style centre of Europe, so Roentgen opened a showroom there, though his furniture was still made in Neuwied. The guild of the maîtres ébénistes disputed his right to sell foreign furniture until, in 1780, a new kind of marquetry, intricate wood inlay giving the effect of pietra dura instead of burnt or engraved veneer, won him admission. Marie Antoinette appointed him ébéniste-mechanicien and had him carry presents and dolls in the latest fashions on his travels. Louis XVI paid him 80,000 livres for a desk 3.4 m high with a musical clock by his partner; it disappeared under Napoleon.

He travelled about Europe with vans of his factory's furniture and kept shops in Berlin and Saint Petersburg. Empress Catherine bought furniture invoiced at 20,000 roubles and added 5000 roubles and a gold snuff-box for the quick fulfilment of a further request, and to her secretaire he fitted a clock marking the date of the Russian navy's victory over the Turks at Chesma. Frederick William II of Prussia made him a Commerzienrat in 1792, and Goethe compared a fairy's box to one of his desks in Wilhelm Meister's Apprenticeship.

In 1793 the revolutionary government declared him an émigré and seized his showroom stock and belongings, and five years later the French invasion closed the Neuwied factory. He died half ruined at Wiesbaden on 12 February 1807. The Encyclopædia Britannica of 1911 judged his forms often clumsy and his bronzes poor, but gave him high distinction as an inlayer and a deviser of mechanism. The most complete private collection belongs to the ducal house of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha, at Callenberg Castle in Coburg, and he is well represented at the V&A Museum in London.
david-soslan: David belonged to the royal house of Alania, called Ovseti or Oseti in the Georgian sources, an Orthodox Christian kingdom in the North Caucasus that often intermarried with the Bagrationi dynasty of Georgia. His second name, Soslan, is the first known use of it as a personal name and comes from Soslan, one of the leading figures of the Ossetian Nart epics.

His ancestry is uncertain. An anonymous chronicler writing under his son George IV Lasha gave him Bagratid descent, and the 18th-century scholar Prince Vakhushti of Kartli traced him to George I of Georgia and named his father Jadaron, an account Mariam Lordkipanidze and Cyril Toumanoff consider credible. In 1946 the archaeologist Evgeniya Pchelina announced the discovery of his supposed tomb in the Nuzal chapel in the Ardon Gorge, a claim most scholars have not accepted.

Tamar married David at the Didube Palace near Tbilisi after divorcing her first husband, the Rus' prince Yury Bogolyubsky. The Armenian chronicler Mkhitar Gosh wrote that she married a relative on her mother's side from the Alan kingdom, named David on his accession. Unlike Yury, who had been the candidate of a powerful party of nobles, David was Tamar's own choice, and he helped defeat the rebellious nobles who rallied behind Yury. Their son George was born in 1192 and their daughter Rusudan, who later succeeded her brother, in 1194.

David appeared in art, on charters and on coins, but he remained a subordinate ruler whose power derived from his wife. He supported her expansionist policy, and in the 1190s led raids against Barda, Erzurum, Geghark'unik', Beylaqan and Ganja. His victories over the Ildegizids at Shamkor in 1195 and over the Seljuqids of Rüm at Basian in 1202 secured Georgia's positions in the eastern and western Caucasian marches.

He died shortly after these campaigns. Medieval Georgian sources praise his handsomeness, military talents, valour and devotion to Tamar. The theory linking him to the Tsarazon, a heroic clan of Nuzal known from Ossetian oral tradition, remains popular among Ossetian historians.
david-toro: José David Toro Ruilova became a major in 1925 and was known for tactical skill and shrewd political instincts. A close associate of General Hans Kundt and President Hernando Siles, he served Siles as minister of development and minister of government in 1930. After Siles resigned in a bid to extend his term, Toro led the cabinet as the sole executive authority, until the ministers were overthrown in the 1930 coup and he went into exile. He later served as military attaché in Argentina and returned to the general staff in the Chaco War, where his decisions in a conflict Bolivia lost were controversial.

Installed in the Palacio Quemado as head of a government junta, Toro faced a large deficit left by the war and the dislocation of the Great Depression. In March 1937 his government nationalised all Standard Oil holdings in Bolivia, accused of irregularities that allegedly included smuggling Bolivian oil to Argentina during the war; the move came a year before the Mexican oil expropriation under Lázaro Cárdenas. It marked the beginning of the end of the Oligarchic Republic that had lasted since 1880.

Toro and the young officers who put him in power called their experiment Military Socialism, but, fearing the economic elites, they did not go as far as reformers wished. His government decreed pay raises, price controls and State Food Stores, a minimum wage, obligatory unionisation of miners, craftsmen and factory workers, and a Secretariat of Peasant Affairs that helped form the country's first legally recognised agricultural workers' union. Caught between reformers on the left and the interests of a mining magnate, he resigned on 13 July 1937.

A year after his fall Toro tried to oust Busch in a coup, failed and went into exile in Chile, where he died on 25 July 1977 at the age of 79. One observer described him as one of the most astute political figures of his day but a pragmatic politician without fixed ideological commitment, who followed rather than led, yet whose regime set the tone for the whole period of military socialist rule.
david-vi-narin: David, of the Bagrationi dynasty, was the son of Queen Rusudan of Georgia and her Seljuk husband, Ghias ad-din. Fearing that her nephew David would claim the throne at her death, Rusudan kept him prisoner at the court of her son-in-law, the Seljuk sultan Kaykhusraw II, and in 1243 sent her own son to the Mongol court to be recognised as heir. She died in 1245 still waiting for his return. Believing him lost, the Georgian nobles proclaimed his cousin, freed on Kaykhusraw's death, as king. In August 1246 both cousins attended the enthronement of Güyük Khan, who recognised Rusudan's son as junior co-king. They became known as David VI Narin, the junior, and David VII Ulu, the senior.

In 1259 David VI rose against the Mongol yoke without drawing his cousin in. The Ilkhanate crushed the revolt in a few short, bloody battles, and David fled to Kutaisi, declared the lands west of the Likhi mountains independent and was proclaimed king of western Georgia by the local nobility. His kingdom took in the duchies of Guria, Mingrelia and Abkhazia, with the ports of Batumi and Poti, and Svaneti and Racha in the mountains. Its trade with the West through Genoese merchants in Abkhazia and the Empire of Trebizond drew many nobles and merchants from eastern Georgia.

He sheltered David VII after his own revolt in 1261, but they could not work together, and in 1262 David VII returned to Tbilisi and submitted to Hulegu Khan; both continued to call themselves king of Georgia. David VI kept friendly relations with the Golden Horde and the Bahri dynasty of Egypt and held off Abaqa Khan's expeditions of the 1270s. In April 1282, while Emperor John II Comnenus was in Constantinople, he invaded the Empire of Trebizond, failing to take the city but occupying several provinces, and in 1284 he helped Theodora seize its crown for a few months.

David VI died at Kutaisi in 1293 and was buried in the chapel of St Andrew at the Cathedral of the Nativity of the Theotokos at Gelati. He was succeeded by his son Constantine I; another son, Michael, later reigned in western Georgia too.
david-vii-ulu: David was the son of King George IV of the Bagrationi dynasty and a woman of non-noble birth, and the Georgian nobility regarded him as illegitimate, so on George's death in 1223 the throne passed to his sister Rusudan. After Georgia became a Mongol vassal in 1236, Rusudan, fearing his claim, sent him into captivity at the court of her son-in-law, Sultan Kaykhusraw II of Rum. He was released after the Battle of Köse Dağ in 1243, when the Mongols subdued the sultanate.

When Rusudan died in 1245 while her son David was at the Mongol court, part of the nobility, believing him dead, proclaimed David Ulu king. In 1246 both Davids attended the enthronement of Güyük Khan at Karakorum. The Mongols divided the nobles into two parties and named David VII the senior ruler, ulu, and his cousin the junior, narin; Baiju Noyan and Batu Khan backed David Ulu. Georgian and Armenian troops served in the Mongol conquests of Alamut in 1256, which David Ulu led in person, and of Baghdad in 1258, and Georgia lost tens of thousands of soldiers in these campaigns.

In 1260, when Hulegu Khan called for Georgian troops for the Levant, David Ulu rebelled. A Mongol army under Arghun Aqa defeated him and Sargis I Jaqeli near Akhaldaba and plundered the country; the king fled to Imereti, and his wife Gvantsa was killed. Peace came in 1262, when he returned to Tbilisi as Hulegu's vassal. His troops fought for the Ilkhanate against the Golden Horde, defending the Siba fortress in 1263 and driving Berke's forces out of Shirvan in 1265. In 1266 the new ilkhan, Abaqa Khan, took Sargis Jaqeli, prince of Samtkhe, under his protection, raising him to David's rank and leaving Georgia divided into three.

In 1270 David led Georgian and Armenian troops for Abaqa against Tekuder, who had taken refuge in western Georgia. He died of a bowel infection that spring, aged 55, and was buried at Mtskheta. He married four times, to the Mongol Jigda-Khatun, the Alan Altun, Gvantsa of Racha and Esukan, daughter of the Mongol general Chormaqan, and was succeeded by his son with Gvantsa, Demetrius II.
davit-bek: Little is known about Davit's early life. Most of what is known about him comes from the History of the Kapanians, written in the mid-18th century by the Mekhitarist monk Ghukas Sebastatsi from the accounts of Stepanos Shahumyan of Meghri and other participants in the rebellion. Most 18th-century manuscripts call him a Georgian Armenian from Mtskheta, though Armenians of Tiflis were then often called Mtskhetians, and a colophon written at Astrakhan in 1746 names him the son of Alikhan. He was an officer of Vakhtang VI, vali and king of Kartli.

With the Safavid state collapsing in 1722 and Peter the Great advancing in the Russo-Persian War of 1722–1723, the Armenian meliks of Kapan and Artsakh asked Vakhtang for military aid. He sent Davit with some 2,000 Armenian soldiers. Davit made the fort of Halidzor his base and, supported by peasants and meliks, defended the Armenian districts from Muslim tribes, while also fighting meliks who opposed the rising. In the spring of 1724 a force of 2,000 from Karabakh under Avan Yuzbashi and Ivan Karapet joined him in Kapan.

When the Ottomans invaded Iran and Eastern Armenia in 1724, taking Tiflis, Yerevan and Hamadan, the Armenians allied with the Iranians against them. After his victory over a larger Ottoman army at Halidzor, Davit's forces drove the Turks from Kapan and captured the Ottoman-controlled Meghri Fortress. Tahmasp II of Iran then made him governor of a vassal Armenian principality, and Davit campaigned against the Ottomans at Ordubad and Agulis.

The circumstances of his death in 1728 are uncertain: some scholars believe he died fighting the Turks, others attribute it to illness. Command of the Armenian forces in Syunik passed to his comrade-in-arms Mkhitar Sparapet. Davit Bek later inspired the historical novel David Bek by Raffi in 1882, a film by Hamo Beknazarian in 1944, the opera David Bek by Armen Tigranian, first performed in 1950, and the 1978 film Star of Hope by Edmond Keosayan.
davos: Davos lies on the Landwasser river in the Rhaetian Alps, between the Plessur and Albula Ranges. The municipality covers nearly the whole valley of the Landwasser and its side valleys, an area of 284 square kilometres. Its centre is two adjacent villages, Davos Dorf and Davos Platz, 1,560 metres above sea level, just below the Wolfgang Pass, which carries a road and a Rhaetian Railway line towards Klosters and the Prättigau. The name is first recorded in the 13th century as Tavaus and may derive from a word for a ravine.

Rhaeto-Romans settled the area in the High Middle Ages. Davos is first mentioned in 1213. From about 1280 the barons of Vaz allowed German-speaking Walser colonists to settle and gave them extensive self-administration rights; an agreement of 1289 freed the people of Davos from personal taxes. Davos became the largest Walser settlement area in eastern Switzerland, and natives still speak a dialect atypical for Grisons. After the last baron of Vaz died in 1338, Davos passed to the Count of Toggenburg, and later to the Counts of Montfort, who sold it to Duke Sigmund of Tyrol in 1466.

In 1436 the League of the Ten Jurisdictions was founded in Davos. An agreement of 1438 confirmed its rights, and in 1450 the League allied with the League of God's House. Davos made a treaty with the Grey League in 1471 and refused to follow Austrian orders, and a compromise placed it under the House of Matsch, with Austria keeping a right to repurchase it.

From the middle of the 19th century Davos became a health resort. Doctors, among them Alexander Spengler, judged the microclimate of the high valley excellent for lung disease patients. Robert Louis Stevenson wintered there in 1880, and a Davos sanatorium inspired the Berghof in Thomas Mann's novel The Magic Mountain. The painter Ernst Ludwig Kirchner lived there from 1917. The sanatoria attracted many German patients, and during the Second World War Davos was a centre of Nazi activity in Switzerland. It was also a centre of speed skating and later a ski resort.

Davos has a permanent population of 10,832 (2020), most of whom speak German. It is a tourist community and regional centre with one of Switzerland's largest ski resorts. HC Davos hosts the Spengler Cup, an international ice hockey tournament first held in 1923. Since 1971 the town has hosted the annual meeting of the World Economic Forum. Seven of its sites are listed as Swiss heritage sites of national significance, among them the Kirchner Museum.
dawachi: Dawachi belonged to the highest rank of the Dzungar aristocracy and traced his descent directly to Erdeni Batur (died 1635), the founder of the Dzungar Khanate. His father was a second cousin of Galdan Tseren, Khong Tayiji of the Dzungars from 1727 to 1745. As a noyon Dawachi roamed with his nomadic camps in Tarbagatai and the Mongolian Altai and had over 30,000 people under his rule.

Galdan Tseren's reign had restored much of the khanate's political, military and economic influence in Central Asia, but after his death in 1745 his three sons fought over the succession, and the anarchy that followed undid most of those gains. Lama Dorji seized the throne in 1750 after killing his brother Tsewang Dorji Namjal. Dawachi and his Khoit-Oirat ally Amursana opposed him, and in 1751 a pre-emptive strike by Lama Dorji forced Dawachi to flee into the territory of the Kazakh Khanate.

After the death of Lama Dorji, Dawachi claimed the title of taisha on the strength of his lineage. Amursana, a prince of simpler descent and of Khoit rather than Dzungar origin, had married a daughter of Ablai Khan, leader of the Kazakh Khanate, and won the backing of several Oirat clan leaders, and he demanded that the khanate's lands be divided between them, as he said he had been promised. Dawachi refused and attacked him in 1754. Amursana fled east to Khovd and swore allegiance to the Qianlong Emperor, and most of the Khoshut followed him to the Qing.

In late 1754 and early 1755 the Qianlong Emperor ordered a final advance on Ili, mobilising about 200,000 soldiers, many of them Khalkha Mongols. The army under General Ban Di left Uliastai in March 1755 and reached Bortala in June. Dawachi's men deserted in large numbers on learning that Amursana was with the enemy, and an embassy led by his son, offering vassalage, went unanswered.

Driven south-west to the Gedeng Mountains by a Qing army under Zhaohui, Dawachi made a last stand with 10,000 men and was routed. He was captured by Hakim Beg Khojis, the Muslim governor of Us-Turfan, and sent on to Beijing. The Qianlong Emperor treated him with leniency, granting him a princely title and allowing him to marry a princess of the imperial family. Dawachi died in 1759 from excessive drinking.
dawda-jawara: Dawda Kairaba Jawara was born on 16 May 1924 at Barajally in the central river region of The Gambia, the son of Almammi Jawara, a well-to-do trader from an aristocratic family, and Mamma Fatty. As a child he attended local Arabic schools to memorise the Quran. He was later educated at the Methodist Boys' School in Banjul and at Achimota College in the Gold Coast, and trained as a veterinary surgeon at Glasgow, Liverpool and Edinburgh.

He returned in 1953 as a veterinary officer. Travelling the country to vaccinate cattle, he made contacts among cattle owners, district chiefs and village heads, who later formed the bulk of his early political support. Adults in the colony area around Bathurst had the vote, but those in the protectorate did not. In 1959 the People's Progressive Society changed its name to challenge the urban-based parties, and Jawara became secretary of the party and was elected to the House of Representatives in 1960.

After the elections of 1962 Jawara became prime minister, self-government followed in 1963 and independence came on 18 February 1965, with Elizabeth II remaining head of state. In 1970 The Gambia became a republic and he was elected its first president. On 29 July 1981 an attempted coup led by Kukoi Samba Sanyang was defeated with the help of Senegalese troops, whom Jawara had asked for aid; several hundred people were killed. In December 1981 treaties in Dakar created the Senegambian Confederation, with Abdou Diouf as president and Jawara as vice-president; it collapsed in 1989.

In 1985 his government began the Economic Recovery Program, an adjustment programme drawn up with economists from the Harvard Institute for International Development and the International Monetary Fund. In December 1991 he announced that he would not seek re-election in 1992, but after the announcement was met with panic he agreed to stand again and won 56% of the vote.

On 22 July 1994 soldiers led by Lieutenant Yahya Jammeh took the capital. Jawara was taken to Senegal by an American warship and lived in exile until 2002, and the new ruling council dissolved the constitution. He returned as an elder statesman but was forbidden to take part in politics, and he died on 27 August 2019. His portrait appeared on Gambian dalasi banknotes and coins from 1971 to 1994. He was knighted in the 1966 New Year Honours and was the last living Gambian to have received a knighthood under the monarchy.
dawit-i: Dawit was a younger son of Emperor Newaya Krestos, whose throne name was Sayfa Ar'ad, and of Lazzab Warqa, and was never meant to reign. When their father died in 1372 the throne passed to his elder brother Newaya Maryam. According to the History of the Patriarchs of the Egyptian Church, Dawit took the throne with the help of his sister Dil Sefa, under the throne name Qwestantinos. The irregular succession was criticised in monastic circles, especially at Asbo under its abbot Tewodros, while the abbot of Debre Hayq Estifanos supported him and was rewarded with land.

No royal chronicle covers his years, which are known from saints' lives, land grants and later sources; historians see them as a time of consolidation. Early in his reign he led troops beyond his northern frontier to defend the Copts of Upper Egypt, until the Patriarch of Alexandria, Matthew I, was made to persuade him to withdraw. According to al-Maqrizi he later sent 22 camels laden with gifts to Berkuk, the first Burji Mamluk sultan, among them an enslaved eunuch, Jawhar al-Qunuqba'i, who became a treasury official in Cairo.

Against Ifat he set up royal camps at Tobya and Tilq and garrisoned Bali, Dawaro and Hadiya. The date and place of Sa'ad ad-Din's death are disputed; Amélie Chekroun placed it within Dawit's reign in 2020, using Yemeni Rasulid records of the arrival of the sultan's sons at Ta'izz. An embassy of his had reached Venice by 23 June 1402, asking for artisans. In 1400 he had Abba Filipos of the Ewostathian movement, which kept both Saturday and Sunday as Sabbaths, imprisoned at Debre Hayq; in 1404, advised by Giyorgis of Sagla, he freed him and allowed the Saturday Sabbath in their monasteries.

A noted horseman, he was killed when his horse kicked him in the head; the traveller James Bruce said the mark was still visible on his skull. His body was later moved by Zara Yaqob to Debre Nagwadgwad and then to the monastery of Daga Estifanos on Lake Tana. His son Tewodros I succeeded him. Dawit encouraged missionary work in Gojjam and endowed the church with lands; his translation of the Miracles of Mary is the oldest surviving illustrated book commissioned by an Ethiopian emperor.
dawit-ii: Dawit was the son of Emperor Na'od and Empress Na'od Mogesa and a male-line descendant of the medieval Amhara kings, which made him a member of the House of Solomon. His political centre and palace were in Shewa. He is better known by his birth name Lebna Dengel, and he also bore the macaronic name Wanag Segad, perhaps after a victory over Emir Mahfuz of Adal.

In contrast to earlier emperors he had only one wife, Seble Wongel, whom he married around 1512-13. They had eight children, four sons and four daughters. The Empress Mother Eleni, though in her seventies, acted as regent until he came of age in 1516. She sent the Armenian Mateus to Portugal to ask for help against the Muslim states, which she knew were assisted by larger Muslim powers such as the Ottoman Empire.

In 1516 the monk Gebre Andrias killed Emir Mahfuz of Adal at the Battle of Fatagar, and Dawit then ravaged Adal. Contemporaries concluded that the Muslim threat was over. A Portuguese embassy led by Dom Rodrigo de Lima reached Massawa on 9 April 1520 and Dawit's camp on 19 October. Dawit denied that Mateus had authority to negotiate treaties, against Eleni's advice, and the Portuguese left after a stay of six years.

After the death of Sultan Abu Bakr ibn Muhammad in 1520, the imam Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi took control of the Adal Sultanate. Dawit had bought only two swivel-guns from the Portuguese and fourteen muskets from the Turks, and so was ill equipped against an invasion that used thousands of firearms. The two armies fought at Shimbra Kure in March 1529 without a clear result. In 1531 Ahmad fired the first cannon in the Horn of Africa and scattered the army of the general Eslamu. He surprised the emperor at Amba Sel on 27 October, and Dawit was almost captured. The invaders then poured into Bet Amhara, pillaging churches, and Dawit withdrew behind the Abay River to Gojjam.

Dawit's eldest son Fiqtor was killed on 7 April 1537, and another son, Menas, was captured on 19 May 1539 and sent to Yemen. Dawit sent João Bermudes to Lisbon to ask for military help, and King John III of Portugal promised ships and four to five hundred soldiers. In 1539 Ahmad asked for Dawit's daughter in marriage and Dawit refused. He then wandered for months, pursued by Ahmad's troops, before he died of sickness on 2 September 1540.

His son Gelawdewos succeeded him. A younger son, Yaqob, is said to have hidden in Menz in Shewa, and Yaqob's grandson Susenyos I became emperor in 1604 and began the Gondar line of the Solomonic dynasty. The Ethiopian Church commemorates Dawit as a saint.
dawud-pasha: Dawud Pasha was born Davit Manvelashvili in Tbilisi, of Georgian origin. In his time Ottoman Iraq was nominally part of the Ottoman Empire but in practice largely autonomous. Mamluks were originally freed slaves who had converted to Islam and were assigned military and administrative duties, and Mamluk rulers governed the territory that became Iraq from 1704 to 1831, gaining increasing autonomy from the Sultan in Constantinople. In 1749 the Sultan extended the authority of the Mamluk governor of Basra to include the province of Baghdad, which began a period of Mamluk rule that lasted until 1831.

After seizing control of Baghdad Eyalet around 1816 to 1817, Dawud Pasha began modernisation programmes that included clearing canals, establishing industries and reforming the army with the help of European instructors. His political and economic policies united the provinces, although their external borders remained ill-defined. Britain had recognised the strategic importance of the Middle East after Napoleon's invasion of Egypt and had negotiated the establishment of a British consulate in Baghdad. Dawud Pasha reduced the influence of the British consul and compelled the British East India Company to begin paying duties on imported goods. Under his rule the Baghdadi Jews were persecuted, and many leading families, such as the Sassoon and Judah families, fled to India.

He is said to have established the first newspaper of Iraq, Jurnal al-Iraq, in Baghdad in 1816, but this is disputed, because no copies survive and neither the Ottoman archives nor travellers of the time mention it.

At the instigation of the British government, according to the account, the Sultan moved to seize back control of Baghdad. In 1830 Mahmud II decreed Dawud Pasha's dismissal, and in the following year an army under Ali Ridha Pasha ousted him and reimposed direct Ottoman rule on Iraq. He lived until 1851, and at the end of his life he was a custodian of the shrine at Medina, the burial place of the Prophet Muhammad.
day-o: The song is a call and response work song sung from the point of view of dock workers on the night shift. Its words tell how daylight has come, the shift is over, and the workers want their bananas counted so that they can go home. Belafonte's album Calypso also carried a shorter reprise, Star O, in which the day shift ends when the first star is seen in the sky. The first recording was made by the Trinidadian singer Edric Connor and his band the Caribbeans, as Day Dah Light, on the 1952 album Songs from Jamaica. Louise Bennett recorded it in 1954.

In 1955 the American songwriters Lord Burgess and William Attaway wrote a version of the lyrics for The Colgate Comedy Hour, where Harry Belafonte performed it. Belafonte based his version on the recordings of Connor and Bennett, and recorded it for RCA Victor; it came out in 1956 on his album Calypso and as a single, reached number five on the Billboard charts in 1957 and became his signature song.

Also in 1956 the folk singer Bob Gibson, who had heard the song in Jamaica, taught his version to the folk band the Tarriers, whose recording added the chorus of another Jamaican folk song, Hill and Gully Rider. It became their biggest hit and was covered by the Fontane Sisters, Sarah Vaughan and Steve Lawrence, and in 1957 by Shirley Bassey, whose recording was her first single to chart in the United Kingdom.

In a 2011 interview with Gwen Ifill on PBS News Hour, Belafonte called it "a song about struggle, about black people in a colonized life doing the most grueling work," which he had honed into an anthem that the world loved. Stan Freberg and Billy May released a parody in 1957 that reached number 25 in the United States, and Belafonte reportedly disliked it.

Freddie Mercury of Queen drew his call and response at Live Aid in 1985 from the opening of the song, and its chorus is used in many Major League Baseball stadiums to draw answers from the crowd. The 1956 Belafonte recording is heard in a dinner scene of the 1988 film Beetlejuice, and Lil Wayne's 2010 song 6 Foot 7 Foot takes its title from it.
dayak-people: Dayak is a loose term for more than 200 Austronesian ethnic groups native to Borneo, found chiefly in the central and southern interior, often in highlands or near rivers. Each has its own dialect, customs, laws and territory. The name is commonly thought to come from a Bruneian and Melanau word for interior people, related to a Kenyah word for upstream. Dutch and German writers used it for any non-Muslim native of Borneo, so the difference between Dayak and non-Dayak natives could be understood as a religious one. James Brooke wished to use it only for the Land Dayaks, or Bidayuh, and the Sea Dayaks, or Iban.

In the early 1900s educated people from these groups, such as Hausman Baboe, adopted the name as a unifying term in Kalimantan. In 1954 Tjilik Riwut sorted the groups into 18 tribes and 403 sub-tribes.

Dayak languages belong to several subgroups of the Malayo-Polynesian family, including Land Dayak, Malayic and Barito, and about 170 languages and dialects are spoken on the island. Historically most Dayaks were swidden cultivators who supplemented their living with forest produce, fishing, hunting and occasional wage labour. In the traditional longhouse, sometimes more than 200 metres long, households had separate apartments and shared areas for cooking, ceremonies and blacksmithing. The people living in it were governed by its customs.

Many groups regard tattoos as sacred and as marks of origin, rank or rites of passage. Beads, including heirloom beads called pesaka, were used in rituals and passed down in families. The short mandau, a machete with an upward protrusion on the handle, could be drawn very quickly, which mattered in headhunting. The indigenous religion of the Dayak, called Kaharingan in Indonesia, is a form of animism in which shamans guide the souls of the dead and heal the sick by retrieving souls.

The Dayaks were once feared for the practice of headhunting, called ngayau. In 1894 the Tumbang Anoi Agreement, a meeting of Dayak groups from all over Kalimantan at Damang Batu, ended the tradition by agreement, since it was held to cause conflict between groups. Headhunting resurfaced in the mid-1940s, when the Allied powers encouraged it against the Japanese occupation, and again in the late 1960s and around the turn of the century in violence involving ethnic Chinese and Madurese settlers.

Since the 19th century many Dayaks have converted to Christianity, brought by missionaries of the Rheinische Missionsgesellschaft and later the Basler Mission, and some groups, such as the Bakumpai, to Islam. Dayak soldiers served with the Sarawak Rangers, whose successor is the present-day Royal Ranger Regiment.
dayan-khan: Dayan Khan was born Batumongke, the son of Bayanmongke, the Bolkhu jinong or crown prince of the Borjigin clan, and Shiker of the Uriyangkhai. His father and his uncle Manduul Khan came to blows, and Bayanmongke fled and was murdered. Manduul's taishi Ismayil took Shiker and her property. To save the child, Shiker gave him to the Bakhay family to nurse, and he was cared for by commoners and minor nobles because of his Borjigin blood. When Manduul Khan died suddenly in 1467, Mandukhai Khatun, his widow, adopted the boy and had him treated for a serious illness.

Mandukhai, a direct descendant of Kublai Khan, had the boy enthroned as khan under the title Dayan, and later married him. She kept great influence over court and army. Together they reunified the eastern Mongols and defeated the Oirats, who had revolted against Borjigin rule since the 14th century. In 1483 they led armies against Ismayil, who fled to Hami and was killed there. By 1495 Batumongke had won the Three Guards, tributaries of the Ming dynasty, and incorporated them into his Six tumens.

His relations with the Ming dynasty broke down after one of his envoys, sent to arrange open trade, was killed at the Ming court. Mongol raids on the borderlands became almost constant. In 1500 the khan and Mandukhai moved to the Eight White Yurts in Ordos and attacked Ningxia. A Ming counterattack the next year nearly captured him, and he withdrew to the Kherlen River, but large raids continued through 1507. In 1517 he moved against Beijing, and the Ming forces of the Zhengde Emperor held him off at the Battle of Yingzhou.

The three Right Wing tumens (Ordos, Tümed and Yöngshiyebü) invited Dayan Khan to rule them. His son Ulusbold was killed in a riot while being enthroned as jinong, and Dayan Khan was first defeated at Turgen Stream. In 1510 he crushed the Right Wing tumens and killed the Ordos elder Mandulai. He enthroned his son Barsubolad as jinong in 1513 and abolished old Yuan titles such as taishi and chingsang.

He organised the eastern Mongols into six tumens, the Left Wing of Khalkha, Chahar and Uriankhai and the Right Wing of Ordos, Tümed and Yöngshiyebü, each serving as both a military unit and a tribal administration. He divided them among his sons, which created a decentralised but stable Borjigin rule for a century. Civil war among Chinggisid princes was unknown until the reign of Ligden Khan (1604-34). Altan Khan and Ligden Khan were among his descendants.
dayfa-khatun: Dayfa Khatun was born in Damascus, a daughter of al-Adil, Sultan of Egypt, in the Kurdish Ayyubid family. In 1212 she was married to her first cousin az-Zahir Ghazi, Emir of Aleppo, who had asked for her hand to end his conflict with al-Adil; the match ended the rivalry between the two branches of the family. The chronicler Ibn Wasil recorded that Ghazi rose and took several steps towards her when she entered. She bore him al-Aziz Muhammad, heir to Aleppo, who succeeded his father in 1216 under the atabek Shihab al-Din Toghril.

When her son died, his heir An-Nasir Yusuf was seven years old. A regency council was formed of Shams ad-Din Lu'lu' al-Amini, Izz ad-Din Umar al-Majalli, the vizier Jamal ad-Din al-Qifti and her own slave Jamal ad-Dawla Iqbal az-Zahiri, who acted as her secretary and deputy. Dayfa did not sit on the council, but every decision needed her approval and her signature; Ibn Wasil wrote that she had the final say on all state affairs.

Her regency coincided with the conflict between her brothers al-Kamil in Egypt and al-Ashraf in Damascus. After al-Ashraf died in 1237, she and other rulers renewed the coalition of the rulers of Syria against al-Kamil under another brother, as-Salih Ismail, but al-Kamil took Damascus and died in March 1238 before he could turn on Aleppo. She then kept Aleppo out of the Ayyubid wars and in 1240 obtained from Sultan as-Salih Ayyub a declaration that he would respect its independence. When a Khwarezmian army of about 12,000 men threatened the city in 1240 and 1241, forces from Homs helped drive it off.

She founded, with her own resources, the Madrasa al-Firdaws, a complex of school, mausoleum and other spaces whose inscription calls her the merciful queen, and the Khanqah al-Farafira, a house for elderly, divorced and widowed women given to Sufism, the only surviving khanqah in Aleppo. Both stood outside the citadel walls. After her death in 1242 Shams al-Din Lu'lu' led the regency until An-Nasir Yusuf began to rule on his own.
daylamites: The Daylamites lived in the highlands of Daylam, part of the Alborz range between Tabaristan and Gilan. They spoke Daylami, a now-extinct Northwestern Iranian language similar to that of their neighbours the Gilites. They first appear in records in the late 2nd century BCE, when Polybius mentions them, though he miscalls them "Elamites". Under the Sasanian Empire they served as high-quality infantry. The Byzantine historian Procopius described them as people who lived on inaccessible mountainsides, had never become subject to the Persian king and marched with the Persians as mercenaries, each man carrying a sword, a shield and three javelins.

The Daylamites resisted the Arab conquest of their homeland for several centuries under their own local rulers, and warfare in the region was endemic, with raids and counter-raids on both sides. The Abbasids occupied parts of Daylam but never controlled it effectively; al-Mansur proclaimed a jihad against it in 759 or 760, and the campaigns brought little but spoils and captives. After 781 the Nestorian monk Shubhalishoʿ began converting them to Christianity but made little headway. During the reign of Harun al-Rashid, Alids fleeing persecution began the gradual conversion of the Daylamites to Shia Islam, and in the 9th century many adopted Zaidi Islam.

From the 9th century Daylamite foot-soldiers became an important part of armies in Iran, and the Abbasids and the Ghaznavids employed them, and they served in the Seljuq army. Between 934 and 936 Ali ibn Buya, known as Imad al-Dawla, led the Daylamite conquest of Fars and Kerman, and his brother Ahmad conquered Khuzestan. In 946 the Buyids took Baghdad from the Hamdanids. When Adud al-Dawla died in 983 he controlled Iraq and parts of the Jazira, and held territories directly or indirectly from Khorasan to the Byzantine frontier in Syria and from Oman to the Caspian. The Seljuk Turks ended Buyid power in the mid-11th century.

The Daylamites were most likely adherents of some form of Iranian paganism, with a minority of Zoroastrians and Nestorian Christians. They fought on foot behind tall shields painted grey, forming a wall and using javelins and battle-axes from behind it; their short two-pronged spears could be thrust or thrown. Their lack of cavalry led the Buyids to add Turkic horsemen to their armies. According to the geographer Estakhri they practised agriculture and kept herds but only a few horses, grew rice, fished and made silk textiles. Daylamite women took part in agriculture like men, and the people strictly practised endogamy. The Zaza, who call themselves Dimli, are considered one of the Daylamite groups that spread westward during the expansion.
dayton-agreement: The basic elements of the settlement had been proposed in international talks as early as 1992, but the negotiations that led to Dayton followed the failure of earlier peace efforts and the Croatian military Operation Storm of August 1995, together with a government offensive against the Republika Srpska conducted alongside NATO's Operation Deliberate Force. In September and October 1995 the Contact Group, above all the United States and Russia, pressed the leaders of the three sides to attend negotiations. A US team led first by Anthony Lake and then by Richard Holbrooke carried out five rounds of shuttle diplomacy from August to October, and the parties adopted principles for a settlement on 8 and 26 September.

The conference was held from 1 to 21 November 1995. The main regional participants were Slobodan Milošević, president of Serbia, whom the Bosnian Serbs had empowered to speak for them, Franjo Tuđman, president of Croatia, and Alija Izetbegović, president of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was led by US Secretary of State Warren Christopher and Holbrooke, with Carl Bildt for the EU and Igor Ivanov for Russia as co-chairmen. The secure site was chosen to take the parties out of their comfort zone, to keep them from negotiating through the media and to house over 800 staff. The agreement was initialled on 21 November and signed ceremonially in Paris on 14 December 1995, with witnesses including Bill Clinton, Jacques Chirac, John Major and Helmut Kohl.

The agreement made Bosnia and Herzegovina a single sovereign state composed of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republika Srpska, a complete state and not a confederation. It retained a central government with a rotating state presidency, a central bank and a constitutional court. The constitution is Annex 4, and a boundary line between the two entities was drawn. Before it, Bosnian Serbs controlled about 46% of the territory, Bosniaks 28% and Bosnian Croats 25%; afterwards the Serb share was 49%, the Bosniak 30% and the Croat 21%. The NATO-led IFOR, deployed on 20 December 1995, handled military implementation, the Office of the High Representative civil implementation, and the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe the first elections in 1996.

Scholars differ on the settlement. Charles-Philippe David calls it the most impressive example of conflict resolution, and it has been praised for establishing lasting peace. Critics, including Patrice McMahon and Jon Western, argue that a decentralised system undermined the authority of the state, and others point to its complex government, its dependence on international actors and its division of Bosnia into three constituent nations and two entities by ethnic identity.
dazexiang-uprising: The rising was the first against the Qin dynasty after the death of Qin Shi Huang, and it is also named after its two leaders, Chen Sheng and Wu Guang. Both were army officers ordered to march their bands of commoner soldiers north to take part in the defence of Yuyang. Flooding from a severe rainstorm stopped them halfway, in what is now Anhui province. Dazexiang, where the revolt began, means Big Swamp Village.

Qin law required execution for anyone who reached a government post late, whatever the cause of the delay. Deciding that they would rather fight than be put to death, Chen and Wu organised a band of 900 villagers against the government. The reigning emperor, Huhai, had killed his benevolent brother Fusu to take the throne, so the rebels rose up in Fusu's name.

Two stories are told of how the leaders won followers. In one, they wrote King Chen Sheng on a piece of silk and hid it in the belly of a fish, which a soldier bought and opened in surprise. In the other, they imitated animal cries to proclaim that Da Chu would flourish under King Chen Sheng.

Once his men declared Chen king of the former Kingdom of Chu, he and Wu became the centre of armed risings across China. Within a few months their strength had grown to around ten thousand men, mostly discontented peasants. Their force was no match for the trained Qin soldiers, however, and in less than a year both leaders were assassinated by their own men.

Although it failed, the rising set the example that Liu Bang and Xiang Yu followed. Its spirit is summed up in a saying attributed to Chen Sheng, rendered as "Are kings and nobles given their high status by birth?", taken to mean that anyone, whatever their birth, can rise high. The main source is Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian, whose chapter 48 is a biography of Chen Sheng. Of Wu Guang, Chen's deputy, little is recorded beyond what that joint biography says.
de-administrando-imperio: Constantine VII, born in 905, became co-emperor in 908 but was too young to rule, and Romanos I Lekapenos took over the imperial government after being crowned co-emperor in December 920. Constantine ruled personally from January 945 until his death in November 959. A scholar-emperor, he gathered a circle of educated men who wrote three unfinished books, De Administrando Imperio, De Ceremoniis and On the Themes, and a biography of his grandfather Basil I.

De Administrando Imperio had at least one anonymous collaborator. Its date is debated: chapters 29 and 45 give dates corresponding to 948/949 and 951/952, while other scholars place its compilation after 952 and before his death. The author never gave it a title; it opens with a salutation to his son.

The work joins two earlier treatises, one on the peoples neighbouring the empire and one on its provinces, to which Constantine added his own instructions for his son Romanos II. According to its preface it has four parts: a key to foreign policy towards the northerners and Scythians, the diplomacy to pursue with them, a survey of the surrounding nations and a summary of recent imperial administration. Chapters 1 to 8 and 10 to 12 explain policy towards the Pechenegs and Turks.

Chapters 12 to 40 hold traditional accounts, mixed with legends, of how the Saracens, Lombards, Venetians, Serbs, Croats, Magyars and Pechenegs came to occupy their lands. Chapters 43 to 46 deal with the north-east, Armenia and Georgia, and chapters 49 to 52 give instructions on taxing new provinces and on civil and naval administration. Its geographic and historical information is often confused and filled with legends, but is in essence reliable. The Greek is plain, since the emperor said he avoided lofty Atticisms.

Four copies survive. Johannes Meursius published the first edition in 1611 and gave it the Latin title by which it is known. Anselmo Banduri produced another in 1711, and Immanuel Bekker one in 1840. The first modern edition, by Gyula Moravcsik, with an English translation by R. J. H. Jenkins, appeared in Budapest in 1949, with commentaries following in 1962. Because it was written as a manual for his successor, it is regarded as one of the most important sources for Byzantium and its neighbours.
de-beers: The name De Beers comes from two Afrikaner brothers, Diederik Arnoldus de Beer and Johannes Nicolaas de Beer, who owned a farm named Vooruitzicht in the Boshof District of the Orange Free State. After diamonds were found on their land they were forced by the increasing demands of the British government to sell it on 31 July 1871 to the merchant Alfred Johnson Ebden for £6,600.

The farm became the site of the Big Hole and the De Beers mine. Cecil Rhodes got his start by renting water pumps to miners during the diamond rush that began in 1869, and invested the profits in buying up the claims of small mining operators. The Rothschild family financed his expansion. De Beers Consolidated Mines was formed in 1888 by merging the companies of Rhodes and the diamond magnate Barney Barnato.

In 1889 Rhodes agreed with the London-based Diamond Syndicate that it would buy a fixed quantity of diamonds at an agreed price, which regulated output and kept prices up; supply was cut during the slump of 1891 to 1892. During the Second Boer War Kimberley was besieged, and Rhodes placed the company's resources at the defenders' disposal, with its workshops making shells, an armoured train and a gun named Long Cecil. When Rhodes died in 1902 De Beers controlled 90 per cent of world diamond production.

The Premier Mine near Pretoria, registered in 1902, yielded the Cullinan Diamond in 1905. Its owner refused to join the cartel and sold through the dealers Bernard and Ernest Oppenheimer, but production was soon absorbed into De Beers. Ernest Oppenheimer joined the board in 1926 and became chairman in 1929, and he consolidated the company's monopoly until his death in 1957.

His son Harry Oppenheimer expanded it into several countries. De Beers kept prices high by buying rivals' stones, stockpiling and limiting supply. Its share of rough diamonds fell from as high as 90 per cent in the 1980s as producers in Canada and Australia sold outside its channel, and in 2011 Anglo American bought the Oppenheimers' 40 per cent stake.

De Beers advertised diamonds as a symbol of love and commitment. In 1947 the copywriter Frances Gerety coined the slogan A Diamond is Forever for the agency N. W. Ayer & Son, and in 2000 Advertising Age named it the best advertising slogan of the 20th century. Mining takes place in Botswana, Namibia, South Africa and Canada, in Botswana and Namibia through joint ventures with the governments. The company has been criticised for profiting under apartheid, though Harry Oppenheimer opposed that system, and for price fixing and monopoly behaviour.
de-ceremoniis: Its Greek title is often given as Explanation of the Order of the Palace, taken from the preface, or as On the Order of the Palace. The revision under Nikephoros II, who reigned from 963 to 969, may have been supervised by Basil Lekapenos, the imperial parakoimomenos. The revised compilation is preserved at Leipzig, in the university library. Among its appendices are the Three Treatises on Imperial Military Expeditions, a war manual Constantine VII wrote for his son and successor, Romanos II.

In its incomplete form, chapters 1 to 37 of the first book describe the processions and ceremonies of religious festivals, among them the Elevation of the Cross, Christmas, Epiphany, Palm Sunday, Good Friday, Easter, Ascension Day and the feasts of saints such as Demetrius and Basil, which often lasted many days. Chapters 38 to 83 cover secular rites, including the triumphal feasts at the Hippodrome such as the Lupercalia.

The rules fix the emperor's progresses between the palace and particular churches, the stations along the way, the ritual actions and the acclamations of named participants: ministers, members of the senate and the leaders of the Blues and the Greens, the factions of the Hippodrome races. They also say whether the procession went on foot, mounted or by boat. Some acclamations were in a debased Latin, although Latin had not been a language of administration for more than three centuries.

The chapters taken from Peter the Patrician deal with administrative ceremonies: the appointment and investiture of officials, the reception of ambassadors, including those of Persia, the proclamation of the Western Emperor and the appointment of the president of the senate. The second book follows a similar plan, with religious feasts and descriptions of the palace buildings, secular ceremonies, receptions and Hippodrome festivities, and customs introduced by Constantine and Romanos.

Johannes Heinrich Leich and Johann Jakob Reiske published an edition in Leipzig in 1751 and 1754, and a Greek and Latin edition followed at Bonn in 1829 and 1830 in the Corpus Scriptorum Historiae Byzantinae. Albert Vogt published a French translation of the first book from 1935, and Gilbert Dagron and Bernard Flusin a five-volume French edition in 2020. The English translation is by Ann Moffatt and Maxeme Tall.
de-humani-corporis-fabrica: The Fabrica grew out of the lectures Andreas Vesalius gave at Padua, in which he departed from common practice by dissecting a corpse himself. Dissections had been done by a barber surgeon under a doctor of medicine, who was not expected to do manual work. The book also rests on Renaissance advances in visual representation and in printing with refined woodcuts. Vesalius published it at the age of 28 and dedicated it to Charles V; he wanted one of the foremost printers, Johannes Oporinus of Basel, and his written directions to the printer were so valuable that Oporinus included them. Because the Church strictly prohibited dissection, Vesalius says he had to take the bodies of executed criminals in secret.

The work has seven books. The first, about a quarter of the whole, treats bones and cartilages, many gathered from cemeteries. The second covers ligaments and muscles and the order in which to dissect them. Books 3 and 4 treat veins, arteries and nerves, Book 5 the organs of nutrition and generation, and Books 6 and 7 the heart and the brain. Each of the last two closes with a chapter on dissecting that organ.

Galen's anatomy had been largely unchecked until then. The Fabrica corrected some of his worst errors, such as that the great blood vessels began in the liver, that the lower jaw was in two parts and that men had fewer ribs than women. Older accounts said this turned the Church against Vesalius, but modern scholarship sees that as anti-clerical bias.

The book recouped its considerable cost and brought Vesalius European fame, partly through cheap unauthorised copies. He became physician to Charles V. The more than 250 illustrations are generally attributed to the studio of Titian. A cheaper Epitome appeared in 1543 and was more widely seen, and a second edition followed in 1555. More than 700 copies of the two editions survive. A second-edition copy sold at Christie's in February 2024 for $2,228,000 was found to be Vesalius's own, with his handwritten annotations.
de-motu-cordis: The full Latin title means An Anatomical Exercise on the Motion of the Heart and Blood in Living Beings. William Harvey, a royal physician, had studied arts and medicine at Padua in the early 1600s, where he furthered his training in anatomy under Hieronymus Fabricius ab Acquapendente, and received his MD degree in April 1602.

Others had come part of the way before him. In the thirteenth century Ibn Al-Nafis proposed the pulmonary circulation; in 1553 Michael Servetus said that blood flows from the heart to the lungs and mixes there with air; between 1570 and 1590 Cesalpino suggested, against the Galenists, that the blood moved in something more like a circulation than an oscillation; and in 1603 Fabricius described the valves of the veins, which hinder blood from flowing away from the heart.

Harvey investigated the effect of ligatures on blood flow and argued for a double circulation: blood returned to the heart is sent through the lungs and back to the heart before it passes into the main circulation. His quantitative argument rested on the output of each beat. He observed that two ounces of blood leave the heart with each beat, so that at 72 beats a minute it throws 540 pounds of blood into the system every hour, an amount that could only be the same blood returning. The one-way valves of the heart and veins showed the direction of the flow. As Harvey put it, "There must be a motion, as it were, in a circle."

The book is counted a landmark in the history of physiology, both for the discovery of the complete circulation and for its experimental, quantitative and mechanistic method, which treated the heart not as a mystical seat of the spirit and faculties but as a pump. It had an immediate and far-reaching influence on Harvey's contemporaries: Thomas Hobbes said that Harvey was the only modern author whose doctrines were taught in his lifetime. The one stage Harvey could not see, where arteries and veins divide into capillaries, was observed in a frog's lung three years after his death.
de-revolutionibus-orbium-coelestium: Copernicus first outlined his system in a short, anonymous manuscript, the Commentariolus, which he circulated among friends; a physician's library list of 1514 describes a manuscript that matches it. By the 1530s a substantial part of the main work was complete, but he hesitated to publish until Cardinal Nikolaus von Schönberg urged him to in 1536. In 1539 the young mathematician Georg Joachim Rheticus came to Frauenburg to study with him, and his Narratio Prima of 1540 summarised the theory and was well received. Under Rheticus's pressure Copernicus gave the book to Bishop Tiedemann Giese, to be printed by Johannes Petreius at Nuremberg.

The book follows the layout of Ptolemy's Almagest, which it updated and replaced. Book I gives the general vision: the heavens and the Earth are spherical, the celestial bodies move in regular circles, and the Earth rotates on its axis and circles the Sun. Book II covers spherical astronomy and a catalogue of the fixed stars, Book III the precession of the equinoxes and the Sun, Book IV the Moon, Book V the positions of the five planets, and Book VI their deviation in latitude from the ecliptic.

Copernicus placed the motionless Sun at the centre, with Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn around it and the Moon circling the Earth. Holding that celestial motions must be uniform and circular, he still needed epicycles. Only after Kepler proposed ellipses in 1609 were deferents and epicycles abolished. An unsigned preface, added by the Lutheran preacher Andreas Osiander, who supervised the printing, presented the theory as a calculus consistent with observation, not a claim of literal truth. Rheticus was furious, and Giese urged the Nuremberg council to issue a correction, which it did not. Johannes Kepler later demonstrated that Osiander wrote it.

Demand was low at first: an initial print run of 400 did not sell out, and the book was technical. Owen Gingerich's census of surviving copies showed, against Arthur Koestler's claim that it was a book nobody read, that nearly all leading astronomers owned and read it, though they mostly ignored the cosmology and used the new planetary models. Erasmus Reinhold's Prutenic Tables of 1551, based on Copernicus's methods, were used in the calendar reform of 1582.

Martin Luther was quoted in 1539 rejecting the idea, and Philipp Melanchthon wrote against it in 1549. On 5 March 1616 the Sacred Congregation of the Index suspended the book until corrected. It was withdrawn, not banned, and nine sentences that stated the heliocentric system as certain were to be changed. After corrections were approved in 1620, reading was permitted, but only to qualified scholars. The book left the Index in 1758.
de-stalinization: Joseph Stalin died on 5 March 1953. The collective leadership that followed him, made up of Georgi Malenkov as premier, Lavrentiy Beria as head of the Ministry of the Interior and Nikita Khrushchev as First Secretary of the Party, began the reforms that came to be called de-Stalinization. The term itself gained currency after the dissolution of the Soviet Union and was not used in Khrushchev's time, when the effort was described as overcoming the cult of personality. Denouncing Stalin was dangerous, since he had been placed on a pedestal at home and among communists abroad.

The first phase has been called silent de-Stalinization. Beria began the release of Gulag prisoners before he was arrested on 26 June 1953 and executed on 23 December. The revision of Stalin's policies was done in secret and often without explanation, with unpublicised rehabilitations of figures such as Marshal Mikhail Tukhachevsky.

About 90,000 prisoners returned from the camps in 1954 and 1955 alone, which made secrecy hard to keep. In December 1955 Khrushchev proposed a commission to investigate Stalin's activities. It found that of 1,920,635 people arrested for anti-Soviet activities, 688,503 were executed.

De-Stalinization became official on 25 February 1956, when Khrushchev addressed a closed session of the 20th Party Congress in the speech On the Cult of Personality and Its Consequences. He set out some of Stalin's crimes, condemned his treatment of the Old Bolsheviks and denounced his dictatorial rule. Some historians hold that Khrushchev meant to free officials from fear of repression, others that he meant to put the blame on Stalin and spare the Party. At the 22nd Congress in 1961, Stalin's body was moved on 31 October from Lenin's Mausoleum to the Kremlin Wall Necropolis, and on 11 November Stalingrad was renamed Volgograd.

Stalin's name was taken off cities, buildings and the state anthem, and hundreds of his monuments were removed across the USSR and the Eastern bloc. A resolution of 25 October 1956 called the Gulag labour system inexpedient, and it was closed by an order of 25 January 1960. Former prisoners often met hostility on their return.

The speech was central to the Khrushchev Thaw, and China under Mao Zedong and Albania under Enver Hoxha cited it as a cause of the Sino-Soviet split and condemned Khrushchev as a revisionist. In North Korea an attempt to remove Kim Il Sung in August 1956 failed. Historians regard the start of the process as a turning point. It stalled under Brezhnev and accelerated under Mikhail Gorbachev, and Polly Jones and Anne Applebaum have both described it as fragile.
dead-sea: The Dead Sea is an endorheic lake with no outlet streams, and its main tributary is the Jordan River. It lies in the Jordan Rift Valley, formed by the Dead Sea Transform, a fault along the boundary between the African Plate and the Arabian Plate. In the late Pliocene and early Pleistocene the valley was repeatedly flooded from the Mediterranean, forming the Sedom Lagoon, which deposited rock salt up to 2.3 km thick. As the climate became more arid, Lake Lisan shrank and grew saltier, leaving the Dead Sea as its last remainder.

Historical English names include the Salt Sea, the Lake of Sodom, from the biblical account of its destruction, and Lake Asphaltites, from Greek and Latin. The Hebrew Bible records dwelling in caves near the sea before the Israelites came to Canaan and extensively in the time of King David. Greek and Jewish writers report that the Nabateans held a monopoly over the sea. The sixth-century Madaba Map indicates that trade across it was prevalent in the Byzantine period, and Greek Orthodox monks settled in the remote region, where Mar Saba is still a place of pilgrimage.

The Jewish village of Ein Gedi, inhabited continuously since the 5th century BCE, was destroyed by fire in the 7th century. From the seventh century the area declined and its population fell. Sugarcane was grown near the shores from the Crusader period and reached its peak under the Mamluks. Christopher Costigan explored the Jordan and the Dead Sea by boat in 1835, followed by Thomas Howard Molyneux in 1847, William Francis Lynch in 1848 and John MacGregor in 1869.

The Dead Sea lies between Jordan to the east and the West Bank and Israel to the west, and its shore is the lowest land-based elevation on Earth. It is about 304 m deep and, with a salinity of 34.2% measured in 2011, among the saltiest bodies of water, so that macroscopic life cannot live in it. Its surface area fell from 1,050 km2 in 1930 to 605 km2. Asphalt for Egyptian mummification and, in modern times, potash have been taken from it, and the area is also a health resort.
dead-sea-scrolls: The first scrolls were found between November 1946 and February 1947 by Bedouin shepherds, among them Muhammed edh-Dhib, who fell into a cave near what is now the Qumran site and found seven scrolls in jars. They included the Isaiah Scroll, the Habakkuk Commentary and the Community Rule. They passed through several hands, among them the cobbler and antiques dealer Khalil Eskander Shahin, known as Kando, and Metropolitan Athanasius Yeshue Samuel.

Scholars did not find the original cave for two years. It was rediscovered on 28 January 1949 by a Belgian United Nations observer and an Arab Legion officer, and in November 1951 Roland de Vaux began a full excavation of Qumran. Further caves followed, among them the third, with the Copper Scroll, on 14 March 1952. In the fourth cave the fragments were torn into up to 15,000 pieces, which scholars assembled in a room called the scrollery.

About 40 per cent of the identified texts are copies of books of the Hebrew scriptures, about 30 per cent are Second Temple texts that were not canonised, such as the Book of Enoch, the Book of Jubilees and the Wisdom of Sirach, and the remaining 30 per cent are sectarian writings not known before, such as the Community Rule, the War Scroll and the Pesher on Habakkuk. Parts of all but one of the books of the Hebrew Bible are present; the Book of Esther is missing.

Before the discovery the oldest Hebrew manuscripts of the Bible were Masoretic texts of the 10th century CE, such as the Aleppo Codex. The biblical manuscripts among the scrolls go back to the 2nd century BCE, and they showed both the stability of the Masoretic tradition and substantial textual variation before the text was standardised about 100 CE.

Who wrote the scrolls is debated. The Qumran-Essene hypothesis of Roland de Vaux and Józef Milik, almost universally held until the 1990s, holds that the Essenes, or another sectarian group living at Khirbet Qumran, composed them and hid them in the caves during the Jewish Revolt between 66 and 68 CE. Others argue that they came from libraries in Jerusalem and were hidden by people fleeing the Romans in 70 CE. Palaeography dates fragments from 225 BCE to 50 CE according to Cross and Avigad, and radiocarbon tests support a date in the last two centuries BCE and the first century CE. Most of the scrolls are held in the Shrine of the Book at the Israel Museum in Jerusalem, completed in April 1965.
dean-barrow: Dean Oliver Barrow was born on 2 March 1951 in Belize City, then in British Honduras, where he grew up. He attended St. Michael's College in Belize, took a law degree at the University of the West Indies at Cave Hill in Barbados in 1973 and a Certificate of Legal Education at the Norman Manley Law School in Jamaica in 1975, and later studied at the University of Miami.

He entered the legal profession in 1974, working with his maternal uncle Dean Lindo, and became a partner in Lindo's firm in 1977. He later founded his own firm, Barrow and Williams, with Rodwell Williams. Among its more controversial clients were Lord Ashcroft and his associated businesses, including Belize Bank and Belize Telemedia Limited.

Barrow entered electoral politics in December 1983, winning a seat on the Belize City council as one of a slate of nine. In 1984 he stood for the newly created Queen's Square constituency, defeated Ralph Fonseca of the People's United Party and joined the first cabinet of Manuel Esquivel as attorney-general and minister of foreign affairs. He held his seat in 1989, when his party lost power, and became deputy leader in 1990 after the death of Curl Thompson. Back in government in 1993, he added the ministry of national security to his former posts; his detractors called him Minister of Everything.

In the heavy defeat of 1998 he was one of only three party candidates to win, and he replaced the defeated Esquivel as party leader and Leader of the Opposition. The general election of 7 February 2008 gave his party 25 of 31 seats, and he was sworn in the next day as the country's first black prime minister, serving also as minister of finance. He won a reduced majority in 2012 and a third consecutive victory in November 2015, which he said would be his last election as leader.

Citing his health, he at first intended to step down by the end of 2019, but on 18 November 2018 his cabinet urged him to stay until the general election of 2020, and he agreed. He did not contest Queen's Square in that election and endorsed his sister, Denise Barrow, to succeed him. He has returned to private practice as head of litigation at Barrow and Williams. His eldest son, Moses Michael Levi Barrow, a former rapper under the name Shyne, was elected to the House of Representatives in 2020 and later became leader of the party and of the opposition.
debal: Debal, also written Daybul, Daibul or Dēwal, was a commercial town and port of Sindh. Arabic histories of the early eighth century record it as Daybul. One view derives the name from the Sanskrit Devalaya, abode of God; the Chach Nama derives it from Dēwal, temple, after a temple that stood there. Its people were mostly of the Med tribe, and at the time of Muqaddasī's visit its merchants spoke Sindhi and Arabic.

Its exact site has long been uncertain. The maps of Ibn Hawqal and Istakhri place it on the west bank of the Indus at the shore. Firishta, around 1600, held that Debal was Thatta, as did most early British writers, among them Richard Francis Burton; H. M. Elliot in 1867 preferred Karachi and placed the temple on Manora Island, while Malcolm Robert Haig in 1894 argued for the ruins of Kakar Bukera on the Baghar branch of the Indus.

According to modern archaeologists Debal was founded in the first century CE and soon became the most important trading city of Sindh, home to thousands of Sindhi sailors, among them the Bawarij. The tenth-century geographer Ibn Hawqal described its huts, the dry land around it that supported little farming, and how well its people kept their fishing vessels and trade. The Abbasids built its first large stone structures, a city wall and a citadel, and an earthquake in 893 is reported to have destroyed the port.

Debal was the first city stormed by Muhammad bin Qasim. The ninth-century historian Al-Baladhuri recorded a massacre of part of the population that lasted three days, after which Qasim marked out a quarter of the town for a Muslim garrison. In 1221 Jalal al-Din Mangburni entered it unopposed when its ruler Hasrar fled. Soon afterwards the Indus changed course and the town declined; Ibn Battuta's description of Sindh in the early 1300s does not mention it, and its trade passed to Lahari Bandar.

Excavations at Banbhore between September 1958 and April 1965, directed by F. A. Khan, found 14 Kufic inscriptions on the collapsed northern wall of its congregational mosque. A study of them by Muhammad Abdul Ghafur in 1966 concluded strongly that Banbhore was Debal, as N. B. Baluch had argued in 1952 on philological grounds without archaeological evidence.
debarwa: In the medieval period Debarwa was among the most important settlements of the region. The Ethiopian monk Brother Antonio told the Venetian scholar Alessandro Zorzi that it was the chief city of the Bahr Negash, and the Portuguese traveller Francisco Álvares, who visited it, found the ruler's principal palaces on a high rock above the Mereb River, his house like a fortress guarded by over 300 mounted men. The town had over 300 households, a Thursday market of 300 to 400 traders who mostly bartered, and two linked churches, of St. Michael for men and of Peter and Paul for women.

Ahmed ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi overran the region in 1535, and when the Portuguese force of Cristóvão da Gama spent the rainy season of 1542 there, Miguel Castanhoso found the land depopulated. After seizing Massawa in 1557 the Ottomans occupied the town and built a fort with a long wall and a very high tower, but attacks by the local people forced them back to the coast. In 1561 the Bahr Negash Yeshaq, rebelling against Emperor Menas, ceded Debarwa to the Turks for their help; in 1576 Emperor Sarsa Dengel took it and destroyed the fort and the mosque.

Charles-Jacques Poncet, who visited in 1699, called it the capital of the kingdom of Tigra, but it was beginning to be overshadowed by Adwa, and the office of Bahr Negash had been divided between two holders. A typhus epidemic in 1893, after the Great Famine of 1888-1892, left the town decimated.

Debarwa is a market town about 25 kilometers south of Asmara and the capital of the Debarwa (Tsilima) district in the Debub region. Most of its people are Bihér-Tigrigna Tigrinya and belong to the Eritrean Orthodox Tewahdo Church. The area has deposits of gold, copper, silver and zinc; a mine operated near the town by Hitachi was shut down in the 1960s at the outbreak of the Eritrean War of Independence.
debre-berhan: Debre Berhan lies in the Semien Shewa Zone of the Amhara Region, about 130 kilometres north-east of Addis Ababa on Ethiopian Highway 2. At 2,840 metres above sea level it is the highest town in Africa. It has a subtropical highland climate and is one of the coolest towns in the subtropical zone of Ethiopia. The historian David Buxton thought the town was bound to regain importance because it commands an important focus of routes, and the road to Asmara passes through its easy gap, avoiding impassable gorges.

Emperor Zara Yaqob founded the town after a light seen in the sky, which he took as a sign of God's approval for the stoning of a group of heretics 38 days earlier. He ordered a church built, then an extensive palace and a second church dedicated to Saint Cyriacus, and spent 12 of the last 14 years of his life there. The historian Richard Pankhurst dates the church to 1456 and argues that the light was Halley's Comet. His son Baeda Maryam spent the first part of his reign there but then returned to the itinerant court, a camp that moved constantly because the needs of the court and army for firewood and food were so heavy.

In the 16th century Emperor Lebna Dengel mustered his troops there against Ahmad ibn Ibrahim, who after the Battle of Amba Sel mustered his own army there twice, in 1535 for campaigns against Tigray, Begemder and Gojjam. He ordered the buildings of Zara Yaqob destroyed. The town regained importance under Asfaw Wossen of Shewa (1775-1808), who built a palace there. His son Sahle Selassie rebuilt it after it was ravaged by Abichu Oromo and built the church of the Selassie. The treaty of Wadara of 1878 required that the capital of Shewa be moved there from Liche. Emperor Menelik II rebuilt the church in 1906.

The town is the administrative centre of the North Shewa Zone and was home to a population of 65,231 at the 2007 census, of whom 94.12 percent reported Ethiopian Orthodox Christianity. Most people speak Amharic as a first language. It has a long tradition of rug making and was the site of Ethiopia's first wool factory, which began production on 1 January 1965. Debre Berhan University, one of thirteen founded in 2007, is in the town. None of Zara Yaqob's buildings survives.
debre-libanos: Debre Libanos is a monastery of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church in the North Shewa Zone of the Oromia Region. The complex stands on a terrace between a cliff and the gorge of a tributary of the Abbay River, the Blue Nile. Tekle Haymanot is said to have prayed for 29 years in a cave in the cliffs above, which holds a spring whose water is considered holy and draws pilgrims. He died in about 1313, was buried in the cave and was moved into the monastery about 60 years later.

Tekle Haymanot founded it in 1284 as Debre Atsbo, after returning from Debre Damo, and it took the name Debre Libanos in the 15th century. It founded daughter houses, and its chief abbot, the Ichege, was the second most powerful official in the Ethiopian Church after the Abuna. On 21 July 1531, during the invasion of Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi, his follower Ura'i Abu Bakr set the monastery on fire despite its community's offer of ransom. Its buildings were not fully rebuilt until after Emperor Iyasu the Great visited in 1699.

From the 17th century the Ichege and the monks were the chief supporters of the Sost Lidet doctrine against the House of Ewostatewos. The Ichege lived at Gondar while the capital was there and followed it to Debre Tabor, Mekele and Addis Ababa. After the attempt on his life on 19 February 1937, Governor-General Rodolfo Graziani blamed the monks and planned the massacre himself. On 21 May 297 monks and 23 laymen were killed, and between 1,700 and 2,100 civilians died in the executions of 21 and 26 May. In November 360 survivors were deported to the Danane camp near Mogadishu, where about half of the deportees died.

None of the original buildings survive. The church over Tekle Haymanot's tomb, designed by Hector Corfiato, was ordered by Emperor Haile Selassie in 1961; beside it stand an older Church of the Cross and five religious schools. A cross-shaped tomb near the car park holds the remains of the victims of 1937. Abuna Basilios, the first Ethiopian-born archbishop and first patriarch of the Church, is buried here, and the manuscript Tweed MS150, once kept at the monastery, was returned to Ethiopia in 2016.
debre-markos: Debre Markos, Amharic for Mount of St. Mark, is a city and separate woreda and the administrative seat of the East Gojjam Zone in the Amhara Region of Ethiopia. It lies 300 kilometres north-west of Addis Ababa on the road to Gondar, at an elevation of over 2,400 metres, and covers 73.5 square kilometres. Its climate is subtropical highland, with temperatures averaging between 14 and 20 °C and a rainy season that peaks in July. Mount Chokea, about 60 kilometres to the north at 4,100 metres, is the source of more than 40 rivers.

The town was originally called Manqwarar, meaning Cold Place, and was founded in 1853 by Dejazmach Tedla Gwalu, then ruler of Gojjam. In 1867 his rival Ras Adal Tessema burned Tedla Gwalu's houses and made the town his capital. In 1869 it became the seat of Ras Adal, who later took the name Tekle Haymanot and the title Negus of Gojjam, and in the 1880s he built the Church of Markos and named the town after it. In 1877 the town suffered further destruction when Menelik II, King of Shewa, captured it. According to Richard Pankhurst, its population then fluctuated greatly with the army: between 20,000 and 40,000 when the negus was in residence, and 5,000 to 6,000 when he was away.

The explorer Pellegrino Matteucci reached the town on 3 June 1879 and found Ras Adal's restored palace on a hill, with soldiers camped in the valley below.
