It began as one of several principalities held by Muhammad Ghori's Turkic slave-generals, who divided the Ghurid lands among themselves.

The rise of the sultanate belonged to a wider movement of Turkic nomads from the Central Asian steppes into Muslim lands. Muslim rulers enslaved Turks and raised many of them as army slaves, called Mamluks, and some became rulers. Qutb ud-Din Aibak, a former slave of Muhammad Ghori, was the first sultan of Delhi.

The history is usually divided into five periods: Mamluk (1206 to 1290), Khalji (1290 to 1320), Tughlaq (1320 to 1414), Sayyid (1414 to 1451) and Lodi (1451 to 1526). Under the Khalji and Tughlaq dynasties conquests continued deep into southern India, and the sultanate reached its largest extent under the Tughlaq Muhammad bin Tughluq, when it held most of the subcontinent. Razia Sultana reigned from 1236 to 1240. The sultanate repelled attacks by the Mongols of the Chagatai Khanate.

Timur's devastating raid on Delhi in 1398 changed northern India. Rival Hindu powers such as the Vijayanagara Empire and the Kingdom of Mewar re-emerged, and the Bengal and Bahmani sultanates asserted independence. In 1526 Babur, a Timurid ruler, invaded northern India and conquered the sultanate, which the Mughal Empire succeeded.

Chroniclers such as Ziauddin Barani called the state the Empire of Delhi, and Ibn Battuta called it Hind and Sind. Its early elite consisted largely of first-generation immigrants from Iran and Central Asia. The sultans generally accepted Hindu officials and vassals in the administration, and non-Muslim subjects paid the jizya as dhimmis. Alauddin Khalji replaced private markets with government-run markets and imposed strict price controls.

The campaigns brought destruction. The historian Richard Eaton tabulated 37 instances of Hindu temples desecrated or destroyed between 1234 and 1518, and notes that sultans also ordered temples protected or repaired. Sources record the sack of cities in Gujarat and large killings, among them 30,000 at Chittor under Alauddin Khalji and 180,000 in Odisha under Firuz Shah Tughlaq.
The Hindustani language began to emerge in this period, and Amir Khusrau wrote in a form of it he called Hindavi. Mosques and tombs under high domes and arches introduced Central Asian styles.
delian-league: After the Greek victories at Plataea and Mycale in 479 BCE, the allied fleet besieged Sestos and then captured Byzantion in 478 BCE, but the behaviour of the Spartan general Pausanias alienated many allies and he was recalled. Sparta was then eager to end its part in the war. Its king Leotychidas had proposed moving all the Greeks of Asia Minor to Europe, but the Athenian commander Xanthippus rejected this, saying the Athenians would protect the Ionians, who had been their colonists.

A congress on the island of Delos then founded a new alliance. According to Thucydides its official aim was to 'avenge the wrongs they suffered by ravaging the territory of the king'. Members swore to have the same friends and enemies and dropped iron ingots into the sea to symbolise the permanence of the alliance.

Members could provide ships or pay a tax into the common treasury, and most chose to pay. The Athenian politician Aristides was occupied with fixing the tax of new members. Under Cimon the League expelled the remaining Persian forces from the Aegean, and Cimon forced Karystos in Euboea to join and conquered Skyros. Athens treated attempts to leave harshly. Naxos was defeated in about 471 BCE, and Thasos, which seceded in 465 BCE after Athens founded Amphipolis near its mines, surrendered after more than two years of siege, lost its walls, ships and mines and had to pay tribute.

Thucydides saw this as the point where the alliance became a hegemony. In 454 BCE Pericles moved the treasury to Athens, allegedly to keep it safe from Persia; Plutarch records that his rivals saw it as using the money for building projects such as the Parthenon.

In 460 BCE Athens sent a large fleet to support a revolt in Egypt against Persia, and the expedition was destroyed; Isocrates puts the loss at some 20,000 men and modern estimates at 50,000 men and 250 ships. Cimon died during the blockade of Citium on Cyprus. Some writers report a peace with Persia, the Peace of Callias, in 450 BCE, while others think it a later invention.

Athens began to plant kleruchiai, quasi-colonies serving as garrisons, and officials supervised the tribute. After an unsuccessful revolt, Mytilene on Lesbos lost the land of the whole island to Athenian settlers, and Melos was conquered and its men put to death. By 431 BCE the League's threat to Spartan hegemony and Athens's heavy administration led to the Peloponnesian War.

The Spartans, aided by the Persians and by Athenian internal strife, defeated the Athenian empire after 27 years of war, and the League was dissolved in 404 BCE under Lysander. Athens founded the Second Athenian League in 377 BCE against Spartan and then Theban power but never recovered its former strength.
della-gherardesca: The House of Gherardesca was an ancient noble family of the Republic of Pisa, of Longobard origin, which probably dates back as early as the 11th century. It was one of the most prominent families first of Pisa, then of Volterra and eventually of Florence. Its members were of Ghibelline sympathies. Constantine I of Gallura, who ruled Gallura on behalf of the Archdiocese of Pisa, may have been one of them.

In Pisa the family had a long rivalry with the House of Visconti, another Ghibelline family. In 1237 the Archbishop and the Emperor Frederick II intervened to reconcile the two houses, without success. The Gherardesca also took an interest in Pisa's affairs in Sardinia. In 1230, when Ubaldo of Gallura, a Visconti, invaded the Giudicato of Cagliari, they drove him back in the name of Benedetta and the young William II.

When Cagliari was divided in 1258, the family received its south-western third. Around 1272 Count Ugolino della Gherardesca founded the mining town of Villa di Chiesa, today Iglesias, in the Cixerri. A Gherardesca woman married John Visconti, Judge of Gallura, who had received the north-eastern third, and the marriage finally reconciled the two families.

The family reached its height in Pisa under Ugolino in the 1270s and 1280s. He had to share power with his nephew Nino Visconti, but the two soon quarrelled, and the Pisans arrested Ugolino and deposed Nino from Gallura. After Ugolino's betrayal at the Battle of Meloria, the House of Orlandi also turned against the Gherardesca.

The family survived the fall of Ugolino, who died in 1289, and produced churchmen and public figures in later centuries, among them Emilia della Gherardesca, duchess of Mantua, who died in 1349, the bishop Cosimo della Gherardesca and the archbishop Tommaso della Gherardesca. A Gherardesca Chapel stands in the church of Saint Francis in Pisa.
della-rovere: The name Della Rovere means of the oak tree. The family had humble origins in Savona, in Liguria, and gained power and influence through nepotism and ambitious marriages arranged by its two popes. Francesco della Rovere was born in 1414 into a poor family, the son of Leonardo della Rovere of Savona. He became a Franciscan, rose to Minister General of his order and then to cardinal, and had a reputation for unworldliness until his election as pope in 1471. As Sixtus IV he claimed descent from a noble Della Rovere family, the counts of Vinovo in Piemonte, and adopted their coat of arms.

Sixtus IV at once set about giving power and wealth to his nephews of the Della Rovere and Riario families. Within months of his election he made Giuliano della Rovere, the future Julius II, and Pietro Riario both cardinals and bishops, and four other nephews also received the red hat. He made Giovanni della Rovere, who was not a priest, prefect of Rome and arranged for him to marry into the da Montefeltro family, the dukes of Urbino. Sixtus built the Sistine Chapel, which is named after him.

Guidobaldo da Montefeltro, who had no children, adopted his sister's son Francesco Maria I della Rovere, a nephew of Julius II. Through the intercession of Julius, Guidobaldo named him heir to the Duchy of Urbino in 1504, and Francesco Maria inherited it in 1508, beginning the line of Della Rovere dukes. Julius II, pope from 1503, was a patron of Michelangelo, Raphael and other artists and began the demolition and rebuilding of St Peter's Basilica. The Basilica of San Pietro in Vincoli in Rome was the family church. Members of the family were also dukes of Sora and lords of Senigallia.

The Della Rovere dukes of Urbino were Francesco Maria I (1490 to 1538), Guidobaldo II (1514 to 1574) and Francesco Maria II (1549 to 1631). In the reign of Pope Urban VIII the duchy was incorporated into the papal dominions. The last descendant of the family was Vittoria della Rovere, the only child of Federico Ubaldo, who lived from 1622 to 1694. She married Ferdinando II de' Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany, and their children were Cosimo III, the longest-reigning monarch of Tuscany, and Francesco Maria de' Medici, a prince of the Church.
delminium: Delminium lay in the land of the Illyrian Delmatae, and its name shares a root with the tribal name and with Dalmatia; it is thought to be connected to Albanian words for sheep and shepherd. Marcus Terentius Varro used the form Delmatia because it matched the name of the tribe's chief settlement, and the grammarian Velius Longus held that Delmatia was the correct spelling. Karl Patsch first placed the site near Tomislavgrad after excavations between 1896 and 1898, locating it 9 km south-east of the town at the Lib mountain.

On the mountains around Tomislavgrad the Illyrians built 21 forts as watchtowers and defences. As the Romans conquered the Ardiaei to the south, the Delmatae were among the last bastions of Illyrian autonomy; they attacked Roman posts near the Neretva, Greek merchant towns and the Daorsi, and ringed their capital with smaller forts. Writers of the time called Delminium a large city, almost inaccessible, and some 5,000 people are assumed to have lived there.

War with the Romans began in 156 BCE. The Roman generals Figulus and Cornelius Scipio Nasica took and burned the town, reportedly shooting burning arrows at its wooden houses, but resistance ended only with the Great Illyrian revolt, crushed in 9 CE. Roads from Salona and Narona on the coast then met at Delminium, and the town was rebuilt in 18 and 19 CE under Emperor Tiberius, with a forum on the site of the present-day Nikola Tavelić basilica.

Finds include altars to Diana, to the Illyrian god Armatus and to Libera, and an altar tablet dedicated to Mars by a soldier of the IX Legion. The forum was destroyed in the middle of the 5th century. The Goths ruled the town from 493 to 537, it came under the Byzantine Empire in 573, and by the middle of the 7th century it was inhabited by Slavs.

The name survives as Duvno, which developed from Delminium through a late antique form, Delminio. Remains of the Roman roads that crossed there still exist, and Delminium is also the name of a Latin bishopric once seated at the site.
delos: Delos lies near Mykonos, close to the centre of the Cyclades, and covers only 3.43 square kilometres. Stone huts found on the island show that it has been inhabited since the third millennium BCE. The island had been a holy sanctuary for a millennium before Olympian mythology made it the birthplace of Apollo and Artemis.

Between 900 BCE and 100 CE Delos was a major cult centre, where Dionysus and Leto, mother of the twins Apollo and Artemis, were also revered. Athens carried out purifications of the island. In the 6th century BCE the tyrant Pisistratus ordered all graves in sight of the temple dug up. In the sixth year of the Peloponnesian War, on the instruction of the Delphic Oracle, the whole island was cleared of the dead, and a decree forbade burial or birth there. After the Persian Wars the Delian League, founded in 478 BCE, met in the temple, and its treasury stayed there until Pericles removed it to Athens in 454 BCE.

In the Hellenistic period a Phoenician colony traded widely, and inscriptions show a Samaritan community and a Jewish presence. In 167 or 166 BCE, after the Roman victory in the Third Macedonian War, the Roman Republic ceded Delos to the Athenians, who expelled most of the original inhabitants. Strabo writes that the Romans made it a free port, partly to damage the trade of Rhodes. Traders bought tens of thousands of slaves there, captured by Cilician pirates or in the wars that followed the break-up of the Seleucid Empire, and Delos held the largest slave market of the region.

After Corinth was destroyed in 146 BCE Delos took over part of its role as a trading centre. Attacks by the forces of Mithridates VI of Pontus in 88 and 69 BCE greatly reduced its prosperity and population, and before the end of the first century BCE Puteoli replaced it as the main focus of Italian trade with the east. The island was eventually abandoned around the eighth century CE.

Excavations on the island are among the most extensive in the Mediterranean. The remains include the Doric Temple of the Delians dedicated to Apollo, the Terrace of the Lions given by the people of Naxos shortly before 600 BCE, of which seven lions remain, and houses with floor mosaics such as the House of Dionysus. UNESCO inscribed Delos on the World Heritage List in 1990.
delphic-hymns: Both hymns were likely written for performance at the Athenian Pythaids of 128 BCE, special religious processions of the Athenians to Delphi held on certain occasions, usually after omens. The First Hymn was long dated around 138 BCE and credited simply to an Athenian, because the heading naming its composer is damaged, but a careful reading shows that it names Athenaios son of Athenaios. The Second Hymn is dated precisely to 128 BCE and credited, in its heading and in a separate inscription, to Limenios son of Thoinos, an Athenian.

Both hymns are monophonic, a single melodic line. The First Hymn, in vocal notation and cretic metre throughout, is a paean in three verses followed by what may have been a dance, almost all lost. Its singers call on the Muses to leave Mount Helicon, describe the Athenian delegation sacrificing young bulls and Arabian incense to the sound of the aulos and kithara, and recall how Apollo took the prophetic tripod after killing the snake that guarded it and thwarted an invading army of Gauls.

The Second Hymn, headed Paean and Prosodion to the God, has ten sections: nine in cretic metre form the paean, and the tenth, in aeolic rhythms, is the processional prosodion. It tells of Apollo's birth on Delos, his visit to Attica, his killing of the Python and his defeat of marauding Gauls with a snowstorm, and closes with a prayer to Apollo and Artemis to protect Athens and Delphi and for the continued dominion of the victorious Roman empire. It is written in instrumental notation and changes key often.

After Théophile Homolle found the fragments in 1893, Henri Weil restored the Greek text and Théodore Reinach transcribed the music into modern notation; the use of vocal notation in one hymn and instrumental notation in the other made the reconstruction easier. The signs can be read thanks to a treatise by Alypius, a musicographer of the 3rd century CE. The First Hymn was first performed publicly in modern times in June 1894 at the Sorbonne in Paris, during the convention for the establishment of the modern Olympic Games.
demak-sultanate: Demak lay on Java's north coast, at the site of the present-day city. It began as a port fief of the Hindu-Buddhist Majapahit kingdom, and Muslim traders from China, Gujarat, Arabia and kingdoms such as Samudra Pasai and Malacca brought Islam to the northern ports. Tradition attributes the foundation to Raden Patah, a Javanese noble related to Majapahit royalty, who set up an Islamic learning centre at Glagah Wangi, a base of the missionaries known as the Wali Songo. After the fall of Kertabhumi at Trowulan in 1478, Demak stopped sending tribute to the Majapahit court and declared its independence. The kingdom was established, by a chronogram, in 1481, and Raden Patah built a Grand Mosque and made members of the Wali Songo his advisers.

Demak gained hegemony over the ports of Semarang, Jepara, Tuban and Gresik, and overlordship of Jambi and Palembang in Sumatra. It defeated Daha, the successor of Majapahit, in 1518. Pati Unus led fleets of Javanese ports against the Portuguese at Malacca, with about 100 ships in 1513 and 375 in 1521. Both failed, and the losses hurt the ports badly. Trenggana, crowned in 1522, sent Fatahillah in 1527 to take Banten and Sunda Kelapa from the Kingdom of Sunda, creating the vassal Sultanate of Banten, and conquered the last Hindu-Buddhist remnants of Majapahit. He was killed in 1546 campaigning against Pasuruan.

His death set off a civil war. Sunan Prawata was killed in 1549 on the orders of Arya Penangsang of Jipang, who took the throne but was overthrown by a coalition of vassals led by Hadiwijaya of Pajang. In 1568 Hadiwijaya moved Demak's regalia to Pajang and made Demak its vassal, ending the sultanate.

Demak lived by trade, importing spices and exporting rice to Malacca and the Maluku Islands, and Tomé Pires wrote that it had more inhabitants than any other port in Sunda or Java. As the first Islamic polity in Java it has a venerated status among Indonesian Muslims, and the Great Mosque of Demak is widely believed to be the oldest surviving mosque in Indonesia.
demaratus: Demaratus was born into the Eurypontid dynasty of Sparta as the firstborn son of King Ariston. Herodotus reports that his birth was accompanied by a prophecy of future prominence, and that his name meant wished by the people. According to Herodotus, Ariston doubted that the child was his own. Remembering when he had married the woman and counting the months on his fingers, he swore an oath that Demaratus could not be his son. As the boy grew up Ariston repented the oath and treated him as his own. When Ariston died, Demaratus became the fifteenth ruler of the Eurypontid line, around 515 BCE.

Demaratus shared the kingship with Cleomenes I of the Agiad dynasty, and the two became rivals. When Cleomenes tried to make Isagoras tyrant in Athens, Demaratus tried to frustrate the plan. Aegina was one of the states that gave earth and water to Persia, and Athens appealed to Sparta to punish this submission. Cleomenes crossed to the island to arrest those responsible, but Demaratus interfered and did his utmost to bring Cleomenes into disfavour at home.

In retaliation Cleomenes urged Leotychidas, a relative and personal enemy of Demaratus, to claim the throne on the ground that Demaratus was the son not of Ariston but of Agetus, his mother's first husband. Leotychidas had a private grievance: he had been promised Perkalon, the daughter of Chilon, but Demaratus had taken her as his own wife. Cleomenes bribed the Delphic oracle to pronounce in favour of Leotychidas, who became king in 491 BCE. Cleomenes then returned to Aegina with Leotychidas and seized ten leading citizens, whom he left at Athens as hostages.

Forced to flee after his deposition, Demaratus went to the Persian court, where he was given the cities of Teuthrania and Halisarna, near Pergamum. He accompanied Xerxes I on the invasion of Greece in 480 BCE. Herodotus records that Xerxes questioned him about the Greeks, and that Demaratus spoke favourably of them even though they had exiled him. In Herodotus's account he told the king that the Spartans, though free, accepted law as their master, and that the law forbade them to flee in battle whatever the number of their enemies.

Demaratus is one of several Greek aristocrats who took refuge in the Achaemenid Empire after reversals at home; Themistocles and Gongylos were others. Such exiles were generally rewarded with land and rule over cities in Asia Minor. No year is known for his death. His sons Eurysthenes and Prokles ruled Halisarna and Teuthrania after him, and his descendants held the area for about eighty years.
demchugdongrub: Demchugdongrub was born on 8 February 1902 into the Plain White Banner of the Chahar, a prince of the Borjigin clan and the only son of Namjil Wangchuk, chief of the Xilingol League. His name joins Tibetan words for Chakrasamvara and Siddhartha. On his father's death in 1908 the six-year-old inherited his title with Qing approval, and he studied Mongolian, Chinese and Manchu. After the fall of the Qing, Yuan Shikai raised him to a higher princely rank in 1912.

In 1933 the Mongol princes of Chahar and Suiyuan met him at Bailingmiao and agreed to form a confederation of the Inner Mongolian banners, warning Nanjing they would seek Japan's help if obstructed; Nanjing authorised a Mongol autonomy committee. In August 1935 he met Jirō Minami, commander of the Kwantung Army, and promised close cooperation in return for money. In April 1936 a conference with the Japanese officer Ryūkichi Tanaka adopted plans for a Mongolian state and a military government, which made an aid agreement with Manchukuo in July.

His Inner Mongolian Army, poorly trained and short of rifles, was beaten in Suiyuan by Fu Zuoyi, general of the warlord Yan Xishan, in 1936; Fu took Bailingmiao on 24 November and virtually annihilated the force. After the Second Sino-Japanese War began in 1937, Japan placed him at the head of the Mengjiang United Autonomous Government, set up in Kalgan on 1 September 1939 and nominally subject from 1940 to Wang Jingwei's government. He made a state visit to Tokyo in February 1941, and Time called him an exalted puppet of the Japanese in 1945.

He fled Kalgan in August 1945 and received asylum from the Kuomintang. In August 1949 he set up a Mongolian Autonomous Government in Alxa Banner, but fled before the advancing People's Liberation Army and crossed to Outer Mongolia on 29 December 1949. Interned and arrested there early in 1950, he was handed to China on 18 September 1950 and pardoned in April 1963. He worked at an Inner Mongolian history museum in Hohhot until his death on 23 May 1966. Some see him as a Mongol nationalist, others as a traitor and pawn of Japan.
demeter: In Greek tradition Demeter is the second child of the Titans Rhea and Cronus and the sister of Hestia, Hera, Hades, Poseidon and Zeus. Hesiod's Theogony, from about 700 BCE, tells how, like her siblings except Zeus, she was swallowed as a newborn by her father and freed when Zeus made Cronus disgorge his children. In the earliest conceptions she is the goddess of grain and threshing, and her functions were extended to the earth in general, so that she was often identified with Gaia. Her religious tradition rests on ancient agrarian cults that predated the Olympian pantheon.

Demeter presided over crops, grains and food, but also over sacred law and the cycle of life and death. Her cult titles include Sito, she of the grain, and Thesmophoros, giver of customs. In the Homeric Hymn to Demeter, Hades abducted her daughter Persephone with the permission of Zeus. Demeter searched for nine days until the sun god Helios told her what had happened. In her grief the seasons halted and living things began to die. Zeus sent Hermes to bring Persephone back, but Hades had made her eat pomegranate seeds, which bound her to the Underworld for part of every year.

Her search took her to Eleusis, where King Celeus took her in as an old woman and she nursed his sons Demophon and Triptolemus. When she tried to make Demophon immortal in the hearth's flames, his mother Metanira cried out, and Demeter abandoned the attempt. She and Persephone then taught Triptolemus the secrets of agriculture.

Her two major festivals were sacred mysteries. The Thesmophoria, held on 11 to 13 October, was open to women only, and the Eleusinian Mysteries to initiates of any gender or social class; the Eleusinian Mysteries promised the initiated a happy afterlife. Major cults are known at Eleusis, Megara, Corinth, Delos, Pergamon, Akragas and Enna. Around 205 BCE her worship merged with that of the Roman goddess Ceres, with a Greek-inspired rite brought from southern Italy by Greek priestesses who were granted Roman citizenship. In art Demeter is shown with flowers, fruit and grain, sometimes with Persephone, and Marcus Manilius assigned her the constellation Virgo.
demetrias: Demetrias stood in Magnesia, in ancient Thessaly in east central Greece, at the head of the Pagasaean Gulf near the modern city of Volos. Its position commanded the interior of Thessaly and the neighbouring seas. Its site is at Aivaliotika, about 3 kilometres south of Volos.

Demetrius Poliorcetes founded the city and relocated to it the inhabitants of Nelia, Pagasae, Ormenium, Rhizus, Sepias, Olizon, Boebe and Iolcos, whose lands were afterwards part of its territory. It soon became important and was a favourite residence of the Macedonian kings. Philip V of Macedon called it one of the three fetters of Greece, with Chalcis and Corinth.

In 196 BCE the Romans, who had beaten Philip V at the Battle of Cynoscephalae the year before, garrisoned the town. Four years later the Aetolian League took it by surprise, and the Aetolians allied with Antiochus III of the Seleucid Empire. After Antiochus returned to Asia in 191 BCE, Demetrias surrendered to Philip, whom the Romans allowed to keep it. It stayed with Philip and his successor until the Macedonian monarchy was overthrown at the Battle of Pydna in 169 BCE. Under Roman rule it lost importance but became the capital of the Magnesian League, and under Constantine the Great it became a Christian episcopal see, now a titular see of the Catholic Church.

Procopius says Justinian I rebuilt Demetrias, though other evidence suggests urban life may have ended by the start of the 6th century. Slavic Belegezitai settled its territory in the 7th or 8th century, and the Saracens sacked it in 901 or the year after. After the Fourth Crusade the town went to the exiled Byzantine empress Euphrosyne Doukaina Kamatera. The Catalan Company sacked it in 1310, and from 1333 it was gradually abandoned for neighbouring Volos. The Ottoman Empire captured it in 1393.

About 11 kilometres of walls and the acropolis survive. Excavations have uncovered a theatre, the Heroon above it, an aqueduct, the sacred agora and the Anaktoron, the royal palace on a hilltop east of the city, which was occupied until the middle of the second century BCE and later used by the Romans as a cemetery. Two early Christian churches stood there, the Basilica of Damokratia in the northern port and the Cemetery Basilica outside the walls to the south.
demetrios-angelos-doukas: Demetrios was born around 1220, the younger son of Theodore Komnenos Doukas and Maria Petraliphaina, and so a great-great-grandson of the Byzantine emperor Alexios I Komnenos. Unlike most of his relatives, who avoided the surname Angelos because of the disastrous reigns of the Angelid emperors, he used the name Angelos Doukas in a manuscript notice dated 25 September 1244.

His father had ruled Epirus from 1215 and, after taking the Latin Kingdom of Thessalonica in 1224, founded the Empire of Thessalonica as a rival to the Empire of Nicaea. Theodore was defeated and captured by Ivan Asen II of Bulgaria at the Battle of Klokotnitsa in 1230 and later blinded. On his release he overthrew his brother Manuel in Thessalonica and installed his eldest son John as emperor, but in 1244 John III Doukas Vatatzes forced John to accept Nicaean overlordship and take the lesser title of Despot.

On John's death in 1244 Demetrios succeeded him, while Theodore oversaw affairs from Vodena. An embassy announced the succession to Nicaea, as the terms of vassalage required, and Vatatzes confirmed it. Young and dissolute, Demetrios inspired little loyalty among Thessalonica's leading families, who came to prefer rule by Nicaea, by then the strongest of the Byzantine successor states.

In 1246 Vatatzes took much of Thrace and most of Macedonia from Bulgaria in a three-month campaign. At Melenikon an envoy of the Thessalonian conspirators offered to deliver the city in return for a guarantee of their privileges, which Vatatzes granted. Demetrios twice refused to come and pay homage, and a few days after the Nicaean army appeared, its supporters opened a gate.

Demetrios fled to the citadel but was persuaded to yield by his sister Irene, who had won clemency for him from Vatatzes. Thessalonica was absorbed into the Nicaean state under the governor Andronikos Palaiologos. Demetrios was exiled to the fortress of Lentiana in Bithynia, where he probably died at an unknown date. His father, isolated at Vodena, apparently took no part in these events.
demetrios-palaiologos: Demetrios was born in 1407, a son of Emperor Manuel II Palaiologos; John VIII and Constantine XI were his elder brothers and Thomas his younger. Made Despot of Lemnos in 1422, he refused to live on the island and in 1423 fled to the court of King Sigismund of Hungary, returning only in 1427. Although firmly against union with the Catholic Church, he went with John VIII to the Council of Florence in 1437, because John did not dare leave him behind in the east.

In April 1442, having made a deal with Sultan Murad II and posed as champion of the anti-unionist cause, he attacked Constantinople with Ottoman support; he was repulsed and briefly imprisoned. When John VIII died in 1448 he hurried to the capital, but their mother, Helena Dragaš, held the regency until Constantine arrived. To keep him away from the city, Constantine made him Despot of the Morea in 1449. He ruled the south and east from Mystras while Thomas held Corinthia and the north-west.

After the fall of Constantinople the brothers ruled as Ottoman vassals for a tribute of 10,000 ducats, raised to 12,000 after Ottoman troops helped them put down an Albanian revolt in 1453–1454. Demetrios leaned towards the Ottomans while Thomas hoped for a crusade. Mehmed II's campaign of 1458 took Corinth and much of the north, and in 1459 Thomas rose against his brother. In 1460 Mehmed invaded again, and Demetrios surrendered Mystras without a fight on 29 May, seven years to the day after Constantinople fell.

Mehmed received him kindly and gave him Lemnos, Imbros, parts of Thassos and Samothrace and the town of Enos, where he lived for seven years in relative comfort with his wife, Theodora Asanina, and her brother Matthew Palaiologos Asen. In 1467, after Matthew's people were accused of cheating the government of revenue from a salt monopoly, the sultan stripped him of his lands. He was then given a small estate in Adrianople, where his only child, Helena, lived. After her death he became a monk, and he died in 1470, leaving no descendants.
demetrios-ypsilantis: Demetrios Ypsilantis belonged to the Phanariote noble family of the Ypsilantis and was the second son of Prince Constantine Ypsilantis of Moldavia and Elisavet Ypsilanti. He was educated at a French military school and served in the Imperial Russian Army, distinguishing himself as a Russian officer in the campaign of 1814. He was also a member of the Filiki Eteria and the younger brother of Alexandros Ypsilantis.

In 1821 he took part in the uprising in Wallachia led by his brother Alexandros, and after its failure he went to the Morea as the representative of the Filiki Eteria and of his brother. He was among the most prominent Phanariote leaders of the early revolt, but local chiefs and the civilian faction headed by Alexandros Mavrokordatos hampered him, which slowed the organisation of a regular army. He took part in the sieges of Tripolitsa and Nafplion and in the Battle of Dervenakia, which secured Greek control of the Morea.

On 15 January 1822 he was elected president of the First National Assembly at Epidaurus. After a failed campaign in central Greece and his failure to win a commanding position at the national convention of Astros, he was forced to retire in 1823. After Ibrahim landed in the Morea, he fought in the defence of Nafplion at the Battle of the Lerna Mills. In 1828 Ioannis Kapodistrias appointed him commander of the troops of eastern Greece in the new regular army, and on 25 September 1829 he forced Aslan Bey to capitulate at the Pass of Petra, ending active operations of the war.

He was known for an affair with Manto Mavrogenous, a heroine of the war. He died of illness in Nafplion on 16 August 1832. The city of Ypsilanti in Michigan, founded in 1823 during the Greek struggle for independence, is named after him, and a bust of him stands at the base of its water tower.
demetrius-i-of-macedon: Demetrius was the son of Antigonus I Monophthalmus, founder of the Antigonid dynasty, and his wife Stratonice. He served with his father in the Second War of the Diadochi. At the Battle of Paraitakene he commanded the cavalry on the right flank, and his success there prevented the battle from being a complete loss. After the Battle of Gabiene he was one of the few who implored his father to spare the captured Eumenes.

At twenty-one he was left to defend Syria against Ptolemy I and was defeated at the Battle of Gaza, though he partly repaired the loss at the Battle of Myus. In 310 BCE he was soundly defeated when he tried to expel Seleucus I Nicator from Babylon, and as a result of this war Antigonus lost almost two thirds of his empire, as all the eastern satrapies fell to Seleucus.

In 307 BCE Demetrius sailed to Athens with 250 ships, expelled the garrison placed there under Demetrius of Phalerum and took Munychia. The Athenians worshipped him as a tutelary deity under the title Soter, Saviour. In 306 BCE he destroyed the naval power of Ptolemaic Egypt at the Battle of Salamis and conquered Cyprus. Antigonus then took the title king and gave it to his son as well.

His siege of Rhodes in 305 BCE failed, but his siege engines earned him the name Poliorcetes. They included a battering ram 55 metres long needing a thousand men to work it and a wheeled tower called Helepolis, 38 metres tall. The Rhodians afterwards used the abandoned bronze to build the Colossus of Rhodes. Antigonus and Demetrius were defeated at the Battle of Ipsus in Phrygia in 301 BCE by a coalition of Seleucus, Cassander and Lysimachus. Antigonus was killed.

In 294 BCE Demetrius took Athens after a long blockade and established himself on the throne of Macedon by murdering Alexander V, the son of Cassander. He took Thebes in 291 BCE after a rebellion by the Boeotians. His rule was continually threatened by Pyrrhus of Epirus, and in 288 BCE the combined forces of Pyrrhus, Ptolemy I and Lysimachus, helped by discontented subjects, obliged him to leave Macedon.

He then attacked provinces of Lysimachus in Asia, but famine and pestilence destroyed most of his army. Abandoned by his troops, he surrendered to Seleucus and died in confinement in 283 BCE after three years. His son Antigonus II Gonatas received his remains, which were buried at Corinth with a splendid funeral. Demetrius's descendants held the Macedonian throne until the Romans conquered Macedon in 168 BCE. Plutarch wrote a biography of him, paired with Mark Antony.
demetrius-ii-aetolicus: Demetrius was born in 275 or 274 BCE, the only child of King Antigonus II Gonatas and Phila, the daughter of Seleucus I. He had an elder half-brother, Halcyoneus, who died in an unknown battle before Antigonus's death in 239 BCE. Demetrius had already distinguished himself in his father's lifetime by defeating Alexander II of Epirus at Derdia and so saving Macedonia, about 260 BCE. Information about his life comes mainly from inscriptions; Plutarch writes of him in the Life of Aratus, and Polybius mentions him rarely.

On his accession in 239 BCE Demetrius faced a coalition of enemies that included the Aetolian and Achaean Leagues, usually rivals, who were now allied against Macedonian power. He dealt this coalition severe blows and took Boeotia from its alliance, invading it in 236 BCE, when the Boeotians submitted immediately. The revolution in Epirus, which replaced the monarchy with a republican league, gravely weakened his position. In 234 BCE he hired Agron for military aid against the advancing Aetolians.

His kingdom extended into Euboea, Magnesia, Thessaly and its environs. He married four times, though the order of the marriages is disputed: Stratonice, daughter of the Seleucid king Antiochus I, who left him when he took a second wife; Nicaea, widow of Alexander of Corinth; Phthia, daughter of Alexander II of Epirus; and Chryseis, probably a former prisoner of war who became his concubine.

At some point in 230 to 229 BCE, at an unknown place in north-western Macedonia, the Dardani defeated Demetrius. He died shortly afterwards, in the next spring, aged about 45. The Macedonian nobility judged his nine-year-old successor, the future Philip V, too young to rule, and Antigonus III Doson was made regent. Chryseis later married Antigonus. The exact location of Demetrius's tomb is unknown but was probably at Beroea or Aegae.
demetrius-ii-nicator: Demetrius II was a son of Demetrius I Soter. While he was a young boy, his father fought Alexander Balas for the Seleucid throne and lost; his father, mother and older brother were all killed. The boy fled to Crete, where guardians raised him. In 147 BCE, while Balas was occupied with a revolt in Cilicia, Demetrius returned to Syria with a force of Cretan mercenaries led by a man called Lasthenes.

In 145 BCE Ptolemy VI Philometor of Egypt marched into Syria in support of Balas but switched sides, sealing the alliance by marrying his daughter Cleopatra Thea to Demetrius. Ptolemy and Demetrius defeated Balas at the Battle of the Oenoparus river; Balas fled to Arabia and was killed, and Ptolemy died of his wounds three days later. Demetrius then cut his soldiers' wages and debased the coinage, and punished Antioch severely, so that Cretan mercenaries slaughtered citizens who resisted.

The Antiochenes rose and besieged him in his palace until Jewish troops restored his control, burning much of the city. The general Diodotus proclaimed Balas's infant son king as Antiochus VI Dionysus, and many soldiers defected to him. Demetrius lost Apamea and Antioch and held out in Seleucia Pieria. Mithridates I of Parthia had taken advantage of the division to seize Mesopotamia, and in 139 or 138 BCE Demetrius marched east to recover it.

He was at first successful but was defeated in the Iranian mountains and taken prisoner in July or August 138 BCE. Mithridates kept him in Hyrcania, married him to a Parthian princess named Rhodogune and, when Demetrius twice tried to escape, humiliated him on the second occasion with a gift of golden dice. In Syria his younger brother Antiochus VII Sidetes took the throne and married Cleopatra Thea. In 130 BCE Phraates II released Demetrius, hoping to start a civil war between the brothers, and Demetrius regained his throne.

The Seleucid kingdom was by now a shadow of its former self, and Cleopatra Thea detested her returned husband. Around 128 BCE Demetrius led an expedition into Egypt to support Queen Cleopatra II against her brother Ptolemy VIII; ancient sources condemned it as foolish. At Pelusium his own troops mutinied, and Ptolemy VIII sent Alexander II Zabinas to fight him. In 126 BCE Demetrius was defeated in a battle at Damascus.

He fled to Ptolemais, but Cleopatra Thea closed its gates against him, and he was captured and killed on a ship near Tyre, having been denied temple asylum. Alexander II succeeded him, while his widow ruled at Ptolemais in co-regency with two of their sons. Pietro Metastasio's libretto Demetrio, first set by Antonio Caldara in 1731, drew on his story.
demetrius-of-phalerum: Demetrius was born in Phalerum, an ancient port of Athens, around 350 BCE, the son of Phanostratus, a man without rank or property, and the brother of the anti-Macedonian orator Himeraeus. He was educated in the school of Theophrastus together with the poet Menander, and perhaps also studied under Aristotle. He began his public career about 325 BCE, at the time of the disputes concerning Harpalus, and soon gained a reputation for public speaking. He belonged to the pro-oligarchic party of Phocion and acted in that statesman's spirit.

After the death of Phocion in 317 BCE, Cassander, King of Macedon, placed Demetrius at the head of the administration of Athens, an office he held for ten years. He instituted extensive legal reforms, among them a sumptuary law restricting funerary luxury, which is known from a mention in Cicero and is visible in the cemeteries of Athens that archaeologists have recorded. He also had the Homeric and other poems recited on the stage by rhapsodists, as a less costly amusement than tragedy. Lower-class Athenians and pro-democratic factions resented the limits he set on the democratic franchise and saw him as a pro-Macedonian puppet.

Tradition says the Athenians erected 360 statues to him, though Stephen V. Tracy argues that this story is not historical. In 307 BCE Demetrius Poliorcetes, an enemy of Cassander, captured Athens, and Demetrius fled. His enemies had him condemned to death, and all his statues but one were demolished. He went first to Thebes and, after Cassander's death in 297 BCE, to the court of Ptolemy I Soter at Alexandria, where he lived on the best terms with the king and devoted himself mainly to literary work.

Under Ptolemy II Philadelphus, Demetrius fell into disfavour, apparently for supporting the wrong candidate, and was sent into exile in Upper Egypt, where he is said to have died of a snake bite. His writings on history, politics, philosophy and poetry, including a collection of Aesopic fables, have all been lost, and the treatise On Style that bears his name may be by a later writer. According to Strabo, he inspired the creation of the Mouseion, the home of the Library of Alexandria, modelled on Aristotle's school. The Letter of Aristeas says he organised the library under Ptolemy I, though other sources credit Ptolemy II.
demetrius-of-pharos: Demetrius came from the Greek colony on Pharos, modern Hvar in Croatia, and ruled the island from his stronghold at Stari Grad under the Illyrian king Agron. After Agron died in 230 BCE he served the regent, Queen Teuta. In 229 BCE an Illyrian fleet, arguably under his command, defeated the Achaeans and Aetolians off Paxos, and the people of Korkyra had to accept an Illyrian garrison under him. When the Romans came to relieve the city he believed Teuta had slandered him, surrendered Corcyra to them and guided their campaign, so that Rome won quickly and Teuta fled to Rhizon.

In or around 222 BCE Demetrius married Triteuta, the mother of the young king Pinnes, and became official regent of the Ardiaean Kingdom. He renewed ties with Macedonia, and an Illyrian corps of 1,600 men under him fought at the Battle of Sellasia. He detached the Atintani from Rome, allied with the Histri, and in 220 BCE sailed south of Lissus with Scerdilaidas and ninety lembi in breach of the treaty, plundering the Cyclades before raiding the Aetolian coast in return for Macedonian help.

When Rome moved against him, he garrisoned Dimallum and stationed 6,000 of his best men on Pharos. The consul Aemilius Paullus took Dimallum by assault within seven days, then drew Demetrius out of his fortifications with a small decoy force and attacked his army from two sides. Demetrius escaped to the court of Philip V of Macedon, and Philip refused Rome's demand to hand him over.

Demetrius became one of Philip's most trusted advisers. According to Polybius, he turned the king's ambitions toward Illyria and Italy after Hannibal's victory at Lake Trasimene in 217 BCE, and the alliance between Philip and Hannibal in 215 BCE provided for his lost lands to be restored to him. Polybius also blamed him for the king's turn to tyranny after the massacre at Messene in 215 BCE, when Demetrius urged Philip to hold the citadel. He was killed the following year trying to take the city.
demetrius-the-fair: Demetrius was born and raised in Macedonia, the only child of King Demetrius I of Macedon and his fifth wife, Ptolemais, whom the king married at Miletus around 287 or 286 BCE and who was a daughter of Ptolemy I Soter. Through his father he was a half-brother of Stratonice of Syria, queen of the Seleucid Empire; through his mother he was a nephew of Ptolemy II Philadelphus, Arsinoe II and Ptolemy Keraunos, and a cousin of Ptolemy III Euergetes. He was surnamed the Fair because many of his contemporaries thought him beautiful.

His first wife was Olympias, daughter of Polycletus of Larissa, who probably died before he went to Cyrene. Their sons were Antigonus III Doson, later king of Macedon, and Echecrates, whose son Antigonus was named heir by Philip V of Macedon shortly before Philip's death in 179 BCE and was then executed by Perseus.

Little is known of him until the death of Magas of Cyrene. Magas's widow, Apama II, was Demetrius's niece, the daughter of Stratonice and Antiochus I Soter. She summoned him from Macedonia and offered him her only child, Berenice II, so that he would become king of Cyrenaica and protect it from the Ptolemaic dynasty. He accepted, married Berenice and took the throne without opposition, but grew ambitious to the point of recklessness.

Some time after the marriage Demetrius and Apama became lovers. Berenice quarrelled with them both and consented to his assassination, and he died in Apama's arms. Callimachus's poem Coma Berenices, lost but known through a Latin version by Catullus, apparently refers to this deed when it reminds the queen of the brave act by which she gained a royal marriage.
demetrius-zvonimir: Zvonimir's origin is uncertain. Some historians believe he belonged to the native Trpimirović dynasty, while others reject this and suggest another prominent Croatian noble family. His early engagement to the Hungarian princess Helen, a daughter of Béla I, suggests an exceptional lineage. He served as ban under King Peter Krešimir IV, to whom he was related, and Peter Krešimir later appointed him duke and declared him heir. Around 1063 he sought protection from King Solomon of Hungary while the Croatian king faced a rebellion in Dalmatia and an attack by the Carantanian army of Ulric I. With help from Géza I and Solomon he restored authority in the March of Dalmatia between 1064 and 1067.

In March 1074 Normans from southern Italy under Count Amico of Giovinazzo invaded Dalmatia and captured a Croatian king, certainly Peter Krešimir, who died by November. Venice expelled the Normans in February 1075, and Zvonimir probably helped. Venice was close to Byzantium and the Holy Roman Empire and unfavourable to the Holy See, which drew the papacy and Zvonimir together. He was crowned at Salona, today Solin, in the Basilica of Saint Peter and Moses by Gebizon, a representative of Pope Gregory VII, and took the forename Demetrius at the coronation. He swore fealty to the pope, pledged Peter's Pence and promised to support Church reform, which made the kingdom a vassal of the Holy See and ended its relations with Byzantium.

His reign is described as relatively peaceful, and he ruled from Knin. He tried to gain firmer control by replacing local nobles in the administration with court nobles, his own supporters and high clerics. Around 1079 the pope intervened on his behalf when Duke Vecelin prepared an attack from Istria, and in the 1080s Zvonimir sent naval troops to support the Norman invasion against Alexios I Komnenos.

Accounts of his death differ. The last document issued in his lifetime is dated 8 October 1087. Thomas the Archdeacon and a charter of 8 September 1089 indicate natural causes, which historians have mostly accepted since the sixteenth century, though some argued for a violent death. Later sources name 20 April and the village of Kosovo near Knin, and are tied to the allegation of assassination, now often considered a medieval legend.

He was married to Helen, sister of Ladislaus I of Hungary. Their son Radovan died before him, and they had two daughters, Vinica and Claudia. Without a descendant to succeed him, Zvonimir was followed by Stephen II, the last of the Trpimirović dynasty, who ruled briefly until his death in 1091. Ten years of anarchy followed, and Ladislaus intervened, either invited by Croatian nobles or at the request of his sister.
demir-kapija: The place was known in Classical times as Stenae, from the Greek word for gorge. On Mount Ramniste, at the foot of the town, stand the ruins of a fortress from the Paeonian era, about 3,000 years old, one of only three known Paeonian structures in Macedonia. The fortress is also said to date from the era of the Macedonian dynasty, around 450 BCE, as a lookout over troop movements to the north.

In the Middle Ages the town was a Slav settlement called Prosek, and in the thirteenth century it was the seat of Dobromir Hriz, with Strez as its well-known commander. The present name comes from the Ottoman Turkish Demir Kapi, meaning iron gate. Remains from the Paeonian, Ancient Macedonian, Roman, Byzantine, early Christian, Ottoman and Samuil periods have been found.

Demir Kapija is a small town and the seat of Demir Kapija Municipality. The Vardar flows through a gorge near it, and a cave called Bela Voda is 955 metres long. The road through the gate leads to the Valandovo and Gevgelija valley, and the town has a railway station on the line from Niš in Serbia to Thessaloniki in Greece.

The gorge is recognised as an Important Bird Area of 10,500 hectares, home to rock partridges and Egyptian vultures among others, and is a national monument of nature. King Aleksandar Karadjordjevic had a summer home and winery built here, and wine is still produced in the area under the Agropin name.
democedes: Democedes was born in Croton, in Magna Graecia. His father, Calliphon, was a priest and physician there at the time of Pythagoras. Herodotus, who tells his story in great detail and calls him the most skilful physician of his time, places his first posts in the civil service of Aegina and Athens, after which he entered the service of Polycrates. In 522 BCE Polycrates, his entourage and Democedes were seized by the Persian governor Oroetes, and Democedes was sent to Susa.

When Darius I sprained his ankle while hunting and his Egyptian doctors could not help him, Democedes healed it. He was then held in such esteem that he could eat in the king's presence and lived in what the Persians regarded as luxury, the first of many Greek physicians at the Persian court, though he always wished to go home. He later cured Darius's wife Atossa of a breast ulcer, an episode described as the first recorded diagnosis and treatment of inflammatory mastitis, and was rewarded with leave to visit Greece.

According to Herodotus, Democedes went west still in Persian custody, with fifteen Persian nobles on a reconnaissance mission of two triremes and a large merchant ship from Sidon that recorded the harbours and strategic sites of Greece. At Taras, the ruler Aristophilides removed the Persian ships' oars and briefly imprisoned the Persians as spies, letting Democedes slip away inland to Croton before the Persians were freed to go on. At home he was sheltered from Persian reprisals and married the daughter of the wrestler Milo of Croton.
democratic-labour-party-barbados: The Democratic Labour Party, known colloquially as the Dems, was founded by Errol Barrow, James Cameron Tudor, Frederick Smith, known as Sleepy, and 26 others, all former members of the Barbados Labour Party who broke away to form a more left-leaning alternative. Because of that common origin the two parties have remained ideologically close, both broadly described as centre-left and social-democratic, in a politics largely driven by personalities and by the state of the economy.

In the general election of 1956 the party won 19.9% of the vote and four seats. In 1961 it received fewer votes than the BLP but won a majority of the seats, and Barrow became Premier. After the party held power in the 1966 election, this time with a plurality of the vote, Barrow became the country's first prime minister.

The DLP won a third successive election in 1971 but lost to the BLP in 1976, and stayed in opposition until 1986, when it took 24 of the 27 seats. It held power at the election of 1991 and lost in 1994. It returned in 2008 under David Thompson, who became prime minister; after his death in 2010 Freundel Stuart succeeded him and led the party to a narrow victory in 2013. The DLP governed from 15 January 2008 to 24 May 2018.

The election of 2018 left the party with no members in the House of Assembly. Stuart stepped down, and Verla De Peiza, unopposed in a leadership election on 1 August 2018, succeeded him as leader and president. After the 2022 election again returned no DLP members, De Peiza resigned on 21 January 2022, and Ronnie Yearwood was elected president on 1 May 2022.

In February 2024 Ralph Thorne left the BLP and became Leader of the Opposition; he joined the DLP shortly afterwards as its leader, the party's first MP since 2018. Yearwood and the secretary general, Steve Blackett, were expelled from the party on 24 August 2024 after a dispute lasting months. At the 2026 election the BLP again won every seat, Thorne lost his own, and he stepped down as leader. David Estwick, a former minister of youth, culture and sport, was elected to succeed him, defeating Stephen Lashley by 217 votes to 136.
democratic-party-of-albania: The party was founded on 12 December 1990 as an anti-communist movement. Avdyl Matoshi, Azem Hajdari, Sali Berisha and Gramoz Pashko took a major part in its founding. Most of its followers were dissidents who had been persecuted under the communist regime of Enver Hoxha. In the elections of 1991, the first since 1923 to allow more than one party, the ruling Labour Party had the greater advantage, including influence over the media, and the opposition could not reach the countryside. The Democratic Party promised membership of the European Community, strong ties with the United States and a free-market economy. It came second.

The party won the parliamentary elections of 22 March 1992. Sali Berisha became the second President of Albania, an office that then held executive powers, and Aleksandër Meksi became prime minister. In 1997 the collapse of pyramid investment schemes led to civil unrest, especially in the south, and many investors blamed the government. The Socialist Party, the reformed successor of the Labour Party, won the elections of 29 June 1997. On 12 September 1998 Azem Hajdari was assassinated, and Berisha accused the Socialist government of the killing.

The party lost the elections of 24 June 2001 and alleged irregularities; observers reported irregularities too, though not how far they affected the result. In 2005 it won 56 of the 140 seats, and with its allies held 79, so that Berisha became prime minister. Albania joined NATO in 2009. The party and its alliance won the elections of 28 June 2009. After defeat in 2013 Berisha resigned as leader, and on 23 July 2013 Lulzim Basha won the first leadership vote of all members.

The party is regarded as centre-right, with conservative and conservative-liberal views, and it supports NATO and Albania's accession to the European Union. Its headquarters stand in Tirana, about 50 metres from the parliament. After a third defeat in 2021 the party split between supporters of Basha and of Berisha. On 11 December 2021 Berisha's faction held a national council that voted to remove Basha, who did not recognise the result. In 2024 the Court of Appeal upheld a ruling that recognised the decisions of that council.
democratic-party-of-socialists-of-monten: The party's history begins in the political turmoil of Yugoslavia in the late 1980s. After Slobodan Milošević took power in the League of Communists of Serbia, rallies he organised ousted the leaderships of the League's branches in Vojvodina, Kosovo and Montenegro, an episode known as the Anti-bureaucratic revolution. In Montenegro it brought to power a leadership allied with Milošević, including Momir Bulatović, Milo Đukanović and Svetozar Marović.

The League of Communists of Montenegro won the December 1990 election, the first relatively free multi-party election in Socialist Montenegro, taking 83 of 125 seats. It had the whole established party structure at its disposal while its rivals started from nothing. On 22 June 1991 it renamed itself the Democratic Party of Socialists of Montenegro.

Under Bulatović as president the party aligned Montenegro with Serbia, its sole partner in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia from 1992, and won the elections of 1992 and 1993 and of 1996. In July 1997 the party's national committee chose Milica Pejanović-Đurišić to replace Bulatović as party president, and the split made a confrontation between Đukanović and Bulatović inevitable.

Đukanović narrowly won the presidential election of October 1997. Bulatović formed the Socialist People's Party of Montenegro from his defeated faction, which kept a unionist position. Đukanović opposed Milošević, Montenegro received economic aid from the United States, and the government gradually took control of customs and the economy and introduced the Deutsche mark and then the euro.

After Milošević's overthrow on 5 October 2000 the party moved toward independence. A negotiation mediated by the European Union in 2003 set a three-year wait before a referendum, and the party led the pro-independence campaign. With 55.5 per cent in favour, Montenegro became independent on 3 June 2006. The party remained the strongest in the elections of 2006, 2009 and 2012, usually governing with the Social Democratic Party of Montenegro and minority parties. Filip Vujanović, a former vice-president of the party, was president of Montenegro from 2002 to 2018, and Đukanović succeeded him in 2018.

At the 2020 parliamentary election the party ran independently and the opposition parties won, ending its thirty years in government. A controversial religious freedom law and corruption scandals had marked the run-up. In 2023 Milatović defeated Đukanović in the presidential election, and Đukanović resigned the party presidency after 24 years. Danijel Živković was elected to succeed him, and the party stood in opposition after the parliamentary election of 11 June 2023.
democratic-party-uganda: The party grew out of the religious divisions of Buganda, where Roman Catholics, Protestants of the Church of England and followers of Islam had long competed for influence over the Kabaka; by the 1950s the Protestants had gained the most. A majority in Buganda wanted autonomy with the Kabaka as its symbol, while most other Ugandans, and part of the Buganda elite, above all Catholics, wanted a unitary modern state. Those Catholics formed the core of the DP, which spoke for the grievances of Catholics who had faced discrimination since the battle of Mengo of 1892.

The Kabaka saw its members as disloyal and set up a more popular rival party, Kabaka Yekka (The King Only). With little hope in Buganda, the DP under Benedicto Kiwanuka sought support among the other Bantu-speaking peoples of southern Uganda and became the country's first national political party. In 1966 Milton Obote, by then prime minister, turned the army against the Kabaka, who fled into exile; Kabaka Yekka was banned and Kiwanuka imprisoned.

After Idi Amin overthrew Obote in 1971, Kiwanuka accepted a ministerial post but was murdered by Amin's agents, and all parties were banned. The DP re-emerged after Amin's fall in 1979 as the main political force in Buganda and the south, while Obote's Uganda People's Congress held the north. Under Paul Ssemogerere, leader from 1980, it challenged the UPC in the 1980 elections, widely believed to have been rigged in Obote's favour by the military junta that ruled after Amin. The DP took its seats, to its supporters' disappointment, while one of its younger leaders, Andrew Kayiira, took up arms with the Uganda Freedom Movement.

Once in power, Yoweri Museveni outflanked the DP in Buganda by allowing the Kabaka's son to return and be crowned as a ceremonial king, and the party did badly in the elections of 2006. Ssemogerere led it for 25 years until he retired in November 2005; John Ssebaana Kizito followed him, and in February 2010 Norbert Mao was elected party president. In the general election of 18 February 2011 the party won 11 of 238 elected seats, and on 13 August 2020 16 of its members of parliament crossed to the NUP, leaving it with 4.
democratic-progressive-party: The party's roots lay in the Tangwai movement, which formed in opposition to the Kuomintang's one-party rule during martial law. It was founded as an alternative, but still illegal, party on 28 September 1986 by eighteen organising members at the Grand Hotel Taipei, with 132 people joining in attendance. Its members contested the 1986 election as nonpartisan candidates, since competing parties remained illegal until the following year. The early members drew heavily on family members and defence lawyers of political prisoners and on intellectuals and artists who had spent time abroad, all committed to democracy and to freedom of speech, press, assembly and association.

At its founding the party held three factions: the Kang group, led by Kang Ning-hsiang, the New Tide faction, led by Wu Nai-ren and Chiou I-jen, and the Progress Faction, led by Lin Cheng-chieh, who opposed independence. In 1991 the party charter came to advocate a new constitution and a Republic of Taiwan by referendum, and many pro-unification members left. In 1999 a party congress resolved that Taiwan was already an independent country under the name Republic of China, and that constitutional changes should be approved by referendum. The pressure the party put on the Kuomintang is credited with the political reforms of the 1990s, notably the direct election of the president and of all members of the National Assembly and Legislative Yuan.

The party won the presidency with Chen Shui-bian in March 2000, with a plurality, ending 91 years of Kuomintang rule in the Republic of China. In 2002 it became the first party other than the Kuomintang to reach a plurality in the Legislative Yuan, though an opposition coalition kept control of the chamber. Chen was narrowly re-elected in 2004. After the party lost the 2008 elections, Tsai Ing-wen became its leader, the first woman to lead a major party in Taiwan. On 16 January 2016 she won the presidency and the party gained a majority of 68 of 113 seats in the Legislative Yuan, its first. Lai Ching-te won the presidency in January 2024.

The National Party Congress selects, for two-year terms, the 30 members of the Central Executive Committee and the 11 members of the Central Review Committee, and the Central Executive Committee chooses the 10 members of the Central Standing Committee. For many years the party officially recognised factions among its members, including the New Tide, Formosa, Justice Alliance and Welfare State Alliance factions, which often reflected the time at which members had entered the party. In 2006 it ended that recognition. The party is a longtime member of Liberal International, and its platform includes democracy, human rights, social welfare and a distinct Taiwanese identity.
democratic-republic-of-the-congo: The Democratic Republic of the Congo covers 2,345,408 km2, the second-largest country in Africa after Algeria, and straddles the Equator, with one-third of its land to the north and two-thirds to the south. The Congo Basin occupies nearly the whole country and holds the Congo rainforest, the second-largest in the world after the Amazon, crossed by the Congo River and tributaries such as the Kasai, Sangha, Ubangi and Aruwimi.

Plateaus merge into savannas in the south and southwest, and the Rwenzori Mountains lie in the far east. The name is taken from the Congo River, which early European sailors named in the 16th century after the Kingdom of Kongo. Mobutu Sese Seko renamed the country Zaire in October 1971.

People lived in the area as early as 90,000 years ago, and the expansion of Bantu peoples brought major change in the first millennium BCE. Organised states emerged, among them early federated states around Pool Malebo, the Kingdom of Kongo, which ruled near the mouth of the Congo River from the 14th to the 19th century, and the Luba and Lunda Empires, which ruled between the 15th and 19th centuries.

King Leopold II of Belgium ruled the Congo Free State as his personal possession until 1908, using forced labour and concessionary companies to extract rubber, and violence, disease and exploitation caused catastrophic population loss. The 1904 Casement Report and diplomatic pressure led to its annexation as the Belgian Congo in 1908. Belgian rule continued direct control, racial segregation and forced labour. The Congolese National Movement under Patrice Lumumba won the elections of May 1960, and Lumumba became prime minister on 24 June 1960.

After the assassination of Lumumba and a series of secessionist movements, Mobutu seized power in 1965 and imposed a personalist dictatorship. His overthrow in 1997 ended the First Congo War, and the Second Congo War of 1998–2003 caused an estimated several million deaths and the assassination of President Laurent-Désiré Kabila.
The country has a population of about 116 million, with French as the official language, Lingala the most widely spoken of over 200 indigenous languages, and over 250 ethnic groups.
democratic-republic-of-yemen: Al-Beidh announced the state on Aden Radio, proclaiming the creation of the Democratic Republic of Yemen as an independent state with its capital at Aden. It was meant as an alternative regime for the whole country rather than only a southern state: al-Beidh called it the nucleus for a unified Yemen, built on the Document of Pledge and Accord, which he described as a document of national consensus.

Al-Beidh was head of state and led a Presidential Council whose members were Abdal-Qawi Makkawi, a former leader of FLOSY, Abdurrahman Al-Jifri, Sulaiman Nasir Muhammad and Salim Salih Muhammad. A government was announced on 2 June 1994, with Haidar Abu Bakr al-Attas as Prime Minister and Minister of Finance. Besides figures of the Yemeni Socialist Party such as al-Beidh and al-Attas, the leadership drew in members of other South Yemeni and South Arabian groups, among them Abdallah al-Asnaj, who had strongly opposed the Socialist Party's one-party rule in the former People's Democratic Republic of Yemen.

The war of the summer of 1994 between the Republic of Yemen and the new state lasted from May until 7 July and cost between 1,000 and 7,000 lives. Supporters of Ali Nasir Muhammad's faction of the Yemeni Socialist Party fought with the government's forces and tribes, and Islamist parties were hostile to the southern government.

The government of the Republic of Yemen, which won the war, describes it as a war in defence of unity. Many people from the southern governorates call it a war of occupation and claim that lands and properties were seized for officials and tribal sheikhs from the north. After the war Ali Abdullah Saleh appointed prime ministers from the south in an effort to win southern support.
democratic-republican-party: The party, known at the time as the Republican Party, originated in Congress to oppose the nationalist and economically interventionist policies of Alexander Hamilton, Secretary of the Treasury under President George Washington. Washington had won the first presidential election of 1788 to 1789 unanimously, at a time when no formal national parties existed. The Republicans and the opposing Federalist Party each became more cohesive during Washington's second term, partly through the debate over the Jay Treaty. Members generally called themselves Republicans and feared that the Federalists, whom they denounced as supporters of monarchy and aristocracy, threatened the principles of republicanism.

Jefferson lost the 1796 presidential election to the Federalist John Adams. The Alien and Sedition Acts, passed under Adams, restricted speech critical of the government, and numerous journalists aligned with the Republicans were prosecuted under the Sedition Act, sparking a backlash. Jefferson and Madison drafted the Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions in response. After the elections of 1800 the transfer of power was peaceful. Jefferson's administration eliminated the whiskey excise, shrank the army and navy, repealed the Alien and Sedition Acts, reduced the national debt and completed the Louisiana Purchase. Madison, who followed him in 1809, led the country through the War of 1812.

After the war Madison and his allies established the Second Bank of the United States and adopted protective tariffs, a move away from the party's earlier emphasis on states' rights and a strict reading of the Constitution. The Federalists collapsed after 1815, beginning the Era of Good Feelings under James Monroe, who tried to end party conflict. The party was strongest in the South and on the western frontier and weakest in New England. It built networks of newspapers in major cities, and its techniques later became standard American practice.

Without an effective opposition the party divided, factions having already formed among moderates, radicals and the Old Republicans, who accused later administrations of betraying republican principles. After the 1824 presidential election it split into rival groups. The coalition built by Andrew Jackson and Martin Van Buren became the Democratic Party. The supporters of John Quincy Adams and Henry Clay formed the National Republican Party, which later became part of the Whig Party. Because the party was diverse and changing, both major parties could claim to stand for Jeffersonian principles. Slavery divided it from the start, though in 1807 Congress outlawed the international slave trade with Jefferson's support.
democratic-revolutionary-party: From its creation the party had strong ties to the military regime that had ruled Panama since the coup of 1968. Having signed the Canal Treaties with the United States, General Omar Torrijos committed himself to restoring at least nominal civilian rule and created the party as his political vehicle. Most of its members identified with his social policy and the legacy of the treaties. After his death the regime fell into a crisis of power, and two generals resigned before Manuel Noriega took control.

Under Noriega, who persecuted politicians opposed to him, the party was manipulated from above: he named presidents, ministers and legislators loyal to himself, and the party had no internal democracy. Nicolás Ardito Barletta Vallarino, president from 1984 to 1985, was its first president of the republic. The assassination of the dissident Hugo Spadafora in 1985 began the turmoil that ended with the United States invasion of Panama in 1989.

After democracy was restored in 1990, a group led by Ernesto Pérez Balladares, Francisco Sanchez, Mitchell Doens, Tomas G. Duque and Gerardo Gonzalez rebuilt the party, widening members' participation and holding primaries for the first time, the first party in Panama to do so. Pérez Balladares won the nomination in 1993 with 66% of the vote and the presidency in 1994. After defeat in 1999, when Mireya Moscoso was elected, Martín Torrijos became secretary and won the presidency in 2004 with 47.4% of the vote at the head of the Patria Nueva alliance, while the party took 41 of the 78 seats in the National Assembly.

Deep divisions between Balbina Herrera, winner of the 2008 primaries, and Juan Carlos Navarro contributed to defeat in 2009. In August 2012 Navarro's Ola Azul movement won all ten seats of the executive committee, chosen by 4,200 delegates of the National Congress, the first time one candidate had done so. Navarro won the primaries of March 2013 with 95% of the vote, but came a distant third in 2014, the party's worst result, and resigned as secretary-general. Carlos Perez Herrera succeeded him, and in 2019 the party's candidate Laurentino Cortizo won the presidency in a close race.
democritus: Many anecdotes about Democritus survive, but modern scholars doubt their accuracy. According to Aristotle he was born in Abdera on the coast of Thrace, though some called him a Milesian. Apollodorus put his birth in 460 BCE, and Democritus called himself forty years younger than Anaxagoras. His father, Hegesistratus, was said to be wealthy enough to have received Xerxes on his march through Abdera.

Democritus spent his inheritance on travel. He is said to have crossed much of Asia, and he wrote on Babylon and Meroe. Diodorus Siculus states that he lived in Egypt for five years. He also bought the works of Greek philosophers, and Leucippus, founder of atomism, is said to have influenced him most. Nearly eighty treatises are attributed to him, but none of his original work survives, and much of what is known comes from Aristotle.

Early sources credit Leucippus with creating atomism, while later sources credit only Democritus, so their separate contributions are hard to tell apart. Democritus held that the universe was originally nothing but tiny atoms moving in chaos until collisions joined them into larger units. Atoms are too small for the senses, infinite in number and kind, and always moving in the void. Ordinary objects are complexes of atoms, and sensory qualities exist only by convention. The only true realities, he said, are atoms and the void.

In ethics he made peace of mind the aim of action, to be reached through moderation and freedom from fear and passion. His moral advice survives mostly as maxims. In mathematics, Archimedes reports that Democritus had already asserted that a cone is one-third of a cylinder with the same base.

Ancient accounts say that he lived to a very great age, some claiming over a hundred years. He seems to have died in poverty, though his fellow citizens esteemed him and honoured him with money and bronze statues. He was known in antiquity as the laughing philosopher for his emphasis on cheerfulness. His atomic picture partly resembles the 19th-century understanding of atoms, which led some to regard him as more of a scientist than other Greek philosophers.
demosioi: Demosios meant public or of the state, and the plural generally named the class of public slaves at Athens, though some may have been privately owned slaves leased to the state. The word had other uses: some priesthoods were called demosioi, presumably because of a tie to the state rather than servitude, and the phrase demosioi aethloi referred to athletic games sponsored by the state. The police corps of archers was also called the Speusinioi, after the first organiser of the service.

The scholar S. Waszynski proposed three classes: the scythai, a police force; the ergatai, labourers kept at forced work; and the hyperetai, who held positions of trust as assistants to officials or were skilled in some exceptional way. The scythai, ergatai and lower hyperetai were paid at subsistence level and lived in barracks provided by the state, while some higher hyperetai seem to have earned a competitive daily wage and enjoyed a degree of independence unusual for a slave. A demosios who failed in his duties apparently faced a standard punishment of fifty lashes.

The archers served under officers called toxarchoi. They first camped in tents in the agora and were later moved to the Areopagus, and some attended officials in person, among them the Prytaneis, the Probuli and police officers such as the Astynomi and Agoranomi. In the courts and assembly demosioi worked as checking-clerks, the antigrapheis, a role for which their liability to torture made them especially useful; the state trained them. At the Battle of Arginusae demosioi rowed in the galleys, and elsewhere they kept up public roads and waterways.

Some demosioi were put in charge of weights and measures, and this office survived very late in the Roman Empire as the demosioi zygostatai. Texts from Roman Egypt mention demosioi iatroi, public doctors elected, hired or bought by a city to keep medical practitioners there; their honours and privileges have led some historians to doubt that demosioi were slaves at all. Luciano Canfora and Gérard Walter argued that the belief comes from misreading the few texts, while others hold that only some demosioi were slaves.
demosthenes: Demosthenes was born in 384 BCE, the son of a wealthy sword-maker, also named Demosthenes, of the deme of Paeania. His rival Aeschines claimed his mother Kleoboule was Scythian by blood, an allegation some modern scholars dispute. He was orphaned at seven; his guardians Aphobus, Demophon and Therippides mishandled his inheritance. He began to learn rhetoric because he wished to take them to court; being of delicate physique, he could not take the usual gymnastic education. Plutarch says he overcame a stammering pronunciation by speaking with pebbles in his mouth and practised before a large mirror. At twenty he delivered his first judicial speeches, successfully claiming what remained of his inheritance.

He then made his living as a logographer, writing speeches for use in private suits, and as an advocate, and he stopped advocacy once he entered politics. He first spoke publicly on politics in 354 BCE. In 357 BCE he was among the first volunteer trierarchs, and in 348 BCE he paid for a theatrical production as a choregos. Between 355 and 351 BCE he wrote prosecutions such as Against Androtion and Against Leptines, which show his principles on foreign policy: the importance of the navy, of alliances and of national honour.

Most of his major orations opposed Philip II of Macedon, who had seized Amphipolis and Pydna in 357 BCE. In 352 BCE he called Philip the worst enemy of Athens, and in 351 BCE, in the First Philippic, he told the Athenians that if anything happened to Philip they would soon raise up a second one. After Chaeronea Philip made peace with Athens on lenient terms, and Demosthenes was chosen to deliver the Funeral Oration. When Philip was assassinated in 336 BCE, Demosthenes rejoiced and played a leading part in the uprising of Athens against the new king, Alexander the Great. Alexander moved swiftly to Thebes, which submitted, and when the Athenians begged mercy he admonished them but imposed no punishment.

After his efforts against Macedon failed, the revolt met a harsh reaction. Antipater sent men to track him down, and Demosthenes killed himself to avoid arrest by Archias of Thurii. He was among the Athenian politicians who published their speeches, which survived in Athens and in the Library of Alexandria. Sixty-one orations attributed to him survive, though some are pseudonymous. The Alexandrian Canon listed him among the ten great Attic orators, and Cicero praised him as the perfect orator.
demosthenes-general: Demosthenes was the son of Alcisthenes. His military career is first recorded in 426 BCE, when he led an Athenian invasion of Aetolia that failed: about 120 Athenians died, among them his second-in-command Procles, and his allies also lost heavily. Fearing for his life, he did not return to Athens. Later that year, while patrolling the Ionian Sea with twenty ships, he answered the call of the Acarnanians against Ambracia and defeated a Spartan army under Eurylochus, who was killed, at the Battle of Olpae.
