He allowed the Portuguese to ransack and burn Buddhist temples in his kingdom, among them the highly venerated Temple of Kelaniya. The Portuguese military occupation of Kotte during his reign ended in 1565, when the unrelenting attacks of King Sitawaka Rajasinghe forced them to withdraw.

Dharmapala died on 27 May 1597. He is remembered as the first Christian king in Sri Lankan history, and most Buddhist Sinhalese have despised him for abandoning the religion of his birth for that of foreign conquerors whose rule they saw as a reign of terror. The Portuguese takeover of Kotte under his bequest was resisted by the Sinhalese Buddhists and completed only during the captaincy of Dom Jerónimo de Azevedo (1594–1612).
dharmawangsa: His full regnal name was Sri Maharaja Isyana Dharmawangsa Teguh Anantawikramottunggadewa, and he belonged to the Isyana dynasty. He succeeded Sri Makutawangsa Wardhana, whose son or son-in-law he was, and was a grandson of Mpu Sindok. His sister, Princess Mahendradatta, married Udayana, raja of the Warmadewa dynasty of Bali; their son was Airlangga. He was the last Hindu raja of the kingdom, which the accounts also call Mataram.

Dharmawangsa extended his power over several areas, including Bali, and established a colony in West Kalimantan. He was the patron of the translator who rendered the Mahabharata into Old Javanese. In 990 he launched a naval invasion of Srivijaya in Sumatra and tried to capture Palembang, but the invaders were driven back; the attack was reported by ambassadors to China in 992.

In 1016 Haji Wurawari of Lwaram rose against him and destroyed the palace at Watugaluh. The attack came during the wedding ceremony of the king's daughter, so the court was unprepared, and Dharmawangsa was killed fighting together with most of the royal family. For this death he was given the posthumous name Wijayamreta Wardhana, meaning powerful in glorious death.

Javanese accounts record the catastrophe as the pralaya, the debacle that ended the kingdom. With the king dead and the capital fallen, the state collapsed into disorder, and unrest and violence continued for several years. Airlangga, then 16 years old, escaped the attackers and later founded the Kahuripan kingdom as its successor.
dharwad: Dharwad, formerly Dharwar, is a city in the northwestern part of Karnataka and the headquarters of Dharwad district. It lies 430 km northwest of Bangalore on NH-48, between Bangalore and Pune, at 750 metres above sea level. It forms a contiguous urban area with Hubballi and merged with it in 1962 to form the twin cities of Hubballi-Dharwad. The name is derived from the Sanskrit dwarawata, from dwara, door, and wata or wada, town. For centuries the town was a resting place for travellers and a gateway between the Malenadu, the western mountains, and the Bayalu Seeme, the plains.

The Chalukyas ruled Dharwad in the 12th century, and an inscription at the Durgadevi temple names a ruler, Bhaskara Deva, in 1117. In the 14th century the district was overrun by the Bahmani Sultanate and then annexed to the Hindu kingdom of Vijayanagar. According to local tradition an official named Dharav built the fort in 1403.

After the defeat of Vijayanagar at the Battle of Talikota in 1565 Dharwad was for a few years practically independent under its Hindu governor. In 1573 the sultan of Bijapur, Adil Shah, captured the fort and annexed the town. His second fort raised its strategic importance and drew later conquerors.

Aurangzeb took the fort in 1685. When the Mughal empire broke up, Dharwad fell to the Maratha Empire. Hyder Ali of Mysore overran the province in 1764 and captured the fort in 1778, and the Marathas retook it in 1791. After the final defeat of the Peshwa by the British in 1818 the region joined the Bombay Presidency of the East India Company. Rulers such as Baba Saheb of Nargund and Kittur Chennamma opposed the British expansion in the early 19th century. The Dharwad Municipal Council first came into existence on 1 January 1856.

Dharwad is called the cultural capital of Karnataka. Musicians from North India halted there on the way to the court of Mysore, and the region became a centre of Hindustani classical music, especially the Kirana and Jaipur-Atrauli gharanas. It is the home of the singers Gangubai Hangal and Mallikarjun Mansur, and of the Kannada writers Da Ra Bendre, V. K. Gokak and Girish Karnad, who won the Jnanpith Award. Karnatak College was founded in 1917 and Karnatak University in 1949. Dharwad peda, a sweet of milk and sugar, has been accorded a Geographical Indication. The twin cities had a population of 943,857 in the census of 2011.
dhatusena: Dhatusena, in some records Dasenkeli, was the first king of the Moriyan dynasty, but his ancestry is uncertain. The Cūḷavaṃsa makes him of royal lineage, descended from a family that had fled the capital some three hundred and seventy-five years before, and the Mahavamsa names his father as Dhata of Ambilayagugama. In 433 Tamil invaders, apparently linked to the Pandyan dynasty and known as the Six Dravidians, killed King Mittasena and took the Anuradhapura Kingdom, while Sinhalese leaders withdrew to Ruhuna in the south. Dhatusena was raised by his uncle, the monk Mahanama, who ordained him to hide him from the invaders.

Dhatusena organised a rebellion and claimed the kingship in 455. Three of the six invading rulers had already died fighting among themselves, two more were defeated, and the last, Pithiya, was beaten in a final battle around 459, after which Dhatusena was crowned at Anuradhapura. He confiscated the villages of the invaders' keenest supporters and persuaded those who had fled to Ruhuna to resettle the north.

He built eighteen large and eighteen small irrigation tanks. Kala Wewa and Balaluwewa, joined together, cover 6,380 acres, and the Yodha Ela, or Jayaganga, carries water about 54 miles from Kala Wewa to Tissawewa, falling only 95 millimetres in each kilometre. The 13-metre Avukana Buddha statue is attributed to him, as are 18 vihara and lightning rods on the three main dagobas of Anuradhapura, and a redaction of the Pali Tipitaka took place in his reign.

His son Kasyapa I was born to a non-royal concubine, while Moggallana I, son of the royal consort, was the rightful heir. When the army commander Migara, Dhatusena's nephew and son-in-law, severely tortured his wife, the king's daughter, after a quarrel, Dhatusena had Migara's mother burned alive. In revenge Migara helped Kasyapa overthrow and imprison the king in 473. Told that his father hid great treasure, Kasyapa had him show it; Dhatusena led him to Kala Wewa, took up water in his hands and said this was his only treasure. Kasyapa had him walled up alive, or by another account buried in the reservoir's bund, while Moggallana fled to India.
dhian-singh: Raja Dhian Singh was born on 22 August 1796. He was a brother of Raja Gulab Singh of Jammu, who later founded the Dogra dynasty of the princely state of Jammu and Kashmir, and of Suchet Singh, who also served the empire; the three were known as the Dogra brothers. He became wazir in 1818 under Maharaja Ranjit Singh and held the office for twenty-five years, longer than any other wazir of the Sikh Empire.

After Ranjit Singh died on 27 June 1839 and Kharak Singh was crowned on 1 September, Dhian launched a palace coup on 8 October 1839 in which Chet Singh Bajwa, the emperor's favourite courtier, was killed. Having spread a rumour that Kharak Singh meant to sell the empire's sovereignty to the British East India Company, he imprisoned him; the emperor later died of slow poisoning by lead and mercury.

Dhian then placed Kharak's eighteen-year-old son Nau Nihal Singh on the throne. On 5 November 1840, the day of his father's funeral, Nau Nihal was struck by a collapsing stone gate at Lahore Fort, which also killed Udham Singh, son of Gulab Singh. Dhian had him carried inside and barred visitors, even his mother Chand Kaur; early eyewitnesses reported only minor injuries, but he was later pronounced dead with his head smashed. Alexander Gardner noted that of the five artillerymen who carried him, two died mysteriously, two never returned from leave and one disappeared.

When Sher Singh moved against Chand Kaur on 13 January 1841, Dhian negotiated the ceasefire that led to her abdication and Sher's accession. Chand Kaur was killed in her palace on 11 June 1842 by servants Dhian had put in place.

On 15 September 1843 Dhian Singh and Sher Singh were both killed in a plot led by Ajit Singh Sandhawalia; Dhian was shot and his body cut into pieces. His son Hira Singh killed the assassins the next day and on 17 September became prime minister at 24, with the five-year-old Duleep Singh crowned emperor. Hira Singh was killed in a coup on 21 December 1844, a year before the First Anglo-Sikh War broke out. A descendant of Dhian, Jagat Dev Singh of the Poonch ruling family, held the throne of Jammu and Kashmir in 1925 and 1926.
dhiban: Dhiban lies in Madaba Governorate, about 70 kilometres south of Amman. The ancient town occupies a tell of about 15 hectares beside the modern one, on the King's Highway, a major trade route of antiquity, which helps explain why the site was settled on and off for some 5,000 years. The Hebrew Bible calls it Divon or Divon Gad, from its occupation by the tribe of Gad, and says it was taken from the Moabites by the Amorite king Sihon before passing to the Israelites.

According to the Mesha Stele, Mesha ruled from Divon after his father had ruled it for 30 years, so it was probably Moabite from at least the late 10th century BCE. In the Iron Age the tell was artificially enlarged, with retaining walls, towers and a monumental city wall, perhaps built in the 9th or 8th century BCE, and a necropolis with family tombs lay to the northeast.

In the early 6th century BCE the Neo-Babylonian Empire destroyed the town. It became part of Nabataea in the mid-1st century BCE and passed to Rome with the Nabataean kingdom in 106 CE; in the 4th century Eusebius described it as a very large village, and excavations have found a bath and two churches of the period.

After the Muslim conquest the town was refounded under the Umayyad Caliphate or the Abbasid Caliphate; the date is debated. In 1261 the Mamluk sultan Baybars granted it as a tax farm to the son of an Ayyubid prince. It prospered in the 1200s and 1300s, growing einkorn, barley, grapes, figs, lentils and chickpeas with cistern irrigation, and supplying meat to nearby towns. It declined after 1356, when Hisban lost its place as capital of the al-Balqa region to Amman, and was abandoned in the early Ottoman period.

Families of the Bani Hamida, a bedouin tribe, settled the site in the 1950s, and the town now has about 15,000 inhabitants, most of them Muslim. The tell remains Jordanian government property. Excavations began with the American Schools of Oriental Research in 1950–1953, and since 2004 the Dhiban Excavation and Development Project has worked there.
dhimiter-progoni: Dhimitër was a son of Progon of Kruja, the archon who held Krujë and its surroundings from at least the 1190s, and he followed his brother Gjin Progoni in power in 1207–08. Before 1204 Arbanon had been an autonomous principality of the Byzantine Empire. The empire's collapse in the Fourth Crusade removed Byzantine overlordship, but the agreements dividing the empire awarded Albania to the Republic of Venice, which became his chief opponent, together with the Despotate of Epiros in his later years.

To defeat Venetian claims he considered leaving Eastern Orthodoxy for Catholicism in 1208–09, since Venice could not claim land held by a Catholic ruler. Pope Innocent III instructed Nicolaus, the Catholic archdeacon of Durrës, to prepare a mission, but Progoni dropped the matter after defeating Đorđe Nemanjić, Grand Prince of Zeta and a Venetian vassal. His wife Komnena was a granddaughter of Emperor Alexios III Angelos, which brought him the title panhypersebastos. He was excommunicated for seizing church property after the death of the Catholic archbishop of Durrës.

He granted merchants of the Republic of Ragusa free passage through his lands. In 1210 Venice agreed to accept Michael I Komnenos Doukas of Epiros as its vassal, and in 1212 it let the coastal duchy of Durrës pass to him. Surrounded by hostile powers, Arbanon seems to have shrunk by the end of his life to the land between the Shkumbin and the Drin.

A Latin inscription in the church of Gëziq at Ndërfandë in Mirdita, made after his death, shows that he had been received back into the Catholic Church and had paid for the church, dedicated to Shën Premte. It also served as his will: having no sons, he named his nephew Progon, son of Gjin, as protosevastos and successor. His widow was soon married to Gregory Kamonas. Historians have suggested that the Dukagjini family, recorded in the same region some 70 years later, were related to or descended from the Progoni. Later rulers presented their realms as heirs of his principality, beginning with Charles I of Anjou's Kingdom of Albania in 1272.
dhimmi: Dhimmi, 'protected person', refers to the state's obligation under sharia to protect the life, property and freedom of religion of non-Muslims in return for their loyalty and payment of the jizya tax. The status was first applied to Jews, Christians and Sabians, the People of the Book, and was later extended to Zoroastrians, Hindus, Jains and Buddhists; Muslim governments in the Indus basin readily gave it to the Hindus and Buddhists of India.

The Pact of Umar is traditionally held to be an agreement between the caliph Umar and the Christians of Jerusalem in the seventh century, but academic historians believe its present form was the work of later jurists who attributed it to Umar, and that much of it was borrowed from the Theodosian and Justinian codes.

Adult, free, healthy men paid the jizya; women, children, the elderly, slaves, the disabled and travellers were exempt. Dhimmis did not pay the zakat paid by Muslims but their own religious dues, and they did not bear arms or perform military service. Islamic law forbade the enslavement of free dhimmis. The communities kept their own leaders, courts and personal and religious laws, such as the Jewish Halakhic courts, and a qadi usually could not interfere unless the parties chose Islamic law.

Restrictions included bans on building new places of worship or repairing old ones without Muslim consent, on loud prayers and church bells, on teaching children the Quran and on seeking converts among Muslims. Dhimmis were made to wear distinctive dress and to avoid riding on saddles, and in Mamluk Egypt they could not ride even donkeys inside cities. Forced conversion was forbidden, but cases of it are well documented.

Historians judge the system differently. Marshall Hodgson describes an official policy that dhimmis should feel inferior and know their place. Bernard Lewis holds that the restrictions on Jews were social and symbolic rather than practical, and María Rosa Menocal argues that Jews under the caliphate were better off than in Christian Europe.

In the 19th century pressure from European powers and from Muslim reformers gradually relaxed the inequalities. The Ottoman Reform Edict of 18 February 1856, issued partly under pressure from France, Austria and the United Kingdom, proclaimed equality between Muslims and non-Muslims, abolished the jizya and allowed non-Muslims to join the army. The dhimma and the jizya are no longer imposed in countries with a Muslim majority.
dhofar: Dhofar lies in south-western Oman between the Arabian Sea and the Dhofar Mountains, a semi-circular range that runs into the sea at Ras Hamar and Mirbat. It has three distinct physical tracts: a cultivated coastal belt, Al Haffah, a desert plain about 60 km long, and the mountains. From mid-June to mid-September the south-west monsoon, known locally as Khareef, brings clouds that are trapped by the mountains, so that Dhofar is unique on the southern Arabian coast in having monsoon rainfall for about three months. The uplands rise to between 900 and 1,200 metres and slope away northwards towards the Empty Quarter. Frankincense grows wild in the dry northern wadis, where the dry air determines its quality.

A site at Aybut Al-Auwal has yielded stone tools of the Arabian Nubian Complex, dated by two luminescence estimates to about 106,000 years ago, and Bronze Age tomb complexes have been found at Hodor. Dhofar was a major exporter of frankincense in ancient times, some of it traded as far as China. Al-Baleed, near Salalah, was home to the Manjawi civilisation from the 12th to the 16th centuries. Marco Polo, writing about 1300, called Dufar a great and noble city whose people were Muslims, with a Count subject to the Sultan of Aden. Before Omani rule it was part of the sultanate of Kathiri, and was later controlled mostly by the Al-Hakli (Qara) tribes.

In 1876 Sayyid Fadhl bin Alawi, who had come from Mecca, made himself de facto ruler and claimed allegiance to the Ottomans, but local sheikhs expelled him in 1879. The Sultan of Muscat administered Dhofar as a separate holding, and in the 1917 Gazetteer of Arabia frankincense made up most of its trade. During the First World War it supplied much of the food and grain for the British Army in Mesopotamia. From 1963 the Omani Civil War was fought there between the Sultan's forces and the Dhofar Liberation Front and then the Popular Front for the Liberation of Oman and the Persian Gulf. The campaign was declared over in December 1975.

Dhofar is the largest of the eleven governorates of Oman by area, covering 99,300 square kilometres, and its capital and largest city is Salalah, which has an international airport and a major seaport. It has ten wilayats. The local Arabic dialect, Dhofari Arabic, differs from that of the rest of Oman, and many people speak Modern South Arabian languages such as Shehri, also called Jibbali, and Harsusi. The Al Kathiri are the largest tribe in Salalah and Dhofar. The region has long been known as a source of frankincense.
dholavira: Dholavira lies at Khadirbet in Bhachau Taluka of Kutch District, Gujarat, on the island of Khadir Bet in the Kutch Desert Wildlife Sanctuary, within the Great Rann of Kutch. It takes the name of a modern village 1 kilometre to the south, and it is known locally as Kotada timba. The site lies on the Tropic of Cancer, between two seasonal streams, the Mansar in the north and the Manhar in the south. Earthquakes have repeatedly struck it, among them a severe one around 2600 BCE.

A resident of the village, Shambhudan Gadhvi, found the site in the early 1960s and tried to draw official attention to it. J. P. Joshi of the Archaeological Survey of India recorded it in 1967 or 1968. The Survey has excavated it since 1990 under Ravindra Bisht, with 13 field seasons between 1990 and 2005. Bisht defined seven stages of occupation. Radiocarbon dates and comparison with Amri II-B pottery led to the first two being renamed the Pre-Harappan Dholaviran Culture, dated c. 3500 to 3200 BCE and c. 3200 to 2600 BCE. The city declined slowly after about 2100 BCE and was briefly abandoned before being reoccupied.

Finds include animal bones, gold, silver, terracotta ornaments, pottery and bronze vessels, and archaeologists believe the city was an important trading centre linking settlements in south Gujarat, Sindh and Punjab with western Asia. Excavation uncovered 225 seals and 60 clay impressions, most of them square stone stamps with an animal above which ran writing. The unicorn appears on 65 per cent of them. A bead-making industry produced about 12,000 beads of steatite, carnelian, agate, lapis lazuli and other materials, and the largest collection of stone bead-drilling tools known from an Indus site, between 1,500 and 1,600 pieces, came from here.

85 metres. Unlike Harappa and Mohenjo-daro it was built to a geometrical plan of three divisions, the citadel, the middle town and the lower town, each with its own defences, gateways and streets. The citadel, defended by double ramparts, was the most heavily fortified part. Beside it stood the bailey, where important officials lived.

Seven hemispherical mud-brick constructions, some shaped like a spoked wheel, were built over rock-cut chambers and held burial goods but, with one exception, no skeletons. Dholavira is one of the five largest Harappan sites. It was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site, Dholavira: a Harappan City, on 27 July 2021.
dhruva-dharavarsha: Dhruva, also known as Kalivallabha, replaced his elder brother Govinda II on the Rashtrakuta throne. According to the historian Kamath, the Karhad plates of Krishna III show that Govinda had become unpopular with his subjects through his misconduct as a monarch, including excessive indulgence in sensual pleasures. Dhruva's inscriptions give him the titles Kalivallabha, Srivallabha, Dharavarsha, Maharajadhiraja and Parameshvara, standard royal epithets of medieval Indian kings that are also found in Jain donor inscriptions across the Deccan.

Dhruva set out to extend the frontiers of the Rashtrakuta dominion. In the Deccan he humbled the Eastern or Vengi Chalukya king Vishnuvardhana IV in 784 and made an alliance with him by marrying his daughter Silabhattarika, as the Jetvai grant of 786 records. He defeated Shivamara II, the Western Ganga ruler of Gangavadi, imprisoned him and made his own son, Prince Kambarasa, governor there. He also forced the Pallava king Nandivarman II to accept Rashtrakuta suzerainty and pay him with many elephants, campaigning towards Kanchi in 785 and again against the Western Ganga Dynasty in 788.

In the north he subjugated the rulers of Kanyakubja. His victories over Vatsaraja and Dharmapala brought him wealth and fame but no permanent gains of land, although one historian has claimed that his empire stretched from Ayodhya in the north to Rameshvaram in the south.

Under Dhruva the Rashtrakutas emerged as a pan-Indian power. His queen, Sila Mahadevi, who bore the titles Paramesvari and Paramabhattarika, ruled with him. He is recorded as a patron of the Jain teacher Virasena, under whose guidance the Dhavala, a commentary on the Jain canon Shatakhandagama, was written; his inscriptions show sustained royal support for Jain monks, temples and scholars, while the dynasty also supported Hindu sects such as Shivism and Vaishnavism. He was succeeded by his third son, Govinda III.
dhulbahante: By tradition the clan descends from Said Saleh Abdi Mohamed Abdirahman bin Isma'il al-Jabarti, known as Dhulbahante, who is buried at Badweyn; his mother is said to have come from the Arap clan of the Isaaq, a link that has encouraged an affinity between the two clans. The clan's homeland straddles the Haud and the Nugaal Valley, and those who settle on either plateau are called the Reer Hawd and the Reer Nugaaled. In Somaliland the Dhulbahante live almost entirely in the Sool region, and also in Erigavo district of Sanaag and Buuhoodle district of Togdheer.

The clan is led by hereditary chiefs with the title of Garad, a title first used by the ancestor Garad Shirshore and most widespread among the Dhulbahante, who have 13 active Garads. Its two major sub-clans are the Mohamoud Garad and the Farah Garad, while the others form a loose confederation called the Baho Nugaaled. The anthropologist I.M. Lewis counted 50 groups that pay diyya, blood money for their members, gathered into four lineages of unequal size.

In the 19th century the explorer Cruttenden described the Dhulbahante as horsemen armed with two spears and a shield, whose horses were held to descend from the stud of Suleiman. Most of the fighters of the Dervish Movement came from the clan, whose members were camel herders and warriors and had signed no treaty of protection with the British; those of Buuhoodle were its first and most persistent supporters. Garad Ali Garad Mohamoud, who wished to stay autonomous under neither the British nor the Dervishes, quarrelled with Sayyid Mohamed Abdullah Hassan, who ordered his assassination.

In 1998 the Dhulbahante joined other Harti clans in founding the State of Puntland, and voters in Sool were less supportive of Somaliland's 2001 referendum on its constitution and independence. After Somaliland took control of Las Anod in 2007, the clan's chiefs met at Boocame in November 2007, rejected Somaliland's secession and demanded the withdrawal of its forces. In 2009 the SSC Movement, led by Saleban Essa Ahmed, was founded to remove Somaliland from Dhulbahante territories.
di-qing: Di Qing's home of Xihe in Fenzhou lies in present-day Fenyang, Shanxi. He bore tattoos on his face and excelled in mounted archery. His command of Yanzhou, which covered parts of present-day Shaanxi, came in the reign of Emperor Renzong of Song, and it was there that he first fought in the war between the Song and the Western Xia.

In battle he let his hair hang loose and disheveled under his bronze mask as he charged. He was close to the Song ministers Yin Zhu, Han Qi and Fan Zhongyan, and it was Fan's gift of the Zuo Zhuan that turned him to scholarly pursuits. Beyond his post at the Bureau of Military Affairs he held high offices, including that of Grand Preceptor. His night raid on Kunlun Pass took place on the 15th day of the first lunar month of 1053.

He died at the age of 48 and was posthumously honoured with the titles of Chancellor of the Imperial Secretariat and Chancellor of the Imperial Ministry. In folklore he is the Astral God of Military Arts, Wuquxing, while the Song figure Bao Zheng is the Astral God of Civil Arts, Wenquxing.

The three Qing novels known together as the Romance of Di Qing are attributed to Li Yutang: Pavilion of Ten Thousand Flowers, Five Tigers Conquering the West and Five Tigers Conquering the South. Di Qing is the central character of all three, and Yang Zongbao of the Yang clan and Bao Zheng also appear as protagonists. In this fiction his father is a civil officer named Di Guang and his mother Meng Shi, and his aunt Di Qianjin marries the Eighth Prince, an uncle of Emperor Renzong.
di-xin: Di Xin was the younger of three sons of Di Yi. His elder brother Zi Qi had a mother of low birth, while Di Xin's mother was the principal consort, so he was made heir and took the throne after his father's death. He was born Zi Shou, and the Zhou called him Shou, King of Shang. Di Xin is his temple name, recorded in bronze inscriptions of his own time. The name King Zhou, in which zhou means a horse's crupper, was a derogatory title given after his death. Later texts describe him as tall, strong and quick-witted, able to fight beasts bare-handed.

Di Xin moved the Shang capital to Mo, later renamed Zhaoge, in modern Qi County in Henan. Bronze inscriptions record his wars with the Renfang, Linfang and Hufang, and a long campaign against the Renfang in the east, a Dongyi people, which Zhou accounts say wore the Shang down. Oracle bones show him performing the ancestral rituals of the Shang religion. Zhou writers noted with horror that he gave office to fugitives on merit and also appointed women, whom the Shang state held in high respect.

The Zhou portrayed him as a tyrant who drank, indulged his favourite Daji and tortured his subjects. The Book of Documents lists six charges against him, and Sima Qian adds the Lake of Wine and Forest of Meat and the death of his uncle Bi Gan, whose heart he is said to have had cut out. Doubts began early. In the Analects, Zigong says that the wickedness of Zhou was not as great as the name implies. The Southern Song scholar Luo Mi thought such stories were largely imitation, and historians of the Doubting Antiquity School noted that the accusations grew more numerous in later sources.

Around 1046 BCE King Wu of Zhou attacked at the Battle of Muye. The Li gui bronze is the only contemporary record of the battle. When defeat was clear, Di Xin is alleged to have put on his finest clothes and burned himself at the Deer Terrace Pavilion. Another text says that King Wu killed him with an axe. His son Wu Geng was left to rule part of the old Shang lands, but joined the Rebellion of the Three Guards, which the Duke of Zhou crushed within three years. Di Xin's brothers Zi Qi and Zi Yan later ruled the state of Song. Chinese tradition made him, with Jie of Xia, the model of the tyrant whose fall justifies a change of dynasty.
di-yi: Di Yi, personal name Zi Xian, was a king of the Shang dynasty whose capital was at Yin, in modern Anyang, Henan. His reign is preserved in oracle bone inscriptions and bronzeware. He was the older brother of Jizi and Bi Gan and had three sons, Weiziqi, Weizhong and Di Xin. Sima Qian records that because Weiziqi and Weizhong were of lower birth, Di Xin became heir and so the last Shang ruler. After the fall of the Shang, Weiziqi was awarded the State of Song.

His reign is marked by a significant war with the Yufang to the west, begun in his ninth year and led on the other side by Yan, the Earl of the Yufang. According to Ma Panpan, it began with the Yufang attacking a western kingdom, and Di Yi responded by ordering western tian ministers to counter-attack. After this campaign he spent about five months at Huo, with divinations about his army's prospects, and then moved to Hedongzhao to campaign against the Yinmeifang.

Earlier oracle bone scholarship held that he campaigned against the Renfang in his tenth year. Stylistic analysis has cast doubt on this, since the term ziyong appears only in Di Xin's reign, usually in accounts of wars with the Renfang, and Ma Panpan concluded that Di Yi probably did not take part and that the war belongs to Di Xin.

Most later accounts were written from the viewpoint of the conquering Zhou and should be treated with caution. According to the Bamboo Annals he ordered Nanzhong to fight the Kun and built Shuofang, roughly modern Ordos. The Book of Changes twice records that he gave his younger sister in marriage to King Wen of Zhou. Sima Qian says his reign did not improve the economic problems inherited from Wu Yi, and the Book of Han says he was infatuated with a deity and died of shock. Bronze inscriptions of Di Xin's reign name him with the epithet Civil and Military.
diadochi: When Alexander the Great died on 10 June 323 BCE he left an empire of many essentially independent territories, stretching from Macedon and the Greek city-states to Bactria and parts of India, and including Anatolia, the Levant, Egypt, Babylonia and most of the former Achaemenid Empire. His companion cavalry, the hetairoi, were officers without fixed rank whom he assigned where needed. At his death these men became the Diadochi, who knew where they had stood but not where they would stand, and without Alexander they had to make their own appointments.

The generals disputed rule between Alexander's half-brother Arrhidaeus and his unborn child with Roxana. A compromise made Arrhidaeus king as Philip III, to rule jointly with Roxana's child if it was a son, with Perdiccas as regent. At the Partition of Babylon Ptolemy received Egypt, Lysimachus Thrace, Antigonus Phrygia, Lycia and Pamphylia, and Eumenes of Cardia Cappadocia and Paphlagonia, while Antipater and Craterus were to rule Macedon and Greece. Greek cities rose in the Lamian War, which ended with the Battle of Crannon on 5 September 322 BCE.

War between the generals followed. Perdiccas was murdered by his own generals during an invasion of Egypt, and Antipater became regent. When he died in 319 BCE, passing over his son Cassander in favour of Polyperchon, civil war broke out. In 310 BCE Cassander secretly murdered Alexander IV and Roxana. At the Battle of Ipsus in 301 BCE Antigonus I Monophthalmus was killed fighting a coalition of Cassander, Lysimachus and Seleucus I Nicator, and the unified empire was finally broken up.

The Diadochi founded the Ptolemaic, Seleucid and Antigonid dynasties, which ruled for centuries in Egypt, the Levant, Asia Minor, Mesopotamia, Persia and Macedon. The Antigonid kingdom fell to the Roman Republic, a rump Seleucid kingdom in Syria was conquered by Pompey in 64 BCE, and Egypt was annexed to Rome in 30 BCE. The term is an ancient Greek word meaning successors; its Latin form entered modern history writing in the 19th century through Johann Gustav Droysen, who divided the age into the period of the Diadochi and that of the Epigoni, their sons.
diaeus: Diaeus, called Diaios in Greek, came from Megalopolis and was probably a son of Diophanes of Megalopolis, a successful general of the Achaian League in 192/91 BCE, who was himself the son of an earlier Diaios. A member of the Arkadian aristocracy within a confederation that by then took in the whole Peloponnese, he was elected strategos of the League in 150 BCE, succeeding Menalkidas of Sparta.

Menalkidas, charged with a capital offence by Kallikrates of Leontion, saved himself by bribing Diaeus with three talents. Blamed for this, Diaeus sought a quarrel with Lakedaimon to divert attention. When the Roman senate answered a Spartan appeal over disputed land by leaving all causes except those of life and death to the Achaian council, he ignored the exception. The dispute led to war; outmatched, the Spartans sought terms, and Diaeus had 24 of their leading citizens banished. They fled to Rome, and Diaeus went there to oppose them. On returning, Menalkidas told the Spartans that Rome favoured their independence while Diaeus assured the Achaians of the opposite, though the senate had decided nothing.

When a Roman decree separated Sparta and other states from the League, Diaeus took a leading part in stirring the Achaian anger and the violence that brought war with Rome. On the death of Kritolaos in office he resumed command under the League's law, enlarged the army with freed slaves and a strict levy, and divided his forces, sending some to garrison Megara. From Corinth he imprisoned envoys of the Roman general Metellus, releasing them for a talent, and had Sosikrates and Philinos of Corinth tortured to death for urging negotiation.

Defeated by Lucius Mummius Achaicus at the Battle of Corinth, Diaeus made no further attempt to hold the city. At Megalopolis he killed his wife so that she would not be captured, and then took poison. With his death the Achaian League came to an end, dissolved by Mummius.
diagoras-of-rhodes: Diagoras belonged to the Eratidea family of Ialysos on Rhodes. He descended from Damagetus, king of Ialysus, and on his mother's side from the Messenian hero and king Aristomenes. Besides his Olympic success he won the boxing four times at the Isthmian Games, twice at the Nemean Games and at least once at the Pythian Games. In his seventh Olympian ode Pindar set these victories beside the myths of Rhodes, praising the boxer who walks a straight course on a road that hates arrogance.

His three sons were all Olympic champions. The eldest, Damagetos, won the pankration in 452 and 448 BCE, and the second, Akousílaos, won the boxing in 448 BCE; the two carried their father around the stadium on their shoulders. According to legend a spectator shouted that Diagoras should die now, since he would not ascend to Olympus besides, and he died on the spot. The youngest son, Dorieus, was even more successful than his brothers.

Another legend, told by Pausanias, concerns his daughter Kallipáteira. Women other than the priestess of Demeter were barred from watching the games, but she entered disguised as a man. Discovered and tried before the Hellanodíkai on pain of death, she argued that she of all women had the right, with a father, three brothers, a son and a nephew among the victors. The judges acquitted her, and according to Pausanias trainers were afterwards required to strip before entering the arena.

Nigel Nicholson argues that Diagoras tied his family to his victories through statues and oral tradition so that he would be remembered as a mortal champion and not replaced in later tales by a god or hero. In 2018 the Turkish press reported that a pyramid-shaped structure near Turgut, south-west of Marmaris, was his tomb; its Hellenistic inscription names a Diagoras slain in battle and his wife Aristomacha, and earlier scholars had not linked it with the 5th-century boxer. Rhodes International Airport bears his name.
diaguita: The Western or Chilean Diaguitas lived mainly in the Transverse Valleys of the Norte Chico that cut through semi-arid mountains, and the Eastern or Argentine Diaguitas in what are now La Rioja and Catamarca and parts of Salta, San Juan and Tucumán. The name was first applied to these peoples and their archaeological cultures by Ricardo E. Latcham in the early 20th century. They were not a unified people: their speech seems to have varied from valley to valley, and they were divided into several chiefdoms.

Their culture is traced back to the El Molle complex of 300 to 700 CE, replaced in Chile by the Las Ánimas complex of 800 to 1000 CE, from which the archaeological Diaguita culture emerged around 1000 CE. Its classical period was marked by advanced irrigation and by pottery painted in black, white and red. Shells found high in the Andean valleys show trade between coast and interior.

The Inca Empire is generally held to have taken Diaguita lands through warfare that severely depopulated the Transverse Valleys; why it came, for minerals or for labour for the Chilean mines, is disputed. The Incas appointed kurakas and settled mitmas there, and the Diaguitas adopted pottery designs from Cuzco and Inca methods of farming and metalworking. The eastern Diaguitas did not all accept Inca rule.

The first large Spanish encounter came in April 1536, when the expedition of Diego de Almagro reached the valley of Copiapó; there may then have been about 20,000 Diaguitas in what is now Chile. Under García Hurtado de Mendoza (1557–1561) rebel Chilean Diaguitas were decimated. On the eastern side the Spanish ringed the valleys with Santiago del Estero, Tucumán, Salta, La Rioja and Jujuy, and founded Londres in their midst in 1607. The Calchaquí Diaguitas rose in 1630, nearly destroying La Rioja, and the last rebels fought until 1642–1643.

In Chile the Diaguita languages may have been largely lost as the people mixed with Mapuche-speaking populations, and Mapuche communities in the southern Diaguita lands may go back centuries before the Spanish. Today 90,794 people in Argentina identified as Diaguita or Diaguita-Cacano in the 2022 census, and Chile, where 153,231 were counted in 2024, has recognised the Diaguitas as an Indigenous people since 2006.
dialogue-of-a-man-and-his-ba: The text was probably written during the reign of Amenemhat III in the Middle Kingdom. Its composition is earlier than that, since corrections and misreadings in the surviving text show it to be a copy. It belongs to the genre of sebayt, a form of Egyptian wisdom literature, and takes the form of a dialogue between a man struggling with the hardship of life and his ba. The Egyptian concept of the soul had nine parts, of which the ba, commonly translated as "soul", was thought to represent a person's psyche or personality and to live on after death, able to move between the physical and spiritual worlds. Egyptian art usually shows the ba as a human-headed saddle-billed stork.

The text concerns the inner struggle of a man who is drawn to death as a release from his troubles but fears that a premature death might harm his afterlife. The surviving part contains three speeches by the man and four by the ba. At first the ba urges death as an escape from hardship, and the man objects that a premature death would deny him a proper afterlife. On reflecting on burial and funeral rites, though, they seem less permanent and more futile, and the ba then urges him to ignore his misery and embrace life.

The man replies with four litanies on social injustice, the lack of help from others, the attraction of death as release and the fortunate state of the afterlife. The roles reverse, and in its last speech the ba compromises: death should be accepted as the end of life, not as an immediate solution, so that the man and the ba can reach a proper afterlife together.

The original papyrus was bought in Egypt in 1843 by the German Egyptologist Karl Richard Lepsius and belongs to the Ägyptisches Museum und Papyrussammlung of the Berlin State Museums. The first edition appeared in 1859, and the text has since been translated into English at least 26 times, with widely differing interpretations. The traditional reading takes it as a commentary on suicide and the funerary cult. More recent scholars read it as a psychological struggle to accept the sorrows and the goodness of life, and some see the man's turmoil as a metaphor for the unstable politics of the 12th Dynasty after the First Intermediate Period.

In 2017 Papyrus Mallorca II was identified as part of the same manuscript, supplying a third-person introduction that calls the speaker "the sick man" and names a woman, Ankhet, who now seems to have been an audience for the debate.
diana-mythology: Diana was an ancient goddess common to all the Latin tribes, with independent origins in Italy. She was first a goddess of the wilderness and the hunt, and early Roman inscriptions celebrate her chiefly as a huntress. Her primary sanctuary was a woodland grove overlooking Lake Nemi, where she was worshipped as Diana Nemorensis, Diana of the Wood. Evidence suggests that worship there flourished from at least the 6th century BCE until the 2nd century CE. Legend said that Orestes and Iphigenia founded the sanctuary after fleeing from the Tauri.

Tradition says King Servius Tullius dedicated her temple on the Aventine Hill, outside the pomerium, in keeping with her being a goddess of all the Latins and not of the Romans alone. Worship probably spread into the city from about 550 BCE, as she became combined with the Greek Artemis, a process that culminated in her appearance beside Apollo at the first lectisternium in Rome in 399 BCE.

Early Roman gods were numina, powers without bodily form, and Diana probably had little mythology when Rome was founded. Under Greek influence she became the daughter of Jupiter and Latona, twin of Apollo and, usually, a virgin goddess. In Ovid's version of the story of Actaeon, the young hunter came upon her bathing in a grotto, and she turned him into a deer, so that his own dogs tore him apart.

She was also a goddess of the countryside, of crossroads, of the Moon and of childbirth. Her earliest epithet was Trivia, from the three-way crossroads she guarded, which also pointed the way to the underworld. As Diana Lucina she protected women in labour. At Nemi she was venerated from the late 6th century BCE as a triple goddess, Diana, Luna and Hecate. She was also a household goddess: Horace had an altar to her in his villa.

Sermons and other church documents show that Diana worship persisted in remote communities of post-Roman Europe, though many of the cults were probably local goddesses or nymphs that Christian writers called Diana. Gregory of Tours reported that the deacon Vulfilaic found an image of Diana on a hill at what is now Margut and destroyed it. James George Frazer reinterpreted the rites at Nemi in The Golden Bough, and Charles Godfrey Leland's Aradia made her Queen of the Witches. Diana is revered in modern neopagan religions, among them Roman neopaganism and Wicca.
diane-de-poitiers: Diane de Poitiers was born on 9 January 1500 at the Château de Saint-Vallier, to Jean de Poitiers and Jeanne de Batarnay. As a girl she was briefly in the retinue of Anne de Beaujeu and was educated in the principles of Renaissance humanism, including Greek and Latin, rhetoric, finance, law and architecture. On 29 March 1515, at fifteen, she married Louis de Brézé, seigneur d'Anet and Grand Seneschal of Normandy, who was 39 years her senior. They had two daughters, Françoise and Louise.

After Louis died in 1531 she wore black and white for the rest of her life, the permitted colours of mourning and the symbolic colours of the two sides of the moon, playing on her name. She kept her husband's offices and revenues, and her legal skill impressed Francis I, who allowed her to manage her inherited estates without a male guardian.

In 1526 the princes Francis and Henry were sent to Spain as hostages for their father, who had been captured at Pavia. Diane, a lady-in-waiting, gave Henry his farewell kiss, and at a tournament in 1531 he wore her colours. In 1533 Henry married Catherine de' Medici, to whom Diane was related as a second cousin, and it is generally believed that Diane became his mistress in 1534. She remained his lifelong companion for the next 25 years.

After Francis I died in 1547, Henry II banned Francis's mistress Anne de Pisseleu from court and confiscated her duchy of Étampes. Diane became Duchess of Valentinois in 1548 and Duchess of Étampes in 1553. Henry trusted her to write many of his official letters, which were signed jointly as HenriDiane, and she directed the education of his children until 1551. He entrusted her with the Crown Jewels and gave her the Château de Chenonceau. She was a major patron of French Renaissance architecture, commissioning Philibert de l'Orme to remodel the Château d'Anet and to build the arched bridge at Chenonceau in 1555.

In 1559 Henry was severely wounded in a jousting tournament, wearing Diane's favour rather than his wife's. Catherine took control, and Diane was not admitted to his deathbed or invited to his funeral. She was obliged to exchange Chenonceau for the Château de Chaumont and lived out her remaining years at Anet in comfortable obscurity. She died on 25 April 1566.

During the French Revolution her tomb was opened and her remains thrown into a mass grave. When French experts exhumed her remains in 2009 they found high levels of gold in her hair, and it has been suggested that the drinkable gold she reportedly took to preserve youth contributed to her death. She was reburied at Anet in May 2010.
diarmait-mac-mael-na-mbo: Diarmait belonged to the Uí Cheinnselaig, a kin group of south-east Leinster centred on Ferns. His father, Donnchad mac Diarmata, was better known by the epithet Máel na mBó, Baldy of the Cattle, and his mother was Aife, daughter of Gilla Pátraic mac Donnchada, king of Osraige. The last of his ancestors counted as king of all Leinster, Crimthann mac Énnai, had died in the late 5th century, though his great-grandfather Domnall mac Cellaig (died 974) was among the kings of the Uí Cheinnselaig.

The power of the Uí Cheinnselaig had been broken at the battle of Áth Senaig in 738, and the rival Uí Dúnlainge of northern Leinster dominated the province until the time of Brian Bóruma. The decline of the Clann Cholmáin kings of Mide and the defeat of the Uí Dúnlainge at the battle of Clontarf in 1014 turned the balance back. Leinster's kings were also well placed to profit from the Viking towns: Wexford, Waterford and Dublin, the most important of them, all lay in or near the province.

Diarmait made an alliance with Niall mac Eochada, king of Ulaid, which put pressure from north and south on the kingdoms of Mide, Brega and Dublin, ruled by the High King. Having claimed the title of King of Leinster and installed his son Murchad as King of Dublin, he ruled two of the most powerful and wealthy towns of the island and could bid for the High Kingship. The surviving sons of King Harold Godwinson of England fled to him after the Battle of Hastings in 1066, and in 1068 and 1069 he lent them the fleet of Dublin for their attempted invasions of England.

Diarmait was killed near Navan in County Meath on 7 February 1072, in battle against Conchobar Ua Maelsechalinn, king of Mide. The Annals of the Four Masters record that he was slain and beheaded in the battle of Odhbha, together with many hundreds of the foreigners and Leinstermen, and add a lament that his death would bring neither peace nor armistice. He is also known as the ancestor of Diarmait MacMurrough.
diarmait-mac-murchada: Diarmait was a son of Donnchadh mac Murchada, King of Leinster and Dublin, who was killed in 1115 fighting Domnall Gerrlámhach, King of Dublin, and buried by the citizens with the carcass of a dog. He became king unexpectedly after the death of his older brother Énna. The High King Toirdelbach Ua Conchobair, fearing a rival, sent Tigernán Ua Ruairc to oust him; Ua Ruairc slaughtered the livestock of Leinster, but Diarmait regained his throne with the help of the Leinster clans in 1132. His reputed abduction of Ua Ruairc's wife Derbforgaill, whom other sources describe as a willing guest at Ferns, deepened the enmity between the two kings.

Between 1140 and 1170 Diarmait commissioned Irish Romanesque buildings at Baltinglass Abbey, St Saviour's Priory in Glendalough, Ferns Abbey and Killeshin Church, and founded convents in Dublin, at Aghade and at Kilculliheen. He married Mór, half-sister of St Lawrence O'Toole, in 1153 and presided at the synod of Clane in 1161 where O'Toole was installed as archbishop of Dublin.

After his exile, Henry II allowed him to recruit soldiers in his realms, among them Robert FitzStephen and Maurice FitzGerald, who were promised lands in Wexford. They landed at Bannow Bay and took Wexford in May 1169, then raided Ossory. Ruaidrí Ua Conchobair negotiated with him at Ferns, letting him keep Leinster in return for recognising Ruaidrí as High King; some historians hold that he secretly promised to bring in no more foreigners. After FitzGerald's arrival in 1170, Diarmait marched on Dublin, which surrendered, and Strongbow's marriage to Aoife followed the fall of Waterford.

Grief-stricken at the death of his youngest son, Conchobar, a hostage of the High King, Diarmait retreated to Ferns and died about 1 May 1171; his reputed grave is in the cathedral graveyard there. Henry II's larger invasion that year created the Lordship of Ireland. Remembered as Diarmait na nGall, Diarmait of the Foreigners, he was often called a traitor in histories written after 1800, though his aim was to become High King himself. Gerald of Wales, whose kinsmen fought for Strongbow, described him as a man who preferred to be feared by all rather than loved by any.
dick-king: Richard Philip King was born on 26 November in Dursley, Gloucestershire. His family emigrated to the Albany district of the Cape Colony among the 1820 Settlers and in 1828 moved on to the frontier at Port Natal. In the company of the Reverend Francis Owen he met the Zulu king Dingane and came to know Captain Allen Gardiner. He hunted elephants with Alexander Biggar and Jan Gerritze Bantjes, the scribe of the Boer leader Petrus Lafras Uys, who was surveying the bay as a possible port for a new Boer homeland.

After the killing of the Voortrekker leader Piet Retief and his delegation at Dingane's kraal in 1838, King was sent on foot to warn the Voortrekker camps some 200 km inland. Walking day and night, he arrived as the Zulu attacks began near present-day Estcourt on 17 February 1838 and helped defend a laager; about 600 Boers died in the attacks. He then joined the force of 20 to 30 European men under Robert Biggar, with some 1,500 Zulus who had deserted Dingane, that was overwhelmed at Ndondakusuka on 17 April 1838 by an army under Mpande and Nongalaza. King was among the few who escaped to the bay.

In 1842 a British garrison under Captain Charlton Smith was defeated by the Boers of the Republic of Natalia at Congella and besieged in its camp by Andries Pretorius. Warned by the trader George Christopher Cato, King and his 16-year-old servant Ndongeni slipped away before daybreak on 26 May, swimming their horses beside a boat to the Bluff. Ndongeni had to turn back halfway, having no saddle or bridle, but King forded 120 rivers and reached Grahamstown in 10 days, a journey that normally took 17. He returned on the Conch, which reached the bay on 24 June with reinforcements in time to save the garrison from surrender or starvation.

Ndongeni received a farm on the Mzimkulu river and King one at Isipingo, where he managed a sugar mill until his death there on 10 November 1871. His statue, mounted on his horse Somerset, was unveiled on the north shore of Durban Bay on 14 August 1915, and Kings Park, Kingsmead and Kingsway High School in Durban are named after him.
dictionnaire-de-trevoux: The work's full title was Dictionnaire universel françois et latin; it was called the Dictionnaire de Trévoux, first unofficially and later officially, after the town near Lyon where it first appeared. The first edition of 1704 was close to a reprint of the 1701 edition of Antoine Furetière's Dictionnaire universel, first published in 1690, with a small number of revisions and added articles and a Latin-French dictionary in its last volume. It came in two or three folio volumes, printed and bound in different ways: one set of three runs A-D, E-N and M-Z, another A-F, G-R and S-Z.

The much expanded second edition of 1721, in five folio volumes, was again printed at Trévoux. Further editions followed in Paris in 1732, in five volumes, and in 1743, in six. In its turn the publisher Pierre Antoine of Nancy brought out two editions in competition with the original series, and editions appeared at Nancy in 1734 and in 1738-42. Antoine then agreed to cooperate on the edition of 1752, issued at Paris or Nancy in eight or nine volumes, including a supplement of one or two volumes. An abridged edition in two or three quarto volumes came out in Paris in 1762, and the last edition in 1771.

From the second edition of 1721 onwards the Dictionnaire de Trévoux was respected and widely used across the 18th century. Its successive editions grew from a near copy of Furetière's work into a reference work of many volumes, and it became an important source for Ephraim Chambers' Cyclopaedia of 1728 and the Encyclopédie, published in 1751-72.
dicuil: The dates of Dicuil's birth and death are unknown, and everything known of his life comes from his own writings. He was possibly born in the Hebrides, and the scholar J. J. Tierney suggested a date around 760 to 770. He called Ireland our own island and wrote that he had lived on some of the islands north and north-west of Britannia and visited others. He probably belonged to one of the many Irish monasteries in the Frankish kingdom, and from 814 to 816 he taught in one of the schools of Louis the Pious. On grounds of style it has been suggested that he was the same person as the anonymous poet and grammarian known as Hibernicus exul.

At the court school he wrote an astronomical computus in five books of prose and verse, preserved in a manuscript from Saint-Amand, now at Valenciennes, and in another from Saint Martin at Tours. It covers calendars and 19-year lunar cycles, the distances between the Earth, the heavens and the seven planets, the reckoning of Easter and Lent, intercalary days and the speeds of the Moon, Sun and stars, and gives two methods of calculating triangular numbers.

The De mensura orbis terrae, completed in 825, was based on a survey of the world made by order of Emperor Theodosius II in 435, a copy of which the Carolingian court owned. In nine sections it treats Europe, Asia, Africa, Egypt and Ethiopia, the area of the Earth, five great rivers, certain islands, the Tyrrhenian Sea and six high mountains, drawing on Pliny the Elder, Solinus, Orosius and Isidore of Seville. In all he quotes or cites thirty Greek and Latin writers.

Although mainly a compilation, the geography is the only detailed source for the surveys of Theodosius II, and its generally exact quotations help scholars establish the texts of the authors it cites. It also preserves reports from travellers of Dicuil's day, among them the monk Fidelis, who travelled along the canal then still joining the Nile to the Red Sea. Editions were published by C. A. Walckenaer in 1807, G. Parthey in 1870 and Tierney in 1967, whose edition is the only complete English translation.
didda: Didda was a daughter of Simharāja, King of Lohara, and on her mother's side a granddaughter of Bhimadeva Shahi, one of the Hindu Shahi of Kabul. Lohara lay in the Pir Panjal range, on a trade route between western Punjab and Kashmir. At the age of 26 she married Ksemagupta, King of Kashmir, uniting the two kingdoms. She had great influence on affairs even before her regency, and coins have been found that appear to bear both her name and her husband's. Most of what is known of her comes from the Rajatarangini, written by Kalhana in the twelfth century.

When Ksemagupta died in 958 of a fever caught after a hunt, their young son Abhimanyu II succeeded and Didda ruled as regent. She drove troublesome ministers and nobles from office, came close to losing control when they rebelled, and, with the support of others, some of them bribed, executed the captured rebels and their families. Abhimanyu died in 972 and was followed by his small son Nandigupta, which unsettled the Dāmaras, the feudatory landlords.

In 973 she disposed of Nandigupta, in the phrase of the scholar Stein, and of his younger brother Tribhuvanagupta in 975, leaving the youngest grandson Bhimagupta on the throne. After the death of the counsellor Phalunga she took as her lover a herdsman named Tunga, and in 980 had Bhimagupta tortured to death and ruled alone, with Tunga as prime minister. She and Tunga dealt with the discontent of the Dāmaras by force and diplomacy.

Didda died on 8 August 1003, at the age of 79. She is one of the very few female monarchs in Indian history and is sometimes called the Catherine of Kashmir, after Catherine the Great of Russia. Stein judged that her statesmanlike instinct and political ability, in spite of the defects of her character, showed in her remaining the last in peaceful possession of the throne and bequeathing it to her family in undisputed succession.

As heir she adopted a nephew, Samgrāmarāja, eldest son of Udayaraja, though Vigraharāja, who had murdered her parents, pressed claims to Kashmir and Lohara in her lifetime. She fought no wars with neighbours; Mahmud of Ghazni's expedition to Kashmir came in 1015 and failed before the fort of Loharkot.
didessa-river: The Didessa, Dhedheessa in Oromo, rises in the mountains of Gomma and flows north-west to meet the Abay where that river has curved to its southernmost point before turning north. Its drainage area of about 25,800 square kilometres covers parts of the Benishangul-Gumuz Region and the West Welega Zone of the Oromia Region. Its right-bank tributaries include the Enareya, Aet, Wama and Angar, and its chief left-bank tributary is the Dobana. Alexander Bulatovich, who explored the river in the mid-1890s and questioned people living along it, held that below the Angar junction it is free of rapids and could be navigable.

The early 20th-century explorer Herbert Weld Blundell thought the name Didessa had replaced a much older one, finding no use of it before 1861, when d'Abbadie made inquiries in Western Shoa. At his visit in 1905 the Handak forest on the right bank was a favourite haunt of elephants, and at the meeting of the Didessa and the Abay gold-washing began in earnest, continuing along the Nile and down the Dabus; he described quartz pebbles and outcrops strewn over some 15 miles, from which gold washed into the streams.

Although people had lived in the area for a very long time, the river's course from near Nekemte to the Abay was apparently first traced only in 1935, by Dunlop and Taylor. Dejazmach Habte Maryam, the local official in Nekemte, told them that nobody, as far as he knew, had followed it to the junction, warning of the lack of paths, thick bamboo forest, fever and steep mountains, and calling the country fit only for monkeys.

On 14 June 2021 construction of the Anger Irrigation Dam on the Didessa was launched by Shimelis Abdisa, President of the Oromia regional state, and Sileshi Bekele, Minister of Water, Irrigation and Energy, with three years planned for the work.
didyma: Didyma stood on a headland that formed the Milesian Peninsula, in the domain of the city of Miletus. It was the largest and most significant sanctuary on Miletus's territory. The natural link between the two was by sea, but the harbour of Miletus silted up with sediment from the Meander River. A Sacred Way of about 20 kilometres, built in the 6th century BCE and used for festival processions, touched the harbour of Panormos and carried ritual waystations and statues of noblemen and noblewomen, as well as animal and mythological figures. Some of these statues, excavated by Charles Thomas Newton in the 19th century, are now in the British Museum.

The name means twins in Greek, though some suggest a Carian origin. Herodotus and Pausanias placed the origin of the oracle before the Ionian settlement of the coast, but finds are so scarce that the sanctuary cannot be proved archaeologically before the late 8th or early 7th century BCE. Until the Persians destroyed it in 494 BCE, it is supposed to have been administered by the Branchidae, who claimed descent from Branchus, a beloved of Apollo. The priestess sat above the sacred spring, and the Branchidae interpreted her utterances.

After the naval battle of Lade, the Persians under Darius burned the sanctuary in 494 BCE and carried the bronze cult statue of Apollo to Ecbatana. The spring was reported to have ceased to flow. Delphi and Ephesus were rebuilt swiftly, but Didyma remained a ruin until Alexander the Great freed Miletus from the Persians in 334 BCE. The Branchidae marched off into Persian territory, so the oracle's personnel and tradition were broken. Callisthenes, Alexander's court historian, reported that the spring flowed again in 331 BCE.

The first temple of Apollo, built around 700 BCE, surrounded the sacred spring and a laurel tree. A new temple followed from the middle of the 6th century BCE, and planning of the Hellenistic temple began after 334 BCE. Its stylobate measured 51 by 109 metres, and it was surrounded by a double file of Ionic columns, each 19.70 metres high. Its frieze was known for monumental heads of Medusa.

The remains lie a short distance north-west of modern Didim in Aydın Province, Turkey, and the town takes its name from them. Excavations by French and German teams, from 1895 and from 1905 to 1913, uncovered the temple, and in 2013 the foundations of a temple of Artemis were identified. A theatre and baths also belonged to the sanctuary.
die-drome: Die lies in the valley of the Drôme, surrounded by the Glandasse mountain, 2,041 metres high, a massive and steep rocky barrier that separates the area, the Diois, from the Vercors Plateau. It is a commune and a subprefecture of the Drôme department, and its territory is part of a regional natural park. It was a county in the High Middle Ages and was the see of a Catholic diocese, with its church serving as the cathedral.

Habitation in the Neolithic is confirmed by the excavations at Chanqueyras, and a large engraved standing stone and two small menhirs found near the wine cooperative are now in the museum. Late Bronze Age remains were found at La Roche de Marginal. A first settlement seems to have appeared at the beginning of the Roman era, on a small pass beside the Drôme, at the crossroads between the valley and the track to Trièves, and there is much evidence of extensive urbanisation in the 1st century.

At the beginning of the 2nd century Die gained monumental architecture and replaced Luc-en-Diois as the Roman provincial capital of the Celtic people of the northern Voconces. It received the formal status of a colony towards the end of the 2nd century or during the 3rd, and it became an important centre of worship of the goddess Cybele. When the empire showed signs of weakness, between 285 and 305, a wall just over a mile long was built around the town, enclosing 25 hectares and using fragments of funerary monuments. The town had two main gates, that of Saint-Pierre to the west, demolished in 1891, and that of Saint-Marcel to the east.

The first recorded bishop of the ancient diocese of Die was Nicaise in 325, the only Gallic church representative at the First Council of Nicaea. The diocese was merged with that of Valence in 1276, separated at the end of the 17th century and suppressed during the French Revolution.

Die has fewer than 5,000 inhabitants and is the economic and social centre of the Diois. It is best known for its sparkling wine, Clairette de Die, and the cooperative winery is the largest employer of the Diois. Its museum shows the Roman remains and the story of the Diois from prehistory, through its time as an episcopal city in the Middle Ages, to the devastation of the religious wars. Historic monuments stand within the Gallo-Roman walls.
die-gedanken-sind-frei: The original lyricist and composer of the song are unknown. An early version, shaped as a dialogue between a captive and his beloved, was published under the title "Lied des Verfolgten im Thurm. Nach Schweizerliedern" (Song of the persecuted in the tower. After Swiss songs) in Des Knaben Wunderhorn, Vol. III, the folk poetry collection of Achim von Arnim and Clemens Brentano, which appeared around 1805.

Both text and melody are found in Lieder der Brienzer Mädchen (Songs of the girls from Brienz), printed in Bern, Switzerland, between 1810 and 1820. Hoffmann von Fallersleben took the song into his collection Schlesische Volkslieder mit Melodien (Silesian folk songs with melodies), published by Breitkopf & Härtel in 1842, where he gave its source as Neukirch bei Schönau. His rendering became the most popular version.

Each verse ends with the refrain that thoughts are free. The singer says that no one can guess his thoughts, which fly past like shadows at night; no person can know them and no hunter can shoot them. He thinks what he wants and what delights him, though quietly and as is fitting, and no one can deny him his wishes.

One verse praises wine and the singer's girl. Another declares that even if he is locked in the darkest dungeon, his thoughts will tear the gates and walls apart. The last renounces sorrow for laughter of the heart. The order of the verses varies today. The rhyme scheme is a, B, a, B, C, C, d, d, in which the capital letters mark two-syllable feminine rhymes.

From the time of the Carlsbad Decrees and the Age of Metternich, the song was sung in protest against political repression and censorship, above all by the banned Burschenschaften, the student fraternities. After the failure of the German Revolution of 1848 it was itself banned. In 1898 Gustav Mahler set the Arnim and Brentano text for voice and orchestra in his Des Knaben Wunderhorn collection.

The song was important to some anti-Nazi resistance movements in Germany. In 1935 guards at the Lichtenburg concentration camp ordered prisoners to stage a performance for Adolf Hitler's 46th birthday, and the imprisoned lawyer Hans Litten recited the song in reply. In 1942 Sophie Scholl of the White Rose played it on her flute outside the walls of Ulm prison, where her father Robert Scholl was held for calling Hitler a scourge of God. The American musician Pete Seeger released an adaptation in 1966.
die-stem-van-suid-afrika: The anthem was first recorded in 1926, when Betty Steyn performed its first and third verses in England for the Zonophone record label. It was sung in public for the first time on 31 May 1928, at the raising of the new South African national flag. In 1938 the government proclaimed it one of two co-national anthems, together with "God Save the King".

From 1952 it was sung in English as well as Afrikaans, and both versions had official status. "God Save the Queen" ceased to be a co-national anthem in May 1957, though it remained the royal anthem until 1961, when South Africa stopped being a Commonwealth realm. The poem originally had three verses; the government asked Langenhoven to add a fourth with a religious theme.

The song is uplifting in tone and speaks throughout of commitment to the Vaderland (Fatherland) and to God. One verse expresses dedication to the Afrikaners and another recalls the Great Trek of the Voortrekkers. The English version is for the most part a faithful translation of the Afrikaans, with a few minor changes; it leaves out the specific mention of Afrikaners, to avoid alienating British-descent whites who were not counted as Afrikaners.

Many black South Africans disliked the anthem, seeing it as triumphalist and closely tied to the apartheid regime. State President P. W. Botha, by contrast, was fond of it. When South African teams returned to international sport in the early 1990s, agreements were made with the African National Congress that it would not be sung at rugby matches. At a test against New Zealand in 1992 the crowd nevertheless sang it, and an instrumental recording was played over the loudspeakers, which caused controversy. At the 1992 Summer Olympics in Barcelona the South African team used Beethoven's setting of Schiller's "Ode to Joy" instead.

A commission seeking a new anthem in 1993 received 119 entries and chose none. The song kept its status after the 1994 general election and shared it with "Nkosi Sikelel' iAfrika" until 1997, when a composite anthem joined parts of both. Its place in the later anthem has been disputed: some South Africans have called for those parts to be removed because of the apartheid connection, while others defend them as a reconciling gesture. The Afrikaans version remained popular with Afrikaner nationalist groups.
die-wacht-am-rhein: The Swabian merchant Max Schneckenburger, inspired by the success of Nikolaus Becker's song Der Deutsche Rhein, wrote the poem Rheinwache, later renamed Die Wacht am Rhein. Its five original stanzas make a thunderous call to all Germans to defend the German Rhine, so that no enemy sets his foot on its shore, as the fourth stanza puts it. Two more specific stanzas were added by others. The poem was first set to music in Bern by the Swiss organist J. Mendel and performed by the tenor Adolph Methfessel for the Prussian ambassador, von Bunsen, but that version did not become popular.

Unlike the older Heil dir im Siegerkranz, which praised a monarch, the song belongs with others of the period such as the Deutschlandlied that called on Germans to put aside the rivalries of the kingdoms and principalities and form a unified German state. Karl Wilhelm, musical director of the city of Krefeld, received the poem in 1854, seven years after Schneckenburger's death, and wrote the music generally sung with it. He performed it with his men's chorus on 11 June, the silver wedding anniversary of Wilhelm of Prussia, later the emperor Wilhelm I. The setting became popular when sung at Dresden.

After the Franco-Prussian War and the founding of the German Empire, which included Alsace-Lorraine, the song stood beside Heil dir im Siegerkranz as an unofficial second national anthem. Otto von Bismarck honoured the composer and gave the author's family an annual pension. From the First World War to 1945 it remained one of the most popular songs in Germany. The Wehrmachtbericht radio report began with its tune until 1941, and the German offensive of 1944 known as the Battle of the Bulge took Watch on the Rhine as its code name. The French-German enmity was ended in 1963 by the Élysée Treaty. The tune gave Yale University its song Bright College Years, with words by Henry Durand in 1881.
die-zeit: Die Zeit, German for The Time, is a national weekly newspaper published in Hamburg. Its first edition appeared on 21 February 1946. The founding publishers were Gerd Bucerius, Lovis H. Lorenz, Richard Tüngel and Ewald Schmidt di Simoni, and Marion Gräfin Dönhoff joined as an editor in March 1946. The paper appeared under the lettering that Carl Otto Czeschka designed in 1946, inspired by The Times, which shows the British coat of arms between its two words. The paper's founding editorial, Unsere Aufgabe, set out the publishers' own view of its mission.

Dönhoff was publisher of Die Zeit from 1972 until her death in 2002, and in 1983 the former chancellor Helmut Schmidt joined her. Josef Joffe and Michael Naumann later joined them. Editors-in-chief have included Richard Tüngel, Josef Müller-Marein, Dönhoff herself from 1968 to 1972, and Theo Sommer from 1973 to 1992. The paper's first masthead carried a version of the Hamburg crest, but the Hamburg Senate objected that it was a misuse of a state emblem for commercial purposes, and on 27 June 1946 the crest was replaced by the key and crown of the coat of arms of Bremen, with the approval of Bremen's mayor Wilhelm Kaisen. That design is still used as the logo of the whole publishing group.

The Zeitmagazin first appeared as a supplement in 1970, ended in 1999 and was reintroduced on 24 May 2007. A redesign by Mario Garcia in January 1998 introduced the headline type Tiemann-Antiqua and body text in Garamond. The online edition, Zeit Online, merged with Tagesspiegel Online and zoomer.de in 2009 and has published some stories in English. Since March 2017 part of its content has been available only for payment.

The publishing house, Zeitverlag Gerd Bucerius, is owned by the Georg von Holtzbrinck Publishing Group and Dieter von Holtzbrinck Media. The paper appears on Thursdays and is printed in Mörfelden-Walldorf. It is divided into sections including Politik, Streit, Dossier, Geschichte, Wirtschaft, Wissen and Feuilleton. It is regarded as highbrow and as centrist and liberal or left-liberal in outlook, and it often publishes dossiers, essays and excerpts of lectures that look at a single topic from several viewpoints, often in long and detailed articles.

Its large Nordisch format is a trademark, often mocked in literature and cabaret, though in fact it is no bigger than that of a dozen other German newspapers. The circulation was 500,000 in 1993 and 504,072 in the second half of 2012, with an estimated readership of just over 2 million, which made it the most widely read German weekly.
diego-columbus: Diego Columbus was born in Porto Santo, Portugal, in 1479 or 1480, the child of Christopher Columbus and Filipa Moniz Perestrelo. He became a page at the Spanish court in 1492, the year of his father's first voyage. With his half-brother Fernando he was a page to Prince Don Juan, and in 1497 to Queen Isabella.

He spent most of his adult life trying to regain the titles and privileges granted to his father and denied in 1500. His marriage to María de Toledo y Rojas, a niece of the 2nd Duke of Alba and a cousin of King Ferdinand, greatly helped his cause. Ferdinand had forced the match.

In August 1508 Diego was named Governor of the Indies, the post his father had held, and he reached Santo Domingo in July 1509. He made his home there in the Alcázar de Colón, which still stands. In 1511 a royal council declared Hispaniola, Puerto Rico, Jamaica and Cuba to be under his power by right of his father, confirmed his titles of viceroy and admiral as hereditary but honorific, and gave him a tenth of the net royal income. Uraba and Veragua were excluded. Factions soon formed between his followers and Ferdinand's royal officials, and in 1514 the king recalled him. He spent five years in Spain pressing his claims, and in 1520 Charles restored his powers.

He returned to Santo Domingo on 12 November 1520, during a native revolt near the Franciscan missions on the Cumana River. In 1521 he invested in Bartolomé de las Casas's plan to settle the Cumana area. Its failure was blamed on Diego and cost him the king's confidence. On 26 December 1522 enslaved Jolof workers on his sugar plantation began the first major slave rebellion in the Americas. Many escaped into the mountains and founded maroon communities among the surviving Taíno; many others were captured, and Diego had them hanged.

Charles reprimanded Diego in 1523 for his defiance of royal power on Cuba and for the Cumana failure, and recalled him to Spain. He died there on 23 February 1526, and his rents, offices and titles in the New World fell into dispute among his descendants. In 1536 a compromise made his son Luis Colón de Toledo Admiral of the Indies. Luis gave up all other rights in return for an annuity of 10,000 ducats, Jamaica as a fief, an estate on the Isthmus of Panama and the titles of Duke of Veragua and Marquess of Jamaica.
diego-de-almagro: Diego de Almagro was born of humble origins, the illegitimate son of Juan de Montenegro and Elvira Gutiérrez, in the village of Almagro or in Malagón in Ciudad Real, and took his surname from the village. In Seville he served in the household of Luis Gonzalez de Polanco, who used his influence to secure him a passage to the New World after Almagro stabbed another servant.

He landed at Santa María la Antigua del Darién, in Panama, on 30 June 1514, with the expedition of Pedro Arias Dávila. There he received an encomienda and farmed, and on an expedition under Gaspar de Espinosa he became a close friend of Francisco Pizarro and Hernando de Luque. By 1524 the three had formed an association to conquer lands to the south. He lost an eye to an arrow at Punta Quemada.

After Pizarro's defeat of the Inca army under Atahualpa at the Battle of Cajamarca in 1532, Almagro joined him with more men and arms. In August 1534 he founded Santiago de Quito near Lake Colta, to forestall Sebastián de Belalcázar, and in December of that year Trujillo, which he named after Pizarro's birthplace.

Charles V divided the conquered lands between Nueva Castilla, for Pizarro, and Nueva Toledo, for Almagro. Almagro left Cuzco on 3 July 1535 with about 750 Spaniards, following the Inca trail and then crossing the Andes, where cold and hunger killed Spaniards and, above all slaves unused to the climate. He took possession of Chile in the Copiapó valley and explored as far as the Aconcagua. Almagro found neither gold nor cities, and his troops plundered local property and carried off captives as porters and slaves.

Almagro returned to Cuzco in 1537. On the night of 8 April 1537 his men seized the city and imprisoned Hernando and Gonzalo Pizarro, and on 12 July 1537 they defeated an army sent by Francisco Pizarro at the Battle of Abancay. Hernando was freed in return for control of Cuzco. In April 1538 the Almagristas were beaten at Las Salinas and Rodrigo Orgóñez was killed. Almagro fled to Cuzco but was captured, and his appeal to the king was ignored.

He was garrotted in his dungeon and beheaded on 8 July 1538. His son Diego de Almagro II, called El Mozo, was proclaimed governor of Peru by the conspirators who killed Pizarro on 26 June 1541. He was defeated at Chupas on 16 September 1542 and executed in Cuzco.
diego-de-landa: Diego de Landa Calderón was born on 12 November 1524 in Cifuentes, Guadalajara, Spain, and became a Franciscan friar in 1541. He was sent to Yucatán as one of the first Franciscans, arriving in 1549, to bring the Roman Catholic faith to the Maya peoples after the Spanish conquest. The Franciscan order held a spiritual monopoly granted by the Spanish crown, and Landa worked to strengthen its power and convert the Maya.

His first post was the mission of San Antonio in Izamal, which remained his main residence. According to Cogolludo, his chief Franciscan biographer, he walked the length of the peninsula preaching in remote villages, and at Cupules he came upon a group of 300 about to sacrifice a boy, whom he released.
