After hearing that Catholic Maya continued to worship idols, Landa ordered an Inquisition at Maní, which ended on 12 July 1562 with an auto de fé in which a disputed number of Maya codices, 27 books according to Landa, and about 5,000 alleged cult images were burned. The Inquisition used physical abuse: Maya nobles were jailed pending interrogation, and many nobles and commoners were hoisted by their bound hands, often with stone weights on the ankles or lashes to the back.

At his later trial Landa denied that any deaths or injuries directly resulted. He believed in a large underground network of apostasy led by displaced native priests and held that a papal bull, Exponi nobis, justified his actions. Bishop Toral sent him back to Spain to stand trial, and he was strongly condemned before the Council of the Indies. In 1569 a committee of doctors absolved him, and after Toral died in 1571 Philip II appointed Landa the second bishop of Yucatán.

Landa wrote the Relación de las cosas de Yucatán, a catalogue of Maya religion, language, culture and writing, around 1566 on his return to Spain. The original is lost; the surviving text is an abridgement made around 1660, rediscovered in the 19th century and published in a French-Spanish edition by Charles Etienne Brasseur de Bourbourg in 1862. It is the main contemporary source for Maya history.

For the writing system Landa asked two literate informants of a ruling dynasty to write the sign for each letter of the Spanish alphabet. The result was later judged inaccurate, until in the 1950s the Soviet linguist Yuri Knorozov showed that it was not an alphabet but a syllabary, which proved instrumental in the decipherment.
diego-de-losada: Losada was born in 1511 into a minor noble family, the son of Álvaro Pérez de Losada, Lord of Rionegro, and Catalina de Osorio. He grew up in Rionegro del Puente and at fifteen entered the service of the Count of Benavente, where he received a military education alongside other young nobles, among them Pedro de Reinoso. In 1533 the two sailed to the Caribbean, reaching Puerto Rico and soon afterwards Venezuela.

He first joined the expedition of Antonio Sedeño, which sought wealth along the Meta River and by 1536 had reached Maracapana and the Venezuelan savannah. The campaign was marked by severe abuses against Indigenous peoples and quarrels among the Spaniards. After the Audiencia ordered Sedeño's arrest he was poisoned on the return journey, and Losada took command of one faction and made his way to Coro.

Governor Juan Pérez de Tolosa made him field marshal, and in 1546 he took part in the arrest and execution of Juan de Carvajal, an official who had defied royal authority. He joined campaigns south of El Tocuyo and the founding of Nueva Segovia de Barquisimeto in 1552, held encomiendas and municipal offices in Barquisimeto and El Tocuyo, and married Catalina de Rojas.

In 1565 Governor Alonso Bernáldez de Quirós charged him with subduing the Caracas region, a commission confirmed by Pedro Ponce de León. Leaving El Tocuyo in January 1567 with a large force, he met fierce resistance from Indigenous groups led by Guaicaipuro, and founded the city probably on 25 July 1567. He then set up Nuestra Señora de Carballeda to secure access to the coast, and in 1568 he crushed a confederation of caciques formed to attack the settlement.

After the death of Governor Ponce de León in 1569, Losada sought the governorship of Venezuela, presenting his credentials in Santo Domingo and petitioning the Crown, but the post went to another candidate. He returned to Venezuela and died soon afterwards. The place and date of his death are uncertain.
diego-de-montemayor: Historians dispute Montemayor's date and place of birth and the identity of his parents; Antonio Morales Goméz and Carlos Pérez Maldonado have given 1530, without proving it. The Catalogo de Pasajeros a Indias records a Diego de Montemayor sailing for New Spain from Sevilla, a resident of Málaga, son of Juan de Montemayor and Mayor Hernández and husband of Inés Rodríguez. His probable first wife, Inez Rodríguez, came with him from Spain to the New World in 1548.

Montemayor became governor of Nuevo León in 1588, after he had reconquered the province. His Monterrey was the third attempt at a settlement there: the earlier ones, Santa Lucia and San Luis Rey de Francia, were led by Alberto del Canto, later his bitter enemy, and by Luis de Carabajal y Cueva. He named the new city Ciudad Metropolitana de Nuestra Señora de Monterrey, partly to win the favour of the viceroy, Gaspar de Zúñiga y Acevedo, Count of Monterrey. He brought forty settlers from Saltillo: nine married couples, three single men, fourteen boys, four girls and one Indian named Domingo Manuel.

He may have married three times, to Inez Rodríguez, María de Esquivel and Juana Porcalla de la Cerda, and had a child by each: Inez, Diego and Estefanía. His third wife turned her attention to Alberto del Canto while Montemayor was often away during the Chichimeca War. When he confronted her over the affair he drew his sword and killed her. He fled north into the wilderness but was eventually cleared of all charges, perhaps because a law of the time allowed a man to kill an unfaithful wife.

Estefanía married Alberto del Canto and had three children with him, but the two separated in 1596 and she returned to Monterrey with her father; her children took the name Montemayor. Montemayor never carried out his vow to kill del Canto. He died about 1611 in Monterrey and is believed to be buried where the Convento de San Francisco once stood. The city he founded is the capital of the Mexican state of Nuevo León.
diego-de-vargas: Diego de Vargas Zapata y Luján Ponce de León y Contreras was appointed governor of New Mexico in 1688, but he did not arrive to take up his duties until 22 February 1691. The colonists driven out by the Pueblo Revolt had been living in exile at El Paso del Norte, now Ciudad Juárez. The Spanish return was prompted by fears of French advances into the Mississippi valley and by the wish for a defensive frontier against nomadic peoples on the northern borders.

In 1692 Vargas marched on Santa Fe with a small force of soldiers and Pueblo auxiliaries, seven cannons and one Franciscan priest, accompanied by the Zia war captain Bartolomé de Ojeda. He promised clemency to the Pueblo people assembled there if they swore allegiance to Charles II of Spain and returned to the Christian faith, and after long persuasion they agreed. Vargas wrote to the Conde de Galve, viceroy of New Spain, that it was the thirteenth town he had reconquered in this manner. He also reached a peace with Luis Tupatu, who was made governor of thirteen villages of northern New Mexico.

Vargas returned on 16 December 1693 with about 800 people, among them 100 soldiers. After the recapture of the town, the 70 Pueblo warriors who had held it were executed on 30 December, and about 400 women and children of their families were sentenced to ten years' servitude among the colonists. In 1696 fourteen pueblos rose again, killing five missionaries and thirty-four settlers, and Vargas's retribution was severe and prolonged. Many Pueblo people fled to the Apache or Navajo or onto the Great Plains.

Vargas had prayed to the Virgin Mary as La Conquistadora for a peaceful re-entry, and the feast he held in her honour continues as the Fiestas de Santa Fe. A re-enactment of his entry, The Entrada, drew protests from Native Americans from 2015 and was later removed from the fiesta. On 18 June 2020 the city removed his statue, which was afterwards displayed at the New Mexico History Museum. Like many wealthy subjects of the Spanish Empire, Vargas owned slaves; he freed his coachman Ignacio de la Cruz.
diego-gelmirez: Diego Gelmírez, also written Xelmírez, was probably born at Catoira, where his father Gelmiro was custodian of the castle. He was educated at the court of Alfonso VI, king of León, Galicia and Castile. In 1092 Raymond, count of Galicia, made him his notary and secretary, and in 1093 he administered the church of Compostela. After the death in 1095 of Dalmatius, the first bishop of Compostela, the people of the see asked the king to name Diego administrator again during the vacancy.

The pope authorised a new election in 1099, and Diego was elected in 1100, anointed at Easter 1101 and granted a pallium by Pope Paschal II the following year, though his see was not yet a metropolitan one. Alfonso VI gave him secular rule of the city, and he worked to make Compostela a major place of pilgrimage. In 1120 Pope Callixtus II raised the see to an archbishopric and appointed him papal legate to Spain.

In Galicia's civil wars he changed sides more than once. Late in 1109 or early in 1110 he took the lead, with the knight Arias Pérez, of a brotherhood opposed to Pedro Fróilaz de Traba, guardian of the heir Alfonso Raimúndez. When he negotiated the surrender of Castrelo de Miño in 1110, Arias had him arrested with Pedro and Alfonso. Released, Diego joined the separatists and in 1111 crowned Alfonso Raimúndez King of Galicia in opposition to Queen Urraca and her husband Alfonso the Battler.

Urraca stripped him of his secular authority late in 1113 at the demand of townspeople seeking communal rights, but restored it within a year. In 1120, according to the Historia Compostelana, she ordered the leading men of Galicia to do homage to him as their lord, yet in the summer of 1121 she had him arrested at Castrelo; popular support forced his release. That year he razed an illegal castle built by Munio Peláez near Compostela. In 1126, after Urraca's death, he put down Arias's rebellion, besieging him at Lobeiro and Tabeirós until he surrendered. The Historia Compostelana, covering his episcopacy from 1100 to 1139, records these quarrels as a kind of gesta of his life.
diego-lopez-v-de-haro: Diego López was the son of Diego López III de Haro and Constanza de Bearne, and through his paternal grandmother, Urraca Alfonso de León, a great-grandson of King Alfonso IX of León. His brother Lope Díaz III de Haro also held the lordship of Biscay. Born most likely around 1250, he married the infanta Violant of Castile, daughter of King Alfonso X of Castile, in 1282. Their children included Lope Díaz IV de Haro and María Díaz de Haro, who married Juan Núñez II de Lara.

On 25 April 1295, after the death of King Sancho IV of Castile, he used the instability at the court of the young Ferdinand IV of Castile to take the lordship of Biscay, which belonged by right to his niece, María Díaz I de Haro; this earned him the nickname el Intruso. That summer the infante John of Castile, her husband, turned the lordship over to him, and in 1300 María renounced her claim in return for other towns. On 15 June 1300 he made the fishing village of Bilbao a town under the authority of the lords of Biscay.

The infante John soon pressed his wife's claim again. Diego López sided with the infante Henry of Castile, and on Henry's death in 1303 he and Juan Manuel, Prince of Villena, inherited his possessions. In 1304 the king confiscated his lands, and at the Cortes of Medina del Campo in 1305 he arrived with three hundred knights, refused to give up Biscay and appealed to the pope. After Pope Clement V declared the renunciation of 1300 invalid, an agreement of 1307 let him keep Biscay for life, to pass to María on his death, and the king made him Mayordomo mayor.

In 1309 he joined Ferdinand IV's war against the Kingdom of Granada. He argued without success for an attack on Gibraltar rather than the siege of Algeciras that the king chose, and stayed with the king when the infante John and others deserted the camp in October 1309. Late that year he fell ill with gout. He died in the camp at Algeciras in the winter of 1310 and was buried in the Monasterio de San Francisco de Burgos, where Violant also lay, and María Díaz I de Haro took possession of Biscay.
diego-luis-de-san-vitores: San Vitores was born in Burgos on 12 November 1627 to the nobleman Don Jerónimo de San Vitores and Doña María Alonso Maluenda, and was baptised Diego Jerónimo de San Vitores y Alonso de Maluendo. His parents wanted him to follow a military career, but he chose religion, entering the Jesuit novitiate in 1640 and being ordained a priest in 1651. Granted a mission in the Philippines, he stopped at Guam on the way in 1662 and vowed to return. Three years later, through his ties to the royal court, he persuaded King Philip IV of Spain and Queen Mariana of Austria to order a mission there.

He sailed from Acapulco in 1668 and landed at the village of Hagåtña, where Chief Kepuha greeted him and Kepuha's family gave land for the mission. On 2 February 1669 San Vitores founded the first Catholic church at Hagåtña, dedicated to the sweet name of Mary. According to the Guampedia editor Tanya Champaco Mendiola, the Chamorros at first welcomed the missionaries and hundreds converted, but the enthusiasm faded as the teaching that the baptised were equal unsettled their caste system and the Jesuits rejected the veneration of ancestors, whose skulls families kept in places of honour in their homes.

After Kepuha died in 1669 relations worsened, and in 1671 the Chamorro–Spanish War began, led on the Chamorro side by Maga'låhi Hurao; peace was negotiated after several attacks on the mission. San Vitores had wanted to follow Francis Xavier, who used no soldiers in India, but he came to think a military presence necessary to protect the priests. In 1672 he ordered churches built in four villages, including Merizo. Later that year, as Chamorro resistance grew, he was killed together with his sacristan Pedro Calungsod.

His cause for beatification was opened on 16 March 1695, and after years of advocacy by Oscar Calvo, Pope John Paul II beatified him in Rome in 1985. He remains a contested figure. Chamorro writers such as the poet Craig Santos Perez criticise him, and scholars including Vince Diaz, Cynthia Ross Wiecko and Francis X. Hezel link the mission to a war of conquest and to the collapse of the Chamorro population, which the first Spanish census of 1710 found reduced to a few thousand; Wiecko attributes most of the decline to introduced diseases and part of it to the wars.
diego-portales: Portales was born in Santiago on 16 June 1793, the son of José Santiago Portales y Larraín, a superintendent of the royal mint. He studied at the Colegio de Santiago and attended law classes at the National Institute in 1813, then followed the men of his family into trade. He married his cousin Josefa Portales y Larraín on 15 August 1819; their two daughters died within days of birth and she died in 1821. He never remarried, but had three children with Constanza Nordenflicht.

In 1821 he left the Mint and opened a trading house, Portales, Cea and Co., in Valparaíso with a branch in Lima. It took over the government monopoly, or estanco, on tobacco, tea and liquor in return for servicing Chile's foreign debt, but in the disorder of the time the monopoly could not be enforced and the firm went bankrupt. His political followers kept the name estanqueros.

Portales became the intellectual leader of the conservatives, the pelucones, and in 1827 founded the satirical journal El Hambriento against the liberal pipiolos. After the conservative victory in the Revolution of 1829 he was named Minister of the Interior and Foreign Affairs and Minister of War and Navy on 6 April 1830, and held these posts again under Fernando Errázuriz Aldunate and José Joaquín Prieto. He never took the presidency, fearing to be bound by factional promises, but he repressed liberals, purged opponents from the army, set up a civil militia and made Catholicism the state religion. In a letter of 1822 he had called democracy an absurdity in countries lacking civic virtue and argued for a strong central government of virtuous men.

During the war with the Peru-Bolivian Confederation the government imposed martial law. On 3 June 1837 Colonel José Antonio Vidaurre seized Portales at the barracks of Quillota and marched on Valparaíso; when Rear Admiral Manuel Blanco Encalada defeated him at the Battle of Barón, Captain Santiago Florín had Portales shot on 6 June. The murder turned opinion behind the war. Historians such as Ramón Sotomayor Valdés and Alberto Edwards have praised him, while Benjamín Vicuña Mackenna, Sergio Villalobos and Gabriel Salazar take a negative view. His remains were found in Santiago's Metropolitan Cathedral in March 2005 and reburied there on 20 June 2006.
diego-rivera: Diego Rivera was born on 8 December 1886 in Guanajuato, the son of a well-to-do couple. He began drawing at three, and from the age of ten studied at the Academy of San Carlos in Mexico City. The governor of Veracruz sponsored his further study in Europe, where he arrived in 1907. He settled in Paris among the artists of Montparnasse, and Amedeo Modigliani painted his portrait in 1914. From 1913 to 1917 he embraced Cubism, and around 1917, inspired by Paul Cézanne, he turned to Post-Impressionism, with simple forms and large patches of vivid colour.

Rivera returned to Mexico in 1921 to join the government mural programme planned by José Vasconcelos, which included José Clemente Orozco, David Alfaro Siqueiros and Rufino Tamayo. His first significant mural, Creation, was painted in January 1922. That year he joined the Mexican Communist Party, and his later murals, in fresco only, treated Mexican society and the 1910 Revolution in large, simplified figures and bold colours with an evident Aztec influence. The series at the Secretariat of Public Education in Mexico City was begun in September 1922 and finished in 1928.

In 1929 he was expelled from the party because of suspected Trotskyite sympathies. In the United States he painted in San Francisco, and in 1931 the Museum of Modern Art in New York held a retrospective. From 1932 to 1933 he painted the twenty-seven frescoes of Detroit Industry, partly paid for by Edsel Ford. His mural Man at the Crossroads for Rockefeller Center was destroyed in 1933 after he refused to remove a portrait of Lenin, and he repainted it in 1934 in Mexico City.

Rivera was an atheist. His fresco A Dream of a Sunday Afternoon in the Alameda Park, painted in 1946, included a sign reading that God does not exist, and the work was not shown for nine years until he agreed to remove the inscription. It also gave the figure of La Calavera Catrina, created by José Guadalupe Posada, indigenous features. He married Frida Kahlo in 1929, divorced her in 1939 and remarried her in 1940. He died on 24 November 1957, and the government of Mexico has declared his works historic monuments.
diego-rodriguez-porcelos: Diego Rodríguez Porcelos was the second Count of Castile, succeeding his father Rodrigo in 873. Unlike his father he did not govern Álava, which fell to Count Vela Jiménez. Between 882 and 884, under the mandate of King Alfonso III of Asturias, he directed the repoblación, the resettlement, of Burgos and Ubierna.

Shortly before 882 he built a castle at Pancorbo, from which he faced a large Arab army trying to annex the valley of the Ebro in two campaigns, in 882 and 883. He also built a defensive line along the river Arlanzón, and the outpost he founded in 884 grew into the city of Burgos. He appears to have restored the episcopal see of Oca, the ancient Auca.

The chronicles do not agree on when and where he died. The most probable account is that of the Chronica Naierensis, which records that he was killed at Cornudilla on 31 January 885, most likely in battle against Muslim troops loyal to the Banu Qasi. His body was supposedly buried in the hermitage of San Felices de Oca, at present-day Villafranca Montes de Oca. After his death his successors divided Castile into many counties, until 932.

The name of the mother of his children, who were probably very young at his death, is not known. His son Gómez Díaz appears in 932 as alférez of Count Fernán González, and Gonzalo Díaz is recorded on 3 February 921 giving watermills on the Arlanzón to the Monastery of San Pedro de Cardeña. A third son, Fernando Díaz, was count in Lantarón and Cerezo. In Burgos an equestrian statue of Diego by the sculptor Juan de Ávalos, made in 1983, stands near the Museum of Human Evolution, and a sixteenth-century statue of him is part of the Arco de Santa María.
diego-silang: Diego Silang y Andaya was born on 16 December 1730 in Aringay, then part of Pangasinan and now in La Union. His father was Pangasinense and his mother Ilocano. He was baptised on 7 January 1731 in Vigan, in the then undivided province of Ilocos, where as a boy he worked as a messenger for a local Castilian priest. Fluent in Spanish, he carried correspondence from the Ilocos to Manila, journeys on which he first saw the injustices of colonial rule.

Spain was allied with France in the Seven Years' War, and the British seizure of Manila in October 1762 inspired risings in the far north of Luzon. Silang at first wanted to replace Spanish functionaries in the Ilocos with native-born officials and offered to lead Ilocano forces on the Spanish side. The Spanish administrators instead transferred their powers to the Catholic Bishop of Nueva Segovia, who rejected the offer. The revolt drew on grievances over Spanish taxation and abuses and on Silang's belief that church and government in the Ilocos should be led by trained Ilocano officials.

Joaquín Martínez de Zúñiga, writing in 1805, gave a hostile account. He called Silang very quick and artful and said he persuaded the chiefs and many commoners, especially those of Vigan, that to keep the Catholic faith they must arm against the Spaniards and deliver them to the English. Armed men demanded that the alcalde give up his staff of government to the vicar-general; he did so and escaped from the province. The rebels then demanded of the bishop-elect, a Dominican named Ustariz, an exemption from the tribute, while Silang gathered troops for wider operations.

Silang was killed on 28 May 1763, aged 32, by a friend, a Spanish-Ilocano mestizo named Miguel Vicos, whom church authorities had paid and who was helped by Pedro Becbec. Gabriela Silang was forced to retreat to what is now Abra, led her troops towards Vigan and was driven back; she and her men were hanged on 20 September 1763, she last of all. The Philippine Navy has named two frigates after Diego Silang, one in service from 1976 to 1990 and one that entered service in 2025.
diego-velazquez: Velázquez was born in Seville, the first child of Juan Rodríguez de Silva, a notary, and Jerónima Velázquez, and was baptised on 6 June 1599. His paternal grandparents were Portuguese and had moved to Seville decades earlier. When offered knighthood in 1658 he claimed descent from the lesser nobility in order to qualify, though his grandparents may have been tradespeople. Raised in modest circumstances, he showed an early gift for art and was apprenticed to Francisco Pacheco, a learned teacher who encouraged his students' intellectual development. A contract of 17 September 1611 formalised a six-year apprenticeship.

By the early 1620s Velázquez had established his reputation in Seville. After the death of the court painter Rodrigo de Villandrando in December 1622, the Count-Duke of Olivares summoned him to court, and on 30 August 1623 Philip IV sat for him. The king was pleased, and Olivares commanded him to move to Madrid, his home for the rest of his life. He spent a year and a half in Italy from 1629 and returned in January 1631. For the Palacio del Buen Retiro he painted equestrian portraits of the royal family and The Surrender of Breda, his only surviving painting of contemporary history, in which the Spanish general stands before his Dutch counterpart as an equal.

He made a second journey to Italy in 1649, accompanied by his assistant Juan de Pareja, then a slave, and painted Pope Innocent X in Rome. He returned to Spain in 1651. In 1652 the king chose him as aposentador mayor, responsible for the court's quarters, an office that interfered with his painting. Las Meninas, completed in 1656, four years before his death, is regarded as his masterpiece.

He began in a precise tenebrist style and later developed a freer manner with bold brushwork. He used Caravaggio's realism and chiaroscuro only as a starting point, with a fluid handling of light and shade closer to Titian's. On his first trip to Italy he adopted canvases prepared with a light-gray ground, which gave greater luminosity and a cool, silvery range of colour. He painted directly from life. He is estimated to have produced between 110 and 120 known canvases, and no etchings or engravings.

His reputation languished in the 18th century, but by its end his importance was recognised, and in 1778 Goya made etchings after his paintings. In 1957 Pablo Picasso recreated Las Meninas in 44 variations.
diego-velazquez-de-cuellar: Little is known of Velázquez's early life. He was born in Cuéllar, in the Segovia region of Spain, around 1465, served for a time in the Spanish military in Naples and then lived in Seville. In September 1493 he was one of 1,500 men who sailed with Columbus on his second voyage, and he never returned to Spain. On Hispaniola he gained the regard of Bartholomew Columbus and became a trusted lieutenant of the governor Nicolás de Ovando. In July 1503 he put down a Taíno revolt at Jaragua and then founded Salvatierra de la Zabana and other towns. By 1511 he was one of the wealthiest men on the island.

King Ferdinand instructed Diego Columbus to conquer Cuba in the hope of gold and Native labour, and Velázquez was chosen to lead the expedition, which he had to finance himself. He sailed in January 1511 with four ships and three hundred men, among them Hernán Cortés and Pedro de Alvarado. A Taíno force led by Hatuey, formerly a chief from Hispaniola, resisted and was defeated after two months. According to Bartolomé de las Casas, Hatuey was captured and burned alive. Baracoa was settled by August 1511, and Pánfilo de Narváez became second in command.

In 1513 three expeditions went west; Narváez defeated a force of 2,500 Taínos under the chief Caguax, the last significant resistance. By 1515 Velázquez had founded Bayamo, Trinidad, Sancti Spiritus, Havana, Camagüey and Santiago de Cuba, which became the capital.

He rewarded relatives and associates with encomiendas, and by 1522 the encomenderos controlled almost 3,000 Indian labourers. From Cuba he sent Francisco Hernández de Córdoba to the Yucatán in 1517 and Juan de Grijalva in 1518. He then chose Cortés to lead a third expedition, but doubted him and tried to replace him. Cortés sailed in February 1519 with ten ships and about 500 men. When Velázquez sent Narváez against him in 1520 with about 1,000 men, Narváez was defeated and most of his force joined Cortés. Velázquez lost a large fortune, and Cuba was left depopulated.

Diego Colón sent Alonso Zuazo in January 1521 to replace Velázquez, but Velázquez was restored in July 1523. In 1522 Carlos I recognised Cortés as governor of New Spain. Velázquez died on 11 or 12 June 1524 and was buried under the altar steps of the new cathedral in Santiago. At his death he was said to be the richest Spaniard in the Americas. He had founded towns that remain important and made Cuba a centre of trade and a staging point for expeditions of conquest.
dieric-bouts: Dieric Bouts, also called Dirk Bouts in some museums and institutions, may have studied under Rogier van der Weyden, and his work was influenced by van der Weyden and by Jan van Eyck. He was married twice and had four children. His two daughters went to convents, and his two sons became painters who carried the Bouts workshop into the mid-16th century. The elder, Dieric the Younger, appears to have continued his father's style until his early death in 1491, and the younger, Aelbrecht, developed a style unmistakably his own.

Bouts' earliest work is the Triptych of the Virgin's Life in the Prado in Madrid, dated about 1445. In 1464 the Leuven Confraternity of the Holy Sacrament commissioned from him the Altarpiece of the Holy Sacrament for St Peter's Church. Its central panel, the Last Supper, shows Christ as a priest consecrating the Eucharistic host rather than focusing on the betrayal by Judas. It is the first Flemish panel painting of the subject, and its four servants, dressed in Flemish clothes, are most likely portraits of members of the confraternity.

After he became city painter of Leuven in 1468, Bouts received commissions for the Town Hall. The first was an altarpiece of the Last Judgment (1468–1470), of which two wings survive in Lille and a fragment of Christ in Stockholm. The second was the Justice Panels (1470–1475), which occupied him until his death in 1475. He finished one panel and began a second, both showing the life of the 11th-century Holy Roman Emperor Otto III; they are now in Brussels, and the other two panels planned were never completed.

Many of his authentic works are small devotional panels, usually of the Virgin and Child, such as the Davis Madonna in New York. His 1462 Portrait of a Man in the National Gallery in London is the first instance of a sitter in three-quarter view before a discernible background with a glimpse of landscape through a window.

Bouts was among the first northern painters to use a single vanishing point, as in his Last Supper, where the lines of the central room converge above Christ's head. The small side room has its own vanishing point, and neither falls on the horizon of the landscape seen through the windows. Only the Last Supper and the Justice Panels are definitely his; the Last Judgment panels and the triptych of the Martyrdom of St Erasmus are fairly secure attributions, and many others are disputed. A retrospective, Dieric Bouts, Creator of Images, was held at the museum of Leuven in 2023.
dies-irae: The Dies irae is a Latin sequence, a medieval poem with accentual stress, rhymed lines and a trochaic metre. It is attributed to Thomas of Celano, a Franciscan, or to Latino Malabranca Orsini, a lector at the Dominican studium at Santa Sabina in Rome. Some sources trace it much further back, to Gregory the Great, Bernard of Clairvaux or Bonaventure. The text is found, with slight differences, in a 13th-century Franciscan calendar missal in the national library at Naples. The manuscript must date from 1253 to 1255, since it lacks the name of Clare of Assisi, who was canonised in 1255.

The hymn appears to draw on the Vulgate text of the prophet Zephaniah, 1:15-16, a day of wrath and tribulation, and on images from the Book of Revelation, from Matthew's account of the sheep and goats and from the Jewish prayer Unetanneh Tokef.

The poem describes the Last Judgment. A trumpet summons souls before the throne of God, where the saved are delivered and the unsaved cast into eternal flames. The last two stanzas differ in structure from the rest. The penultimate, the Lacrimosa, has two rhyming couplets in place of rhyming triplets, and the final stanza, Pie Iesu, has assonance instead of rhyme, with catalectic lines. Some scholars therefore think they were added to suit the poem to liturgical use.

The Dies irae was for centuries the sequence of the Requiem Mass in the Roman Rite, and it appears in the Roman Missal of 1962. Its place in the Mass is evident in the great settings by Mozart and Verdi. The liturgical reforms of 1969 and 1970 removed it from funerals and other Masses for the dead, on the ground that it overemphasised judgment, fear and despair. It was kept in an edited form as a hymn in the Liturgy of the Hours on All Souls' Day and in the last week before Advent.

The first polyphonic settings that include it are by Engarandus Juvenis in 1490 and Antoine Brumel in 1516. The plainchant melody, in the Dorian mode, became one of the most quoted in music, after Berlioz used it in the Symphonie fantastique. Walter Scott quoted its first two stanzas in The Lay of the Last Minstrel, and Goethe used three in the Cathedral scene of Faust. William Josiah Irons made an English version in 1849.
diesel-engine: In 1878 Rudolf Diesel, then a student at the Polytechnikum in Munich, attended the lectures of Carl von Linde, who explained that steam engines convert just 6 to 10 percent of heat energy into work, whereas the Carnot cycle allows much more. According to Diesel this gave him the idea of a highly efficient engine working on that cycle. He was also shown a fire piston, a traditional fire starter based on rapid compression.

Diesel sought firms to build the engine and, with help from Moritz Schröter and Max Gutermuth, persuaded both Krupp in Essen and the Maschinenfabrik Augsburg. He obtained a patent on 23 February 1893, signed a contract with Krupp on 10 April, and on 24 April both firms agreed to build a single prototype at Augsburg. In the winter of 1893 and 1894 he redesigned the engine and added an air-blast injection system. After the engine ran for 88 revolutions in February 1894 the Maschinenfabrik Augsburg's stock rose by 30 percent. The engine still caused problems, and Krupp considered cancelling its contract before a third prototype was rushed together.

In a diesel engine only air, or air mixed with exhaust gas, is compressed in the cylinder. The compression raises its temperature enough to ignite atomised fuel injected at high pressure, so no spark plug is needed. Torque is controlled by changing the amount of fuel injected rather than by throttling the air, and the engine is also called a compression-ignition engine. Its fuel efficiency is better than most other combustion engines because of the high compression ratio and the lack of throttling, reaching up to 43 percent in passenger cars and 55 percent in large two-stroke marine engines. High-speed engines above 1,000 rpm power trucks, buses, tractors and cars, while slow-speed engines run below 300 rpm.

In 1893 Diesel suggested that the engine might power lorries, and the first diesel lorries came to market in 1924. The first diesel locomotives appeared in 1913, and diesel engines later replaced steam on all non-electrified railways. Nearly all modern diesel locomotives are diesel–electric, the engine driving a generator that powers electric traction motors. Large ships use slow two-stroke diesels, and submarines are usually diesel–electric.

Before the Second World War diesel engines also powered aircraft, including the airship Hindenburg. Diesels drive construction and farm machinery and stationary generators. In passenger cars they were long popular in bigger models and have been used in smaller cars in Europe since the 1980s.
diessenhofen: Diessenhofen is first mentioned in 757, as Deozincova, in a deed of the Abbey of St Gall that refers to an Alamanni village. Stone and Bronze Age objects, a hoard of Roman coins from 251 to 270 and the remains of three towers of the Danube-Iller-Rhein limes show earlier settlement. In 1178 Count Hartmann III of Kyburg raised the village to a town and probably appointed a family of ministeriales as its stewards. He used the castle and the bridge over the Rhine to defend his possessions on both banks, and gave the town a measure of self-government. By 1245 at the latest it was the centre of a bailiwick.

After the Kyburgs died out in 1264 the town passed to the Habsburgs. By 1320 the citizens chose a town council of eight to twelve members. Diessenhofen was captured in 1460 after a ten-day siege during the Swiss conquest of Thurgau, but kept its high and low courts, its customs and tax rights and its castle. After 1574 it also gained rights over the left bank of the Rhine and the possessions of Paradise Monastery.

The town lies on the south shore of the High Rhine, opposite the German town of Gailingen am Hochrhein, in the municipality's 10.12 square kilometres. About 42 per cent of the land is farmed and about 36 per cent forested. The district has been known since the Early Middle Ages as the granary of Thurgau for its grain fields, and viticulture is mentioned there in the 9th century. The town was largely self-supplied until the 19th century and collected food from farms for Schaffhausen and Zürich. Bridge and transit tariffs gave most of its income until the abolition of internal tariffs in 1848.

Diessenhofen had 4,085 inhabitants in December 2020 and is part of Frauenfeld District. Its Altstadt centres on the Siegelturm, a tower where seals and official documents are kept, and the covered bridge over the Rhine, rebuilt in 1814, leads to Gailingen. Unterhof Castle, the Rhine bridge, the city walls with the Siegelturm and the former Dominican monastery of St Katharinental are listed as Swiss heritage sites of national significance. One of the three data centres of the bank messaging network SWIFT has been in the town since 2009.
diet-of-porvoo: During the Finnish War between Sweden and Russia, the acting Governor-General of Finland, Göran Magnus Sprengtporten, drew up a plan for its government, which the Emperor confirmed on 1 December 1808. A delegation of the Finnish estates had already sworn loyalty to the Emperor in Saint Petersburg that autumn, and Sprengtporten was charged with preparing a diet. Turku and Hämeenlinna lay too far from the Russian border, and a large fire had left Helsinki without suitable premises, as Loviisa also lacked them, so Porvoo was chosen.

The diet sat from 25 March to 19 July 1809. It opened in Porvoo Cathedral; the clergy met in the Borgå Gymnasium, whose lecture hall served as the main chamber, the nobility and burghers in the town hall and the peasants in the house of the lawspeaker Anders Fabian Orraeus. The nobility sent 75 representatives under Count Robert Wilhelm De Geer, the clergy 8 under Jakob Tengström, bishop of Turku, the burghers 20 and the peasants 31; 130 of the 205 noble families were not represented.

The central ceremony took place in the cathedral on 29 March, when Alexander gave his sovereign's pledge and the estates swore their oaths to him as Grand Duke. His promise to uphold the Christian doctrine, the constitutional laws and the privileges of each estate was taken to confirm the Swedish Instrument of Government of 1772 as Finland's constitution, though it could also be read as respecting only the existing subordinate laws.

The diet had asked to be called again after the war, which the Treaty of Fredrikshamn ended on 17 September 1809, but the estates did not meet again for five decades. Finns later read the pledge and the oaths as a mutual act neither side could dissolve, and Leo Mechelin described the link with Russia as a personal union of sovereign states, whereas many Russian researchers saw Finland's position as resting on the Emperor's goodwill. Osmo Jussila has argued that the idea of a treaty between equals was a device of the later struggle for independence. Finnish historians still disagree whether the diet was Finland's first meeting of the estates or a traditional lantdag.
diet-of-worms: In June 1520 Pope Leo X issued the bull Exsurge Domine, which listed 41 purported errors in Martin Luther's Ninety-five Theses and other writings. Luther was excommunicated in January 1521 and summoned by the emperor to the diet at Worms. Frederick III, Elector of Saxony, obtained a promise of safe passage, which was essential after the treatment of Jan Hus, tried and executed at the Council of Constance in 1415 despite a promise of safe conduct. The diet sat from January to 25 May 1521 at the Bischofshof palace, with Emperor Charles V presiding.

Luther reached Worms on 16 April. On 17 April the spokesman Johann von Eck asked whether a collection of 25 titles was his and whether he would revoke them. Luther asked for time and was given until 4 p.m. the next day.

On 18 April he said the books were his but not all of one sort: some had been well received even by his enemies, some attacked abuses of the papacy, and some were harsh attacks on individuals. He would not reject the first two kinds and, if shown by Scripture that he was wrong, he would reject the third. He concluded that unless convinced by Scripture or clear reason he could not and would not recant, since it was neither safe nor right to go against conscience. According to tradition he added, Here I stand, I cannot do otherwise.

He was not arrested. Given safe conduct, he left for Wittenberg, but Frederick III, fearing for his safety, had men stage a highway attack and take him to Wartburg Castle, where he stayed disguised as a knight from early May 1521 to early March 1522. The Edict of Worms, issued on 25 May 1521, declared him a heretic and an enemy of the state and permitted anyone to kill him without legal consequence. The diet also let Charles V reform the administration of his lands, appointing his brother Ferdinand as Archduke and Imperial Lieutenant.

The Edict was never enforced in Germany, because of rising support for Luther among the people and the protection of certain princes. In the Habsburg Netherlands, under Charles V's direct rule and his regent Margaret of Austria, it was enforced against Luther's active supporters. Jacob Proost, prior of the Augustinian monastery in Antwerp, was arrested in December 1521 and made to recant in February 1522, and the monks Jan van Essen and Hendrik Vos were burned at the stake in Brussels on 1 July 1523. The Diets of Nuremberg of 1522 and 1524 failed to carry out the Edict. Historians such as Carter Lindberg see Luther's stand as crystallising the principle of the authority of Scripture over ecclesiastical hierarchy.
diet-of-worms-1495: During the 15th century the need for an imperial reform became ever clearer, with proposals such as the Reformatio Sigismundi ranging from the restoration of absolute imperial power to an Imperial Government of the electors. From the Frankfurt election of 1486 the Imperial Estates tried to make their support depend on reform, which Emperor Frederick III resisted. When Maximilian announced on 24 November 1494 that the diet would meet on 2 February 1495, he wanted help against Charles VIII of France, whose Italian campaign threatened Pope Alexander VI, Imperial Italy and Milan, and planned a march to Italy linked to his coronation in Rome.

Maximilian reached Worms on 18 March and stayed until September. The Estates refused his request for urgent aid and pressed for reform instead, even as the French conquered the Kingdom of Naples. On 27 April he agreed to discuss an Imperial Government, the Eternal Peace and an Imperial Court before aid and taxes, and on 1 June he was promised 100,000 guilders of emergency aid. The Imperial Government, which would have handed power to a council, in effect an oligarchy of electors, remained the main point of dispute.

Berthold of Henneberg, Elector of Mainz and spokesman of the Estates, mediated between the two sides while pressing hard for reform. After Charles VIII withdrew from Italy at the end of June, the electors and princes dropped the Imperial Government by 28 June and the money was granted. The texts of the Eternal Peace, the Imperial Court, the handling of peace and war and the Common Penny were published on 7 August. Some 147 imperial estates attended, nearly half of the whole; of the seven electors only five came, Bohemia and Brandenburg staying away.

Several of the reforms could not be put into effect at once, or at all, but the Eternal Peace and the Imperial Court laid foundations of the later constitutional state, and the king came to accept the diet as a powerful political tool; the term Reichstag came into common use only after it. The Old Swiss Confederacy rejected the imperial tax and the court, one of the causes of the Swabian War in 1499, and after its victory the Treaty of Basel implicitly exempted it. An Imperial Government was set up at the Diet of Augsburg in 1500 and dissolved in 1502.
dietrich-klagges: Klagges, born on 1 February 1891, was the youngest of a forest ranger's seven children and trained as a teacher at a seminar in Soest. Discharged from military service in 1911 because of an ear infection, he re-enlisted in 1915, was badly wounded at Neuve Chapelle on 1 April 1915 and left the army in 1916 to return to teaching. He belonged to the German National People's Party from 1918 to 1924, briefly to the German Völkisch Freedom Party, and joined the Nazi Party on 13 June 1925. From 1921 he wrote völkisch, antidemocratic and antisemitic articles.

Dismissed from the Prussian school service in 1930 for his party work, he turned to Brunswick, where the Nazis had entered the coalition government. As Interior and Education Minister from 15 September 1931 he imposed professional bans on Social Democrats and Jews in the civil service. His first plan to naturalise Hitler, a professorship at the Braunschweig Technical College in an invented subject, leaked and failed. Hitler never forgave him the public ridicule and curbed his power after a visit on 17 July 1935.

Appointed Ministerpräsident on 6 May 1933, Klagges joined the SS in 1934 and became SS-Obergruppenführer in 1942. He sought to make Brunswick a Nazi model state, independent of Prussia, brought institutions such as the SS Ensigns' School and the German Research Centre for Aviation to Braunschweig, and linked it to the Autobahn and the Mittellandkanal. The Auxiliary Police, answerable directly to him, struck at labour organisations, Social Democrats, Communists and Jews. He was responsible for at least 25 deaths, among them eleven communists and labour organisers murdered by the SS at Rieseberg on 4 July 1933. The deportation of Braunschweig's Jews began on 21 January 1941.

Taken prisoner by American troops on 12 April 1945, Klagges was sentenced in 1946 by a military court in Bielefeld to six years. In 1950 he was sentenced to life for crimes including the Rieseberg murders; after the Bundesgerichtshof set that aside in 1952, he was resentenced to fifteen years. Released from the Lingen penitentiary on 2 October 1957, he lived in Bad Harzburg, edited right-wing writings, kept contact with neo-Nazi groups and in 1970 won a retroactive pension of about DM 100,000. He died in 1971.
dietrich-of-haldensleben: Dietrich, also called Theoderich or Theodoric, was born between 928 and 935. He founded a comital branch named after its residence at Haldensleben in Eastphalia and may have been a son of Count Wichmann the Elder and of Frederuna, a sister of Queen Matilda. He held large estates along the Elbe and Saale rivers and was count in the Schwabengau, later also in the Nordthüringgau and the Derlingau.

A follower of the Ottonian dynasty, Dietrich supported King Otto I of Germany in 953 against the revolt of his son Duke Liudolf of Swabia. He also fought, without success, against the Polabian Slavs settled on the Elbe at the eastern edge of his home territory. When Margrave Gero died in 965, Otto, emperor since 962, made Dietrich margrave of the Northern March beyond the Elbe, the largest part of the former Marca Geronis. Contemporary sources also give him the title of dux, or duke.

He was a harsh overlord. With Archbishop Adalbert of Magdeburg he enforced the Christianization of the local Slavic population, and he had a hand in the execution of his rival Gero, Count of Alsleben. The chronicler Thietmar of Merseburg blamed his pride for the rising of 983, telling that he once refused to let a kinswoman marry a Slav he called a dog. After the rising Adam of Bremen and the Annalista Saxo record that he lost the march, and Lothar I succeeded him as margrave. He later appeared again as a Saxon general, supporting the minor King Otto III of Germany against the Bavarian duke Henry the Wrangler.

According to the Annals of Quedlinburg, Dietrich died on 25 August 985. He married a woman whose name is unknown. Their son Bernard I, father of Bernard II, Margrave of the Nordmark, became margrave himself in 1009. Their daughter Oda married Mieszko I, Duke of Poland, and Mathilda married the Hevelli chieftain Pribislaw, killed in battle on 28 December 994. Another daughter, Thietberga, married Dedo I, Count of Wettin.
digambara: Digambara, Sanskrit for sky-clad, names one of the two major schools of Jainism, the other being Svetambara, the white-clad. Digambaras hold that they are the original followers of Mahavira, who taught that nakedness symbolised complete detachment and spared a monk the distraction of acquiring and washing garments. In tradition the schools divided in the time of Chandragupta Maurya (c. 324-297 BCE). A twelve-year famine struck Magadha, and a group of monks led by Bhadrabahu, said to be the last who knew the complete original canon, migrated south to Karnataka and kept to strict asceticism, including nudity. Monks who stayed in the north under Sthulabhadra took to wearing white robes. Digambaras say the northern group kept beliefs and practices they consider heretical.

The oldest archaeological evidence for Digambaras is the Mangalam inscriptions, which record stone beds made for Digambara monks by workers of the Pandyan king Netunceliyan I, around 270 BCE. Statues of tirthankaras from Mathura dated to the second century CE or later are naked, and Svetambara iconography appears there only from the late fifth century.

Digambara monks own nothing. They are wandering mendicants who carry a community-owned picchi, a broom of fallen peacock feathers used to brush insects from their path or seat so as not to kill them. The tradition shares the Jain principles of aparigraha, non-attachment, ahimsa, non-violence, and anekantavada, the many-sidedness of reality. Digambaras maintain that women cannot attain nirvana, while Svetambaras hold that women, and eunuchs, can. The two schools have differed in dress, temples and iconography, attitudes to female monastics, legends and the texts they treat as important.

Digambara monastic lineages trace their descent to Mahavira, among them the Mula Sangha and the Kashtha Sangha. For most of the second millennium CE ascetic life centred on lineages of bhattarakas. In the seventeenth century a lay movement at Agra led to the division into Terapanthi and Bisapanthi sub-sects, and the Terapanthis, led by Pandit Todarmal and Banarasidas, rejected the bhattarakas' authority.

From about the middle of the first millennium CE the Western Ganga, Rashtrakuta and Chalukya dynasties of the Deccan and south India patronised Digambara teachers. Under the Rashtrakuta dynasty the scholar Jinasena advised King Amoghavarsha I (r. 814-878 CE), and he and his disciple Gunabhadra wrote the Mahapurana. Jain caves at Ellora, such as the Indra Sabha, contain Digambara images. Kundakunda, author of the Samayasara and Pravacanasara, is regarded as the tradition's most significant scholar-monk. Digambara communities live today across India, including Rajasthan, Maharashtra, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu.
dijon: Dijon lies in a plain drained by two small converging rivers, the Suzon, which crosses the town mostly underground from north to south, and the Ouche on its southern side. South of the town rises the côte, the hillside of vineyards that gives the department its name. The city is about 310 km south-east of Paris and has a climate that is oceanic with continental influence. The Canal de Bourgogne passes through the city and links the Yonne and the Seine in the north-west with the Saône to the south-east; these waterways were largely completed before the 19th century and were the main means of industrial transport until railways took over in the mid-19th century.

The earliest archaeological finds within the city limits date to the Neolithic period. Dijon later became a Roman settlement called Divio, which may mean sacred fountain, on the road from Lyon to Paris. Saint Benignus, the city's apocryphal patron saint, is said to have introduced Christianity to the area before being martyred.

The province was home to the Dukes of Burgundy from the early 11th until the late 15th century, and Dijon was a place of great wealth and power and one of the major European centres of art, learning and science, with Dijon Abbey having great influence. The Palace of the Dukes of Burgundy now houses the city hall and the Museum of Fine Arts. In 1513 Swiss and Imperial armies invaded Burgundy and besieged Dijon, which the governor, Louis II de la Trémoille, defended. After long negotiations he persuaded the besiegers to withdraw. The population, which had called on the Virgin Mary for help, saw this as a miracle and began to venerate Notre-Dame de Bon-Espoir, Our Lady of Good Hope.

Dijon was occupied by anti-Napoleonic coalitions in 1814, by the Prussian army in 1870–71, and by Nazi Germany from June 1940. It was liberated by the French Army and the Resistance on 11 September 1944. Henry Darcy built a system of purified water for its citizens a quarter-century before Paris had one.

Dijon is the prefecture of the Côte-d'Or department, with 161,830 inhabitants in the commune in 2023. Its historic centre keeps Capetian, Gothic and Renaissance buildings, half-timbered houses of the 12th to 15th centuries and roofs of glazed terracotta tiles in geometric patterns. The Well of Moses, a sculpture by Claus Sluter, is among its best-known works. In 2015 UNESCO registered the historic centre as part of the Climats, terroirs of Burgundy World Heritage site. Dijon mustard dates from 1856, when Jean Naigeon substituted verjuice for vinegar.
dikwa: Dikwa lies in Borno State in north-eastern Nigeria, in a region with a semiarid climate, a long dry season and a short wet one, and an annual rainfall of 380 to 810 millimetres. Rabih az-Zubayr preferred it to the old Bornu capital because it had better communications and a superior water supply.

When Rabih conquered the Kanem–Bornu Empire in 1893, he destroyed its capital at Kukawa, stayed there for a time and then settled on Dikwa, which he fortified heavily and kept as his capital for the rest of his rule. In 1900 he was killed by a French army, reinforced by local Bornu forces, at the Battle of Kousséri. The al-Kanemi dynasty, which had ruled the empire before his invasion, was restored with French and local support, and with Kukawa in ruins Dikwa remained the capital in the empire's last years under the shehus Sanda Kura, Masta Gumsumi and Abubakar Garbai.

In 1902 all of the empire's lands passed under European colonial rule, and under a treaty of 1893 Dikwa fell under German control. From 1902 to 1916 it was the capital of what the Europeans called German Borno, the present Dikwa Emirate. After the First World War the British administered the town and the emirate, first under a League of Nations mandate and then under a United Nations trusteeship agreement. In 1942 the emirate's capital moved to Bama, though the emirate kept the name Dikwa. A United Nations plebiscite in 1961 made the town and the emirate officially part of Nigeria.

Dikwa is the headquarters of a local government area of Borno State with an area of 1,774 square kilometres. Africapolis counted 25,300 inhabitants in 2010, while the 2006 census gave an estimate of 105,909 that, as elsewhere in Nigeria, is to be treated with caution.
dili: Dili lies on the northern coast of the island of Timor, on a small area of flat land hemmed in by mountains, facing the Ombai Strait of the Savu Sea. The central mountain range of Timor runs to the south and reaches the coast to the west and east of the core city. The climate is a rather dry tropical savanna one, with a rainy season from November to April and a dry season from May to October.

Early records about Timor are sparse, and the archives of Dili were destroyed in 1779, 1890, 1975 and 1999. Dili became the chief port and economic hub of what is now Timor-Leste when it was designated the capital of Portuguese Timor in 1769.

When the Pacific War began in 1941, Australian and Dutch troops were sent to Dili despite Portuguese objections, and the Japanese invaded in response. The Japanese left the Portuguese governor nominally in place but took over the administration, and much of Dili was destroyed by the invasion and by later Allied bombing. An Australian official told the Portuguese governor of the Japanese surrender on 23 September 1945, and the city returned to Portuguese control.

In 1975 a civil war between Timorese political parties led to a declaration of independence and then an Indonesian invasion. Under Indonesian rule the city was developed, with landmarks such as the Immaculate Conception Cathedral and the Cristo Rei of Dili, and its population passed 100,000. Resistance met violent repression, and a massacre in Dili brought international pressure that led to an independence referendum. After the vote for independence violence broke out, and up to 70 per cent of the country's infrastructure was destroyed in 1999, including 68,000 homes in Dili. A period of United Nations rule followed, and in 2002 Dili became the capital of independent Timor-Leste.

Dili is the capital and largest city of Timor-Leste and its chief port, with an international airport inside the city limits. The language of the locality is Tetum. The 2022 census counted 324,269 people in the Dili Municipality. Most of the country's universities are in the city, and the Immaculate Conception Cathedral and Cristo Rei remain its landmarks.
dillenburg: Dillenburg lies on the eastern edge of the Westerwald range, in the narrow valley of the Dill, which flows from the border of Hesse and Westphalia to Wetzlar and empties into the Lahn. The Dietzhölze flows into the Dill in the town. It was formerly the seat of the old Dillkreis district, now part of the Lahn-Dill-Kreis, and it lies on the Orange Route, a German-Dutch holiday road that joins places associated with the House of Orange-Nassau.

Dillenburg is first mentioned in a document of 1254 and was the ancestral seat of the Orange branch of the House of Nassau. The first castle on the Schlossberg was of wood, so that no pictures of it exist, and it was destroyed in the Dernbacher Feud. William I of Orange-Nassau, who was born in Dillenburg, organised the Dutch resistance against Spain from exile between 1567 and 1572. The land was administered by the presidents of the House of Nassau-Dillenburg. In the Seven Years' War the stately home was destroyed in 1760, and a street, Wilhelmstraße, was built out of its remains.

In 1797 one of the earliest schools of forestry in Europe, founded a decade earlier at Hungen by Georg Ludwig Hartig, was moved to Dillenburg. It continued there until 1805, when Hartig lost his position as Inspector of Forests for the Prince of Orange-Nassau after Napoleon dissolved the principality.

In the 19th century the building of the Deutz–Gießen railway and the use of iron ore found on the Lahn, Dill and Sieg brought the Industrial Revolution to the region, with many mines, foundries and metalworking works. Branch lines were built from Dillenburg to places such as Gönnern and Ewersbach. In the Second World War the town was a target of Allied attacks because of its marshalling yard, and Niederscheld, now part of the town, was bombed because parts for the V-2 rocket were built at the Adolfshütte. Ore mining later became ever less profitable, and the last blast furnace, in Oberscheld, ceased operations.

The Wilhelmsturm, built between 1872 and 1875 on the Schlossberg, is the landmark of the town and houses the Orange-Nassau Museum. The casemates beneath the former castle, from the 16th century, are among the biggest defensive works in Europe, and parts of them have been excavated and may be toured. Other buildings include the Evangelical Town Church of 1491, the Dillturm of 1597 and the Untertor, or Lower Gate, of 1344, with alterations in 1594 and 1737. The town is twinned with Breda, Diest, Hereford and Orange. In November 2017 its name was officially extended to Oranienstadt Dillenburg, to recall its connection with the House of Orange-Nassau.
dillingen-an-der-donau: Dillingen an der Donau lies in Swabia in Bavaria, Germany, and is the administrative centre of the district of Dillingen. Besides the town proper, the municipality includes the villages of Donaualtheim, Fristingen, Hausen, Kicklingen, Schretzheim and Steinheim. Schretzheim is notable for an Alemannic cemetery of the 6th to 7th century, with 630 row graves.

The counts of Dillingen ruled from the 10th to the 13th century, and in 1258 the territory was turned over to the prince-bishops of Augsburg. After the Reformation they moved to the Catholic city of Dillingen and made it one of the centres of the Counter-Reformation. A university there was closed by Napoleon in 1804, its philosophical and theological faculties still existed in the 20th century, and in 1971 it became part of an academy for teacher training.

In 1800, during the War of the Second Coalition, French armies under Jean Victor Moreau fought Habsburg regulars and Württemberg contingents under Pál Kray, who had taken refuge in the fortress at Ulm. Moreau approached from the east and, after a small group captured a foothold on the northern bank of the Danube, moved against the fortress on both sides of the river. This culmination of the Danube Campaign of 1800 forced Kray to abandon Ulm and withdraw into eastern Bavaria.

Natives and residents include the painter Heinrich Vogtherr, the theologian Johann Michael Sailer, who taught there and became Bishop of Regensburg in 1829, and the priest and hydrotherapist Sebastian Kneipp, who began his theological studies in Dillingen in 1848. The town is twinned with Bondeno in Italy, Brand-Erbisdorf in Germany and Naas in Ireland.
dilmun: Dilmun was an East Semitic-speaking civilisation of Eastern Arabia, mentioned from the 3rd millennium BCE onwards. It lay in the Persian Gulf on a trade route between Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley Civilisation, close to the sea and to artesian springs, and it encompassed Bahrain, Kuwait and eastern Saudi Arabia. Its land was then fertile, thanks to wells that have since dried and to a much wetter climate. Its people wrote cuneiform in the Akkadian language, and its main deity was Inzak, whose spouse was Panipa. In Sumerian myth Dilmun is a paradisiacal land in the story of Enki and Ninhursag, and the place where the flood hero Ziusudra was taken by the gods to live forever.

Dilmun was an important trading centre from the late 4th millennium to 800 BCE. It first appears in Sumerian clay tablets of the late 3rd millennium BCE found in the temple of Inanna at Uruk, and an inscription of Ur-Nanshe of Lagash, around 2300 BCE, says that the ships of Dilmun brought him wood as tribute. Metals such as copper, wood, perfumes and pearls came from Dilmun to Ur, and timber, ivory, lapis lazuli and gold also reached Mesopotamia. Weights and measures at Dilmun were identical to those of the Indus and not to those of southern Mesopotamia.

From around 2050 BCE Dilmun seems to have been at its peak, with Qal'at al-Bahrain probably its capital and the largest royal burial mounds raised. A decline is visible from around 1720 BCE and a recovery from about 1650 BCE. From at least 1500 BCE Dilmun was probably ruled by the Mesopotamian Sealand dynasty and then by the Kassite dynasty of Babylon. Assyrian inscriptions of 1250 to 1050 BCE claim its tribute, and Babylonian records of 567 BCE place it under the king of Babylon. Its commercial power declined between 1000 and 800 BCE as piracy flourished. The name fell from use after Babylon collapsed in 538 BCE, and the area was later called Tylos in the Hellenistic period.

The Barbar Temple was the first part of Dilmun society to be rediscovered, by Geoffrey Bibby and Peter Glob from 1954. Dilmun is generally located in the Gulf region, though one archaeologist, Theresa Howard-Carter, proposed in 1987 an unidentified mound near the Shatt al-Arab between Qurnah and Basra, and some scholars think the name first denoted the eastern province of modern Saudi Arabia.
dilmun-burial-mounds: The Dilmun Burial Mounds are necropolis areas on the main island of Bahrain, dating to the Dilmun and the Umm al-Nar cultures. The cemeteries lie in the north of the island, on hard stony ground slightly above the arable soils, while the south is mainly sandy desert. Bahrain has long been known as an island with a very large number of burials, and the mounds, which once covered a number of square kilometres, were said to form one of the largest cemeteries of the ancient world.

Recent studies suggest that the local population alone could have produced an estimated 350,000 ancient grave mounds over some thousands of years. The graves differ in era, style and size across the moundfield, and research under the Bahrain National Museum continues in order to fix a firm timeline and to understand the societies that built them.

Each tumulus has a central stone chamber enclosed by a low ring-wall and covered with earth and gravel. Most mounds measure about 4.5 by 9 metres across and stand 1 to 2 metres high. The smaller ones usually hold a single chamber, generally rectangular with one or two alcoves at the northeast end.

The dead were usually laid on their right sides with their heads toward the alcove, accompanied by few goods: a little pottery, shell or stone stamp seals, baskets sealed with asphalt, ivory objects, stone jars and copper weapons. The skeletons include both sexes, with a life expectancy of about 40 years, and babies were generally buried at or outside the ring-wall.

From 10 to 19 February 1889 the British explorer J. Theodore Bent and his wife Mabel excavated some of the mounds and found ivory, charcoal and ostrich eggshell, now in the British Museum. At A'ali, in Mound 8, they found three cuneiform inscriptions, all variants of a text naming the palace of the son of Ri'mum, servant of Inzak of Akarum. The same text turned up on the surface at Qal'at al-Bahrain. In the 1950s a Danish group digging at Qal'at al-Bahrain, the Bronze Age capital, opened tumuli with items of about 4100 to 3700 BP, and many others later excavated more graves.

The mounds are a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Efforts to protect them have met opposition from religious fundamentalists who regard them as un-Islamic and have called for them to be built over with housing. In a parliamentary debate on 17 July 2005 Sheikh Adel Mouwda, leader of the Salafist al Asalah party, argued that housing for the living was better than graves for the dead.
dilwara-temples: The earliest temple was built by Vimal Shah, a Jain minister of Bhima I, the Chaulukya king of Gujarat, and the Luna Vasahi by the Porwad brothers Vastupal and Tejpal, ministers of Virdhaval, the Vaghela ruler, in memory of their late brother Lunig. The Pittalhar temple was built by Bhima Shah, a minister of Sultan Begada of Ahmedabad, and its five-metal statue of Rishabhanatha, of about four tonnes, was installed in 1468–69. The Parshvanatha temple was built by Sangvi Mandlik and his family in 1458–59, and the small Mahavir Swami temple in 1582.

The five temples stand in one high-walled compound among forested hills near the Mount Abu settlement in Sirohi District, and are named after the village of Dilwara or Delvara. The main buildings of the first three have an axis from the sanctuary through a closed and then an open mandapa to a rangamandapa, a hall for dance or drama, and are ringed by screens of small devakulika shrines, a plan that became distinctive of the Jain temples of western India. In the Vimal Vasahi 59 such shrines face the image of Rishabhanatha, and Prithvipal, a descendant of Vimal Shah, added an elephant court in 1147–49.

The Luna Vasahi, dedicated to Neminatha, follows the plan of the older temple with finer carving. From the dome of its main hall hangs a large ornamental pendant, ringed by 72 seated tirthankaras and 360 small figures of monks, and 38 of its 130 pillars are carved. The three-storey Parshvanatha temple, the tallest, is built of grey stone.

Allauddin Khilji attacked and damaged the temples in 1311, and Bijag and Lalag of Mandore repaired them in 1321. They were reconsecrated on 25 April 1906 and repaired again between 1950 and 1965, so that older marble with a yellow patina stands beside newer white stone. With Shatrunjaya, Girnar, Sammed Shikharji and Ashtapad they are one of the five principal pilgrimage places of the Śvētāmbara Jains, and their very pure white marble came to be regarded as essential in later temples of the Māru-Gurjara style.
dima-hasao: From about 1500 the area was part of the Dimasa Kingdom, also called the Kachar kingdom, which had its capital at Maibang and Dimapur. In the colonial period Khaspur in the present Cachar district became its administrative centre, and an internal schism divided the old kingdom. The last Dimasa king, Govinda Chandra Hasnusa, assigned the hilly tract to Kashi Chandra, who soon declared independence and was murdered by the king.

Kashi Chandra's son Tularam Senapati kept up the struggle and, with British help, carved out his own territory; in 1829 David Scott, the British agent, recognised him as ruler of the hilly tract. After Tularam died in 1850, Angami raids and an incident at Semkhor village opened the way to British influence, and in 1852 the territory was annexed to the Nowgong district of British Assam.

The subdivision was abolished in 1866 and shared among three districts, and in 1880 the present area became a subdivision of Cachar with its headquarters first at Gunjung and from 1895 at Haflong. On 17 November 1951 the United Mikir and North Cachar Hills District was created, and on 2 February 1970 the North Cachar Hills became a district of their own. On 30 March 2010 it was renamed Dima Hasao, which means Dimasa Hills in the Dimasa language.

Dima Hasao covers 4,888 square kilometres, with Haflong as its headquarters, and is one of two autonomous hill districts of Assam. It has Sixth Schedule status under the Constitution of India and is administered by the Dima Hasao Autonomous Council, which controls almost every department except the police and law and order.

It has three subdivisions: Haflong, Maibang and Diyungbra. Its tribal population includes Dimasa Kachari, Zeme Naga, Hmar, Kuki, Karbi and Khasi people. At Maibang stands a rock-cut temple of the goddess Ranachandi, or Mahamaya, carved from a single block of black sandstone. Jatinga village is known for birds that appear to fall dead between September and November.
dimapur: Many historians explain the name as the city of the Dimasa people, from the Dimasa Kachari words di, water, ma, big, and pur, settlement. The Ahom chronicles, the Buranjis, sometimes call it Che-din-chi-pen, brick town, and European scholars also described it as the Brick City. The city is said to have been founded by the Kachari king Mahamanipha, who ruled from 1330 to 1370, and it remained the capital of the Kacharis until the Ahom ruler Suhungmung captured it.

Between 1406 and 1439 the Ming dynasty had political contacts with the Dimasa and neighbouring kingdoms. In 1406 the Ming made the Dimasa kingdom a tusi and set up a Pacification Superintendency, with Lawangpa as superintendent, and the chieftain sent horses and local products as tribute. The ruins in Dimapur include a brick wall nearly 2 miles long and two tanks about 300 yards square, which show a city of considerable size. In the early 19th century the Dimasa chiefs, with the help of Brahmins, claimed descent from Hidimba.

Dimapur is the largest city and municipality in Nagaland, near the border with Assam on the banks of the Dhansiri River, a tributary of the Brahmaputra. During the Second World War it was the centre of action between British India and Imperial Japan and an important logistics hub and staging post for the Allied offensive. Reinforcements came through it by rail and road after the Japanese reached Kohima, about 77 kilometres away, and an airfield supplied forces in Burma.

The city is the main gateway and commercial centre of Nagaland, and its railway station is the second busiest in north-east India. Its population is a mix of people from all over India, and it is known as Mini India. Christianity and Hinduism are its largest religions. The ruins of the Kachari Rajbari are a national heritage site, and the Dimapur Jain Temple was built in 1947.
dimasa-people: The name Dimasa is explained as people of the big waters, referring to the Lohit, an upper tributary of the Brahmaputra known in Dimasa as Dilao. Another name used within the community, Ha-Tseng-Sa or Ha-Cheng-Sa, means people of the soil, and may be the older one. Dimasa tradition holds that sixty thousand lunar months ago the people left their ancestral land in a severe drought and, after long wandering, settled where the Dilao meets the Brahmaputra. They belong to the Bodo-Kachari family of peoples, with the Boro, Tripuri, Rabha, Garo and Tiwa.

The Dimasa kingdom was one of the early states of Assam that followed the downfall of the Kamarupa kingdom. After political troubles in the 18th century the Dimasa ruler moved south into the plains of Cachar, and the people divided: the hill Dimasa kept their traditional way of life and political exclusiveness, while many in the plains converted to Hinduism in the 19th century. These are known as Barmans and are recognised as a Scheduled Tribe under the name Barmans in Cachar, to distinguish them from the Barman Kacharis of western Assam.

Dimasa society is sealed: each member takes a father's line from one of the male clans, called sengphong, holder of the sword, and a mother's line from one of the female clans, jalik or julu. The clans are spread over twelve territorial sacred groves, the daikhos, held to be the houses of the gods. Most Dimasa keep their animist and shamanic faith in spiritual beings known as madai; in Cachar it has blended with Hinduism.

The village headman, the Khunang, holds executive and judicial powers, assisted by the Dillik and the Daulathu. The Dimasa language is agglutinative, has six vowels and sixteen consonants, and is written in Latin and Eastern Nagari scripts; the 2011 census counted 137,184 native speakers. Since 1994, 27 January has been the Busu Dima festival day in Dima Hasao.
dimitrie-cantemir: Dimitrie Cantemir was born in Silişteni, Moldavia, on 26 October 1673, the son of Constantin Cantemir and Ana Bantăș, a learned daughter of a local noble family. His surname is of Turkic or Tatar origin. In 1685 the Ottoman overlords named Constantin voivode of Moldavia. Although Constantin himself was illiterate, he educated his sons Dimitrie and Antioh thoroughly, and Dimitrie learned Greek and Latin as a child. Between 1687 and 1710 he spent most of his time in Constantinople as a hostage or envoy, learning Turkish, studying Ottoman history at the Patriarchate's Greek Academy and composing Ottoman music. When Constantin died in 1693 Dimitrie briefly succeeded him but was passed over within three weeks in favour of Constantin Duca.

Appointed voivode again in 1710, Cantemir believed that Ottoman Turkey was collapsing. By a secret agreement at Lutsk he placed Moldavia under Russian control and joined Peter the Great in his war against the Turks. The campaign ended in failure at Stănilești in July 1711, and the Cantemirs were forced into exile in Russia. Native voivodes of Moldavia were replaced by Greek phanariots. In 1712 Peter presented him with the Bogorodskoye District. Cantemir was made a Russian prince by Peter and a prince of the Holy Roman Empire by Charles VI, and lived on an estate at Dmitrovka near Oryol. He died there on 21 August 1723, the day he was awarded his German title, and in 1935 his remains were returned to Iași.

Cantemir was a polyglot, speaking and writing eleven languages, and wrote as philosopher, historian, composer, musicologist, linguist, ethnographer and geographer. In 1714 he became a member of the Royal Academy of Berlin. His History of the Growth and Decay of the Ottoman Empire circulated in manuscript for years, was printed in London in 1734 and remained the standard work on the Ottoman Empire until the middle of the 19th century; Edward Gibbon used it. Later scholarship contests many points because some of his sources were doubtful.

For the Berlin Academy he wrote the Descriptio Moldaviae in 1714, covering geography, ethnography and economy, and drew a manuscript map of Moldavia which was the first real map of the country. His Chronicle of the Antiquity of the Romano-Moldavo-Wallachians asserted the Latin origin of the Romanian language. A Hieroglyphic History of 1705 is considered the first Romanian novel. In music he composed about forty Ottoman pieces and preserved 350 traditional instrumental works in a notation of his own in Edvar-i Musiki.
dimitrov-constitution: The Dimitrov Constitution was the second constitution of Bulgaria and formed the legal basis for communist rule in the country. Georgi Dimitrov, the country's first communist leader, guided its framing. It guaranteed equality before the law, freedom from discrimination, freedom of speech, press and assembly, and the inviolability of person, home and correspondence. A clause prohibiting any activity that would jeopardise the attainments of the national revolution of 9 September 1944, however, left these rights without effect in practice.

Citizens were guaranteed employment but required to work in a socially useful capacity. The constitution prescribed a planned national economy and provided for a national welfare system. Unlike the Soviet constitution on which it was modelled, it allowed private property, provided that it was not used to the detriment of the public good.

The constitution set up a highly centralised structure. The National Assembly, defined as the highest organ of state power, was elected for four years and met in regular session twice a year; in practice it did little more than approve decisions already made at the highest levels of the Bulgarian Communist Party. Between sessions its powers passed to a Presidium of a president and 18 members, which could also declare war, make peace, amend the constitution and approve the national economic plan.

Executive authority lay with a Council of Ministers appointed by the Presidium, whose chairman, the prime minister, was almost always the leader of the Communist Party. Judges at every level were appointed by the National Assembly, and the judiciary lost all independence. Local government was exercised by people's councils, which elected executive committees responsible to the Presidium. In 1971 the constitution was replaced by the Zhivkov Constitution.
din-eidyn: The name is Brittonic, meaning the dun or hillfort of Eidyn, a district that took in at least the fortress and perhaps much of the land south of the Firth of Forth; Carriden, eighteen miles west, may preserve it as Caer Eidyn, though Kenneth H. Jackson held that Eidyn meant the fortress alone. Iron Age hill forts stood at Arthur's Seat, Castle Rock and other hilltops, and archaeologists generally identify Castle Rock as Din Eidyn, since it was an important centre continuously from Roman times into the Middle Ages.

Castle Rock has been inhabited since the Bronze Age, perhaps the longest nearly continuous occupation of any site in Scotland, though it began as a minor fortified village beside others. Its defensible position gave it an advantage over Arthur's Seat. In the Roman era it held a prosperous settlement of the Votadini, probably with a hillfort, but was dwarfed by Traprain Law. After Traprain Law was abandoned early in the 5th century, Din Eidyn became the chief political centre of the Gododdin kingdom.
