Y Gododdin tells of 300 warriors from across the Brittonic world gathering there to feast before a raid on Catraeth, probably Catterick, around 600; Ifor Williams read Mynydawc Eidyn as the ruler who summoned them, while John Koch and Graham Isaac read the name as a mountain. By the 7th century the lords of Din Eidyn may have held only their own district. The Annals of Ulster record the siege of Etin in 638, after which the fortress stayed with the Angles for most of three centuries. The Chronicle of the Kings of Alba says the Scots took it under King Indulf, who ruled from 954 to 962.

Castle Rock is the site of Edinburgh Castle. The Angles replaced the Brittonic din with the Old English burh, giving Edinburgh, and the name became Dùn Èideann in Scottish Gaelic. In Welsh tradition Eidyn long remained the northern frontier of the Britons, where Arthur's warriors fought on the Mountain of Eidyn.
dinant: Dinant lies in the Upper Meuse valley, in the Ardennes, where the river cuts deeply into the western Condroz plateau. Between the rock face and the river the original settlement had little room, and the town grew into a long, thin line along the river shore. The navigable river carried the raw materials of its brassware to the workshops and the finished goods away, and the limestone cliffs above supported a quarrying industry producing black marble and bluestone. Its name comes from the Celtic Divo-Nanto, meaning Sacred Valley.

The area was populated in Neolithic, Celtic and Roman times. Dinant is first mentioned as a settlement in the 7th century, when Perpète of Maastricht, Bishop of Tongeren, moved his main residence there and founded the church of Saint Vincent. In the 11th century the emperor Henry IV granted the Prince-Bishopric of Liège market and justice rights over the town, which became one of its 23 principal cities, the bonnes villes. The first stone bridge on the Meuse dates from the end of that century.

In 1466, during the Liège Wars, Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy, and his son Charles the Bold punished an uprising by casting 800 burghers into the Meuse and setting fire to the city. Late medieval Dinant and its rival Bouvignes specialised in dinanderie, objects cast and finished in a silvery brass alloy, among them aquamaniles, candlesticks and altar furniture, supplied through the Meuse valley and the Rhineland. After the Bishopric of Liège was ceded to France in 1795, the dinanderies fell out of fashion and the economy rested on leather tanning and playing cards.

On 15 August 1914 French and German troops fought for the town in the Battle of Dinant, and on 23 August Saxon troops of the German Army summarily executed 674 inhabitants, the largest massacre committed by the Germans in 1914. In 1940 Erwin Rommel's 7th Panzer Division took the town on 13 May after crossing the Meuse.

Dinant is a town of the province of Namur, in Wallonia, about 30 km south of the city of Namur. Its landmark is the Collegiate Church of Notre Dame, rebuilt in Gothic style after falling rock from the cliff partly destroyed the Romanesque church in 1227, with an onion-domed tower. Above it rises the Citadel, first built in the 11th century and rebuilt in 1821.
dinavar: Dinavar lay in the centre of the ancient region of Media. Its position made it the entrance to the Jibal and a crossroads between the culture of Iran and that of the peoples on the other side of the Zagros Mountains. Under the caliphs its district bordered Hulwan to the west, Masabadhan to the south, Hamadan to the east and Adharbayjan to the north.

The town is first attested as a foundation of the Seleucid Empire, though it may be older, and like neighbouring Kangavar it had a Greek population. Under the Sasanian Empire it was an important fortified place, reportedly attacked by the Khazars early in the 6th century. It was conquered in 642, after the Sasanian defeat by the Arabs at the Battle of Nahavand. Under the Umayyad caliph Mu'awiya I it was renamed Mah al-Kufa and made one of the two districts of the Jibal, the other being Karmisin (Kermanshah).

Dinavar flourished under the Umayyad and Abbasid caliphates; in the 10th century Ibn Hawqal described it as only a third smaller than Hamadan. It produced scholars such as Ibn Qutaybah (died 889), Fakhr-un-Nisa and Abu Hanifa Dinawari (died 896), whose Kitāb al-akhbār al-ṭiwāl is an early effort to combine Iranian and Islamic history. It was sacked by Mardavij in 931 and, according to Ibn Athir, plundered by Turkmen of the Iva tribe in 1172/73.

The 14th-century geographer Hamdallah Mustawfi knew Dinavar as a small town in his Nuzhat al-Qulub, and Timur destroyed it by the end of that century. Only a field of ruins remains, in Dinavar District of Sahneh County, Kermanshah Province.
dinefwr-castle: The ruined castle, also known as Old Dynevor Castle, lies on a ridge on the northern bank of the Towy, with a steep drop of one hundred feet to the river. A fortified entrance with a restored length of battlement leads into the space enclosed by the walls, from which stairs climb to the battlements and towers; a narrow spiral staircase reaches a high tower looking over the deer park to the north and the valley to the south and west. The keep is entered through the cellar at its base, and a well and several garderobes survive.

Tradition holds that Rhodri the Great first built a castle here, though no remains of that age have been dated, and that it became the chief seat of his grandson Hywel Dda. Rhys ap Gruffydd, ruler of Deheubarth from 1155 to 1197, is thought to have rebuilt it. Giraldus Cambrensis tells how a follower of King Henry II of England, sent to scout the castle, was led by a Welsh cleric along the hardest route, and the planned attack was abandoned.

Rhys's son Rhys Gryg, unable to resist Llywelyn the Great of Gwynedd, dismantled the castle, but Llywelyn restored it and held it until his death in 1240; the earliest parts of the present castle are thought to date from this time. Rhys ap Maredudd helped King Edward I of England take Dinefwr in 1277, apparently on a promise that he would have it, but Edward did not keep the promise and had him executed in 1291.

In English hands the castle was burnt during the rebellion of Llywelyn Bren in 1316, given in 1317 to the king's favourite Hugh Despenser, and besieged without success by the forces of Owain Glyndŵr in 1403. Sir Rhys ap Thomas rebuilt it extensively late in the 15th century; after his grandson Rhys ap Gruffydd was executed for treason in 1531 the crown confiscated it, though the family later recovered it.

When Newton House was built nearby in 1660, the keep was adapted as a summer house, which burned down in the 18th century. The castle is a Grade I listed building, owned by the Wildlife Trust of South and West Wales and managed by Cadw, which since 2024 has used the Welsh name Castell Dinefwr in English. It lies within Dinefwr Park.
dingane: Dingane came to power in 1828 by assassinating his half-brother Shaka at KwaDukuza, with the help of another brother, Umhlangana, and of Shaka's bodyguard Mbopa. After the death of Nandi, Shaka's mother, Shaka's behaviour had become increasingly erratic, and many relatives accused him of killing her. The true mastermind of the murder was, according to the account given, Shaka's paternal aunt Mkabayi kaJama, who saw Dingane as the best choice for the next king. Dingane and Mkabayi then conspired to kill Mbopa and Umhlangana, leaving Dingane sole ruler.

Dingane built his capital, umGungundlovu, in 1829 and enlarged it five years later, on the layout of a Zulu military settlement: a central parade ground ringed by barracks, with the royal enclosure on the south side. He never married officially and kept at least 500 women and attendants in the enclosure, divided into the black and white isigodlo. The missionary Francis Owen, who lived near the capital, described a rule in which ministers and servants acted only on the king's command, and he recorded Dingane's reply to his preaching: "I and my people believe there is only one God – I am that God."

Dingane lacked Shaka's military and leadership skills, and rebel chiefs broke away from his rule. Some who fell out of favour fled the country. The subjects of the chief Signabani who could not flee with him were rounded up and massacred. The unrest was made worse by armed conflict with the newly arrived Voortrekkers.

In November 1837 Dingane signed a deed ceding land to the Voortrekkers under Piet Retief, in return for the recovery of stolen cattle. On 6 February 1838 he had Retief and his party killed at the hill kwaMatiwane, and his forces killed the undefended trek party of about 500 Boers and servants, an event the Boers called the Weenen massacre. A Voortrekker attack led by Andries Potgieter and Piet Uys ended in a Zulu victory at Italeni, where Uys was killed. Dingane's army then attacked Andries Pretorius's encampment at the Battle of Blood River, under the command of Ndlela kaSompisi, and was defeated; an estimated 3,000 Zulus died.

In January 1840 Pretorius and 400 Boers helped Mpande revolt against his half-brother. At the Battle of Maqongqo many of Dingane's men deserted to Mpande. Dingane had Ndlela executed and took refuge with a few followers in Nyawo territory in the Lubombo mountains, where a group of Nyawo and Swazi assassinated him in the Hlatikhulu Forest. His grave lies near Ingwavuma.
dingiswayo: Dingiswayo was born Godongwana, a son of the Mthethwa king Jobe kaKayi, and his line is traced back to Mthethwa I. With his brother Tana he plotted against their father; the plot was discovered, Tana was killed and Godongwana escaped. Nursed back to health by a sister, he went into exile and changed his name to Dingiswayo, which means one in distress or in exile. During his exile he was exposed to European ideas, and the Tembe prince Makhasana ka Mwayi taught him about trade.

On his father's death he returned to Oyengweni, his tribal home, and displaced his brother Mawewe without resistance; Mawewe fled, was lured back and killed. Dingiswayo acquired the horse and gun of Dr Andrew Cowan of the 83rd Regiment, who with Captain Goddard Edward Donovan had been exploring a southern approach to the interior and was possibly murdered by chief Phakathwayo. He adopted western drill and formation movements under a chain of command and, by Mthethwa's account, added seven new regiments, one of them of women, to the three of his father.

He widened Mthethwa power more by diplomacy and assimilation than by force. He made Nqoboko kaLanga chief of the Sokhulu, bound to report to Oyengweni, and on the death of Senzangakhona backed Shaka's claim to the Zulu chiefship, sending Ngomane kaNqomboli to him as adviser. With Shaka as his general he drove the Amangwane under Matiwane across the Buffalo river in about 1812, the first of the Mfecane migrations.

Dingiswayo combined several smaller peoples against his chief rival to the north, Zwide of the Ndwandwe. In an attempted invasion of Zwide's territory he was captured and beheaded at Ngome, near Nongoma; his grave is on the north bank of the Tugela River. The Mthethwa forces scattered and re-formed under Shaka, who later defeated Zwide. His career is seen as a watershed in the history of south-east Africa: he built the region's first disciplined and highly organised army, and Shaka extended his ideas into a rigidly disciplined society.
dinguiraye: El Hajj Umar Tall founded Dinguiraye after he was forced to leave the town of Diegunko in the Imamate of Futa Jallon, buying the land from the Kingdom of Tamba with gold. His community soon grew to as many as 10,000 people. The engineers Samba Ndiaye and Johnny Bambara built the large mosque he commissioned and the town's tata, its fortified wall. Dinguiraye lay on trade routes linking the Niger river to the coast, and caravans went back and forth to Freetown. Alarmed at his new neighbour's rising power, King Dyimba Sako of Tamba attacked and was defeated.

Umar Tall left Dinguiraye on 21 May 1854 to campaign in the north and never returned, leaving his son Habibou in command. After Umar's death in 1864 his son Ahmadu succeeded him; Habibou joined a rebellion in 1870 and was captured and imprisoned. Leadership passed to Ahmadu's cousin Saidou, who was killed in battle in 1876, and Aguibou Tall arrived to take over as governor in late 1878 or early 1879.

Cut off from the rest of the Toucouleur Empire, Aguibou sought French protection, and in May 1891 Dinguiraye was annexed to the French colonial empire. Aguibou was soon made Faama of Massina and his son Makki led the town, until in 1899 the French removed him, sent him into exile and ended even Dinguiraye's nominal independence.

Dinguiraye is a small town of Guinea, remembered as the first capital of the Tukulor Empire. It is known for the large mosque begun in Umar Tall's time, long covered with a thatched roof, which still stands in the centre of the town. It had 47,250 inhabitants in 2014.
dingzhou: Dingzhou is a county-level city in the prefecture-level city of Baoding in Hebei Province, China. It lies about halfway between Baoding and Shijiazhuang, 196 kilometres south-west of Beijing and 68 kilometres north-east of Shijiazhuang. It was formerly romanised Tingchow and was known as Ding County or Dingxian. Its population was 1.1 million in 2020, and it is divided into 3 subdistricts, 13 towns, 8 townships and 1 ethnic township.

In early imperial China the place was known as Lunu. A tomb about 4 kilometres south-west of the city, dated to 55 to 8 BCE, was excavated in 1973. It held fragments of Han literature, among them manuscripts of Confucius's Analects, the Taoist Wenzi and the Six Secret Teachings, a military treatise; four further manuscripts remain unpublished. The occupant is unknown, but Chinese archaeologists have speculated that it was one of two kings of the Zhongshan fiefdom under the Former Han, either Liu Xiu or Liu Xing.

The city took its present name around 400 CE, when it became the seat of Ding Prefecture under the Northern Wei, displacing the earlier An Prefecture. In the mid-6th century its territory held 834,211 people in 177,500 households. Under the Tang, the territory held only 86,869 people in 25,637 households in 639 but had recovered to 496,676 people in 78,090 households by 742. As the seat of the often de facto independent jiedushi of Yiding Province it was also known as Anxi. In 1055, under the Song, it became the home of the 84-metre Liaodi Pagoda.

The Liaodi Pagoda is China's tallest surviving pre-modern pagoda, and the city also has a well-preserved Confucius temple. Under the early Republic it was called Dingxian, and from 1926 to 1937 the county hosted the Ting Hsien Experiment of the Rural Reconstruction Movement, run by the National Association of Mass Education Movement. Dingzhou is one of the transport hubs of North China, on the Jingguang, Jingshi and Shuohuang railways.
dinh-lien: Đinh Liễn, also called Đinh Khuông Liễn, was the eldest son of Đinh Bộ Lĩnh, who reigned as Đinh Tiên Hoàng. He spent his childhood fighting for his father's cause during the Anarchy of the 12 Warlords. When he was a toddler his father's enemies held him hostage, and his father tried to kill him so that they would lose their leverage; Liễn later forgave him.

When his father took the throne, Liễn received the title Nam Việt vương, king of Nam Việt. In 973 he was sent to Song China with tribute, and Song Taizu named him Grand Preceptor of Inspection, Jiedushi of Tĩnh Hải quân and Governor of the Protectorate General to Pacify the South. In 975 the Song court raised him to Prince of Giao Chỉ. The Song regarded him as the ruler of Vietnam, although his father held power in fact.

In 978 Đinh Tiên Hoàng named the four-year-old Đinh Hạng Lang crown prince, over the objections of officials. Liễn felt wronged by his father once more, and in the spring of 979 he sent his men to kill his half-brother, to the distress of his father and his father's wives. To console them he had masons carve the Uṣṇīṣa Vijaya Dhāraṇī Sūtra on 100 columns dedicated to the dead boy and other souls. Their remains, forgotten for almost 1,000 years, were found in 1963.

Liễn never received the title of crown prince. In the winter of 979 his father was assassinated, and Liễn was killed as well when he came upon the fleeing assassin. Đỗ Thích, who had saved members of the Đinh family many times during the Anarchy of the 12 Warlords, was hastily executed by Nguyễn Bặc. Accusations were also made that Lê Hoàn was involved in the killings, even that he planned the end of the Đinh dynasty.
dinh-phe-de: Đinh Toàn, also recorded as Đinh Tuệ, was born in 974 at Hoa Lư, the son of Đinh Bộ Lĩnh and of the empress Dương Vân Nga, one of five consorts on whom Đinh Bộ Lĩnh conferred that title. He was the second son, after Đinh Liễn and before Đinh Hạng Lang. When Đinh Bộ Lĩnh named Đinh Hạng Lang crown prince, Đinh Liễn killed his youngest brother in anger. A minor official, Đỗ Thích, then dreamed that he would take the throne and assassinated both Đinh Bộ Lĩnh and Đinh Liễn, leaving Đinh Toàn the last heir, enthroned at the age of six.

As a child he was emperor in name only, and all power lay with the regent Lê Hoàn. Some modern historians suggest that Dương Vân Nga plotted with Lê Hoàn in the killings to put her son on the throne, but this is not confirmed. Two officials, Đinh Điền and Nguyễn Bặc, feared that Lê Hoàn would replace the dynasty and suspected him of a liaison with the dowager empress; they moved against him and were quickly crushed.

The prince consort Ngô Nhật Khánh fled to Champa and persuaded its monarch, Parameshvaravarman I, to send a fleet against the capital at Hoa Lư, but a sudden storm sank many of the ships. In 980, hearing of Đinh Bộ Lĩnh's death, the Song emperor sent an army to invade Đại Cồ Việt, as the country was then called. Because the emperor was too young, the dowager empress and the court enthroned Lê Hoàn, who as Lê Đại Hành fought the Song army twice and drove the invaders out, and with his accession the Đinh dynasty came to an end.

After he was deposed, Đinh Toàn received the noble title Vệ Vương. In 1001, while putting down the rebellion of Cửu Long in Thanh Hóa Province, he was struck by an arrow and died at once, at the age of 27. Later historical works gave him the name by which he is known, Đinh Phế Đế, the deposed emperor of the Đinh dynasty.
dinh-tien-hoang: Đinh Bộ Lĩnh was born in 924 in Hoa Lư, south of the Red River Delta in what is now Ninh Bình Province. His real name was allegedly Đinh Hoàn. He grew up in a local village during the disintegration of the Tang dynasty, which had dominated Vietnam for centuries, and became a local military leader at a very young age. The first independent Vietnamese polity had emerged when the warlord Ngô Quyền defeated the forces of the Southern Han at the First Battle of the Bạch Đằng River in 938, but the Ngô dynasty was weak and could not unify the country.

Faced with anarchy as twelve warlords competed for control, and with the threat of the Southern Han, which saw itself as heir to the ancient kingdom of Nan Yue, Đinh Bộ Lĩnh sought to unify the Vietnamese. When the last Ngô king died in 965 he seized power and founded a new kingdom with its capital in his home district of Hoa Lư. To establish his legitimacy he married a woman of the Ngô family. In his first years he avoided antagonising the Southern Han, but in 968 he adopted the title of emperor, Hoàng Đế, declaring independence from Chinese overlordship, and called his kingdom Đại Cồ Việt. He became known as Đinh Tiên Hoàng, the Former Đinh Emperor.

After the Song dynasty annexed the Southern Han in 971, he sent a tribute mission to the Song in 972. Emperor Taizu of Song recognised him as Giao Chỉ Quận Vương, King of Giao Chi, a title that implied vassalage. In exchange for tribute payable every three years, Đinh Bộ Lĩnh obtained a non-aggression agreement. He also reformed the administration and the armed forces, established a royal court with a hierarchy of civil and military officials, and set up a harsh justice system in which treason was punished by cooking in a vat of boiling oil or by being fed to a caged tiger.

In 979 a palace official, inspired by a dream, killed Đinh Bộ Lĩnh and his eldest son Đinh Liễn while they slept in the palace courtyard. The general Nguyễn Bặc quickly arrested and executed the killer. The throne passed to the emperor's surviving six-year-old son. The Song dynasty sent an army to exploit the turmoil, and Lê Hoàn, commander-in-chief of the army, took power, dethroned the child, removed his opponents at court and defeated the Song invasion. He proclaimed himself emperor and founded the Early Lê dynasty, still calling the country Đại Cồ Việt. Đinh Bộ Lĩnh is regarded as a significant figure in the establishment of Vietnamese independence and political unity in the 10th century.
dinmukhamed-kunaev: Kunayev was born on 12 January 1912 at Verny, now Almaty, the son of a Kazakh clerk. He studied at the Institute of Non-Ferrous and Fine Metallurgy in Moscow, and by 1939 was engineer-in-chief of the Pribalkhashatroi mine, when he joined the Communist Party. From April 1942 to 1946 he was deputy chairman of the Council of People's Commissars of the Kazakh SSR and oversaw the setting up of factories evacuated to Kazakhstan. He was president of the Academy of Sciences of the Kazakh SSR from 1952 and chairman of the Council of Ministers from 1955. His rise was closely tied to that of Leonid Brezhnev, with whom he formed a friendship that lasted until Brezhnev's death.

On 19 January 1960 Kunayev was elected first secretary of the Communist Party of Kazakhstan, the first Kazakh to hold the post. He supported the Virgin Lands campaign, which brought a large influx of Russian settlers. In 1962 he was dismissed after disagreeing with Khrushchev's plans to transfer lands in southern Kazakhstan to Uzbekistan. He returned as first secretary in 1964, when Khrushchev was ousted, and held the post for 22 more years. He became a full member of the Politburo in 1971.

In his second term the Virgin Lands Territory was abolished, new regions such as Turgai and Jezkazgan were formed in the north, and areas given to Uzbekistan were returned, so that the republic's territory grew for the first time since 1936. Supporters credit him with the building of oil refineries at Pavlodar and Chimkent and with backing Kazakh writers whose books were refused elsewhere.

At the 16th Congress of the Kazakh party in February 1986 Kunayev was criticised by Nursultan Nazarbayev, chairman of the Council of Ministers. He was removed under pressure from Mikhail Gorbachev, who accused him of corruption, and on 16 December 1986 the Politburo replaced him with Gennady Kolbin, an ethnic Russian who had never lived in Kazakhstan. The decision set off three days of street rioting in Almaty, called Jeltoqsan, or December in Kazakh. Kunayev died of a heart attack on 22 August 1993 at Akshi and was buried at the Kensai cemetery in Alma-Ata on 25 August.
dinuzulu-kacetshwayo: After the Anglo-Zulu War the British broke Zululand into thirteen smaller territories, one of which Cetshwayo administered. They later restored him as paramount leader but left his relative Usibepu, or Zibhebhu, with his lands intact. On 22 July 1883 Usibepu attacked Cetshwayo's new kraal at Ulundi, wounding the king, who fled to Eshowe. Dinuzulu succeeded his father on 20 May 1884. To contest the succession he first appealed to the British and, receiving no answer, offered land to Boer farmers of the Vryheid and Utrecht districts if they would fight for him.

Led by General Louis Botha, the Boers formed Dinuzulu's Volunteers and, after several clashes, defeated Zibhebhu at the Battle of Ghost Mountain, also called the Battle of Tshaneni, on 5 June 1884. The Nieuwe Republiek they founded on the land he awarded was recognised by Germany and Portugal. Britain annexed the coastal plains to keep the Boers from building a harbour, and the republic joined the Zuid Afrikaanse Republiek at its own request in 1888.

For leading a Zulu army against the British over the annexation of the coastal plains, Dinuzulu was exiled to Saint Helena for seven years. He lived at Rosemary Hall, Maldivia and Francis Plain House with an entourage of about 20, including two of his wives, his uncles, a doctor and translators, and there he learned to write and played the piano and organ. After his release the British installed him as their government's induna. Accused after the Bambatha rebellion of having ordered it, he protested his innocence but was sentenced in March 1908 to four years' imprisonment.

When his old friend Louis Botha became Prime Minister of the Union of South Africa, he had Dinuzulu released to the farm Uitkyk in the Transvaal, where he died on 18 October 1913. After a state funeral he was buried at Nobamba in the Khosini Valley and was succeeded by his son Solomon kaDinuzulu. His statue stands beside Botha's in Durban. Beads said to come from his necklace, claimed to have been found by Robert Baden-Powell, were later presented to Scout leaders after Wood Badge training, and the beads given today are replicas, though how Baden-Powell obtained them is disputed.
diocese-of-dresden-meissen: Meissen grew from a castle built by King Henry I the Fowler about 928 to protect German colonists among the pagan Wends. At the Synod of Ravenna in 967 it was decided to create the bishoprics of Meissen, Merseburg and Zeitz as suffragans of the Archbishopric of Magdeburg; a record of its endowment by Otto I in 971 survives. The first bishop, Burchard, died in 969, and the conversion of the Wends was the chief task of his successors, completed in the 13th century chiefly through Cistercian monasteries such as Dobrilugk and Neuzelle.

Bishop Benno (1066–1106) was imprisoned by Henry IV in 1076, sided with Pope Gregory VII and was deposed after the Synod of Quedlinburg in 1085, but made peace with the emperor and was restored in 1086. Wittigo I (1266–1293) began the Gothic cathedral of Meissen, and the bishops, prince-bishops of the Holy Roman Empire from the 13th century, were often disputed in that position by the Margraves of Meissen. In 1405 Pope Boniface IX made Meissen an exempt diocese directly under the Holy See.

John VII of Schleinitz (1518–1537) opposed Martin Luther and urged the canonisation of Benno in 1523, but after the death of Duke George of Saxony in 1539 the Reformation triumphed. The last bishop, John of Haugwitz, resigned, became a Lutheran and married. In 1567 the Holy See separated the Lusatian parts of the diocese and made them the Apostolic Prefecture of Meißen at St. Peter's in Bautzen, under Johannes Leisentritt. After Prussia took Lower Lusatia and eastern Upper Lusatia, their parishes went to the Prince-Bishopric of Breslau in 1821.

In 1921 Pope Benedict XV refounded the diocese with its seat at Bautzen, absorbing the Apostolic Vicariate in the Saxon Hereditary Lands, which had served the Catholic diaspora in the rest of Saxony from Dresden since 1743. Between 1945 and 1948 the number of parishioners more than doubled with refugees and expellees from former Eastern Germany and Czechoslovakia, while four parishes east of the Lusatian Neisse were lost to Poland.

The seat moved to Dresden in 1980. The diocese covers most of the Free State of Saxony and parts of Thuringia in nine deaneries, and since 1994 it has belonged to the ecclesiastical province of Berlin. Its central church is Dresden Cathedral, the former court church built from 1739 to 1755, and its patron saint is Benno of Meissen.
diocese-of-rottenburg-stuttgart: In 1803 Prince Primate Karl Theodor von Dalberg appointed a vicar general for the new state of Württemberg, the auxiliary bishop Franz Karl Joseph Fürst von Hohenlohe-Waldenburg-Schillingsfürst, who consecrated the present co-cathedral in Stuttgart. The vicariate's first seat was Ellwangen Abbey, but in 1817 it moved to Rottenburg. The diocese itself was established on 16 August 1821 by the papal bull De salute animarum, on territory separated from the suppressed Diocese of Konstanz, and its formation was complete with the enthronement of the first bishop, Johann Baptist von Keller, on 20 May 1828.

Keller served until his death in 1845. Among his successors were Karl Joseph von Hefele, bishop from 1869 to 1893, Paul Wilhelm von Keppler, from 1898 to 1926, and Johannes Baptista Sproll, from 1927 to 1949. Franz Xaver von Linsenmann held the see only from July to September 1898 and was never consecrated a bishop. On 18 January 1978 the diocese was renamed Rottenburg-Stuttgart. Walter Kasper, bishop from 1989 to 1999, went on to preside over the Pontifical Council for Promoting Christian Unity and was created a cardinal in 2001. Gebhard Fürst held the see from 2000 to 2023, and Klaus Krämer followed him in 2024.

The diocese is a suffragan of the metropolitan Archdiocese of Freiburg and covers the territory of the former Kingdom of Württemberg. Its cathedral is St. Martin's in Rottenburg and its co-cathedral St. Eberhard in Stuttgart. It has three minor basilicas: St. Vitus in Ellwangen, the former abbey church and first seat of the vicar general; St. Martin in Ulm's Benedictine Wiblingen Abbey; and St. Martin of Tours and St. Oswald in Weingarten. In 2014 it served 1,872,849 Catholics, 37.0% of the population, over 19,500 km² in 1,096 parishes and 45 deaneries, with 1,016 priests.
diocles-of-carystus: Little is known of the life of Diocles, also called by the Latin name Diocles Medicus, the physician. He lived not long after Hippocrates, to whom Pliny says he was next in age and fame, and lived and worked in Athens. There he wrote what may be the first medical treatise in Attic, rather than the Ionic customary in Greek medical writing. He belonged to the medical sect of the Dogmatici. He invented the Spoon of Diocles, a surgical instrument for drawing out weapons such as barbed arrowheads lodged in the body.

His most important work was in practical medicine, above all diet and nutrition, but he also wrote the first systematic textbook on animal anatomy, and several sources say he was the first to use the word anatomy for the study. He held that health requires an understanding of the nature of the universe and its relation to man, and he stressed that nerves are the channels of sensation and that interference with them is directly involved in disease. It was once said that he first explained the difference between veins and arteries, but this does not seem to be correct.

Of his writings only titles and some fragments remain, preserved by Galen, Caelius Aurelianus, Oribasius, Athenaeus in the Deipnosophistae and other ancient writers. A Letter on Preserving Health addressed in his name to a king Antigonus, on the diet fitting each season of the year, was inserted by Paul of Aegina at the end of the first book of his medical compendium; if genuine, it was probably written to Antigonus II Gonatas, king of Macedon. It resembles letters ascribed to Hippocrates. Philip van der Eijk has collected and translated the fragments into English, with a commentary in a separate volume.
diocletian: Diocletian was born Diocles to a family of low status in the Roman province of Dalmatia, probably at or near Salona. The first forty years of his life are mostly obscure. He was an Illyrian soldier who served under Aurelian and Probus, and in 282 Emperor Carus made him commander of the Protectores domestici, the elite cavalry attached to the imperial household, which earned him a consulship in 283.

After Carus died in 283, his sons Numerian and Carinus became joint emperors. Numerian was found dead in a closed coach in Bithynia, and Eutropius and Aurelius Victor both describe the death as an assassination. The army proclaimed Diocles emperor under the name Diocletianus, and he defeated Carinus at the Battle of the Margus.

Diocletian judged that rule by one man was too dangerous, since Aurelian and Probus had been assassinated. In 286 he raised Maximian to the rank of Augustus to rule the West, while he governed the East. On 1 March 293 each appointed a junior colleague with the title Caesar: Constantius for Maximian and Galerius for Diocletian. This rule of four is known as the Tetrarchy. He campaigned against the Sarmatians and Carpi, built forts along the Danube, and in 299 made a favourable peace with Persia after Galerius had sacked Ctesiphon.

He separated and enlarged the civil and military services, reorganised the provinces and established new administrative centres at Nicomedia, Mediolanum, Sirmium and Treverorum, nearer the frontiers than Rome. He styled himself an autocrat, with an imposing court ceremony. He turned requisition into a tax based on heads and land, tied to a regular census. His Edict on Maximum Prices of 301, an attempt to curb inflation, was counterproductive and quickly ignored.

In 303 Diocletian ordered the persecution of Christians. According to Lactantius, he first believed that excluding Christians from the bureaucracy and army would be enough, while Galerius pushed for their extermination. It became the last, largest and bloodiest official persecution of Christianity in the empire, and it failed to eliminate it.

Weakened by illness, he left office on 1 May 305, the first Roman emperor to abdicate voluntarily. He retired to a fortified palace near Spalatum on the Dalmatian coast, which forms the historic core of Split. His tetrarchic system collapsed after his abdication, and civil wars followed until Constantine defeated Licinius in 324.
diodorus-siculus: Diodorus gives his birthplace in his own work as Agyrium in Sicily, now called Agira. Apart from his writings, antiquity provides almost nothing about his life. The only other notice is in the Chronicon of Jerome, which records under the year of Abraham 1968, equated with 49 BCE, that Diodorus of Sicily, a writer of Greek history, became illustrious. His English translator, Charles Henry Oldfather, remarked on a striking coincidence: one of only two known Greek inscriptions from Agyrium is the tombstone of a Diodorus, the son of Apollonius. The last work attributed to him is dated to 21 BCE.

His universal history, which he named Bibliotheca historica or Historical Library, was written between 60 and 30 BCE and ran to forty books. Books 1 to 5 and 11 to 20 survive; fragments of the lost books are preserved in Photius and in the Excerpts of Constantine Porphyrogenitus. The first section, books I to VI, treats the mythic history of non-Hellenic and Hellenic peoples up to the destruction of Troy and is geographical in plan. It describes ancient Egypt in book I, Mesopotamia, India, Scythia and Arabia in book II, North Africa in book III, and Greece and Europe in books IV to VI.

The second section, books VII to XVII, covers the world from the Trojan War to the death of Alexander the Great. The third, from book XVII to the end, runs from Alexander's successors to either 60 BCE or the beginning of Julius Caesar's Gallic Wars. Because the end is lost, it is unclear whether Diodorus reached the Gallic War, as he promised at the start, or stopped at 60 BCE, perhaps old and tired from his labours.

The title acknowledges that the work was assembled from many sources. The authors on whom he drew include Hecataeus of Abdera, Ctesias of Cnidus, Ephorus, Theopompus, Hieronymus of Cardia, Duris of Samos, Diyllus, Philistus, Timaeus, Polybius and Posidonius.
diodotus-i: Bactria, the region of the Oxus valley in modern Afghanistan and Tajikistan, was conquered by Alexander the Great between 329 and 327 BCE, and he settled veterans there. Seleucus I incorporated it into the Seleucid Empire between 308 and 305 BCE, and his son Antiochus I established firm control between 295 and 281 BCE, founding or refounding cities on the Greek model and opening mints. Diodotus became Seleucid satrap of Bactria during the reign of Antiochus II. The importance of the post suggests he was a man of standing. Some scholars think he later married a daughter of Antiochus II, but this is uncertain. Excavations at Ai Khanoum show irrigation works and civic building in these years, and probably raiding by steppe nomads.

The Roman historian Justin records that Diodotus, governor of the thousand cities of Bactria, defected and proclaimed himself king. The date is unclear. Scholars favouring a high chronology place his independence around 255 BCE under Antiochus II, and those favouring a low chronology around 245 BCE at the start of the reign of Seleucus II. Frank Holt sees a gradual process in which Diodotus and other eastern satraps gathered more autonomy, probably beginning in the 250s BCE. Jens Jakobsson argues for a sudden break in 246 or 245 BCE, during the Third Syrian War. The excavations show no destruction, so the change seems to have been peaceful.

Diodotus divided his territory into satrapies, two of them, Aspionus and Turiva, on the Parthian border. Justin and Strabo stress the prosperity of the kingdom. According to Strabo, Diodotus drove Arsaces, leader of the Parni, out of Bactria and stayed hostile to the Parthians for the rest of his reign.

His coinage tells much of the story. As satrap he issued coins in the name of Antiochus II. Holt thinks he then introduced silver tetradrachms bearing a diademed male head, probably his own and apparently ageing over time, with Zeus hurling a thunderbolt on the reverse, though the legend still read Of King Antiochus. A wreath on late issues may commemorate a victory over the Parthians and the title Soter, saviour. Later Greco-Bactrian kings, Agathocles and Antimachus, struck coins in his memory naming him Diodotus Soter.

He died around 235 BCE, probably of natural causes, and was succeeded by his son Diodotus II, who made peace with the Parthians. Diodotus II was later killed by a usurper, Euthydemus, who founded the Euthydemid dynasty. Some historians have suggested that Diodotus had a daughter who married Euthydemus, but no explicit evidence supports this.
diodotus-ii: Diodotus II Theos, Diodotus the God, was the son of Diodotus I Soter, who rebelled against the Seleucid Empire. The Seleucids gained control of Bactria between 308 and 305 BCE and made it a satrapy. Diodotus I ruled it as satrap in the 260s BCE and drifted into independence under Antiochus II Theos, proclaiming himself king some time between 255 and 245 BCE. Surviving literary sources mention the younger Diodotus only in passing, since Apollodorus of Artemita's Parthian History, which told his career, is lost. Most of what is known must be reconstructed from coins.

Coins of Diodotus I came from two mints, one showing a mature man and the other a similar but younger figure. Frank L. Holt proposes that the younger figure was Diodotus II, who held a portion of the realm as co-regent, as Seleucid crown princes had held the east. Where this region lay is unknown. Holt tentatively places it in the west, exposed to Parthian raids, with its base at Bactra.

Diodotus II probably succeeded as sole king around 235 BCE. His father had expelled Arsaces I of the Parni from Bactria, and Arsaces had gone on to seize Parthia from the Seleucids. Diodotus I had remained opposed to the Parni and so aligned with the Seleucids. His son reversed that policy. According to Justin, Arsaces, relieved by the death of Diodotus I, made peace and an alliance with the son, and later defeated Seleucus II, who had come to punish the rebels. This battle took place around 228 BCE. It is unclear whether Diodotus fought in it or only stayed neutral.

He continued his father's minting on two mints, in gold staters and silver tetradrachms, with a diademed head on the obverse and Zeus about to hurl a thunderbolt on the reverse. After a break the legend changed from King Antiochus to King Diodotus, which seems to mark a final renunciation of Seleucid authority. Large bronze issues found at Ai-Khanoum show growing use of money in Bactria.

Around 225 BCE Euthydemus I killed Diodotus and took the throne, founding the Euthydemid dynasty. Excavations show that Ai-Khanoum was besieged around 225 BCE, which Holt connects with the seizure of power, and the evidence points to a civil war. Holt proposes that the alliance with Arsaces answered this war, while W. W. Tarn thought Euthydemus rebelled because of the alliance. Tarn's claim that Euthydemus was Diodotus's brother-in-law has no evidence behind it. The later Graeco-Bactrian kings Agathocles and Antimachus I struck coins in memory of Diodotus Theos.
diogenes-the-cynic: Diogenes was born in Sinope, a Milesian colony on the Black Sea, the son of Hicesias, a money-changer. He and his father were accused of debasing the currency. Ancient sources disagree on who was responsible, and modern scholars are divided: some see the episode as a fiction symbolising his aim to revalue the currency, meaning to challenge conventional values, while others point to debased Sinopean coins as evidence of a historical core. It is unclear whether he was banished or fled. Plutarch notes that the hardships of exile made him a philosopher.

Diogenes advocated a shameless life lived according to nature rather than social convention. He lived by begging, sheltered in a large ceramic storage jar, and was said to wander the marketplace by day with a lit lamp, saying that he was looking for a man, that is, a wise man. Asked where he came from, he answered kosmopolitēs, a citizen of the world. Plato is said to have called him Socrates gone mad.

According to Diogenes Laertius, he wrote dialogues, letters and tragedies, none of which survive. The best-known anecdote has Alexander the Great, probably in 336 BCE at the Isthmus of Corinth, ask whether he wanted anything; Diogenes replied that Alexander should stand a little out of his sun, and Plutarch reports Alexander as saying that if he were not Alexander he would be Diogenes.

Ancient sources give several accounts of his death, among them self-asphyxiation, a raw octopus and an infected dog bite. A story that he died on the same night as Alexander is probably legend, and one modern scholar thinks he most plausibly died of old age, in or near Corinth. The Corinthians arranged his funeral and buried him outside the city walls. After his death Cynicism diverged: one branch, founded by Zeno of Citium, evolved into Stoicism, while another, beginning with Crates of Thebes, preserved his principles until Sallustius of Emesa in the 5th century CE. His attitude to the rich gave the word cynicism its modern sense.
diogo-cao: Little is known of the early life of Diogo Cão, who is also called Diogo Cam. According to tradition he was born in Vila Real, Portugal, around 1452, and his grandfather Gonçalo Cão had fought for Portuguese independence at the Battle of Aljubarrota. By 1480 he was sailing off the coast of Africa in the service of King João II, and there is a record that he returned to Portugal with captured Spanish ships.

The Treaty of Alcáçovas of 1480 confirmed Portugal's monopoly on trade and exploration along Africa's west coast. João II sent a fleet in 1481 to build the fortress of São Jorge da Mina on the Gold Coast and restarted the programme of exploration southward. Cão was chosen to lead the first voyage, in 1482.

Cão filled his ship with stone pillars, called padrões, surmounted by the cross of the Order of Christ and engraved with the Portuguese royal arms, to be erected at significant landmarks. He stopped at São Jorge da Mina to resupply, reached the mouth of the Congo River and marked it with a padrão on Shark Point. He sailed a short way up the river and began modest trade with the people of the Bakongo kingdom. Told that their king lived farther upriver, he sent four Christian native messengers to find him, and went on south along the coast of present-day Angola, raising a second padrão at Cabo de Santa Maria.

On his return to the Congo he found that his messengers had not come back, and he took four local men visiting his ship to Portugal. He reached Lisbon by 8 April 1484, where João II ennobled him and granted him an annuity and a coat of arms showing two padrões. On the second voyage, of 1484 to 1486, he carried the four men home and sailed about 170 kilometres up the Congo to the Yellala Falls, where an inscription records his passage. He set up two more padrões, at Cabo Negro and Cape Cross, the latter probably marking the end of his progress southward.

Information about his death is scanty and contradictory. A legend on Martin Behaim's globe reads hic moritur, here he dies, which seems to place his death on the African coast in 1486, but the historian João de Barros never mentions it. All four of his pillars have been found on their original sites. Those of the Kongo estuary, Cabo Negro and Cabo de Santa Maria are in the Museum of the Lisbon Geographical Society, and the Cape Cross pillar, long in Berlin, has been returned to Namibia. Fernando Pessoa's poem Padrão, in his book Mensagem, takes Cão as its subject.
diogo-de-azambuja: Diogo de Azambuja was born at Montemor-o-Velho and became a knight of the Order of Aviz in the service of the Infante Dom Pedro, son of the regent Peter, Duke of Coimbra. When Peter was defeated and killed at the battle of Alfarrobeira in 1449, Azambuja followed his master into exile. In 1458 he fought for Afonso V in the conquest of Alcácer-Ceguer in Morocco, received several honours and became a counsellor of the king. In the War of the Castilian Succession he was wounded in the leg while retaking the town of Alegrete from the Castilians.

In 1481 John II gave him command of a fleet of nine caravels and two ships carrying 600 soldiers and 100 masons and carpenters, with stone and other materials for a fortress on the Gulf of Guinea. A defensible position was chosen and, despite resistance from the local population, the building was practically complete within 20 days. It was the best-known exploit of his long life.

Contacts for trade with the local people followed. Azambuja sent the fleet back to Lisbon with word that the mission had succeeded and stayed behind as captain with a garrison of 60 soldiers, holding the post until 1484. The fortress is now known as Elmina Castle.

The king rewarded him with the post of alcaide-mor of Monsaraz and a place on the Privy Council, and despite his age and disabled leg he remained in royal service for many years. In 1506, when he was over 70, Manuel I put him in charge of building the fortress of Castelo Real at Essaouira, in southern Morocco, to protect Portuguese interests. Azambuja built it and also took the city of Safi, where he remained captain until 1509, at the age of 77. He then returned to Portugal, where he died in 1518.
diogo-gomes: Probably a native of Lagos, Gomes began as a page in the household of Prince Henry the Navigator and had become a cavaleiro, or knight, by 1440. He took part in the slave raid led by Lançarote de Freitas of Lagos on the Arguin banks in 1445, and claimed to have captured 22 Berber slaves by himself. On 12 June 1451 he was named a royal clerk.

Around 1456 Prince Henry sent him down the West African coast in command of three vessels. He is said to have reached the Rio Grande, now the Geba River in Guinea Bissau, before strong currents and his crew's fear of the ocean's edge turned him back. On the way home he ascended the Gambia some 50 leagues to Cantor, an entrepot of the Mali gold trade, where he gathered news of the gold mines, of Timbuktu and of the Trans-Saharan routes. He also seems to have won over a chief named Numimansa and his court to Christianity and Portuguese allegiance.

From 1459 Gomes was receiver of royal customs at Sintra. On a voyage of 1462, which some historians date to 1460, he traded with the Serer of Sine and Saloum, met the Genoese captain António de Noli, and sailed to the Cape Verde islands, where he claimed to have been the first to land on and name Santiago, a priority Alvise Cadamosto contested. Noli reached Lisbon first and secured the island's captaincy. Gomes then served Ferdinand of Viseu and King Afonso V of Portugal, later as a magistrate in Sintra and Colares.

Late in life Gomes dictated his memoirs to the German cartographer Martin Behaim, perhaps around 1499, and they were written down in Latin as De prima inuentione Guineae. Apart from the official chronicle of Gomes Eanes de Zurara, they are the only surviving contemporary attempt at a chronological account of the discoveries under Henry. Historians read them with caution because of their self-promotion, errors and hasty Latin, but they hold details found nowhere else, such as the rediscovery of the Azores. The single manuscript was found in Munich in 1845 and printed in 1847.
diomedes: In myth Diomedes was the son of Tydeus and Deipyle. Tydeus, an Aetolian of royal blood and the son of Oeneus, king of Calydon, was exiled for killing relatives and found refuge at Argos, where King Adrastus gave him his daughter Deipyle in marriage. Tydeus died among the Seven against Thebes, and according to the Iliad Diomedes was then a small child. He later succeeded his maternal grandfather Adrastus as king of Argos.

According to Homer, Diomedes came to Troy with 80 ships, a contribution third only to those of Agamemnon (100) and Nestor (90), with Sthenelus, his charioteer and probably closest friend, and Euryalus fighting under him. He is the key fighter in the first third of the Iliad. He is the only human besides Heracles granted strength to fight immortals, and he wounded both Ares and Aphrodite in a single day, yet he retreated before Apollo, which some interpreters read as his keeping within mortal limits.

Diomedes was a companion of Odysseus, and both were favourites of Athena. After the seer Helenus revealed that Troy would not fall while the Palladium, an image of Athena, stood inside its walls, the two stole it, and Diomedes is generally regarded as the one who carried it to the ships. After Troy fell, Diomedes and Nestor decided to leave at once, and Diomedes reached Argos four days later, one of the few Achaean commanders to return safely.

Tradition says Diomedes went to Daunia in Apulia, where King Daunus gave him land and his daughter Euippe in return for help against the Messapians. He built Argyrippa, hosted Aeneas there and gave back the Palladium, as an oracle had told him to give it to a Trojan. The Greeks and Romans credited him with founding many towns in southern Italy, among them Arpi, Beneventum, Brundusium, Canusium, Venafrum, Ancona, Adria and Venusia.

Strabo lists four traditions of his end: he went home to Argos and died, he stayed at Urium, he disappeared on the island of Diomedea in the Adriatic, whose birds were said to be his companions, or he stayed among the Heneti and was mysteriously deified. Pindar says Athena made him immortal. Hero cults of Diomedes are attested in Cyprus, Metapontum and along the Adriatic coast. At Argos his shield was carried through the streets with the Palladium at the festival of Athena. In the Inferno Dante places him in the Eighth Circle of Hell, among the counsellors of fraud.
dionisio-de-herrera: José Dionisio de la Trinidad de Herrera y Díaz del Valle was born on 9 October 1781 into a land-owning family. He studied at the University of San Carlos of Guatemala, where he took a law degree and came into contact with the liberal ideas of the French Revolution. He was the uncle and tutor of Francisco Morazán, later a Liberal Central American general. His first public office, in 1820, was that of secretary of the town government of Tegucigalpa.

Herrera became head of state of Honduras on 16 September 1824, after Central America had won independence from Spain and from Mexico, with Colonel José Justo Milla as his deputy. He decreed the first territorial divisions of Honduras, creating the departments of Comayagua, Tegucigalpa, Santa Bárbara, Yoro, Olancho and Choluteca, and promulgated the state's first constitution on 11 December 1825. He survived an assassination attempt on 3 November 1826.

On 10 May 1827 Milla, aided by Honduran Conservatives, overthrew him in a coup, and Herrera was held prisoner in Guatemala until 1829. He then took office as head of state of Nicaragua on 12 May 1830 and held it until November 1833, relying on Morazán's support. His attempts at Liberal reforms there failed in the face of opposition from the clergy.

Elected head of state of El Salvador in 1835, Herrera declined the office. He retired from politics in 1838 and worked as a teacher in San Vicente, El Salvador, where he remained until his death on 13 June 1850. His nephew and former pupil Morazán, whose support had kept him in office in Nicaragua, became a leading Liberal general of Central America.
dionysia: The Dionysia consisted of two related festivals, the Rural Dionysia and the City Dionysia, held in different parts of the year. The rural festival was originally held at Eleutherae in Attica to celebrate the cultivation of vines, and took place in the winter month of Poseideon. Its central event was a procession in which phalloi were carried, accompanied by basket-carriers and bearers of loaves, water jars and goatskin bags of wine. Contests of dancing and singing followed, and in larger towns such as Piraeus and Eleusis there may have been dramatic performances. Aristophanes parodied the rural festival in The Acharnians, and his description is the earliest surviving account.

The City Dionysia was established under the tyranny of Peisistratus in the 6th century BCE. It was held probably from the 10th to the 16th of the month Elaphebolion, in March and April, and was run by the archon, who chose two assistants and ten curators. By tradition it began when Eleutherae joined Attica and brought a statue of Dionysus to Athens, where it was at first rejected; Dionysus then sent a plague, which ended when the Athenians accepted the cult. On the first day citizens, metics and delegates from colonies carried the statue to the Theatre of Dionysus.

The next day, at the proagon, playwrights announced the titles of their plays and judges were chosen by lot. Tradition holds that Thespis gave the first tragedy at the festival in 534 BCE. In the 5th century BCE three playwrights each presented three tragedies and a satyr play on successive days, and from 487 or 486 BCE comic poets also competed, each with one play. Most surviving Greek tragedies, including those of Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides, were first performed in the Theatre of Dionysus. Winners received a wreath of ivy.

Tragic output continued through most of the 4th century BCE, and at least one older play was revived each year. New plays were written until the 2nd century BCE, when new works of comedy and tragedy appear to have ceased. Drama continued, but prizes went to wealthy producers and prominent actors rather than to the long-dead playwrights. Knowledge of the winners comes from damaged inscriptions, the Fasti, the Didascaliae and the Victors Lists. Modern followers of Hellenism celebrate the Dionysia as a holiday.
dionysius-i-of-syracuse: Dionysius was the son of Hermocrates, a prominent Syracusan general, and began his working life as a clerk in public office. His achievements in the war against Carthage that began in 409 BCE led to his election as supreme military commander in 406 BCE, and in the following year he seized total power.

He seized it with the help of mercenaries, initially 600 men and later 1,000, granted to him as a bodyguard after he faked an attack on his own life. Having consolidated his position he imposed them on the whole community, which signalled the end of democracy in Syracuse. He was married at the same time to Aristomache, who bore him a daughter, Arete, and to Doris of Locris, mother of his son Dionysius II.

Dionysius fought a war with Carthage from 397 to 392 BCE with mixed success. He failed to drive the Carthaginians out of Sicily, and at his death they still held at least a third of it. In southern Italy he led an expedition against the Italiote League in 387 BCE, joined by the Lucanians, devastated the lands of Thurii and Croton, and took Rhegium in 386 after a long siege, selling its inhabitants as slaves. Sparta did not condemn his autocracy and even helped establish it, and he allowed Sparta to conscript mercenaries and assisted it in the Corinthian War with mercenaries and ships.

Around 387 to 385 BCE he began an intensive colonisation of the Adriatic, to dominate the sea routes to the grain markets of the Po Delta, gain access to Epirus and the riches of Delphi. He made pacts with the Illyrians and the Senones, and founded or settled Ancona, Adria, Issa and Lissos. This gave him control of the routes that carried Po Valley grain to Greece.

Sources differ on his death in 367 BCE. According to some he drank himself to death after his tragedy The Ransom of Hector won a prize at the Lenaia festival in Athens. Cicero and Diodorus Siculus report natural causes shortly after the news of the victory. Others say his physicians gave him an overdose of a sleeping potion at the instigation of his son Dionysius the Younger, who succeeded him, and Justin claims a conspiracy of his own kin, though a modern historian finds no evidence for it.

The ancients regarded him as the worst kind of despot, cruel, suspicious and vindictive. He was one of the first Greek rulers given divine honours in his lifetime, and his innovations in military technique, such as siege engines, became standard under Alexander the Great and later generals.
dionysius-ii-of-syracuse: Dionysius II was the son of Dionysius the Elder and Doris of Locri. When his father died in 367 BCE he was under thirty and completely inexperienced in public affairs. He inherited supreme power and began to rule under the supervision of his uncle Dion. Dion disapproved of the young man's lavishly dissolute lifestyle and invited his own teacher, Plato, to visit Syracuse. Together they tried to make the government more moderate, with Dionysius as an ideal philosopher-king, as Plato's Seventh Letter describes.

Under the influence of Dion's opponents Dionysius conspired with the historian Philistus and banished his uncle, taking complete power in 366 BCE. Without Dion his rule grew unpopular, since he was mostly incompetent at governing men and commanding soldiers. When Plato appealed for Dion's return, Dionysius interfered with Dion's property and finances and gave his wife to another man. In the Seventh Letter Plato describes a test of Dionysius's philosophical progress, which, in Plato's account, he failed by claiming to know already the most important matters and by disdaining further training.

Dion formed a small army at Zacynthus and returned to Sicily in 357 BCE, to the delight of the Syracusans. Dionysius was then at Caulonia in Italy, and Dion took all of Syracuse except the island citadel. Dionysius sailed back and tried attacks and peace treaties, but without success, and then left for Locri, putting his son Apollocrates in charge of the citadel. In Locri he made himself tyrant and treated the people with great cruelty.

Dionysius did not return to Syracuse until 346 BCE, eight years after Dion's assassination by his officers. When he left Locri the remaining troops were driven out and the locals took revenge on his wife and daughters. He regained power in Syracuse only because of its political instability: many other cities in Sicily had defected and were ruled by local tyrants, and several joined the Syracusans in an attack that forced him back into the citadel.

In 344 BCE Timoleon arrived and began his invasion of Sicily. Dionysius, aware that he could not win and out of respect for Timoleon, arranged the surrender of the citadel and received safe passage to Corinth. He lived there in increasingly miserable conditions. The anecdote of the Sword of Damocles is often wrongly attributed to him, since it concerns his father, and a tradition makes him a schoolteacher at Corinth.
dionysus: Dionysus is the god of wine-making, orchards, fruit, vegetation, fertility, festivity, ritual madness, religious ecstasy and theatre. Nineteenth-century scholars often regarded him as a foreign deity admitted late into the Greek pantheon, since his myths so often show a god who travels abroad and struggles for acceptance on his return. Later evidence has shown him to be among the earliest gods attested on the Greek mainland. His name, written di-wo-nu-so, appears on Linear B tablets from Mycenaean Pylos that link him with offerings of wine. His worship was firmly established by the seventh century BCE.

Wine was a religious focus of the cult and was regarded as the god's earthly incarnation. It could ease suffering, bring joy and inspire divine madness. His thyrsus, a fennel stalk sometimes wound with ivy, was both a wand and a weapon against those who opposed him. His procession was made up of female followers, the maenads, and of satyrs. In the Orphic tradition the first Dionysus was a son of Zeus and Persephone, dismembered by the Titans and reborn. In another account Zeus took the infant from the womb of Semele, a daughter of Cadmus, after she was killed by a thunderbolt, and so he is called the one with two mothers.

In myth he discovered the vine, was driven mad by Hera, and was cured by the goddess Cybele. He travelled through Asia and to India, and when Alexander the Great reached a city called Nysa near the Indus, the locals said that Dionysus had founded it.

The Rural Dionysia, held in the winter month of Poseideon, centred on a procession followed by dramatic performances and competitions. The Anthesteria, an Athenian festival at the beginning of spring, opened the wine vats and was believed to let the dead rise from the underworld. In Rome the cult was established around 200 BCE in the Aventine grove of Stimula, near the temple of Liber Pater, with whom Bacchus was identified. The Roman state treated independent festivals of Bacchus, the Bacchanalia, as subversive, and made their celebration a capital offence except in forms it approved and supervised. The festivals' sacred dramas were the initial driving force behind the development of theatre in Western culture.
dioscorus-i-of-alexandria: Dioscorus' origins are unknown, though it is known that he was not a Copt. He served as dean of the Catechetical School of Alexandria and as personal secretary to Cyril of Alexandria, whom he accompanied to the First Council of Ephesus in 431. He rose to be archdeacon and had been made Cyril's designated successor. In the struggle against Nestorius, Cyril and Dioscorus held to the Alexandrian formula of one nature of God the Word incarnate, against the Antiochene formula of two natures after the union.

Dioscorus succeeded Cyril in the summer of 444. Cyril's nephew Athanasius, a wealthy priest and possible rival, accused him of harassment, and at Chalcedon the deacon Ischyrion accused him of laying waste to property. In 448 Flavian, Bishop of Constantinople, held a synod that condemned the archimandrite Eutyches. Eutyches appealed and received the support of Dioscorus. In 449 Emperor Theodosius II convened the Second Council of Ephesus and asked Dioscorus to preside. It reinstated Eutyches and deposed Flavian and several other bishops, among them Theodoret. Pope Leo I called it a robber synod. In 450 Dioscorus had ten bishops sign a document excommunicating Leo. Flavian was exiled and died within days, and the accounts given at Chalcedon differ on who was responsible.

The Council of Chalcedon in October 451 questioned Dioscorus' conduct. It deposed him for violations of canon law rather than heresy, because he did not attend from the third session onward despite an imperial summons. Proterius was appointed patriarch and met a riot in Alexandria, since the native Christians continued to support Dioscorus. He died in exile at Gangra in Paphlagonia in September 454, and his supporters elected his disciple Timothy, creating the split between the Coptic and the Melchite churches.

The Coptic, Syriac and other Oriental Orthodox churches venerate him as a saint, while Eastern Orthodox and Catholic churches have often deemed him a heretic. Some theologians argue he was deposed for administrative errors rather than heresy. In 1973 Pope Shenouda III of Alexandria declared a common faith in the nature of Christ with Pope Paul VI.
dipavamsa: The chronicle is believed to have been compiled from the Atthakatha and other sources, probably by several Buddhist monks or nuns of the Anuradhapura Maha Viharaya. It was likely the first completely new Pali text composed in Sri Lanka, and among the last to be composed anonymously. Because it pays close attention to the nuns of the island and describes Theri Sangamitta, daughter of Ashoka, as particularly proficient in history, Hugh Nevill suggested that it came from a community of nuns rather than from monks.

Its preamble promises the chronicle of the Buddha's visits to the island, the arrival of the Tooth Relic and the Bodhi tree, the advent of the doctrine, the rise of the teachers, the spread of Buddhism and the coming of Vijaya. It names three visits of the Buddha, to Kelaniya, to Deegavapi and to the place in Anuradhapura where the Bo-sapling was later planted, but none to Sri Pada. Its Vijaya legend is less supernatural than the later one: the ancestor of Vijaya is an outlaw named Sinha who attacked caravans, and Vijaya, sent away for cruel conduct with seven hundred followers, lands at Tamba-panni on the day the Buddha passed away.

The Dipavamsa praises the Theravada of the Mahavihara as a great banyan tree and calls the seventeen other schools thorns on it. It tells the story of Dutugamunu in only ten stanzas, where the Mahavamsa gives it ten chapters.

In the 5th century King Dhatusena of Anuradhapura ordered the chronicle to be recited at the Mahinda festival held each year in the city. It served as source material for the more coherently organised Mahavamsa, and the chronology of kings in the two is believed to be largely correct from about the time of Ashoka's death. Hermann Oldenberg edited and translated it into English in 1879, and B. C. Law studied it in 1947. Tilman Frasch has shown that Burma kept a longer and less corrupt text than the Sinhalese manuscripts Oldenberg used; one such manuscript is in the John Rylands Library.
dipendra-of-nepal: Dipendra Bir Bikram Shah Dev was born on 27 June 1971 at the Narayanhiti Royal Palace, the eldest child of Birendra, then Crown Prince of Nepal, and Princess Aishwarya. He was educated at Kanti Ishwori High School in Kathmandu and Budhanilkantha School, then at Eton College in the United Kingdom and Tri Chandra College, and later joined the Nepalese Military Academy at Kharipati. He studied geography at Tribhuvan University for a master's degree and was a doctoral student there, and he received further military training and pilot training.

He was interested in social services and sports, became a karateka while studying in the United Kingdom and received a black belt at around the age of 20. He was a patron of the National Sports Council and the Nepal Scouts, and he wrote articles for Nepalese periodicals, often on nationhood and nationality.

On 1 June 2001 Dipendra opened fire at a party in a house on the grounds of the Narayanhiti Royal Palace. According to the official inquiry's findings he shot and killed his father King Birendra, his mother Queen Aishwarya, his younger brother Prince Nirajan, his younger sister Princess Shruti, his uncle Prince Dhirendra, his aunts Princess Shanti and Princess Sharada, his cousin Princess Jayanti and his uncle-in-law Kumar Khadga Bikram Shah, before shooting himself in the head. Because his father was dead he succeeded as king while in a coma. He died on 4 June 2001, after three days as king, and his uncle Gyanendra succeeded him.

His motives remain unknown. A leading theory holds that he wished to marry Devyani Rana, whom he had met in England, and that his parents objected and told him he would have to give up his right to succeed to do so. Other theories hold that he was unhappy with the shift from absolute to constitutional monarchy after the 1990 People's Movement.
diploma-ottonianum: Pope John XII, not yet 26, had lost a war against Pandolfo Testa di Ferro of Capua, while Berengar of Ivrea, in effect King of Italy, and his son Adalbert occupied many strongholds of the Papal States. The pope turned to Otto I, who came to Italy with a powerful army; Berengar avoided battle and withdrew to his castles. Otto reached Rome on 31 January 962 and swore to recognise John as pope and ruler of Rome and to issue no decrees without his consent, while John swore to keep faith with Otto and make no alliance with Berengar and Adalbert.

On 2 February the pope crowned Otto emperor. Ten days later, at a Roman synod held at Otto's wish, John founded the Archbishopric of Magdeburg and the Bishopric of Merseburg, gave the pallium to the archbishops of Salzburg and Trier and confirmed Rather as Bishop of Verona. The emperor issued the diploma the next day.

The diploma confirmed the Roman Church in its possessions, especially those granted by the Donation of Pepin and by Charlemagne. Future popes were to be elected in canonical form, but consecrated only after the necessary pledges had been given to the emperor or his envoys. In effect the emperor became the guarantor of papal independence while keeping the right to confirm elections. Like other 10th-century documents, the surviving text seems to be a duplicate of the original, but the authenticity of its contents is considered certain.

Historians debate whether it was a gain in prestige for the papacy or a political triumph for the emperor. The alliance soon broke down: John sent envoys to the Magyars and the Byzantine Empire to form a league against Otto, who returned to Rome in November 963 and had a synod depose him and make Leo VIII, a layman, pope.

The diploma was confirmed at Easter 1020 in the Diploma Heinricianum of Pope Benedict VIII and Emperor Henry II at Bamberg; the historian Hanns Leo Mikoletzky called it a frequently overrated document. From the reign of Pope Leo IX the papacy gradually freed itself from imperial interference, and in 1059 Pope Nicholas II's bull In nomine Domini gave the election of popes to the cardinals alone, ending the emperor's privilege.
diponegoro: Diponegoro was born on 11 November 1785 in Yogyakarta. In his youth the VOC was dissolved, the British invaded Java and Dutch rule returned. He advised his father during the British period and helped British forces so far that Stamford Raffles offered him the sultan's title, which he declined. When his father died in 1814, the Dutch supported his younger half-brother Hamengkubuwono IV, although the late sultan had urged that Diponegoro succeed him.

A devout Muslim who lived in seclusion, Diponegoro was alarmed by the laxity in religious observance at his half-brother's court and by its pro-Dutch policy. Famine and plague spread in 1821. After Hamengkubuwono IV died in 1822 in mysterious circumstances, leaving an infant heir, Diponegoro was passed over again, though he believed he had been promised the succession.

Dutch rule was unpopular with farmers because of rising taxes and failed harvests, and with nobles who had lost the right to lease land. Many believed Diponegoro to be the Ratu Adil, the just ruler foretold in the Pralembang Jayabaya, and the eruption of Mount Merapi in 1822 and a cholera epidemic in 1824 suggested that a cataclysm was near. The Java War began in 1825. Diponegoro's guerrilla tactics, ambushes and denial of supplies inflicted heavy losses on the Dutch at first. General De Kock then adopted a strategy of fortified camps and mobile forces, and from 1829 Diponegoro lost the initiative.
His forces also attacked the Chinese minority in Java, for example at Ngawi and along the Bengawan Solo, and the relationship between the Chinese and the Javanese was never the same afterwards.

In March 1830 Diponegoro was invited to negotiate at Magelang under a flag of truce and was taken prisoner on 28 March. He saw this as a betrayal, while the Dutch said he had surrendered, and the painters Raden Saleh and Nicolaas Pieneman later depicted the scene in opposite ways. He was taken to Manado in 1830 and moved to Fort Rotterdam in Makassar in July 1833. His wife and some followers went with him. There he wrote his autobiography, the Babad Diponegoro.

Diponegoro died in Makassar on 8 January 1855, aged 69, and was buried in Kampung Melayu on land the Dutch donated; his tomb is visited by pilgrims today. Indonesians remember his struggle as an inspiration for the National Revolution, and in 1973 he was made a National Hero of Indonesia. An army regional command, a university in Semarang and warships are named for him. In March 2020 King Willem-Alexander of the Netherlands gave a kris identified as Diponegoro's to Indonesia, although there is doubt whether it is the original.
directorate-of-ukraine: The Directorate was set up on 13–14 November 1918 at a session of the Ukrainian National Union, in rebellion against the Ukrainian State of Hetman Pavlo Skoropadsky, who could no longer rely on Germany and Austria-Hungary after the defeat of the Central Powers. Its forces, led by the newly re-formed Sich Riflemen, were joined by most of Skoropadsky's troops in a month-long civil war, and the Russian officers he formed into a Special Corps could not stop them. On 19 December 1918 the Directorate's troops took Kyiv, and on 26 December it issued its declaration abolishing the Hetman regime.

The Directorate had five members from various parties and groups and was meant to govern until a new council could be elected; the Central Rada was not restored. The Labor Congress of Ukraine, meeting on 23–28 January 1919, confirmed it as the supreme body for the protection of the republic, with power to enact laws in the congress's absence, while the Council of People's Ministers held executive power. It restored the rights of peasants and workers under the Central Rada's laws, planned to give land beyond small holdings to land-poor peasants, and brought back the eight-hour working day and the right to strike.

Major fighting broke out in January 1919, Kyiv fell in February and the government moved to Vinnytsia. Vynnychenko resigned on 10 February in the hope of talks with the Entente, and Petliura became chairman on 11 February. By May its armies held only a narrow strip around Brody; a ceasefire with Poland let them retake Podilia and make Kamianets-Podilskyi their capital, and in July the forces of the Western Ukrainian Republic joined them. Red counter-attacks and a typhus epidemic later drove them out of Ukraine.

A treaty with Poland in April 1920 provided for joint operations under Polish command and recognised a border on the Zbruch river. Polish and Ukrainian forces retook Kyiv, but the Soviet counter-offensive drove them back. The Directorate dissolved on 10 November 1920, and two days later its executive authority passed to a single person. The Treaty of Riga of 1921 gave the Soviet Union the rest of Ukraine, which became the Ukrainian SSR.
diretas-ja: The movement grew during a deepening economic crisis, with annual inflation of 239% in 1983, which brought professional bodies and trade unions into politics. It joined people of many backgrounds in the single cause of a direct vote for president: party politicians such as Ulysses Guimarães, Tancredo Neves, André Franco Montoro, Fernando Henrique Cardoso, Leonel Brizola and Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, artists such as Chico Buarque de Holanda, Gilberto Gil and Fernanda Montenegro, sectors of the Catholic Church and other religions, and the football club Corinthians, which printed Diretas Já on the back of its shirts.

The first public protest took place in the town of Abreu e Lima, in Pernambuco, on 31 March 1983, followed by protests in Goiânia on 15 June and in front of São Paulo's Pacaembu Stadium on 27 November. On 25 January 1984, the anniversary of the city of São Paulo, the campaign's first major assembly filled the Praça da Sé, made possible by Montoro as governor of São Paulo. By then the military regime had lost much of its prestige, and even low-ranking soldiers whose pay had fallen with inflation voiced discontent.

On 16 April 1984 a final demonstration in São Paulo's Anhangabaú Valley drew an estimated crowd of over 1.5 million, the largest political demonstration Brazil had seen. That month President Figueiredo tightened press censorship and promoted arrests and police violence. The amendment, named the Dante de Oliveira law after its author, came to the vote on 25 April 1984: it won 298 votes to 65, but 112 pro-government deputies abstained, the Chamber lacked a quorum, and the bill died.

Although the amendment failed, the movement became a catalyst for the opposition and a voice for popular discontent. The return to democracy ended with civilian rule in 1985 and a new constitution in 1988, which provided for the direct presidential election of 1989. Fernando Collor de Mello won it, the first democratically elected president since 1961.
dirham: The word dirham ultimately comes from drachma, the Greek coin. The Greek-speaking Byzantine Empire lay partly in the Levant and traded with Arabia, and the coin circulated there in pre-Islamic times and afterward. Near the end of the 7th century it became an Islamic currency, bearing the name of the sovereign and a religious verse. The Arabs introduced their own coins. The Ottoman dirham was based on the Sasanian drachm, written drahm in Middle Persian, which was itself based on the Greek dram or drachma.

The dirham, also spelled dirhem or drahm, is a unit of currency and of mass, and it was historically a silver coin. As a unit of mass it was used across North Africa, the Middle East and Persia, with varying values. The Islamic dirham was 8 daniq, and ten dirhams were equal to seven mithqal, or 2.975 grams of silver. In the late Ottoman Empire the standard dirham was 3.207 grams, and 400 dirhems made one oka. In Egypt in 1895 it was equivalent to 47.661 troy grains, or 3.088 grams.

The Islamic dirham was struck in many Mediterranean countries, including Al-Andalus, and the Byzantine Empire struck a related silver coin, the miliaresion. Between the 10th and 12th centuries it could be used as currency in Europe, notably in areas with Viking connections such as Viking York and Dublin.

Jewish law mentions the dirham as a unit of weight, for example for the silver pledged in marriage contracts and for the quantity of flour from which a portion of dough must be separated. Maimonides, in his commentary on the Mishnah, used the Egyptian dirham to estimate that quantity, and later rabbis gave differing weights for it, from about 3.0 to 3.36 grams. The name dirham remains the name of the currencies of Morocco, the United Arab Emirates and Armenia.
diriyah: The ruins of old Diriyah lie on either side of the narrow valley known as Wadi Hanifa. Built almost entirely of mud brick, they are divided into three districts, Ghussaibah, Al-Mulaybeed and Turaif, set on hills overlooking the valley. Turaif is the highest. Part of the city wall, also of mud brick, still stands along the edges of the wadi with some high observation towers. The modern town stands lower, at the foot of the hill, and north of it in the valley lie gardens, palm groves and small farms.
