According to the chroniclers of Nejd, the city was founded in 1446-47 by Mani' Al-Muraydi, an ancestor of the Saudi royal family. He and his clan came from the area of Al-Qatif in eastern Arabia at the invitation of Ibn Dir', then ruler of a group of settlements that now make up Riyadh, and the settlement was named after him. It first occupied Ghusaybah and Al-Mulaybeed, and Turaif was settled later. By the 18th century Diriyah was a well-known town in Nejd.

Muhammad ibn Saud emerged from a struggle within the ruling family, the Al Miqrin, and became emir. In 1744 he took in the religious scholar Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab, and he agreed to implement his views. The First Saudi State was born, with its capital at Diriyah. Within decades Ibn Saud and his descendants subjugated all of Nejd and the eastern and western regions of Arabia. Their conquest of Mecca and Medina drew the anger of the Ottoman Empire and led to the Ottoman-Saudi War of 1811 to 1818.

In 1818 an Egyptian army under Ibrahim Pasha entered Diriyah after a siege of about six months, destroyed the houses and cut down every tree in the palm groves. The Egyptians were estimated to have lost 10,000 men and the Saudi forces 1,800. When the Saudis revived their fortunes in 1824 and again in 1902, they made their capital at Riyadh. The area was resettled in the late 20th century, and a new town founded in the late 1970s is now the seat of its own governorate.

Among the historic structures are Salwa Palace, the largest on the site, which rises four storeys and was probably finished by Saud ibn Abdul Aziz, imam from 1803 to 1814; the Saad bin Saud Palace; and the mosque of Imam Muhammad bin Saud, where Imam Abd al-Aziz bin Muhammad was assassinated while leading prayer in November 1803. At-Turaif District was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2010.
dirk-iii-count-of-holland: Dirk III, also called Dirik or Theodoric, was count of the area that became Holland, then often called West Frisia, from 993 to 27 May 1039. The name Holland was first used for it only in 1101. Most of the territory was boggy and subject to constant flooding and so sparsely populated, with settlement mainly in the coastal dunes and on raised ground near the rivers.

Dirk belonged to the house of Holland. His mother, Luitgard of Luxemburg, was regent from 993 to 1005, while he was a minor. She was the sister-in-law of Emperor Henry II, and with his help she kept the county for her son. She went on to use her family connections to win imperial help for Dirk, and an imperial army once helped him suppress a Frisian revolt.

Before 1018 Dirk was a vassal of Henry II, but the bishops of Trier, Utrecht and Cologne all contested ownership of his fief, which lay in a strategic position. Traders from Utrecht, the largest trading town of the German kings in the area, had to pass through his lands by the Rhine and Vecht to reach the North Sea, and another route ran from Tiel to England.

Along that route Dirk built a stronghold at Vlaardingen, in a newly habitable area where many Frisians had settled at his invitation. He was not permitted to levy tolls or hinder trade, but he defied imperial rule and, with the Frisians there, stopped passing ships and demanded tolls. Merchants of Tiel complained to the king and to Bishop Adelbold of Utrecht of violence by his men. Henry decided to end Dirk's rule and awarded his lands to Adelbold.

A large imperial army, supplied by the region's bishops and commanded by Godfrey II, Duke of Lower Lorraine, marched on Vlaardingen. In the Battle of Vlaardingen in 1018 it was destroyed. Many imperial commanders died and Godfrey was captured. Dirk kept his lands, went on levying tolls and later gained more land to the east at the expense of the Bishop of Utrecht. After Henry's death in 1024 he supported Conrad II for the kingship.

Dirk is thought to have gone on pilgrimage to the Holy Land around 1030, hence his nickname Hierosolymita, the Jerusalemite. He died on 27 May 1039 and was buried at Egmond Abbey. He had married Othelindis, perhaps a daughter of Bernard I, Duke of Saxony, and was succeeded by his sons Dirk IV and then Floris I. After his death imperial armies tried several times to reclaim the lands of the Frisian counts, and Robert I, Count of Flanders, helped Dirk V, Dirk III's grandson, to restore Frisia to the counts.
dirty-war: In 1955 the Argentine military removed Juan Perón from the presidency in the Revolución Libertadora, and Peronism was then proscribed. Resistance came from workplaces and trade unions, and over the following decade leftist guerrilla groups arose, among them the Uturuncos and the People's Guerrilla Army. Perón died on 1 July 1974 and was succeeded by his vice-president and third wife, Isabel Perón. Paramilitary groups, mostly the Triple A death squad run by José López Rega, carried out hundreds of killings in these years. The exact start of the repression is debated: some date it to 1969, others to the Trelew massacre of 1972, the Triple A in 1973 or Isabel Perón's decrees of 1975 against the guerrillas. The military overthrew her on 24 March 1976.

The military junta used the name Dirty War, claiming that a war with different methods was needed to keep social order and eradicate subversives. Human rights groups have rejected the term because it implies a civil war and a justification for the killings. At the 1985 trial the prosecutor Julio Strassera called it a euphemism. The targets were guerrillas and sympathisers, but also students, trade unionists, writers, journalists and artists. Estimates of those killed or disappeared run from 13,000 to 30,000, many of them impossible to document.

Victims were held incommunicado in clandestine detention centres, at least 340 by later findings, and tortured. About 3,000 deaths are estimated at the Navy Engineering School alone. Some prisoners were drugged and thrown alive from aircraft over the Río de la Plata in what became known as death flights, one of which was organised by the navy captain Adolfo Scilingo. Children born in the camps or taken with their parents were given to other families; the Grandmothers of the Plaza de Mayo had records of 172 at the time of the national inquiry. The Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo held their first vigil in 1977.

Economic collapse, public discontent and the Falklands War ended the junta. After the 1983 elections President Raúl Alfonsín set up the National Commission on the Disappearance of Persons, led by the writer Ernesto Sábato, which documented the disappearance of nearly 9,000 people by name. In 1985 the nine members of the juntas were tried, and Jorge Rafael Videla was sentenced to life imprisonment. Nearly 300 people were prosecuted.

Laws that had granted pardons were repealed by Congress in 2003 and declared unconstitutional by the Supreme Court in 2005, and prosecutions resumed in 2006. In that year 24 March was made a public holiday, the Day of Remembrance for Truth and Justice.
discourses-on-livy: The Discourses on Livy (in Italian, Discorsi sopra la prima deca di Tito Livio) take as their subject the first ten books of Livy's History of Rome, which relate the expansion of Rome through the end of the Third Samnite War in 293 BCE. Machiavelli, a Florentine, also discusses what can be learned from many other eras, including contemporary politics. He saw history as a way to learn useful lessons for the present, and as an analysis that later generations could build on, provided they did not forget the works of the past. He often describes Romans and other ancient peoples as superior models, but he also describes political greatness as something that comes and goes among peoples in cycles.

The work has a dedicatory letter and three books with 142 numbered chapters in all. Machiavelli dedicated it to two friends, Zanobi Buondelmonti and Cosimo Rucellai, because they deserved to be princes even if they lacked principalities. He divides Rome's actions into those taken by public or private counsel and those inside or outside the city. Book I treats the city's internal actions by public counsel, and Book II public counsel outside the city. The single remaining book treats private counsel in both spheres.

In Book I he names six forms of government, three good and three bad: monarchy, aristocracy and democracy slip into tyranny, oligarchy and anarchy. Rome, he says, was a republic that mixed the three, and the mixture kept their violent tendencies in check. In Book II he argues that money is not the sinew of war, and he also says republics are better than principalities. Book III opens with the claim that a republic or sect must be drawn back often toward its beginning to live long. He gives the sack of Rome by the Gauls in 387 BCE as an example, and says that Saint Francis and Saint Dominick renewed the religion of his time in this way.

Francesco Guicciardini, Machiavelli's close friend, wrote critical notes on many chapters. He thought many of the recommendations too vicious and warned against taking as an absolute rule what Machiavelli said, who was always extremely partial to extraordinary and violent methods. Jean-Jacques Rousseau considered the Discourses and the Florentine Histories more representative of Machiavelli's true philosophy than The Prince. In The Social Contract he wrote that the contradiction between The Prince and the Discourses showed that this thinker had been studied only by superficial or corrupt readers. The Discourses were written around 1517 and published after his death, with papal privilege, in 1531.
disentis-abbey: Tradition placed the foundation in 614 and attributed it to the local saints Placidus and Sigisbert, holding that the Avars destroyed the monastery in 670 and martyred its abbot and thirty monks, and that Charles Martel and Saint Pirmin rebuilt it about 711. Later research places the foundation in the early 8th century: excavation shows that the first traceable building on the site dates from about 700 and was destroyed about 940, a destruction attributed to raiding Saracens. The abbey is dedicated to Saint Martin of Tours.

In the 12th-century Passio Placidi, Sigisbert is a wandering Frankish monk inspired by Columbanus and Luxeuil, and Placidus a local landowner who supported him and was murdered by Victor, the praeses of Chur. The Testament of Tello, Bishop of Chur, dated 765, already records very extensive properties; Tello left the abbey his wealth in the lower Surselva between Flims and Trun. The abbey and its territories were known as Cadi, from Casa Dei, House of God.

Charlemagne visited in 800 and made many benefactions. As a Reichskloster, answerable directly to the emperor, the abbey drew its importance from the Lukmanier Pass, crossed by Otto I and Frederick Barbarossa, and gained estates reaching into Lombardy. Udalric I (1031–55) was the first abbot made a prince of the empire. The abbey's subjects used their own seal from 1285 and had their own Landammann from 1371, and Cadi became an autonomous commune of the Grey League.

The abbey joined the Swiss Congregation in 1617; its buildings were refurbished in the Baroque style between 1683 and 1704, and the church of St. Martin was built in 1712. In 1799 Napoleon's soldiers burned and plundered it, destroying books, archives, a 7th-century manuscript chronicle and the printing press of 1729, whose melted type later became organ pipes. The abbey lost half its estates, and its feudal territory was abolished under the Helvetic Republic. Abbot Anselm Huonder rebuilt it.

Disentis escaped the dissolution that ended most religious houses of the time, and in 1880 it opened a secondary school. The community follows the Rule of St. Benedict, runs a grammar school and a gymnasium where about a third of the students board, and keeps a comprehensive Romansh library.
dispositio-achillea: Also known as the Constitutio Achillea or the Achillean House Law, the disposition was set out in the last will and testament of Elector Albert III Achilles of Brandenburg. The Mark Brandenburg was to stay undivided and pass whole to the eldest son, who at Albert's death would be John Cicero. This matched a requirement of the Golden Bull, which held that electorates must be indivisible.

The younger sons, Frederick I and Siegmund, were to inherit the Franconian margraviates of Brandenburg-Ansbach and Brandenburg-Kulmbach, later called Brandenburg-Bayreuth, and to draw lots to decide which of them took which principality. Any further sons were to receive no land and to pursue an ecclesiastical career, though Albert had no more.

Strictly, the disposition settled only how the lands of one margrave were to be shared among his sons. In time, however, it came to be accepted as a principle of succession in the House of Hohenzollern, and in 1541 it was confirmed, together with the House Treaty of Regensburg, as a binding house law of the dynasty. Its central rule, the indivisibility of the Mark Brandenburg, thus became part of the family's own law and no longer rested only on a clause of the Golden Bull.

The settlement also laid the ground for the gradual separation of the Mark Brandenburg from the Hohenzollern family's original lands in Franconia. The two margraviates it created there, Brandenburg-Ansbach and Brandenburg-Kulmbach, were reunited with Prussia, the successor state of the Mark, only in 1791.
dissolution-of-czechoslovakia: Czechoslovakia was created with the end of Austria-Hungary after the First World War. In 1918, at a meeting in Pittsburgh, Tomáš Garrigue Masaryk and other Czech and Slovak representatives signed the Pittsburgh Agreement, which promised a common state of two equal nations, Slovaks and Czechs. The Czechoslovak Constitution of 1920, however, specified a single Czechoslovak nation. Political tension followed between Czechoslovakists and those seeking greater autonomy for the Slovaks. In March 1939, under pressure from Adolf Hitler, the First Slovak Republic was created as a German satellite state, and after the war the two parts were reunited in the Third Czechoslovak Republic. In 1969 the Czech Socialist Republic and the Slovak Socialist Republic became constituent states of the federation.

After the Velvet Revolution of 1989 ended communist rule, many Czechs and Slovaks wanted to keep a federal state. By 1991 the Czech Republic's GDP per capita was some 20 per cent higher than Slovakia's, and transfer payments from the Czech budget to Slovakia stopped in January 1991. Czech parties had little presence in Slovakia and the reverse. The government demanded continued control from Prague, while Slovaks asked for decentralisation, and leading Slovak parties, notably the Slovak National Party, advocated looser complete independence and sovereignty.

Historians debate whether the dissolution was inevitable, pointing to differences between the two nations dating from Austria-Hungary and to the 1968 constitution with its minority veto, or the result of events between 1989 and 1992. The partition took effect at the end of 1992, and, unlike the breakup of Yugoslavia, it brought no violence. No referendum was held, and the decision was unpopular at the time.

The national territory was divided along the existing internal borders, with disputes over a few places settled by negotiation, compensation and a treaty. Most federal assets, including army equipment and rail and air infrastructure, were divided in a ratio of two to one, the approximate ratio of the Czech and Slovak populations. The two states first kept the Czechoslovak koruna, but adopted separate currencies in February 1993. Each republic kept its own symbols, the Czech lion and the Slovak double cross. Neither state claimed to be the sole successor, Czechoslovakia's membership in the United Nations ended, and both were admitted as new states on 19 January 1993.

A customs union remained until both countries joined the European Union on 1 May 2004. On the dissolution all Czechoslovak citizens became citizens of the Czech Republic or Slovakia according to criteria such as residence and birthplace. Soon afterwards polls showed many people on both sides had opposed the split.
dissolution-of-the-holy-roman-empire: Since the Middle Ages Western Europeans had regarded the Holy Roman Empire as the legitimate continuation of the ancient Roman Empire, its emperors having been proclaimed Roman emperors by the papacy, and the emperors claimed a universal authority over Christendom. The rise of sovereign territorial states in the 16th and 17th centuries undermined that claim. By the 18th century contemporaries described the empire as irregular and sick: it had no standing army, no central treasury and an elective monarch with little central control. Samuel von Pufendorf called it a monstrosity. Most still believed it could be revived, and the Reichstag passed the Imperial Recess as late as 1803.

The empire held its own in the French Revolutionary Wars until Prussia left the war to attend to the Second and Third Partitions of Poland. When Napoleon took the title Emperor of the French in 1804, Francis II answered on 11 August 1804 by proclaiming himself Emperor of Austria as well, a hereditary title meant to keep parity with other rulers. After the defeat at Austerlitz on 2 December 1805, the Peace of Pressburg of 26 December granted Bavaria, Baden and Württemberg full sovereignty while leaving them nominally within the empire.

On 12 July 1806 those three states and thirteen lesser princes formed the Confederation of the Rhine, a French satellite. Karl Theodor Dalberg resigned as archchancellor of Germany on 31 July, and on 1 August a French envoy told the Reichstag that Napoleon no longer recognised the empire. On 6 August Francis II abdicated and released all imperial states and officials from their obligations. The step was meant above all to prevent Napoleon, drawn to the legacy of Charlemagne, from claiming the imperial title and making Francis his vassal.

Reactions ranged from indifference to despair. Vienna's people were horrified, and the Bavarian envoy Rechberg said he was furious at having signed away the German name. Legal commentators held the abdication lawful but doubted the emperor's power to dissolve the empire, and some subjects refused to accept its end: as late as October 1806 farmers in Thuringia thought the news a plot by their local authorities. Many Germans compared the fall to that of Troy.

The title and the idea of the empire were never formally abolished, and the Savoyard kings of Italy styled themselves Perpetual Vicar of the Holy Roman Empire until 1946. The imperial regalia remained with the Habsburgs and are kept in the Imperial Treasury at the Hofburg in Vienna, and the Austrian emperors went on acting as protectors of the Catholic Church.
dissolution-of-the-soviet-union: Mikhail Gorbachev was elected General Secretary on 11 March 1985, just over four hours after the death of Konstantin Chernenko. He meant to revive a stagnating economy and came to see that this required reforming political and social structures. His glasnost allowed nationalist movements and ethnic disputes to be expressed and to grow into dominant political forces. Commentators also point to chronic economic stagnation and the burden of the arms race with the United States.

In 1989 limited competitive elections were held for a new Congress of People's Deputies, and the revolutions of 1989 in the Warsaw Pact countries increased pressure for republican autonomy. Estonia was the first republic to declare state sovereignty, on 16 November 1988, and Lithuania the first to declare independence, in March 1990. In 1990 all fifteen republics held competitive elections, and the Communist Party lost them in five.

On 17 March 1991 a Union-wide referendum was held in which 77.85 per cent of voters endorsed keeping a reformed Soviet Union; the Baltic republics, Armenia, Georgia and Moldova boycotted it. In August 1991 communist hardliners tried to overthrow Gorbachev. The coup failed, but the turmoil weakened the central government, and many republics declared independence in the following days and months.

On 8 December the leaders of the Russian, Byelorussian and Ukrainian republics signed the Belovezha Accords, declared that the Soviet Union no longer existed and set up the Commonwealth of Independent States. Kazakhstan was the last republic to declare independence, on 16 December. Gorbachev resigned on 25 December and passed his powers, including control of the nuclear launch codes, to Boris Yeltsin, and the Soviet flag was lowered from the Kremlin. On 26 December the Soviet of the Republics formally dissolved the Soviet Union.

The dissolution marked the culmination of the revolutions of 1989 and the end of the Cold War. Russia became the recognised successor state and continued the Soviet seat at the United Nations. Several successor states kept close links with Russia through the Commonwealth, while the Baltic states moved towards the West. The end of Soviet aid brought crisis to Cuba and North Korea, and disputes over territory and minorities led to conflicts in some successor states.
divashtich: Divashtich, also spelled Devashtich, Dewashtich and Divasti, was the son of Yodkhsetak, of a noble Sogdian dehqan family from Samarkand that traced its descent to the Sasanian king Bahram V Gur. The family bore the title of sur and had ruled parts of Sogdia since the 6th century; Divashtich was the last of its five members to bear that title. Like most of his subjects he followed a Sogdian form of Zoroastrianism, shaped by other religions, in which gods such as Nanaya were worshipped.

In about 706 he was elected king of Panjikant, succeeding the Turkic prince Chukin Chur Bilga, and the city reached the height of its prosperity under him. He shared power with other princes. Some of his coins name a certain Nana, either the goddess Nanaya or Chukin Chur Bilga's daughter, whom he may have married. When Tarkhun, ruler of Samarkand, was overthrown in 709/710 for his pro-Muslim policy and replaced by Gurak, Tarkhun's two sons fled to Divashtich's court, strengthening his own claim to Samarkand.

After the invasion of the Arab general Qutayba ibn Muslim, Divashtich and other Sogdian rulers acknowledged the Umayyad Caliphate in about 712. While Gurak sought help from the Tang dynasty, Divashtich stayed loyal, so much so that he was even thought a Muslim. In 719 he had to hand Tarkhun's sons to al-Jarrah ibn Abdallah, governor of Khorasan, and as late as 721 he corresponded with the new governor, Abd al-Rahman ibn Nu'aym al-Ghamidi. In 720, however, he and Karzanj are named as leaders of an anti-Arab rebellion in Sogdia.

The rebels' ally at-Tar of Farghana betrayed Karzanj to the Umayyad general Sa'id ibn Amr al-Harashi, who defeated him at Khujand and massacred more than 3,000 Sogdian inhabitants of the city. Al-Harashi then beat Divashtich in battle in 722. Divashtich fled to the fortress of Kal'ai Mug, about 60 kilometres from Panjakent, and surrendered. The Umayyad governor of Iraq wanted him freed, but al-Harashi had him crucified on a Zoroastrian burial building and sent his head to Iraq, a choice that later counted in al-Harashi's removal. His son Tarkhun was taken to Iraq as a prisoner; a descendant, Mikal ibn Abd al-Wahid, founded the Mikalid family of Khorasan.
diviciacus-aedui: Diviciacus, also written Divitiacus, was an aristocrat of the Aedui who took part in the decision-making of the clans, as Julius Caesar describes in The Gallic War. His name may mean avenger. His date of birth is unknown, though he was an adult by the late 60s BCE. In 63 BCE he survived the Battle of Magetobriga, where the Sequani and Arverni, with Germanic troops under the Suebi king Ariovistus, massacred the Aedui, who then became tributary to the Sequani.

After that defeat he went to Rome and spoke before the Senate to ask for military aid. He stayed as a guest of Cicero, who wrote of his knowledge of divination, astronomy and natural philosophy and is the source that names him as a druid. Caesar, who knew him well, praised his skill as a diplomat without calling him a druid.

Following Caesar's victory over the Helvetii, Diviciacus was the chief spokesman of the Gallic delegation to him. He set out the harm Ariovistus had done to the Aedui and pointed out that the lands of the Sequani, their old enemies, were also occupied. The request gave Caesar the occasion for the next phase of his conquest of Gaul, in which he confronted and defeated Ariovistus. When Caesar defeated the anti-Roman Dumnorix in battle, he spared his life because Diviciacus begged him not to punish his brother. Dumnorix was later killed trying to escape from Caesar's control.

The scholar Delamarre has argued that, besides being a druid, Diviciacus may have held the office of Uergobretos, the annually elected chief magistrate of the Aedui, at some time before 52 BCE. If so, his mix of religious and political duties paralleled Caesar's own as Pontifex Maximus and magistrate. The date of his death is unknown, but Cicero speaks of him in the past tense in 44 BCE.
divico: Divico is known only from the first book of Caesar's Bellum Gallicum. His name means the avenger, from the Gaulish stem diuic-, to avenge or punish, and belongs to a family of Gaulish names that includes that of the druid Diviciacus. He first appears commanding the Tigurini during the migration of the Cimbri and Teutoni. In the Roman defeat of 107 BCE, remembered at Rome as the clades Cassiana, the consul was killed and the surviving soldiers were sent under the yoke. When Marius destroyed the Cimbri and Teutoni in 102 and 101 BCE, the Tigurini, who had stayed back in the Alps, escaped and returned to Helvetia.

In 58 BCE the Helvetii set out to migrate westward. After Caesar blocked them and bridged the Arar in a single day, they sent envoys, and Caesar names Divico as their head. In his account Divico offered peace if the Helvetii were granted land, warned Caesar not to trust in one Roman defeat, and, when hostages were demanded, replied that the Helvetii were used to receiving hostages, not giving them.

The historian Gerold Walser doubted that one man led in both 107 and 58 BCE, since the envoy would have been about seventy-five. He read the embassy as a literary set-piece that changes nothing in the war and serves Caesar's self-presentation as the late avenger of the defeat, a role linking him to Marius and to his own family through the legate Lucius Piso, killed at Agen.

In the 19th and early 20th centuries Divico became central to the Swiss national myth. Olivier Curty has shown how the Tigurini's victory was transferred to the Helvetii as a whole after the federal state was founded in 1848. In Charles Gleyre's painting Les Romains passant sous le joug of 1858 Divico still stands aside with his face hidden, but from the late 19th century he became the emblematic Helvetian leader, a hero of the kind of Vercingetorix. Karl Jauslin's Die Schweizergeschichte in Bildern of 1888 placed him between William Tell and Arnold von Winkelried, and he stayed in Fribourg primary-school textbooks until the early 1970s.
divine-comedy: Dante Alighieri belonged to the Guelphs, who in general favoured the papacy over the Holy Roman Emperor. Florence's Guelphs split around 1300 into the White Guelphs and the Black Guelphs, and the White Guelphs later supported greater imperial power in Italy. Dante was among the White Guelphs exiled in 1302 after troops under Charles of Valois entered the city at the request of Pope Boniface VIII, who supported the Black Guelphs. The exile lasted the rest of his life and shows throughout the poem, from prophecies of his banishment to the damnation of some of his opponents.

The work was originally titled Comedìa. Dante used the word because poems in the ancient world were classed as high (tragedy) or low (comedy), and low poems had happy endings and everyday language. The adjective Divina first appears in Giovanni Boccaccio's Trattatello in laude di Dante, written between 1351 and 1355.

The poem has 14,233 lines in three cantiche, Inferno, Purgatorio and Paradiso, each of 33 cantos, and an introductory canto brings the total to 100. Its verse form is terza rima, in tercets of eleven-syllable lines. The story is told in the first person and runs from the night before Good Friday to the Wednesday after Easter in the spring of 1300. Virgil guides Dante through Hell and most of Purgatory, Beatrice from the end of Purgatorio, and Bernard of Clairvaux through the last cantos.

Hell has nine circles, Mount Purgatory nine rings crowned by the Garden of Eden, and Heaven nine celestial spheres beneath the Empyrean. Each punishment in Hell is a contrapasso, a symbolic instance of poetic justice: in Canto XX the fortune-tellers must walk with their heads turned backwards. Allegorically the poem represents the soul's journey towards God.

According to the Italian Dante Society, no manuscript in Dante's own hand survives, although some 800 copies from the 14th and 15th centuries are listed. Giovanni da Serravalle made the first complete translation, into Latin prose, in 1416, and Enrique de Villena completed a Castilian prose version in 1428. The first printed edition appeared at Foligno on 11 April 1472, in 300 copies, of which fourteen survive.

The poem was recognised as a masterpiece in the centuries after it was written, largely fell into obscurity during the Enlightenment, and was rediscovered in the English-speaking world by William Blake and the Romantic writers of the 19th century. Erich Auerbach held that it inaugurated literary realism in modern fiction. In 1919 Miguel Asín Palacios argued that Dante drew on the Islamic tradition of Muhammad's night journey to heaven, but Francesco Gabrieli and other scholars have not found the claim convincing.
division-of-korea: Korea had been a nominal protectorate of Japan after the Russo-Japanese War ended in 1905 and was formally annexed in 1910, when Emperor Gojong was deposed. Nationalist and radical groups struggled for independence but never united in one movement, and the Korean Provisional Government in exile in the Republic of China gained wide recognition only with the Second World War.

At the Cairo Conference in November 1943 Franklin D. Roosevelt, Winston Churchill and Chiang Kai-shek declared that Korea would in due course become free and independent. Roosevelt raised a trusteeship with Joseph Stalin at Tehran and Yalta, and Stalin did not object but wanted it short. The Soviet Union declared war on Japan on 8 August 1945 and advanced quickly into the north, which made the United States anxious that it would occupy the whole peninsula.

On 10 August 1945 two young officers, Dean Rusk and Charles Bonesteel, were told to define an American zone at very short notice. No experts on Korea were consulted. Rusk later said that had he known Korean history he would almost surely have chosen a different line. Soviet troops entered Pyongyang on 24 August and found a committee under the nationalist Cho Man-sik, and the Soviet administration allowed local People's Committees to function. Koreans there enjoyed more autonomy than people in Soviet-controlled Eastern Europe, though Soviet soldiers also looted and were accused of rape.

The Moscow Conference of December 1945 agreed a trusteeship of up to five years, which Koreans opposed. A US-Soviet Joint Commission met in 1946 and 1947 and failed. Crossing the parallel without a permit became illegal in May 1946, and Lyuh Woon-hyung, the last senior politician committed to left-right dialogue, was assassinated on 19 July 1947. After the matter went to the United Nations, elections were held in the south only, over the objection of the commission's chairman, K. P. S. Menon. Strikes followed, and a rising on Jeju island was put down at a cost of 25,000 to 30,000 lives.

The Republic of Korea was proclaimed on 15 August 1948, and the Democratic People's Republic of Korea followed on 9 September. Each claimed the whole peninsula, and armed skirmishes along the border continued until North Korean forces invaded the South on 25 June 1950. A UN force led by the United States intervened.

The North overran 90 per cent of the south before a counter-attack drove it back, and UN troops then crossed the parallel in October despite warnings from the People's Republic of China. The war lasted until 1953, ended in stalemate and left the peninsula divided by the Korean Demilitarized Zone. Both regimes regarded the division, after more than a millennium of unity, as controversial and temporary.
divrigi: Divriği lies on a gentle slope on the south bank of the Çaltısuyu river, a tributary of the Karasu, which flows into the Euphrates. It is the district capital of Divriği District in Sivas Province and has about eleven thousand people. Large iron mines lie nearby, and the Hittites may already have mined and used the ore of the area.

In the 9th century the town was known as Abrik. It was founded around 850 by Karbeas, the leader of the Paulicians, an Armenian sect regarded by its opponents as heretical, and the Paulicians fortified it and made it the capital of their state, with the support of Arabs and the emir of Malatya. Later called Tephrike in Greek, it was recaptured by the Byzantine Empire during the reign of Emperor Basil I. It was temporarily renamed Leontokome, after Emperor Leo VI, and made into a thema.

In the early eleventh century the town was part of the territory given to the Armenian king Seneqerim-Hovhannes of Vaspurakan in exchange for his own lands. After the Battle of Manzikert it came under the Sultanate of Rûm, and the Mengüjeks built the Great Mosque and hospital. The traveller Evliya Çelebi recorded that the town's people included Greeks and Turkomans as well as Armenians and Kurds.

The Great Mosque and Hospital of Divriği, of the 13th century, stand on UNESCO's World Heritage List for the carving and architecture of both buildings. A medieval castle, mostly of the thirteenth century, crowns a steep hill above the town. The railway arrived in 1937, and iron ore from the nearby mines is still exported by it. Most of the district's villages are inhabited by Alevis.
divrigi-great-mosque-and-hospital: Divriği was founded in the 9th century under Byzantine rule. After the defeat of the Byzantines at Manzikert in 1071 Turkish tribes occupied it, and in the 12th century the Mengujekid dynasty controlled it and nearby Erzincan. The dynasty later divided into two branches, one ruling from Divriği and the other from Erzincan, and it was related by marriage to the Seljuks of Konya. The Mengujekid rulers were patrons of arts, science and literature, which may explain why exceptional artists were present, and itinerant artisans moving from patron to patron probably gave rise to the eclectic architecture.

The complex stands in the upper town, below the citadel. The mosque adjoins the hospital, with which it shares its southern qibla wall, and a mausoleum is attached to the hospital. The north portal of the mosque gives the date 626 AH (1228–1229) and names its patron as Ahmadshāh ibn Sulaymān, a ruler of the Divriği branch. The inscription on the hospital portal calls it a dār al-shifā' (house of healing) and ascribes its foundation to Tūrān Malik. The chief architect, Khurramshāh ibn Mughīth al-Khilātī, came from Ahlat.

The mosque's north portal is marked by the density of its high-relief carving. Inside, stone piers support stone vaults, and the central bay was probably open to the sky. A wooden minbar of 1243 signed by Ibrahīm ibn Ahmad al-Tiflīsī survives. The hospital portal, on the west, is less dense and in places seems unfinished; rooms and iwans surround a covered courtyard with a pool, and one room served as a dynastic tomb chamber.

Inscriptions record several major restorations between the 15th and 19th centuries, and more followed in the 20th. The carving and eclectic architecture place the complex among the most important works of architecture in Anatolia, and it was inscribed on UNESCO's World Heritage List in 1985.
divya-upadesh: Prithvi Narayan Shah fell ill before his death on 11 January 1775 and was reportedly distraught that his kingdom might collapse and his work be undone. He gathered his courtiers, brothers and cousins, royal priests and scribes and gave his final counsel to his successors and to the country. The teachings were written down but mostly passed on by word of mouth. In the early 1950s a worn manuscript was found in the home of a descendant of a noble of his court, and another with a descendant of an employee of another noble. Baburam Acharya and Yogi Naraharinath reconciled the two and published them as one book in 1952–53.

The counsel calls Nepal a garden of four castes and thirty-six sub-castes and asks that the castes take turns in leading its institutions. It favours merit over nepotism, warns politicians against lucrative commerce, asks for care of soldiers' needs and of the families of soldiers killed, and wants a learned priest in every court to interpret the law. It treats bribery as the biggest enemy of justice, calling both giver and taker enemies of the country. Shah says his life's work had been to protect Nepal from foreign empires, though his first motive for conquest had been to rule the Nepal Valley, and he warns against incoming foreign investment.

The work is regarded as the first essay in Nepali literature, is taught in the Master of Arts (Nepali) course of Guwahati University, and is often cited by politicians and commentators. New editions appeared in 1996–97 and 2002–03. Historians consider it a late manuscript, perhaps first written down under Rana Bahadur Shah or Rajendra Bikram Shah, and its authenticity is disputed.

Kamal P. Malla argued that its language differs so much from Prithvi Narayan Shah's verified letters that the two could hardly be the work of one man, and that King Mahendra brought the text forward in the late 1950s to legitimise the Shah monarchy; Pradhan and Maharjan shared such doubts. The historian Yogesh Raj accepts that its authorship and dating are controversial but finds no reliable evidence that Mahendra produced it. Several vamsavalis, among them the Padmagiri of 1825, do not mention the deathbed counsel.
diwan-dina-nath: Dina Nath came of a Kashmiri Brahmin family of the governing aristocracy of Kashmir, which moved to Delhi in 1815 during the oppressive rule of the Afghan governors of the valley. He was closely related to Diwan Ganga Ram, head of the military accounts and keeper of the privy seal at Lahore, at whose instance Maharaja Ranjit Singh invited him to Lahore in 1815 and made him a mutsaddi, or writer, in the department of military accounts.

When Ganga Ram died in 1826, Dina Nath took over as head of military finance, accounts and estates and as commander of the GhorCharas, the lancer cavalry, and became keeper of the privy seal. After the death of Diwan Bhawani Das in 1834 the Maharaja placed him at the head of the civil and military finance office. Lepel Griffin called him the Talleyrand of the Punjab.

After Ranjit Singh's death his influence grew, and he is said to have made no enemies at court. He refused to side with Rani Chand Kaur or Sher Singh, who on taking the throne trusted him fully. After the First Anglo-Sikh War he signed the treaty with the British, and in December 1846 he became president of the council set up to govern the Punjab, with British support. He was one of six signatories of the Treaty of Lahore of 1849, under which the ten-year-old Dalip Singh surrendered the Koh-i-noor to the Queen of England.

During the revolt of the Sikh army in 1848 some claimed that he had encouraged the rising at heart, though these stories were perhaps invented by his enemies. After the annexation of the Punjab he was confirmed in his jagirs, worth Rs. 246,460, which he held until his death at Lahore in 1857. There he had laid out a garden and a small haveli around a shrine to Shah Bilawal near Mughalpura, of which only remnants survive, and he commissioned the Well of Dina Nath, which according to legend has always been dry.
diwanus: Diwanus, also called Diwan or Diwane, was the capitaneus of the Bartians and a son of Kleckis, whose name means bear in Old Prussian, so that he is sometimes known by a nickname from that word. His first great success came in 1263, when Schippenbeil fell after almost three years of siege. Twenty knights and their men who sallied out against the Bartians and Sudovians were all killed, one of the order's heaviest losses of knights in the 13th century. The rest of the garrison escaped through Galindia to Masovia; Diwanus pursued them with a few of his best men and killed three knights, but was seriously injured.

With every major Teutonic castle in Bartia fallen, the Bartians could send men to help other Prussian clans, and Diwanus led minor expeditions into Pogesania and Chełmno Land. In 1271 he and the Pogesanian leader Linko besieged a border castle, were driven off by knights from Christburg and found their way home blocked at the Dzierzgoń River. By night half the Prussian army crossed the river at a distance and fell on the knights from the rear while the other half charged straight across: at the Battle of Paganstin twelve knights and 500 men were killed.

The Prussians then assaulted Christburg and almost captured it, but cavalry from Elbing caught them looting and many of the infantry perished. Diwanus blocked the roads to Christburg and three times intercepted supply vessels on the river, yet the castle refused to surrender. In 1273 he brought 800 men against the small outpost of Schönsee, held by three knights and a few sergeants who dressed every soldier as a knight to hide their weakness. Brother Arnold shot and killed him in the attack; the leaderless Bartians went home and withdrew from the uprising, which was lost within a year.
diyala-river: The Diyala is a tributary of the Tigris, 445 kilometres long. It rises near Hamadan in the Zagros Mountains of Iran and descends through the mountains, forming the border between Iran and Iraq for some 32 kilometres. It flows southwest of the Hamrin Mountains and enters the Tigris below Baghdad. The upper reaches cannot be navigated because of narrow defiles, but the valley is an important trade route between Iran and Iraq. In the early Islamic period its lower course formed part of the Nahrawan Canal, and Diyala Governorate in Iraq is named after it. In Kurdish the river is called Sirwan, said to mean roaring sea or shouting river.

The valley flourished from the Jemdet Nasr and Early Dynastic periods to the Akkadian period. At Eshnunna (Tell Asmar) twelve statues of the Early Dynastic period were found in the Tell Asmar Hoard. A brightly coloured pottery known as Scarlet Ware, painted with haematite and with pictorial scenes, developed around 2800 BCE along the river. It was traded to Susa and was also popular in Luristan, because the valley carried one of the main routes between southern Mesopotamia and the Iranian plateau. Eshnunna became especially prominent in the Larsa period.

In 693 BCE the Assyrians and the Elamites fought the Battle of Diyala River. Herodotus calls the river the Gyndes and says that Cyrus the Great dispersed it into 360 channels as a punishment after a sacred white horse perished in it. In March 1917 the British Empire defeated the Ottoman Empire at the confluence with the Tigris, which led to the fall of Baghdad.

The University of Chicago Oriental Institute excavated the lower Diyala basin from 1930 to 1937 and the University of Pennsylvania in 1938 and 1939, at Tell Agrab, Tell Asmar, Ishchali (ancient Neribtum) and Khafaje (ancient Tutub). Henri Frankfort and others led the work, which covered the period from the late Uruk to the end of the Old Babylonian period. Of some 12,000 objects, most stayed unpublished, and the Diyala Database Project, begun in 1992, has been publishing them. The Hamrin Dam Salvage Project excavated further sites from 1977 to 1981. Dams now control the river, among them Darbandikhan and Hemrin in Iraq.
diyar-bakr: Diyar Bakr, meaning abode of Bakr, was the northernmost of the three provinces of the Jazira, or Upper Mesopotamia, the others being Diyar Mudar and Diyar Rabi'a. The medieval geographer al-Baladhuri held that all three were named after the Arab tribes settled there by Mu'awiya during the Muslim conquests of the 7th century. Diyar Bakr was settled by the Rabi'a subgroup of the Banu Bakr, so the two provinces are sometimes called Diyar Rabi'a together.

The province covered both banks of the upper Tigris, from its sources to about where the river turns from an eastward to a south-eastward course. Besides Amida, its main city, it included Mayyafariqin, Hisn Kaifa and Arzan. In early Islamic times it was usually part of the Jazira, but it was sometimes joined to the Armenian province to the north. In later Turkish usage the name came to mean only the western part around Amid, which became known as Diyarbakır.

In the late 9th century the region was held by an autonomous dynasty founded by Isa ibn al-Shaykh al-Shaybani, and in the mid-10th century it passed to the Hamdanids. After the Marwanid emirate, it was annexed by the Seljuk Empire in 1084–1085. When the Seljuk realm broke up after the death of Malik-Shah I in 1092, small emirates took over the region, the Artuqids of Mardin the most important of them.

In the late 12th century the province came under Ayyubid control, and by the mid-13th century it was divided between the Ayyubids in the east and the Seljuks of Rum around Amida in the west. The Mongols conquered it around 1260 and let local rulers govern as their vassals. In the 14th century the Aq Qoyunlu took the region, disputing it with the Qara Qoyunlu and the last Ayyubid princes. The Safavids occupied it for a time in the early 16th century before it came under Ottoman control in 1516.
diyar-mudar: Diyar Mudar, meaning abode of Mudar, was the westernmost of the three provinces of al-Jazira, or Upper Mesopotamia, the others being Diyar Bakr and Diyar Rabi'a. The medieval geographer al-Baladhuri held that all three were named after the main Arab tribes that settled there during the Muslim conquests of the 7th century, the Mudar in this case.

The province spread over both banks of the middle Euphrates, from the area of Samosata to the town of Anah, and took in the Balikh valley and the lower reaches of the Khabur. Raqqa in the south and Edessa, called al-Ruha in Arabic, in the north were its main cities; Harran and Saruj, now Suruç, were others.

In early Islamic times Diyar Mudar was usually part of al-Jazira. After the Hamdanids took it in the mid-10th century, Sayf al-Dawla detached it from the Jazira and the Hamdanids of Mosul and placed it under his Emirate of Aleppo, while the revived Byzantine Empire attacked the region. When Hamdanid control ended, the Banu Numayr gained the upper hand: Waththab ibn Ja'bar al-Numayri was autonomous governor of Harran by 1002, and the Byzantine general George Maniakes took Edessa in 1032.

From then on the north was mostly under Christian rule and subject to Armenian colonisation, while Arab nomadic tribes dominated the land from Harran to the Euphrates. Seljuk raids in the 1060s and 1070s failed to take the region. After the Battle of Manzikert, Philaretos Brachamios made Thoros governor of Edessa and Diyar Mudar. By 1086 the Seljuk sultan Malik-Shah I had united the province, but the Crusades divided it again between the Christian County of Edessa in the north and a Muslim south until the mid-12th century. The Ayyubids won it under Saladin and held it until the Mongol invasion of the Levant in 1260.
diyar-rabia: Diyar Rabi'a was the easternmost and largest of the three provinces of the Jazira, or Upper Mesopotamia, the other two being Diyar Bakr and Diyar Mudar. According to the medieval geographer al-Baladhuri, each of the three was named after the main Arab tribe settled in it.

The province took in the upper reaches of the river Khabur and its tributaries, with the regions of Tur Abdin and Beth Arabaye, and both banks of the Tigris from near Jazirat ibn Umar in the north to the boundary with Iraq near Tikrit in the south, including the lower courses of the Upper Zab and the Lower Zab. Its main city was Mosul, in Arabic al-Mawsil, and the province's other important urban centres were Balad, Jazirat ibn Umar, al-Sinn, Barqa'id, Sinjar, Nisibis, Mardin and Ra's al-'Ayn.

In the 690s the region became part of the province of the Jazira, whose oversight was given to Muhammad ibn Marwan, who governed from Harran. Diyar Rabi'a was probably not yet a separate administrative subdivision during the Umayyad period and seems to have been created as one only in Abbasid times. During the Abbasid period the region was plagued by the raids of the Qarmatians.

In the mid-10th century the province came under the control of the Hamdanid dynasty, a family native to the region whose power was centred at Mosul. The Buyids put an end to the Hamdanid emirate in 980, and Diyar Rabi'a then passed to the Uqaylids. They held it until the Seljuq conquest in the late 11th century.
diyarbakir: Diyarbakır stands on a high plateau on the banks of the Tigris, where the historic fortress rises, and is the administrative centre of Diyarbakır Province in southeastern Turkey. It is considered one of the oldest continually inhabited cities in the world, with settlement since c. 8,000 BCE. In antiquity it was Amida. After the Muslim conquests of the 7th century it became Diyar Bakr, the abode of the tribe of Bakr, a portion of which had been ordered to settle in the lands near the city. In Turkish it was also called Kara Âmid, Black Amid, after its black basalt walls.

The first major civilisation in the region was the Hurrian kingdom of the Mitanni. Nearly every polity that controlled Upper Mesopotamia later ruled the city, among them the Arameans, Assyrians, Achaemenid Persians, Seleucids and Parthians. The Roman Republic gained control in 66 BCE, and in 359 Shapur II of Persia captured Amida after a siege of 73 days. Syriac Christianity took hold between the 1st and 4th centuries, and the Byzantine emperor Theodosius II made Amida capital of Mesopotamia Prima. The walls were built in antiquity and restored and extended by the emperor Constantius II in 349.

Amida fell in 639 to the armies of the Rashidun Caliphate, and the Great Mosque was built afterwards in the city's centre. The city belonged to the Umayyad and Abbasid caliphates, and forces loyal to the caliph al-Mu'tadid recovered it in 899. It then fell under the Hamdanid dynasty, the Buyid dynasty and the Marwanids. The Ottomans conquered it in 1514 under Sultan Selim I, and the Safavid governor was evicted and killed in the Battle of Chaldiran that followed. The Armenian Catholic diocese had some 5,000 members in 1903 but lost most of its population in the Armenian genocide of 1915, when its last bishop was killed with some 600 of his flock.

Diyarbakır is the largest Kurdish-majority city in Turkey. Its walls form a circle of about 5.5 kilometres around the old city, with four gates and 82 watch-towers. The Diyarbakır Fortress and Hevsel Gardens Cultural Landscape was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2015. The Great Mosque, built by the Seljuk sultan Malik Shah in the 11th century, is one of the oldest in Turkey and is built in alternating bands of black basalt and white limestone.
djedars: The tombs stand on two hills in the mountainous Frenda area, about 30 km south of Tiaret: three on Jabal Lakhdar and ten on Jabal Arawi, also called Ternaten, 6 km to the south. The name comes from the Arabic jidār, wall, used locally for ancient ruins. Each has a square body, from 11.55 m to 46 m a side and up to 4 m high, under a stepped top that may once have reached 13 m. In the larger ones removable steps hide a passage down to the funerary chambers.

They were built mostly of dry stone, from local limestone and sandstone and from blocks, old tombstones and building fragments taken from earlier sites. Their likeness to the much smaller Berber tombs called bazinas marks them as indigenous Berber architecture, despite their Roman building techniques and Christian imagery. The largest tomb at Ternaten held polychrome murals of Christian scenes and reused Latin inscriptions dated from the time of Septimius Severus to 494.

The three tombs of Jabal Lakhdar are thought to be the oldest. Remains of a wooden coffin from Jedar B gave a radiocarbon range of 410 to 615 CE. Because their Christian symbols are unobtrusive, their occupants are thought to have ruled Christian subjects without being Christian themselves. Jedar F, the largest at Ternaten, may belong to the 6th or 7th century and seems built for several occupants, perhaps a dynasty. Some scholars link the tombs to Zenati-speaking migrants from the Sahara and to rulers such as Masuna, Mastigas and Garmul.

The first known mention dates from 947, when the Fatimid caliph Ismail al-Mansur was shown the tombs of Jabal Lakhdar during a campaign. French military expeditions described them from 1842, and in 1882 La Blanchère of Algiers University tied them to a king named by Procopius, a view no longer held. Fatima Kadria Kadra's study of 1968–70, published in 1983, remains the definitive reference.
djemal-pasha: Ahmed Djemal was born on 6 May 1872 in Mytilene on Lesbos, the son of Mehmed Nesib Bey, a military pharmacist. He graduated from the Kuleli Military High School in 1890 and from the staff college in Istanbul in 1893. Posted to the II Army Corps in 1896 and later to the Salonica frontier, he came to sympathise with the Committee of Union and Progress, a secret reformist party, and joined it in 1898. After the Young Turk Revolution of 1908 he sat on its central committee. He governed the Adana Vilayet from 1909 to 1911, where he helped Armenian victims of the Adana massacres and was praised by Christian missionaries as a competent administrator, and he served in the Balkan Wars.

Djemal became Minister of the Ottoman Navy in February 1914 and, with Talaat and Enver, one of the Three Pashas who effectively ruled the empire during the First World War. He had first favoured an alliance with France. In October 1914 he authorised the Black Sea strike that brought Russia, Britain and France into war against the empire. In 1915 he was given full military and civil powers in Syria. His two attacks on the Suez Canal failed, and wartime hardship and natural disasters turned the population against Ottoman rule.

Between 1915 and 1916 he had 34 Syrian and Lebanese politicians and nationalists executed, among them the men hanged in Damascus and Beirut on 6 May 1916. Arabs called him as-Saffah, the Butcher. Some people in Aleppo praised him for a water pipeline that saved the city from drought in 1917. Historians contest his role in the Armenian genocide: he favoured forced assimilation and conversion, and his policies allowed some Armenians to survive. Wolfgang Gust says he preserved perhaps 150,000 lives while helping to kill another 150,000.

After the empire's defeat in October 1918 Djemal fled with other leaders of the Committee to Germany and Switzerland, and a military court sentenced him to death in absentia. In 1920 he went to Central Asia as a military adviser to the Afghan army. He was assassinated in Tiflis on 21 July 1922 by members of the Armenian Revolutionary Federation, as part of Operation Nemesis, a plan to kill the surviving chief perpetrators of the Armenian genocide. He was buried at Erzurum. In Syria and Lebanon 6 May is Martyrs' Day, a national holiday marking the executions of 1916, and the squares where they took place were renamed Martyrs' Square.
djenne: Djenné sits on the floodplain between the Niger and Bani rivers at the southern end of the Inland Niger Delta, in central Mali. The annual flood begins in July and reaches its maximum in October, and the town then becomes an island reached by causeways. Some 2.5 kilometres to the south-east lies the archaeological site of Djenné-Djeno, one of the earliest and most important urban sites in West Africa, first settled around 200 BCE according to excavations by Susan and Roderick McIntosh. The present town was first settled after 1000 CE.

Djenné-Djeno developed into a large walled urban complex between 300 and 850 CE. After 1100 its population declined, and by 1400 it was abandoned, for reasons that are unknown. Djenné itself survived as a centre of regional trade. Between the 15th and 17th centuries much of the trans-Saharan trade in salt, gold and slaves passing through Timbuktu went through it, and both towns were centres of Islamic scholarship. Seventeenth-century chronicles give conflicting accounts of its relation to the Mali Empire. Sonni Ali conquered it in 1471 after a siege of about six months, and under the Songhai it had about 40,000 people.

A Moroccan army defeated the Songhai at Tondibi in 1591, and the Mali Empire's attempt to fill the void was beaten outside Djenné's walls in 1599. The town formed part of the Segou kingdom from 1670 to 1818 and the Massina Empire from 1818 to 1861. René Caillié, in 1828, was the first European to visit it. French forces occupied it in April 1893 and made Mopti the regional capital, so that Djenné's importance declined.

Djenné is a town and urban commune of the Mopti Region. It is noted for its Sudanese-style architecture, in which nearly all buildings, among them the Great Mosque, are of sun-baked earthen bricks coated with plaster, and the adobe needs replastering at least every other year. The town is a centre of Islamic scholarship, with Quranic schools that draw students from outside the region. In 1988 UNESCO named the Old Towns of Djenné, comprising four archaeological sites, a World Heritage Site.
djerba: Djerba covers 514 square kilometres in the Gulf of Gabès and is administratively part of the Medenine Governorate. In the time of the ancient Greeks it was known as Lytos or Meninx, and it is speculated to have been the island of the lotus-eaters where Odysseus was stranded. The city of Girba, which gave the island its name, was a suffragan bishopric of the Roman province of Tripolitania.

Archaeological and genetic evidence show that the ancestors of the Berbers have lived in the region for more than 20,000 years. The island was settled by the Phoenicians, who came from Tyre and Sidon, in the 12th century BCE according to the account followed here. They spread the pottery industry and the making of purple dye, and are thought to have introduced olive trees. Prosperity continued under the Romans, and the Vandals under King Gaiseric conquered the island after reaching the Maghreb in 429 CE.

Djerba was taken by Arab forces in 665, during the invasion of Tunisia in which the Ibadi sect prevailed. It was sometimes subordinate to the Aghlabids and sometimes to the Rustamids but always semi-independent, until the Fatimid Caliphate controlled the area from 909 to 972. Normans held it from 1135 to 1159, when the Almohad Caliphate drove out their garrison. The Ottomans entered part of Ifriqiya in 1574, and the island suffered under French colonial rule from 1881 until independence in 1956.

Djerba is the largest island of North Africa. According to oral history its Jewish minority has lived there continuously for more than 2,500 years, since the destruction of the Temple of Jerusalem, and the first physical evidence known to historians, from the 11th century, comes from the Cairo Geniza. The El Ghriba synagogue has been in use for over 2,000 years. The wetland of Djerba Bin El Ouedian, a habitat for migratory birds, was listed as a Ramsar site in 2007, and in 2023 the island was designated a World Heritage Site.
djibo-bakary: In the early 1950s Bakary rose to prominence as general secretary of the PPN, founded as the Nigerien branch of the RDA. He clashed with the RDA's leader, Félix Houphouët-Boigny, who was steering the party towards a pro-French line and away from the French Communist Party; Bakary argued that such a change should have followed a democratic debate inside the party. A three-man mission sent by Houphouët, made up of Hamani Diori, Ouezzin Coulibaly and Mamadou Konaté, removed him as general secretary.
As Diori and Boubou Hama took control of the PPN, Bakary founded a new party, Sawaba, and was expelled from the PPN. He served as Mayor of Niamey from 1956 to 1958.

From 20 May 1957 to 14 December 1958 Bakary was Vice President of the Council of Government, and from 26 July to 10 October 1958 President of the Government Council of Niger, the first Nigerien to hold local executive power since the start of French colonial rule. In July 1958, at the congress of the African Regroupment Party in Cotonou, he denounced what he called Charles de Gaulle's economic blackmail of the colonies, opposed his constitutional referendum and demanded immediate independence, carrying a majority of the delegates with him.

Jacques Foccart, Pierre Messmer and Houphouët-Boigny then decided that he should be brought down. The colonial administrator Louis Rollet, seen as too conciliatory, was replaced by Don Jean Colombani, who ran a massive campaign for a yes vote and worked with General Raoul Salan to bring death squads into villages seen as Sawaba strongholds. The yes side won, the French authorities pushed Bakary out of power and replaced him with his cousin Diori, and a new election to the Territorial Assembly, again marked by repression, consolidated Diori's position.

Bakary, an important figure of Niger's independence movement, died on 16 April 1998. After the 2023 coup d'état in Niger the military government began renaming places that bore French names, and the Avenue General Charles de Gaulle became the Avenue Djibo Bakary in his honour.
djinguereber-mosque: The name comes from the Koyra Chiini jiŋgar-ey beer, grand mosque. It is one of three mosques of Timbuktu associated with the community of scholars and students known today as the University of Timbuktu. According to Ibn Khaldun, one of the main sources on 14th-century Mali, Abu Ishaq al-Sahili was said to have received 12,000 mithkals of gold dust for the work. More recent studies doubt his part. The historian J. O. Hunwick has shown that the Arabic sources firmly attest al-Sahili only as the designer of a royal audience chamber at the city of Mali, and scholars trace the mosque's style mainly to the mosques of the Sahara and to traditional African building.

Apart from its minaret and a small part of the northern facade, both of limestone, the building is made entirely of earth with fibre, straw and wood. It has three inner courts, two minarets and twenty-five rows of pillars running east to west, with prayer space for 2,000 people.

Under Askia Dawud of the Songhai Empire, the Qadi of Timbuktu, Aqib ibn Mahmud, began a renovation in 1570. The work caused a quarrel between the ruler and the qadi, who resented the link between the rebuilt mosque and a secular power.

The mosque was inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 1988 and placed on the list of sites in danger in 1990 because of sand carried by spreading desert. The Aga Khan Trust for Culture financed a restoration from 2006, whose first phase brought drainage, new rendering and the replacement of about half the roof beams; the wood now has to come from Ghana, as the local trees once used have gone. Heavy rains in 1999, 2001 and 2003 brought down many earthen buildings in the town. On 26 February 2010, during Mawlid, a stampede at the mosque killed around 26 people. On 1 July 2012 militants of Ansar Dine destroyed two earthen tombs at the mosque, and it was listed as in danger again.
djoser: Djoser, also read Zoser, was a pharaoh of the Third Dynasty and is often counted as the founder of the Old Kingdom. In contemporary inscriptions he is known by his Horus name Netjerikhet, meaning divine of body. He was the son of King Khasekhemwy and Queen Nimaathap, though whether he directly succeeded Khasekhemwy has been uncertain. The Egyptologist Toby Wilkinson argues from burial seals in Khasekhemwy's tomb at Abydos that Djoser was his direct successor and the founder of the dynasty.

Manetho gives him a reign of twenty-nine years and the Turin King List nineteen. Wilkinson's reconstruction of the Royal Annals gives twenty-eight complete or partial years. Djoser sent expeditions to the Sinai Peninsula, where the local inhabitants were subdued and turquoise and copper were mined. The painted limestone statue of Djoser found at Saqqara in 1924 to 1925 is the oldest known life-sized Egyptian statue.

His main monument is the step pyramid at Saqqara, the earliest colossal stone building in ancient Egypt. It began as a nearly square mastaba, and five smaller steps were piled on top. It was once 62 metres high, with a base of about 125 by 109 metres, covered in polished white limestone. Beneath it lies a maze of corridors and chambers, with a burial chamber at the bottom of a shaft 28 metres deep, sealed by a plug stone of 3.5 tons. More than 40,000 stone vessels were found in the galleries.

Imhotep, Djoser's head of the royal shipyard and overseer of all stone works, directed the construction. Manetho credits Tosorthros with discovering how to build with hewn stone, which modern scholars think he meant to ascribe to Imhotep, later deified by Greeks and Romans as Aesculapius.

The date of his death is uncertain, and his relationship to his successor Sekhemkhet is not known. The Famine Stela, probably made in the Ptolemaic period but claiming to date from his reign, tells how Djoser rebuilt the temple of Khnum at Elephantine and so ended a seven-year famine. Some regard it as a legend. A papyrus of the 2nd century CE from Tebtunis preserves a long demotic story about Djoser and Imhotep. The Egyptian historian al-Nuwayri, who lived from 1279 to 1333, described him as a wise ruler and said the Copts held a feast in his honour called the vine festival.
djoumbe-fatima: Djoumbé Fatima, also known as Djoumbé Soudi or Queen Jumbe-Souli, was the daughter of Ramanetaka, also known as Sultan Abderahmane, a Malagasy prince who had left Madagascar after the death of King Radama I, whose brother-in-law he was. Her mother, Ravao, daughter of Andriantsiahofa of Imamo West, was Merina. Fatima was a cousin of King Radama II of Madagascar and had a sister, Jumbe-Salama, who died young.

When her father died in 1842, Ravao ruled for a time as regent and in 1843 married his former adviser, General Ratsivandini. The couple divorced in 1846, and Ravao died by poison in 1847. Ratsivandini became the young queen's tutor and began to arrange her marriage to the sultan of Zanzibar.

France had recently acquired Mayotte and wished to extend its presence on Mohéli. The French sent a governess, Madame Droit, to the queen and arranged her coronation in 1849, at the age of 12. Two years later Fatima dismissed the governess and married Saïd Mohammed Nasser M'Kadar, a cousin of the sultan of Zanzibar, who became prince consort and ruled beside her until the French ousted him in 1860. Like most of the island's people she was Muslim, and she did not convert to Christianity, although the missionary David Griffiths worked on Mohéli.

In 1863 a French delegation visited her, recorded by the photographer Désiré Charnay, who found her melancholy and sickly, dressed in a robe of silk and gold with her face covered. The delegation was sent to persuade her of the advantages of becoming a French colony, and she resisted. Her palace overlooked the sea beside a garrison of 28 soldiers. She later married twice more and gave up the throne for her son, before being restored by the French and ruling until her death in 1878.

Three sons were born of her marriage to M'Kadar, two of whom ruled Mohéli: Mohamed bin Saidi Hamadi Makadara and Abderremane bin Saidi Hamadi Makadara, who reigned from 1878 to 1885. From her relationship with Emile Fleuriot de Langle, an assistant to the explorer Joseph-François Lambert, came two more children, among them Salima Machamba, born at Fomboni in 1874, who became sultana of Mohéli in 1888, married a French gendarme, Camille Paule, and died in France in 1964.
djurdjura: The Djurdjura, Adrar n Jerjer in Berber and Jabal Jurjura in Arabic, is a massif of the Tell Atlas in Kabylie made up of two distinct ranges. The northern range holds the Haïzer and Akouker subranges; the southern range holds the highest summit, Lalla Khedidja, known in Kabylian as Tamgut Aâlayen. Close behind it at 2,305 metres stands Ich n'Timedouine, in the centre of the massif and the highest point of the Akouker.

Adrar n'Hayzer, at 2,164 metres the highest point of the Haïzer, rises above Bouira and the high valley of Oued Dhous, and the Thaletat, a rocky mountain of 1,638 metres with a very unusual shape, lies in Tizi Ouzou Province. At the eastern end the Tirourda Pass crosses the range at 1,750 metres. To the north rises the Kweryet, about 1,500 metres high, which gave its name to the old commune of Douar N'Kweryet, a grouping of villages of the Ouacifs (At Wasif) and the Ouadhia (Iwadhiyen).

The Romans knew the range as Mons Ferratus, the Iron Mountains. The medieval traveller Ibn Batuta crossed it on his way to Béjaïa, travelling with a caravan from the Mitidja, a plain near Algiers, towards Tunis on his journey of the Hajj.

Part of the range is protected within the Djurdjura National Park. At Tikjda, at a height of 1,478 metres, there is a ski resort, with sites such as the Point de Vue du Djurdjura and the Gouffre de l'Akouker.
dmitri-shostakovich: Dmitri Dmitriyevich Shostakovich was born on 25 September 1906 (12 September in the old style) in Saint Petersburg, the second of three children of Dmitri Boleslavovich Shostakovich and Sofiya Vasilievna Kokoulina. His paternal grandfather, Bolesław Szostakowicz, was of Polish and Lithuanian descent and had taken part in the January Uprising of 1863-1864; he was exiled to Narym in 1866 and later became a banker in Irkutsk. Shostakovich pursued a dual career as pianist and composer, and in 1927 he was among the Soviet contestants in the first International Chopin Piano Competition in Warsaw. He became internationally known after the premiere of his First Symphony in 1926.

His relationship with the Soviet government was complex. His opera Lady Macbeth of the Mtsensk District, first performed in 1934, was at first a success. On 26 January 1936 Joseph Stalin attended a performance with Vyacheslav Molotov, Andrei Zhdanov and Anastas Mikoyan and left without speaking to anyone; the work was later condemned, which put the composer's career at risk. After the German invasion of 1941 he stayed at first in Leningrad, was refused for military service because of poor eyesight, and served as a volunteer in the Conservatory's firefighter brigade.

In 1948 he and other composers, including Sergei Prokofiev and Aram Khachaturian, were denounced for formalism under the Zhdanov decree. Most of his works were banned and his family lost privileges. The censure was rescinded in 1956. In 1960 he joined the Communist Party, which was required for the chairmanship of the RSFSR Union of Composers; his son recalled that this reduced him to tears, and he later told his wife that he had been blackmailed.

His output is dominated by fifteen symphonies and fifteen string quartets. His music is broadly tonal, with sharp contrasts, elements of the grotesque and ambivalent tonality, and shows the influence of Gustav Mahler. He often quoted himself, as with the theme of Katerina's aria from Lady Macbeth in his Eighth and Fourteenth String Quartets. His song cycle From Jewish Folk Poetry was not approved in 1949 and could not be performed until after Stalin's death. Whether he used music as covert dissent is disputed. Solomon Volkov's 1979 book Testimony, which claimed to be his memoirs, alleged coded anti-government messages. Shostakovich died on 9 August 1975 in Moscow and was buried in Novodevichy Cemetery.
dmitrov: Dmitrov lies 65 kilometres north of Moscow, on the Yakhroma River and the Moscow Canal, at an altitude of 179 metres. It is the administrative centre of Dmitrovsky District in Moscow Oblast and one of the oldest urban areas in the oblast. Its name means Dmitri's, and it is explained by the fact that the patron saint of Vsevolod, the son of Yury Dolgoruky born where the town was founded, was Saint Demetrius.

Yury Dolgoruky founded the town in 1154. In the 13th century the settlement marked the point where the borders of the Grand Duchy of Moscow, Tver and Pereslavl-Zalessky met. It belonged to the princes of Galich-Mersky, who lived far to the north, until 1364, when it was incorporated into the Grand Duchy of Moscow. Dmitry Donskoy and his grandson Vasily II each granted Dmitrov as an appanage to a younger son, so that it became the capital of a tiny principality. It received town rights in 1374.

The reign of Ivan III's son Yury Ivanovich, from 1503 to 1533, began the golden age of the town. During it the black-domed Assumption Cathedral in the kremlin and a smaller monastery cathedral of Sts. Boris and Gleb were built. The town then passed to Yury's brother Andrey of Staritsa. In 1569 it was seized from Vladimir of Staritsa and added to the Oprichnina, and it declined afterward. It suffered further damage in the Time of Troubles, when the Poles ransacked it.

The Grande Armée briefly occupied Dmitrov in 1812. The anarchist prince Peter Kropotkin spent his last years there after the Russian Revolution. Soviet archaeologists excavated the local kremlin in the 1930s. In November 1941 German troops occupied the town and crossed the Moscow-Volga Canal from there.

Dmitrov had a population of 65,574 at the 2021 census. It is a railway junction, on the branch from Moscow's Savyolovsky terminal to Savyolovo and the branch to Alexandrov, and a cargo port on the Moscow Canal. The kremlin's Assumption Cathedral recalls the town's golden age.
dmitry-donskoy: Dmitry Ivanovich was born in Moscow on 12 October 1350, the eldest son of Ivan II of Moscow and his second wife, Alexandra Velyaminova, daughter of Vasily Velyaminov, the tysyatsky (military commander) of Moscow. Ivan died on 13 November 1359, when Dmitry was nine. Real power then rested with his father's advisers, led by Velyaminov, while Metropolitan Alexius supervised the boy's education and wielded significant influence in the government.

In 1360, amid political turmoil in the Golden Horde, the khan Nawruz Beg gave the Grand Principality of Vladimir to Dmitry Konstantinovich of Suzdal. In 1362 Dmitry Ivanovich received a patent (yarlyk) from the rival khan Murad and, with the Moscow boyars and his cousin Vladimir Andreyevich of Serpukhov, drove his rival from Vladimir. In January 1366 he married the rival's youngest daughter, Eudoxia, which secured peace between the two principalities.

After taking the throne of Tver in 1366, Mikhail Aleksandrovich challenged Moscow with Lithuanian support. A Lithuanian army came to his aid, but the new stone walls of Moscow withstood the siege. In 1370 Dmitry invaded Tver again, and the Lithuanian grand duke Algirdas, finding him well prepared, proposed a truce and withdrew. Mikhail received a patent from Mamai in 1371 but could not enforce it, and a treaty negotiated by Alexius had Algirdas recognise the grand principality as Dmitry's patrimony. On 1 September 1375 Mikhail acknowledged Dmitry as his elder brother.

From 1374 Dmitry refused to pay tribute to Mamai. In 1378 his forces defeated a Mongol army at the Battle of Vozha River. In 1380 Mamai himself led a large force against Moscow. Sergius of Radonezh blessed Dmitry before the Battle of Kulikovo, and the battle opened with a single combat in which the Russian champion Alexander Peresvet and Temir-Murza of the Horde killed each other. Dmitry won, and from the battle took his name Donskoy, 'of the Don'. Tokhtamysh then deposed Mamai and overran Moscow in 1382; Dmitry pledged loyalty to him and was reinstated as grand prince of Vladimir.

Dmitry died in Moscow on 19 May 1389. He was the first grand prince to bequeath his titles to his son, Vasily I of Moscow, without consulting the khan. He had at least twelve children with Eudoxia. In Russian historiography he is regarded as a national hero and a central figure of medieval Russia. The Russian Orthodox Church canonised him as a saint on 6 June 1988, with his feast day on 19 May.
dmitry-milyutin: Count Dmitry Alekseyevich Milyutin was born on 10 July 1816 and graduated from the Moscow University School in 1833 and the Nicholas Military Academy in 1836. Unlike his brother Nikolai Milyutin, who chose civil administration, he volunteered for the Caucasian War and, after a grave wound, returned to the academy as a professor. His study of military statistics, the first comprehensive one, won the Demidov Prize for 1847, and in 1852 and 1853 he published a five-volume history of the war of 1799 against France, in which he held up Suvorov and his Italian campaign as models.

Milyutin analysed the causes of Russia's defeat in the Crimean War and drew up radical proposals for reform, which Alexander II approved; a few years before his appointment he had taken part in the capture of Imam Shamil. As minister he introduced the levy system and created military districts across the country. Service became compulsory for all men, nobles included, at 21 for six years instead of 25. Military education was reformed and elementary schooling offered to every draftee; before his reforms the army had no permanent barracks and lived in dugouts and shacks.

During the Russo-Turkish War of 1877 and 1878, when three assaults on Pleven had failed and many advised retreat, he ordered the siege continued in a more orderly way, and afterwards set up a commission on the supply failures. He was made a count and received the Order of Saint Andrew. Milyutin strongly advocated the deportation that formed the latter stage of the Circassian genocide, arguing that eliminating the Circassians was to be an end in itself.

After the Congress of Berlin he took over the direction of foreign policy from the ailing Alexander Gorchakov. The assassination of Alexander II in 1881 and the rise of Konstantin Pobedonostsev, who sought to reverse the liberal reforms, led him to resign. In 1898, on the 80th anniversary of Alexander II, he was made field marshal, the last in the history of the Russian Empire. He died in Simeiz on 7 February 1912. His reforms are regarded as a milestone in Russian history.
dmitry-of-pereslavl: Dmitry Alexandrovich was born in 1250. After the early death of his elder brother Vasily he became the chief heir of Alexander Nevsky, who left him in charge of Novgorod as early as 1259. When Alexander died in 1264, the Novgorodians expelled Dmitry to his native Pereslavl-Zalessky, giving his youth as the reason. Four years later, at 18, he was welcomed back and, with his future son-in-law Daumantas of Pskov, led the town's militia against the Livonian Knights at the Battle of Rakvere.

Through the following decade Dmitry struggled for Novgorod with his uncles Yaroslav III and Vasily of Kostroma, and only after their deaths in 1276 did he take the thrones of Vladimir and Novgorod. Two years later he founded the fortress of Koporye, which he meant to hold himself; the Novgorodians revolted and forced him out of Koporye and Novgorod.
