The oldest possible sign of a changed relationship comes from graves of the Khvalynsk and Samara cultures on the middle Volga, about 4800–4400 BCE, where horse bones lie with those of sacrificed cattle and sheep. At Botai settlements, with 50 to 150 pit houses, 65 to 99 percent of the discarded bones were horses, and pottery residues point to mare's milk; layers of dung and a corral at Krasnyi Yar suggest the animals were penned. Taylor and Barrón-Ortiz argued in 2021 that Botai shows intensive use of wild horses rather than true domestication.

Bones from Bell Beaker sites in eastern Hungary of about 2500 BCE show the size changes of penned herds. Studies of DNA found 125 genes linked to domestication, and scientists suggest that genes for stronger backs (GSDMC) and docility (ZFPM1) made the spreading lineage suited to riding.

In the Sintashta and Petrovka chariot graves, horses were buried with pairs of antler cheekpieces whose inner studs pressed on the horse's lips when the reins were pulled, the oldest objects clearly identified as horse tack. Riding may have been practised in the 4th and 3rd millennia BCE, but the clearest effect of horses on ancient warfare came through the chariot. Herodotus described the Sigynnae, who bred horses too small to ride but good at drawing chariots. In the Iron Age mounted archers such as the Parthians made cavalry a weapon of war, and over time the chariot fell out of use.
dominador-gomez: Gómez was born in Intramuros, Manila, the son of Jose Maria Gomez y Medel and Lutgardia Basilia De Jesus of Santa Cruz, Manila. He obtained his bachelor's degree from the Ateneo Municipal in 1881 and studied medicine at the University of Santo Tomas before leaving for Spain in 1887. There he received his licence to practise medicine from the University of Barcelona in 1889 and went on to Madrid for his doctorate. In Spain he was active in the Propaganda Movement as a leading member of the Asociacion Hispano-Filipina and a contributor to La Solidaridad, writing under the pen name Ramiro Franco.

Back in the Philippines, Gómez succeeded Isabelo de los Reyes as head of the Union Obrera Democratica, renamed the Union Obrera Democratica Filipina, in February 1903. Under him the federation launched strikes against American companies in Manila, and he became known for fiery speeches against capitalism and imperialism. On 1 May 1903 he was arrested on charges of sedition and illegal association, and the federation was accused of aiding the resistance of Macario Sakay. Gómez resigned his post and was sentenced to four years' imprisonment and a year of hard labour, but he won early release by taking part in the negotiations for Sakay's surrender.

In 1907 he was elected to the Philippine Assembly for Manila's 1st district. The Assembly expelled him on 1 February 1908 by 40 votes to 38 over legal controversies; he won the special election of 30 March 1908 and resigned on 18 June. Standing again in 1909, he at first lost to Justo Lukban, and in March 1910 the Assembly refused to seat him. In 1911 Lukban's election was voided for lack of residency and Gómez was declared the winner, serving until 1912.

Gómez has been portrayed on screen and on stage: by Nanding Josef in the 1993 film Sakay, by Lorenzo Mara in the 2012 film El Presidente, and by JV Ibesate in Aurelio Sedisyoso, a rock sarswela staged by Tanghalang Pilipino in 2017.
dominate: The term was proposed in the 19th century by the German scholar Theodor Mommsen, who set it against the Principate established by Augustus in 27 BCE. In his view the Principate was a system in which imperial authority was embedded within Roman Republican institutions. The later period, beginning with Diocletian about 284 CE, marked a break in the constitutional basis of the empire, which moved from one legitimised by a republican senate and people to one in which the emperor became the state. The historian Jochen Bleicken credits Mommsen with introducing both concepts to divide the history of the Roman Empire into periods.

Mommsen's lectures, published after his death, described the Dominate of Diocletian and Constantine as sharply different from the Principate. He saw an oriental ruler as its model, an empire divided where it had been united, a new capital, and a reformed administration. The army became a mobile force in which foreigners, above all Germans, served, a finance administration developed, and Constantine reintroduced a universal gold coin, the solidus.

Titles mattered to him. The word dominus, first used of slave-owners, became a title for the emperor as well as for a god, and it appeared on coins under Aurelian combined with deus. Diocletian introduced genuflection in the ceremony of adoration, where earlier emperors had been greeted with a handshake or a kiss. Mommsen noted that the idea of a god on earth could not be reconciled with Christianity, so the god was abandoned, but the lord remained.

Since the start of the 20th century scholars have increasingly rejected the idea of a rupture around Diocletian's time. They accept that significant changes occurred but do not see them as altering the emperor's legal position or the basic structure of Roman government. Mommsen's view was criticised for overemphasising law, and Ronald Syme's work, with its stress on networks of people, challenged it. In 1978 Bleicken argued that the division into Principate and Dominate rested on no genuine constitutional change and that both terms were ill suited to strict periodisation, and that Mommsen's view reflected reactions to absolutism in post-Napoleonic Europe. The Oxford Classical Dictionary now regards the term as nearly obsolete.
domingo-de-monteverde: Juan Domingo de Monteverde y Rivas was born in San Cristóbal de La Laguna on 2 April 1773. Holding the rank of frigate captain, he was sent to Venezuela from Puerto Rico and arrived at Coro in early March 1812 with other Spanish marines. Spain, fighting the Peninsular War against Napoleon's forces, had almost nothing to send to the New World, and the force the governor of Coro gave him to aid the town of Siquisique, which wished to leave the Republic, was poorly supplied.

Monteverde occupied Siquisique on 17 March 1812 after a seven-day march and, without authorisation, pressed on into republican territory. He found recruits easily among pardos, zambos, Canary Islanders and other lower-class people who saw the aristocratic mantuano rulers of the Republic as their enemies, and some mantuanos, among them the Marqués of Casa Leon, joined him. The earthquake of 26 March 1812 strengthened his cause. His vanguard under Francisco Marmól entered Barquisimeto on 2 April, and after a victory on 3 May he was welcomed into Valencia.

Repulsed at San Mateo in June, Monteverde still obtained a capitulation from Francisco de Miranda on 25 July 1812, after Miranda learned of the loss of Puerto Cabello and a rising in Caracas. Miranda was imprisoned and sent to Puerto Rico and later Cádiz, while most republican officials chose the exile the terms allowed. As captain general from June 1812 to 8 August 1813, Monteverde failed to meet the hopes of the people who had carried him to Caracas, and they abandoned him when Santiago Mariño invaded from the east and Simón Bolívar advanced through the Andes.

Monteverde, based at Valencia with his flank on the castle of Puerto Cabello, was defeated at Alto de los Godos on 25 May 1813 and wounded at Las Trincheras on 3 October 1813. Near the end of that year his own officers deposed him at Puerto Cabello, and Field Marshal Juan Manuel Cajigal took over the captaincy general. Monteverde went to Puerto Rico, returned to Spain in 1816 and died at San Fernando, Cádiz, on 15 September 1832 with the rank of brigadier.
domingo-faustino-sarmiento: Sarmiento was born on 15 February 1811 at Carrascal, a poor suburb of San Juan. His mother sold her weaving to build a house, and of the fifteen children of the marriage only Domingo reached adulthood. In the civil wars that followed the election of Bernardino Rivadavia in 1826 he sided with the centralising Unitarians against the rural Federalists, and in 1831 he fled to Chile, where he wrote political commentary and taught. After returning to San Juan in 1836 he founded the journal El Zonda, which a punitive tax forced to close in 1840. He belonged to the Generation of 1837, reformers who advocated republicanism, free trade and freedom of speech.

Between 1843 and 1850 he was frequently in exile. In Chile he wrote Facundo, published in instalments in El Progreso in 1845, which attacked the governor of Buenos Aires, Juan Manuel de Rosas, and contrasted European civilisation with the barbarism of the gaucho and the caudillo. He returned to Buenos Aires in 1855 and was elected president, against the manoeuvres of Bartolomé Mitre, serving from 1868 to 1874.

His government carried out the first national census in 1869, which counted 1,836,490 inhabitants, of whom 71 per cent were illiterate. The Subsidies Law of 1871 funded new schools, and primary schools rose to 1,816, with pupils increasing from 30,000 to 110,000. About 75 teachers, mostly women, were brought from the United States. Immigration rose, with 280,000 arrivals, the railway network grew from 573 to 1,331 kilometres, and about 5,000 km of telegraph lines were laid. The Paraguayan War ended in March 1870.

After his term Sarmiento served as senator and briefly as interior minister, and in 1882 helped pass the law making schools free, mandatory and separate from religion. He died of a heart attack in Asunción on 11 September 1888, aged 77, and was buried in Buenos Aires. Miguel de Unamuno considered him among the finest writers of Castilian prose. He admired the liberty of the United States but warned that liberty could turn into anarchy and civil war.
domingo-martinez-de-irala: Irala sailed for America in 1535 as a member of the expedition of Pedro de Mendoza and took part in the founding of Buenos Aires. He explored the Paraná and Paraguay rivers with Juan de Ayolas, and he was commanding the rear-guard when Ayolas's advance party was wiped out by the Payaguá. Charles V had granted the colony a right, unique in Spanish America, to elect its own commander in such a case, and in August 1538 the conquistadors elected Irala Captain General of the Río de la Plata.

In 1539 he began to move the settlers of Buenos Aires to Asunción, and the older town had been abandoned by 1541. He outlasted the royal appointee Álvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca, whom he sent back to Spain to be tried as a traitor. Juan de Sanabria and his son Diego were named governor in 1547 and 1549 but never took up their commissions, and in 1552 the king confirmed Irala as governor.

Between 1537 and 1541 the conquistadors received women within the cuñadazgo, a Guaraní institution by which caciques sealed alliances by giving women to newcomers, who thereby became brothers-in-law or sons-in-law. After 1541, with the settlers concentrated at Asunción, this system gave way to the rancheadas: mass and violent seizures of Guaraní women, who were bought and sold, used as currency and shipped to the Portuguese port of São Vicente.

A 1545 letter by Pero Hernández records that Irala sold a free Cario woman to Tristán de Vallartas for a scarlet cloak and a velvet jacket. In his testament of 1556 Irala acknowledged nine children by seven Guaraní women, whom he called his criadas, or servants. Modern historians describe the mestizaje of Paraguay as fundamentally a forced sexual relationship.

In 1555 Irala divided land among about 320 colonists as encomiendas, which bound between 17,000 and 20,000 indigenous people; the first encomiendas provoked uprisings. He governed forcefully until his death in 1556, raising churches and public buildings, founding towns and subjugating the native population. Gonzalo de Mendoza succeeded him.
domingos-jose-martins: Martins was born on 9 May 1781, by the accepted account at Fazenda Caxangá in Itapemirim, where Marataízes now stands, though some writers placed his birth in Vitória, in the Captaincy of Bahia or in Portugal. He was the son of the militia captain Joaquim José Martins and Joana Luiza de Santa Clara Martins. According to the priest Joaquim Dias Martins, he left home young to seek his fortune in Bahia, then moved to Lisbon and on to London, where he worked as finance director of the Portuguese company Dourado, Dias e Carvalho and was initiated into Freemasonry of the English tradition.

He was back in Brazil in early 1812, officially inspecting his company's branches, though Francisco Muniz Tavares wrote that the Freemasons had sent him to watch the revolutionary movements. He helped reactivate Freemasonry in the Captaincy of Pernambuco in 1813 and joined the lodges of Cabo and Paraíso, but the historian Breno Andrade finds no documents for the claim that he led the lodges of Brazil. He returned to London in 1815 and later settled in Recife. The merchant Louis-François Tollenare, who disliked him, judged him mediocre but a good speaker.

In 1817 Governor Caetano Pinto ordered arrests over a suspected conspiracy. While being arrested, José de Barros Lima killed Brigadier Manoel Joaquim Barbosa de Castro, and the revolt began. Martins was elected one of its five leaders, for the commercial class. Sent with troops to support Colonel Suassuna, he disagreed with him over tactics, and on 15 April, after crossing the Mererepe River, his force was attacked by the troops of Marcos de Noronha Brito at the Battle of Ipojuca. Wounded, he went into hiding but was denounced and taken prisoner.

Held in Aljube prison, he married Maria Teodora da Costa, daughter of the slave-trader Bento José da Costa, shortly before his execution, and is said to have written the poem Soneto do Patriota there. He was shot on 12 July 1817 at Campo da Pólvora with José Luiz de Mendonça and Father Miguel Joaquim de Castro e Almeida. Espírito Santo later made him a local hero: in 1921 the municipality of Campinho was renamed Domingos Martins, and in 2011 his name entered the Book of Heroes of the Homeland.
domini-di-terraferma: The Domini di Terraferma, also called the Stato da Tera, were one of the three parts of the Republic of Venice's possessions, beside the original Dogado around the lagoon and the Stato da Màr, the maritime territories. At their widest they covered the present-day region of Veneto, the western and central parts of Friuli-Venezia Giulia and the provinces of Bergamo and Brescia in eastern Lombardy.

In the west they reached the Adda River, where they bordered the Imperial Duchy of Milan. In the south the lower Po, the Polesine, formed the border with the Papal States, and in the north the Carnic and Julian Alps separated them from the Inner Austrian duchies of Carinthia and Carniola. In Friuli the easternmost part along the Isonzo River belonged to the Imperial counts of Gorizia.

Venice took the Mestre mainland from the Scaliger lords of Verona in 1337 during the Scaliger War, and Treviso and Bassano del Grappa in 1339. Systematic expansion began with Doge Michele Steno from 1400, who campaigned in the hinterland to secure trade and food for the city. His successors Tommaso Mocenigo and Francesco Foscari extended the territory at the expense of the Scaligeri, the Carraresi of Padua, whose lord Francesco Novello da Carrara was executed in 1406, and the Visconti of Milan.

In 1420 Venice annexed the Friulian lands of the Patriarchate of Aquileia from the Adriatic coast up to Pontebba in the Julian Alps. Emperor Sigismund acknowledged the conquest in 1433 and four years later ceded the territory to Venice as an Imperial fief. In 1523 Emperor Charles V finally gave up all his titles as feudal lord.

With the fall of the Republic the Domini passed briefly under French rule until Napoleon ceded them to Austria by the Treaty of Campo Formio in 1797. They were joined to the Napoleonic Kingdom of Italy in 1805, to the Austrian Kingdom of Lombardy–Venetia in 1815, and to the Kingdom of Italy in 1866 as a result of the Third Italian War of Independence.
dominica-freedom-party: The party was founded in 1968 by a group that included Eugenia Charles, Elkin Henry, Anthony Moise, Eustace Francis, Robert Allfrey, Phyllis Allfrey, E. C. Loblack, Edward Scobie, Loftus Roberts, Antony Agar, Star Lestrade and Martin Sorhaindo. It is a conservative party, sharing many of the social and economic principles of the Conservative Party in the UK, and it belongs to the Caribbean Democrat Union and the International Democrat Union. Charles led it from 1972 to 1995, serving as prime minister from 1980 until her retirement.

After the party lost the 1995 election to the United Workers' Party and Charles stood down, Brian Alleyne briefly led it, followed in 1996 by Charles Savarin, under whom it went on declining. In the election of 31 January 2000 it won two of the 21 elected seats with 13.6% of the vote and joined a coalition government with the Dominica Labour Party, which lacked a majority of its own.

At the general election of 5 May 2005 it lost all its seats, with 3.15% of the vote, the first time since 1975 that it had won none. Prime Minister Roosevelt Skerrit of the Dominica Labour Party, now governing alone, nevertheless appointed Savarin a senator and foreign minister, and many party members criticised his continued support for their former opponents. On 5 August 2007 a new executive chose the businessman Michael Astaphan as political leader.

Its leaders after Savarin were Michael Astaphan from 2007 to 2008, Judith Pestaina from 2008 to 2012, Astaphan again from 2012 to 2017, Kent Vital from 2017 to 2021 and, from 2021, Bernard Hurtault. The party boycotted the general election of 2022, at which the Dominica Labour Party took 19 of the 21 seats.
dominican-liberation-party: The party's founder, Juan Bosch, entered politics in the late 1920s and opposed Rafael Leonidas Trujillo, who took power in 1930. Arrested in 1934 on suspicion of conspiracy and released, he later left for Puerto Rico in self-imposed exile. After Trujillo's assassination he returned and in 1963 became the country's first democratically elected president, but the military overthrew him after a few months. A civil war and a United States intervention followed, and Joaquin Balaguer, one of Trujillo's original supporters, won the presidency.

Bosch rejoined the Dominican Revolutionary Party but left it in the early 1970s, feeling that it worked only for small and wealthy interest groups and not for the people. The PLD he founded in 1973, with a yellow five-pointed star on a purple background as its emblem, stood considerably to the left of the PRD. Bosch ran as its presidential candidate several times between 1978 and 1994 without winning, and retired from politics in 1996 at the age of 87.

Leonel Fernández, Bosch's running mate in 1994, succeeded him as leader and won the presidential election of 1996 in alliance with Balaguer, for more than 30 years Bosch's political enemy. Term-limited in 2000, he returned to office in 2004 with 57.1% of the vote and won again in 2008 with 54%. In the legislative elections of 2006 the party led the Progressive Bloc to 96 of 178 deputies and 22 of 32 senators, and in 2010 it won 31 of the 32 Senate seats.

Danilo Medina won the presidency for the party in 2012 with 51.2% of the vote against Hipólito Mejía of the PRD, and again in 2016. The Odebrecht scandal, in which the Brazilian construction company paid more than 90 million dollars in bribes to the Dominican government between 2001 and 2014, spanned the presidencies of Mejía, Fernández and Medina; it caused wide distrust and gave rise to the Green March protest movement.

At the election of 5 July 2020, postponed from May by the coronavirus pandemic, the PLD candidate Gonzalo Castillo won 37% against 54% for Luis Abinader of the Modern Revolutionary Party, ending sixteen years of PLD presidencies. Fernández, writing in an op-ed, put the defeat down to several factors, among them the Odebrecht scandal and protests against Medina's government.
dominican-order: The order grew out of a medieval ideal in which men of God were no longer expected to stay behind the walls of a cloister but travelled among the people, taking the apostles of the early Church as their example. Two orders of mendicant friars came from it: the Friars Minor, led by Francis of Assisi, and the Friars Preachers, led by the Castilian priest Dominic de Guzmán.

In 1203 he accompanied Diego de Acebo, Bishop of Osma, on a diplomatic mission to Denmark. The south of France was then a stronghold of the Cathars, whom the Church considered heretical. In 1206 Dominic established several women he had reconciled to the faith in a convent at Prouille, near Toulouse, which became the foundation of the Dominican nuns and later his headquarters for missionary work.

Dominic set up a religious community in Toulouse in 1214 and in 1215 gave it an institutional form with the approval of Bishop Foulques of Toulouse. It followed the Rule of Saint Augustine, which made its members canons regular rather than monks, able to carry out ministry and common life while living in individual poverty. Its founding documents name two purposes, preaching and the salvation of souls. Pope Honorius III approved the order by the bull Religiosam vitam on 22 December 1216.

The Pax Mongolica of the 13th and 14th centuries allowed missionaries to travel east. Dominican friars were preaching on the Volga steppes by 1225, and in 1240 Pope Gregory IX sent others to Persia and Armenia. Jordanus Catala de Severac went first to Persia and in 1321 to India, and recorded his observations in a book translated as Wonders of the East. Later, Gaspar da Cruz worked across the Portuguese empire in Asia and in 1569 or 1570 published the first European book devoted wholly to China.

The order's highest authority is the General Chapter, made up of the Chapter of Provincials, the heads of the provinces, and the Chapter of Definitors, who represent each province. This arrangement is unique in the Catholic Church. New legislation takes effect only after three successive meetings approve it.

Friars include ordained priests and non-ordained cooperator brothers. Their life rests on four pillars: prayer, study, community and preaching, and a long period of study precedes the solemn vow. Alongside the friars stand the cloistered nuns, active sisters, whose congregations are largely a product of the 19th century, priestly fraternities, lay Dominicans and associates. Dominican friars numbered 6,058 in 2013 and 5,369 in 2024.
dominican-republic: The country occupies the eastern part of Hispaniola, with the Atlantic Ocean to the north and the Caribbean Sea to the south, and shares a border of 376 km with Haiti. It is the second-largest country in the Antilles by area, after Cuba. The Cordillera Central is the highest range in the West Indies and holds the four highest peaks in the Caribbean, among them Pico Duarte at 3,098 metres. The capital and largest city, Santo Domingo, lies on the southern coast.

The Arawakan-speaking ancestors of the Taíno reached Hispaniola by around 600 CE, and by 1492 the island was divided into five Taíno chiefdoms. Christopher Columbus landed on 5 December 1492 and claimed the island for the Crown of Castile. In 1496 his brother Bartholomew built Santo Domingo, the first permanent European settlement in the Americas. Taíno chiefs such as Anacaona, Caonabo and Enriquillo resisted the conquest, but their numbers fell drastically from smallpox, measles and other diseases, and enslaved people from Africa were imported in their place. The last record of pure Taínos dates from 1864, though Taíno ancestry survived through intermixing.

By the Treaty of Ryswick in 1697, Spain ceded the western third of the island to France. A group of Dominicans declared independence from Spain in November 1821 but were annexed by Haiti in February 1822. Independence came in 1844 after the Dominican War of Independence, and the Spanish were permanently ousted in the Restoration War of 1863–1865. The United States occupied the country from 1916 to 1924. Rafael Trujillo ruled from 1930 until his assassination in 1961, and Joaquín Balaguer held office in 1966–1978 and 1986–1996.

The Dominican Republic is a representative democracy with an elected president and a bicameral Congress. Its culture has a European basis influenced by African and Taíno elements. Santo Domingo's Colonial Zone is a World Heritage Site and holds the first cathedral, palace, monastery and fortress built in the Americas. The name Dominican comes from Saint Dominic.
dominican-restoration-war: Facing an empty treasury and the threat of renewed attack from Haiti, President Pedro Santana asked Spain to take the country back, 17 years after independence. With the United States absorbed in its civil war and unable to enforce the Monroe Doctrine, Spain announced the annexation on 18 March 1861 and made Santana governor-general. Early risings failed: Francisco del Rosario Sánchez, who invaded from Haiti, was captured and executed on 4 July 1861, and Santana himself resigned in January 1862.

Spanish rule soon alienated Dominicans. The bagajes policy let the army seize work animals without compensation, a heavy burden on the farmers of the Cibao. Archbishop Bienvenido de Monzón pressed couples to marry in church, higher tariffs and a tobacco monopoly angered merchants, and rumours spread that slavery would return. When Spanish troops evicted Haitians from border areas, Haitian President Fabre Geffrard began to aid the rebels.

The rising spread through the Cibao, and on 3 September 1863 some 6,000 Dominicans besieged Fort San Luis at Santiago, burning the city; the Spanish garrison evacuated it on 13 September. The rebels set up a government under José Antonio Salcedo and denounced Santana, now leading Spanish forces, as a traitor. Yellow fever, malaria and dysentery took a heavy toll: by March 1864 Spain counted 1,000 killed in action and 9,000 dead from disease.

The fighting swung back and forth. Spain took Azua in December 1863 and Monte Cristi in May 1864, while guerrillas held San Cristóbal and raided supply convoys. On 4 December 1864 José María Cabral won at Neiba, the first Dominican victory over Spain in a conventional battle. Salcedo was overthrown and killed by commanders led by Gaspar Polanco, who was in turn replaced by Benigno Filomeno de Rojas, with Gregorio Luperón as vice-president, in January 1865.

The war was deeply unpopular in Spain, which had spent over 33 million pesos. Queen Isabella II signed the annulment of the annexation on 3 March 1865, and by 15 July no Spanish troops remained. The victory brought a new national pride and showed nationalists in Cuba and Puerto Rico that Spain could be beaten, but it left power with regional caudillos, a system that lasted until the late 20th century. Haiti abandoned its aim of ruling the whole island. 16 August is a national holiday, and the day on which Dominican presidents are sworn in.
dominican-war-of-independence: On 9 November 1821 José Núñez de Cáceres, the former captain general of Santo Domingo, overthrew Spanish rule, and on 9 February 1822 Haiti's president Jean-Pierre Boyer entered the city with the support of frontier leaders. Haitian rule grew unpopular for its heavy taxes and an economic crisis caused by the indemnity Haiti had to pay France. In 1838 Duarte, Mella and Sánchez founded the secret society La Trinitaria, organised in cells of three. On 27 February 1844 some 100 Dominicans seized the fortress of Puerta del Conde, and the Haitian garrison surrendered the next day.

In March 1844 President Charles Rivière-Hérard sent three columns, totalling 30,000 men, east. General Pedro Santana fought them at the Battle of Azua on 19 March, General José María Imbert defeated a column at the Battle of Santiago on 30 March, and on 15 April Dominican schooners sank three Haitian ships off Azua. Hérard was ousted on 3 May, and in July Santana took power in Santo Domingo, pushing the Trinitarios aside. A second Haitian campaign in 1845 was beaten back at Estrelleta and the Battle of Beler.

In March 1849 President Faustin Soulouque invaded with 10,000 troops and burned Azua, but Santana routed his army at the Battle of Las Carreras on 21 and 22 April. Late that year Dominican squadrons bombarded and burned Haitian coastal villages. After a truce mediated in 1851 by the United Kingdom, France and the United States broke down, Soulouque, now Emperor Faustin I, invaded in November 1855 with 30,000 men. José María Cabral defeated 12,000 Haitians at the Battle of Santomé on 22 December 1855, and in January 1856 some 8,000 Dominicans defeated 22,000 Haitians at the Battle of Sabana Larga.

Haiti kept Lascahobas and Hinche. A further invasion was defeated in 1859, but with the country ruined and fearing new attacks, Santana annexed the Dominican Republic to Spain in 1861. The Dominican Restoration War that followed cost Spain thousands of dead and wounded and many more to yellow fever, and Spain withdrew in 1865. Haiti recognised Dominican independence in 1867, and the frontier was settled only in 1936.
dominicus-gundissalinus: Gundissalinus was born in Castile and educated at Chartres, supposedly as a pupil of William of Conches and Thierry of Chartres. From 1148 he was back in Castile, where the capitular archives of Segovia name him archdeacon of Cuéllar, a small town near Segovia; almost nothing is known of the roughly 14 years he presumably spent there.

After Abraham Ibn Daud asked John II, archbishop of Toledo, to begin a series of Latin translations of Avicenna's Kitab al-Shifāʾ, Gundissalinus moved to Toledo in 1161–1162. With Ibn Daud he translated Avicenna's De anima before 1166. Over some twenty years in Toledo he and his collaborators, Ibn Daud and Johannes Hispanus, produced around twenty Latin versions of Arabic works, among them Avicenna's Liber de philosophia prima, al-Ghazali's Summa theoricae philosophiae and writings of al-Farabi, al-Kindi and Isaac Israeli ben Solomon. The Toledo chapter names him for the last time in 1178, and a document in Arabic mentions him in 1181.

His five treatises combine Avicenna and Ibn Gabirol with Boethius and writers of his own time such as the School of Chartres and Herman of Carinthia. De divisione philosophiae divides philosophy into a hierarchy of sciences, joining the schemes of al-Farabi and Avicenna to those of Isidore of Seville and Boethius. De scientiis revises al-Farabi's work of that name, De anima draws on Avicenna's psychology, and De unitate et uno and De processione mundi develop Ibn Gabirol's metaphysics and his doctrine of universal hylomorphism.

The last record of Gundissalinus alive is a meeting of the chapters of Segovia and Burgos held at Segovia in 1190, and he probably spent his last years there. His translations marked the passage from Platonism to the Aristotelianism of 13th-century Latin thought, and he was the first Latin thinker to take up doctrines such as Avicenna's modal ontology and Ibn Gabirol's universal hylomorphism, which entered the philosophical debates of the 13th century. De unitate et uno, long misattributed to Boethius, was translated into Hebrew by Judah ben Moses Romano and commented on by Conrad of Prussia in the 14th century.
dominion: The word dominion means that which is mastered or ruled. The British used it of their colonies and territorial possessions from the 16th century, and it was sometimes applied to Wales from 1535 to around 1800. It was conferred as an official title on the Colony of Virginia about 1660 and on the Dominion of New England in 1686. The later status followed the mid-19th-century achievement of full responsible government in British colonies, whose legislatures could then make laws in all matters except foreign affairs, defence and international trade.

At the London Conference of 1866 Samuel Leonard Tilley proposed the name One Dominion under the Name of Canada for the confederation of the Province of Canada, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, taking it from Psalm 72, verse eight. The British North America Act 1867 began the use of the title Dominion of Canada, though it gave no extra autonomy.

The Imperial Conference of 1907 introduced the idea of the Dominions as self-governing countries, referring to Canada and Australia in this way. In 1919 the self-governing Dominions signed the Treaty of Versailles independently of the British government and became individual members of the League of Nations. The Balfour Declaration of 1926 gave Australia, Canada, the Irish Free State, New Zealand, Newfoundland and South Africa the status of autonomous communities within the British Empire, equal in status and not subordinate to one another, though united by a common allegiance to the Crown.

The Statute of Westminster of December 1931 confirmed their full legislative independence. At the request of Australia and New Zealand it applied to them only when their parliaments confirmed it, in 1942 and 1947. Newfoundland suspended its self-government in 1934 after an economic collapse and joined Canada in 1949.

After the Second World War the empire became the Commonwealth of Nations. India and Pakistan became dominions in 1947 and Ceylon in 1948. At the Commonwealth Prime Ministers' Conference of 1949, when India intended to become a republic, the term Commonwealth country replaced dominion so that realms and republics could both be full members. By 1952 the United Kingdom no longer used the term for member nations, though it stayed in loose use for around thirty more years, mostly for smaller realms where the monarch remained head of state.
dominique-de-gourgues: Little is known of Gourgues's early life. He came from the old and powerful Gourgue family, one of the most important of Bordeaux. He served in the Italian wars under Maréchal de Strozzi, was captured by the Spaniards in 1557 and then by the Turks, and spent several years in the galleys. After his return to France he made a voyage to Brazil and the West Indies, then entered the service of the Duke de Guise and fought against the Huguenots. He was a captain in the army of King Charles IX.

In 1565 troops under Pedro Menéndez de Avilés captured Fort Caroline, in what is now Jacksonville, killed nearly all their prisoners and hung the bodies on trees with the words Not as Frenchmen but as Lutherans; the Massacre at Matanzas Inlet followed. The killings angered Catholics and Protestants alike in France, but Menéndez was rewarded rather than punished. Gourgues, embittered by what he himself had suffered at Spanish hands, resolved to avenge the Protestant colonists although he was a Catholic.

He sold everything he owned, borrowed from his brother Antoine, and chartered three ships with two hundred men, telling them his goal only once they reached Cuba, where they approved it. He then attacked the old Fort Caroline, renamed Fort San Mateo by the Spaniards, with the help of the Saturiwa and Tacatacuru clans of the Timucua, who had been the French fort's allies. The fort soon surrendered, and the French and their allies killed the Spanish prisoners, hanging them under the inscription Not as Spaniards but as murderers.

Gourgues landed at La Rochelle on 6 June 1568. Monluc, governor of Bordeaux, received him warmly, but the court, fearing a break with Spain, was cold, and for several years he lived in obscurity and near poverty at Rouen. Restored to royal favour in 1572, he commanded the largest vessel of the squadron at the Siege of La Rochelle. In 1592 Don Antonio de Crato made him commander of the fleet for a campaign against Philip II of Spain for the crown of Portugal, and he died on the voyage.
dominique-mbonyumutwa: Mbonyumutwa was born in January 1921. He rose to prominence in the late 1950s, when Rwanda was part of the Belgian-administered United Nations trust territory of Ruanda-Urundi. Ethnic divisions between the Tutsi, who held most political power, and the Hutu, who made up most of the population, had come to dominate Rwandan life. He was one of the few Hutu subchiefs in the country and a leader of the Hutu Emancipation Movement Party (Parmehutu) under Grégoire Kayibanda.

He had a working relationship with the Rwandan king, Mutara III Rudahigwa, but his position became less secure after the king died in July 1959. The assault on him came at Byimana in the Southern Province. There had never before been systematic political violence between Hutu and Tutsi, but within a week of the attack self-organised groups of Hutu were committing arson and even murder against their Tutsi neighbours.

He was chosen as president at a people's congress on 28 January 1961, which abolished the monarchy and proclaimed Rwanda a republic. He travelled the country for weeks to establish himself as the king's replacement and to gather support for the new government. The United Nations condemned the new order as "one racist dictatorship [replacing] another", but agreed to oversee a referendum. The monarchy was abolished with 80% of the vote, and a parliamentary election held at the same time gave Parmehutu a majority in the National Assembly, which chose Kayibanda to succeed him.

After he left the presidency, Mbonyumutwa served as a magistrate and then as a member of parliament. Under the next president, Juvénal Habyarimana, he held the honorary post of Chancellor of National Orders until his death on 26 July 1986.
domitian: Domitian was born in Rome on 24 October 51 as the youngest son of Vespasian and Flavia Domitilla Major. He had an older sister, Domitilla the Younger, and an older brother, Titus. The Flavians had risen from relative obscurity to prominence in four generations, gaining wealth and status under the Julio-Claudian emperors. Domitian spent much of his youth in the shadow of Titus, who won military renown in the First Jewish-Roman War, while their father and brother were away commanding armies in Germania and Judaea.

After Vespasian became emperor in 69, Domitian received honours but no responsibilities. In 70 he persuaded Domitia Longina, daughter of the general Gnaeus Domitius Corbulo, to leave her husband and marry him. For about ten years his role stayed largely ceremonial.

After the death of Titus, Domitian was declared emperor by the Praetorian Guard. His reign of fifteen years was the longest since that of Tiberius. He dropped the republican facade kept by his father and brother, moved the centre of government to the imperial court and drastically curtailed the powers of the Senate. According to Pliny the Younger, he believed the empire should be governed as a divine monarchy. He took the office of perpetual censor to control public and private morals.

He revalued the Roman coinage, raising the silver purity of the denarius from 90% to 98%. A financial crisis in 85 forced it down to 93.5%, still above the levels of Vespasian and Titus. Around fifty structures were built, restored or completed in Rome, among them the Stadium of Domitian, the Odeon of Domitian and the Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus on the Capitoline Hill, and the Flavian Palace on the Palatine Hill.

His campaigns were mostly defensive. He developed the Limes Germanicus, a network of roads, forts and watchtowers along the Rhine, and founded the Legio I Minervia in 82. On 1 January 89 Lucius Antonius Saturninus, governor of Germania Superior, rose in revolt with two legions and the Chatti; the rising stayed within his province and was put down.

Domitian was assassinated on 18 September 96 in a plot by court officials. Suetonius gives the main role to the chamberlain Parthenius; the blow was struck by Parthenius' freedman Maximus and Stephanus, a steward of Domitian's niece Flavia Domitilla. The Senate proclaimed Nerva emperor the same day, and condemned Domitian's memory to oblivion.

Most surviving accounts come from senatorial or aristocratic writers such as Tacitus, Pliny the Younger and Suetonius, who wrote after his death. Only the poets Martial and Statius, who praised him extravagantly, wrote during his reign. Since the 20th century, historians such as Brian W. Jones have described him as a ruthless but efficient autocrat whose policies laid foundations for the peaceful second century.
domitius-alexander: Lucius Domitius Alexander was vicarius of Africa before he usurped the imperial title, in the time of the Tetrarchy. The fullest and somewhat confusing account is that of Zosimus. He reports that Maxentius sent his portrait to Africa to gain recognition there as emperor, but the troops resisted because of their loyalty to Galerius. Maxentius then ordered Alexander to send his son to Rome as a guarantee of his loyalty. Alexander refused and was proclaimed emperor by his army. The incident was probably caused by the conflict between Maxentius and his father Maximian in April 308, and Zosimus seems to have confused Galerius with Maximian.

Besides the provinces of north Africa, today's Algeria, Tunisia and western Libya, Alexander also controlled Sardinia. An inscription from Sicca, modern El Kef, bears the names of both Alexander and Constantine I as emperors, which may imply some kind of alliance, although this is uncertain. Salama suggests that the possible pact was made by autumn 310 at the latest. According to Noel Emmanuel Lenski, Constantine seems to have offered support, very cautiously, in order to keep pressure on Maxentius. The usurpation coincided with Constantine's recognition as Augustus and ruined the balance of Tetrarchic power, since there were now five Augusti and only one Caesar.

Maxentius sent his praetorian prefect Rufius Volusianus and a certain Zenas to put down the rebellion. Alexander was taken prisoner and then executed by strangulation, and his troops apparently offered little resistance. Maxentius retaliated with confiscations of the property of alleged supporters of Alexander.
dommoc: Bede's Historia ecclesiastica is the main authority for the founding of the see. After Eorpwald of East Anglia was killed by Ricberht, the kingdom fell back from the faith for three years, until Sigeberht, Eorpwald's brother or half-brother, took possession of it; he had received the Christian sacraments in exile in Gaul. Felix, born and consecrated in Burgundy, came to Archbishop Honorius of Canterbury, who sent him to the East Angles. Bede says Felix took the episcopal seat in the civitas of Dommoc, governed it for seventeen years and died there. William of Malmesbury, writing much later, has Sigeberht and Felix come from Gaul together.

Felix was followed by Thomas, bishop for five years, and Berhtgisl Boniface, for seventeen; both were consecrated by Honorius, who died in 653. Theodore of Tarsus, Archbishop of Canterbury, then appointed Bisi, who attended the Council of Hertford in 673. As Bisi's health failed, Theodore divided the see and created a second bishopric, the See of Elmham. The see of Dommoc lapsed after the Viking Wars of the 860s. A seal matrix of Ethilwald, its last-known bishop, was found at Eye about two hundred years ago.

The site was lost many centuries ago. In the 13th century the monks of Eye claimed it for Dunwich and those of Rochester for Walton near Felixstowe, so the doubt had arisen between the tenth and twelfth centuries. William Camden's Britannia won general acceptance for Dunwich, once a splendid city on the Suffolk coast between Aldeburgh and Southwold, now almost wholly lost to coastal erosion. Stuart Rigold revived the case for Walton, where a Roman shore fort stood beside a large Roman settlement, both since lost to the sea; Bede's word civitas suggests a former Roman site.

The likeness of the names Dommoc and Dunwich may mislead: Dommoc could derive from the Latin dominicum, a church, while Dunwich should mean the wic at the hill. At Walton, Roger Bigod, 1st Earl of Norfolk, founded a priory of St Felix within the fort around the end of the eleventh century, inviting monks from Rochester. Several East Anglian places are linked with Felix's work, and although Dunwich or Walton seems more likely, neither is certain.
domnall-mac-aedo: Domnall was the son of Áed mac Ainmuirech and his consort Land, daughter of Áed Guaire mac Amalgada of Airgíalla. His year of birth is unknown and depends on the disputed date of the convention of Druim Cett, but it fell between about 570 and 590. According to Adomnán's Life of Saint Columba, Domnall met Columba there as a boy, and the saint foretold great success and a peaceful death in old age. Later claims that his father and his brother Máel Cobo had also been high kings are inventions of later writers.

The Annals of Ulster first mention him in 628, when he was defeated at the battle of Both by the high king Suibne Menn of the Cenél nEógain. Soon after, Suibne was killed by Congal Cáech, and Domnall raided Leinster, after which the annalists treat him as high king. In 629 he defeated Congal and the armies of the Ulaid and Dál nAraidi at Dún Ceithirn, and wars among the other Uí Néill kindreds strengthened his hold.

Congal returned in 637 with Domnall Brecc of Dál Riata and the Cenél nEógain, while Domnall had the Síl nÁedo Sláine on his side. On the day of Mag Rath his fleet, led by his nephew Conall Cáel, also won the sea battle of Sailtír off Kintyre. Dál Riata is thought to have lost its lands in County Antrim as a result.

His wife Duinseach died in 641, and Domnall died at the end of January 642, perhaps after a long illness. His nephew Cellach mac Máele Cobo followed him as king of Cenél Conaill. The original compiler of the Annals of Ulster began his list of twelve kings of Ireland with Domnall. His grandsons Loingsech mac Óengusso and Congal Cennmagair both became high kings.
domnall-mor-ua-briain: Domnall Mór, Donall the Great, was the third son of Toirdhealbhach mac Diarmada Ua Briain, King of Munster from 1142 to 1167. He came to the throne in 1168 after his eldest brother, Muirchertach, who had succeeded their father, was killed at the instigation of their cousin Conchobar mac Muirchertach Ua Briain. He was also styled King of Limerick, a title the O'Brien dynasty had held since Brian Boru sacked the Hiberno-Norse city after the Battle of Sulcoit.

In 1169, the year his brother Brian of Slieve Bloom was blinded, Domnall clashed with the High King Ruaidrí Ua Conchobair and had to pay him a tribute of 300 cows. After submitting to Henry II at Cashel in 1171 he fought the Normans in the south-west for many years. In 1175, after his victory over the Cambro-Normans at Thurles, he blinded two of his cousins, Dermot mac Taig Ua Briain and Mathgamain mac Toirdhelbeach Ua Briain, in Limerick, and was driven from Thomond by the High King. In 1176 he drove the Normans from Limerick, and in 1178 he drove out the Uí Fidgenti.

In 1184 part of his lands was enfeoffed to Philip de Braose, who set out with Robert Fitz-Stephen and Miles de Cogan to take Limerick but turned back in a panic as he approached the city. In 1185, when Prince John intervened in Ireland, Domnall defeated the Normans as John plundered the valley of the River Suir. In 1188 he helped the men of Connacht under Conchobar Maenmaige Ua Conchobhair to overcome Jean de Courcy in the Curlew Mountains, and in 1193 the Normans devastated Clare in reprisal.

He founded the Cistercian abbeys of Holy Cross in 1180 and Kilcooly in 1184. The Annals of Ulster call him the last king of Munster, dying in 1194. He is believed to be buried in Saint Mary's Cathedral, Limerick, a church he first organised, where a stone coffin lid said to be his lies near the high altar. He married Orlacan, daughter of Diarmait Mac Murchada, and left three sons and a daughter; his sons Muirchertach Dall, Conchobar Ruadh and Donnchadh Cairbreach fought one another for Thomond.
domodossola: Domodossola lies at the foot of the Alps, in the Toce plain at the crossroads of the Bognanco, Divedro, Antigorio, Vigezzo and Isorno valleys. It stands at the confluence of the Bogna and Toce rivers, 272 metres above sea level, and is the main centre of the Ossola. Much of its municipal territory is mountainous, and the ski resort of Domobianca lies within it, on the slopes of the Moncucco.

The area has been inhabited since prehistoric times. Known as Oscella, the town was the chief town of the Lepontii when the Romans conquered the region in 12 BCE, and a Roman road linking Mediolanum to Lake Maggiore passed through it. Afterwards it belonged to the Ostrogothic Kingdom, whose king Theodoric the Great fortified the nearby Mattarella hill. In the sixth century the Lombards sacked and burned it, and the Franks later drove them out. It then became a fief of the bishop-count of Novara, who built a castle there. A collegiate church of the eleventh century gave it the name Domus Oxile, which gradually became its modern name.

In 1381, after Swiss raids and the conflict between Guelphs and Ghibellines, the town swore fealty to Gian Galeazzo Visconti, Lord of Milan, in exchange for military protection. After the Italian Wars it came briefly under the French, then for nearly two centuries under the Spaniards and in 1706 under the Austrians. The Treaty of Worms of 1743 gave it to the Kingdom of Sardinia, and in 1818 King Victor Emmanuel I made it the capital of the new Province of Ossola. The opening of the Simplon Tunnel in 1906 put it again on a major international route. Industry and hydroelectric plants brought growth, and the population almost doubled between 1881 and 1921.

On 10 September 1944 Italian Resistance forces liberated Domodossola, which became the capital of the Republic of Ossola, one of the largest partisan republics in German-occupied northern Italy. German and Fascist forces crushed the republic on 23 October 1944, and many inhabitants fled to Switzerland to escape reprisals. In 1945 the city flag was awarded the Gold Medal of Military Valor.

Domodossola is a city and comune in the Province of Verbano-Cusio-Ossola in Piedmont, northern Italy. It is the main railway hub in northern Piedmont and an international stopping point between Milan and Brig in Switzerland through the Simplon Pass. Its best-known landmark is the Sacro Monte Calvario, a pilgrimage site and UNESCO World Heritage Site, on the same hill as the remains of the medieval castle of Mattarella. Its name is widely known in Italy from the spelling alphabet, in which D stands for Domodossola.
domoni: Domoni lies on the east coast of Anjouan, also called Nzwani, and is the island's second largest town, with a population of 15,351. It is one of the island's three major towns, with Bambao and Mutsamudu, and is linked to Mutsamudu by a road of about 16 kilometres. The old town is divided into three neighbourhoods: Hari ya muji, Maweni and Momoni. The middle section, Hari ya Muzhi, has been the centre of activity since the 16th century and holds the main plaza, the Friday mosque and many mansions.

According to archaeological finds the town was established in the 12th century. By the 15th century it was a flourishing trading centre, with links to Africa, Persia, Arab lands and India, and artefacts show contact with places as far away as Japan.

The navigator Ibn Majid, who had guided Vasco da Gama to India, confirmed the port as a major trading centre. In the 16th century many chiefs, known as Feni, controlled different parts of the island. Domoni was the capital of the Anjouan sultanate until the end of the 18th century, when Mwenye Fani, who took the name Abdallah I on becoming sultan, moved the capital to Mutsamudu. It has a significant Shirazi population, descended from Sunni aristocratic immigrants from Shiraz in Persia who arrived between the 14th and 18th centuries.

Infighting among the chiefs of Anjouan led them to ask Europeans to broker peace. The Comoros became a French protectorate in 1886, and in 1909 the French made them part of their own country. In 1975 the three islands formed the Republic of the Comoro Islands. Its first president, Ahmed Abdallah, came from Domoni; he was assassinated in 1989 by a presidential guard, and his white mausoleum, with four tall minarets, stands in the town. Tadjidine ben Saïd Massonde was also born there.

The first stone building in Domoni dates from the mid-13th century, and the old houses built by the Shirazi migrants can still be seen. The mosques, built of stone masonry on raised foundations, date from the eleventh and twelfth centuries, were rebuilt in the thirteenth and enlarged in the fourteenth and fifteenth. The Shirazi Mosque has two mihrabs where most have one, and the Friday mosque has the tallest minaret on the island. The town is known for mansions of the 16th and 18th centuries with richly carved Swahili doors, and for its wood carving and embroidery.
don-quixote: In July 1604 Miguel de Cervantes sold the rights to El ingenioso hidalgo don Quixote de la Mancha, later called Part I, to the publisher and bookseller Francisco de Robles for an unknown sum. The licence to publish was granted in September, printing finished in December, and the book came out on 16 January 1605. It was an immediate success. Most of the 400 copies of the first edition went to the New World, and although most were lost in a shipwreck near Havana, about 70 reached Lima and were sent on to Cuzco. For Cervantes and his readers it was a single volume, and the mention of further adventures to be told was conventional rather than a plan for a sequel.

The hero is an hidalgo of nearly 50 from an unspecified place in La Mancha, Alonso Quixano, who lives frugally with his niece and housekeeper. His obsession with chivalric romances leads him to become a knight errant. He dons an old suit of armour, renames himself Don Quixote, names his old workhorse Rocinante and chooses as his lady love Aldonza Lorenzo, whom he renames Dulcinea del Toboso. Cervantes writes that the rest of the book was translated from an Arabic text by the Moorish historian Cide Hamete Benengeli. Don Quixote does not see the world as it is, while his squire, the farm labourer Sancho Panza, brings an earthy wit to his lofty rhetoric.

Part One also holds stories told by figures the two men meet, the longest being The Ill-Advised Curiosity, about the Florentine nobleman Anselmo, who talks his friend Lothario into testing his wife's fidelity. Part Two appeared ten years later and is an early example of metafiction, since its characters have read the first part. The names play on words: Rocinante is a reversal, Dulcinea alludes to illusion, and quixote is a term for the armour that protects the thighs.

Cervantes had probably written no further than Chapter 59 of Part Two by late July 1614. In about September a spurious Part Two by a certain Alonso Fernández de Avellaneda was published at Tarragona. Its author, never identified with any consensus, insulted Cervantes in the prologue, and Cervantes answered in the later chapters of his own Part Two. The book had been translated into French, German, Italian and English within seven years of Part One. It influenced Alexandre Dumas's The Three Musketeers and Edmond Rostand's Cyrano de Bergerac, and inspired works by Pablo Picasso and Richard Strauss, and it gave English the word quixotic and the phrase tilting at windmills, meaning attacking imaginary enemies.
don-river: The Don is the fifth-longest river in Europe. It rises in the town of Novomoskovsk, 60 kilometres south-east of Tula, and flows 1,870 kilometres to the Sea of Azov. Its upper half meanders gently south, while the lower half makes a great eastern curve past Voronezh before the final stretch, an estuary, runs west-south-west. Its basin lies between the Dnieper basin to the west, the lower Volga basin to the east and the Oka basin to the north. The main tributary is the Seversky Donets, and the main city on the river is Rostov-on-Don.

The name derives from the Avestan and Rigveda word dānu. According to the Kurgan hypothesis, the Volga-Don region was the homeland of the Proto-Indo-Europeans around 4,000 BCE. In antiquity some Greek geographers viewed the river as the border between Europe and Asia. The Greeks called it the Tanaïs, which was also the name of a city on it, situated in the Maeotian marshes; they also called it Iazartes, and Pliny gives its Scythian name as Silys. A Greek source traditionally, though not certainly, attributed to Plutarch placed the Amazons of Greek mythology on the Don. Byzantine traders used the river, and it has been a major trading route ever since.

In the early Middle Ages the Khazar Khaganate controlled much of the lower Don and built the limestone fortress of Sarkel on its left bank to defend a vital portage between the Don and the Volga. After the Mongol conquests most of the basin passed to the Golden Horde, which set up the trade outpost of Azak in the estuary, an area speculated to be the source of the Black Death in the mid-14th century. The Don Cossacks, who settled the valley in the 16th and 17th centuries, took their name from the river. Its middle and upper reaches were not mapped accurately before the Tsardom of Russia gradually conquered the area in the 16th century.

The Volga-Don Canal, 101 kilometres long, links the Don with the Volga where the two rivers come within about 100 kilometres of each other, and the Tsimlyansk Dam raises the Don's level there, forming the Tsimlyansk Reservoir. Below it, three dam-and-ship-lock complexes maintain depth for 130 kilometres. The Kochetovsky Lock was built in 1914–19 and doubled in 2004–08. The region is the setting of Mikhail Sholokhov's novel And Quiet Flows the Don.
donald-ii-of-scotland: Domnall mac Causantín, anglicised as Donald II, was the son of Constantine I, Causantín mac Cináeda. The Prophecy of Berchán gives him the epithet Dásachtach, the Madman. He came to the throne on the death or deposition of his cousin Giric, whose date is not certainly known but is usually placed in 889. Giric had killed Donald's uncle Àed mac Cináeda, who reigned from 877 to 879.

The Chronicle of the Kings of Alba says Donald held the kingdom for eleven years, from 889 to 900, and that the Northmen wasted Pictland in his reign. It reports a battle at Innisibsolian in which the Scots defeated the Danes, so that he is thought to have fought the Vikings in the north continuously.

The Annals of Ulster and the Chronicon Scotorum date his death to 900 and call him king of Alba rather than king of the Picts. This change of title is seen as a step towards the kingdom of the Scots, but historians do not generally credit it to Donald. The consensus is that the key changes occurred in the reign of Constantine II, though the reign of Giric has also been proposed.

The Chronicle says he was killed at Opidum Fother, modern Dunnottar, by the Gentiles. It has been suggested that the attack on Dunnottar was no small raid but linked to the ravaging of Scotland attributed to Harald Fairhair in the Heimskringla. The Prophecy of Berchán places his death at Dunnottar but seems to blame Gaels rather than Norsemen, and other sources report that he died at Forres. He was buried on Iona. His cousin Constantine II succeeded him, and Donald's son Malcolm later became king as Malcolm I.
donald-lord-of-the-isles: The Lordship of the Isles was centred on Islay, but under Donald's father, John of Islay, it had grown to take in most of the isles and the mainland lands once held by Somerled, King of the Isles in the 12th century, including Morvern, Garmoran, Lochaber, Kintyre and Knapdale. Donald was a grandson of King Robert II and first cousin of King Robert III, and he took pride in his royal blood, setting the royal tressure around his coat of arms. Historians note that he was one of several magnates, like the Douglas kindred and the Albany Stewarts, who held great lordships with little interference from the crown.

His early years were spent putting down a revolt by his younger brother John Mór, who resented his small inheritance of land in Kintyre and Islay. The rising, begun by the MacKinnons in 1387 and backed by the MacLean and MacLeod kindreds, lasted into the 1390s; the MacKinnon chief was hanged and the Green Abbot of Iona imprisoned for life, while John was forgiven. Donald and his brother Alexander of Lochaber then profited from the fall of Alexander Stewart, Earl of Buchan, the Wolf of Badenoch, and by the end of 1395 the MacDonalds held Urquhart Castle.

After the death of Alexander Leslie, Earl of Ross, in 1402, Donald pressed the claim of his wife Mariota, Alexander's sister. He took Dingwall Castle, the chief seat of the earldom, and sought the support of the captive heir to the throne, James Stewart, and of King Henry IV of England against the governor, Robert Stewart, Duke of Albany. In 1411 he led some 10,000 Islesmen and men of Ross against Albany's ally Alexander Stewart, Earl of Mar, and won a decisive victory at the Battle of Harlaw before returning to the western Highlands and Isles.

Albany then retook Dingwall and Easter Ross, and in 1415 the heiress Euphemia II resigned the earldom to him, but Donald proclaimed himself Lord of Ross and Mariota still held herself the rightful countess. Donald died on Islay in 1423. His son Alexander succeeded him as Lord of the Isles and became Earl of Ross, and another son, Angus, became Bishop of the Isles.
donatello: Donato di Niccolò di Betto Bardi was born in Florence, probably in 1386, judging from his own tax declaration of July 1427, in which he claimed to be 41. His father, Niccolò di Betto Bardi, was a wool-stretcher and a member of the wool workers' guild. Donatello's first appearance in the records is in January 1401, when, aged about 15, he was accused in Pistoia of hitting a German with a stick. He appears to have befriended, and perhaps worked with, the goldsmith Filippo Brunelleschi, some ten years older. All accounts describe him as amiable and well liked but poor at the business side of his career, accepting more commissions than he could handle, and he enjoyed steady Medici patronage.

By early 1408 Donatello had the commission for a life-size prophet for Florence Cathedral, to pair with one by Nanni di Banco; it was not placed as intended and appears to be lost. He also made statues for the niches of Orsanmichele, and developed stiacciato, a very shallow relief, with Saint George Freeing the Princess as an early milestone. Around 1425 he formed a partnership with the architect Michelozzo, which lasted nine years and ended partly because of Donatello's delays on an exterior pulpit for Prato Cathedral. In the 1430s and 1440s he made many dancing children, putti and spiritelli.

His bronze David, now in the Bargello, is his best-known work: the first known free-standing nude statue since antiquity, conceived fully in the round at nearly life size. It was probably commissioned by Cosimo de' Medici between 1434 and 1440. In 1443 he was called to Padua by the heirs of the condottiere Gattamelata, whose equestrian monument, cast mostly in 1447 or 1448 and finished in 1450, was installed in 1453. His ten years there are thought to have stimulated Padua's later table bronzes. He worked in Siena between 1457 and 1461, though ageing.

Donatello remained in Florence after returning from Siena and died in 1466, on 13 December. In his last years, with assistants, he made the reliefs that now form two pulpits in San Lorenzo, assembled in that form only in the following century. His influence can be seen in all Florentine sculpture of the 15th century and well beyond, and most of his major church works remain in place, with the main museum collection in the Bargello. Giorgio Vasari, writing around a century after the events, recognised his stature but made clear errors, placing his birth in 1403.
donation-of-constantine: In many manuscripts, including the oldest, the document is titled Constitutum domini Constantini imperatoris. It was included in the 9th-century Pseudo-Isidorean decretals. Its origin is debated. One suggestion is that an early draft was made shortly after the middle of the 8th century to assist Pope Stephen II in his negotiations with Pepin the Short, who in 754 received the pope's anointing as king; the lands Pepin then gave the pope became the Papal States.

Another view holds that it was a move in Roman church politics to raise the Lateran against the rising Vatican, perhaps composed by a Greek monk in a Roman monastery. The German medievalist Johannes Fried distinguishes the Donation from a shorter, earlier forgery, the Constitutum Constantini, of which he thinks it a later expansion.

The text is dated 30 March without a year, and names as Constantine's co-consul in his fourth term (315) a Gallicanus who held the office in 317. It has Constantine profess Christianity and grant Pope Sylvester I imperial insignia and privileges and the Lateran Palace. Rome, the rest of Italy and the western provinces are made over to the papacy. Sylvester is also given supremacy over the four principal sees of Alexandria, Antioch, Jerusalem and Constantinople.

It rests on the 5th-century Acts of Sylvester, in which the pope rescues the Romans from a dragon and cures the emperor's leprosy through baptism. Because it implied that Sylvester held imperial rank before Constantinople was inaugurated in 330, it also served to reduce the authority of Constantinople.

The earliest known allusion may be a letter of 778 in which Pope Hadrian I urged Charlemagne to follow Constantine's example. Pope Leo IX was the first pope to invoke the decree directly, in 1054, in a letter to Patriarch Michael I Cerularius of Constantinople, citing much of it in the belief that it was genuine. In the 11th and 12th centuries it was often cited in the investiture conflicts. Dante regretted the evil born from the donation.

Doubt had been raised since 1001, when Otto III's chancery denied its authenticity. In the mid-15th century Nicholas of Cusa and Reginald Pecocke concluded independently that it was a forgery. Lorenzo Valla argued from philology that its language could not belong to the 4th century and could most likely be dated to the 8th. Valla's treatise was taken up by Protestant writers such as Ulrich von Hutten and Martin Luther. Caesar Baronius admitted the forgery in his Annales Ecclesiastici, published from 1588 to 1607, after which it was almost universally accepted as such.
donation-of-pepin: In 751 Aistulf, king of the Lombards, conquered what remained of the exarchate of Ravenna, the last vestige of the Roman Empire in northern Italy. In 752 he demanded the submission of Rome and a tribute of one gold solidus per head. Pope Stephen II tried negotiations and bribes, and when they failed, he led a procession through Rome and nailed the violated treaty to a crucifix. He appealed to the Byzantine emperor Constantine V without success, then to Pepin the Short. Stephen was refused by Aistulf at Pavia and became the first pope to cross the Alps, reaching Pepin's estate at Ponthion on 6 January 754.

At Ponthion, the pope in sackcloth and ashes asked Pepin to support the suit of St Peter and the republic of the Romans, and Pepin promised to restore the exarchate of Ravenna and the rights and territories of the republic. In April 754 an assembly at Quierzy-sur-Oise heard him restate the promise and list the territories, and some noblemen left in opposition. The promise was afterwards put in writing. On 28 July 754 the pope anointed Pepin and his sons Charles and Carloman as kings of the Franks and patricians of the Romans.

In spring 755 the Frankish army crossed Mont Cénis and defeated the Lombards near Susa, and Aistulf swore to return Ravenna. As soon as the army left, he broke the treaty and put Rome under siege on 1 January 756. After three months Aistulf lifted the blockade, and in April a Frankish army again defeated the Lombards. Aistulf gave hostages, agreed to pay annual tribute and promised in writing to return the lands.

The treaty of 756 conferred on the pope the territories of Ravenna, including Forlì, the Lombard conquests in the Romagna and in the Duchy of Spoleto and Benevento, and the Pentapolis of Rimini, Pesaro, Fano, Senigallia and Ancona. Envoys of the Empire offered Pepin money to have the lands returned, but he refused, saying they belonged to St Peter. Abbot Fulrad collected the keys of the cities and laid them with the written agreement on the tomb of St Peter. The boundaries can only be approximated, since the text has not survived.

The Donation made the pope a temporal ruler for the first time, over a strip of territory running across Italy from the Tyrrhenian to the Adriatic, though the popes could not exercise effective sovereignty over it. Pepin's successors Charlemagne and Louis the Pious confirmed it in 778 and 817. Scholars debate the terminology, since the lands were technically not Pepin's to give.
donatism: Donatism was a schism from the Catholic Church in the Archdiocese of Carthage, rooted in the Christian community of Roman Africa. During the Diocletianic Persecutions the governor was satisfied when Christians handed over their scriptures as a token repudiation of faith, and critics called those who did so traditores. The Donatists were rigorists: the church must be a church of saints, and sacraments given by traditores were invalid. In 311 Caecilian was consecrated bishop of Carthage by Felix of Aptungi, an alleged traditor. His opponents consecrated Majorinus, who was succeeded by Donatus Magnus, after whom the movement is named.

Constantine gave money to Caecilian for churches damaged in the persecution and nothing to the Donatists, which worsened the dispute. A commission appointed by Pope Miltiades condemned the Donatists in 313, and the Council of Arles in 314 ruled against them again. In 317 Constantine issued an edict threatening death to anyone disturbing the imperial peace and another calling for confiscation of Donatist church property, but by 321 he asked the bishops for moderation. The movement spread mainly among the indigenous Berber population and blended Christianity with local customs. The Circumcellions, as opponents called them, were roving groups who regarded martyrdom as the supreme virtue and sometimes used violence.

Augustine of Hippo campaigned against Donatism as bishop. He taught that a sacrament is valid whatever the character of the priest, and he justified force against the Donatists, though he rejected the death penalty. In 409 a decree condemned them as heretics and ordered them to surrender their churches. Donatism survived the Vandal conquest and the Byzantine reconquest, and it is unknown how long it lasted. In the Middle Ages and the Reformation the charge of Donatism was made against reformers such as John Wycliffe and Jan Hus, who held that the moral failings of priests invalidated their offices.
donato-bramante: Bramante was born Donato di Pascuccio d'Antonio and is also known as Bramante Lazzari. He was born at Fermignano near Urbino, where in 1467 Luciano Laurana was adding an arcaded courtyard and other Renaissance features to Federico da Montefeltro's ducal palace. He knew the painters Melozzo da Forlì and Piero della Francesca, who were interested in perspective. His architecture has eclipsed his painting.

Around 1474 Bramante moved to Milan, a city with a deep Gothic tradition, and built several churches in the new antique style. From 1476 Duke Ludovico Sforza made him virtually his court architect. His commissions culminated in the trompe-l'œil choir of Santa Maria presso San Satiro, built in 1482 to 1486. Space was limited, so he made a theatrical apse in bas-relief that combines perspective with Roman details. He also built the tribune of Santa Maria delle Grazie in 1492 to 1499 and the cloisters of Sant'Ambrogio in 1497 to 1498, and worked on Pavia Cathedral, setting the design and creating the crypt and part of the apse.

In 1499 the French army drove out his Sforza patron, and Bramante went to Rome, where Cardinal Riario already knew him. Cardinal Della Rovere, soon to be Pope Julius II, took notice of him. He designed the cloister of Santa Maria della Pace in 1500 to 1504 and in 1502 the Tempietto of San Pietro in Montorio, built over the spot where Peter was martyred. Though small, it has the strict proportions and symmetry of classical buildings, with slender Doric columns and a dome, and it marked the beginning of the High Renaissance in Rome.

In November 1503 Julius II engaged him for the complete rebuilding of St Peter's Basilica, the grandest architectural commission in 16th-century Europe. The cornerstone of the first great pier of the crossing was laid on 17 April 1506. Bramante planned a centralised Greek cross, which symbolised sublime perfection for him and his generation, with four chapels filling the corners between equal transepts, each capped with a smaller dome around the great dome. The plan was more Romano-Byzantine in form than the church built, and it was fundamentally altered when the nave was extended after his death. Michelangelo later executed a design based on it.

He also planned the Cortile del Belvedere, a vast courtyard linking the buildings of the Vatican, and designed the Palazzo Caprini. Very few of his drawings survive, though some by his assistants do. He wrote about architecture and composed eighty sonnets. He died on 11 April 1514.
donaueschingen: Donaueschingen lies in the Baar basin in the southern Black Forest, in the Schwarzwald-Baar district of Baden-Württemberg. It stands about 13 kilometres south of Villingen-Schwenningen, 24 kilometres west of Tuttlingen and about 30 kilometres north of the Swiss town of Schaffhausen. The town takes its name from the Danube, German Donau, which begins at the confluence here of the Brigach and the Breg, its two source tributaries. An enclosed karst spring in the park of Donaueschingen Palace, the source of the Donaubach, is also known as the source of the Danube. The heights of the municipal area fall from 1,020 metres in the Black Forest to about 660 metres on the Baar plateau and rise again above 900 metres at the Swabian Alb.

The place is first recorded as Esginga in 889, and the modern form of its name is first attested in 1292. In 1283 Rudolph von Habsburg granted the principality of Baar and Donaueschingen to Heinrich von Fürstenberg, a grant that carried the right to brew beer, which is the origin of the Fürstenberg Brewery. In 1488 possession passed to the Count of Fürstenberg-Baar, and from the 18th century the town was the residence of the princes of Fürstenberg, who lived in Schloss Donaueschingen.

In 1806 it came under the rule of the Grand Duchy of Baden and received township in 1810. A large part of the town was destroyed by fire in 1908. It has a tradition as a military garrison: the French military had barracks there from 1945 to 2014, and until the early 1990s the United States Air Force ran a contingency hospital, which was most used in 1989, when it housed refugees leaving East Germany for the West. The Fürstenberg princes were nominally mediatised and deposed as absolute rulers, but they kept much property, including the palace and its gardens. They owned an important manuscript of the Nibelungenlied, Manuscript C, until they sold it in 2001.

The town had 21,750 people in 2015 and is a regional rail hub where four lines join, including the Schwarzwaldbahn and the Höllentalbahn to Freiburg. The long-distance Danube Cycle Trail starts there. The Donaueschingen Festival for contemporary music, founded in 1921 and one of the world's oldest festivals for new music, takes place every October, and guest composers have included Paul Hindemith, Arnold Schoenberg, Pierre Boulez, John Cage and György Ligeti. The Fürstenberg Library holds early copies of five of Mozart's operas, an important source for reviving historically informed performance of 18th-century opera.
donbas: The Donbas lies in south-eastern Ukraine between the middle and lower Donets river in the north and the Azov Upland and Lowland in the south, across the border from Russia. The core area, about 23,000 square kilometres, corresponds roughly to the Donets Ridge, where coal seams reach the surface and which is known as the Old Donbas. Coal elsewhere lies at depths of 500 to 600 metres or more, in areas that became producing regions only after the Second World War.

Nomadic peoples including the Scythians, Alans, Huns, Pechenegs, Kipchaks, Tatars and Nogais lived on this steppe for centuries. It was largely unpopulated until the second half of the 17th century, when Don Cossacks founded the first permanent settlements. The first town, Solanoye (now Soledar), was founded in 1676 for rock-salt working. The area, called the Wild Fields, lay under the Cossack Hetmanate and the Crimean Khanate until the Russian Empire conquered the one and annexed the other in the mid to late 18th century.

Coal was discovered in 1721 and exploited on a large scale from the mid to late 19th century, when the name Donbas came into use. Early steel mills were set up at Luhansk in 1795, near Yenakiieve in 1859 to 1864 and at Lysychansk in 1866 to 1870. The Welsh businessman John Hughes founded Yuzivka, later Donetsk, in 1869 and built a steel mill and collieries. Landless peasants came in large numbers to find work, and poor conditions led to strikes, including a wave in 1905.

The region was incorporated into the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic in 1919. Coal output fell sharply between 1913 and 1920, and pre-war levels returned by 1928 to 1929. Under German occupation in 1941 to 1943, 279,000 civilians were killed in what is now Donetsk Oblast and 45,649 in Luhansk Oblast, and production of 1940 was restored only in 1949. After independence in 1991 industry declined sharply. In 2014 unrest in the region grew into a war that has continued within the wider Russo-Ukrainian war.

The Donbas is usually taken to mean Donetsk Oblast and Luhansk Oblast. Donetsk is considered its unofficial capital, and other large cities include Mariupol, Luhansk, Makiivka, Horlivka, Kramatorsk, Sloviansk, Alchevsk, Sievierodonetsk and Lysychansk. At the census of 2001 the population of the Ukrainian part was about 58 percent ethnic Ukrainian and 38 percent ethnic Russian. The region remains defined by coal, iron and steel.
donegal-castle: The castle stands in the centre of Donegal Town, on a bend of the River Eske near the mouth of Donegal Bay. It consists of a 15th-century rectangular keep with a later wing in the Jacobean style, a small gatehouse that mirrors the design of the keep, and a 17th-century boundary wall; most of the stone is local limestone with some sandstone. The town's Irish name, Dún na nGall, means fort of the foreigner, possibly after a Viking fortress destroyed in 1159, of which no archaeological trace has been found.

The castle was built by Hugh Roe O'Donnell I, chief of the O'Donnells, and in 1474 he and his wife Nuala founded a Franciscan friary further down the river. It was counted among the finest Gaelic castles in Ireland: in 1566 the Lord Deputy of Ireland, Sir Henry Sidney, wrote to William Cecil that it was "the largest and strongest fortress in all Ireland". After the Nine Years' War the O'Donnell leaders left Ireland in the Flight of the Earls of 1607, and during the Plantation of Ulster the castle and its lands were granted to the English captain Basil Brooke, who restored it and added windows and a gable to the keep.
