The Brookes kept the castle until the 1670s, when they moved to near Lisnaskea in County Fermanagh and sold it to the Gore family, later Earls of Arran. It fell into ruin under the Gores in the early 18th century, and in 1898 the 5th Earl of Arran vested it in the Office of Public Works.

The Office of Public Works partly restored the castle in the early 1990s. The tower house received new roofs and floors in the styles of the 15th and 17th centuries, the stonework was repaired and the manor wing partly roofed, some of the oak coming from the Colebrooke Estate near Brookeborough. It is open to the public and hosts events such as Gaelic cultural evenings and Ulster Scots events.
donegal-friary: The friary stands at the mouth of the River Eske where it enters Donegal Bay, west of the town centre. A 17th-century Latin account by one of its friars, translated by Charles Patrick Meehan, tells that Nuala made a journey of about 100 miles with a group of women to Ross Errilly Friary in County Galway, where the Franciscans were holding a provincial chapter, to ask for a house in Tyrconnell. Refused at first, she warned them of God's wrath for the souls that might be lost, and friars went back with her to build beside the wharf at Donegal.

Nuala died later in 1474, before the building was finished, and Hugh Roe O'Donnell's second wife, Fingalla O'Brien, saw the monastery, church and cloisters completed; she later lived in austerity in a small house near the friary. In 1508 Creevelea Abbey in County Leitrim was founded as its daughter house. In the Nine Years' War the friary was used for a meeting between the rebel leaders and envoys of King Philip II of Spain, and Hugh McManus O'Donnell, who had lived many years among the friars, was buried there in 1600.

In the absence of Red Hugh O'Donnell, his cousin Niall Garve O'Donnell came to terms with the English government and made the friary his base. Red Hugh attacked in 1601 but could not retake it. On 10 August 1601 a fire reached a store of Niall Garve's gunpowder, and the explosion destroyed most of the building and killed hundreds of his soldiers, among them his brother Conn Oge O'Donnell.

The friary was never rebuilt. Its friars set up a new base at Bundrowes, near the River Drowes, where Mícheál Ó Cléirigh, Cú Choigríche Ó Duibhgeannáin and Fearfeasa Ó Maol Chonaire worked between 1632 and 1636. A silver chalice made for the Friars of Donegal in 1633 by O'Donnell's silversmith John O'Mullarkey was later in Quebec. In 1992 Pope John Paul II beatified Concobhar Ó Duibheannaigh, a Franciscan of Donegal and Bishop of Down and Conor, hanged, drawn and quartered outside Dublin in 1612.
dong-khanh: Đồng Khánh was born Nguyễn Phúc Ưng Kỷ on 19 February 1864 in the Imperial City of Huế. His childhood name, Chánh Mông, came from the Chánh Mông palace where he was raised. He was the eldest son of Prince Nguyễn Phúc Hồng Cai, a son of Emperor Thiệu Trị, and his concubine Bùi Thị Thanh. His uncle, Emperor Tự Đức, had no children, so he was adopted and given the title Kiên Giang quận công, Duke of Kiên Giang.

After French armies captured Huế and the Imperial City fell, the court regents Nguyễn Văn Tường and Tôn Thất Thuyết took the young Emperor Hàm Nghi out of the Purple Forbidden City. They brought him to Tân Sở in the mountains as the figurehead of a movement against the French. To take away Hàm Nghi's legitimacy, General de Courcy and the résident de Champeaux asked the empress dowager Nghi Thiên to enthrone his elder half brother. With the backing of the governor of Annam, Prince Nguyễn Phúc Ưng Kỷ was crowned as the ninth emperor of Đại Nam on 19 September 1885 and took the era name Đồng Khánh.

Đồng Khánh was pro-French. According to the later historian Trần Trọng Kim, he had a gentle personality, loved luxurious jewellery and adopted French culture, so the colonial government favoured him. After Hàm Nghi fled to Quảng Bình, Đồng Khánh agreed to the French request to travel there and persuade Hàm Nghi and his loyal followers to surrender, but he was unsuccessful. Hàm Nghi was later betrayed by his follower Trương Quang Ngọc, captured by the French and exiled to Algérie.

Đồng Khánh died on 28 January 1889 at the age of 24 and was given the temple name Cảnh Tông. His son, Emperor Khải Định, granted him a longer posthumous name in 1916. He was buried in the Tư Lăng mausoleum at Dương Xuân Thượng village, Hương Thuỷ commune, in Thừa Thiên Province.
dong-son-culture: Scholars traditionally traced bronze-casting technology to China, but discoveries of the 1970s at Isan in Thailand suggested that casting either began in Southeast Asia first and spread into China, or developed there independently. The Đông Sơn bronze industry therefore has a local origin in Southeast Asia and was not brought by migrations out of China. The Gò Mun culture gave rise to the Đông Sơn culture, which was the culmination of the Bronze Age and the opening stage of the Iron Age. Objects related to Đông Sơn have been found in Malaysia, Laos and the Chinese provinces of Yunnan, Guangxi and Fujian.

The Đông Sơn people cultivated rice, kept water buffalo and pigs, fished and sailed in long dugout canoes. They were also skilled bronze casters. Their Heger I drums are decorated with rings of warships and warriors in feather headdresses circling a central sun, on which stylised frogs rest; the scenes also show drummers and other musicians, rice processing, birds, deer and geometric designs. The chief summoned the warriors of the tribe by beating the drum, and drums were also used in mourning and at feasts. The Cổ Loa drum weighs 72 kilograms and would have needed between 1 and 7 tonnes of copper ore. Some Đông Sơn daggers closely resemble Scytho-Siberian styles.

Excavations at Đông Sơn village began in 1924 after a fisherman, Nguyễn Văn Lắm, reported large quantities of bronze objects to the École française d'Extrême-Orient in Hanoi. The Austrian archaeologist Franz Heger had classified bronze drums in 1898. Scholars disagree about who the Dongsonians were. Ferlus concluded from vocabulary for the pestle, oar and sticky-rice pan that they were of Vietic origin and direct ancestors of the Vietnamese, while Keith W. Taylor, Nguyen Phuong and John D. Phan hold there is no evidence they were Vietnamese or their ancestors.

The Đông Sơn drums vanish from Vietnam after the defeat of the Trưng sisters and the arrival of Han material culture, after the Han general Ma Yuan conquered the Red River Plain. More than 120 Han brick tombs in the region point to growing Chinese migration or cultural influence, and the earliest Sino-Vietnamese loanwords date from about then.
dong-son-drum: Each drum has three parts: the head at the top, the barrel or upper body, and the leg at the base. The decoration is realistic, showing stilted houses, people dancing, pounding rice, beating drums and sailing, with animals and birds. The Ngọc Lũ drum, regarded as the most important, has three concentric panels on its head; the innermost shows people performing a ceremony with the drums themselves, with other instruments and rice growing, and the outer two show deer, hornbills and egrets. The Hoàng Hạ drum, found in Hòa Bình Province in 1937, shows four feathered men with spears walking in a line with two musicians.

The drums were played at festivals, in prayers for rain and a good harvest, at weddings and funerals, and to give commands in the army. They also served as funerary objects and as symbols of the power of tribal leaders. In ancient Vietnam they were venerated as cult objects, and excavated drums were worshipped as Thần Đồng Cổ, the bronze drum god, in temples such as the Đông Cổ Temple and the Cao Sơn Temple. The Book of the Later Han records that Ma Yuan melted down drums seized from the Lạc Việt in Jiaozhi to make bronze horses.

The Ngọc Lũ drum was found by accident in 1893 in Hà Nam Province, and drums and other bronzes were excavated in 1924 at the village of Đông Sơn in Thanh Hóa Province. In 1902 F. Heger published 165 large bronze drums and divided them into four types, the first of which takes in these drums. In 1990 the Vietnamese scholar Pham Huy Thong divided them into five groups thought to follow one another in time, from large, intricately decorated drums to smaller ones with waterbirds in flight as their main motif. Drums found in New Guinea are seen as evidence of trade with Java and China.
dong-zhuo: Dong Zhuo, courtesy name Zhongying, was born in Lintao, Longxi Commandery, in the early 140s. He was said to have been a chivalrous youth, physically strong and skilled at archery on horseback, who travelled among the Qiang and Xiongnu. About 165 he joined the Yulin corps of the Imperial Guard and served under Zhang Huan against a Qiang uprising. He held posts as county magistrate, inspector of Bing Province and administrator of Hedong Commandery, and fought in the Yellow Turban Rebellion of 184 and against rebels in Liang Province. In 188 he was named General of the Vanguard but refused the governorship of Bing Province because he did not want to leave his men.

After Emperor Ling of Han died in May 189, General-in-Chief He Jin ordered Dong Zhuo to bring troops to Luoyang against the eunuch faction. He Jin was assassinated before Dong arrived. Finding his 3,000 men too few, Dong had some leave at night and re-enter at dawn so as to seem to be receiving reinforcements. He took command of He Jin's troops, won over Lü Bu and made himself Excellency of Works. That year he deposed Emperor Shao and put Liu Xie, Emperor Xian, in his place, declaring himself chancellor. Rafe de Crespigny describes his conduct towards the court as bullying, oppressive and frequently bloody.

Yuan Shao formed a coalition of regional officials and warlords against him. Dong evacuated Luoyang and moved its people to Chang'an, and his troops ransacked the tombs of the Han emperors and burned the palaces. He later had the Yuan clan in Luoyang killed, and thousands of officials were wrongly accused and executed. He melted bells and bronze statues into coins of unequal weight, which devalued copper cash.

Dong Zhuo had sworn father and son with Lü Bu, but the bond failed after a quarrel in which Dong threw a hand-axe at Lü. With the encouragement of the interior minister Wang Yun, Lü Bu killed him on 22 May 192 at the palace gate, after an attempt to stab him with a ji failed against his armour. His body was left in the street with a lit wick on its navel, and his kin were put to death.

His loyalists Li Jue, Guo Si, Zhang Ji and Fan Chou, refused a pardon by Wang Yun, took Chang'an with an army of about 100,000 and again held the emperor and the court. His death is seen as a destabilising event in the collapse of the Eastern Han dynasty and a precursor to the Wars of the Three Kingdoms.
dongcheon-of-goguryeo: Dongcheon was the grandson of Goguryeo's eighth ruler, King Sindae, and the son of the tenth, King Sansang. His mother was a royal concubine of Sansang, known as the Little Consort, from the Jutong-chon of Gwanno-bu. He was made crown prince in 213 and came to the throne on his father's death. His sons included Prince Yeonbul and the princes Yemul and Sagu, both of whom died in 248.

In 238 Dongcheon joined Wei, one of the three Chinese kingdoms, in destroying the Gongsun family and its hold over the Liaodong Peninsula, but Wei then became a new threat. His attack on a Chinese fortress near the mouth of the Yalu River in 242 led to the Goguryeo–Wei War. After the sack of Hwando the king fled, and his forces later returned to a capital whose buildings lay badly damaged, before moving the capital to present-day Pyongyang in 246; the exact site of the new capital is disputed. According to Mark E. Byington, the destruction was so great that Chinese histories did not mention Goguryeo for the next 50 years.

The 12th-century Samguk sagi tells that the general Yu Yu feigned surrender, killed a Wei officer and then himself, and that the generals Mil U and Yu Okgu then drove out the Wei army and regained all lost land. No Chinese record parallels the story, and Hiroshi Ikeuchi, pointing to its geographical errors and anachronisms, considered it fiction. The Samguk sagi also records that Dongcheon attacked Silla in 245 and made peace in 248, which many read as a flight of Goguryeo refugees into the borderlands with Silla.

In 243 Dongcheon named Yeonbul crown prince. He fell ill and died in the autumn of 248, and Yeonbul succeeded him at once as King Jungcheon. His tomb is said to lie in South Pyongan Province near Pyongyang, and he is said to have been so loved that many people followed him in death.
donghak: Donghak arose as a reaction to seohak, Western learning. Joseon had made Neo-Confucianism its state ideology, and by the 19th century orthodox scholars stood increasingly apart from other Confucian scholars who sought to revive social ethics and reform society. Growing pressure from the West made reform seem more urgent. Ch'oe Cheu was alarmed by the spread of Catholicism, called Cheonjugyo, and by the Anglo-French occupation of Beijing, and he wrote the treatise Dongkyeong Daejeon, the Comprehensive Book of Eastern Learning. It was the first work to use the term Eastern Learning, and it rejected God in the Christian sense and other parts of Christian theology.

Ch'oe called for a return to the Way of Heaven, understood in Confucian terms, with stress on self-cultivation and the improvement of one's own nature. As he wrote, the Way of Heaven lay within one's own mind, so that by improving one's nature one also attained it. The movement had no fixed agenda or systematic doctrine: Ch'oe preferred to improvise as events unfolded and left no practical plan for the paradise on Earth he spoke of, beyond the belief that all people were equal. His call for equality and his Korean nationalism struck a chord among the peasants, and the movement spread rapidly across Korea.

Ch'oe was executed, and the movement passed to Choe Si-hyeong (1829–1898), who systematised its doctrine and was executed in his turn. In 1898 his successor Son Byong-hi took refuge in Japan. Returning after the Russo-Japanese War of 1904, he founded the Chinbohoe, or progressive society, a reform movement meant to reverse the nation's declining fortunes. Through Donghak he led a nationwide campaign to renew old customs: hundreds of thousands of members cut their long hair short and adopted simple, modest clothing, and non-violent demonstrations for social improvement took place throughout 1904. Under Son, its third patriarch, the movement became the religion of Cheondogyo, or Cheondoism, which is followed today in both North and South Korea.
donghak-peasant-revolution: In the late 19th century Korean society faced inequality, corruption and excessive taxation, which set off a series of peasant-led rebellions and weakened the Joseon government's control outside the capital. The Donghak religion arose in this turbulent age. By the 1890s believers were petitioning to overturn the 1863 execution of the founder, Choe Je-u. In November 1892 Jeon Bong-jun led the Samrye Petition, which asked that Donghak not be banned, that Western missionaries and merchants be expelled and that corrupt officials be killed.

The immediate cause was the conduct of Jo Byeong-gap, magistrate of Gobu, who took water taxes from peasants and made them pay taxes on land he had promised to exempt. In March 1894 peasants led by Jeon and Kim Gae-nam rose, and the revolt grew to tens of thousands. In April they defeated government forces at Hwangtojae, luring them into a pass and attacking under cover of fog, and at the Hwangryong River, where they rolled chicken cages downhill to block bullets. Jeon took Jeonju, the largest city in Jeolla, and a truce followed in May by the Treaty of Jeonju.

The government asked for foreign help, and both Qing and Japanese forces landed at Incheon. Japan's anger that the Qing had not informed it under the Convention of Tientsin led to the First Sino-Japanese War.

Growing Japanese dominance alarmed the rebels. On 12 October 1894 a coalition of Northern and Southern forces, put at between 25,000 and 200,000 by different records, marched on Gongju and was decisively defeated at the Battle of Ugeumchi. At Taein on 25 November Japanese firepower destroyed both the rebels and the town. Fighting continued into the spring of 1895, and the rebel leaders were captured in several places in the Honam region, most of them executed by mass hanging in March.
donglin-movement: The Donglin Academy in Wuxi was restored in 1604, in the Wanli era, by Gu Xiancheng (1550–1612) and the scholar Gao Panlong (1562–1626), with the financial backing of local gentry and officials. They were moved by concern over the state of the bureaucracy and its inability to bring about improvement, and turned to moral Confucian traditions as a way to fresh moral judgements. Many of the founders had been among the mandarins who, a few years before, forced the Wanli Emperor to name his first-born son, Zhu Changluo, the future Taichang Emperor, as heir instead of Zhu Changxun, his son by his favourite concubine, Lady Zheng.

The academy became a centre of dissent on public affairs, and the movement gained momentum when the academies of nearby Wujin and Yixing joined it. Its many supporters in the bureaucracy drew it deep into factional politics, carried on through bureaucratic manoeuvring and through educated opinion, the building of reputations and even the reporting of dreams.

Under the Tianqi Emperor its opposition to the eunuch Wei Zhongxian led to the closure of the academy in 1622, and in 1624 its head, Yang Lian, and five other members were tortured and executed. The accession of the Chongzhen Emperor restored the faction's fortunes, and in 1637 Donglin partisans arranged the dismissal of the Grand Secretary Wen Tiren.

The movement marked the growth of literati influence on political life in late imperial China. Its tradition passed to the Fushe movement, centred on Suzhou, before the fall of the Ming dynasty, and to the Changzhou School of Thought under the Qing. China's defeat in the Opium War of 1839–42 revived interest in the Donglin movement as a prominent example of literati solidarity.
dongmyeong-of-goguryeo: The records of Dongmyeong are often regarded as partly mythological, and how far they are historical is debated. Much of his story is taken from an earlier one about the founder of Buyeo, which the Goguryeo monarchy appropriated in the 4th century CE to raise its own standing. The best-known versions are in the Samguk sagi and the Samguk yusa. Chumong, his personal name, was a Buyeo word for an excellent archer, and Dongmyeong, Brilliant Saintly King of the East, is a posthumous name.

In the story, Lady Yuhwa, daughter of Habaek, bore a large egg that animals refused to harm, and a boy hatched from it. He was a master of archery by seven. Daeso, eldest son of Geumwa, king of Eastern Buyeo, feared him, and Yuhwa told him to leave. Pursued, he reached the Eomsa River and, declaring himself a son of the Heavenly God and grandson of Habaek, made fish and turtles form a bridge.

He gathered followers, reached Jolbon Stream and founded Goguryeo, taking the surname Ko at the age of 21. In the first year of his reign he struck the Mohe, who surrendered. He defeated Song Yang, king of Biryu, in an archery contest, and Song Yang submitted in June of 36 BCE and was made Marquis of Damul. Later campaigns subdued the State of Haengin and the Northern Okjeo. In 19 BCE his son Yuri arrived from Buyeo and was named crown prince.

A variant noted by the compilers of the Samguk sagi says that Biryu and Onjo were sons of Soseono by an earlier husband, and that Dongmyeong married her. When Yuri became crown prince, Biryu left with Onjo and Soseono to found a kingdom of his own.

According to the Gwanggaeto Stele, Dongmyeong rode a dragon into Heaven at 39, and only his whip was buried at Yongsan. The Confucian Kim Pusik read this as a metaphor and wrote that he died and was buried there. Goguryeo worshipped him as an ancestral deity, and Balhae and Goryeo succeeded the kingdom. The Hoengseong Ko clan of Korea and the Koma clan of Japan consider him their founder. Other records, among them the tombstone of Go Ja, suggest that Goguryeo was older than the Samguk sagi's chronology allows.
donnchad-ua-cerbaill: Donnchad was a half-brother on his mother's side of Tigernán Ua Ruairc, King of Bréifne: both were sons of Aillend, daughter of Ua Baegelláin, a local ruler of the Fir Manach. His family's base was the Clann Cearbhaill lands in Fearmaigh and west Louth. He rose in the age historians call that of the High Kings with Opposition, roughly 1076 to 1166, when provincial armies repeatedly crossed County Louth, the Kingdom of Midhe was divided again and again, and outside candidates were often imposed as local kings.

Early in his career Donnchad conquered the sub-kingdom of Conaille Muirtheimne in north Louth, around 1130, raided across Meath into Fingal, the Viking settlement north of Dublin, and worked closely with the northern king Muirchertach Mac Lochlainn. By about 1140 he had added Fir Arda Ciannachta and extended his influence around Newry and Bairrche in south County Down. He settled vassal groups of Airgialla on his conquests: the Uí Méith gave their name to Omeath and the Mugdorna to the Mournes.

His church foundations served his power as well as reform. Besides Mellifont he was connected with foundations at Louth, Knock Abbey and Termonfeckin, some of them of the Arrouaisian order. Handing older religious sites from local dynasts to European orders weakened them as bases of opposition. To reflect his conquests, the area of County Louth passed from the see of Armagh to that of Clogher, whose bishop styled himself Bishop of Louth. In 1166, after Muirchertach Mac Lochlainn broke an oath and blinded Donnchad's foster-son Eochaid Mac Duinn Sléibe, king of Ulaid, Donnchad was central to the overthrow and killing of the High King.

According to the Annals of Ulster, Donnchad was mortally wounded while drunk by the battle-axe of one of his own servants, Ua Duibhne of the Cenél nEoghain. He was buried in the sanctuary of Mellifont Abbey, in an arched recess on the north side of the high altar. Before his death he had placed Áed in Macáem Tóinlesc on the throne of Ailech, dividing that kingdom's power for 75 years. By 1193 his family had been eclipsed, and County Louth had been lost to the Norman colony.
donnuban-mac-cathail: Donnubán, also written Donndubán or Donnabán and anglicised Donovan, was the son of Cathal. His pedigree, as set out by John O'Donovan in the appendix to the Annals of the Four Masters, makes him the senior descendant of Oilioll Olum, but the historian Donnchadh Ó Corráin argued that it may be a fabrication meant to link the family to the Uí Chairpre Áebda, or at least that generations are missing. His sons appear as kings of Uí Chairpre, and family tradition holds that his wife was a daughter of Ivar of Limerick, though other relationships with the Norse have been proposed.

Donnubán allied with Ivar of Limerick and with Máel Muad mac Brain, king of Desmond, against the rising Dál gCais under Mathgamain mac Cennétig, king of Cashel, and his brother Brian Bóruma. Máel Muad had been king of Munster until he was deposed around 970. Mathgamain agreed to meet the allies at Donnubán's house, for a reason now lost.

There Donnubán seized him and handed him over to Máel Muad, who put him to death. The Annals of Inisfallen say this was done in violation of the guarantee and despite the interdiction of the elders of Munster. Donnubán's help made Máel Muad king of Munster from 976 to 978. The twelfth-century saga Cogad Gáedel re Gallaib, a fictional political work, casts Ivar rather than Máel Muad as the one who moved Donnubán to act.

Accounts of Donnubán's end differ. Cogad Gáedel re Gallaib, written more than 120 years after the events, has him killed by Brian's army at Cathair Cuan together with Aralt, a son of Ivar, while the family pedigrees place his death at a battle of Croma. The Annals of the Four Masters record only Brian's victory over him and the Norse of Limerick, and the Annals of Inisfallen note under 980 the death of Donnubán, king of Ress, giving no cause. The place called Ress or Ressad has not been identified with certainty. His son Uainide died as king of Uí Chairpre in 982, and Donnubán is the ancestor of the O'Donovan family.
dooars: The Dooars lie south of the outer foothills of the Himalayas and north of the Brahmaputra River basin, a belt about 30 km wide that stretches over about 350 km from the Teesta River in West Bengal to the Dhansiri River in Udalguri district of Assam. They form part of the Terai-Duar savanna and grasslands ecoregion. The name means doors in several languages of the region, after the 18 passages between the hills of Bhutan and the plains, and the Sankosh River divides them into Eastern and Western Dooars.

The Dooars belonged to the Kamata Kingdom under the Koch dynasty and carried the trade between Assam and Bhutan: Assam sent muga silk, endi cloth, dried fish and rice, and received woollen cloth, gold dust, rock salt, yak tails, musk, ponies and blankets. In the early 17th century the combined forces of the Ahoms and Koches checked the advance of the Bhutias, who during the Ahom–Mughal conflicts of the mid-17th century tried to extend their authority southwards.

Under the Ahom king Jayadhwaj Singha, the Druk Desi of Bhutan obtained the Darrang Duars by agreement in return for an annual tribute, the Ahoms holding them each year from June to October. In the last phase of the 18th century, while the Ahoms were occupied with internal rebellions, the Druk Desi took possession of them. Bhutan held the region when British India annexed it in 1865 after the Duar War, losing almost one fifth of its area. The western part became a district called Western Dooars, renamed Jalpaiguri district in 1869.

The region forms the northern bank of the Brahmaputra Valley in Assam and the plains of Kalimpong district, the whole of Jalpaiguri and Alipurduar districts and the upper part of Cooch Behar district in West Bengal. Its towns include Cooch Behar, Alipurduar, Dhupguri, Malbazar and Birpara in West Bengal and Kokrajhar, Bongaigaon and Dhubri in Assam; Siliguri and Jalpaiguri, the largest cities, lie partly in the Terai. Its forests are home to endangered animals such as the Bengal tiger, the Indian rhinoceros and the Indian elephant.
dora-riparia: The Dora Riparia is a left-bank tributary of the Po, mostly flowing in Piedmont in north-west Italy. It is 125 kilometres long, of which 5 kilometres lie in Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur in south-east France, and it drains a basin of 1,231 square kilometres. In Piedmontese it is Dòira Rivaira, and in Occitan Dueira. It rises in the Cottian Alps close to the Col de Montgenèvre in France, where it is called the Piccola Dora or Petite Doire, meaning Small Dora. It takes the name Dora Riparia after meeting the Ripa in the Argentera Valley and the Thuras de Bousson near Cesana Torinese.

At Oulx it grows with its main upper tributary, the Dora di Bardonecchia, and before Susa it is joined by the Galambra and Cenischia. Below Susa it receives only minor tributaries, among them the Gravio, Sessi, Messa and Scaglione. It runs through the Susa Valley, crosses part of the plain of the Po through the territories of Avigliana, Alpignano, Pianezza and Collegno, and joins the Po at Turin. It counts as a stream, torrente, as far as Susa and as a river, fiume, from there to Turin.

Present-day Turin was founded in Roman times at the confluence of the Dora Riparia and the Po. For a long time the Dora was the city's main source of energy. Already in medieval times its water was gathered into canals, called duriae, that drove mills, water wheels and other machinery. Between its confluence with the Stura and the Po lay the Royal Park, the Parco Regio, until the destruction caused by the Battle of Turin in 1706. The Parco della Colletta lies there today, and Ponte Mosca is one of the bridges across the river in the city.

Industrial and urban development in the 20th century badly degraded the river, and renovation work began only in the 1990s. In 1999 the regional environmental protection agency ARPA studied the whole Dora Riparia and the river Sangone and found serious pollution. In 2002 the agro-natural park of the Dora Riparia was created, financed by the comune of Collegno and the region, to preserve the natural habitat and to bring agricultural and river areas together.
dorchester-dorset: Dorchester stands on gently sloping ground beside the south bank of the River Frome, about 7 miles (11 km) north of Weymouth, south of the Dorset Downs and north of the South Dorset Ridgeway. Growth to the north and north-east is limited by the river's floodplain and watermeadows. The chalk hills of the ridgeway carry over five hundred ancient monuments, including barrows, stone circles and hillforts, and many finds from the area are displayed in the Dorset Museum in the town.

The earliest settlements lay about 2 miles (3.2 km) south-west of the modern centre near Maiden Castle, a large Iron Age hill fort that was one of the most powerful settlements in pre-Roman Britain; different tribes lived there from about 4000 BCE. The Romans defeated the local tribes by about 70 CE and set up a garrison from which grew the town they called Durnovaria. It is recorded in the 4th-century Antonine Itinerary and became a market centre, a road junction and staging post, and one of the twin capitals of the Durotriges.

Around 790 the first recorded Viking raid of the period came ashore on the Isle of Portland. Beaduheard, the king's reeve in Dorchester, rode out with a few men, took the newcomers for merchants and was killed with his companions. By 864 the area was held by Saxons who called themselves Dorsaetas, and the town's name passed through Dornwaraceaster to Dorchester.

Fires struck the town in 1613, 1622, 1725 and 1775; the first destroyed 300 houses and two churches, All Saints and Holy Trinity. After the Monmouth Rebellion the town was the site of the Bloody Assizes, presided over by Judge Jeffreys. In 1833 the Tolpuddle Martyrs founded the Friendly Society of Agricultural Labourers; because members swore an oath, they were arrested and tried in the Shire Hall, with cells beneath the courtroom.

Dorchester is the county town of Dorset, with a weekly market, a hospital, schools and a college serving the surrounding area. It has 293 listed structures, among them the Church of St George, with a late 11th-century south door, the Church of St Peter, mostly of 1420 to 1421, Shire Hall, Max Gate and the Roman town house. Thomas Hardy lived at Max Gate and made Dorchester the model for Casterbridge in The Mayor of Casterbridge.
dorchester-on-thames: The village lies about 9 miles (14 km) south-east of Oxford and 3 miles (5 km) north-west of Wallingford, on a low gravel peninsula enclosed by the River Thame to the east and the River Thames to the south and west. Across the Thames rise the chalk Wittenham Clumps, also called the Sinodun Hills. Bede recorded the place in the 8th century as Dorcic, and the Old English form was Dorcanceaster. The first part of the name probably comes from a Common Brittonic word for water, and the suffix marks a Roman-era fortified town.

People lived here from at least the Neolithic period. Beside the village lie the Dyke Hills, the remains of a rare Iron Age valley fort with massive double banks and ditches. After the Roman conquest a walled small town of about 13.5 acres grew up on the site, linked by a Roman road to the military camp at Alchester. Its Roman name is not known: Dorocina is a guess of 18th-century antiquaries.

Pope Honorius I sent Bishop Birinus to convert the West Saxons, and the Diocese of Dorchester served for a time as the religious and political centre of Wessex until the see moved to Winchester in 660. Saint Æthelwold was consecrated Bishop of Winchester at Dorchester in 963, and Remigius de Fécamp was the last Bishop of Dorchester and the first of Lincoln. In the 12th century the church was refounded as an abbey of Augustinian canons; after the Dissolution of the Monasteries a local benefactor bought the building for the parish. J. M. W. Turner painted the meeting of the rivers in Union of the Thames and Isis, exhibited in 1808.

Dorchester Abbey is the parish church and holds a museum in the former 14th-century guest house. The title Bishop of Dorchester was revived in 1939 for a suffragan bishop of the Diocese of Oxford. Gravel digging after the Second World War destroyed much of the parish's Neolithic and Bronze Age archaeology and left a chain of flooded pits, and a bypass of 1981 took through traffic off the High Street.
dorde-stratimirovic: Stratimirović was born in Novi Sad on 7 February 1822, the son of Vasilije Stratimirović, a well-to-do landowner of noble birth from Kulpin. He was taught at home, among others by the writer Milovan Vidaković, attended a Lutheran school in Novi Vrbas from 1832 to 1836, spent a year in the cadet corps at Titel and studied at the Military Engineering Academy in Vienna from 1837 to 1841. After service in Italy he left the army in 1843, settled on the family estate at Kulpin and married the noblewoman Maja Zakin Bajšanski.

Between 1843 and 1848 he became a leading voice among the Serbs of southern Hungary, who sought recognition as a nation with their own language rights and diet. At the Hungarian Parliament in Požun he confronted Lajos Kossuth, who would discuss Serb autonomy only once peace was restored, and later offered no more than a limited form of it; the Serbs then sided with Austria. At the May Assembly in Sremski Karlovci in 1848 he was elected president of the Main Board of the Serbian people. He set up military camps, organised the Serbian People's Army and directed its operations until the arrival of Voivode Stevan Šupljikac.

As leader of the progressive and anti-Austrian circles he clashed with Patriarch Josif Rajačić, who used military setbacks to remove him as supreme commander. After the Hungarian revolution collapsed in 1849 he rejoined the Austrian army, rose from cavalry lieutenant colonel to major general, and until his retirement in 1859 carried out confidential diplomatic missions for Austria in Montenegro, Corfu, Epirus, Serbia and Italy. He sat twice in the Hungarian Parliament and several times in the Serbian People's and Church Parliaments in Karlovac.

From 1873 he lived in Novi Sad. In the Serbian-Turkish war of 1876 he offered his services to the Serbian government, but, suspected of working for Austrian interests, he had to leave Serbia. After 1877 he withdrew from public life to Vienna, where he died on 15 December 1908. Much of his political activity, including his links with the Hungarian emigration and Czech politicians and his work with the court in Vienna, remains unclear. His autobiography was published in Serbian and German by his son Đorđe in 1913.
dordogne: Dordogne is a large rural department in the Nouvelle-Aquitaine region, roughly half-way between the Loire Valley and the Pyrenees. It is named after the river Dordogne and corresponds roughly to the ancient county of Périgord. It is the third largest department of metropolitan France and the largest landlocked one. Four Périgords are distinguished: Périgord Vert, around Nontron; Périgord Blanc, around the prefecture Périgueux; Périgord Pourpre, around Bergerac, a wine region; and Périgord Noir, around Sarlat, which overlooks the valleys of the Vézère and the Dordogne.

The county of Périgord dates back to the time when ancient Celtic Gaulish tribes lived in the area. The name is explained by the Gaulish word Petrocore, meaning four tribes. The Petrocores took part in the resistance against the Roman occupation of Gaul. Gallo-Roman remains include the ruined tower and arena at Périgueux, formerly Vesone, and villa remains at Montcaret. After the province of Guienne passed to the English Crown following the remarriage of Eleanor of Aquitaine in 1152, Périgord came under English suzerainty, and it oscillated between France and England for more than three hundred years until the end of the Hundred Years' War in 1453.

In the late 15th and early 16th centuries the nobility erected most of more than 1,200 châteaux, manors and country houses. In the second half of the 16th century the violence of the Wars of Religion reached a peak partly focused on Périgord, and Bergerac was one of the most powerful Huguenot strongholds. Dordogne is one of the original 83 departments created on 4 March 1790 during the French Revolution, formed from the former province of Périgord.

The prefecture is Périgueux. The population peaked at 505,789 in 1851 and declined to 373,000 by 1975, before rising again to about 417,000 by 2023. The department has more than 1,500 castles, among them Beynac, Biron and Hautefort, along with bastides and abbeys. Writers associated with the region include Michel de Montaigne and Étienne de La Boétie. The caves of Lascaux are closed to the public, and a replica, Lascaux II, is open to visitors.
dordrecht: The municipality covers the whole of Dordrecht Island, bordered by the rivers Oude Maas, Beneden Merwede, Nieuwe Merwede, Hollands Diep and Dordtsche Kil. The city formed along the Thure river in the midst of peat marshes, in the Rhine-Meuse-Scheldt delta. The name appears as Thuredriht around 1120 and seems to mean a thoroughfare: a canal or river through which ships were pulled by rope from one river to another. An older explanation from the Latin trajectum, a ford, was rejected in 1996. English once called it Dort or Dordt, and its inhabitants call it Dordt.

A remark of about 1120 records that Count Dirk IV of Holland had been murdered in 1049 near Thuredrech, which refers to the place. In 1572, four years into the Dutch Revolt, representatives of all the cities of Holland except Amsterdam, together with the Watergeuzen under William II de la Marck, met in Dordrecht in a secret First Assembly of the Free States. The meeting was a rebellious act, since only King Philip II or his stadtholder, then the Duke of Alba, could call the States of Holland.

From 13 November 1618 to 9 May 1619 the Synod of Dordrecht met to settle the dispute between the central tenets of Calvinism and the school of thought of Jacobus Arminius, whose followers, the Remonstrants, had set out their dissent in the Five Articles of Remonstrance of 1610. They were opposed by the Contra-Remonstrants, or Gomarists, led by the theologian Franciscus Gomarus.

Merchants of Dordrecht helped found sugar plantations in the West Indies, which led at the end of the 17th century to a sugar refining industry; the city had 16 refineries in the 18th century, against 120 in Amsterdam and 40 in Rotterdam. Its economic importance nonetheless began to wane in that century. From 1780 to 1787 it was a home of the Patriots, who sought to remove the hereditary stadtholder, until it capitulated to Prussian troops on 18 September 1787.
The opening of the Voorne Canal in 1829 and of the Nieuwe Waterweg in 1883 ended Dordrecht's role as a first-rate sea harbour; by 1910 Rotterdam sent about 200 times as much cargo up the Rhine.

Dordrecht is the fifth-largest city of South Holland, with about 123,000 inhabitants in 2025, and the most important city of the Drechtsteden. Its medieval centre has over 950 monuments, seven historic churches and six museums. The Grote Kerk, built between 1285 and 1470, has a 65-metre tower with a carillon of 67 bells. The Nieuwkerk of 1175 is the city's oldest building, and the Augustinian monastery Het Hof, built in 1275, was the meeting place of the First Assembly of the Free States.
dore-south-yorkshire: Dore lies on a hill above the River Sheaf, the river that gave Sheffield its name. Three streams that meet there, the Limb Brook, the River Sheaf and the Meers Brook, marked the boundary between the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms of Deira, later Northumbria, and Mercia. Besides the Old English root shared with door, a gateway or pass between two kingdoms, the name has been explained from the Welsh dwr, water, which would refer to these streams; the same root is found in Dour in Fife and Kent and in Dorchester in Dorset.

The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle holds the earliest written record of Dore. It places the meeting in 827, a year more likely to have been 829: King Egbert of Wessex, having conquered the Mercian kingdom and all that lay south of the Humber, led an army against the Northumbrians as far as Dore, where they met him and offered terms of obedience and subjection, and then returned home. The submission was that of King Eanred of Northumbria. In 1968 the Dore Village Society put up a plaque on the village green to mark the event.

For centuries Dore remained a small village, with about 500 people in the 19th century. It was a township and chapelry in the parish of Dronfield in Derbyshire. Christ Church, now Grade II listed, was built in 1828, and Dore became a separate parish in 1844 and a separate civil parish in 1866. A 17th-century paper mill on Avenue Farm was turned into a scythe forge by Joshua Tyzack in 1839. In 1931 the parish had 2684 inhabitants, and on 1 April 1934 it was abolished and merged with Sheffield.

On Dore Moor stood the Sheffield Clarion Club House, an independent socialist social centre that continued operating until 1967. The Old School, built in 1821 on the site of an earlier school, was restored and opened as a community centre once the new school had opened.

Dore is now a suburb of Sheffield in South Yorkshire, in the city's unparished area and in the Sheffield Hallam constituency. Dore and Totley railway station lies on the Hope Valley Line between Sheffield and Manchester, and the railway tunnel between Dore and Totley, under a limb of the Pennines to Grindleford in Derbyshire, is the longest main line railway tunnel in England. Abbeydale Park, a former county cricket ground of both Derbyshire and Yorkshire, lies just north of it.
dorestad: Dorestad lay in the present-day province of Utrecht, near Wijk bij Duurstede, close to the fork of the Rhine, where two river trade routes crossed. One ran by the Kromme Rijn to the Frisian north and linked the Rhineland with Scandinavia and the Baltic. The other ran from the Lek to the west coast and joined the Rhineland to England. It was founded in the 7th century at the foot of the former Roman fortress of Levefanum.

The Franks and Frisians fought for control, and the Franks won at the end of the 7th century and held the Frisian coast from 719. They encouraged its growth, and it became known for coins minted under several Frankish rulers. Its growth lasted until the early 9th century, when regional trade gained on luxury trade and the Franks gave the Church of Utrecht a large part of the town. It is thought to have peaked in the 820s and 830s.

Viking attacks fell between 834 and 863, and the town seems never to have recovered fully. The Danish chieftain Hroerekr, whom Frankish kings had set to guard the coast, took control, and the mint closed. The Danes plundered it in 846 and captured it in 850. One view holds that it recovered each time and disappeared in the 860s because the river channel carrying its trade shifted. The site stayed uninhabited until about 1270, when a keep, the nucleus of Duurstede Castle, was built about 800 m to the south.

The most important excavation took place between 1967 and 1977 and exposed about 30 hectares. The settlement covered about 3 square kilometres, large for its time, with a harbour, the Lower town, a trading centre, the Upper town, and farmland inland, joined by a single road. Only the Lower town was excavated, as the river bend had eroded much of the site. The harbour had wooden causeways for unloading, and wine barrels, glassware and lava querns show imports. The Dorestad Fibula was found in an old well in 1969.
dorgon: Dorgon was born on 17 November 1612 in the Aisin-Gioro clan, the 14th son of Nurhaci, and his mother was Nurhaci's primary consort, Lady Abahai. His full brothers were Ajige and Dodo. He began his career in campaigns against the Mongols, Koreans and the Ming under his half-brother Hong Taiji, fighting the Chahar Mongols in 1628 and 1635. When Hong Taiji died in 1643, Dorgon contested the succession with Hong Taiji's eldest son Hooge. They compromised, and Hong Taiji's ninth son Fulin, six years old, became the Shunzhi Emperor, with Dorgon and his cousin Jirgalang as co-regents.

Jirgalang yielded control of state affairs on 17 February 1644, and by early June Dorgon firmly controlled the government and army. On 24 April rebels under Li Zicheng took Beijing and the Chongzhen Emperor hanged himself. The Ming general Wu Sangui, at Shanhai Pass, asked Dorgon's help against the rebels, and the Qing army won a decisive victory over Li Zicheng there on 27 May. Dorgon entered Beijing, ordered his troops not to loot, and installed himself in the Wuying Palace. The Shunzhi Emperor arrived on 19 October 1644 and was enthroned on 8 November, when Dorgon's title was raised to Uncle and Prince Regent; in 1649 it became Emperor's Father and Prince-Regent.

Under his direction Qing armies subdued most of China. After the fall of Yangzhou on 20 May 1645, his brother Dodo ordered the slaughter of its population. On 21 July 1645 Dorgon decreed that all Han Chinese men shave the front of the head and wear the queue on pain of death. The order united Chinese of all backgrounds in resistance, and the army massacred the people of Jiangyin, killing between 74,000 and 100,000. In 1646 he reinstated the civil service examinations. Historians have called him the mastermind of the Qing conquest, and he is also blamed for policies such as land enclosure for Bannermen and the seizure of commoners as slaves.

Dorgon died on 31 December 1650 on a hunting trip at Kharahotun, after an injury, and was posthumously given the title Emperor Yi. In 1651 his enemies, led by Jirgalang, accused him of possessing yellow robes, plotting to seize the throne by calling himself Emperor's Father, and killing Hooge. The Shunzhi Emperor stripped him of his titles and had his remains exhumed and flogged in public. The Qianlong Emperor rehabilitated him in 1778, granting the name zhong, loyal, so that his title became Prince Ruizhong of the First Rank.
doria-family: The name comes from de Auria, from de filiis Auriae, the sons of Auria, later de Oria or d'Oria. According to legend a noble Genoese lady, Auria or Oria della Volta, loved a pilgrim bound for the First Crusade, Arduino di Narbonne, and their children took their mother's name. Some have speculated that the family descended from the Arduinici family of the Piemonte, some of whom were Counts of Auriate. It appears suddenly as a major local power in Liguria in the late 11th century, and documents of 1110 name two members, Martino and Genuardo, as filii Auriae.

The family held fiefs in Sardinia from the 12th to the 15th century and at Dolceacqua, Oneglia and Portofino. Simon Doria was an admiral of the Genoese at the crusaders' assault on Acre in the late 12th century. Oberto Doria, Captain of the People, led Genoa's fleet against Pisa at Meloria, and his brother Lamba defeated the Venetian Andrea Dandolo at Curzola. Tedisio Doria financed the voyage of Vadino and Ugolino Vivaldi in 1291, and Branca Doria appears in Dante's Divine Comedy for murdering his father-in-law, Michele Zanche. Brancaleone Doria ruled the Giudicato of Arborea and nearly conquered all Sardinia in the late 14th century.

Ottone Doria commanded the Genoese crossbowmen hired by the French at the Battle of Crécy in August 1346 and was killed there. Andrea Doria, Prince of Melfi, became perpetual censor of Genoa in 1528 and admiral to Emperor Charles V; his titles passed to Giovanni Andrea Doria, son of his adopted son Giannettino, who was killed in the Fieschi conspiracy of 1547. Members of the family served as doge from Giovanni Battista Doria in 1537 to Giuseppe Maria Doria in 1795.

Dorias helped finance the Portuguese and Spanish voyages: Francesco Doria, a banker at Seville, financed the expeditions of Christopher Columbus, and his granddaughter Clemenza Doria was among the earliest settlers of Portuguese Brazil. Branches bore the titles of Prince of Melfi and Prince of Centola and many lesser ones, and some male children were named after foreign rulers such as Abaqa Khan, Ghazan Khan and Hethum I of Cilician Armenia.
dorians: The Dorians were one of the four major groups into which the Greeks of the Classical period divided themselves, with the Aeolians, Achaeans and Ionians. The earliest literary mention is in the Odyssey, which already places Dorians on Crete. Accounts of their origin vary. One theory, widely believed in antiquity, held that they came from the mountains of northern Greece, such as Macedonia and Epirus. Herodotus presents the events later called the Dorian invasion as transfers of population from Thessaly, and Pausanias has Dorians from Oeta led by Hyllus, a son of Heracles, who built ships at Naupactus to cross the Gulf of Corinth.

Modern scholarship treats the Dorian invasion as a concept meant to explain the replacement of East Greek (Ionian) speech in the Peloponnese by West Greek (Doric) speech in official circles. Its objectives have not been met, though investigation has ruled out speculative hypotheses. Most scholars doubt that it was the main cause of the collapse of Mycenaean civilisation, and the source of the West Greek speakers remains unattested by solid evidence.

Most Dorians settled in the Peloponnese, but they also held Crete, Rhodes, Sicily and parts of southern Italy. In Asia Minor the Dorian Hexapolis comprised Halicarnassus and Cnidus, Kos, and Lindos, Kameiros and Ialyssos on Rhodes. Colonies from Corinth, Megara and the Dorian islands lay along the southern coast of Sicily from Syracuse to Selinus, and Taras was a Spartan colony. In the fifth century BCE Dorians and Ionians were the two most politically important Greek peoples, and Thucydides saw the Peloponnesian War in part as Ionians fighting Dorians. Scholars dispute how far fifth-century Greeks identified themselves in this way, and Thucydides shows that alignment was not always ethnic.

Dorian communities varied from the trade centre of Corinth to the military state of Sparta, yet all Greeks knew which places were Dorian. Dorians were distinguished by the Doric dialect, which kept the long a that became eta in Attic-Ionic, and by a calendar built on festivals, notably the Hyacinthia and the Carneia. Doric colonies kept it. Dorian women are said to have had more freedom and economic power than other Greek women, with Spartan women the freest. The Doric order of architecture, the Dorian mode in music, said by classical writers to be martial, and a prominent cult of Helios are associated with Dorian societies. Tsakonian, a descendant of Doric, is still spoken on the southern Argolid coast.
dorieus: Dorieus belonged to the Agiad dynasty, and his story is known mainly from Herodotus. According to Herodotus, his father Anaxandridas II had married his own niece, and when the marriage stayed childless for a long time the Council of the Ephors, fearing that the line of Eurysthenes would die out, asked him to divorce her. He refused, and the ephors proposed a second wife, though bigamy had been unknown in Sparta. Soon both wives were pregnant: the second bore Cleomenes, and a few months later the first bore Dorieus, followed the next year by Leonidas and Cleombrotus, who may have been twins.

On Anaxandridas's death the council named Cleomenes king as the eldest son. Dorieus challenged the choice and was overruled, although Herodotus calls him the finest young man of his generation and says Cleomenes was close to madness. Dorieus then asked the council for a body of men to found a settlement elsewhere.

Herodotus says he left for Libya in a fit of temper, making the grave mistake of not consulting the Delphic Oracle. After he and his followers had been driven from Cinyps in Tripolitania, he returned to Sparta and heard of land in western Sicily said to belong by right to the Heracleidae, from whom his family claimed descent. This time he consulted the Oracle, was told the land was his for the taking, and sailed again with his followers.

On the way, war broke out between the cities of Croton and Sybaris in southern Italy, and at Croton's request Dorieus took part in its attack on Sybaris. He then founded a colony named Herakleia near Eryx in Sicily, but soon afterwards he and most of his followers were defeated and killed by the Egestaeans with Carthaginian support; the historians Bury and Meiggs date his death to c. 510 BCE. The survivors moved to the southern coast and took Herakleia Minoa.

Herodotus remarks that had Dorieus stayed in Sparta under Cleomenes, who had no sons, he would in time have become king; instead the throne passed to Leonidas, whose deeds in the Persian Wars made him a hero. Dorieus features prominently in the novel The Etruscan by Mika Waltari.
doris-greece: Doris was bounded by Aetolia, southern Thessaly, Ozolian Locris and Phocis. Its heart was the valley of the river Pindus, now called the Apostoliá, a tributary that joins the Cephissus not far from the latter's sources. The valley opens towards Phocis but lies higher than the Phocian towns of Drymaea, Tithronium and Amphicaea. Herodotus placed Doris between Malis and Phocis and gave its breadth as only 30 stadia. A mountain pass led across Parnassus from Doris to Amphissa, and the Dorian town of Cytinium stood at its head.

The four towns of the Doric Tetrapolis were Erineus, Boium, Cytinium and Pindus, also called Akyphas; Erineus, the most important, seems also to have been called Dorium. Tradition held that the land was first called Dryopis after the Dryopes, whom Heracles and the Malians drove out, and that it took its later name from the Dorians who left it to conquer the Peloponnese. Herodotus traced the Dorians through several earlier homelands, but scholars such as Smith doubted that so small a district could have conquered most of the Peloponnese.

During the invasion of Xerxes, Doris submitted to the Persians, and its towns were spared. It was one of the oldest members of the Delphic Amphictyony, and the Lacedaemonians more than once came to its aid when the Phocians and other neighbours attacked it. In the 3rd century BCE the Tetrapolis joined the Aetolian League. Its towns suffered so much in the Phocian, Aetolian and Macedonian wars that Strabo wondered any trace of them was left in Roman times, and in the 6th century CE only Voion is still named, in the Synecdemus of Hierocles.
The modern municipality of Dorida takes its name from the ancient region. Before the local government reform of 2006 it was a province of the same name covering the same area.
dormition-cathedral-moscow: Excavations in 1968 indicated that the site was a medieval burial ground, which supports the view that a wooden church stood there in the 12th century. In the 14th century Metropolitan Peter persuaded Ivan I, known as Ivan Kalita, to build a cathedral to the Theotokos in Moscow like the Cathedral of the Dormition in Vladimir. Work began on 4 August 1326 and the limestone church was consecrated on 4 August 1327.

By the late 15th century it was dilapidated, and in 1472 the Moscow architects Kryvtsov and Myshkin began a new building. In May 1474, as it neared completion, it collapsed in an earthquake. Ivan III then invited Aristotele Fioravanti, an architect and engineer from Bologna, to design a cathedral from scratch.

Fioravanti travelled to Vladimir to study Russian methods of building, and the cathedral there was again taken as a model. The foundation was laid in 1475 and Metropolitan Geronty consecrated the church in 1479. It has six pillars, five apses and five domes, which symbolise Jesus Christ and the Four Evangelists, and is built of white-stone blocks on a raised limestone foundation. Fioravanti did not use the cantilever vaults usual in Russian architecture but introduced groin vaults and transverse arches, and for the upper parts he used larger specially made bricks that reduced weight.

Four of the six interior columns are slender Corinthian columns, which give the interior its light and spacious effect. The design proved popular and became a template for many other Russian churches.

The interior is dominated by frescoes. The iconostasis dates from 1547, with its two highest tiers added in 1626 and 1653 or 1654. Tsars added to it important icons taken from conquered cities, among them an icon of Saint George from the 12th century brought from Veliky Novgorod in 1561. The Theotokos of Vladimir was kept here from 1395 to 1919 and is now in the Tretyakov Gallery.

The cathedral is regarded as the mother church of Muscovite Russia. Ivan the Terrible was crowned here in 1547 as the first Russian Tsar, and monarchs were crowned here until 1896. Metropolitans and patriarchs were installed here, and most are buried in it. Fires in 1518, 1547, 1682 and 1737, looting by Polish-Lithuanian forces in 1612 and French occupation, when it was used as a stable, damaged it. After the 1917 revolution the Bolshevik government closed the Kremlin churches and made the cathedral a museum, and the last Easter service was held in 1918. It was returned to the Russian Orthodox Church in 1991 and is part of the Moscow Kremlin Museums.
dornbirn: Dornbirn stands 437 metres above sea level in the Alpine Rhine Valley, at the foot of the Karren mountain, which belongs to the Bregenz Forest chain at the edge of the Eastern Alps. It lies near the borders of Switzerland, Germany and Liechtenstein, and the river Dornbirner Ach runs through it on its way to Lake Constance. It is the largest city in Vorarlberg, the westernmost Austrian state, and the tenth largest in Austria. It is the administrative centre of a district that also includes Hohenems and Lustenau. Its territory once consisted of four quarters, Markt, Hatlerdorf, Oberdorf and Haselstauden, and by the 20th century two more were formed in the west, Rohrbach and Schoren.

The earliest evidence of human presence in the area dates from the Mesolithic. The name derives from torrin puirron, the settlement of Torro, an Alemannic farmer, and has nothing to do with pears, though the fruit appears on the town emblem. The name is first mentioned in 895 in a document from St Gallen.

Dornbirn became part of the Habsburg Monarchy in 1380. In 1793 it was raised to a market community, and it received municipal status only in 1901. The mountain village of Ebnit was annexed in 1932, and in 1969 Dornbirn became the seat of the new district administration. On 10 August 1881 Emperor Franz Joseph I inaugurated the first telephone service in the Habsburg empire there. The town long ranked as a major centre of the textile industry, which declined seriously from the 1980s. The Mohrenbrauerei, Vorarlberg's oldest operating brewery, was founded in 1834.

The City Museum Dornbirn covers local history, early photography, crafts, agriculture and the textile industry, and Inatura is an interactive natural history museum. Dornbirn is an important commercial and shopping centre and a junction of regional bus lines and of the railway between western and eastern Austria. The Vorarlberg University of Applied Sciences, founded in 1989 as a school of technology, was recognised as a university in 1999.
dornoch-firth: The Dornoch Firth, in Scottish Gaelic Caolas Dhòrnaich, forms part of the boundary between Ross and Cromarty and Sutherland. Compared with the other firths of the east coast it is narrow and winding, yet it holds a wide variety of landscapes. Rounded granite hills covered in heather moor and scree enclose it, their Gaelic names of cnoc, meall and creag pointing to their character, and their lower slopes are often wooded, with oakwoods prominent among plantations that range from those around Skibo Castle to the pines of the Struie Forest.

On 16 August 1809 the firth was the scene of the Meikle Ferry disaster, when an overloaded ferryboat sank with the loss of 99 lives. For long afterwards road traffic between the south and the far north had to go round by Bonar Bridge at the head of the inlet.

In 1991 the Dornoch Firth Bridge opened, giving a shorter route on the A9 road between Inverness and Thurso. Planners had proposed that the bridge should also carry the Far North railway line, which could have saved up to 45 minutes on journeys between Inverness and Thurso or Wick, but that part of the scheme did not win government funding and only a road bridge was built.

The firth is one of 40 national scenic areas in Scotland, covering 15,782 hectares, of which 4,240 hectares are sea below low tide. With Loch Fleet it is a Special Protection Area for birds, among them breeding ospreys and wintering bar-tailed godwits, greylag geese, wigeon, curlews, dunlins, oystercatchers and teal. With Morrich More it is also a Special Area of Conservation, protecting salt meadows, coastal dune heathland and grassland, and it is an important site for otters and harbour seals.
dorothea-of-montau: Dorothea was born on 6 February 1347 at Groß Montau (now Mątowy Wielkie in Poland), west of Marienburg, the daughter of Willem Swarte, a wealthy farmer from Holland. At 17 she was married to Adalbrecht, a swordsmith of Danzig in his forties and an ill-tempered man. Her visions began almost as soon as she was married. Her husband had little patience with them and abused her, but through her humility and gentleness she converted him, and together they went on pilgrimage to Cologne, Aachen and Einsiedeln Abbey in present-day Switzerland.

Of their nine children, four died in infancy and four in the plague of 1383; the surviving daughter, Gertrude, became a Benedictine nun. Adalbrecht died in 1389 or 1390 while Dorothea, with his permission, was on pilgrimage to Rome.

In the summer of 1391 Dorothea moved to Marienwerder (now Kwidzyn). On 2 May 1393, with the permission of the cathedral chapter and of the Teutonic Order, she took up an anchoress's cell built against the cathedral wall, where she spent the rest of her life. She lived austerely, and many visitors came to her for advice and consolation. A devotee of the Passion of Jesus and of the Eucharist, she is said to have borne the stigmata.

Her confessor, the deacon Johannes of Marienwerder, a learned theologian, wrote down what she communicated to him. He composed a Latin life of her in seven books, the Septililium, as well as a German life in four books. The scholar Michelle Sauer has noted that her life bore a close resemblance to that of Saint Jutta of Kulmsee, a Prussian anchoress of the late 13th century.

Dorothea died at Marienwerder on 25 June 1394, the day later kept as her feast. From the moment of her death she was venerated as the guardian of the land of the Teutonic Knights and patron saint of Prussia and Pomerania, and in 1405 some 257 witnesses testified to her virtues and miracles. The formal process for her canonisation was then broken off and not resumed until 1955. Her relics were lost, probably during the Protestant Reformation. Günter Grass made her life, seen through the eyes of her embittered husband, one of the subjects of his 1977 novel The Flounder.
dorset: Dorset is a ceremonial county of South West England with an area of 2,653 square kilometres. It is bordered by Somerset, Wiltshire, Hampshire and Devon, and by the English Channel to the south. Its landscape combines chalk downs, steep limestone ridges and low-lying clay valleys, and the north of the county contains part of Cranborne Chase. The highest point is Lewesdon Hill, 279 metres, in the south-west. The coastline, with Lulworth Cove, the Isle of Portland, Chesil Beach and Durdle Door, is largely part of the Jurassic Coast World Heritage Site because of its geological and palaeontological importance.

The first visitors were Mesolithic hunters from around 8000 BCE. Neolithic settlers arrived around 3000 BCE and made the Dorset Cursus, a monument 10.5 kilometres long. From 2800 BCE Bronze Age farmers cleared woodland and raised round barrows on the chalk hills. In the Iron Age the Durotriges built a series of hill forts, most notably Maiden Castle, one of the largest in Europe. The Romans arrived in 43 CE; the Legio II Augusta under Vespasian captured Maiden Castle, and the Roman settlement of Durnovaria, now Dorchester, was founded nearby. Bokerley Dyke, built by the post-Roman inhabitants, delayed the Saxon advance for almost 150 years.

The name comes from Dorchester: the Saxons called the town Dornwaraceaster, and Dornsæte meant the people of the area. The county developed in the 7th century. The first recorded Viking raid on the British Isles took place in Dorset in 789, and the Black Death entered England at Melcombe Regis in 1348. Dorset's monasteries, among them Shaftesbury, Cerne and Milton, were sold off in the dissolution of 1536-1541 with little resistance.

In the English Civil War the Royalists held the whole county except Poole and Lyme Regis in 1642, but the Parliamentarians had almost reversed this within three years. In 1645 about 2,000 Clubmen, vigilantes weary of the war's depredations, offered battle to Fairfax's army at Hambledon Hill and were routed. Corfe Castle, the last Royalist stronghold, fell in 1646. The Duke of Monmouth's rebellion began when he landed at Lyme Regis in 1685; at the Bloody Assizes in Dorchester Judge Jeffreys heard 312 cases, with 74 accused executed, 175 sentenced to transportation and nine whipped.

In 2021 the ceremonial county had about 779,775 residents. It is largely rural, with many small villages and no cities; the main urban area is a south-eastern conurbation of Bournemouth, Poole and Christchurch, which historically belonged to Hampshire in the case of Bournemouth and Christchurch. Dorchester is the county town. Agriculture was once the principal industry but has declined in favour of tourism. The county has more than 1,500 scheduled monuments and no cathedral.
dorsland-trek: The trekkers came from a divided, poor and isolated Boer community in the Transvaal. Religious grievances weighed most: opposition to the progressive policy of President Thomas Burgers, above all his new education laws, disputes within the Gereformeerde Kerk (Reformed Church) and the search for a New Jerusalem, so that most trekkers belonged to that church. With them went an estimated 130 to 200 labourers known as the mak volk, descendants of the indigenous people of South Africa, most taken as children on the battlefield and raised by the trekkers, who are often left out of accounts of the trek.

A first party of 10 families left in May 1875 and reached Lake Ngami in September; Herero and Nama-Oorlam captains, turned against them by the Cape envoy William Coates Palgrave, refused them land. A second, much larger party camped along the Limpopo, where malaria began to kill, and on 7 May 1877 left Letloche as one disorderly column. At watering places such as Tlhabala and Lethlakane cattle stampeded and died, and people rationed water by the spoon or drank the blood of animals; none died of thirst, but malaria went on killing. A third party left in April 1877, the month Britain annexed the Transvaal.

Along the Okavango, malaria and tsetse fly killed many people and most of the oxen; of one group of 65 under Gert du Preez, all the men died. The parties reunited at Leeupan in July 1878 and from May 1879 stayed for 18 months in Kaokoland. After agreements with Sebastião Nunes da Matta, governor of Moçâmedes, signed on 18 September and 28 December 1880, the Portuguese chose Humpata for their settlement on 4 January 1881.

About 700 people left the Transvaal between 1874 and 1877; roughly 230 died and about as many turned back, and although some 130 babies were born on the way, only 370 reached Angola. Portugal hoped the Boers would help it hold the interior against indigenous peoples and the British. By 1 July 1883 Humpata held 325 Boers and 43 mak volk. From August 1928 to February 1929 the South African government of J. B. M. Hertzog repatriated 1,922 Boers, most to South-West Africa. An obelisk of 1958 at Humpata, where the leader Gert Alberts is buried, and a memorial of 2003 at Cassinga commemorate the trek.
dorylaeum: Dorylaion, Dorylaeum in Latin, was a Phrygian, Greek, Roman and Byzantine settlement. Its earliest town stood at a place now called Karaca Hisar, and about the end of the fourth century BCE it was moved to a new site. Excavations on the mound of Şar Höyük, in the village of Şarhöyük, have run since 1989 and reach back to the 3rd millennium BCE. Around 2500 BCE the town lay at the centre of the Demircihüyük Culture of north-western Anatolia; a Luwian hieroglyphic seal of the Hittite Imperial Period was found there in 2018, and the town was important under the Phrygians in the Iron Age.

In the Roman period Dorylaion was a trading post, and it probably lay on the route of the Apostle Paul's second missionary journey in 50 CE. In the third century, threatened by Gothic raids while the Roman forces in Asia Minor were spread thin, its people built their wall in haste from dedicatory statues. A funerary inscription of the same century, with Hebrew names and a menorah, shows a Jewish presence. As a bishopric of Phrygia Salutaris under the Metropolitan of Synnada it had seven known bishops between the fourth and ninth centuries, among them Eusebius, an opponent of Nestorius and Eutyches.

In the 11th century its lands yielded rich grain harvests, the rivers were full of fish, and the city had stoas, fountains and fine houses. The Seljuk Turks took it after the Battle of Manzikert in 1071, and by 1147 nomads grazed large flocks around it. In 1175 Manuel I Komnenos drove the Turks out and refortified Dorylaion and Soublaion, an event told in a poem possibly by John Tzetzes. Having agreed to destroy it after the Battle of Myriokephalon on 17 September 1176, Manuel kept it, and Kilij Arslan II sent an army that ravaged the Meander valley.

The see is still named among the suffragans of Synnada in the twelfth century but must have been suppressed soon after. The Muslim author al-Harawi, who died in 1215, described Dorylaion as a place of medicinal hot springs on the frontier, at the end of Christian territory.
dos-pilas: Dos Pilas, Guatemalan Spanish for two wells, lies between the Pasión and Salinas rivers in the municipality of Sayaxché, about 8 kilometres from the border with Mexico and 120 kilometres south-west of Tikal. The land is one of forested ridges, wetlands and lakes with heavy rainfall. The city was built in an area with little earlier settlement, 4 km from Arroyo de Piedra, the seat with Tamarindito of the kingdom that had dominated the region since the Early Classic. At its height the Dos Pilas kingdom covered some 3,885 square kilometres. It used the same emblem glyph as Tikal, Mutul.

Bʼalaj Chan Kʼawiil, installed as a child by his father Kʼinich Muwaan Jol II of Tikal, was captured by Yuknoom Chʼeen II of Calakmul and reinstated as his vassal. After the victory over Tikal he made marriage alliances, and his daughter Lady Six Sky was sent to refound the dynasty of Naranjo. His son Itzamnaaj Kʼawiil, king from 698, oversaw a new victory over Tikal in 705, when its lord was captured by his general Uchaʼan Kʼin Bʼalam; tribute in labour and wealth then paid for the El Duende group, a hill terraced into the city's largest pyramid.

Uchaʼan Kʼin Bʼalam, enthroned in 727 probably as regent for the young heir Kʼawiil Chan Kʼinich, captured Yichʼaak Bʼalam, king of the much larger city of Seibal, in 735 and kept him as a vassal. Kʼawiil Chan Kʼinich fought Ahkul and El Chorro in 743 and, two years later, the distant cities of Yaxchilán and Motul de San José. A hieroglyphic stairway at Tamarindito records his forced flight in 761, and the royal family probably moved to Aguateca. Itzan, Cancuén and Machaquila grew stronger as Dos Pilas fell.

The ruins cover about one square kilometre around three complexes on an east-west axis, and are poorly preserved because their stone was stripped for the last defensive walls. Among them are the Main Group with its hieroglyphic stairways, the Bat Palace, where a smashed royal throne was found, and a tomb under Structure L5-1 thought to be Itzamnaaj Kʼawiil's. Twenty-two caves lie around the site. The ruins were first reported in 1953–4 by José and Lisandro Flores, were excavated by Arthur Demarest and Juan Antonio Valdés from 1989 to 1994, and were declared a National Monument on 12 June 1970.
dositej-obradovic: Dositej Obradović was born Dimitrije Obradović, probably in 1739, in the Banat village of Čakovo in the Habsburg monarchy, now Ciacova in Romania. He grew up bilingual in Serbian and Romanian and learned classical Greek, Latin, modern Greek, German, English, French, Russian and Italian. On 17 February 1757 he became a monk in the Serbian Orthodox monastery of Hopovo in Syrmia and took the name Dositej. He translated many European classics into Serbian, including Aesop's Fables, and on 2 November 1760 left the monastery for Hilandar on Mount Athos.

From 1761 he studied Latin in Zagreb and then taught in Serbian schools in Dalmatia, among them Kninsko Polje, Golubić near Knin and Plavno. He was ordained a priest by Vasilije Petrović. He studied Greek on Corfu and in 1782 enrolled at the University of Halle to study philosophy. In 1783 he moved to Leipzig, where he published his first work and studied under Johann Eberhard, a disciple of Christian Wolf. In 1785 he presented his Leipzig books to the British Museum Library in London, the first modern Serbian books it acquired.

More than a third of his life was spent in Austria, where he was influenced by Joseph II and the German Enlightenment. He was also an Anglophile who saw England as the land of spiritual freedom, and his forty years of travel took him across Europe and Asia Minor. During the First Serbian Uprising of 1804 he was in Italy, where he published the poem Vostani Serbije in honour of Karađorđe Petrović and the insurgents. In 1807 he moved to Belgrade at Karađorđe's invitation and became Serbia's first minister of education.

In Belgrade he founded the Velika škola, the first higher education institution in Serbia, which later developed into a university. He helped introduce the literature of western European countries to the Serbs and, with Vuk Karadžić, whom he influenced, is recognised as a father of modern Serbian literature. Because the Serbian population often suffered famine, he also introduced potato cultivation. He died in Belgrade in 1811 and was buried in the Cathedral of Saint Archangel Michael after a large funeral procession.
dost-mohammad-khan: Dost Mohammad Khan was a Pashtun of the Mohammadzai branch of the Barakzai tribe, born in Kandahar in the Durrani Empire. His father, Payandah Khan, chief of the Barakzai, was killed in 1800 by King Zaman Shah Durrani, and his mother belonged to the Qizilbash. He was the eleventh son and spoke Pashto, Persian, Punjabi and Turkish.

His elder brother Fateh Khan helped install Mahmud Shah Durrani in 1800 and restore him in 1809, but Mahmud Shah had him assassinated in 1818. The Barakzai brothers then stripped Mahmud Shah of everything but Herat and divided his lands, and Dost Mohammad received Ghazni, to which he added Kabul, the richest of the Afghan provinces.

Early in his rule the Afghans lost the Peshawar valley to the Sikh army of Ranjit Singh at the Battle of Nowshera in 1823. Ranjit Singh used the dethroned Sadozai prince Shah Shujah Durrani against him, and in 1834 Dost Mohammad defeated Shah Shujah under the walls of Kandahar. In 1837 his son Akbar Khan defeated the Sikhs at the Battle of Jamrud, where the Sikh general Hari Singh Nalwa was killed.

He welcomed the British envoy Alexander Burnes to Kabul in 1837, but Lord Auckland would not accept his advances, and when he renewed relations with Russia the British set troops in motion in 1838. Shah Shuja was restored in Kabul on 7 August 1839 and Dost Mohammad was exiled to Mussoorie in November 1840.

He was restored after Shah Shuja was murdered in April 1842, and, convinced that war with the British would damage Afghanistan, he sought an alliance with them. He subdued the Hazarajat and Bamian in 1843 and put down a Kohistani rebellion in 1846. His son Mohammad Akram Khan invaded Balkh in 1849, and the province was annexed.

On 30 March 1855 Dost Mohammad signed an offensive and defensive alliance with the British, and in 1857 he joined them against Persia. He took no part in the Indian Rebellion of 1857. In 1862 the ruler of Herat captured Farah, which gave him a pretext to attack. Herat fell on 27 May 1863 after a long siege, and he died on 9 June, after forty years in the politics of South and Central Asia.

His son Sher Ali Khan succeeded him, and he was buried at the Gazurgah in Herat. He ruled for 36 years. He had united Kabul, Kandahar and Herat in one state, as few of his predecessors had done, and state revenue rose from about 500,000 rupees at the start of his rule to 7 million by his death.
dost-mohammad-khan-of-bhopal: Dost Mohammad Khan was the son of Nur Mohammad Khan, an Afghan nobleman of the Mirazikhel clan of the Orakzai tribe of Tirah. After killing a cousin who had been betrothed to his fiancée Mehraj Bibi, he was cast out by his family and went to relatives at Jalalabad near Delhi, where he killed a son of his kinsman Jalal Khan in a quarrel. He fled to Delhi, sheltered for about a year with his old teacher Mullah Jamali, and in 1703 enlisted with Mir Fazlullah, Aurangzeb's keeper of arms.

After Aurangzeb's death Dost Mohammad led a band of about 50 Pathan mercenaries in Malwa. He became guardian of the small Rajput principality of Mangalgarh, married the raja's daughter Kunwar Sardar Bai, who took the name Fatah Bibi, and in 1709 leased the Berasia estate. In 1715 he had the Rajput chief Narsingh Deora and his men killed at a parley near Jagdishpur, which he renamed Islamnagar and made his headquarters. When the dowager of Mangalgarh died heirless he took her lands.

Hired by Rani Kamlapati, widow of the Gond ruler Nizam Shah, to avenge her husband, he defeated and killed Alam Shah and received the village of Bhopal in part payment. After the Rani's death in 1723 his soldiers, hidden in litters meant for his family, entered Ginnor fort and killed her son Nawal Shah. He began the Fatehgarh fort at Bhopal on 30 August 1723 and walled the town. His friendship with the Sayyid brothers made an enemy of Nizam-ul-Mulk, who besieged Bhopal and forced him to cede territory, pay tribute and send his son Yar Mohammad Khan to Hyderabad as a hostage.

In his last years he turned to Sufi mystics and drew scholars, physicians, artists and Pashtun settlers to Bhopal. He died of an illness in March 1728 and was buried in the Fatehgarh fort beside Fatah Bibi. The court chose his young son Sultan Mohammad as successor, but the Nizam sent Yar Mohammad back with a thousand horsemen, and he ruled as regent.
dosunmu: Dosunmu was born around 1823. His accession broke with tradition, because he owed it to the British consul Benjamin Campbell, who had gained influence in Lagos after the Reduction of Lagos in December 1851.
