The motte-and-bailey castle now known as Millmount Fort was probably built by the Norman Lord of Meath, Hugh de Lacy, before 1186. The earliest known town charter was granted to Drogheda-in-Meath by Walter de Lacy in 1194. In 1412 the two towns were united and became a county corporate.

In the medieval period Drogheda was an important walled town in the English Pale and often hosted the Irish Parliament, including the one that passed Poynings' Law, the legislation that subordinated the Irish Parliament's lawmaking to the king and his English Council. On Valentine's Day 1468 the Earl of Desmond and his two young sons were executed there on the orders of the Earl of Worcester, the Lord Deputy.

The town was besieged twice during the Irish Confederate Wars. In September 1649, in the second siege, Oliver Cromwell's army breached the walls from the south and took the town, and the Royalist defenders were massacred. Cromwell wrote that the officers were 'knocked on the head', every tenth soldier was killed and the rest were shipped to Barbados. The Battle of the Boyne was fought in 1690 about 6 km to the west, at Oldbridge.

Drogheda is a port town in County Louth, with its southern fringes in County Meath. Newgrange, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, lies 8 km to the west. Landmarks include Millmount Fort, now a museum, the barbican of St Laurence's Gate from the 1300s, the Tholsel of 1770, and St Peter's Church, which houses the preserved head of Saint Oliver Plunkett, executed in London in 1681. The Boyne Viaduct and Mellifont Abbey lie nearby.
drogo-of-hauteville: Drogo was a son of Tancred of Hauteville by his first wife Muriella. Goffredo Malaterra makes him the second son, after William Iron Arm, while Romuald Guarna puts him third, after Serlo and Geoffrey. As Tancred's lands could not support all his sons, Drogo went to southern Italy around 1035 with William and their brother Humphrey to join Rainulf Drengot, Count of Aversa, and fought for Guaimar IV of Salerno against Pandulf IV, Prince of Capua.

In Guaimar's service the Normans and the Lombard forces under Arduin joined the Byzantine general George Maniakes in his attempt to take Sicily from the Saracens, and Drogo fought at the Battle of Messina and the reconquest of Syracuse. After a quarrel over spoils they left, and in 1040 joined a Lombard rebellion against the Byzantines in Apulia. When William was made Count of all the Normans in Apulia in September 1042, with his capital at Melfi, Drogo received Venosa, and in 1045 he occupied Bovino.

Drogo won the succession after a contest with Peter I of Trani, and Guaimar gave him his daughter Gaitelgrima in marriage. He paid homage to Emperor Henry III on 3 February 1047 and was invested as Count of all the Normans in Apulia and Calabria, while Henry stripped Guaimar of the title Duke of Apulia. Drogo received his half-brother Robert Guiscard coldly, sent him to Calabria without a fief and at first opposed his marriage to Alberada of Buonalbergo. He also held Richard Drengot, a claimant to Aversa, prisoner for a time.

After meeting Pope Leo IX, Drogo was killed with several followers on Saint Lawrence's Day, 10 August 1051, as he entered the chapel of his castle to hear mass. Goffredo Malaterra records that the killer was a Lombard man of his entourage. He was buried at the Abbey of Santissima Trinità of Venosa and succeeded by his brother Humphrey. With his first wife, Altrude, he had three children, Richard, Rocca and Eremburga.
drogon-chogyal-phagpa: Phagpa was born in Ngari in West Tibet on 26 March 1235, a son of Sönam Gyeltsen of the Khön clan, which held hereditary power over the Sakya Monastery in Tsang. He was a nephew of Sakya Pandita, who in 1244 set out to the camp of Godan Khan, son of Ögedei Khan, taking the ten-year-old Phagpa and his brother Chakna Dorje with him. On the way Phagpa took novice vows at the Jokhang in Lhasa. At Godan's camp in Liangzhou the brothers learned Middle Mongol and took up Mongol dress.

In 1253 Kublai, brother of Möngke Khan, asked Godan for the 18-year-old lama, who converted him to Buddhism and became his tantric guru in 1258. Under the influence of Kublai's wife Chabi, Phagpa took precedence in religious matters and Kublai in temporal ones. Phagpa defeated Daoist opponents in a debate at Kaiping in 1258, presented Kublai as a chakravartin, a universal ruler, after he took power, and was named State Preceptor in 1260. Mongol sources credit him with first shaping the relationship of priest and patron between state and religion in the Tibeto-Mongolian Buddhist world.

In 1264 Kublai granted him authority over all Buddhist clergy in Tibet and sent him home to persuade local leaders to accept Mongol administration, while his brother Chakna Dorje was made viceroy. His script, adapted from the Tibetan alphabet, was completed in 1269 and won him the new title of Imperial Preceptor, but resistance kept it from wide use, and it fell out of use after the Yuan collapsed in 1368. He mostly lived at Lintao in Gansu and had left the post by 1274 to his half-brother Rinchen Gyaltsen.

Phagpa spent his last years in Tibet strengthening Sakya and Yuan authority and in 1277 convened a general conference of Buddhist hierarchs. He died in the Lhakhang palace at Sakya on 15 December 1280. An unproven rumour that the dismissed pönchen Kunga Zangpo had poisoned him led to a Mongol and Amdo Tibetan intervention the next year and Kunga Zangpo's execution. Later chronicles describe him as ruling the 13 myriarchies of Central Tibet, a tradition recent research has qualified.
drohiczyn: Drohiczyn stands on the bank of the Bug River in Siemiatycze County, Podlaskie Voivodeship. Traces of a Neolithic settlement, La Tène crematoria and ancient graves have been found there, and in ancient times the site lay among dense forests. It is regarded as one of the oldest towns of Podlachia.

In the early Middle Ages the area was inhabited by the Yotvingians, and the fortified settlement was most likely theirs; Rus' chronicles mention it in 1061. In 1142 Grand Duke Vsevolod II of Kiev gave Drohiczyn, as Dorohychin, and Brest to his younger brother Igor. In 1192 Casimir II the Just defeated Ruthenians, Yotvingians and Cumans near the town, and in 1237 Konrad I of Masovia handed it to the Order of Dobrzyń, and Prince Daniel annexed it to Galicia-Volhynia in 1238. After the Mongol invasion Mindaugas took Podlasie into the Grand Duchy of Lithuania in 1241, but the Rus' dukes regained Drohiczyn. In 1253 Daniel of Galicia, strengthened by a victorious war against the Yotvingians, was crowned King of Ruthenia there.

The Lithuanians captured the town again in 1274, and it remained in Lithuania until the Union of Lublin in 1569, apart from the 1380s and 1430s, when Duke Janusz of Masovia held it. It was among the major cities of the Grand Duchy and received Magdeburg rights in 1498. Under Sigismund I the Old it became capital of Podlaskie Voivodeship, established in 1513, and prospered. The Deluge of 1655-1660 brought looting by Swedes and Crimean Tatars, and on 3 May 1657 the army of George II Rákóczi captured the town, killed most residents and destroyed the parish church and castle; Drohiczyn never recovered its greatness.

In 1795 the third partition of Poland divided the town between the Habsburg Empire and Prussia along the Bug, and a fire in 1805 destroyed the town hall's archives. In 1939 the Soviet Union occupied it; residents were deported to Siberia and houses near the river were moved or destroyed, along with two churches. German forces took it in June 1941, and the Jews of the town were sent in autumn 1942 to Treblinka.

Drohiczyn, with a population of 2,110, has Baroque churches and monasteries, regional and diocesan museums and Poland's only Canoeing Museum. Since 1991 it has been the seat of the Roman Catholic Diocese of Drohiczyn.
droitwich-spa: Droitwich Spa lies on the River Salwarpe in northern Worcestershire, about 35 kilometres south-west of Birmingham and 11 kilometres north-east of Worcester. The town stands on massive deposits of salt, and salt has been extracted there since ancient times. Its natural brine holds about 0.25 kilograms of salt per litre, ten times stronger than sea water and rivalled only by the Dead Sea. The name Salwarpe probably comes from sal, 'salt', and weorp, 'to throw up': the river that throws up salt.

In Roman times the settlement, called Salinae, stood at the crossing of several Roman roads, and railway construction in 1847 revealed Roman mosaic pavements. Later it was called Wyche, from the Anglo-Saxon Hwicce, and appears as Saltwich in Anglo-Saxon charters. King John gave the town a charter on 1 August 1215, which added the French Droit, 'right'; James VI and I renewed it on 8 November 1625. A salt tax was levied by the king until 1825, and by the 1600s the Wintour family owned up to 25 salt evaporating pans.

The brine rose naturally at three sites along the Salwarpe. It was fully saturated and so economic to boil, and it was divided into shares, each of 6,912 imperial gallons, which yielded eight long tons of salt in the set boiling period. Brine was first drawn in buckets from pits, the deepest, Upwich, at 30 feet. In 1725 boreholes reached the brine reservoirs and gave an almost unlimited supply, which ended the town monopoly. Pumping brought subsidence to parts of the town.

In the mid-19th century Droitwich became known as a spa. The benefit came not from drinking the almost saturated brine but from floating and swimming in it at the brine baths, first opened in 1830. John Corbett, called the Salt King, industrialised the salt works and redeveloped the town as a spa; he built Chateau Impney nearby for his Franco-Irish wife. The town remained small until the 1960s, when its population was still barely 7,000, and then grew with overspill from Birmingham.

The parish had 25,027 inhabitants in 2021. The Church of the Sacred Heart and St Catherine of Alexandria, styled on the basilicas of Ravenna, has interior walls covered almost entirely with eight tonnes of mosaic glass imported from Murano. St Richard, Bishop of Chichester, was born in the town in 1197, and the Pilgrim Father Edward Winslow in 1595. A BBC longwave transmitting station, built in the 1930s, stands north-east of the town.
dromahair: Dromahair, in Irish Droim Dhá Thiar, apparently meaning the ridge of two demons, takes its name from the ridge of high ground on which it stands above the River Bonet, which flows into Lough Gill. It lies in the hilly north-west of County Leitrim, 10 kilometres from Manorhamilton and 17 kilometres from Sligo. Much of the village was laid out by the Earl of Leitrim on the model of a village in Somerset, and its central streets still follow his plan.

The ridge was the site of Drumlease, an important early church site and a Patrician foundation of the fifth century. During the medieval period Dromahair was the capital of Breifne, a Gaelic confederation stretching from Kells across County Cavan and north Leitrim to County Sligo, and the seat of the O'Rourke kings, whose castle, built around 950, survives as ruins with its banqueting hall. From here Devorgilla, wife of Tiernan O'Rourke, was carried off to Ferns by Dermot McMurrough, King of Leinster, starting a feud that led to McMurrough's exile from Ireland.

Creevelea Abbey, a Franciscan friary founded in 1508 as a daughter house of Donegal Abbey, was in use until the 17th century, when the New Model Army forced the friars out. A fortified house was built for Sir William Villiers around 1629. In 1798 the army of General Humbert, pursued through Leitrim after its victories at Castlebar and Carricknagat, rested at Dromahair and threw captured British artillery into the Bonet. William Butler Yeats named the village in his poem The Man Who Dreamed of Faeryland.

The nave, choir, tower and transept of Creevelea Abbey are well preserved, and the friary is protected as a national monument. The railway station, opened on 1 September 1881 on the Sligo, Leitrim and Northern Counties Railway, closed with the line on 1 October 1957. Parke's Castle stands on the shore of Lough Gill to the north-west.
dromichaetes: The Getae had been federated in the Odrysian kingdom in the 5th century BCE. The Balkan campaigns of Philip II of Macedon between 352 and 340 BCE shattered Odrysian authority, and the Getae profited: by the second half of the 4th century they held sites on both banks of the lower Danube, and the fear caused by the new Macedonian conquests encouraged the Getic tribes to unite. Little is known of Dromichaetes himself, and the fullest account, two fragments of Diodorus Siculus, mixes history with literary motifs.

According to Diodorus his main residence was called Helis. It has traditionally been placed in the Romanian Plain, though sites in the Moldavian Plateau have also been proposed. Another candidate is a fortified settlement near the Getic tomb at Sveshtari in Bulgaria, occupied from about 335 to about 250 BCE, which traded with the Greek colonies of the Aegean and Black Sea and had metal, bone and pottery workshops.

His war with Lysimachus was probably provoked by Lysimachus's expansion, perhaps over control of the Greek colonies. Diodorus suggests two campaigns, in the first of which the Getae captured Lysimachus's son Agathocles, while Pausanias implies the two episodes are versions of one event. Polyaenus tells that Seuthes, a general of Dromichaetes, posed as a deserter and led the invaders into difficult terrain. Having persuaded his assembly that freeing the king would gain more than punishing him, Dromichaetes crowned Lysimachus with a wreath and freed him, keeping high-born hostages such as Clearchus, son of the tyrant Dionysius of Heraclea.

The man and woman buried in the richly decorated Ginina mound tomb near Sveshtari, of the early 3rd century BCE, have tentatively been identified as Dromichaetes and his consort; the unfinished decoration suggests a hasty burial. Citing Justin's report of Celts defeating the Getae before 279 BCE, the historian Peter Delev argued that he may have fallen fighting them. Greek writers retold the captivity of Lysimachus as a moral tale of pride punished and barbarian virtue, and Helis Nunatak in Antarctica is named after his residence.
druid: The word druid comes through French and Latin from the Gaulish druides, and most scholars derive it from a Proto-Celtic compound read as oak-knower or as a priest with strong insight. Classical authors placed druids only in Gaul and Britain. The earliest notices, of the 4th and 3rd centuries BCE, treat them as barbarian philosophers akin to the Persian magi. Because the druids committed nothing of their teaching to writing and cannot be securely identified in the archaeological record, nearly everything known about them comes from outside observers, much of it descended from the lost ethnography of Posidonius.

Diodorus and Strabo, drawing on Posidonius, describe druids arbitrating public and private disputes and even halting armies drawn up for battle. According to Caesar they had a single head who held office for life, and their pupils might remain in instruction for up to twenty years, memorising a great body of verse. The doctrine most often remarked on was the immortality of the soul.

Caesar and the Posidonian authors agree that no sacrifice took place without a druid. Diodorus and Strabo describe divination from a human victim, and Caesar reports victims burned inside a huge wickerwork image. Scholars weigh these reports differently: some note that the barbarity had propaganda value for Rome, while Bruce Lincoln holds that they go back to Greek sources older than any such motive. Excavations in pre-Roman Gaul show animal and human sacrifice, though the priests who officiated are nowhere named.

Augustus forbade the druidic religion to Roman citizens, a decree of the Senate under Tiberius was directed against druids, diviners and physicians, and Suetonius says Claudius abolished their religion. In Ireland, which Rome never reached, medieval literature preserves many druids, but these accounts are generally read as literary constructs of Christian authors.

From the 16th century druids became a screen for reinterpretation. John Aubrey attributed Stonehenge and Avebury to them, though the monuments are millennia older than the Iron Age Celts. In 1792 Edward Williams, known as Iolo Morganwg, invented the Gorsedd Beirdd Ynys Prydain, whose ritual survives in the National Eisteddfod. The Order of Bards, Ovates and Druids was founded in 1964, but modern Druidry has no genuine continuity with the ancient priesthood.
druk-desi: The title, in Wylie transliteration 'brug sde-srid and also known as Deb Raja, joins Druk, the thunder dragon that stands for Bhutan, whose oldest name is Druk-yul, with Desi, meaning regent. Ngawang Namgyal, the Zhabdrung Rinpoche, had fled sectarian persecution in Tibet and made the Drukpa Lineage the state religion. Under his dual system the Je Khenpo led the religious branch and the Druk Desi the civil administration, both under the nominal authority of the Zhabdrung, held to be a reincarnation of Ngawang Namgyal.

The Druk Desi could be a monk or a layman, and by the nineteenth century was usually a layman. He was elected for a three-year term, at first by a monastic council and later by the State Council, the Lhengye Tshokdu, which brought together regional rulers, the Zhabdrung's chamberlains and the Druk Desi himself. In time the office fell under the control of the council's strongest faction of regional administrators.

Government sat at the dzong of Thimphu in spring, summer and autumn and at Punakha, a dzong founded in 1527, in winter. The kingdom was divided into eastern, central and western regions, each under a penlop who acted as tax collector, judge, military commander and procurer for the centre, drawing revenue from land taxes and the trade between Tibet and India. Districts were run by dzongpens from lesser dzongs.

The death of Ngawang Namgyal in 1651 is believed to have been hidden for some 50 years while a reincarnation was sought. In that time the Druk Desi gained power, and civil wars followed; once a successor was found, the Desi would not give up what he had won, and the Zhabdrung was often a child in his control. The Desi in turn lost his hold over the penlops, and the country broke into semi-independent regions. The Constitution of Bhutan of 2008 keeps the dual system but never names the Druk Desi, vesting administrative power in the Druk Gyalpo and civilian offices.
drukpa-kagyu: The Drukpa lineage is a branch of the Kagyu school, one of the Sarma or New Translation schools of Tibetan Buddhism, and one of the lineages known as Red Hat sects. Its founder, Tsangpa Gyare (1161–1211), a disciple of Ling Repa, mastered the practices of mahamudra and the Six Yogas of Naropa when young. Followers hold that as a tertön, a finder of hidden teachings, he discovered the text of the Six Equal Tastes. He was recognised as the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara in human form and as an incarnation of Songtsän Gampo, the first Buddhist king of Tibet, of Naropa and of Gampopa. His title, Gyalwang Drukpa, has passed to the heads of the lineage ever since.

Tsangpa Gyare's nephew Onre Darma Sengye (1177–1237) took the throne at Ralung, the lineage's main seat, and his family's descendants, the hereditary prince-abbots of the Middle Drukpa, held it for centuries. Two disciples founded further sub-schools: Gyalwa Lorepa the Lower Drukpa, and Gotsangpa Gonpo Dorje the Upper Drukpa. In 1222 Phajo Drugom Zhigpo brought the teachings to western Bhutan. The Middle Drukpa produced scholars and siddhas such as Tsangnyön Heruka, author of the Life of Milarepa, and Drukpa Kunley, both disciples of the 4th Gyalwang Drukpa, Kunkhyen Pema Karpo.

After Pema Karpo died in 1592, two candidates were recognised as his reincarnation. Pagsam Wangpo won the backing of the ruler of Tsang, a patron of the Karma Kagyu, and in 1616 his rival Ngawang Namgyal fled to Bhutan. The lineage then divided into the Northern Drukpa in Tibet, headed by the Gyalwang Drukpa, and the Southern Drukpa in Bhutan, headed by the Zhabdrung incarnations.

In Bhutan the Drukpa lineage is the dominant school and the state religion. Since Ngawang Namgyal appointed Pekar Jungne as the first Je Khenpo, successive holders of that elected office have acted as spiritual heads of Bhutan's monasteries. Its leading monasteries include Ralung in central Tibet, Hemis in Ladakh, Kardang in Lahaul, and Punakha Dzong and Tashichho Dzong in Bhutan. Its masters today meet across the old geographical divisions: the first Annual Drukpa Council was held in Kathmandu in April 2009.
drumanagh: The headland is surrounded on three sides by the Irish Sea and forms a peninsula of about 320 by 420 metres, some 12 hectares. Across its neck run three parallel earth banks, about 350 metres long and fairly straight, with ditches in front of them; with the cliffs on the other sides they give a strong defensive position. The earthworks may be Bronze Age, like the somewhat similar ones at Knock Dhu in County Antrim, or Iron Age, and they resemble other Irish forts in the area. An early 19th-century Martello tower stands near the tip of the headland.

Ploughing turned up sherds of Roman Samian ware in the 1950s, but for decades the site was not excavated, while illegal metal detectorists dug up many objects. One collector tried to sell a trove of Roman coins and ornaments at Sotheby's in London in the 1980s; it was impounded and deposited in the National Museum of Ireland, and a legal dispute over ownership has since kept the finds and their provenance from public discussion. Over 40 ingots of copper and brass, and copper mines nearby at Loughshinny, suggest an Iron Age metalworking centre.

Interpretations differ widely. Barry Raftery and Gabriel Cooney have suggested that Gnaeus Julius Agricola, Roman governor of Britain, may have used the fort for an invasion of Ireland in 82 CE; Tacitus records that Agricola entertained an exiled Irish prince and thought the island could be conquered with a single legion. Professor Michael Herity of UCD saw the material as evidence of a rich Irish emporium trading with the Roman world. Richard Warner linked the site with the legend of Túathal Techtmar, an exile said to have returned from Britain with an army. Roman-style brooches from burials on nearby Lambay Island belong to the same debate.

Drumanagh is a Recorded Monument under the National Monuments (Amendment) Act of 1994 and has had a Preservation Order since 1977. Fingal County Council acquired the site in 2017 and in 2018 published a draft plan to protect it from motorbike scrambling and link it to coastal paths. In May 2025 archaeologists from Maynooth University and the Irish Archaeology Field School uncovered there the first intact Roman pot found in Ireland, about 2,000 years old.
drunken-sailor: The first published description of the shanty comes from an account of a whaling voyage of 1839 out of New London, Connecticut, to the Pacific, which gave it as a song performed with very good effect when a long line of men hauled together, with the words Ho! Ho! and up she rises, early in the morning. There are hints that it is older. In Minstrelsy of Maine (1927) the editors Eckstorm and Smyth recorded that a grandmother who sang it claimed to have heard it used for tacking on the Penobscot River, by their reckoning well over a hundred years earlier.

References remain rare. A five-verse text and tune appeared in the third edition of Davis and Tozer's Sailor Songs or 'Chanties', but the song is missing from the other major shanty collections of the 19th century.

The shanty accompanied tasks done at a brisk walking pace, and it probably belonged to the time when crews, especially on warships, were large enough to haul a rope while simply marching along the deck. John Masefield, publishing it in 1906, called it a runaway chorus, seldom used; others called it a stamp and go or walk away shanty, sung in quick time for tacking. Captain W. B. Whall, an English sailor of the 1860s and 1870s, said it was one of only two shanties sung in the Royal Navy, where singing at work was frowned upon, and that it fell out of use as crews shrank on merchant packet and clipper ships.

Later sailors remembered other uses. Richard Maitland, an American sailor of the 1870s, told the collector Alan Lomax in 1939 that it was sung while scrubbing the barnacles from an iron ship's bottom, and Frederick Pease Harlow wrote that it served for hauling halyards hand over hand.

By the 1900s the song had passed ashore. It was sung in glee singing at Eton College, at gatherings of the Savage Club of London by the 1910s, and as a dance tune in the American Midwest, where a catalogue of folk-songs listed it in 1915. Percy Grainger recorded Charles Rosher of London singing it in 1906 and used it in his Scotch Strathspey And Reel (1924); Malcolm Arnold drew on its melody in his Three Shanties for Woodwind Quintet (1943). The shanty revival from the 1920s made it one of the best-known songs of the repertoire. The Irish Rovers have closed their shows with it for over 50 years.
drusus-the-younger: Drusus Julius Caesar was born at Rome around 14 BCE as Nero Claudius Drusus, son of Tiberius and his first wife Vipsania Agrippina. In 4 CE, when Augustus adopted Tiberius on condition that Tiberius adopt Germanicus, he took the name Julius Caesar. Augustus intended Germanicus and Drusus to rule together, as he had once intended for the sons of Marcus Agrippa. Their careers ran in parallel, with the same offices at the same ages, and Cassius Dio likened them to the twins Castor and Pollux. Later in 4 CE Drusus married his cousin Livilla.

Drusus was quaestor in 10 CE. After Augustus died in August 14 CE the legions in Illyricum and on the Rhine mutinied over unpaid bonuses. Drusus was sent with two Praetorian cohorts and the Praetorian prefect Sejanus, and reached the three Pannonian legions at Emona on 26 September. The soldiers demanded discharge after sixteen years instead of twenty. Talks broke down and they stoned his party, but a lunar eclipse convinced them that the mutiny was doomed. Drusus restored order, and according to Tacitus had the leaders executed.

He was consul in 15 CE, and Tiberius then sent him to Illyricum, where he governed from 17 to 20 CE with proconsular imperium. The Germanic tribes had begun fighting among themselves, and Maroboduus, king of the Marcomanni, retreated to Bohemia after an indecisive clash with Arminius. Tiberius refused his request for aid. In the summer of 18 CE Drusus stormed the royal stronghold of the Marcomanni and drove Maroboduus to seek asylum in Rome. The Senate decreed him an ovation, which he received on 28 May 20 CE. After Germanicus died in 19 CE, Drusus was Tiberius's sole heir. He held a second consulship with his father in 21 CE and received tribunician power in the spring of 22 CE.

Drusus died on 14 September 23 CE, at about 35. Tacitus and Suetonius claim that he was murdered amid a feud with Sejanus, who had seduced Livilla and, with her help and that of her doctor Eudemus, poisoned him. The historian Barbara Levick finds the story unlikely, and Ronald Syme thinks Drusus may simply have died of illness.

He received a full funeral and was buried in the Mausoleum of Augustus. Tiberius adopted Germanicus's sons Nero and Drusus and recommended them to the Senate, but neither lived to succeed him. In 37 CE Gaius Caligula became princeps, and Drusus's son Tiberius Gemellus, made joint heir with him, was killed soon after.
druze: The Druze call themselves al-Muwaḥḥidūn, meaning the monotheists. Their faith developed from the Ismaili branch of Shiʿa Islam, but they do not identify as Muslims. The creation of the faith in 1017-1018 is dominated by three men. Hamza ibn Ali ibn Ahmad, an Ismaili mystic from Khorasan, arrived in Fatimid Egypt in 1014 or 1016 and began to preach a unitarian doctrine. The Fatimid caliph al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah became central to it, and in 1018 the preacher ad-Darazī proclaimed him the incarnation of God. The Druze regard ad-Darazī as a heretic, and their name probably comes from his, perhaps applied by opponents.

The most widely accepted theory of the community's descent holds that the Druze come from twelve Arab tribes that migrated to Syria before and during the early Islamic period. After the Ottoman conquest of Syria in 1516 the Ma'an family were acknowledged as feudal lords of southern Lebanon, and Druze villages prospered. The Shihab family succeeded them as leaders in 1697. Feuds between the Qaysite and Yemenite factions, which grouped Druze and Christians alike, ended in the battle of Ain Dara in 1711, after which many Yemenite Druze migrated to the Hauran. Relations between Druze and Maronite Christians broke down from 1840 and led to the civil war of 1860.

In May 1909 the Druze of the Hauran rose against Ottoman authority, led by the al-Atrash family, in a dispute over taxes and conscription. General Sami Pasha al-Farouqi suppressed the revolt; about 2,000 Druze were killed and their leaders executed in 1910.

The Druze number between 800,000 and a million, mostly in Lebanon, Syria and Israel. Arabic is their primary language, and their central text is the Epistles of Wisdom. Core tenets are the unity of God, reincarnation and the eternity of the soul. Most religious practice is kept secret, and the community does not accept converts.

There is no clergy. A few initiates, the ʿuqqāl, hold the faith's secrets, while other members are called juhhāl. Prayer houses are called khalwa, and the Druze avoid iconography, using five colours as a religious symbol. They follow seven moral precepts, the first being truthfulness in speech.
du-gamla-du-fria: Dybeck published the traditional text of the ballad in Folk-lore I and the melody in 1845 in his Runa, where he also published his new text, Sång till Norden. His original lyrics consist of two verses, written in the spirit of Scandinavianism then popular. They refer to the Nordic region but not to Sweden itself, and patriotic sentiment is notably absent from them. Dybeck first wrote the opening as Du gamla, du friska, meaning you ancient, you healthy, and changed it to Du gamla, du fria in the late 1850s. In 1900 a priest who had known him told the opera singer Carl Fredrik Lundqvist of the change, and printings of the friska version then ceased.

The song is the de facto national anthem of Sweden. Like the anthems of Finland and the United Kingdom, it is not defined in the Basic Laws nor recognised by other legislation, unlike the flag and the coat of arms. It is used all the same at official events such as state visits and the Opening of the Riksdag, at sporting events and at the Nobel Prize Award Ceremony. Sweden also has a royal anthem, Kungssången.

After it began to act as a national anthem, various people wrote extra verses to make it more Swedish, among them Lundqvist, Frans Österblom and Louise Ahlén. None is accepted as part of the anthem or normally sung.

The song was regarded as the national anthem from the late 19th century and became predominant in 1893, when King Oscar II stood in acknowledgement of it at a dinner at Lund University. Many still regarded it as unsuitable as an anthem, and a contest of 1899 produced Sverige by Verner von Heidenstam but no new anthem. In 1938 Sveriges Radio began to play it at the close of its daily programming, and by the end of the 1930s its status was effectively established.
A motion to give it legal recognition in 1986 did not pass. In 2000 a Riksdag committee concluded that, since it had already become the national anthem in fact, formal recognition was unnecessary.
du-wenxiu: Du Wenxiu was born in Yongchang, now Baoshan in Yunnan, under the name Yang Xiu, and was raised as a Muslim. Like the sons of other elite Hui families he studied the Chinese classics for the civil service examinations and passed the first at the age of sixteen, gaining the xiucai degree. He won respect among the Hui of Yunnan when he and two others travelled to Beijing to petition the court for redress for the Baoshan Massacre of 1845. When that failed he travelled the trading networks of western Yunnan for his family.

After the rebels took Dali, Du was proclaimed their generalissimo on 23 October 1856. He called on the Han to join the Hui against the Manchu dynasty, wore robes of the Ming style and cited the Nanzhao Kingdom as proof that a Yunnan state could endure. He repaired Dali's main mosque, built five new ones, founded madrasas, promoted Arabic among the Hui elite and printed the first copy of the Quran in China. Han Chinese held a third of the military posts and most civil ones, and Islam, Confucianism and local animism were all honoured.

The fellow Hui leader Ma Rulong defected to the Qing and fought him, while the scholar Ma Dexin tried to mediate between the factions and in 1864 urged Du to surrender, which he refused. Travellers and traders praised the security of the territory under the white banner; the government guarded the passes into Yunnan, lodged traders free and kept duties light, and Du set up a trading company in Burma.

On 25 December 1872 Qing troops encircled Dali. On the advice of his general Yang Rong, Du gave himself up the next morning in the hope of saving the people, asking General Yang Yuke to spare them. The Qing forces nevertheless massacred about ten thousand of the Hui population. Du's head was preserved in honey and sent to Beijing with 24 baskets of the ears of the dead, and his body was buried at Xiadui. The revolt ended in 1873. His life is a major element of Tariq Ali's novel Night of the Golden Butterfly.
du-yuesheng: Du was born on 22 August 1888 in Gaoqiao, and his family moved to Shanghai the next year. By the age of nine he had lost his immediate family: his mother died in childbirth, his sister was sold into slavery, his father died and his stepmother vanished. He returned to Shanghai in 1902, worked at a fruit stall in the French Concession until he was dismissed for theft, and became a bodyguard in a brothel, and joined the Green Gang at 16. A friend introduced him to Huang Jinrong, the highest-ranking Chinese detective in the French Concession Police, for whom he became an enforcer in gambling and opium.

His rise came after Huang's arrest in 1924 for beating the son of Lu Yongxiang, the tuchun then ruling Shanghai: Du's diplomacy and money freed his mentor, and Du, Huang and Zhang Xiaolin became sworn brothers, known as the Three Tycoons of Shanghai. In April 1927 the three formed with Chiang Kai-shek the Chinese Progress Association. On the night of 11 April Du's lieutenant Wan Molin killed the labour leader Wang Shouhua at Du's house, and gang members wearing armbands marked Labor attacked workers and left-wing activists. Chiang rewarded him with the rank of major general and advisory posts.

From 1928 he moved into finance, founding the Zhonghui Bank and becoming a director of the Bank of China and the Bank of Communications. In 1931 he opened a temple to his ancestors; within months its private wings housed a heroin factory. When war with Japan broke out in 1937 he refused to cooperate with the Japanese, unlike Zhang Xiaolin, and went to Hong Kong, while Green Gang men working with Chiang's intelligence chief Dai Li smuggled weapons and goods to the Nationalist forces.

After the war he returned to Shanghai and founded the newspaper Shang Pao. He hoped to become mayor but gave way under pressure from Chiang, and in 1948 his son Du Weiping was sentenced to six months in an anti-corruption campaign led by Chiang Ching-kuo. In April 1949 he moved to Hong Kong, declining approaches from both the Kuomintang and the Communists. His health failed through asthma, and he died on 16 August 1951. He was buried in Xizhi in Taiwan, where the authorities raised a statue of him, though some doubt that the tomb holds his body.
duala-people: Early Duala history is known only from oral tradition. The Duala trace their descent to Mbedi, who lived at Bakota in what is now Gabon or the Republic of the Congo. His sons Ewale and Dibongo migrated north to Pitti on the Dibamba River and parted there after a quarrel: Ewale's followers settled on the east bank of the Wouri estuary and became the Duala, while Dibongo's became the Limba. According to Duala tradition, the Bakoko and Bassa held the estuary when they arrived and were driven inland, probably in the late 17th or early 18th century. The Duala belong to the Sawa, the coastal peoples of Cameroon.

The Duala bought goods and slaves from inland peoples such as the Bakweri, Mungo, Bassa and Bakoko and sold them to Europeans for alcohol, guns, gunpowder, textiles and tools. In the 19th century Ndumb'a Lobe of the Bell lineage styled himself King Bell, and rivals arose, among them King Akwa in 1814 and King Deido. Akwa and Bell signed anti-slavery treaties with the British in 1840 and 1841, and Alfred Saker opened a mission at Douala in 1845. In July 1884 the German explorer Gustav Nachtigal secured treaties ceding land from Kings Akwa, Bell and Deido.

A literate class of clerks, farmers and traders resisted unpopular German measures with petitions and lawsuits. When the administration tried from 1910 to seize land in Douala and remove its people, King Rudolf Duala Manga Bell rallied opposition, and he was executed for high treason in 1914. Under the French mandate after 1918, almost half of the 15–20,000 Duala were traders, planters, chiefs or clerks by the 1930s, but Bamileke migrants made them a minority in Douala, and many supported the Union des Populations du Cameroun when it formed.

The Duala live mainly in the Moungo, Nkam and Wouri divisions of the Littoral, and Douala is their traditional capital. Many in the city live from rents on land they own, while rural Duala fish and farm. Inheritance passes through the male line. Most have been Christian since the 1930s, chiefly Baptist, though belief in ancestors who dwell in the sea and in water spirits called Miengu persists. The Ngondo, an assembly of chiefs, and age groups called miemba hold the community together, and pirogue racing is their traditional sport.
duan-pidi: Duan Pidi belonged to the Xianbei Duan clan of Liaoxi. His father, Duan Wuwuchen, headed the clan from 303 to 311, and his elder brother Duan Jilujuan succeeded him around 310. The Duan had allied with the Youzhou warlord Wang Jun against the Han-Zhao state, and Pidi took part in Jilujuan's attack on Xiangguo in 312. After Shi Le captured and executed Wang Jun in 314, Pidi accepted the city of Ji, submitted to Sima Rui, the Jin leader in the south, and was made Inspector of Youzhou.

In 316 Pidi invited Liu Kun, the Inspector of Bingzhou, who had lost his province to Shi Le, to join him. The two swore an oath of alliance by smearing their lips with blood, married their relatives to each other and petitioned Sima Rui to claim the imperial title. When Jilujuan died in early 318, Pidi's cousin Duan Mobo turned the new chieftain Duan Shefuchen against him, then killed Shefuchen and routed Pidi.

A letter from Mobo seeking to win Liu Kun over was intercepted, and Pidi, urged on by his younger brother Duan Shujun, had Liu Kun arrested and strangled on 22 June, with the consent of the general Wang Dun. Sima Rui did not punish him, but the broken oath cost Pidi the trust of many Han Chinese and Hu followers. Attacked by Mobo and weakened by famine, he lost Youzhou and in 319 fled to Shao Xu at Leling, leaving his wife and children behind.

From 320 Pidi and his brother Duan Wenyang defended Yanci against the Later Zhao general Shi Hu. Wenyang was captured after a cavalry charge, and when Pidi planned to flee south, Shao Xu's brother Shao Ji detained him and surrendered. Shi Le and Shi Hu respected Pidi and made him Champion General, but he kept wearing Jin court dress and holding the staff of authority Sima Rui had given him. Fearing a revolt, Shi Le had him put to death with Wenyang and Shao Xu. The Book of Zhou names him as the ancestor of the Kudi family.
duan-qirui: Duan Qirui was born in Hefei on 6 March 1865. His grandfather was an officer in Li Hongzhang's Huai Army, and his father died early, so his maternal grandmother raised him.

He entered the Tianjin Military Academy in 1885, specialised in artillery and graduated at the top of his class, after which Li Hongzhang sent him to study military science in Germany for two years. Yuan Shikai sponsored him as an artillery commander in the New Army, and he distinguished himself against the Boxers in Shandong. In 1906 he became director of the Baoding Staff College, where he began recruiting his own clique of junior officers. After the Wuchang Uprising of 1911 he retook Hankou and Hanyang for the Qing, then supported Yuan, who named him minister of war in 1912 and premier in 1913.

Duan opposed Yuan's attempt to make himself emperor in late 1915. After Yuan died on 6 June 1916, Duan, Li Yuanhong and Xu Shichang were the three names in the box Yuan had left, and Duan pressured Li into the presidency while he served as premier and dominated the government. He refused to recognise the 1912 constitution. President Li dismissed him in May 1917 when he pressed for war with Germany, but after the failed monarchist restoration of Zhang Xun in July he returned, and China declared war on 14 August 1917.
He secretly negotiated the Nishihara Loans with Japan, the first on 29 September 1917, offering troops in Shandong and railway rights. He built up the Anhui clique with the funds.

The exposure of the loans and the transfer of Shandong to Japan at Versailles contributed to the May Fourth Movement on 4 May 1919. In the Zhili-Anhui War, from 14 to 18 July 1920, his army was defeated by forces led by Wu Peifu, and he fled to a Japanese settlement in Tianjin. After the Second Zhili-Fengtian War, Zhang Zuolin named him Chief Executive on 24 November 1924. On 18 March 1926 his military police dispersed a protest against foreign infringement, and 47 protesters were killed and over 200 injured, including Li Dazhao. The next month Feng Yuxiang deposed him.

Duan exiled himself to Tianjin and later moved to Shanghai, where he died on 2 November 1936. He was known as tough and authoritarian, with little love for public office, delegated authority to his subordinates and favoured a cabinet system. After his retirement he became a devoted Buddhist, and he was well known as a player and patron of weiqi.
duan-ye: Duan Ye was a Han Chinese from Jingzhao Commandery, roughly modern Xi'an, and was probably a low-level official sent by the Former Qin to Liang Province after it conquered the Former Liang in 376; his wife and children remained in Jingzhao. He first appears in 388 under Lü Guang of the Later Liang, when at a feast he told Lü Guang that he applied the laws too harshly, pointing out that the legalists Wu Qi and Shang Yang had both died through their own laws. Lü Guang apologised, and in 396 made him one of his ministers.

In 397, as governor of Jiankang Commandery, Duan Ye was besieged by the Lushuihu rebels of the Juqu family, who had risen after Lü Guang executed their uncles. After 20 days with no help from the capital Guzang, he accepted their offer of leadership, took the title Duke of Jiankang and changed the era name, founding the Northern Liang. He left most affairs of state to Juqu Nancheng.

His state withstood an attack by Lü Guang's son Lü Zuan, took Xi, Jiuquan and Dunhuang commanderies in 398, and moved its capital to Zhangye; in 399 Duan Ye took the title Prince of Liang. With help from Southern Liang it beat off further attacks in 399 and 400. In 400, however, Li Gao seceded with six commanderies and founded the Western Liáng.

Wary of Juqu Mengxun's military skill, Duan Ye demoted him in 401. Juqu Mengxun then reported falsely that Juqu Nancheng was about to rebel, and Duan Ye had Nancheng put to death despite his warning that the charge was a sign of Mengxun's own plans. Mengxun used the killing to raise the people, who held Nancheng in high regard. The general Tian Ang, released from prison to lead Duan Ye's army, surrendered to him, Zhangye fell and Duan Ye was executed despite his pleas. He was described as a kind but weak ruler, unable to keep his subjects in check, who trusted too much in witchcraft and magic.
duarte-barbosa: His father, Diogo Barbosa, was a servant of Álvaro of Braganza and sailed to India in 1501 with the 3rd Portuguese India Armada under João da Nova. While his father was away, Duarte stayed in Kochi with his uncle Gonçalo Gil Barbosa, a factor who had travelled with the fleet of Pedro Álvares Cabral in 1500. In 1502 Gonçalo was moved to Cannanore, and Duarte went with him and learned Malayalam, the local language.

In 1503 Barbosa interpreted for Afonso de Albuquerque in his dealings with the Rajah of Cannanore. In 1513 he signed a letter to King Manuel I of Portugal as Clerk of Cannanore, and in 1514 Albuquerque used him as interpreter in an attempt to convert the King of Kochi. In 1515 he was sent to Kozhikode to oversee the building of two ships for an expedition to the Red Sea. He then returned to Portugal and finished his book, which for a long time was known only through the Italian writer Giovanni Battista Ramusio; the original manuscript was found and published in Lisbon in the early 19th century.

Diogo Barbosa had followed Álvaro of Braganza into exile in Seville and become governor of its castle. There Ferdinand Magellan, who moved to Seville in 1516, befriended him and married his daughter Beatriz, so that Duarte became Magellan's brother-in-law.

Barbosa sailed from Seville on 10 August 1519 with his friend João Serrão. His habit of leaving the expedition to stay with local people annoyed Magellan, who once had him arrested, but on 2 April 1520 Barbosa helped put down a revolt at Puerto San Julián and became captain of the Victoria. According to Antonio Pigafetta, after Magellan's death at the Battle of Mactan he and Serrão were made joint commanders. One of them threatened to enslave Magellan's interpreter Enrique of Malacca, though Magellan's will had freed him, and Enrique's fear has been seen as a reason he may have conspired with Rajah Humabon. At the rajah's banquet near Cebu on 1 May 1521, Barbosa and many others were killed.
duarte-coelho: Little is known of Coelho's birth and childhood. His father was named Gonçalo Coelho, but it is unclear which of six men of that name he was, and the silence of writers of his own time about his ancestry suggests that he was not noble by birth. The story that he sailed to Brazil as a boy with his father in 1503 is unlikely to have any substance.

In 1509 he went to India in the fleet of Fernando Coutinho and served the crown in Asia for about 20 years. He played an important part in the taking of Portuguese Malacca and the capture of Bintan, served as ambassador to Siam and visited China. In 1526 a fleet of brigantines he sent to Sunda Kelapa under the Luso-Sundanese treaty was destroyed by Fatahillah, a naval commander from Cirebon. Back in Portugal by 1530, he went on a diplomatic mission to France and in 1531 led the annual armada to Elmina.

In Asia he had served under Jorge de Albuquerque, twice captain of Malacca, and he married Brites de Albuquerque, Jorge's niece. His grant of 10 March 1534 ran for 60 leagues of coast from the Rio Igaraçu south to the São Francisco River. He arrived on 9 March 1535 with his wife, her brother Jerónimo de Albuquerque and families from northern Portugal, founded the village of Igaraçu and built the Church of Santos Cosme e Damião, the first in Brazil, before moving south to found Olinda.

He died in Portugal, where he had gone to petition the king, leaving Pernambuco in the hands of Brites, helped by Jerónimo. In his twenty years as lord proprietor he fought many battles with the Indigenous peoples, made the colony the main source of sugar for most of Europe and began bringing in enslaved Africans for the plantations. His sons Duarte Coelho de Albuquerque and Jorge Albuquerque Coelho both went with Dom Sebastião to North Africa in 1578 and were captured there, and the rule of the last proprietor was interrupted by the Dutch incursion that began in 1630.
dubai-creek: Dubai Creek is a natural saltwater inlet of the Persian Gulf that extends about 14 kilometres inland and forms a natural port long used for trade and transport. It ranges from 200 to 1,200 metres in width, with an average depth of 6.5 to 7 metres. It ends naturally at the Ras Al Khor Wildlife Sanctuary. Abras, small boats, have traditionally carried people across it, and the two sides are now linked by bridges and a tunnel.

The creek divided the city into Bur Dubai and Deira. Members of the Bani Yas tribe first settled along the Bur Dubai side in the 19th century and established the Al Maktoum dynasty there. In the early 20th century it could not take large ships, which the current also impeded, and served as a minor port for dhows from as far as India or East Africa. It was nonetheless the only harbour in the city and the basis of Dubai's commercial position. The pearling industry, the main sector of the economy until cultured pearls were invented in the 1930s, was based on expeditions from the creek. Fishing also centred on it, and fishing dhows were built on its foreshore.

In 1955 a plan was made to develop the creek by dredging shallow areas, building breakwaters and turning the beach into a quay for cargo. After the first dredging, vessels of 7-foot (2.1 m) draught could cross at all times, and further dredging in the 1960s and 1970s allowed anchorage for coastal shipping of up to about 500 tons. Traffic became continuous, re-export developed, and Dubai gained an advantage over Sharjah, then the other main trading centre of the region. The Al Maktoum Bridge, the first to join Bur Dubai and Deira, was built in 1963.

The creek lost importance as a port with the growth of Jebel Ali Port, though Port Saeed and other small facilities still serve traders from the region and the subcontinent. In September 2007 an extension costing 484 million dirhams was finished, and the Dubai Water Canal, a final 2.2-kilometre stretch inaugurated on 9 November 2016, took the waterway through Business Bay and Jumeirah to the Gulf, adding about 13 kilometres. Landmarks on its banks include the Deira Twin Towers, Dubai Creek Park and the Dubai Creek Golf & Yacht Club.
dubays-ibn-sadaqa: Dubays, also known as Dubays II, was born in 1070 into the Banu Mazyad, an Arab Shi'ite tribe of central Iraq, and was named after his great-grandfather Dubays I ibn Ali, emir from 1017 to 1082. His father Sadaqa, emir from 1086, rose to prominence in the troubled reign of the Seljuk sultan Berkyaruq and was known in early Latin chronicles as the King of the Arabs. When Muhammad I Tapar became sultan in 1105 he moved against his powerful vassal, and Sadaqa was killed in 1108, leaving Dubays the emirate and the Middle Euphrates region.

Dubays preserved his independence at al-Hillah by entering the Seljuk succession wars and changing sides between rival sultans. After Muhammad Tapar died in 1118, Mahmud II's younger brother Mas'ud rebelled with Dubays' support, but in 1120 Aqsunqur al-Bursuqi, with the young officer Zengi among his troops, defeated them in Azerbaijan. Dubays married Guhar Khatun, daughter of the Artuqid Ilghazi of Aleppo, and in 1121 the two allies suffered a heavy defeat by David IV of Georgia at the Battle of Didgori, barely escaping with their lives.

He defeated al-Bursuqi in the summer of 1122, but in March 1123 Zengi beat his forces at the Battle of Mubarraqiyya, and an attack he and Mas'ud then made on Baghdad was crushed. In 1124 he allied with Baldwin II of Jerusalem, recently released from captivity in Aleppo, routed Timurtash at Marj Dabiq and joined the Christian and Muslim siege of Aleppo that began on 6 October 1124. The city's qadi, Ibn al-Khashshab, denounced him for treason and held out until a relief force under al-Bursuqi arrived on 25 January 1125.

The caliph al-Mustarshid, trying to restore Abbasid power in Baghdad, counted him among his chief enemies. When the Banu Kalb captured Dubays and handed him over to Damascus in 1130, Zengi offered a captive son of Buri, atabeg of Damascus, in exchange for his release. On 20 June 1132 the two allies were defeated by the caliph's forces at Hisn al-Baramika, north of Baghdad. In his last years Dubays was closely tied to Mas'ud, sultan from 1133: Mas'ud married his daughter Sufra Khatun, and one of Mas'ud's daughters married his son Sadaqa II. He was also known across the medieval Middle East as a patron of Arabic poetry.
dublin: Dublin lies at the mouth of the River Liffey in east-central Ireland, and its urban area covers about 345 square kilometres. The Dublin Mountains, a low sub-range of the Wicklow Mountains, border it on the south, with flat farmland to the north and west. The Liffey divides the city into the Northside and the Southside, and the city itself was founded where the River Poddle met the Liffey. The Grand Canal on the southside and the Royal Canal on the northside ring the inner city on their way from the west, both connecting with the River Shannon.

The name comes from the Middle Irish Du(i)blind, literally Blackpool, from dubh, meaning black, and linn, meaning pool. It referred to a dark tidal pool on the site of the castle gardens behind Dublin Castle, where the Poddle entered the Liffey. Old Norse Dyflin, Welsh Dulyn and Breton Dulenn all preserve the Middle Irish pronunciation.

Fish traps found during construction of the Convention Centre indicate human habitation 6,000 years ago, and others near St. James's Gate show Mesolithic activity. Ptolemy's map of about 140 CE gives what may be the earliest reference to a settlement nearby, calling it Eblana polis. A Christian ecclesiastical settlement known as Duibhlinn preceded the Viking settlement of about 841, Dyflin, which took its name from it; an excavation in Temple Bar has also found evidence of Anglo-Saxons there before 841. A Gaelic settlement, Áth Cliath, 'ford of hurdles', stood further up the river. The Irish government recognised 988 as the year of the city's first settlement, and Dublin marked its official millennium in 1988.

As the Kingdom of Dublin grew, the city became Ireland's principal settlement by the 12th century, following the Anglo-Norman invasion. It expanded rapidly from the 17th century and, after the Acts of Union in 1800, was briefly the second-largest city in the British Empire and sixth largest in Western Europe. Trinity College was established by Royal Charter in 1592 under Elizabeth I, and Guinness has been brewed at the St. James's Gate Brewery since 1759. After independence in 1922 Dublin became the capital of the Irish Free State, renamed Ireland in 1937.

Dublin is the capital and largest city of Ireland and its economic centre. The historic centre lies between the two canals, with O'Connell Street as its main thoroughfare and Grafton Street and Henry Street as the main shopping streets. The University of Dublin, the oldest university in Ireland, has Trinity College as its sole constituent college; the college was closed to Roman Catholics until 1793. Dublin City Council is led by a Lord Mayor, elected for a yearly term, who lives in the Mansion House.
dublin-castle: The castle was founded as a major defensive work by Meiler Fitzhenry on the orders of King John in 1204, some years after the Norman invasion of 1169. John commanded a castle with strong walls and good ditches for the defence of the city, the administration of justice and the protection of the king's treasure.

It stood on the highest point of central Dublin, beside the dark pool, the Dubh Linn that gave the city its name, where the River Poddle met the then much wider Liffey. Largely complete by 1230, it followed the Norman courtyard plan: a central square with no keep, tall walls and a circular tower at each corner. The Record Tower, from about 1228-1230, is the only part of the original fortification still standing.

The castle was the seat of English, and later British, government in Ireland under the Lordship of Ireland, the Kingdom of Ireland and the United Kingdom. It was the residence of the Lord Lieutenant or viceroy, housed the Chief Secretary for Ireland, served as a garrison and later for intelligence services, and at times held parliament and law courts. The Court of Castle Chamber sat there from about 1570. It was also a prison: Red Hugh O'Donnell and Art and Henry O'Neill escaped in January 1592, and Joseph Holt, a participant in the 1798 Rising, was held in the Bermingham Tower before transportation in 1799.

A fire in 1684 caused severe damage, and rebuilding turned the medieval fortress into a Georgian palace, with the State Apartments built in the 1740s. In 1907 the Irish Crown Jewels were stolen from the castle and never recovered. During the Easter Rising of 1916 twenty-five Irish Citizen Army members seized its entrance and guard room. In the Anglo-Irish War it was the centre of the British effort against separatism, and on the night of Bloody Sunday in 1920 three Irish Republican Army members were tortured and killed there.

After the Anglo-Irish Treaty of December 1921 the complex was ceremonially handed over to the Provisional Government led by Michael Collins. For about a decade it housed courts in place of the Four Courts, damaged in the Civil War. Douglas Hyde was inaugurated there as the first President of Ireland in 1938, and later presidents have been inaugurated in St Patrick's Hall. Elizabeth II was received there in 2011.

Visitors have not always praised the building: the Earl of Arran called it in the seventeenth century the worst castle in the worst situation in Christendom, and John Cornforth called it a piece of English make-do and mend. Today it holds the State Apartments, a museum, the Chester Beatty Library, the Garda Museum and the Revenue Museum, and is managed by the Office of Public Works.
dubricius: According to the accounts of his life, Dubricius was the illegitimate son of Efrddyl, daughter of King Peibio Clafrog of Ergyng. When her father found that she was pregnant he threw her into the River Wye but failed to drown her, and the boy was born at Madley in Herefordshire. The story tells that mother and son were reconciled with Peibio when the child's touch cured him of leprosy.

He is said to have been known as a scholar throughout Britain by early manhood. He founded a monastery at Hentland and then one at Moccas, and taught Welsh saints including Teilo and Samson. Dedications at Porlock and near Luccombe in Somerset may show that he travelled there. He became bishop of Ergyng, possibly with his seat at Weston under Penyard, and probably held sway over Glamorgan and Gwent, the later diocese of Llandaff, though he may have been a bishop only for the ordaining of priests rather than the head of a territorial church. He is said to have resigned his see in favour of Saint David at the Synod of Llanddewi Brefi in 545.

He retired to Bardsey Island, where he was buried. Geoffrey of Monmouth made him a character in the Historia Regum Britanniae, followed by Wace's Roman de Brut, and Alfred, Lord Tennyson later included him in the Idylls of the King. Churches at Ballingham, Whitchurch, Hentland and Hamnish in Herefordshire, at Porlock, at Gwenddwr and Llanvaches in Wales and the Catholic church at Treforest are dedicated to him.

The Roman Martyrology lists him under 14 November as a bishop and abbot who died on Bardsey Island, and the Catholic calendar for Wales keeps that traditional date. He is usually shown holding two crosiers, for the sees of Caerleon and Llandaff.
dubrovnik: Dubrovnik is a city in southern Dalmatia, Croatia, on the Adriatic Sea, a seaport and the centre of Dubrovnik-Neretva County. Its population was 41,562 in 2021. UNESCO inscribed the Old City of Dubrovnik as a World Heritage Site in 1979, recognising its medieval architecture and fortifications. The two names, Dubrovnik and Ragusa, co-existed for centuries. Ragusa, recorded since at least the 10th century, was the official name of the Republic of Ragusa until 1808, while Dubrovnik, first recorded in the Charter of Ban Kulin in 1189, was in widespread use by the late 16th or early 17th century and is usually explained from a Slavic word for oak wood.

The area was inhabited in ancient times by the Illyrian tribe of the Pleraei. According to Constantine Porphyrogenitus, writing around 950, Ragusa was founded in the 7th century by refugees from Epidaurum, a Roman city about 15 kilometres to the south destroyed by Slavs fighting with the Avars. After the fall of the Ostrogothic kingdom the town came under Byzantine protection. In the 12th and 13th centuries it grew into an oligarchic republic and was under the sovereignty of Venice from 1205 to 1358. A fire destroyed most of the city on 16 August 1296, and a new urban plan followed. By the Peace Treaty of Zadar in 1358 it gained relative independence as a vassal of the Kingdom of Hungary.

Between the 14th and 19th centuries Dubrovnik ruled itself as a free state, prosperous from maritime trade, with its highest development in the 15th and 16th centuries, when it was noted for wealth and skilled diplomacy and was a birthplace of Croatian literature. Latin was the official language until 1472, although most of the population spoke Croatian. An earthquake in 1667 almost destroyed the whole city. French forces occupied the republic on 27 May 1806, and in 1808 Marshal Marmont abolished it and joined its territory to the Napoleonic Kingdom of Italy.

After 1815 Dubrovnik belonged to the Kingdom of Dalmatia within the Habsburg Empire. In 1918 it became part of the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, later Yugoslavia. During World War II it was in the Independent State of Croatia, and afterwards in the Socialist Republic of Croatia within Yugoslavia. In 1991, in the Croatian War of Independence, the Yugoslav People's Army besieged the city and shelled it, causing significant damage. After repair and restoration it became one of the best-known tourist destinations of the Mediterranean, often called the Queen of the Adriatic.
duccio: Duccio was born and died in Siena and worked mostly in the surrounding region of Tuscany. Much about his life and family is uncertain, though he is better documented than other Italian painters of his time. Archives record the debts he ran up and the fines he incurred, and some records say he was married with seven children. Gaps of years in the Sienese records have led scholars to speculate that he may have travelled to Paris, Assisi and Rome. Where he studied is debated: many believe he trained under Cimabue, while others think he learned from a Byzantine master in Constantinople.

Little is known of his painting before 1278, when, at the age of 23, he is recorded as having painted twelve account book cases. Only about thirteen of his works survive, and only two can be firmly dated, both major public commissions. The Rucellai Madonna, now in the Uffizi, was commissioned in April 1285 by the Compagnia del Laudesi di Maria Vergine for a chapel in Santa Maria Novella in Florence. The Maestà was commissioned for the high altar of Siena Cathedral in 1308, and Duccio completed it by June 1311.

Duccio's known works are on wooden panels, painted in egg tempera with gold leaf. His style resembles Byzantine art in its gold backgrounds and familiar religious scenes, but he began to soften its sharp lines. He used modelling of light and dark to reveal the figures beneath heavy drapery, so that hands, faces and feet became rounder and more three-dimensional. He was also one of the first painters to set figures in architectural settings, and he gave his figures a tenderness toward one another that makes Christ and the Virgin read as child and mother.

He had many followers, some of them anonymous masters known only through stylistic analysis. Simone Martini, from about 1305, and Pietro Lorenzetti, from about 1310, painted works with affinities to his, though each soon developed an independent style, and Ambrogio Lorenzetti is also named among those he influenced.
ducetius: Ducetius, known in Greek also as Douketios, was a native Sicilian, thought perhaps to have been born near the town of Mineo, but Greek by education and strongly shaped by the Greek civilisation of the island. His story is known through the Greek historian Diodorus Siculus, who wrote in the 1st century BCE and drew on the work of Timaeus.

Sicily had been ruled by the tyrants Gelo and his brother Hiero. After Hiero's death in 467 BCE Syracuse became a democracy, but troubles followed the fall of the tyranny, and in 460 BCE war broke out between Syracuse and its former colony Catana. Because Catana had occupied Sicel land, Ducetius sided with Syracuse, and together they defeated it.

Ducetius then founded the city of Menai, today Mineo, and occupied Morgantina. He made the new city of Palice the seat of his power. It stood near Lago Naftia, then two sacred crater lakes and the sanctuary of a pair of Sicel gods called the Palici, and it grew quickly as a refuge for runaway slaves. He went on to conquer Aetna, south-west of Mount Etna, and to move into the territory of Agrigentum.

Syracuse, although an ally, grew uneasy at his unchecked expansion. When in 451 BCE he took Motyon, a stronghold held by Agrigentum, Syracuse came to Agrigentum's aid but could not defeat him, and that year his Sicel state was at its height. In 450 BCE it was decisively beaten at Nomae. His army scattered among the Sicel towns, Agrigentum retook Motyon, and Ducetius fled to Syracuse, where a general assembly tried him and voted to pay for his exile to Corinth, the city's mother-city, on condition that he never return.

According to Diodorus he nevertheless came back and founded Kale Akte, on the north coast in the present-day province of Messina, supposedly on the instruction of an oracle, with Sicel and Corinthian settlers. Diodorus dates the foundation once to 446 BCE and elsewhere to 440 BCE, the year Ducetius died of illness, so the date is uncertain. Excavations at Caronia have found only sparse remains of the 5th century BCE and show that a Sicel settlement already existed there. The suggestion that he came back without the consent of Syracuse is considered very improbable. After his death the Sicel federation fell apart almost at once, and Palice was sacked and its inhabitants sold into slavery.
duchy-of-croatia: The Roman province of Dalmatia suffered conquest by Goths and Huns, then Slavic intrusions from the mid-6th century, and around 614 the Avars and Slavs sacked its capital, Salona. According to the De Administrando Imperio of Constantine Porphyrogenitus, the White Croats were either invited into Dalmatia by the Byzantine emperor Heraclius and settled there after defeating the Avars, or came across the Sava from Pannonia and settled by themselves; historians have interpreted these accounts in several ways.

The source says they were led by five brothers and two sisters, and that they were later divided into eleven counties. By the early 9th century Croatia had emerged as a political entity headed by a duke, in the basins of the Cetina, Krka and Zrmanja rivers.

The Franks gained control of Pannonia and Dalmatia in the 790s and the first decade of the 9th century. Under the Pax Nicephori of 812 the Byzantines kept the coastal cities and islands while the Franks held Istria and the hinterland. From about 810 Duke Borna ruled most of northern Dalmatia as a Carolingian vassal. Trpimir I, who succeeded about 845 and founded the House of Trpimirović, strengthened his personal rule, attacked Byzantine coastal cities in 846. A charter of 852 names him dux Croatorum.

Domagoj, who founded the House of Domagojević, took the throne in 864; his reign saw piracy that the Pope tried in vain to stop, a revolt against Frankish overlordship, and the establishment of the Byzantine Theme of Dalmatia. In 879 Duke Branimir, who had killed Zdeslav and turned the country towards Rome, received papal recognition as a state from Pope John VIII, now free of Frankish suzerainty. His successor Tomislav allied with Byzantium about 923 and in 926 severely defeated Simeon I of Bulgaria in the Battle of the Bosnian Highlands.

Around 925 Croatia became a kingdom. It is generally said that Tomislav was crowned king in 925, though it is not known when or where, or whether he was crowned at all. He was the first Croatian ruler whom the papal chancellery honoured with the title of king, and the conclusions of the Council of Split of 925 and a letter of Pope John X call him king. Later inscriptions and charters show that his 10th-century successors called themselves kings. The Trpimirović and Domagojević dynasties ruled the duchy from 845 to 1091.
duchy-of-lower-lorraine: Under the Treaty of Prüm of 855 that divided Middle Francia, King Lothair II received regions along the Meuse, Moselle and Lower Rhine, and his realm came to be called Lotharingia. It was later divided, reunited or attached to West and East Francia several times, and early in the 10th century it became a stem duchy. In 953 the German king Otto I gave the governance of the whole duchy to his brother Bruno the Great, Archbishop of Cologne. In 959 Bruno divided it into a southern half, Upper Lotharingia, and a northern half, Lower Lotharingia, and the division became permanent after his death in 965. Scholars debate the exact chronology and nature of these divisions.

Lower Lotharingia was granted to Count Godfrey I of Mons, whose lands lay lower down the Rhine river system. After the death of his son Duke Richar the emperor ruled it directly, until in 977 Otto II enfeoffed Charles, the exiled younger brother of King Lothair of France. Lower and Upper Lorraine were briefly reunited under Gothelo I. After that the lower duchy was quickly marginalised, while Upper Lorraine came to be known simply as the Duchy of Lorraine.

The duchy's significance diminished further, and it was affected by the conflict between Emperors Henry IV and Henry V. Henry IV enfeoffed Count Henry of Limburg, whom Henry V deposed and replaced by Count Godfrey I of Louvain. When Duke Godfrey III died in 1190, his son Duke Henry I of Brabant inherited the title by order of Emperor Henry VI at the Diet of Schwäbisch Hall, and the duchy lost its territorial authority. The remaining imperial fief held by the dukes of Brabant was later called the Duchy of Lothier.

The duchy covered almost all of the modern Netherlands, Belgium and Luxembourg and parts of modern Germany and France, though Frisia was only loosely associated and the dukes had no real control there. After its territorial power was shattered, many fiefdoms came to imperial immediacy in its area, among them the Archbishopric of Cologne, the Prince-Bishopric of Liège, the Bishopric of Utrecht, the Duchy of Limburg, the counties of Guelders, Holland, Jülich, Namur, Cleves and Hainault, and the County of Loon. The County of Leuven and Brussels, the Margraviate of Antwerp and the Duchy of Brabant stayed under the authority of the titular dukes of Lothier.
duchy-of-naples: The Duchy of Naples began as a Byzantine province, constituted in the seventh century in the lands roughly corresponding to the present province of Naples that the Lombards had not conquered in their invasion of Italy in the sixth century. It extended over the Vesuvius zone, the Sorrento Peninsula, the Phlegraean area, the islands of Ischia and Procida, Nola and parts of the present province of Caserta. In 661 Naples obtained from the emperor Constans II the right to be ruled by a local duke, Basil, whose subjection to the emperor soon became merely nominal. Greek was the official language, though the population spoke Latin, and the duchy coined money with the emperor's effigy and Greek inscriptions.

In 763 Duke Stephen II switched his allegiance from Constantinople to Rome, placing Naples under papal suzerainty. Around the beginning of the ninth century Latin replaced Greek in official use and Saint Januarius replaced the emperor on the coins. In 813 Duke Anthimus could ignore Emperor Leo V's call for the fleet to fight Saracen pirates off Sicily; only Amalfi and Gaeta sent contingents. In 840 Duke Sergius I made the succession hereditary, and Naples was thereafter de facto independent. Gaeta, Amalfi and Sorrento took their independence from Naples in the early ninth century.

The city was mainly a military centre, ruled by an aristocracy of warriors and landowners, with a population of between thirty and thirty-five thousand. Its fleet took part in the Battle of Ostia against the Arabs in 849, yet in 836 it asked the Arabs for support against a Lombard siege from Benevento. Dukes such as Gregory IV and John II fought at the Battle of the Garigliano in 915. In 1027 Duke Sergius IV gave the county of Aversa to Norman mercenaries led by Rainulf Drengot, which began a process that eventually ended Naples's independence. In 1137 Duke Sergius VII surrendered to Roger II of Sicily.

The duchy lasted more than five centuries in the Early and High Middle Ages. It outlasted the Lombard principalities of Capua, Salerno and Benevento and the Greek duchies of Amalfi, Gaeta and Sorrento. Under the Normans the city was administered by a palatine count, with little independence left to the Neapolitan patriciate, and commerce was left mainly to merchants from Pisa and Genoa. Norman buildings in Naples were mainly castles, walls and fortified gates, among them Castel Capuano and Castel dell'Ovo.
duchy-of-prussia: As Protestantism spread among the laity of the Teutonic Order's Prussian state, dissent grew against its Catholic rule. Albert, the Grand Master, a member of a cadet branch of the House of Hohenzollern, lacked the military resources to assert the Order's authority after losing a war against Poland, and his bishop, Georg von Polenz, had converted to Lutheranism in 1523. Martin Luther encouraged him to turn the Order's territory into a secular principality under his own rule.

On 10 April 1525 Albert resigned his office, became a Protestant and was granted the title Duke of Prussia by his uncle, King Sigismund I of Poland, in the Prussian Homage at Kraków, in a deal partly brokered by Luther. On 10 December 1525 the Prussian estates established the Lutheran Church by a Church Order. The Order was left with but 55 knights in Prussia.

The duchy had German, Polish (mainly in Masuria) and Lithuanian-speaking (mainly in Lithuania Minor) populations, and the capital remained Königsberg. Albert was formally a vassal of the Polish crown, but he kept self-government, his own army, his own currency, a provincial assembly and substantial autonomy in foreign affairs.

In 1544 Albert founded the Albertina University in Königsberg, which trained Lutheran pastors and theologians, and in 1560 Sigismund II Augustus of Poland gave it the rights and autonomy of Kraków University. Because services were held in native languages, exiled Lithuanian Protestant pastors were appointed professors, which made the Albertina a centre of Lithuanian language and literature.

Albert died in 1568 and his teenage son Albert Frederick inherited the duchy. In 1569 at Lublin the king also enfeoffed Joachim II of Brandenburg and his descendants as co-heirs. George William was invested with the duchy in 1623, which confirmed the personal union known as Brandenburg-Prussia.

During the Second Northern War Charles X Gustav of Sweden invaded and by the Treaty of Königsberg of January 1656 made the duchy a Swedish fief. When the war turned against him he made Frederick William, the Great Elector, full sovereign by the Treaty of Labiau. The Treaties of Wehlau and Bromberg in 1657 confirmed this, with John II Casimir of Poland recognising his full sovereignty. The burghers of Königsberg rejected the change, but in 1662 Frederick William entered the city with troops and forced it to swear allegiance.

Full sovereignty made it possible to raise the duchy to a kingdom in 1701, when Frederick III of Brandenburg became King in Prussia. After the First Partition of Poland in 1772, the former Ducal Prussia was reorganised as the Province of East Prussia.
duchy-of-saxe-coburg: The Coburg lands came to the House of Wettin through Catherine of Henneberg, whose husband, Frederick III, Margrave of Meissen, could take them as her dowry only after her mother Jutta of Brandenburg-Salzwedel died in 1353. By the Treaty of Leipzig of 1485, which divided the Saxon states, they passed to the Ernestine line. After the Ernestines lost the Schmalkaldic War in 1547, Coburg was held by Duke John Ernest, who built the Ehrenburg palace there. The outlawed Duke John Frederick II died in imperial prison, and by the Erfurt Division of 1572 his sons John Casimir and John Ernest received the new principality, with Coburg as their residence.

Their guardian, Augustus, Elector of Saxony, an enemy of their father, ran a corrupt regency with Saxon officials until his death in 1586. In 1596 John Ernest received his own Duchy of Saxe-Eisenach, and John Casimir ruled Coburg alone. Under him Coburg saw a building boom and gained an administrative apparatus that long outlived him. In the Thirty Years War the land served as a staging area for many armies, and its population fell from 55,000 to 22,000. It later passed by lot to Frederick William II of Saxe-Altenburg and in 1672 to Ernest the Pious of Saxe-Gotha.

After the joint rule of his seven sons failed, Albert received a smaller Saxe-Coburg on 24 February 1680, with full sovereignty in the Empire. He modelled his court on those of greater princes, kept a library of 4,757 volumes and rebuilt the Ehrenburg in the Baroque style after it burned in 1690, which ruined the duchy's finances despite the minting of inferior coins.

The dispute after Albert's death lasted thirty-five years between Bernhard I of Saxe-Meiningen and John Ernest IV of Saxe-Saalfeld, ending in 1735 after interventions by Emperor Charles VI. Duke Francis Josias made Coburg his residence, and it remained the seat of the dynasty until the monarchy ended in 1918. In 1826 Saxe-Coburg-Saalfeld became Saxe-Coburg and Gotha, whose later dukes included Alfred, a son of Queen Victoria.
duchy-of-westphalia: The Westphalian lands, once part of the Saxon stem duchy, were Christianized by the archbishops of Cologne after Charlemagne's conquests in the Saxon Wars, and parishes and monasteries such as Grafschaft Abbey, founded by Anno II in 1072, strengthened their hold. During the Investiture Controversy, in 1102, Archbishop Frederick I of Cologne seized half the territory of the counts of Arnsberg, supporters of Emperor Henry IV, and the counties of Werl, Rüthen and Volmarstein soon followed. In 1180 Emperor Frederick Barbarossa granted these lands, with the south-west of the former Duchy of Saxony, to Archbishop Philip of Heinsberg.

The duchy covered roughly the later districts of Olpe and Hochsauerland and neighbouring parts of Soest and the Märkischer Kreis; its lands were mostly mountainous and forested, with metal deposits and brine springs, besides the fertile Hellweg Börde on the trade route from Aachen to Goslar. It formed the largest part of the Cologne electorate.
