Archbishop Engelbert of Berg subdued the nobility after 1220 and joined the duchy's scattered lands, until Frederick I of Isenberg killed him in 1225. The purchase of Werl-Arnsberg in 1368 united the north and south of the Sauerland.

Soest, the richest town of Westphalia, rejected Cologne's rule in the Soest Feud of 1444 to 1449 and passed to the Duchy of Cleves, after which Arnsberg became the administrative capital. The Reformation reached the duchy under Archbishop Herman V of Wied and returned under Gebhard Truchsess von Waldburg, but Ernest of Bavaria and his brother Ferdinand regained it for the archbishopric at the start of the Cologne War in 1583, after which Protestantism survived only on the borders with Waldeck and Hesse.

The duchy suffered in the Thirty Years' War, and in 1794 the archbishops moved there after the French annexed their lands west of the Rhine. The Kingdom of Westphalia created in 1807 did not include it. At the Congress of Vienna the duchy was awarded to Prussia in exchange for lands west of the Rhine and became part of the Province of Westphalia.
dudo-of-saint-quentin: Dudo was a Picard, born at Saint-Quentin in the 960s, and later became dean there. He was a learned man who probably received his education at Liège or perhaps at Laon. By 987 he had become a canon of St Quentin, whose abbacy was held by the counts of Vermandois. Very little else is known about his life beyond his work for the Norman court and the fact that he died before 1043.

In 987 Albert I, Count of Vermandois, sent Dudo on a diplomatic mission to Richard I of Normandy, and the mission succeeded. In the two years before Richard's death in 996 Dudo was a frequent visitor to the Norman court. In a letter to Adalbero, Bishop of Laon, he wrote that Richard had asked him to record the customs and deeds of the Norman land and the rights established in the kingdom of his grandfather Rollo. He wrote the history during a second stay in Normandy, as the duke had urged him to do.

The Historia Normannorum, also called the Gesta Normannorum, was written between 996 and 1015 and dedicated to Adalbero of Laon. It is divided into four parts, alternates between prose and verse in several metres, and covers the Normans from 852 to the death of Duke Richard in 996. Dudo knew Virgil's Aeneid and other Latin authors, but his Latin is affected and obscure. He seems to have used no earlier documents, relying on oral tradition, much of it supplied by Raoul, Count of Ivry, a maternal half-brother of Duke Richard.

Because of this the work reads in places like a romance. Ernst Dümmler and Georg Waitz judged it untrustworthy, while Jules Lair and Johannes Steenstrup, admitting that it mixes in legend, valued it as a source. Leah Shopkow has argued that Carolingian saints' lives, the Vita S. Germani of Heiric of Auxerre and the Vita S. Lamberti of Stephen of Liège, served as models. Dudo also claims that Richard I was sent to learn the Dacian, or Old Norse, tongue, and that the people of Bayeux spoke it more often than Old French.

William of Jumièges, Wace, Robert of Torigni, William of Poitiers and Hugh of Fleury drew heavily on the work for their own chronicles. André Duchesne first printed it in Paris in 1619; later editions appeared in Migne's Patrologia Latina in 1844 and, edited by Jules Lair, at Caen in 1865.
dugout-canoe: A dugout is made from a log of suitable size, from which enough wood is removed to leave the vessel light and buoyant but still strong enough to carry its crew and cargo. The shape is fashioned to reduce drag, with sharp ends at bow and stern. The bark is stripped first. Before metal tools the log was hollowed out with controlled fires, and the burnt wood was removed with an adze. Another method was to chop parallel notches across the interior and split out the wood between them.

Some makers steamed the sides of the hollow log until pliable and bent them outwards to widen the beam and flatten the bottom. For rougher ocean water a dugout can be fitted with one or two outriggers, smaller logs mounted parallel to the hull on long poles.

Dugouts are the oldest boat type archaeologists have found, which probably reflects that massive timbers survive better than other materials such as bark. The Pesse canoe, found in the Netherlands, is believed to be the world's oldest boat and is carbon dated to between 8040 BCE and 7510 BCE. The Dufuna canoe from Nigeria, about 8,000 years old, is the oldest boat found in Africa, and a dugout of similar age from Kuahuqiao in Zhejiang, China, is the earliest found in Asia.

In Denmark, linden-wood dugouts found at Egådalen north of Aarhus are dated to 5210–4910 BCE and are the oldest known boats in Northern Europe. Linden was widely used in ancient Europe because the trees were abundant, grew tall, carved easily and were lighter than other forest trees.

In sub-Saharan Africa dugouts are commonplace from the Limpopo basin to West Africa and have been used for transport, fishing and hunting, once including the dangerous hunting of hippopotamus. Along the river system linking the Niger, Benue, Gambia and Senegal rivers and Lake Chad they carried people and goods along trade routes. A Nok terracotta of the first millennium BCE shows two paddlers with goods in a dugout.

In the Pacific Northwest cedar canoes over 18 metres long are made for everyday and ceremonial use. In the north-eastern woodlands the mishoon was burned out over several days. Pacific island canoes are very large and fitted with outriggers, and the Māori waka carried 40 to 80 warriors. According to Byzantine sources the Slavs built monoxyla, each holding 40 to 70 warriors, which the Rus used in attacks on Constantinople in the 9th and 10th centuries.
dugu-xin: Dugu Xin, whose Xianbei name was Qimitou, was known as Dugu Ruyuan until 540. His father was Dugu Kuzhe, Duke of Sikong, and his mother a lady of the Feilian clan. He lived in the chaotic age of the Northern and Southern dynasties. In 534 Dugu Xin followed Emperor Xiaowu of Northern Wei westward to join the warlord Yuwen Tai, and in the years that followed he led Western Wei forces against the Eastern Wei. After an early defeat he fled to the southern Liang state and stayed there three years before returning to the north-west.

In 537 he took the former Northern Wei capital, Luoyang, from the Eastern Wei, and in 548 he became one of the Eight Pillars of the State. When the Northern Zhou replaced the Western Wei he was created Duke of Wei, but the powerful regent Yuwen Hu soon forced him to take his own life, on 24 April 557. He was given the posthumous name Li, meaning unrepentant.

He is remembered above all through three of his daughters. His first daughter, Empress Mingjing, married Yuwen Yu, Emperor Ming of Northern Zhou. His seventh daughter, Qieluo, Empress Wenxian, married Yang Jian, Emperor Wen of Sui, and bore him five sons and five daughters. His fourth daughter, Empress Yuanzhen, married Li Bing, Duke of Tang. Through these marriages he became, though only after his death, father-in-law to two emperors of two dynasties and maternal grandfather of Emperor Yang of Sui and Emperor Gaozu of Tang; every Chinese emperor from 604 to 907, except Wu Zetian and self-proclaimed rebels, descended from him.

The Sui honoured him as Duke Jing of Zhao and the Tang as Prince of Liang. In 583 Empress Wenxian built a temple to his memory in the capital Daxing, whose remains were found in 1997 on the campus of Xi'an Jiaotong University. Among his sons was Dugu Luo, Duke Gong of Shu.
duke-adolf-friedrich-of-mecklenburg: Duke Adolf Friedrich Albrecht Heinrich of Mecklenburg-Schwerin was born in Schwerin on 10 October 1873. He was the third child of Frederick Francis II, Grand Duke of Mecklenburg-Schwerin, and his third wife Princess Marie of Schwarzburg-Rudolstadt. His younger brother was Prince Hendrik of the Netherlands, prince consort to Queen Wilhelmina of the Netherlands.

From 1907 to 1908 Adolf Friedrich led a scientific research expedition in the region of the Central African Graben and crossed Africa from east to west. In 1908 the Association of Geography of Leipzig awarded him the Eduard Vogel Medal. From 1910 to 1911 he led a second expedition to Lake Chad and the northern rivers of the Congo, reaching the Nile in what is now Sudan. His party explored the little-known forests of the Congo tributaries and the Lake Chad basin, and some groups went on to the Bahr el Ghazal and to southern Cameroon and the islands of the Gulf of Guinea. His two-volume account of it is Vom Kongo zum Niger und Nil.

From 1912 to 1914 he was the last governor of Togoland in German West Africa. After the First World War he served as vice-president of the German Colonial Society for Southwest Africa. In the autumn of 1918 representatives of the Baltic German nobility offered him the throne of the United Baltic Duchy, a short-lived client state on Baltic territories under German occupation. It was proclaimed in Riga on 5 November, with a regency council headed by Baron Adolf Pilar von Pilchau, while he remained in Germany. Germany lost the war by 11 November, so he never took the throne, and the council was dissolved on 28 November 1918.

He was a member of the International Olympic Committee from 1926 to 1956 and the first president of the National Olympic Committee of Germany, from 1949 to 1951. He married twice, first Princess Viktoria Feodora of Reuss-Schleiz in 1917, who died in December 1918 a day after the birth of their only daughter, and then in 1924 Princess Elisabeth of Stolberg-Rossla, widow of his half-brother. He died in Eutin on 5 August 1969. A genus of lizards, Adolfus, a chameleon, Kinyongia adolfifriderici, and a cichlid fish are named after him.
duke-huan-of-qi: Born Lü Xiaobai, a son of Duke Xi of Qi, he was not in line for the throne, since he had at least two older brothers, Zhu'er and Jiu. His tutor Bao Shuya, fearing for his life under the troubled rule of Zhu'er as Duke Xiang, took him into exile in the state of Ju. After Duke Xiang was assassinated in 686 BCE and his successor Wuzhi was murdered a month later, Xiaobai hurried back and seized the government and army before Prince Jiu, backed by his tutor Guan Zhong and Duke Zhuang of Lu, could be installed. Lu's invading army was crushed at Qianshi, and Duke Zhuang executed Jiu and handed Guan Zhong over as a prisoner.

On Bao Shuya's advice the duke spared Guan Zhong and made him chief minister. Together they divided the land and people into regulated units and enforced a merit-based system of government, which let Qi mobilise its resources more effectively than the other, loosely structured Zhou states. In 667 BCE the rulers of Lu, Song, Chen and Zheng chose him as their leader, and King Hui of Zhou named him hegemon, with authority to act militarily in the royal name.

He saved Yan, Xing and Wey from invasions by non-Zhou peoples and in 656 BCE led an alliance of eight states that defeated Cai, a satellite of Chu, then invaded Chu itself, which agreed to halt its northward expansion and attend a meeting at Shaoling, the first of its kind. The historian Cho-yun Hsu wrote that he set up an interstate order guarded by consensus rather than authority.

His power declined after Chu turned east, his alliance was beaten at Loulin in 645 BCE and Guan Zhong died the same year. Six sons by different concubines fought over the succession. The Guanzi says four officials locked the ailing duke in his room and starved him, a story the Zuo Zhuan and the Records of the Grand Historian do not tell. After his death war broke out in Linzi, his body lay unburied for between seven days and three months, and Qi lost its leading place to Jin under Duke Wen.
duke-huan-of-zheng: Duke Huan of Zheng, personal name Ji You, was the founding duke of Zheng, a vassal state of the Zhou dynasty ruled by a branch of the royal house. According to the Records of the Grand Historian he was a son of King Li of Zhou. In 806 BCE King Xuan of Zhou granted him the land of Zheng, north-west of modern Hua County in Shaanxi.

In 773 BCE, the 33rd year of his reign, King You of Zhou made him situ, or minister of land, because of the people's affection for him. Troubled by the instability of King You's rule, Duke Huan asked the court historian Taishi Bo whether he should move his state to the west or to the Yangtze basin. Taishi Bo advised against both: a state in the west would not last among its grasping peoples, and in the south the expanding state of Chu stood in the way.

Following that advice, Duke Huan moved his state east of Luoyang, south of the Yellow River and the Ji River, and named it New Zheng. Neighbouring states, among them Kuai and Guo, offered him ten cities, which were joined to his lands.

In 771 BCE, the 45th year of his reign, the Quanrong attacked the Zhou capital Haojing and killed both King You of Zhou and Duke Huan. His son Juetu took the throne as Duke Wu of Zheng and ruled the state that his father had moved to its new lands in the east.
duke-hui-of-jin: Ji Yiwu was one of the nine sons of Duke Xian of Jin; his mother was Xiao Rongzi. He was a younger brother of Shensheng and Chong'er, the future Duke Wen, and an elder brother of Xiqi. To secure the succession for her son Xiqi, the concubine Li Ji had the older princes sent away from the capital, and Yiwu was posted to defend Erqu, in present-day Ji County in Shanxi.

After Duke Xian died in 651 BCE, the minister Li Ke killed first Xiqi and then the infant Zhuozi, who had been placed on the throne after him, together with Li Ji. Li Ke offered the throne to Chong'er, who declined, and then to Yiwu, who was living in the state of Liang and accepted.

As duke, Yiwu ordered Li Ke to take his own life for the deaths of the two earlier rulers. When Jin suffered famine in 647 BCE, Duke Mu of Qin sold it grain, but when Qin went hungry the next year Yiwu refused to return the favour, against the advice of his minister Qing Zheng. Duke Mu invaded, and in the battle at Han Yiwu's chariot stuck in the mud; Qing Zheng walked away, the Jin troops fled and the duke was taken to Qin as a captive.

He was to be killed as an offering to the gods, but his half-sister Bo Ji, Duke Mu's wife, mourned for him, and Duke Mu spared him and made an alliance with Jin. Once restored, Yiwu had Qing Zheng killed and sent assassins after Chong'er, who escaped to Qi. In 643 BCE he sent his son, Crown Prince Yu, to Qin as a hostage.

Yiwu fell gravely ill in 638 BCE, and Crown Prince Yu and his wife Huai Ying fled Qin to reach Jin before he died. He died in the ninth lunar month of 637 BCE and was given the posthumous name Duke Hui, the Benevolent Duke of Jin. Crown Prince Yu succeeded him as Duke Huai.
duke-mu-of-qin: He was the son of Duke De of Qin and the younger brother of Duke Cheng. In his own day he would simply have been called the Duke of Qin; Mu, meaning solemn, is a posthumous name given by his successors. He married Mu Ji, a daughter of Duke Xian of Jin, and gave his own daughter Huai Ying in marriage to two of Duke Xian's sons. These ties gave rise to the saying "the Friendship of Qin and Jin" for alliances built on marriage. Among his advisers were Baili Xi and Jian Shu, and he is also remembered as the master of Bole, the horse expert of later folklore.

After Duke Xian's death, Jin fell into a succession struggle among his sons. When Jin suffered a famine, Duke Mu sent food and farming tools, but when famine struck Qin in turn, Jin attacked instead of repaying the help, and the two states fought for several years. Duke Mu then invited Duke Xian's son Ji Chong'er from the court of Chu, and when Duke Hui of Jin died he sent his army to install Chong'er, defeating the Jin army at the Battle of Gaoliang. Chong'er, now Duke Wen of Jin, was grateful, and with his eastern front calm Qin turned on the peoples of the west; with the help of You Yu, Duke Mu brought eight western tribes to submit.

In 627 BCE he planned a secret attack on the State of Zheng, but his army turned back, and on its way home it was ambushed and badly beaten by Jin at the Battle of Yao, near present-day Luoning County in Henan. Three years later Qin won a major victory over Jin in revenge. Duke Mu then held a funeral for those killed at Yao, refused to advance further east and kept to Qin's old policy of expanding westward.

His son Ying succeeded him as Duke Kang of Qin. Duke Mu is remembered in the poem Huang Niao of the Classic of Poetry, which tells of three men of the Ziche clan, Ziche Yansi, Ziche Zhongheng and Ziche Qianhu, who served and followed him until they died.
duke-of-atholl: The dukes descend from Sir William Murray of Castleton, who married a daughter of John Stewart, 1st Earl of Atholl, and was killed at the Battle of Flodden in 1513. His descendant Sir John Murray was made Lord Murray of Tullibardine in 1604 and Earl of Tullibardine in 1606. The 2nd Earl married Lady Dorothea, daughter of the last Stewart Earl of Atholl, and their son John Murray was created Earl of Atholl in 1629. His son was raised to Marquess of Atholl in 1676 and married Lady Amelia Anne Sophia, daughter of James Stanley, 7th Earl of Derby.

The dukedom was created by Queen Anne in 1703 for the 2nd Marquess. His heir William Murray, Marquess of Tullibardine, joined the Jacobite rising of 1715, was attainted and removed from the succession, so the title passed to a younger son, James, the 2nd Duke, who in 1736 also succeeded James Stanley, 10th Earl of Derby, as Baron Strange and Lord of Mann. His nephew John, the 3rd Duke, son of the Jacobite general Lord George Murray, married his cousin Charlotte, Baroness Strange, and the couple sold their sovereignty over the Isle of Man to the British Crown for £70,000.

The 4th Duke was made Earl Strange in the Peerage of Great Britain in 1786, which gave the dukes a seat in the House of Lords, and sold the family's remaining properties and privileges to the Crown for £409,000. The 7th Duke added the surname Stewart in 1865 and in 1893 restored the spelling Atholl in place of Athole. When the unmarried 9th Duke died in 1957, the British titles became extinct, and his distant cousin, the 10th Duke, had no seat in the Lords until he was elected a Scottish representative peer in 1958.

The duke is hereditary chief of Clan Murray, and his heir uses the courtesy title Marquess of Tullibardine. The family seat was historically Blair Castle in Perthshire, which the 10th Duke placed with most of his estates in a charitable trust before his death in 1996. In 1883 the 7th Duke's estates covered 201,640 acres in Perthshire. The dukes are traditionally buried beside the ruined St Bride's Kirk in the castle grounds, and the holder of the title commands the Atholl Highlanders, the only legal private army in Europe.
duke-of-aveiro: King John III of Portugal granted the title in 1535 to his second cousin John of Lencastre, who was already Marquis of Torres Novas. He was the son of Infante George, Duke of Coimbra, a natural son of King John II. The family name Lancastre recalls Philippa of Lancaster, the wife of King John I and daughter of John of Gaunt. The second duke, George, died at Alcácer Quibir in 1578.

The dukes strongly supported Philip II of Spain in the Portuguese succession crisis of 1580 and became the second house of the kingdom after the Braganzas. Raimundo, the 4th duke, kept the house's loyalty to the Habsburg monarchy after the revolution of 1640, so the new Braganza kings confiscated his property and in 1668 gave it to his uncle Peter, Archbishop of Évora and general Inquisitor, who died without issue in 1673. His niece Maria de Guadalupe, wife of the Spanish Duke of Los Arcos, was recognised as duchess in 1679 on condition that she return to Portugal; she left her husband and recovered the estates, while King Carlos II of Spain created a separate Spanish title, Duchess of Aveyro, in 1681.

José de Mascarenhas da Silva e Lancastre, the 8th duke, came from a collateral line descended from a daughter of the 3rd dukes. Accused of taking part in the Távora affair, he was executed by the Marquis of Pombal on the orders of King Joseph I.

All the family's possessions were confiscated, its arms removed from public places, its houses demolished and its lands salted. On the site of the Lisbon palace a stone memorial recorded the sentence of 12 January 1759 and forbade any building there for all time. Only the palace of the dukes at Azeitão survives, its arms defaced. The title then lay in abeyance until 1939, when Duarte Nuno, Duke of Braganza, authorised its personal use by the Count of Alcáçovas.
duke-of-shao: Lord Shao, posthumously named Kang, was head of the minor polity of Shao as well as founder of the lineage of Yan. Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian says only that he belonged to the same ancestral temple group as the Zhou royal house. Wang Chong's Lunheng calls him the elder brother of the Duke of Zhou, and Huangfu Mi made him a son of King Wen by a concubine. Maria Khayutina has argued from the order of lineages in the Gu Ming chapter that his lineage was founded before those of King Wen's sons.

King Wu appointed him Grand Protector, one of the Three Excellencies, the highest ministers at the capital. When King Wu died two years after the conquest, Lord Shao sided with the Duke of Zhou, and after three years they suppressed the Rebellion of the Three Guards. Power was then shared between them and the young King Cheng: Lord Shao held the lands west of the twin capitals Feng and Hao, the Duke of Zhou those to the east. Lord Shao surveyed the site of the new capital Luoyi and had its rammed earth walls built in a month.

Two chapters of the Shangshu, Jun Shi and Shao Gao, come from this period. The traditional reading takes Jun Shi as the Duke of Zhou's plea to Lord Shao to stay in office. Another reading sets the two against each other, with Lord Shao arguing that Heaven's mandate passes to the eldest son and the Duke of Zhou stressing the need for capable ministers.

Lord Shao served four kings, Wen, Wu, Cheng and Kang. In the Gu Ming chapter, which describes King Kang's inauguration, he is listed first among the participants and reads the command of accession. The Lunheng claims he lived more than a hundred years, and inscriptions from the middle of King Kang's reign tend to support it. The ode The Sweet Pears in the Classic of Poetry is said to honour him, asking that the tree where he camped be spared.
duke-of-zhou: Ji Dan, Duke Wen of Zhou, was the fourth son of Ji Chang, King Wen of Zhou, and Queen Tai Si. He was born when the Shang dynasty was in perceived decline, with rulers that the Chinese classics record as corrupt or immoral, chief among them Di Xin. From a young age he was noted for filial conduct and moral aptitude. After King Wen died, his brother Ji Fa, King Wu, took up the plan to take the Shang capital of Yin, and Ji Dan joined him with a much larger role in government. His part at the Battle of Muye is unclear: later accounts make him a strategist, while the earliest materials show him as a soldier or not at all.

After the victory King Wu gave fiefs to relatives and followers. Ji Dan was offered Lu but stayed at Haojing, so that his son Bo Qin took Lu, and he became the Duke of Zhou because his fief lay in Zhou. He was credited with elaborating the doctrine of the Mandate of Heaven, by which Shang injustice had offended Heaven, which commanded the reluctant Zhou to replace them. King Wu died three years after taking power and left the kingdom to his young son King Cheng. The Duke of Zhou became regent, codified the system of territorial administration and founded a new capital at Chengzhou around 1038 BCE. According to the traditional narrative he gave up power once King Cheng came of age.

The regency was not unquestioned. Some held that Wu Geng, the heir of Di Xin, should rule, and this led to the Rebellion of the Three Guards, led by Wu Geng and three of the duke's brothers. Within five years the duke defeated them and other rebels, and his armies pushed east and brought more land under Zhou control.

Tradition attributes to the Duke of Zhou the authorship of the I Ching and the Classic of Poetry and the establishment of the Rites of Zhou. His campaign in the east is remembered in the poem Po Fu of the Classic of Poetry. Later emperors regarded him as a paragon of virtue, and in 1008 the Zhenzong Emperor gave him the posthumous title King of Exemplary Culture. He is known in popular belief as the God of Dreams, from the passage in the Analects where Confucius laments that he has not dreamt of the Duke of Zhou for a long time, which was meant to say that his governmental ideals had faded.
duke-town: The Efik had become a power on the coast of the Bight of Biafra by the early 18th century. They lived by fishing and farming in large fortified villages along the waterways, in a loose federation with no paramount ruler, and the Duke and Eyamba families were among their leaders. The town stood on the east bank of the Calabar river, where its people could dominate the trade with European ships anchored there. The name Calabar was given to the coast by the Portuguese explorer Diogo Cao and was not used by the Efik.

Most of those sold from Calabar were Igbo. From 1725 to 1750 roughly 17,000 enslaved Africans were sold to European traders there, and from 1772 to 1775 more than 62,000. In 1767, during a feud with Old Town, the leaders of Duke Town arranged with six British slave ships to lure Old Town's leaders aboard under promise of safety; they were seized, some kept as slaves and others handed over for execution.

Britain outlawed its own slave trade in 1807, but traders from other European nations bought slaves at Calabar until 1841, when King Eyamba V of Duke Town and King Eyo of Creek Town agreed to end it, and palm oil became the main export. A United Presbyterian mission under Hope Masterton Waddell was founded in 1846. In 1850 the kings agreed to suppress the sacrifice of wives and slaves at a great man's death. The chiefs accepted British protection in 1884, and Old Calabar was the headquarters of the Niger Coast Protectorate until 1906.

The town is part of the modern city of Calabar, and its traditional rulers are still recognised. Since an agreement of 1970 a single ruler, the Edidem, represents the Efik, the office alternating between Duke Town and Creek Town.
duke-wen-of-jin: Chong'er, of the Ji clan, was a son of Duke Xian of Jin; Wen, the Cultured, is his posthumous name. In his father's later years the concubine Li Ji schemed to make her son Xiqi heir, and the crown prince Shensheng took his own life in 656 BCE. In the civil war that followed, the Li Ji Unrest, Duke Xian campaigned against his own sons. Chong'er fled north with able followers, among them Zhao Cui, Hu Yan, Xian Zhen and Jie Zhitui. In 651 BCE he refused an offer of the throne, which went to his half-brother Yiwu, Duke Hui of Jin.

After Duke Hui's attempts to have him killed he moved in 644 BCE to Qi, and from 639 BCE he wandered through Cao, Song, Zheng, Chu and Qin. After Duke Hui's death, Duke Mu of Qin escorted him home with an army.

Duke Wen reorganised the state into three armies, upper, middle and lower, each under a general and a lieutenant-general, and gave the men of his exile high posts. Jin absorbed many neighbouring states and made others vassals. He backed the Eastern Zhou court, and when King Xiang of Zhou was driven out by his brother in 635 BCE, Duke Wen's coalition restored him.

When Chu invaded Jin's ally Song in 633 BCE, he led troops of Qin, Qi and Song against it. Legend says he kept a promise made at the Chu court by pulling back three she, about 30 km, before the battle, and used the retreat to draw the Chu commander Ziyu into an ambush. At a meeting of rulers at Jiantu he was confirmed as hegemon.

He died in 628 BCE and was succeeded by his son Duke Xiang of Jin, and the hegemony stayed with Jin for nearly a century. His reforms kept Jin stable and strong for decades, but the houses of Wei and Zhao, raised by their military posts at his court, later came to dominate it, leading to the partition of Jin two and a half centuries later. Sima Qian tells how his follower Jie Zhitui refused reward and withdrew to Mount Mian; later legend has Jie die in a forest fire set to drive him out, an origin story of the Cold Food Festival, which is not attested before the Han.
duke-wu-of-qin: Duke Wu, whose personal name is unknown, was the eldest son and crown prince of Duke Xian of Qin. When his father died in 704 BCE at the age of 21, the ministers Fuji and Sanfu set him aside and placed his younger half-brother Chuzi on the throne. Six years later, in 698 BCE, the same ministers murdered Chuzi and installed Duke Wu, the original crown prince, in his place.

In 697 BCE, the first year of his reign, Qin attacked the Pengxi tribe of the Rong people, and its army advanced east to Mount Hua. In 695 BCE Duke Wu had Sanfu, Fuji and their clans executed for the murder of Chuzi. The counties he set up at Gui and Ji in 688 BCE lay in present-day Tianshui and Gangu in Gansu. The following year he established the counties of Du and Zheng in the east, in present-day Xi'an and Hua County in Shaanxi, and conquered the minor state of Xiao Guo.

Duke Wu died in 678 BCE after a reign of 20 years and was buried at Yong, in present-day Fengxiang in Shaanxi. Although he had a son named Bai, he was succeeded by his younger brother, Duke De of Qin, who moved the capital to Yong and enfeoffed Bai at the old capital, Pingyang.

Sima Qian names Duke Wu as the ruler who began the practice of funerary human sacrifice in Qin. A later ruler, Duke Mu, who died in 621 BCE, had 177 people buried with him, among them several senior officials. The practice lasted for almost three centuries until Duke Xian, also called Shixi, banned it in 384 BCE.
duke-xian-of-jin: Duke Xian, personal name Ji Guizhu, was named after Guizhu, a Rongdi leader whom his father and predecessor, Duke Wu, had captured alive. He moved the capital from Quwo to Jiang. On the advice of his official Shi Wei he killed or exiled almost all the members of the ducal clan of Jin, securing the throne for his own descendants. He expanded his army into two forces of 10,000 men each, some say 12,500.

In 672 BCE he destroyed the Li Rong tribe and took two of its women, Li Ji and her younger sister Shao Ji. In 661 BCE he conquered Geng, Huo and the old state of Wei; he gave Wei to his official Bi Wan and Geng to Zhao Su, whose descendants later founded the states of Wei and Zhao. In all he is said to have annexed 17 states and subjugated 38 others. Before the campaign against Guo, the Yu official Gong Zhiqi warned his ruler in vain that the teeth are cold when the lips are lost; the use of Yu became one of the Thirty-Six Stratagems.

In 656 BCE Li Ji, who wished her son Xiqi to be heir, poisoned food that the crown prince Shensheng had sent to his father after a sacrifice. Accused of plotting, Shensheng killed himself, and his half-brothers Chong'er and Yiwu fled after Li Ji accused them too.

Gravely ill in 651 BCE, Duke Xian could not attend the meeting of states called by Duke Huan of Qi at Kuiqiu, and he entrusted Xiqi to Xun Xi as chancellor. He died in the ninth month of that year. Li Ji put the 15-year-old Xiqi on the throne, but Li Ke killed him about a month later, and then killed the infant Zhuozi and Li Ji herself, while Xun Xi hanged himself. Yiwu then became ruler as Duke Hui of Jin. At Duke Xian's death Jin was one of the largest and most powerful states in China.
duke-xiang-of-qin: Duke Xiang, whose personal name was possibly Ying Kai, was not the eldest son of Duke Zhuang of Qin. The eldest of the three sons, Shifu, was the legal heir but refused the throne, preferring to devote his life to fighting the Rong tribes to avenge their grandfather Qin Zhong, who had been killed in battle against the Rong in 822 BCE. Xiang was made crown prince instead.

Qin, the westernmost of the Zhou states, bore the brunt of the long war with the western Rong. Soon after his accession, in 777 BCE, Duke Xiang married his younger sister Mu Ying to a Rong leader called King Feng, apparently to make peace. The following year he moved the Qin capital east from Quanqiu, also called Xichui, in present-day Li County in Gansu, to Qian, in present-day Long County in Shaanxi. Quanqiu soon fell to the Rong, and Shifu, who had led its defence, was captured and released a year later.

In 771 BCE King You of Zhou deposed Crown Prince Yijiu, son of Queen Shen, in favour of Bofu, son of his favourite concubine Bao Si. The Marquis of Shen, the queen's father, rebelled, allied with the Quanrong, attacked the Zhou capital Haojing and killed King You at Mount Li, and the feudal rulers set Yijiu on the throne as King Ping of Zhou. With Haojing ruined and still threatened, the capital was moved east, the start of the Eastern Zhou dynasty.

Duke Xiang was the first Qin ruler granted a noble rank by the Zhou king. With it Qin rose from a minor attached state, or fuyong, to a major vassal state. The land west of Qishan that King Ping promised to Qin had been the heartland of Zhou.

Duke Xiang died in 766 BCE, the 12th year of his reign, while campaigning against the Quanrong at Qishan, and was succeeded by his son, Duke Wen of Qin. He was buried at Quanqiu, and his tomb has been found in Li County in Gansu Province.
duke-xiang-of-song: Duke Xiang, whose personal name was Zifu, came to the throne of Song in 650 BCE, in the Spring and Autumn period. His wife Wang Ji, of the Ji clan of Zhou, was a daughter of King Hui of Zhou and an elder sister of King Xiang of Zhou. After the death of the hegemon Duke Huan of Qi in 643 BCE, he intervened in the war over Qi's succession on behalf of his ally Prince Zhao: allied with Cao, Wey and Zou, his troops invaded Qi, defeated Prince Zhao's rival brothers and crowned him Duke Xiao of Qi.

His rising influence led him to seek the place of hegemon himself and to make war on Chu. In 641 BCE he made a covenant with the small states of Cao and Zhu, and ordered the viscount of Zeng to be sacrificed as a victim for arriving too late at their first covenant. In 638 BCE he attacked Zheng and met the troops of Chu marching to save it. Rather than strike by surprise, he waited for the enemy to cross the river, to display his benevolence, ren, as a junzi. At the Battle of Hongshui his troops were thoroughly defeated by the stronger and fully prepared enemy, and he was badly hurt.

He died the following year and was succeeded by his son Wangchen, who ruled as Duke Cheng of Song from 636 to 620 BCE. Despite his failure to expand his power, some historians count him among the Five Hegemons. His conduct at the river became a byword; Mao Zedong once said, "We are not Duke Xiang of Song and have no use for his idiotic virtue and morality."
duke-xiao-of-qin: Duke Xiao, personal name Ying Quliang, was the son of Duke Xian. Before his birth Qin had suffered a long period of instability under Duke Li, Duke Zao, Duke Jian and Duke Chu, and the state of Wei had taken the Hexi region west of the Yellow River. Duke Xian stabilised the borders, moved the capital to Liyang and fought to recover Hexi, but died before he could. Isolated in the far west, Qin was left out of the alliances of the Central Plains states and treated as a barbarian country.

On his accession Duke Xiao issued an edict recalling the hegemony of his ancestor Duke Mu and promising office and land to anyone with a plan to strengthen Qin. Shang Yang, from Wei, answered it, bringing the Canon of Law of Li Kui, and won the duke over at a fourth audience with practical strategies. Against nobles such as Gan Long and Du Zhi, the duke issued the Land Reclamation Order in 359 BCE and made Shang Yang Left Assistant Chancellor in 356 BCE.

The first reforms brought household registration, collective responsibility, rewards for military merit, a twenty-rank system of military nobility and the end of hereditary privileges. After the capital moved from Liyang to Xianyang, a second phase abolished the well-field system, allowed private ownership and sale of land, introduced poll taxes, standardised weights and measures and burned private philosophical texts. King Xian of Zhou granted the duke the title of hegemon.

Qin turned on Wei, killing 7,000 Wei soldiers at Yuanli in 354 BCE and taking the old Wei capital of Anyi in 352 BCE. After Wei's defeat by Qi at Maling in 341 BCE, Shang Yang lured the Wei commander Prince Ang to a parley, seized him and routed his army, and King Hui of Wei ceded part of Hexi. Shang Yang was enfeoffed with 15 towns as Lord Shang.

Gravely ill in 338 BCE, Duke Xiao offered the throne to Shang Yang according to the Strategies of the Warring States, but he declined. The duke was buried at Di Yu and succeeded by his son, King Huiwen of Qin, under whom Shang Yang was accused of treason and executed. Xiao, meaning filial, was his posthumous name, and he was the last ruler of Qin styled duke. His reforms prepared the unification of China by his descendant Qin Shi Huang.
duke-zhuang-of-zheng: Duke Zhuang was born in 757 BCE with the ancestral name Ji and the given name Wusheng, meaning difficult birth, a reference to a breech presentation. He was the elder of the two sons of Duke Wu of Zheng and was groomed for the throne. His mother, Wu Jiang, preferred his younger brother Duan, and repeatedly asked Duke Wu to make Duan heir, but she was refused.

Wusheng became ruler of Zheng in 743 BCE. His mother asked that Duan be given the city of Zhi as a fief; Zhuang refused but allowed any other city, and against his courtiers' advice he granted Jing, the second largest city of Zheng and an important fortress. Duan, urged on by his mother, built walls, stockpiled arms and recruited soldiers. Zhuang dismissed his ministers' warnings, saying he had no clear proof of a plot and could not take up arms against his brother.

While Zhuang was away in Luoyang on diplomatic business, his mother wrote to Duan, ordering him to revolt and promising to open the gates of the capital. Zhuang, aware of the plan, returned in time to raise an army and defeated Duan at Yan, north of present-day Yanling County, in the summer of 722 BCE. A saying attributed to him about his brother runs that one who repeatedly commits undutiful acts will surely bring himself down.

King Ping of Zhou appointed Zhuang Left Advisor, but King Huan removed him from office, and Zhuang refused to attend the royal court. Zhuang also led campaigns in the name of the Zhou king against the Rong people and other Zhou states.

Zhuang died in 701 BCE, and his sons fought a long war of succession from 701 to 680 BCE. Of his 11 sons, Hu became Duke Zhao, but Duke Zhuang of Song intervened and the minister Ji Zu installed Tu as Duke Li. Duke Zhao was later restored and then murdered by the vice minister Gao Qumi, who set up Men; Duke Xiang of Qi had Men and Gao Qumi killed, and Ji Zu made Yi duke. In 680 BCE Duke Li returned with Qi troops, defeated Yi and restored himself, and all later dukes of Zheng descended from him.
dukhan: Dukhan lies in the western municipality of Al-Shahaniya, west of the capital, Doha; it was formerly part of Al Rayyan municipality. Its name means smoke, a reference to the clouds that gathered round the summit of Jebel Dukhan, the smoky mountain, and later to the gas flares of the oil camp. The oil field sits on the Dukhan anticline, a group of folds about 80 kilometres long that runs parallel to the west coast. To the north lies the Dukhan Sabkha, a salt flat that holds the lowest point of Qatar, 6 metres below sea level. The area is also among the most important Paleolithic sites of the peninsula.

Oil exploration in the area began in 1935, and the settlement was built as a camp for staff of the Qatar Petroleum Company. Operations stopped during the Second World War, and supplies of water, food and machinery came from Bahrain through the shallow harbour of Zekreet. The first barrel of oil was exported on 31 December 1949, and the full development of the fields was completed in 1954. Natural gas was found in the Khuff Reservoir in 1959, a year after the Dukhan power station was commissioned.

The first road to Doha was built in 1940, and the journey by car took about three hours; Dukhan Airport, built in the late 1930s, was the country's first airport until Doha International Airport opened in 1959. The fenced camp had eight residential zones, schools, a hospital, two mosques and a church, and in the 1940s communities grew up outside it, notably in the Khatiyah sector. In the 1950s the government had Dukhan build settlements for Bedouins, among them Al Zeghain, Afjan, Zekreet and Al Da'asa. Al Khotba Mosque, built in 1942, is one of the oldest in the region.

The town is administered by the state oil company, QatarEnergy, and entry requires a gate pass from it. Its three oil-producing sectors are Khatiyah, Fahahil and Jaleha. The Dukhan Highway, a four-lane motorway of about 66 kilometres, links it to Doha.
dule-temple: The Dule Temple, whose name means Temple of Solitary Joy, goes back at least to the early Tang dynasty, though the year of its founding is unknown and no Tang building survives. In 755 An Lushan held a rally there at the start of his rebellion against the Tang emperor, and the name may refer to him, since he was also known as An Dule, or to the Dule River north-west of the city. The front gate (shanmen) and the Guanyin Pavilion were rebuilt in 984, the second year of the Tonghe era of the Liao dynasty, by local architects and craftsmen working with Tang techniques.

The complex faces south. The shanmen is a single-storey gate 10 metres tall, with ridge ornaments (chiwen) of the Liao period, two Liao clay guardian figures, frescoes of the Four Heavenly Kings from the Qing dynasty and a plaque said to be in the hand of the Ming prime minister Yan Song (1480–1567). The Guanyin Pavilion, about 23 metres high and made of more than one thousand pieces, is built around the statue of the Eleven-Headed Guanyin, the largest of its kind in China, flanked by Liao statues of attendants.

Rings of columns and bracket sets (dougong) let worshippers see the figure from several levels, and an octagonal caisson covers the open space at its centre. The murals inside were added in a restoration of 1753.

In 1928 soldiers of the warlord Sun Dianying, who looted the nearby Eastern Qing Tombs, used the main hall as barracks and left bullet holes in its timbers, and in 1929 the temple became the Jixian Village Normal School. In the early 1930s it was studied by the Japanese scholar Sadako Sekino and by Liang Sicheng, who in 1966 proposed protecting it with lightning rods, doors and windows. It was listed in 1961 among the first National Priority Protected Sites. The Tangshan earthquake of July 1976 brought down parts of the White Tower, and a survey in 1982 found that the top of the statue had moved about 15 centimetres to the south-west.
duleek: Duleek lies in County Meath, 8 km south-west of Drogheda and 35 km north of Dublin city centre, close to the River Nanny. It is the centre of a civil parish of the same name. Its Irish name, Damhliag, is made of the words daimh and liag, house of stones, and refers to the early stone-built St. Cianán's Church, whose ruins can still be seen in the village.

Duleek began as an early Christian monastic settlement. Tradition holds that Saint Patrick established a bishopric there about 450 and placed it in the care of Saint Cianán on 24 November 489, and that Patrick and several contemporaries spent a winter at the monastery while compiling the Seanchas Mór, the first written compilation of the Brehon Laws. The settlement was sacked several times by the Norsemen between 830 and 1149. In April 1014 the bodies of Brian Ború and his son lay in state at Duleek on their way to Armagh.

The Normans pillaged Duleek in 1171. Hugh de Lacy, the first Anglo-Norman Lord of Meath, built a motte castle and established a manor there, and in 1180 he granted St. Cianán's Church and lands to the Augustinians. In the 12th century the old monastery was reconstituted as Saint Mary's Abbey, and the Diocese of Duleek was absorbed into the Diocese of Meath. About 1172 Augustinian monks from Llanthony in Monmouthshire founded the Grange of Saint Michael on lands given by the De Lacy family; its ruins stand in the townland of Abbeyland, near Duleek House.

Later centuries left their own marks. The Wayward Cross outside the village was put up in 1601 by Janet Dowdall in memory of her husband, Sir William Bathe of Athcarne Castle. The village's four crosses and the lime tree on its green recall Duleek's part in the struggle between William III and James II. During World War II, known in Ireland as The Emergency, German bombers struck the village by accident on 1 January 1941, causing minor damage and no casualties.

The 2022 census counted 4,899 people in Duleek, twice the number of 2002. A 10th-century high cross with New Testament scenes on its west side stands north of the church, and a segment of another cross is kept inside it. The Duleek Heritage Trail links the historic sites of the village centre.
duleep-singh: Duleep Singh was born on 6 September 1838, the youngest son of Maharaja Ranjit Singh and the only child of Maharani Jind Kaur. After Ranjit Singh died in 1839, he lived quietly with his mother at Jammu. In 1843, after the assassinations of Maharaja Sher Singh and Dhian Singh, they were recalled to Lahore, and on 16 September the Panch, the military council, proclaimed the five-year-old Maharaja with Jind Kaur as regent.

The British East India Company declared war on the Sikhs on 13 December 1845. After winning the First Anglo-Sikh War it kept the boy as nominal ruler but replaced the Maharani with a Council of Regency and later imprisoned and exiled her. Thirteen years passed before he was allowed to see her again. After the Second Anglo-Sikh War the Punjab was annexed on 29 March 1849 and he was deposed at the age of ten. He was given a pension of 120,000 rupees a year and told he could live anywhere but the Punjab. His property, worth 15 million rupees, including the Koh-i-Noor diamond, was taken from him.

He was placed in the care of Dr John Login and sent to Fatehgarh, with tight limits on whom he could meet. Company policy was to Anglicise him in every respect. On 8 March 1853, before he turned fifteen, he converted to Christianity with the approval of Lord Dalhousie, who expected the conversion to destroy any remaining influence he had in the Punjab. The conversion remains controversial, and he later regretted it. In May 1854 he was sent into exile in Britain.

In Britain Queen Victoria befriended him and was godmother to several of his children. He lived at Castle Menzies in Perthshire and later bought the 17,000-acre Elveden estate in Suffolk, which he turned into a game preserve. In 1861 he was allowed to go to India to meet his mother and bring her to England, and in 1863 he returned with her ashes. He married Bamba Müller in Alexandria in 1864.

Disaffected, in debt and with his pension reduced, he reverted to Sikhism and tried to return to India. In 1886 he sailed for home, but the British stopped him at Aden and made him return to Europe, which left him more bitter. He tried to find allies among other European powers and threatened an invasion of India through the North-West Frontier, but this was not taken seriously. Later he apologised to Queen Victoria and his pension was resumed. He died in Paris, and as the British feared unrest, his wish to be buried in India was refused; he lies in Elveden Church beside his wife Bamba. All his children died without legitimate issue.
dulo-clan: The Dulo were a ruling dynasty of the Bulgars, who were of Turkic origin. Their elite is generally considered related to the Huns and the Western Turkic Khaganate, and the clan is said to descend from the rulers of Old Great Bulgaria, a centralised monarchy, unlike earlier Hunno-Turkic entities, which were tribal confederations. Its exact origin is obscure. Some researchers link it to the five Duolu tribes of the Western Turks, and Omeljan Pritsak connected its name with that of an old Xiongnu ruling house, though Peter B. Golden regards the Turkic and Xiongnu associations as speculative. Etymologies of the name are also speculative.

Most of what is known comes from the Nominalia of the Bulgarian khans. It lists Avitohol, who lived 300 years, and Irnik, who lived 150, as Dulo, and rulers of Old Great Bulgaria and of the First Bulgarian Empire traced descent from Attila through Irnik, possibly Attila's attested son Ernak. Historians disagree. Josef Marquart identified Avitohol with Attila, while Jean W. Sedlar thought the Attila connection doubtful. Vasil Zlatarski held that Irnik and Ernak were different persons, since the Nominalia gives Irnik's accession as 437, before Attila's death in 453.

Kubrat, a member of the clan, revolted against the Pannonian Avars and founded Old Great Bulgaria in what is now Ukraine. In the second half of the 7th century his sons split the family and spread across Europe: Bezmer in Ukraine, Kotrag on the Volga, Kuber in Balkan Macedonia, Asparukh on the Danube and Alcek at Sepino, Bojano and Isernia. Bezmer was the last Dulo ruler north of the Danube, and Asparukh the first south of it, followed by Tervel and then Sevar, the last Dulo ruler of Bulgaria. According to Theophanes, in 761 or 762 the Bulgars rose up, killed their hereditary lords and set up Teletzes as king, which historians usually read as a massacre of the Dulo.

In the pagan period succession in the clan followed traditions brought from the Eurasian steppe, including the rulers' divine ancestry. The Khan stood at the head of the clan as head of state, military leader and probably high priest of the Bulgar god Tangra. Mercia MacDermott claimed that the clan held the dog sacred and that a Bulgarian expression, he kills the dog, meaning he gives the orders, recalls a Dulo khan sacrificing a dog to Tangra for the whole community.
dumat-al-jandal: The name means Dumah of the Stone, and the town is also called Al-Jawf, the depression, after the Wadi Sirhan. It lies north of the Nafud desert, 37 kilometres from Sakaka, within an oasis enclosed by the Dumat al-Jandal Wall. It stood where branches of the incense trade route met, one linking India and South Arabia with Lower Mesopotamia, another linking the Persian Gulf through the Wadi Sirhan with southern Syria. Some scholars identify it with Dumah, one of the twelve sons of Ishmael in the Book of Genesis.

A triangular megalithic platform 35 metres long, surrounded by burials and dating to the 6th millennium BCE, was reported in 2020. Assyrian inscriptions of 845 BCE call the town the capital of an Arab kingdom sometimes named Qedar, and the Esarhaddon Prism of 673–672 BCE calls it the strong city of the Arabians. Five ruling queens are known, among them Zabibe, Šamši, Tabūʿa and Teʾelḫunu, the last also high priestess of Atarsamain; the town had an important temple of Ishtar.

Roman-Nabataean pottery shows a prosperous community under the Nabataeans, and a large open-air Nabataean banqueting hall, used from the late 1st century BCE, was found in 2011. Porphyry reports that a boy was sacrificed there each year. Trajan brought Dumah into the Roman Empire in 106, and it was for over four centuries the easternmost settlement of the Limes Arabicus. Its market fairs, disputed between Arab clients of the Byzantines and the Sasanians, specialised in slavery and prostitution.

Lying about fifteen days' march from Medina, the town was raided three times on Muhammad's orders. The expedition of July 626 found the Ghaṭafān fled, and in 630 Khalid ibn al-Walid captured it for the new Islamic state; in 631 he destroyed the idol Wadd of the Banu Kalb.

Dumat al-Jandal is the historical capital of what is now al-Jouf Province of Saudi Arabia. The Umar Mosque, wrongly attributed to Caliph Umar, has a stone prayer hall and a tapering minaret and faces Marid Castle across a street. The nearby Al-Dar'i Quarter of stone houses and lanes, dating to the middle Islamic age, survives from the old town.
dumbarton-rock: Dumbarton Rock is a plug of basalt 73 metres high that overlooks the town of Dumbarton. It formed between 330 and 340 million years ago, in the Early Carboniferous period, when volcanic activity was widespread around what is now Glasgow, and the softer outer part of the volcano weathered away. Dumbarton Castle, built on it, has the longest recorded history of any stronghold in Scotland. Archaeological finds show a strategically important settlement there at least as far back as the Iron Age, and its people traded with the Romans.

The first written record of the settlement is a letter that Saint Patrick wrote to King Ceretic of Alt Clut in the late 5th century. From the 5th century until the 9th the rock was the centre of the independent Brythonic Kingdom of Strathclyde, and Alt Clut became a metonym for the kingdom. About 570 its king was Riderch Hael, who appears in Welsh and Latin works.

In 756 a joint force of Picts and Northumbrians captured the fortress after a siege, only to lose it again a few days later. The Irish-based Viking kings Amlaíb Conung and Ímar then besieged it, and it fell in four months after its water supply failed. They are recorded as returning to Ireland with 200 ships and many British, English and Pictish captives. Dumbarton Rock then does not appear in the record until the 13th century.

In medieval Scotland it was an important royal castle, and Sir John Menteith is believed to have taken William Wallace through it after his capture. After the Scottish defeat at Halidon Hill on 19 July 1333, its governor Malcolm Fleming of Fulwood sheltered the young King David II and his wife Joan, and later sent them to France; Fleming held the castle against an English siege and was created the first Earl of Wigtown.

In the war of the Rough Wooing Mary, Queen of Scots was lodged there by 22 February 1548, and sailed for France on 7 August 1548. During the Marian Civil War Lord Fleming held it for her until forces of Regent Lennox climbed the rock with ladders and took it in the early hours of 2 April 1571.

Threats from Jacobites and the French in the eighteenth century led to new structures and defences at the castle, which was garrisoned until the Second World War. Inventories survive from 1510, 1571, 1580, 1644 and 1668, listing its guns, furniture and rooms.
dummer: The Dümmer, officially Dümmer See, covers 13.5 square kilometres, or 16 within its ring dyke including the silted zones. It averages about one metre deep, about 1.50 metres at most, and lies at an elevation of 37 metres. It stretches up to 5 kilometres from north to south and 3.4 kilometres from west to east, with flat beaches on its western and eastern shores. The lake sits in the Dümmer depression, and to the west the Damme Hills rise to 145 metres. Fens and raised bogs surround it, within the Dümmer Nature Park of just under 500 square kilometres.
The River Hunte flows through the lake and leaves it by several branches, the largest called the Lohne; others include the Grawiede and the Ompteda Canal. All rejoin 3 kilometres north of Diepholz.

The name is first recorded as diummeri in 965. It probably joins dummerig, moist or shaded, with Meer, the traditional word in north-western Germany for still waters surrounded by marshes. Remains of New Stone Age settlements have been found on its shores. The open water belongs to the district of Diepholz, part of the Electorate of Hanover from the late 16th century, while the western shore lies in the district of Vechta, which belonged for centuries to the Diocese of Münster and passed to Oldenburg in 1803 after the German Mediatisation.

Springs and heavy rain once caused regular floods, so in the 1940s work began on dykes around the lake, using foreign forced labour on a large scale between 1941 and 1945. Without the yearly floods, algae spread and took oxygen from most other life, and the dyking also caused heavy silting. Locks were later used to control high water.

The Dümmer is a resort for water sports and a breeding and resting place for water birds on a route used by migrants. Large parts of its western and southern shores are nature reserves, though the lake suffers from heavy nutrient pollution caused by intensive farming.
dummers-war: The Treaty of Utrecht of 1713 gave mainland Nova Scotia to Britain, but the land between the Kennebec River and the Isthmus of Chignecto stayed contested, and the Wabanaki Confederacy, which had not been party to the treaty, claimed it as its own. After the peace, New Englanders settled east of the Kennebec and fished off Nova Scotia from a permanent station at Canso, which the Miꞌkmaq raided. Massachusetts built forts around the mouth of the Kennebec, and at Arrowsic in 1717 the Kennebec sachem Wiwurna objected to new settlements while Governor Samuel Shute insisted on the colonists' right to expand.

Shute blamed the Jesuit Sébastien Rale for Wabanaki resistance. Early in 1722 Colonel Thomas Westbrook's 300 soldiers surrounded Norridgewock to seize him; Rale escaped, but his strongbox held letters promising the Indians enough ammunition to drive out the settlers. The Abenaki answered by raiding Fort George at Brunswick, and on 25 July 1722 Shute declared war.

Lieutenant Governor William Dummer ran the war after Shute sailed for England late in 1722. Wabanaki raids struck Arrowsic, Brunswick and the Kennebec settlements, the Miꞌkmaq and Maliseet blockaded Annapolis Royal and seized fishing vessels, and in 1723 Westbrook burned the empty Penobscot village. On 22 August 1724 rangers under Jeremiah Moulton and Johnson Harmon attacked Norridgewock, killing Rale, a leading chief and nearly two dozen women and children. In the west, Chief Gray Lock raided towns in Massachusetts, and Fort Dummer, built near present Brattleboro, became Vermont's first permanent colonial settlement. On 9 May 1725 Chief Paugus's Pequawket war party ambushed Captain John Lovewell's company near Fryeburg; Lovewell and Paugus were both killed.

Dummer announced a cessation of hostilities with the Penobscot on 31 July 1725, though Chief Loron rejected the British claim of sovereignty over his people. Treaties followed in December 1725 and June 1726, and only Gray Lock stayed out of the peace reconfirmed at Falmouth in 1727. The Indian population of the Kennebec and Penobscot declined, many withdrawing to St. Francis and Bécancour, and western Maine came more firmly under British control. The Miꞌkmaq and Maliseet refused to declare themselves British subjects, and Nova Scotia had peace for 18 years. Lovewell's Fight was later told in song and story, by Henry Wadsworth Longfellow and Nathaniel Hawthorne among others.
dumnorix: Dumnorix, whose name is spelled Dubnoreix on coins, was the younger brother of Divitiacus, the Aedui druid and statesman. The Aedui were allies of Rome, and the two brothers stood on opposite sides of that alliance: Divitiacus led the pro-Roman faction and would later aid Julius Caesar in his conquest of Gaul, while Dumnorix led those who, in Caesar's words, thought it better to be dominated by their fellow Gauls than by the Romans. Both brothers appear in Caesar's Commentaries on the Gallic War, the main account of his life.

His name carries the Gaulish suffix -rix, related to the Latin rex and indicating kingship or rule, as in Ambiorix, Orgetorix and Vercingetorix. Dumno- is related to the Gaelic domhan, world, so the name may be translated as king of the world.

Before Caesar's governorship of Transalpine Gaul, the Helvetii chieftain Orgetorix conspired with Dumnorix and Casticus of the Sequani to make themselves kings in their own tribes and then rule all of Gaul by their combined power. Orgetorix married his daughter to Dumnorix to seal the alliance, but the plot was discovered and Orgetorix died soon after amid rumours of suicide.

Dumnorix then used his influence to persuade the Sequani to let the Helvetii migrate through their territory. When Caesar arrived in 58 BCE and opposed the migration, he required the Aedui to supply his soldiers with grain. Dumnorix, popular and followed by a large body of personal retainers, delayed the supply. His retainers formed a sizeable part of the Gallic cavalry screening Caesar's pursuit of the Helvetii, and at a key moment in one engagement he withdrew his unit, handing the Helvetii the victory.

Liscus, the chief magistrate or Vergobretus of the Aedui, revealed to Caesar that Dumnorix was behind both the withheld grain and the cavalry's flight. Divitiacus interceded for his brother, and Caesar placed Dumnorix under surveillance instead of punishing him.

Caesar chose Dumnorix as one of the Gaulish leaders he would take as hostages on his second expedition to Britain, fearing trouble in his absence. Dumnorix pleaded fear of the sea and religious obligations, then claimed that Caesar meant to have them all killed out of sight of their people. Finally he fled the camp with the Aeduan cavalry. Pursued by the rest of Caesar's horsemen, he was killed shouting that he was a free man and a citizen of a free state, and the Aeduan cavalry returned to Caesar's service.
dumyat: Though small, Dumyat's characteristic shape is an important part of the scenery around Stirling, and it is often pictured with the nearby Abbey Craig. The hill has two principal summits, Castle Law to the west and Dumyat proper to the east. A prominent gully running almost straight up the southern scarp was long the favourite route to the top. It was formed by erosion along a fault where soft pyroclastic rocks meet harder andesite and basalt, part of the disturbance caused by the Ochil Fault.

Further gullies branch from the main fault into Dumyat, among them Raeburn's Gulley and Siart Gulley. Today many walkers start from Sheriffmuir and take a longer, gentler path to the summit, passing just north of Castle Law, while a third route climbs from the east through Menstrie Glen.

On the summit of Castle Law the remains of a hill fort, originally occupied by the Maeatae, are still clearly visible, and the fort is a scheduled monument. Excavation by Murray Cook and Gordon Noble of Aberdeen University has produced radiocarbon dates showing at least two periods of use, around 500 BCE and between the 5th and 7th centuries CE.

The exposed hill and the surrounding moor are suitable only for sheep farming, and sheep folds and the ruins of a shepherd's stone house stand on its slopes. Copper and barytes were once mined there on a small scale. The scree of Castle Law is a source of agates, and occasionally of smoky quartz and citrine, along with quartz, calcite, barytes and the copper ores malachite and azurite.

The hill is a popular climb for visitors to Stirling and the Trossachs, close to the Wallace Monument. On the top stand a memorial to the Argyll and Sutherland Highlanders, a trig point and a cairn with a beacon, commissioned for the Queen's Silver Jubilee in 1977, carried up by the Menstrie Scout Group and lit as part of the UK chain of jubilee beacons.
dunadd: Dunadd takes its name from the River Add: in Scottish Gaelic it is Dún Ad, fort on the Add, and in Old Irish Dún Att. The rocky crag lies a little north of Lochgilphead. The land around it, now largely reclaimed, was once boggy ground known in Gaelic as the Mòine Mhòr, the Great Moor, which added to the strength of the site. Studies of sea-level change in the region argue that the crag was an island or a promontory into historic times, and that falling sea levels left the fort open to siege and seizure in the 6th to 7th centuries.

The site was first occupied in the Iron Age before it became a seat of the kings of Dál Riata, a Gaelic kingdom that spanned the northern Irish coast, Argyll and the Scottish islands. Besides the footprint, basin and boar, the summit rock bears an inscription in the ogham script, read as referring to a Finn Manach and dated to the late 8th century or after.

The Annals of Ulster mention Dunadd twice. For 683 they record the siege of Dún At and the siege of Dún Duirn, without naming the outcome or those involved. For 736 they record that Aengus son of Fergus, king of the Picts, laid waste Dál Riata, seized Dún At and bound in chains two sons of Selbach, Donngal and Feradach. The fort was still occupied after 736, at least into the 9th century.

Later sources show that the place kept some importance. In 1436 Alan son of John Riabhach MacLachlan of Dunadd was made seneschal of the lands of Glassary, and the MacLachlans of Dunadd lived below the fort. In June 1506 commissioners appointed by James IV, among them the earl and bishop of Argyll, met there to collect rents and settle feuds.

Dunadd was excavated in 1904–1905, 1929 and 1980, and its finds, dating from the 6th to the 8th centuries, include tools, weapons, quernstones and moulds for fine metalwork; they form one of the most important groups from any early medieval site in Scotland. Glass beads found at Bruach An Druimein, seven kilometres to the north, match those of Dunadd in composition. The fort is an ancient monument in the care of Historic Scotland and is open to the public.
dunama-dabbalemi: Dunama, also called Dunama Selmami and numbered Dunama II, was a son of mai Selema II, also known as Abd al-Jalil, and of Dibala, who came from the tribe of the Maghárma. He succeeded his father in the early 13th century. Besides later oral history and documents of Kanem–Bornu, a few details of his reign were recorded by the contemporary Arab geographer Ibn Sa'id al-Maghribi.

Dunama built up a large cavalry force early in his reign and has been credited with introducing cavalry to Central Africa, perhaps inspired by the Mamluk horsemen of Egypt; the import of mail armour may also have begun under him. His wars against non-Muslim neighbours were justified as jihad. He brought the whole of Fezzan under Kanem, fought a long war against the Toubou, raided the shores of Lake Chad with a fleet and campaigned against the Sao as far south as Mafoni. His authority reached Kano in the west, the Ouaddaï highlands in the east and the Adamawa Plateau in the south.

A fervent Muslim, he made the Hajj twice and pressed his subjects to abandon their traditional practices. Later accounts say he opened the mune, a sacred object whose nature is unclear, an act widely seen as having brought the empire misfortune. He had a hostel built in Cairo for Kanem's pilgrims and students, and in 1257 sent an embassy with a giraffe to the Hafsid sultan Muhammad I al-Mustansir of Tunisia. Slaves captured in his southern wars were sold north across the Sahara for horses and other scarce goods.

Late in his reign the traditionalist Bilala grew alienated and his sons, who led many of his campaigns, became effective governors of the outer territories; one king list speaks of a civil war caused by the greed of his children. Dunama died at Zamtam in Bornu and was succeeded by his son Kade I Aujami, but a succession conflict among his sons soon broke out and lasted for decades.
duncan-i-of-scotland: Duncan, in Gaelic Donnchad mac Crinain, was nicknamed An t-Ilgarach, the Diseased or the Sick. His ancestry is not certain, but modern texts make him the son of Crínán, hereditary lay abbot of Dunkeld, and Bethóc, a daughter of King Malcolm II. Earlier histories that follow John of Fordun supposed that he had ruled Strathclyde as an appanage between 1018 and 1034, an idea modern historians discount, though the Oxford Dictionary of National Biography supports it. Unlike the aged king of Shakespeare's Macbeth, the historical Duncan appears to have been a young man.

Malcolm II died on 25 November 1034 and Duncan succeeded him without apparent opposition. He may have been Malcolm's acknowledged successor, or tánaiste. The early part of his reign seems to have been uneventful, perhaps because of his youth. Macbeth is recorded as his dux, a word that meant a war leader, and since the dukes of Francia had replaced the Carolingian kings of the Franks half a century earlier, and England's Godwin of Wessex was also called dux, Macbeth may have been the power behind the throne.

In 1039 Duncan led a large Scottish army south to besiege Durham, and the expedition ended in disaster, though he survived. The following year he led an army north into Moray, Macbeth's domain, apparently on a punitive expedition. He was killed in action at the battle of Bothnagowan, now Pitgaveny near Elgin, by the men of Moray under Macbeth, probably on 14 August 1040.

Duncan is thought to have been buried at Elgin and later moved to the island of Iona. A variant of the Chronicle of the Kings of Alba gives his wife the Gaelic name Suthen, while John of Fordun, writing in the 14th century, made her a kinswoman of Siward, Earl of Northumbria, who would help restore her son Malcolm to the throne. Duncan had at least two sons.

Malcolm III, also called Máel Coluim mac Donnchada, was king from 1058 to 1093, after he assassinated and usurped Lulach, Macbeth's stepson. The second son, Donald III, or Domnall Bán, was king afterwards. Máel Muire, Earl of Atholl, is a possible third son, though this is uncertain. Duncan is the historical basis of the King Duncan of Shakespeare's Macbeth, written in 1606, in which he is killed in his sleep by Macbeth.
duncan-stewart-colonial-administrator: Duncan George Stewart was born on 22 October 1904 at Witkleifontein in the Transvaal Colony, now part of South Africa, to British parents posted there. He was educated in England at Winchester College and Oriel College, Oxford, where he took a BA. He was married and had three children.

Stewart joined the Colonial Administration Service in 1928. He served as a district officer in the Oya Territory of Nigeria, as colonial secretary in the Bahamas, as secretary of finance in Mandatory Palestine and as secretary of the governors' conference in South Africa. In 1948 he was made a Companion of the Order of St Michael and St George. His record was regarded as exceptional, and Lord Listowel, minister of state for colonial affairs, named him governor and commander-in-chief of Sarawak in succession to Charles Arden-Clarke.

Only a couple of weeks after taking office, Stewart made his first official visit within the colony, to Sibu, on 3 December 1949. Press reports described large and cheerful crowds. After he had inspected an honour guard and met a group of schoolchildren, a youth, Moshidi bin Sedek, approached holding a camera and asking for a picture, and as Stewart posed Rosli Dhobi stabbed him. Both youths were arrested on the spot.

Despite a deep wound, Stewart is reported to have tried to carry on until blood seeped through his white uniform. He was taken to Kuching for treatment and then flown to the General Hospital in Singapore, where he died on 10 December 1949. The two youths and two other conspirators were convicted of his murder and hanged.

Documents released in the late 20th century show that the British government knew that Anthony Brooke, whom opponents of the cession hoped to restore to the throne of Sarawak, had not been involved, but kept silent so as not to provoke Indonesia, newly independent after its war with the Netherlands, while the UK was already facing the Malayan Emergency.
dundrennan-abbey: The abbey stands at Dundrennan, near Kirkcudbright, and was built in the Romanesque style. Although it is extensively ruined, with the transepts as its main surviving parts, it is noted for the purity and restraint of its architecture, which reflects the austere Cistercian ideal. It was built of a very hard-weathering grey sandstone, so that its original forms and mouldings are well preserved.

In the mid 12th century the abbey's founder, Fergus of Galloway, also revived the Bishopric of Whithorn, a see first set up by the Northumbrians, whose last recorded bishop, Beadwulf, was noted around 803. On 9 December 1125 Pope Honorius II ordered the bishop-elect, a cleric named Gille Aldan, to appear before Archbishop Thurstan of York, who needed a third suffragan. A deal between York and Fergus probably kept the Galwegian church independent of both Man and Scotland.

Alan of Galloway was buried at the abbey. After the Battle of Langside in 1568, Mary, Queen of Scots spent her last night in Scotland here and sailed from Port Mary across the Solway to Workington; shortly afterwards she was imprisoned by the English. In 1587, after the Scottish Reformation, its lands passed to the Crown, and the buildings fell into ruin once they were used to house livestock.

Historic Environment Scotland maintains the abbey as a scheduled monument. In the 1990s it funded excavations of the south-east corner of the cloister, which found a warming house, a novices' day room, a great drain and the undercroft of a latrine block. With geophysical survey and test trenches, they traced the building in five periods, from about 1170 to about 1600.
dungan-people: Dungan is a term used in territories of the former Soviet Union for Muslims of Hui origin; Turkic-speaking peoples in Xinjiang also sometimes call Hui Muslims Dungans. In Central Asia the Dungans call themselves Hui. The name is of obscure origin. One theory derives it from the Turkic word doñan, one who turns, comparable to the Chinese hui, and another from Donggan, Eastern Gansu, the region many Dungans trace their ancestry to, though the character gan differs. Central Asian Turkic and Tajik speakers have used it for Chinese-speaking Muslims for several centuries, and English and German writers used it from the 1830s.

The Dungans of the former Soviet republics descend from Hui who fled China after the Hui Minorities' War, also called the Dungan Rebellion, of the nineteenth century. According to Rimsky-Korsakoff, three groups crossed the Tian Shan into the Russian Empire in the severe winter of 1877-1878. About 1,000 people from Turpan, led by Ma Daren, reached Osh. A second group from Didaozhou in Gansu, led by the ahong Ma Yusuf, settled in the spring of 1878 at Yrdyk near Karakol; they numbered 1,130. A third, from Shaanxi, led by the rebel Bai Yanhu, settled at Karakunuz, now Masanchi, and numbered 3,314.

Under the Treaty of Saint Petersburg of 1881, which required Russian withdrawal from the Upper Ili basin, the Hui and Uyghur people of the Kulja area could move to the Russian side; Russian statistics record 4,682 Hui who did so between 1881 and 1883, settling at Sokuluk and in southeastern Kazakhstan and northern Kyrgyzstan. Some Dungans served in the Red Army in the Second World War. In February 2020 a conflict between ethnic Kazakhs and Dungans at Korday in Kazakhstan left ten dead according to official Kazakh sources, and about 600 people fled to Kyrgyzstan.

The Dungan language, which Dungans call the Hui language, is close to the Zhongyuan dialect of Mandarin spoken in southern Gansu and western Guanzhong in Shaanxi. It is tonal, preserves archaic Qing-era vocabulary, has loanwords from Russian, Arabic, Persian and Turkic, and is uniquely written in the Cyrillic script. More than two-thirds of Dungans also speak Russian.

Dungans keep elements of Chinese culture in cuisine and dress, and they practised foot binding until 1948, when the Soviet government banned it. Traditional marriage practices with matchmakers remain widespread. The Shaanxi Dungans hold more closely to Chinese customs than the Gansu Dungans. They have been counted in censuses as separate from Chinese, with 36,900 in Kazakhstan in 1999 and 58,409 in Kyrgyzstan in 2009. The nineteenth-century explorer Henry Lansdell noted that they abstained from spirits and opium and worked in farming, gardening and trade.
dungannon: For centuries Dungannon's fortunes were tied to the O'Neill dynasty, which ruled a large part of Ulster until the 17th century. The O'Neills were traditionally inaugurated at Tullyhogue Fort, an Iron Age mound some four miles north-east of the town, where the O'Hagan clan were stewards. In the 14th century they built a castle on Castle Hill. Hugh O'Neill, 2nd Earl of Tyrone, burned it in 1602 as Crown forces under Lord Mountjoy closed in near the end of the Nine Years' War. After the Flight of the Earls in 1607, the lands were confiscated in the Plantation of Ulster, and Dungannon and its castle were granted to Sir Arthur Chichester.

Sir Phelim O'Neill seized the town at the start of the Irish Rebellion of 1641 and issued the Proclamation of Dungannon, setting out the rebels' aims and professing loyalty to Charles I. The town changed hands several times in the Irish Confederate Wars, and in 1689 a Jacobite force occupied Castle Hill, which hosted King James II on his way to the Siege of Derry.

In 1782, as the most central town of Ulster, Dungannon was chosen for a convention of the Volunteers, who had formed for defence against the French in the American War of Independence. Delegates from 147 corps met at the Presbyterian church on Scotch Street and resolved that the British Crown's claim to overrule the Irish Parliament in Dublin was unconstitutional and illegal. Further conventions followed in 1783 and 1793, when the Volunteers divided over Catholic emancipation and parliamentary reform. Local veterans split between the Orangemen and the United Irishmen, and martial law from January 1797 broke the local United Irish organisation.

The town became a linen centre; by 1802 a surveyor described it as one of the most prosperous in the north of Ireland in the linen trade. A workhouse opened in 1842 and closed in 1948, and a memorial commemorates those sheltered there, including victims of the Great Famine.

Dungannon had 16,282 people at the 2021 census and is the second-largest town in the historic County Tyrone. In 1963 protests against housing allocation began a campaign that led to Northern Ireland's first civil rights march, from Coalisland to Dungannon, on 24 August 1968. During the Troubles almost 50 people were killed in and around the town. The poultry processor Moy Park, founded in 1943 in the neighbouring village of Moygashel, is the largest employer, and since the 1990s the food industry has drawn workers from abroad, including Lithuania, East Timor, Portugal, Brazil and Mozambique. Since 2015 the town has shared local government with Magherafelt and Cookstown in the Mid-Ulster District Council.
dunhuang: Dunhuang lies in an oasis in the far northwest of Gansu, with Crescent Lake and the Singing Sand Dunes nearby. It commands the western entrance to the Hexi Corridor, which leads to the north Chinese plains and the ancient capitals of Chang'an and Luoyang, and it stands where the southern Silk Road meets the road from India via Lhasa to Mongolia and southern Siberia. Its name is usually taken to mean Blazing Beacon, after the watchtowers lit to warn of raiding nomads, though scholars have proposed several other derivations.

By the 3rd century BCE the area was dominated by the Xiongnu, and it came under Chinese rule after Emperor Wu defeated them in 121 BCE. Dunhuang became one of four frontier garrison towns, and the Great Wall was extended to it. By the 2nd century CE the town had more than 76,000 people and served as a supply base for caravans crossing the desert. The first Buddhist caves of the area were cut in 353. Under the Sui and Tang it was a main stop on the routes between China and the rest of the world, and Sogdian merchants founded large colonies there.
