After the An Lushan Rebellion weakened the Tang, the Tibetan Empire occupied the city until the local general Zhang Yichao expelled the Tibetans in 848. From 848 to about 1036 the city, under the Guiyi Circuit, was a multicultural entrepôt with one of the largest Sogdian communities in China. The Tanguts of Western Xia captured it in 1036, and the Mongols took it in 1227. Under the Ming it declined as trade moved to the southern sea routes. The present town was founded in 1725, east of the ruined old city.

Dunhuang is a county-level city in the prefecture-level city of Jiuquan. The Mogao Caves, 25 kilometres southeast of the city, hold 735 caves noted for Buddhist murals and statues and for the hoard of manuscripts found sealed in one cave. Other sites include the Yumen Pass, built in 111 BCE, the Yang Pass and the White Horse Pagoda. The manuscripts and artefacts from Dunhuang have been digitised by the International Dunhuang Project.
dunkeld: Dunkeld lies on the north bank of the Tay opposite Birnam, close to the Highland Boundary Fault, about 25 kilometres north of Perth on the A9, and is often called the Gateway to the Highlands. Its name, from the Gaelic Dùn Chailleann, means fort of the Caledonians, probably the hill fort on King's Seat just north of the town, which suggests the place mattered as far back as the Iron Age. Much of the surrounding countryside is the River Tay (Dunkeld) National Scenic Area, and the Birnam Oak nearby is believed to be the last tree of the Birnam Wood named in Shakespeare's Macbeth.

Dunkeld is said to have been founded by Caustantín son of Fergus, king of the Picts, who died in 820, and a Pictish monastery stood there. The relics of St Columba were divided between Dunkeld and Kells in Ireland to keep them from Viking raiders. For a time Dunkeld was the chief church of eastern Scotland, a place it yielded to St Andrews in the 10th century. Danish Vikings raided it in 903, but it flourished into the 11th century. Alexander I revived the see, and by 1300 the diocese held sixty parish churches.

The cathedral choir dates to the 13th and 14th centuries, the nave to the early 15th, and the tower and chapter house to 1450 to 1475. It was stripped after the Reformation, and its nave has been roofless since the early 17th century. On 21 August 1689 the Cameronian Regiment under William Cleland, who died in the fight, held the town against the Jacobites in the Battle of Dunkeld, which destroyed most of the old town. Thomas Telford's bridge of 1809 changed the town's layout.

The rebuilt town is one of the most complete 18th-century country towns in Scotland, and the National Trust for Scotland has restored about twenty of its houses. The choir of the cathedral is still the parish church, the nave and tower are in the care of Historic Environment Scotland, and murals of about 1490 survive beneath the tower vault.
dunkirk: Dunkirk lies on the North Sea, 10 kilometres from the Belgian border, in the department of Nord. Its name derives from West Flemish dun, dune, and kerke, church, and so means church in the dunes. French Flemish, the local variety of Dutch, was commonly spoken there until the middle of the 20th century.

A fishing village arose in the late 10th century in a flooded coastal area held by the Counts of Flanders. About 960 Count Baldwin III had a wall built to protect it from Viking raids, and monks of Bergues Abbey drained the surrounding wetlands. The name is first mentioned in a tithe privilege of 27 May 1067. From 1384 it passed with Flanders to the Burgundian dukes and later to the Habsburg Netherlands. It was briefly held by Dutch rebels from 1577, and after Spanish forces retook it in 1583 it became a base for privateers known as the Dunkirkers. It changed hands between Spain, France and England until Charles II of England sold it to France on 17 October 1662 for £320,000.

In the First World War the city was bombarded from 1915, including by the German gun Lange Max in 1917, and its population fell from 39,000 in 1914 to 7,000 in the autumn of 1917. In 1940 more than 400,000 Allied soldiers were trapped around the port. Churchill ordered every available ship and boat to collect them, and 338,226 men, among them 123,000 French soldiers, were evacuated in Operation Dynamo. German forces held Dunkirk as a fortress until its commander surrendered on 9 May 1945.

Dunkirk is a port city with a commune population of about 86,000, and its harbour is the third largest in France. Its economy rests on steel, food processing, oil refining, shipbuilding and chemicals. Two of its belfries belong to the group of belfries of Belgium and France inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2005.
dunnottar-castle: Dunnottar, from the Gaelic Dùn Fhoithear, fort on the shelving slope, stands about 2 miles (3 km) south of Stonehaven. The ruins cover 1.4 hectares of a headland surrounded by cliffs that drop 160 feet (50 metres) to the North Sea. A narrow strip of land joins it to the mainland, and a steep path leads to the gatehouse. Its position let its owners control the coastal terrace between the cliffs and the hills of the Mounth, the route to and from north-east Scotland. The principal buildings are the 14th-century tower house, the gatehouse, the chapel and the 16th-century palace, which includes the Whigs' Vault.

A chapel is said to have been founded by St Ninian in the 5th century. The Annals of Ulster record two sieges of Dún Foither in 681 and 694, and the Chronicle of the Kings of Alba says that King Donald II was killed at Dunnottar in a Viking attack in 900. Excavations in the 1980s found no firm evidence of early medieval fortification, and Pictish stones at the nearby sea stack of Dunnicaer have led to speculation that Dún Foither lay elsewhere.

In 1297, according to the poet Blind Harry, William Wallace captured it from the English and burned prisoners in the church. In 1336 Edward III had it rebuilt as a base, and Sir Andrew Murray destroyed the defences again the same year. From about 1359 it passed to the Keiths, who became Earls Marischal in the mid 15th century and held it until the 18th. George Keith, 5th Earl Marischal, rebuilt it from 1581 with a palace around a quadrangle.

In 1651 the Honours of Scotland, the crown, sceptre and sword, were placed at Dunnottar against Cromwell's army. During the blockade Elizabeth Douglas, wife of the lieutenant-governor Sir George Ogilvie, and Christian Fletcher, wife of the minister of Kinneff, smuggled them out, and they were buried under the floor of the Old Kirk at Kinneff. Ogilvie surrendered on 24 May 1652.

In 1685, 167 Covenanters, 122 men and 45 women, were held in a cellar of the castle. Five died there and many of the rest were transported to Perth Amboy, New Jersey. After George Keith, 10th Earl Marischal, took part in the Jacobite rising of 1715, his titles and estates were forfeited in 1716. The York Buildings Company bought the estate in 1720 and dismantled much of the castle.

Lord Cowdray bought the castle in 1919, and his wife began repairs. It is a scheduled monument, designated in 1970, and is open to the public. Parts of the 1990 film Hamlet were shot there, and the castle was chosen as the home of Merida in the film Brave.
dunsterforce: After the Russian Revolution of 1917 the Tsarist armies dissolved, leaving the Caspian Sea and the route from Baku to Krasnovodsk and Central Asia open to the Central Powers. The Eastern Committee of the War Cabinet, judging that British India had been drained of troops, decided to send a mission of picked men to train local recruits at Tiflis. The force was formed in December 1917 from fewer than 350 Australian, New Zealand, British and Canadian officers and NCOs drawn from the Western and Mesopotamian fronts, the largest number from the Australians.

Lieutenant-General William Marshall, commanding the Mesopotamian Expeditionary Force, had severe doubts and called it a mad enterprise that would obstruct the main campaign. Dunsterville arrived in Baghdad on 18 January and on 27 January set off along the Persian road with a small party in Ford cars and vans.

In July 1918 Captain Stanley Savige led a party of five officers and fifteen NCOs towards Urmia and was caught up in the flight of about 80,000 Armenians and Assyrians after the Ottoman Army took the town. The party helped hold off the pursuit, and by the time the rearguard reached Bijar on 17 August only four of its men recovered before the war ended. The rest of the force, reinforced by the 39th Infantry Brigade, drove about 350 kilometres from Hamadan to Baku in 500 Ford vans and armoured cars and fought in the Battle of Baku from 26 August to 14 September. It was disbanded two days after leaving the city.

The Centrocaspian Dictatorship fell on 15 September, when Ottoman-Azerbaijani forces occupied Baku, but the armistice of 30 October obliged the Ottomans to leave. The RAF official historian H. A. Jones wrote in 1937 that the force had failed to reach Tiflis or raise a Caucasian army, but had denied the cotton crop and Baku's oil to the Germans; rumours of its strength also tied down Ottoman troops in Kurdistan. The Australian official historian Charles Bean judged that it had stopped the agents of the Central Powers getting into Iran, and its officers returned to their units, joined Indian battalions or stayed with North Persia Force.
dunwich: Dunwich lies on the North Sea coast within the Suffolk & Essex Coast & Heaths National Landscape, about 148 kilometres north-east of London, 14 kilometres south of Southwold and 11 kilometres north of Leiston. The port grew as a sheltered harbour where the River Dunwich met the sea. Storms and other coastal processes moved the river's mouth 4 kilometres north to Walberswick, and the town lost its reason for being; its sea defences were no longer kept up, and erosion steadily wore it away.

Dommoc was the seat founded by Sigeberht of East Anglia for Saint Felix in about 629–631 and held by bishops until about 870, when the Danes took the kingdom; the historian Rory Naismith speaks of a bishopric of Dunwich, while Richard Hoggett places Dommoc at Walton Castle. The Domesday Book of 1086 gives Dunwich three churches and an estimated 3,000 people. The Earl of Leicester besieged it without success in 1173.

A storm surge on 1 January 1286 destroyed buildings at the town's eastern edge, and two more surges followed in February and December 1287. A storm in 1347 swept some 400 houses into the sea, and the Grote Mandrenke of about 16 January 1362 destroyed much of what was left. All eight medieval churches were lost in time: St Peter's fell between 1688 and 1697, and All Saints', abandoned in the 1750s, went over the cliff between 1904 and 1919. The borough kept the right to send two members to Parliament until the Reform Act 1832 and was one of the most notorious rotten boroughs.

Dunwich is now a small village with a parish meeting instead of a council. The ruins of the 13th-century Franciscan friary of Greyfriars and the Leper Hospital of St James survive, and a buttress of All Saints' tower stands in St James's Church, built in 1832. Sonar and diver surveys from 2008 have mapped the ruins of St Peter's and St Nicholas's churches under the sea, the largest medieval underwater site in Europe, and their results are shown in Dunwich Museum.
duong-dinh-nghe: Dương Đình Nghệ was born in 874 in Ái Châu, modern Thanh Hóa. Some sources, among them Chinese works such as the History of Song and the Zizhi Tongjian, write his name Dương Diên Nghệ, a confusion of two similar-looking characters. He grew up as the Tang dynasty declined. Around 905 Khúc Thừa Dụ had taken the office of jiedushi of Tĩnh Hải quân, beginning native rule, and Dương served three generations of the Khúc clan as a swordsman and commander, an esteemed general under Khúc Hạo.

In 919 Khúc Thừa Mỹ sought investiture from the Later Liang, angering the Southern Han, whose king Liu Yan sent his general Li Ke Zheng against Tĩnh Hải quân in 923; Chinese sources say 930. Khúc Thừa Mỹ was captured and taken to China, and the Southern Han installed Lý Tiến as administrator, with a large army in the fortified garrison of Đại La. In Ái Châu Dương gathered 3,000 warriors whom he regarded as adopted sons, training them at wrestling grounds he set up.

In 931 he marched north and besieged Đại La. Lý Tiến fled back to China; Dương took the fortress, killed the relief commander Trình Bảo in a counter-attack and drove the remaining Chinese forces to the border. He cultivated a circle of young commanders, among them Ngô Quyền, who married his daughter Dương Thị Ngọc.

He was murdered in March 937. After his death the Dương clan kept an indirect influence on politics: Ngô Quyền, Đinh Bộ Lĩnh and Lê Hoàn all married women of the clan, and these women played crucial roles in deciding the succession. The historian Keith Weller Taylor contrasts him with Khúc Thừa Mỹ, who pursued an idealised vision of Tang civilisation: Dương was ready to use practical political power and, by building local authority against the Southern Han, prepared the ground for Vietnamese national consciousness. He is counted among the national heroes of Vietnam.
duong-van-nga: Sources differ on her origins. Some make her the daughter of a subordinate of the warlord Dương Đình Nghệ from Ái province, now Thanh Hóa, while others say that she came from Hoa Lư, the home town of Đinh Tiên Hoàng. As one of his wives she bore his youngest son, Đinh Toàn, in 974.

After Đỗ Thích murdered Đinh Tiên Hoàng and his eldest son Đinh Liễn at the end of 979, the six-year-old Đinh Toàn came to the throne as Đinh Phế Đế. As empress dowager she held the regency with Lê Hoàn, who was made viceroy. The court faced a revolt by the officials Đinh Điền and Nguyễn Bặc, which Lê Hoàn quickly put down, an attack by Ngô Nhật Khánh with forces from Champa, and an invasion by the Song dynasty. With the general Phạm Cự Lượng and most of the court she chose to give the throne to Lê Hoàn in 980, founding the Early Lê dynasty.

The chronicles tell this differently. In the Đại Việt sử lược and the Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư it was Phạm Cự Lượng who proposed the abdication. The Khâm định Việt sử thông giám cương mục holds that she had an affection for Lê Hoàn and played the main part, a view Trần Trọng Kim shared in his Việt Nam sử lược.

Lê Hoàn made her his empress with the title Đại Thắng Minh, the same title her first husband had borne, and she became the first woman in Vietnamese history married to two emperors. The Confucian historian Ngô Sĩ Liên condemned the union as a grave breach of Confucian morals, and Ngô Thì Sĩ mocked the repeated title. She died in 1000, the same year as Lê Thâu, Lê Hoàn's eldest son. She is still worshipped with Lê Đại Hành and his sons in his temple at Hoa Lư, and her life has been the subject of chèo and cải lương plays and of a novel.
dupplin-cross: The cross is carved from Old Red Sandstone and stands about 2.5 metres tall and 1 metre across the arms. It is a high cross, a free-standing stone cross of a kind fairly common in Ireland, Northumbria and Dál Riata but rare among the Picts. Fragments of shattered crosses, probably thrown down at the Reformation of the 16th century, show that more once existed there, and in the 18th century a second, the Cross of Dronachy, was recorded at Invermay, fallen and broken.

Its faces carry religious and martial scenes and the animals typical of Pictish carving. A rider with an oversized head and a ponytail is shown as a man of authority. On the obverse a man fights bears with his bare hands, and the sides show a harpist, probably David, and hunting dogs. Of the inscription only the words CUSTANTIN FILIUS FIRCUS can still be read, taken as the Latin form of the Gaelic name Caustantín son of Fergus.

Thomas Pennant first recorded the cross in 1769 on a hillside in Strathearn, north of Forteviot and Dunning across the River Earn. Because the inscription implies that it was carved during or shortly after Caustantín's reign, it gives a fixed point in the chronology of Pictish sculpture. The Latin text also uses the Gaelic name of the king's father, which shows that Gaelic was spoken at the time. In 2002 the cross passed into the care of Historic Scotland and was placed under the tower of St Serf's Church, which dates from the 11th or 12th century.
dur-kurigalzu: Dur-Kurigalzu stood in southern Mesopotamia near the confluence of the Tigris and Diyala rivers, about 30 kilometres west of the centre of modern Baghdad, at the mound now called Aqar Quf. The prefix Dur is Akkadian for fortress, and the royal name Kurigalzu is believed to mean shepherd of the Kassites. The city lay on an east-west limestone ridge and drew fresh water from the Euphrates through the Isa Canal, known in antiquity as the Patti-Enlil Canal.

The city served as the capital of Babylonia during the reign of Kurigalzu I and as either the capital or at least an important city in the period after. It appears on the toponym lists in the funerary temple of the Egyptian pharaoh Amenophis III at Kom el-Hettan. A wall enclosing about 425 hectares was built by Kurigalzu I and rebuilt by Kurigalzu II. The city was occupied until the fall of the Kassite dynasty in the 12th century BCE and was then largely abandoned, although the temple area was still active in the 7th century BCE and in the Neo-Babylonian period.

The ziggurat, dedicated to the god Enlil, has a base of 69 by 67 metres and stands about 52 metres high. Its core is of sun-dried brick with reed mats set in every seventh layer, and its baked bricks bear Kurigalzu's name and his dedication of the temple E-U-GAL to Enlil. The royal palace covered 420,000 square metres. Wall paintings from the palace at Tell al-Abyadh show processional scenes, clusters of fruit and geometric bands in red, blue, yellow, white and black.

Western visitors confused the ziggurat with the Tower of Babel from the 17th century onwards; Bengt Bengtsson Oxenstierna visited the site in 1616, and Henry Rawlinson identified the ancient name in the mid-19th century. Taha Baqir and Seton Lloyd excavated in 1942-1945 and recovered over 100 Kassite cuneiform tablets, which name two palaces as the Palace of the Mountain Sheep and the Palace of the Stag. The site was placed on Iraq's Tentative List for UNESCO World Heritage in January 2025, and an Iraqi-Italian expedition from the University of Bologna has worked there since 2022.
durad-brankovic: Đurađ Vuković Branković, also George Branković, was born on 22 February 1377, the son of Vuk Branković and Mara Lazarević, a daughter of Prince Lazar Hrebeljanović. His wife was Eirene Kantakouzene, a Byzantine princess. Despot Stefan Lazarević had appropriated lands that were part of Vuk's hereditary holdings, which led to a conflict between the two cousins that lasted ten years. After they reconciled, the childless Stefan made Đurađ his heir. When Stefan died on 19 July 1427 and Đurađ succeeded him, he was 50 and a man of great experience.

After Stefan's death King Sigismund of Hungary took over Belgrade, which was ceded to him, and Đurađ kept southern and western Mačva with the king's approval. The Ottoman sultan answered the change of throne by sending an army into Serbia, which took Niš and Kruševac and besieged Novo Brdo. In 1429 John VIII Palaiologos formally granted Đurađ the title of Despot. Like other Christian rulers of Eastern Europe he lived under Ottoman vassalage, but he often sought Christian alliances while keeping up the appearance of loyalty to the sultan.

In 1439 the Ottomans captured Smederevo and he fled to Hungary, where he held large estates, and then to Zeta. Dubrovnik refused an Ottoman demand to hand him over, saying it was a free city that took in anyone who sought shelter. Murad II, who was married to Đurađ's daughter Mara, made peace with Hungary at Szeged in 1444. The peace restored Đurađ's rule, though he had to give his vast estates to John Hunyadi, and on 22 August 1444 he peacefully took possession of the evacuated Smederevo.

The peace was broken by Hunyadi and King Władysław III of Poland in the Crusade of Varna, and in 1448 Hunyadi's army was beaten by Murad II at Kosovo Polje. Because of a personal feud, Đurađ held Hunyadi at Smederevo for a short time on his retreat. After Hunyadi's victory over Mehmed II at the siege of Belgrade on 14 July 1456 Đurađ regained Serbia, but he died before the end of that year, aged 79. His library held Serbian, Slavonic, Latin and Greek manuscripts and made Smederevo a centre of Serbian culture. Following disputes among his widow and three sons, the Ottomans annexed Serbia three years after his death.
durad-crnojevic: Đurađ was the eldest son of Ivan Crnojević, lord of Zeta, and of Voisava Arianiti, a member of the Albanian nobility. His paternal grandmother, Mara Kastrioti, was a sister of Skanderbeg, and through his mother he was a grandson of Gjergj Arianiti. He styled himself Duke of Zeta and was known for his learning in astronomy, geometry and other sciences. His first wife was Yela Thopia; in 1490 he married Isabetha Erizzo, daughter of the Venetian nobleman and diplomat Antonio Erizzo.

His short rule is remembered less for its politics than for its printing. With the help of Hieromonk Makarije he founded the first Serbian printing house and printed five books: the Oktoih prvoglasnik, the Oktoih petoglasnik, the Psaltir s posljedovanjem, the prayer book known as the Trebnik and, probably in 1496, the Četvorojevanđelje. These books became a lasting contribution to Serbian culture.

After the Ottomans forced him out of Zeta in 1496, the Venetians imprisoned him for a time in 1497, accusing him of collaborating with the Ottomans, and again from 30 July to 25 October 1498, this time because the Ottomans insisted on it. In exile in Venice he and his wife lived in the Palazzo Zaguri.

In the spring of 1500 Đurađ went to Scutari at the invitation of Feriz Beg, who sent him on to Istanbul. There he formally ceded his possessions to the sultan, who granted him a timar in Anatolia to hold as a sipahi. He had written his testament in Serbian Cyrillic on 22 October 1499; an Italian translation was later copied into an official document, witnessed by Doge Leonardo Loredan, which declared the will valid in January 1517. The testament is valued as a literary work of its time.
durad-i-balsic: Đurađ was the eldest of the three sons of Balša I, a petty nobleman who held a single village under the Serbian Emperor Stefan Uroš IV Dušan and was said to be kin to Nemanja. After Dušan's death in 1355 the family began taking Lower Zeta. In 1362 the brothers murdered Đuraš Ilijić, who held Upper Zeta, and were then recognised as provincial lords of Zeta in the charters of Stefan Uroš V.

In 1363 Đurađ went to war against the Thopia family of northern Albania, allied with the Matarangos of the south. Karl Thopia captured him in a skirmish in the spring of 1364, and he was held until 1366, when the Republic of Ragusa mediated his release; in 1367 he is called the baron of maritime Serbia. To further their coastal ambitions the brothers converted from Orthodoxy to Catholicism, formally in 1369.

Đurađ waged war on Kotor from 1368, hoping to win suzerainty over the town, and besieged it in 1369; Kotor turned to the Kingdom of Hungary, and peace was made by spring 1370, probably through Venetian mediation. Bar paid him an annual tribute of 2,000 ducats, and Venice complained of armed ships at Bar, Budva and Ulcinj, which Stefan Uroš V said were Đurađ's. Among the towns he took from the lands of Nikola Altomanović were Trebinje, Konavle and Dračevica, though historians differ on how he acquired them.

In 1371 he expelled his first wife Olivera, sister of King Marko, and took Prizren from Marko, and a year later Peja. On 30 November 1373 the brothers issued an edict for Ragusa confirming the laws of Stefan Uroš V and recognising the sovereignty of the Serbian Empire. In 1375 Đurađ and Lazar Hrebeljanović convened the assembly that chose Jefrem as Serbian Patriarch.

Đurađ died in Skadar, and rule over Zeta passed to his younger brother Balša II. His neighbours used the moment: the Bosnian Ban Tvrtko I took the rest of his coastal lands by the Bay of Kotor, and Vuk Branković sent forces into Metohija and seized Prizren. His son Konstantin became a local Zetan lord, and descendants of his illegitimate son were among the founders of the League of Lezhë in 1444.
durad-ii-balsic: Đurađ II was the son of Stracimir, one of the three Balšić brothers who came to rule Zeta in the 1360s, and of Milica Mrnjavčević, daughter of King Vukašin Mrnjavčević. When his uncle Balša II was killed fighting the Ottomans at the Battle of Savra on 18 September 1385, Đurađ inherited parts of Zeta and northern Albania, including Scutari, Drivast and Lezhë, under the family's rule of seniority, and made Ulcinj his seat.

His lands soon shrank. Pal Dukagjini took Lezhë and the Drin area, the Jonima family seceded, Vuk Branković took Peć and Prizren, and in Upper Zeta Radič Crnojević opposed him, leaving Đurađ a strip of land between Lake Skadar and the Adriatic Sea. In 1386 he recognised Prince Lazar Hrebeljanović as his sovereign and married his daughter Jelena Lazarević, joining Lazar and Vuk Branković in a family alliance over the Serbian realm. Yet he also kept ties with the Ottomans, and his troops fought beside Lala Şâhin Paşa at the Battle of Bileća in 1388.

After Tvrtko I died in 1391, Đurađ seized Kotor. His cousin Konstantin entered Ottoman service, and Đurađ turned against the Ottomans, converting to Catholicism. Late in 1392 Yiğit Bey captured him in battle, and to win his release he surrendered Scutari, Drivast and Sveti Srđ and agreed to pay tribute. In October 1395 he retook them and in April 1396 handed Scutari, Lake Skadar with its islands and Sveti Srđ to Venetian administration for 1,000 ducats a year.

In May 1396 he defeated the Crnojević brothers and killed Radič. The Hungarian King Sigismund, returning from his defeat at Nicopolis, made him Prince of Hvar and Korčula. Relations with Venice worsened, and in early 1401 Venice stopped paying the tribute; unable to get Ottoman help, Đurađ accepted its demands, and Venice resumed the payment.

In late summer 1402 his brother-in-law Despot Stefan Lazarević, returning from the Battle of Angora, stayed at his court, and Đurađ raised an army that helped him win at Tripolje near Gračanica in November. He died of his wounds in April 1403 and was buried in the Church of Saint Catherine in Ulcinj. His seventeen-year-old son Balša III succeeded him. Đurađ founded the Beška Monastery on Lake Skadar, and most historians identify him with the epic hero Banović Strahinja.
durance: The Durance has its source on the northern slope of the Sommet des Anges, above Montgenèvre, in the south-western Alps. It flows through Briançon, Embrun, Sisteron, Manosque and Cavaillon, receives the Verdon as its largest tributary, and joins the Rhône south of Avignon. The name is documented as Druentia in the 1st century CE and probably means the flowing one, from a Proto-Indo-European root meaning to run. The river keeps its name rather than the Clarée or the Guisane, which are longer where they join it, because the Durance valley is an old and important trade route, whereas the valleys of those two are effectively dead ends.

From antiquity until the 19th century the river was known for the difficulty of crossing it: its wide bed, strong current, changes of course after floods and inconstant flow hindered fords, and the only durable ones were at Mirabeau and Pertuis. In pre-Roman times it was the border between Celto-Ligurian peoples such as the Cavares and the Salyes. In the 12th century a flood swept away the town of Rama, and the flood of 1843 carried off several newly built suspension bridges. In the Middle Ages the county of Forcalquier stretched along the river, and the monks of Boscodon Abbey were given the privilege of floating timber down it in 1191.

The first known irrigation canal, the Canal Saint-Julien, was dug in 1171. The Adam de Craponne canal, 50 kilometres long, was dug in nine months in 1554. From 1839 to 1854 the engineer Franz Mayor de Montricher built the Marseille Canal, 80 kilometres long, to supply the city with drinking water, and it allowed the Marseille area to develop quickly. Freight on the river ended in the 20th century under competition from road and rail; there were ten raftmen left in 1896 and one in 1908.

A law of 1955 defined the Durance-Verdon project for producing electricity, supplying irrigation and drinking water and limiting floods. Over forty years it required 23 dams and water extraction points and the supply of 33 hydroelectric power stations. Most of the flow was diverted into canals downstream from Serre-Ponçon, whose lake is also a tourist attraction. The river and its valley are a protected Natura 2000 area. The Palais Longchamp in Marseille, built between 1862 and 1869, has a monument celebrating the arrival of the Durance's water, and the writer Jean Giono used the river in his imagined Provence.
durand-line: The Durand Line was established towards the end of the Great Game, the rivalry between the British and Russian empires, and made Afghanistan a buffer zone between their interests. Earlier, in the First Anglo-Afghan War, British-led Indian forces invaded in 1839 and were defeated in 1842. After the Second Anglo-Afghan War, which began in 1878, the Treaty of Gandamak of 1880 had Afghanistan cede control of various frontier areas to British India. In 1893 the government of India sent Mortimer Durand to Kabul to sign an agreement with Emir Abdur Rahman Khan fixing the limits of their spheres of influence and improving diplomatic relations and trade.

The single-page agreement, dated 12 November 1893, has seven short articles, among them a commitment not to interfere beyond the line. It created the Wakhan Corridor as a buffer between the British and Russian empires and gave Nuristan, then known as Kafiristan, and parts of Chitral to Afghanistan, while Afghanistan gave up claims to Waziristan and Chageh. It also permitted arms imports from British India and raised the subsidy paid to Afghanistan from 1.2 to 1.8 million rupees.

A joint survey began in 1894 and covered some 1,300 kilometres of the border. Three boundary commissions worked on it: the Asmar commission along Chitral, the Afghan-Waziristan commission and the Baluch-Afghan commission. At Nashagam on 9 April 1895 Nasrat and Bashgal were ceded to Afghanistan, and the Baluchistan section was completed on 13 May 1896. In 1896 the stretch from the Kabul River to China was declared demarcated by its continuous watershed ridge. The section near the Khyber Pass was demarcated after the Third Anglo-Afghan War, and the treaties of 1919 and 1921 confirmed the Indo-Afghan frontier. A short adjustment was made at Arundu in 1933 and 1934.

Pakistan inherited the line in 1947. On 26 July 1949 a loya jirga in Afghanistan declared that Afghanistan recognised neither the line nor any similar line and that all earlier agreements were void. In 1950 the British government held that Pakistan was in international law the inheritor of the rights and duties of the old Government of India and that the Durand Line was the international frontier. In 1956 the SEATO council likewise recognised that the sovereignty of Pakistan extended up to the line.

The line runs largely through mountains, south of the Hindu Kush, with its eastern end in the Karakoram and its western part in the lower, sparse Registan Desert. The Kunar, Kabul, Kurram and Gomal rivers cross it, and the Khyber Pass is the main land connection between Central Asia and the Indian subcontinent. Twelve Afghan provinces lie along the border, and in Pakistan it adjoins Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Balochistan and Gilgit-Baltistan.
durango-city: The city stands at about 1,890 metres above sea level in the Valley of Guadiana, on the northwestern edge of the Central Mexican Highlands. Since the prehistoric period the area was a conduit for influences from north and south, between Aridoamerica and Mesoamerica. The first inhabitants were a people called the Nahoas, nomads who came from the north about 2,000 years ago. By the Post Classic period the area was inhabited by the Zacatecans and the Tepehuanos, who had migrated from the north-west.

Durango was founded on 8 July 1563 by the Spanish explorer Francisco de Ibarra, who named it after his hometown of Durango in the Spanish province of Biscay; the name is of Basque origin. He also named the surrounding area Nueva Vizcaya. The site was chosen for its proximity to the Cerro del Mercado, which was believed to contain large amounts of silver, though an important iron deposit was found in the end. Under Spanish rule the city was the capital of the province of Nueva Vizcaya in New Spain, which consisted mostly of what became the Mexican states of Durango and Chihuahua.

In 1826 the official name became Victoria de Durango, in honour of Guadalupe Victoria, the first president of Mexico and a native of the state. The diocese of Durango was erected in 1620 and became an archdiocese in 1891.

Victoria de Durango is the capital and largest city of the state of Durango. Its historic centre holds the largest concentration of historic monuments in northern Mexico, many in colonial and Baroque styles, and centres on the cathedral and the Plaza de Armas. The Cathedral Basilica became the cathedral in 1621, burned in 1634 and was rebuilt in the middle of the 18th century at the height of the city's mining prosperity. A mining tunnel that also served as a secret passage runs beneath it and is now a museum. The city's patron saint is Saint George, whose feast day is 23 April.
durban: Durban lies on the Natal Bay of the Indian Ocean, on the east coast of South Africa. North of the harbour and city centre is the mouth of the Umgeni River, and the flat city centre rises to the hills of the Berea on the west, while the Bluff runs along the coast to the south. The Zulu name, eThekwini, comes from itheku, meaning bay or lagoon. The city has a humid subtropical climate with hot, wet summers and mild, dry winters. Its natural harbour is one of the few between Port Elizabeth and Maputo, and it became a busy port of call for ship repairs after the port opened in the 1840s.

Archaeological evidence from the Drakensberg suggests that hunter-gatherers lived in the area from about 100,000 years ago, until agro-pastoralists from the north gradually absorbed them. Vasco da Gama sailed along the coast at Christmas 1497 and named it Natal, Portuguese for Christmas. In 1686 survivors of the wrecked Dutch East India Company ship Stavenisse were taken in by the Abambo people, a group of the Hlubi.

In 1823 James Saunders King and Lieutenant Francis George Farewell, former Royal Navy officers, sheltered from a storm in the Bay of Natal. In 1824 Farewell, with the trading company J. R. Thompson and Co. and with Henry Francis Fynn, set up a trading station at the bay and opened trade with Shaka, the Zulu king, who granted them land around it. The settlement was named after Sir Benjamin D'Urban in 1835 and became a borough in 1854. The Natal Railway Company opened South Africa's first operating steam railway, between the Point and the town, in 1860, and in the same year indentured labourers from British India began to arrive.

The Voortrekkers founded the Natalia Republic in 1839, with Pietermaritzburg as its capital. To keep Port Natal, Governor George Thomas Napier sent a force under Captain Thomas Charlton Smith, which built a fortified camp in May 1842. After its attack on a camp at Congella failed, the Voortrekkers besieged it. The trader Dick King and his servant Ndongeni rode to Grahamstown in 14 days to fetch reinforcements, and the siege was lifted. Britain annexed the republic in 1843. Natal became a province of the Union of South Africa in 1910, and Durban received city status in 1935.

Durban is the third most populous city in South Africa and the largest in KwaZulu-Natal, and its harbour is the busiest port in sub-Saharan Africa. It is the seat of the eThekwini Metropolitan Municipality, formed in 1999. Its people include large Zulu, Indian, White and Coloured communities, and the Indian community has influenced its cuisine, culture and religion. Its architecture runs from Victorian to contemporary, with Art Deco on many buildings.
durga: Durga's name means the impassable or unassailable one and is related to durg, a fortress. Words of this root occur in the Vedic literature, but the Vedic texts lack the legends later told of her. Asko Parpola reads a cylindrical seal from Kalibangan as showing a Durga-like goddess of war associated with the tiger, which would take her image back to the Indus Valley civilisation. In 1916 the historian Ramaprasad Chanda proposed that she developed from a mountain goddess worshipped by the dwellers of the Himalaya and the Vindhyas. Inscriptions of the 6th century CE already mention her victory over Mahishasura, and the Devi Mahatmya, composed between about 400 and 600 CE according to scholars, presents her as a well-established demon-slaying goddess.

In the Devi Mahatmya and the Devi Bhagavata Purana, the central texts of Shaktism, Durga is the embodiment of creation, preservation and destruction and is identified with Brahman, the ultimate reality. She is best known as Mahishasura-mardini, the slayer of the half-buffalo demon Mahishasura, who had won from Brahma the boon that only a woman could kill him. The gods gave form to their combined energy as a many-armed warrior woman, the Himalayas gave her a lion, and she killed the demon with her trident when he took buffalo form.

She is shown riding a lion or tiger with between eight and eighteen hands, each holding a weapon given by a male god, yet her face is calm. Shakta Hindus read the weapons as symbols of self-discipline, prayer and devotion. In Bengal she is a mother, of Ganesha, Kartikeya, Lakshmi and Sarasvati, although she is generally regarded as independent and not the consort of any god.

Her worship is most prominent in the east and north-east of the subcontinent. Durga Puja, held in the month of Ashvina, usually in September or October, is a major festival in Bengal, Odisha, Assam, Jharkhand and Bihar; clay images are worshipped for nine days and then immersed in water. Manuscripts of the 14th century give rules for it, and royalty and wealthy families sponsored public celebrations from at least the 16th century. In Nepal the festival is Dashain.

Images of her slaying the buffalo demon have been found at Buddhist sites in Afghanistan, Indonesia and north-eastern India, and in Indonesia at least 135 statues of Durga, dating from the 6th century onwards, have been found. Bankim Chandra Chatterjee's song Vande Mataram drew on her image as mother goddess.
durgadas-rathore: Durgadas was born on 13 August 1638, the son of Askaran Rathore, a jagirdar of Drunera and a minister under Jaswant Singh, the ruler of Marwar. He was a distant relative of the royal family, descended from Karana, a son of Rao Ranmal. When Jaswant Singh died in Afghanistan in December 1678 without an heir, Aurangzeb imposed direct rule over Marwar. Two of the late ruler's queens then gave birth to sons, one of whom died soon after, leaving Ajit Singh as the sole heir.

Aurangzeb had the infant Ajit Singh brought to Delhi and held under house arrest at Noorgarh. Durgadas and other nobles of Jodhpur attacked the Mughal contingent in Delhi and rescued the child and the widowed queens. Ajit Singh was hidden first at Balunda, then in the Aravalli Hills near Abu Sirohi, and later at Nandlai in Mewar, where Rana Raj Singh I offered him refuge. Tahir Beg and Inder Singh Rathore, sent to capture Durgadas, both failed.

Through guerrilla warfare Durgadas harassed Mughal outposts and made Mughal officers pay tribute. He encouraged the princes Muazzam and Akbar against their father, and kept Aurangzeb's granddaughter Saif-un-nissa in his care before returning her. After Aurangzeb's death in 1707 he and Ajit Singh seized Jodhpur. In the Rajput Rebellion of 1708 to 1710 he routed Saiyid Hussain Khan Barha at Kaladera in July 1708 and helped win the victory at Sambhar alongside Raja Jai Singh II of Jaipur.

Ajit Singh grew jealous of his fame, and Durgadas turned against him after Ajit Singh had the loyal noble Mukund Das murdered. Durgadas was exiled and his name erased from the Marwari chronicles, although the Mughals offered him the title of Rao, and Maharana Amar Singh II of Mewar gave him the jagirs of Rampura and Vijaypur. He died on the banks of the Shipra River in Ujjain on 22 November 1718. The historian Jadunath Sarkar praised his honour and constancy, and India issued a postage stamp in his memory in 1988 and coins in 2003.
durgasimha: Durgasimha was a Brahmin by birth and belonged to the Smartha Bhagavata sub-sect of Hinduism, a community that gives equal importance to the gods Shiva and Vishnu. He was a native of Kisukadu Nadu, another name for ancient Karnataka, and lived at the Sayyadi agrahara, a Brahmin school of higher learning. At the court of King Jayasimha II, also known as Jagadekamalla, who reigned from 1018 to 1042, he held the office of minister of war and peace, the Sandhi Vigrahi.

His Kannada Panchatantra contains 60 fables, 13 of them original stories, and its central theme has a strong Jain bent. Every story turns on morality and ends with a summary section, the Katha Shloka. As a minister, Durgasimha treated the fables as a book of political science, or Rajniti. The scholar R. Narasimhachar dated the work to about 1025, while the Kannada poet and scholar Govinda Pai placed it on 8 March 1031, from the concluding stanza of the manuscript.

The original Sanskrit Panchatantra is lost; it was an independent Sanskrit work of around 300 CE, give or take a century or two, and its putative author Vishnu Sharma may be a story-telling figure rather than a real person. Durgasimha worked from the so-called Southern Panchatantra, a version close to the original that also gave rise to other Indian vernacular versions and to the Hitopadesha.

Durgasimha, or his source, gave the work an origin story of its own. In his account Pushpadatta, an attendant of Shiva, overheard the god telling a great story to his consort Parvati; Gunadhya, a reincarnation of Pushpadatta and court poet of King Shalivahana, later set it down in Paishachi as the Brihatkatha. A Sanskrit selection of five stories from it by Vasubhaga Datta gave the Panchatantra its name. Modern scholars hold that the original Brihatkatha did not include the Panchatantra, which a later version made in Kashmir or north-western India seems to have inserted.
durham-castle: Construction of the castle, of the motte and bailey design favoured by the Normans, began in 1072 under William the Conqueror, six years after the Norman Conquest and soon after the Normans first came to the North. The work was supervised by Waltheof, Earl of Northumbria, until he rebelled against William and was executed in 1076. Stone was cut from the cliffs below the walls and moved up with winches. The bishop of Durham, Walcher at the time, was appointed by the king to exercise royal authority on his behalf, with the castle as his seat, and after he bought the Earldom of Northumbria he began a line of prince-bishops.

The prince-bishops were entitled to raise an army, levy taxes and mint their own coinage, which gave them virtual autonomy as a defence against Scottish incursions and internal rebellions. Walcher built the castle as both a bishops' palace and a stronghold, with inner and outer baileys and a keep, and in May 1080 rebels from Northumbria besieged it for four days and killed him. In 1177 King Henry II seized the castle after a disagreement with Bishop Pudsey. Bishop Thomas Hatfield rebuilt the keep in the 1300s, and Bishop Antony Bek created the Great Hall in the early 14th century, now 14 metres high and over 30 metres long.

The Norman Chapel is the oldest accessible part of the castle, dated to 1075 or shortly after 1080. Its architecture is Anglian in character, possibly because forced Anglian labour was used. In the 15th century its windows were almost blocked by the expanded keep, and it fell into disuse until 1841. In the Second World War it served as a Royal Air Force command and observation post and it was re-consecrated in the 1950s. Tunstall's Chapel was built in the 16th century.

The bishops lost their temporal powers under the Durham (County Palatine) Act 1836. Auckland Castle had become the bishops' residence in 1832, and Bishop William Van Mildert donated Durham Castle to the University of Durham. University College moved in during 1837, after Bishop Edward Maltby had completed renovations. Since 1986 the castle and Durham Cathedral have been a World Heritage Site together, and seventeen elements of the castle are listed at Grade I. The castle is home to over 100 students and can be visited only on guided tours.
durham-university: Between around 1286 and 1291 the Benedictine monks of Durham established a hall at the University of Oxford. In 1381 it received an endowment from Thomas Hatfield, Bishop of Durham, and became Durham College, which was surrendered to the Crown in 1545 after the Reformation. Attempts to form a university in the city itself were made under King Henry VIII and under Oliver Cromwell, who issued letters patent in 1657 for a college. A proposal to let it confer degrees met opposition from Oxford and Cambridge, and the scheme was abandoned at the restoration of the monarchy in 1660.

The university came into being through the Durham University Act 1832, passed at the instigation of Archdeacon Charles Thorp with the support of the bishop of Durham, William van Mildert, and given royal assent by King William IV on 4 July 1832. It opened on 28 October 1833 and received a royal charter on 1 June 1837. Degrees were at first open only to members of the Church of England. Early accommodation was in the Archdeacon's Inn, now Cosin's Hall, and in 1837 the university was granted the use of Durham Castle, formerly the bishop's palace.

In the early twentieth century the Newcastle division, made up of Armstrong College and the Durham University College of Medicine, grew to outnumber the Durham colleges. A reform of 1909 made the university federal, with its seat fixed in Durham. From 1959 new colleges were founded on the Elvet Hill site, beginning with Grey College, named after the second Earl Grey, prime minister when the university was founded.

Durham is a collegiate university: academic departments provide research and teaching, while 17 colleges are responsible for domestic arrangements and welfare. Graduates have long used the Latin post-nominal letters Dunelm, from Dunelmensis, meaning of Durham. The estate includes 83 listed buildings, from the 11th-century Durham Castle to the 1960s students' union, and the university manages the Durham World Heritage Site with Durham Cathedral. Its library, founded in January 1833 with a gift of 160 volumes from Bishop van Mildert, includes Bishop Cosin's Library, founded in 1669.
duris-of-samos: Duris claimed descent from Alcibiades. His son Scaeus won the boys' boxing at the Olympic Games while the Samians were in exile, that is, before 324 BCE, when Athenian cleruchs held the island after expelling its people; Duris was therefore probably born close to 350 BCE. Some modern works call the victor his father rather than his son, which the meagre ancient sources do not support. His brother was Lynceus of Samos, author of comedies, letters and the essay Shopping for Food.

Many 20th-century works make Duris a pupil of Theophrastus at Athens, but this rests only on a conjectural emendation by Adamantios Korais of the text of Athenaeus; the manuscripts say that Lynceus and his correspondent Hippolochus studied under him. How Duris became tyrant of Samos, how long he ruled and what happened under him are unknown.

His main history ran from the Battle of Leuctra to the death of Lysimachus in 281 BCE, and was continued by the Histories of Phylarchus. His life of Agathocles was a source for books 19 to 21 of the Historical Library of Diodorus Siculus, and his annals of Samos were arranged by the lists of the priests of Hera. Fragments survive of eight works: 33 of the Histories, 13 of On Agathocles, 22 of the Annals of Samos, and a few of On Laws, On Games, On Tragedy, On Painters and On Sculpture. Over thirty fragments of the history are known through quotations, among them those in Plutarch.

He died at an unknown date after 281 BCE. Few later readers praised him. Cicero called him industrious, Plutarch used his work while doubting its trustworthiness, Dionysius of Halicarnassus disparaged his style and Photius found its arrangement faulty. Plutarch's Life of Pericles cites his exaggerated account of cruelty and destruction when Athenian forces under Pericles subdued Samos. Critics who took him for a pupil of Theophrastus tried to relate tragic history to the teachings of the Peripatetic school, a debate that stayed inconclusive.
durlach: Durlach lies on the left bank of the Pfinz at the foot of the Turmberg, a vineyard-covered hill at the northernmost tip of the Black Forest, crowned by a ruined castle with a watch-tower that looks west over Karlsruhe and the Rhine valley. A staircase climbs the hill, and the Turmbergbahn, a historic funicular railway, runs to the top. The district of Karlsruhe has roughly 30,000 people and is divided into Alt-Durlach, Dornwald-Untermühl, Hanggebiet, Bergwald, Aue, Lohn-Lissen and Killisfeld.

The Emperor Frederick II granted Durlach to the margrave Hermann V of Zähringen as an allodial possession. Margrave Charles II made it the residence of the rulers of Baden-Durlach in 1565, and it kept that rank after the French almost wholly destroyed it in 1689. Margrave Charles III William, wanting more room, founded Karlsruhe in 1715, which soon replaced it as capital.

In 1846 Durlach hosted a congress of the Liberal Party of the Baden Parliament, and in 1849, during the Baden Revolution, Prussian troops and insurgents fought there. Karlsruhe, by then larger and joined to it by a canal and an avenue of poplars, absorbed the town in 1938. During the Second World War 329 people were killed in Durlach. Georg Friedrich von Reichenbach and the historian Ernst Ludwig Posselt (1763–1804) were born there.

The Karlsburg Castle in the centre, built in 1565 and later used as barracks, now holds museums; the old town hall, a church with a fine organ and a statue of Charles II in the market-place also survive. The factories that once made Pfaff sewing machines, brushes, chemicals, tobacco, beer, vinegar, chicory and pipe organs have mostly gone, and information technology firms, the largest Fiducia IT AG, have taken their place.
durrani-empire: Ahmad Khan, of the Sadozai lineage of the Abdali tribe, was the son of Muhammad Zaman Khan, who had served as governor of Herat, and a commander under Nader Shah. After Nader Shah's death in June 1747 a loya jirga, or grand council, met near Kandahar for nine days. The two chief contestants were Hajji Jamal Khan of the Mohammadzai and Ahmad Khan. A holy man, Mohammad Sabir Khan, spoke for Ahmad Khan, reputedly placed sheaves of wheat or barley in his turban and crowned him with the title Durr-i-Durran, Pearl of the Pearls, from which the tribe took the name Durrani.

Ahmad Shah took Qalati Ghilji and Ghazni from the Ghilji and Kabul and Peshawar from the Mughal governor Nasir Khan. In 1749 the Mughal emperor Ahmad Shah Bahadur ceded Sindh and the Punjab to save his capital, and Ahmad Shah then took Mashhad from Shahrukh Afshar and subdued the peoples north of the Hindu Kush. He sacked Delhi in 1757. In 1762 his forces killed thousands of Sikhs in the Punjab, in what Sikhs call the Vaḍḍā Ghallūghārā, and destroyed the Golden Temple at Amritsar, yet the Sikhs rebuilt it and he never subdued them. He died east of Kandahar in 1772.

His son Timur Shah Durrani took the throne in November 1772 and made Kabul the capital. Timur's sons fought one another: Zaman Shah, who succeeded in 1793, was blinded and replaced by Mahmud Shah in 1801, and Shuja Shah ruled from 1803 to 1809. On 7 June 1809 Shuja signed with the British East India Company the first Afghan pact with a European power. By 1818 the Sadozai rulers held little more than Kabul and the land within 160 kilometres of it. Kashmir was lost to the Sikh Empire at the Battle of Shopian in 1819, and Ayub Shah was deposed in 1823.

The army was based on cavalry armed with flintlocks, who made hit-and-run attacks. Its core was 10,000 mounted ghulams, or slave-soldiers, carrying blunderbusses; a third of them were Qizilbash who had served Nader Shah. The bulk of the army was irregular Afghan tribal cavalry armed with lance and broadsword, and infantry played a very small part. Ahmad Shah balanced tribal alliances and hostilities, a balance his successors upset when they tried to rule without the other Durrani chiefs. The Barakzai under Dost Muhammad Khan later displaced the dynasty at Kabul, and the empire is regarded as the foundation of the modern Afghan state.
durres: Durrës lies on the Bay of Durrës, on a flat alluvial plain between the mouths of the Erzen and the Ishëm rivers, on the Adriatic coast of Albania. The municipality stretches from the mouth of the Ishëm at the Cape of Rodon, across the Bay of Lalzi, to the Shkëmbi i Kavajës in the south, and the climate is a hot-summer Mediterranean one.

The area was inhabited from the Eneolithic, and from protohistoric times by Illyrian peoples. Greek colonists from Corinth and Corcyra founded the city in 627 BCE, on the coast of the Taulantii, an Illyrian tribe. A flourishing commercial centre emerged, and the construction of a Doric-style treasury at Olympia by the citizens of Epidamnos about the 6th century BCE suggests that it was among the richest cities of the Greek world. After the Illyrian Wars the Roman Republic made Dyrrachium its sole name.

The city became part of the Roman Empire and then of the Byzantine Empire, and the Via Egnatia began there and ran east across the Balkans to Constantinople. Its bishopric was created around 58 and became an archbishopric in 449. The Byzantine walls were built in the sixth century, after the Visigoth invasion of 481. In the late 10th century it passed to Samuel of Bulgaria; around 1005 his governor, Ashot Taronites, fled to Constantinople and offered the city to Emperor Basil II, and it returned to Byzantine rule.

The Ottomans ruled from 1501 until 1912 and renamed it Dırac. The city did not prosper in the first two centuries and became a den of piracy; its significance for the Ottomans lay in its castle and its salt deposits. After Ismail Qemali raised the Albanian flag on 26 November 1912, Serbia occupied the city three days later. It became Albania's second national capital, after Vlorë, on 7 March 1914 under Prince Wilhelm, and remained so until 11 February 1920, when the Congress of Lushnjë made Tirana the capital.

Durrës is the second most populous city of Albania, with roughly 2,500 years of recorded history. Its port is one of the largest on the Adriatic, with daily ferries to Bari in Italy. The Amphitheatre of Durrës, once seating 20,000, is the largest amphitheatre in the Balkans and is on Albania's tentative list for World Heritage status. The Durrës Archaeological Museum holds the mosaic known as The Beauty of Durrës.
durrow-abbey: Durrow lies about 5 kilometres north of the centre of Tullamore. Its old name, Daru, means plain of the oaks, and the site keeps some of the only remaining pre-medieval oak in Ireland. A line of oaks beside the fields marks the route of the Slighe Mhór, the Great Highway along the Esker Riada. Nearby is Mag Lena, where a synod of Irish clerics met in 630 to settle the controversy over the date of Easter.

Bede called Durrow Monasterium nobile in Hiberniâ, and it was an important centre from which further monasteries were founded; later Armagh and Durrow were called the Universities of the West. The community was close to Clann Cholmáin: Domnall Midi was apparently buried there in 763, men of Durrow fought those of Clonmacnoise in 764 during a succession struggle, and they joined Donnchad Midi in a raid into Munster in 776. Vikings raided Durrow often, but it was not wholly destroyed until the Norman invasion.

The Book of Durrow was at the abbey by 916 at the latest, though it may have been made elsewhere. In July 1054, according to the Annals of the Four Masters, monks at Durrow saw a bright star appear overnight, the only known European sighting of the supernova of 1054. Hugh de Lacy, Lord of Meath, built a motte there using the abbey's stones and was killed at the site in 1186 by one of his workmen.

The site keeps a large ecclesiastical enclosure, five Early Christian grave slabs, a high cross of the mid-ninth century, a holy well and other remains; a complete cross-head is in the National Museum of Ireland. A church of the late eighteenth or early nineteenth century stands on the footprint of earlier churches, beside Durrow Abbey House, rebuilt in the 1920s after a fire. The Irish Government bought the abbey and the monastic site in 2003 to protect them from commercial development.
durvinita: Durvinita, a son of the preceding king Avinita, ruled from 529 to 579 CE. His brother disputed his accession with the support of the Pallavas and Kadambas, a quarrel recorded in the Nallala and Kadagattur inscriptions, but Durvinita took the throne by force of arms. He defeated the Pallavas at the Battle of Anderi, and the Gummareddipura inscription praises his victories at Alattur, Porulare and Pernagra, which may have carried his power into the Kongudesa and Tondaimandalam regions of the Tamil country.

To keep the Pallavas at bay he gave his daughter in marriage to the Chalukya Vijayaditya; the Nagara record names Pulakesi II instead, which is unlikely given their dates. When the Pallavas attacked the Chalukyas he fought on their side, beginning a friendship with the Chalukyas and their successors that lasted more than 600 years. The Gummareddipura and Uttanur plates call him Lord of Punnata.

Durvinita knew both Sanskrit and Kannada. The Nallala grant, issued in the 40th year of his reign, calls him an expert in poetry, stories, dramas and commentaries, and the Avanti-sundari-katha-sara, attributed to Dandin, says the Sanskrit poet Bharavi stayed at his court for a time. Ganga inscriptions credit him with a Kannada commentary on Canto 15 of Bharavi's Kirātārjunīya and with a Sanskrit Brihatkatha (Vadda-katha), and Amoghavarsha's Kavirajamarga counts him among the early writers of Kannada prose, though none of his Kannada works survive. The inscriptions also style him Shabdavatara-kara, although the grammar Shabdavatara is the work of his tutor Pujyapada.

Durvinita was a devout Jain and a disciple of Pujyapada. Inscriptions show him patronising Jain monks of the Desiga-gana and Kundakunda traditions, and the Madikeri copper plate honours a Jain lineage traced to Gunachandra Bhattara; an inscription of 977 CE records that he had a Jain temple (basadi) built. He is said to have taken part in public debates in which Buddhist scholars were defeated, which strengthened Jainism in the Western Ganga kingdom and contributed to the decline of Buddhist influence in parts of Karnataka. His reign ended in 579, and he is seen as the most successful ruler of his dynasty.
dusan-simovic: Dušan Simović was born on 28 October 1882 in Kragujevac. He attended elementary school and two years of high school there, then left to enter the Military Academy in Belgrade, drawn by an interest in military matters. He completed its course in 1900 and was promoted to second lieutenant of artillery, and finished the Higher School of the Military Academy in 1905. In October 1908 he married Snežana Tadić, a pharmacist from Valjevo; they had three sons and four daughters. He rose to serve as Chief of the General Staff of the Royal Yugoslav Army.

Simović joined other officers in the March 1941 coup against the government of Dragiša Cvetković and became prime minister on 27 March 1941. He did not repudiate the Tripartite Pact. He assured the German minister Viktor von Heeren that his government remained committed to it, and he told the American minister Arthur Bliss Lane that Yugoslavia was too weak to fight Germany and that an openly anti-German policy would break national unity, since most Croats favoured a pro-German course. He named Momčilo Ninčić, formerly president of the Yugoslav-German friendship society, as foreign minister.

Crowds in Belgrade had cheered the coup, and Winston Churchill's speech portrayed it as anti-Axis, which gave the impression that it aimed at undoing the Pact. The historian Sima M. Cirković called it a legend that Simović repudiated the Pact, noting that he continued Prince Paul's policy of pro-Allied neutrality. Tim Judah wrote that Simović learned, as Paul had, that Britain offered words but no military support. Hitler, furious, ordered an invasion of Yugoslavia on 27 March 1941 under the codename Operation Punishment.

On 4 May 1941 Simović issued a statement in Jerusalem calling the Sporazum one of the cornerstones of state policy, endorsed by only two of the Serb parties. He reached London with King Peter II on 21 June 1941, where British journalists took to the picture of a teenage king guided by a patriotic general. Peter came to dislike Simović's tutoring, which he found overbearing. Simović returned to Belgrade in June 1945, testified for the prosecution in the 1946 trial of Draža Mihailović, wrote several books on military subjects and died in Belgrade on 26 August 1962.
dusans-code: At Easter, 16 April 1346, Stefan Dušan held a great assembly at Skopje at which the Serbian Archbishopric was raised to a patriarchate, and the first Serbian Patriarch, Joanikije II, crowned Dušan Emperor and autocrat of Serbs and Romans. The Code was promulgated at a state council in Skopje on 21 May 1349, in the name of the Orthodox synod, the patriarch, the clergy and the lords of the empire. A second part, about half the size of the first, was added later at a council in Serres.

The Code had 201 articles in all. Four of them invoke the Law of the Sainted King, Stefan Uroš II Milutin, which suggests that a lost code of Milutin existed. Most early manuscripts pair Dušan's Code with an abridged Syntagma of Matthew Blastares and a short so-called Code of Justinian, drawn mostly from the Farmer's Law, and scholars such as A. Solovjev and Soulis hold that the council issued all three together.

Since civil and criminal law were covered by the other two parts, Dušan's articles dealt mainly with public law and procedure: courts and their jurisdictions, ordeals and juries, taxes, grazing rights, landholding, inheritance, and the position of slaves and serfs. Serfs owed labour dues but could bring complaints against their lord before the Emperor's court. Byzantine influence brought executions and mutilations in place of traditional fines. Punishment depended on social class, and commoners were forbidden to hold councils on pain of having their ears cut off.

The Church held a privileged position but was bound to feed the poor, and simony was banned. Catholics were called half believers, Catholic proselytism and mixed marriages were forbidden, and heretics such as the Bogomils were strongly penalised. Villages and frontier lords were made liable for brigands and raiders in their lands, which the historian Fine reads as a sign of the state's weak hold on rural and border areas.

The Code remained in force under Stefan Uroš V and in the Serbian Despotate until its annexation by the Ottoman Empire in 1459. Serbian communities under Ottoman rule, and areas under the Republic of Venice such as Grbalj and Paštrovići, continued to refer to it. The original manuscript is lost; 24 manuscripts are known today, the oldest the incomplete Struga manuscript of 1373, and the most complete the Hilandar, Bistrica and Prizren texts of the 15th century.
dushanbe: Dushanbe lies in the Hisar Valley, at 750 to 930 metres above sea level, at the confluence of the Varzob and the Kofarnihon rivers. The Hisar range, which reaches up to 4,000 metres, bounds it on the north and east, and the Babatag, Aktau, Rangontau and Karatau mountains bound it on the south, so that it is an intermontane basin. The climate has hot summers and chilly winters, and the surrounding mountains shield the city from the extremely cold air of Siberia. Before the 1960s most of the city stood on the left bank of the Varzob, but construction later carried it across.

In the Stone Age Mousterian tool-users lived in the Hisar Valley. The Hisar, Bishkent and Vakhsh cultures, whose stone tools were found within modern Dushanbe at the confluence of the Varzob and Luchob, are thought to have inhabited it in the second millennium BCE, keeping cattle, farming and weaving. The area was later settled by the Achaemenid Empire, Greco-Bactria, the Kushan Empire and the Hephthalites, and in the Middle Ages by settlements such as Hulbuk, with its palace. Islam was introduced in the eighth century.

The town first appears in the historical record in 1676, in a letter from the Balkh khan Subhonquli Bahodur to Tsar Fyodor III, although the Balkh historian Mahmud ibn Wali mentioned the area in the 1630s. It was called Kasabai Dushanbe, the town of Monday, after a large bazaar held each Monday. Its place between caravan routes to Karategin and the Alay Valley, and to Afghanistan through the Anzob Pass, helped the market grow. It then had a population of about 7,000 to 8,000. From the 17th to the early 20th century it was controlled at times by the Beg of Hisor, by Balkh and finally by Bukhara, before the Russian Empire conquered it.

The Bolsheviks captured Dushanbe in 1922, and in 1924 it became the capital of the Tajik Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic, which began its rapid growth. When the Tajik SSR separated from the Uzbek SSR in 1929, its capital was renamed Stalinabad on 19 October 1929, incorporating the nearby districts of Shohmansur, Mavlono and Sari Osiyo. The old name returned in late 1961 as a result of de-Stalinization. During the middle of the 20th century the city had a majority Russian and Eastern European population. Dushanbe became the capital of an independent Tajikistan on 9 September 1991, and the Tajik Civil War of the 1990s checked its growth.

Dushanbe is the capital and largest city of Tajikistan and holds most of the country's major hospitals. Its sights include the Tajikistan National Museum, the National Museum of Antiquities, Rudaki Avenue and the National Library. Its electricity is mainly hydroelectric, from the Nurek Dam, and its trolleybus system dates from 1955.
dusseldorf: Düsseldorf lies at the centre of the Lower Rhine basin, where the Düssel flows into the Rhine, and most of the city is on the east bank. It lies in the middle of the Rhine-Ruhr metropolitan region. Its name comes from the small river Düssel, with the suffix dorf, meaning village, so that the literal meaning is village on the Düssel. It reflects the original character of the settlement as a fishing and farming community on the riverbanks.

In the 7th and 8th centuries the odd farming or fishing settlement stood where the Düssel meets the Rhine, and the city grew from such settlements. In 1186 Düsseldorf came under the rule of the County of Berg, a state of the Holy Roman Empire. In 1263 the Count of Berg granted ferry rights to its inhabitants, and it gained city rights in 1288 after the Battle of Worringen.

In the Late Middle Ages and Renaissance it grew into a regional political and cultural centre under the Dukes of Berg and later as the capital of the United Duchies of Jülich-Cleves-Berg. In the 17th and 18th centuries it became known for its court culture and early art academy. During the Napoleonic era it was briefly part of the Grand Duchy of Berg. After the Congress of Vienna in 1815 the Rhineland, including Düsseldorf, was incorporated into the Kingdom of Prussia. The city lost its status as a capital but became the seat of a regional governor and it industrialised rapidly in the 19th century; its population passed 100,000 in 1882.

In the Second World War Düsseldorf was the location of a Nazi prison with forced labour subcamps and of five subcamps of the Buchenwald concentration camp, and the city's Rabbi, who had fled to the Netherlands, died in Auschwitz in 1943. The city entered the British occupation zone on 21 June 1945, and in 1946 it became the capital of the new state of North Rhine-Westphalia. Its population peaked at just over 705,000 in 1962.

Düsseldorf is the capital of North Rhine-Westphalia and, with 619,444 inhabitants in 2025, the second-largest city in the state after Cologne. It is an international business and financial centre, known for its fashion and trade fairs, and it has the largest Japanese community in Germany. The Kunstakademie Düsseldorf, its academy of arts, counts Joseph Beuys, Emanuel Leutze, August Macke and Gerhard Richter among its members.
dutch-conquest-of-the-banda-islands: The volcanic Banda Islands were the only source of nutmeg and mace. A Dutch fleet reached them in 1599, and Jacob van Heemskerck signed contracts with Bandanese chiefs. The Bandanese preferred free trade, selling to the highest bidder, while the Dutch East India Company (VOC), founded on 20 March 1602, wanted a monopoly. In late May 1609 chiefs lured the commander Pieter Willemsz Verhoeff into an ambush, killing 46 Dutchmen in all, Verhoeff among them; the Dutch plundered villages and imposed a treaty, building Fort Nassau on Banda Neira.

The Bandanese went on selling to English, Malay, Javanese and Makassarese traders, and by 1614 the Heeren XVII, the VOC's governing body, resolved to conquer the whole archipelago. In April 1616 Jan Dirkszoon Lam took Ai, where about 400 islanders, many of them women and children, drowned fleeing to Run, then held by the English. The English under Nathaniel Courthope held Run for over four years.

On 26 October 1620 Governor-General Jan Pieterszoon Coen wrote that Banda must be subjugated again and populated with other people. His fleet of 19 ships, with 1,655 Dutch soldiers and 286 Japanese mercenaries, reached Fort Nassau on 21 February 1621. Attacking Lontor, the main island, on 11 March, it held the whole island by the end of 12 March. The orang kaya, Lontor's upper class, accepted Dutch sovereignty, but many islanders fled to the hills and fought on. After confessions extracted by torture on 21 April, Coen deported at least 789 orang kaya and their families to Batavia, and 24 were beheaded by the Japanese mercenaries on 8 May. Villages were destroyed, and many islanders starved or leapt from the cliffs rather than surrender.

Coen himself reported that about 2,500 died of hunger and misery or by the sword. The historian Hans Straver estimated that of 4,500 to 5,000 people on Lontor, 1,700 were enslaved and 2,500 died of famine and disease, while several hundred escaped to the Kei Islands and eastern Seram. Vincent Loth and Charles Corn put the islands' population before the conquest at about 15,000, of whom only 1,000 survived, and Peter Lape estimated that 90% were killed, enslaved or deported. The Dutch planters (perkeniers) worked the islands with slaves from the Dutch East Indies, India and China; the native Bandanese numbered 100 by 1681. The English renounced their claim in the Treaty of Breda of 1667.
dutch-east-india-company: After the Dutch Revolt began, the Portuguese used an international syndicate operating from Hamburg, which cut Dutch merchants out of the Asian trade, while their system could not raise its supply of pepper to meet demand. In 1580 the Portuguese crown had been united with the Spanish crown, with which the Dutch Republic was at war, so the Portuguese Empire became a fitting target. Dutch merchants such as Jan Huyghen van Linschoten and Cornelis de Houtman gained firsthand knowledge of the secret Portuguese routes.

The English formed a monopoly company in 1600, and in 1602 the States General followed, founding the United East India Company on 20 March by amalgamating existing companies, with a 21-year monopoly on Asian trade. Any citizen of the Dutch Republic could buy shares, which were traded in open-air markets, one of which became the Amsterdam Stock Exchange.

The charter let the company build forts, keep armies, make treaties and strike its own coins. For a time it monopolised nutmeg, mace and cloves and sold them at 14 to 17 times the price it paid in Indonesia, while as sole buyer it forced down the prices paid to producers in the Spice Islands. Jan Pieterszoon Coen, governor-general from 1619, stormed Jayakarta on 30 May 1619 and founded Batavia as headquarters. In the 1620s almost the entire native population of the Banda Islands was driven away, starved or killed so that Dutch plantations could grow nutmeg.

After 1730 the company declined, squeezed out of Persia, Suratte, the Malabar Coast and Bengal, while corruption and private trading by its staff spread. It paid dividends averaging about 18% for almost 200 years, but went bankrupt and was formally dissolved in 1799, and the government of the Batavian Republic took over its possessions and debt.

The headquarters were in Amsterdam, with a board of directors known as the Heeren XVII. At its height the company had 25,000 employees in Asia and 11,000 en route, recruited across north-west Europe and from local Asian labour markets. Posts included Batavia, the Cape Colony from 1652 and Dejima in Japan from 1641. Between 1602 and 1795 about one million seamen and craftsmen left Holland, and only about 340,000 returned. Twenty-five million pages of its records survive and were added to UNESCO's Memory of the World register in 2003.
dutch-empire: The Dutch rebel provinces declared independence from the Spanish Empire with the Act of Abjuration of 1581. In 1580 Philip II brought Portugal into the Iberian Union with Spain, which closed all Portuguese markets to the United Provinces, and in 1595 the Dutch set sail to acquire Asian goods for themselves. By 1600 Dutch traders had penetrated the Asian spice trade but lacked capital, and in 1602 the States General merged several enterprises into the semi-state-owned Dutch East India Company, the VOC, which was granted a monopoly over Asian trade. The Dutch West India Company followed in 1621 for the Atlantic, the Americas and the west coast of Africa.

Dutch activities abroad were at first commercial ventures that controlled shipping routes through strategically placed outposts rather than large territories. By the mid-17th century the two companies exercised quasi-governmental powers to negotiate treaties, wage war and administer territory. The conquest of the Banda Islands from 1609 to 1621, also called the Banda genocide, followed a collapse in negotiations over the Dutch nutmeg monopoly; under Jan Pieterszoon Coen massacres, deportations, starvation and disease left the islands severely depopulated. The West India Company took Pernambuco from Portugal in 1630 and by 1650 controlled the sugar and slave trades. The Cape of Good Hope was founded in 1652 as a victualling station.

Wars with England between 1652 and 1784 cost many settlements, and the rise of the British East India Company weakened Dutch influence. After the French invasion of 1795 made the Batavian Republic, Britain occupied Dutch colonies in Asia, South Africa and the Caribbean. After the Japanese occupation of 1942 to 1945 the Dutch East Indies became Indonesia, and Suriname became independent in 1975.

Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten remain autonomous constituent countries of the Kingdom of the Netherlands. Names of Dutch origin survive in New York, among them Brooklyn, Harlem and Staten Island, and the Dutch Fort Zeelandia still stands in Paramaribo. Between 1800 and 1950 Dutch engineers built roads, railways and irrigation systems in Indonesia, which became the material base of the colonial and later Indonesian state. Dutch is the official language of Suriname, Aruba, Bonaire and Curaçao, and Indonesian inherited many words from Dutch.
dutch-golden-age: In 1568 the Seven Provinces that later signed the Union of Utrecht rebelled against Philip II of Spain, beginning the Eighty Years' War. Antwerp, then arguably the most important port in the world, fell to Spain on 17 August 1585 after a siege, and the division between the Northern and Southern Netherlands was established. Under the terms of the surrender, Protestants unwilling to reconvert were given four years to leave. More Protestants moved north between 1585 and 1630 than Catholics moved south, and many settled in Amsterdam, which became one of the most important ports and commercial centres in the world by 1630. The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 brought the Dutch Republic formal recognition of its independence.

The Dutch East India Company (VOC), founded in 1602, was among the first multinational corporations, financed by shares that established the Amsterdam Stock Exchange. It received a Dutch monopoly on Asian trade, which it kept for two centuries, and became the largest commercial enterprise of the 17th-century world. The Bank of Amsterdam was established in 1609. The Republic's position between the Bay of Biscay and the Baltic let its ships carry goods between the two, and the Dutch share of European shipping was well over half during most of the period. From 1640 the VOC held a monopoly on trade with Japan through Dejima, and until 1854 the Dutch were Japan's sole window to the Western world.

The prosperity came with violence. In 1621 Jan Pieterszoon Coen had almost all the inhabitants of the Banda Islands massacred, and about 1.7 million people were enslaved by Dutch slavers between the 17th and 19th centuries. Calvinism was the state religion, though bitter controversy between strict Calvinists and Remonstrants was settled in favour of the former at the Synod of Dort in 1618–19.

The Republic attracted scientists and thinkers from across Europe. The University of Leiden, founded in 1575, became a gathering place for intellectuals, and René Descartes, Jan Amos Comenius and Pierre Bayle all lived and published there. Wealthy merchants rather than nobles were the patrons of art. Dutch painting led in developing still life, landscape and genre painting, canals were dug and merchants built houses along them, and the book trade flourished, with the House of Elzevir producing reliable pocket editions of classical Latin texts. Conflicts with neighbouring powers and declining economic influence ended the period, usually dated to the Rampjaar of 1672. Since 2019 the Amsterdam Museum has stopped using the phrase Golden Age, saying it hides the colonial past and slavery.
dutch-hanseatic-war: The war was fought over trade and the control of Baltic shipping. For years tension had grown as Hanseatic merchants tried to keep Dutch trade with Livonia small, and the Dutch had begun to use privateers against German ships. The County of Holland acted independently of the rest of the Burgundian Netherlands, of which it was then part.

On 14 April 1438 the Dutch authorities declared war on the six Wendish cities, Hamburg, Lübeck, Lüneburg, Greifswald, Stettin and Anklam, and on the County of Holstein.
