On 23 April the League told its members and advised them to ship goods through Flanders rather than Holland or Zeeland. In May the Dutch mobilised every suitable ship in Holland and ordered 79 new vessels to be built.

There was little real fighting. For much of 1438 to 1440 the Dutch fleet patrolled the Øresund, but the Wendish fleet blocked the passage and kept it from going far into the Baltic Sea. The State of the Teutonic Order declared itself neutral, and the towns of Prussia refused to give military help to the Hanseatic side. The opening for peace came in 1440, when Eric of Pomerania was forced from the throne of Denmark. His successor, Christopher of Bavaria, though nominally allied with the Hanseatic cities, wanted a settlement and gave Dutch merchants the same rights in Denmark as Hanseatic ones.

Peace was made in September 1441 by the Treaty of Copenhagen. Each side granted the other free trading rights, which gave the Dutch unrestricted access to Baltic trade once more and worked in the long run to their benefit rather than that of the German cities. The settlement also obliged the Dutch to pay costly reparations.
dutch-indonesian-round-table-conference: Sukarno declared Indonesian independence on 17 August 1945. The Dutch, who had been expelled by the Japanese occupation of the Dutch East Indies in 1942, regarded the Indonesian leaders as collaborators and sought to regain the colony, and the conflict grew into the Indonesian National Revolution. Earlier talks produced the Linggadjati Agreement and the Renville Agreement. On 28 January 1949 United Nations Security Council Resolution 67 called for an end to the latest Dutch offensive and the restoration of the republican government.

The Roem–Van Roijen Agreement of 1949 effectively endorsed that resolution, and the republican government, in exile for over six months, returned to its temporary capital at Yogyakarta on 6 July 1949. Inter-Indonesian Conferences held there from 31 July to 2 August agreed the outline of a federal constitution, so that the republic and the federal delegates would negotiate as one.

With the help of the United Nations Commission for Indonesia, the delegations agreed a Charter of Transfer of Sovereignty, a statute of union, a draft constitution and economic, social and military agreements. The Dutch–Indonesian Union was to be a consultative body without powers, headed by the Dutch queen in a symbolic role. Dutch troops were to be withdrawn as soon as possible, and the Netherlands received most-favoured-nation status.

Two issues nearly broke the talks. On the colonial debt, the Indonesian delegations objected to paying what they saw as the costs of Dutch military action against them, but after intervention by the United States member of the commission they agreed on 24 October to take over about ƒ4.5 billion. On Western New Guinea, the Dutch argued that it had no ethnic ties with the rest of the archipelago; in the early hours of 1 November a compromise put off its status to negotiations within a year.

The Central Indonesian National Committee ratified the agreement on 14 December, and both houses of the Dutch parliament did so on 21 December by the required two-thirds majority. The dispute over Western New Guinea lasted twelve years. After the United States of Indonesia was dissolved into the Republic of Indonesia in 1950, Indonesia nationalised Dutch companies and stopped paying the debt, resuming payments after 1962; the last instalment was made in 2002. Some journalists have called the settlement the price of independence.
dutch-portuguese-war: After the Iberian Union of 1580, Philip II of Spain, fighting the Dutch Revolt, cut the Netherlands off from the spice markets of Lisbon, and the Dutch had to send their own expeditions east. The VOC was founded in 1602 to share the costs and win a share of the spice trade. On 25 February 1603 three VOC ships seized the Portuguese galleon Santa Catarina, whose sale doubled the Company's capital. The scandal produced Hugo Grotius's Mare Liberum of 1609, which argued that the sea was international territory.

In Asia the Dutch made Batavia, conquered by Jan Pieterszoon Coen in 1619, their base against the Portuguese capital at Goa. A battle off Malacca in 1615 destroyed Portuguese naval power in Southeast Asia, and Malacca fell in 1641. They failed four times to take Macau, colonised Taiwan from 1624 and took Colombo in 1656, driving the last Portuguese out of Ceylon in 1658.

In the Atlantic the Dutch West India Company took Salvador in 1624, but it was retaken in 1625; in 1630 the Dutch took Olinda and Recife and founded New Holland. Portuguese settlers rose in 1645, and the Second Battle of Guararapes in 1649 began the end of Dutch rule, which closed with the expulsion from Recife in 1654. In Africa Elmina fell in 1637, and in 1641 the Dutch took Luanda with Kongo and Queen Nzinga of Ndongo, but Salvador Correia de Sá retook it in 1648.

After Portugal broke from Spain in 1640 the war went on. The Dutch demanded Brazil back in May 1654, and the fleet resumed large operations in 1657, with blockades that crippled Portuguese trade. In 1661 Portugal agreed to pay eight million guilders and to cede Ceylon and the Maluku Islands, and on 6 August 1661 the Dutch Republic ceded Brazil to Portugal by the Treaty of The Hague. Portugal kept Goa, Diu and Macau but had lost Hormuz and Malacca.
dutch-reformed-church: Efforts to form a Reformed church began in the southern provinces with a secret meeting of Protestant leaders at Antwerp in 1566. After an attack by the forces of the Duke of Alba in 1568, many Netherlanders fled to the German city of Wesel, where a synod adopted the Belgic Confession and the Heidelberg Catechism and provided for the offices of pastor, elder, teacher and deacon. The first synod of 23 Dutch Reformed leaders met at Emden in October 1571 and is generally taken as the founding of the church. It affirmed the Wesel decisions and set up presbyterian church government.

Before 1795 the church was a public or privileged church. It was never formally adopted as the state religion, but the law required every public official to be a communicant member, and its members could keep their businesses open on Sundays. The Synod of Dort of 1618 expelled the Arminians and added the Canons of Dort to the confessions, which together with the Belgic Confession and the Heidelberg Catechism formed the Three Forms of Unity. The government, which had instigated the expulsion, then forbade synods, and none met until after the end of the Republic in 1795, when the church was disestablished.

In the 17th and early 18th centuries the Nadere Reformatie, or Further Reformation, led by Gisbertus Voetius and Wilhelmus à Brakel, drew on English Puritanism. In 1816 King William I imposed a new form of government under which civil authorities chose the commissioners to the National Synod. In 1834 the minister Hendrik de Cock of Ulrum seceded with his congregation after being told not to preach against colleagues he thought mistaken; the Afscheiding eventually took 120 congregations out of the church. Abraham Kuyper led a further separation, the Doleantie, in 1886.

Dutch migrants carried the church abroad. It reached New Amsterdam in 1628, Ceylon through the Dutch East India Company in 1642, and Pernambuco during the Dutch settlement of Brazil; the Groote Kerk built in 1755 still stands in Galle. In South Africa it produced the Three Sister Churches, and the church became a crucial part of Afrikaner nationalism. In 1766 its ministers founded Queen's College in New Jersey, later Rutgers. Secularisation in the 1960s reduced attendance, and in 2004 the church, with about 2 million members in 1,350 congregations, merged with the Reformed Churches in the Netherlands and the Evangelical Lutheran Church to form the Protestant Church in the Netherlands. Some members left to form the Restored Reformed Church.
dutch-republic: Until the 16th century the Low Countries consisted of duchies, counties and prince-bishoprics, almost all under the supremacy of the Holy Roman Empire. Seven provinces of the Spanish Netherlands revolted against Spanish rule, formed a mutual alliance in 1579 in the Union of Utrecht and declared their independence in 1581 in the Act of Abjuration. In 1588, when the States General could not agree on a new monarch, they confederated.

Each province kept a high degree of independence from the federal assembly, the States General. Each was led by a stadtholder, an office nominally open to anyone but usually given to a member of the House of Orange. Under the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 the republic gained about 20 percent more territory, governed directly by the States General as Generality Lands.

With only around 1.5 million inhabitants, the republic controlled a worldwide network of trade routes through the Dutch East India Company and the Dutch West India Company. Amsterdam became the hub of world trade, and by the mid-1660s had about 200,000 people. Refugees helped the economy, among them Portuguese and Spanish Jews, Protestants from Antwerp, French Huguenots and English Dissenters. Nearly half of Amsterdam's residents in the 17th and 18th centuries were first-generation immigrants.

After the death of William II in 1650 the regents allowed no new stadtholder in Holland for 22 years, and Johan de Witt became the dominant figure. The republic fought three naval wars against England between 1652 and 1674. In the Disaster Year of 1672 England, France, Münster and Cologne attacked it, Johan de Witt and his brother Cornelis were lynched and William III was appointed stadtholder.

After William III died in 1702 the office stood vacant in Holland, Zeeland and Utrecht until William IV was appointed in 1747. In this Second Stadtholderless Period the republic lost its great-power status and its primacy in world trade. Unrest in the 1780s was suppressed by a Prussian invasion supporting the stadtholder. Defeated by France, the republic ended in the Batavian Revolution of 1795, when the stadtholder was expelled.

The republic was a predecessor of the present-day Netherlands and its first independent nation state. It was more tolerant of different religions and ideas than contemporary states. Painters such as Rembrandt and Johannes Vermeer and scientists such as Hugo Grotius, Christiaan Huygens and Antonie van Leeuwenhoek worked under it, and the 17th century became known as the Dutch Golden Age.
dutch-water-line: Early in the Eighty Years' War against Spain the Dutch Republic learnt that flooding low-lying land was an excellent defence, as the Siege of Leiden showed in 1574. Once Holland was free of Spanish troops, Maurice of Nassau planned to defend it with a line of flooded land guarded by fortresses, running from the Zuiderzee down to the river Waal. His half-brother Prince Frederick Henry began the work in 1629, building sluices in the dykes and forts and fortified towns at strategic points, with guns covering the dykes that crossed the line.

The water was kept deep enough to make an advance on foot precarious and shallow enough to rule out boats other than the flat-bottomed gun barges of the defenders. Ditches and trous de loup were hidden below the surface, the trees along the dykes could be felled as abatis, and in winter the level could be changed to weaken the ice. Frost was the line's weakness: freezing nearly made it useless in 1672, and in 1794 and 1795 the revolutionary French armies crossed it only because the floods had frozen solid.

After 1815 King William I of the United Kingdom of the Netherlands extended the line east to include Utrecht, and in the 19th century it gained forts with round gun towers like Martello towers. It was mobilised but never attacked in the Franco-Prussian War of 1870 and in World War I. Before World War II many pillboxes were added, the most numerous being 570 unarmed structures of the Type P Shelter, but the army chose the Grebbe Line as its main defence. In 1940 German airborne troops seized the bridges at Moerdijk, Dordrecht and Rotterdam, and the bombing of Rotterdam forced the surrender.

After the war a third line on the IJssel was planned against a Soviet invasion, to be flooded by diverting the Rhine and the Waal; it was never tested and was dismantled in 1964. From 1815 to 1940 around 50 billion euro in today's terms was spent on the New Dutch Water Line. Many of its forts survive, some used for overnight stays or, like Fort Hoofddijk with Utrecht University's botanical garden, for other purposes. On 26 July 2021 the line joined the Defence Line of Amsterdam as the Dutch Water Defence Lines World Heritage Site.
dutch-west-india-company: When the Dutch East India Company (VOC) was founded in 1602, some Amsterdam traders objected to its monopoly and looked for other routes to Asia. Trade with the Caribbean was hampered by Spain, which refused to make peace if a West India Company were established, and during the Twelve Years' Truce the Dutch sailed to South America under foreign flags. After the truce expired in April 1621, the company was founded. Among its promoters were Reynier Pauw, Willem Usselincx and Jessé de Forest. On 3 June 1621 the States-General granted it a charter giving a 24-year monopoly on trade and colonisation in West Africa and on the American coast between Newfoundland and the Straits of Magellan.

Like the VOC, the company had five chambers, in Amsterdam, Rotterdam, Hoorn, Middelburg and Groningen, and a board of 19 members, the Heeren XIX. Funding was arranged only in 1623, when the States General and the VOC pledged one million guilders, and the capital of 2.8 million florins was smaller than the VOC's original 6.5 million. Investors came slowly, in part because shareholders had no control over the directors' policy, and the company offered foreign investors equal standing. Unlike the VOC it had no right to deploy military troops, and in 1623 it had 15 ships trading along the West African coast and Brazil.

After a plan to seize the Portuguese colonies failed, privateering became a major aim, and Piet Hein's capture of the Spanish silver fleet was its most spectacular success. The Dutch held Portuguese territory in north-eastern Brazil from 1624 to 1654, with Mauritsstad, present-day Recife, as the capital of New Holland, before being driven out. In North America the company allowed investors to found patroonships in New Netherland from 1629, of which Rensselaerswyck was the most successful, and Manhattan with Fort Amsterdam served as the first capital. It also held posts on the Gold Coast, the Slave Coast and briefly Loango-Angola. Fur and sugar were the main trade goods in the Americas, while African posts traded enslaved people, gold, copper and ivory.

In 1662 the company obtained asiento subcontracts with the Spanish Crown to deliver 24,000 enslaved Africans, and it made Curaçao a centre of the Atlantic slave trade. It could not repay its debts and was dissolved in 1674, but a second West India Company was chartered the same year with the same area and fewer directors. Sint Eustatius became its most profitable asset, and from 1738 it outsourced the slave trade to private enterprise. After the Fourth Anglo-Dutch War of 1780–1784 the British took Sint Eustatius, Berbice, Essequibo, Demerara and some forts on the Gold Coast. In 1791 it was decided not to renew the charter, and the territories passed to the States General.
dutty-boukman: Boukman is said to have been a Muslim cleric in Senegambia before his capture, and in Saint-Domingue some of his followers called him Zamba Boukman. Modern sources make him a leader of the maroons and a Vodou houngan, or priest, a claim not found in earlier accounts.

His French name came from the English nickname Book Man, which scholars such as Sylviane Anna Diouf have read as Islamic in origin, since man of the book is a synonym for a Muslim in many parts of the world. Dutty probably refers to Dutih, the plantation where he was enslaved, and the historian Laurent Dubois argues he may have practised a blend of traditional African religion and an Abrahamic faith.

As a coach driver he met Jean-Jacques Dessalines, enslaved less than a mile away, and he worked with Jeannot Bullet, Jean-François and Georges Biassou to prepare the revolt. Contemporary accounts place the Bois Caïman ceremony at the Choiseul plantation, the last of several meetings held over weeks. A black pig was sacrificed and an oath taken, and the attendees drank its blood. The speech attributed to Boukman first appears in an account by Hérard Dumesle of 1824, which does not name him and is likely a dramatisation. A second meeting of about two hundred people at Morne Rouge fixed the date of the rising.

On 22 August 1791 Boukman gathered enslaved people from estates including Dutilh, Héron and Noé, who elected him their commander. The next night he led them north to recruit more, and joined other fighters into a force of about fifteen thousand that marched on the city of le Cap to lay siege to it.

Boukman was killed on 7 November 1791 defending a rebel base at Fond Bleu. The French displayed his head under the words The head of Boukman, leader of the rebels, to dispel his aura of invincibility. The rebels mourned him, and when some demanded the execution of all white prisoners, Jean François prevented it. Haitians later admitted him to the pantheon of loa, the guiding spirits; the band Boukman Eksperyans is named after him, and he appears in Victor Hugo's Bug-Jargal and Guy Endore's novel Babouk.
dutugemunu: Most of what is known of him comes from the Mahavamsa, which gives some six of its 35 chapters to his story. Much of it is legend, but inscriptions confirm many aspects, and the basic account is generally accepted. His mother was Viharamahadevi, daughter of Tissa, king of Kalyani. According to the chronicle, the young Gamani Abhaya mocked his father for refusing to make war on Elara, who had ruled from Anuradhapura for 45 years, and sent him a piece of women's jewellery; the name Dutthagamani, the disobedient one, is said to come from this quarrel.

On Kavantissa's death his younger brother Tissa seized the royal elephant Kandula and their mother. Dutugemunu lost a first battle at Culanganiyapitthi but defeated Tissa near Mahagama, and the brothers were later reconciled through Viharamahadevi and the monks, Tissa becoming one of his foremost generals. Marching north with war elephants, monks and the Ten Giant Warriors his father had recruited, he subdued as many as 32 Tamil rulers, according to the Mahavamsa, including at a four-month siege of Vijitanagara. He killed Elara with a spear at the eastern gate of Anuradhapura, then had him cremated and built a tomb at which passers-by were to dismount and pay respect.

The chronicles credit him with between 68 and 99 religious foundations, among them the Mirisavetiya stupa and the Lohapasada, or Brazen Palace, a nine-storey chapter house for monks named after its copper-tiled roof. His son Saliya gave up the throne rather than give up Asokamala, a woman of the Chandala caste.

He died before the plasterwork of his great stupa was finished. The Mahavamsa describes the dying king carried by palanquin to the unfinished monument, and a folk tale adds that his brother Tissa draped it in white cloth so that he died believing it complete. He was succeeded by his brother Saddhatissa rather than by Saliya. After his death he was called Dharma Gamini, but posterity knows him as Dutugemunu. His life is the subject of the 2015 film Maharaja Gemunu.
duwa: Duwa, also known as Du'a, was the second son of Baraq. In 1282 Kaidu appointed him head of the Chagatai Khanate, hoping to make peace with the sons of Baraq, who had ravaged Central Asia for much of the previous ten years. The appointment kept the Chaghataids loyal to Kaidu until Kaidu's death. Duwa was already a seasoned commander: in 1275 he had destroyed a force in Uyghuria loyal to Kublai Khan, and with Kaidu he took Beshbalik from the Yuan the following year.

He then besieged Kara-Khoja near Turpan for six months with his brother Buzma. The Mongol princes failed to take the city by assault, and the Uyghur ruler, Idiqut Khochqar, had the siege lifted only by giving Duwa his daughter in marriage, and probably by paying compensation as well.

In early 1295 Duwa invaded the Ilkhanate, supported by Kaidu's son Sarban. He stayed eight months in Mazandaran and pillaged many cities on the way back, sacking Fushang, before Kaidu recalled him. In the winter of 1298 he struck the Yuan garrisons, but was then defeated at what is now Kebuduo. In 1298 or 1299 he made his son Kutluk Khoja head of the Qara'unas, a Mongol group that controlled much of Khurasan. He was wounded and defeated in a battle of 1301, shortly before Kaidu died.

Duwa passed over Kaidu's chosen heir, Orus, and had Kaidu's firstborn son Chapar enthroned in 1303. Around 1304 a general peace among the Mongol states ended the Kaidu–Kublai war, which had lasted more than thirty years. Duwa then turned on Chapar: fighting broke out in 1305 or 1306, and with Yuan help he forced Chapar to surrender, deposing him in 1307 in favour of his brother Yangichar. Duwa died the same year and was succeeded by his son Könchek.

Duwa freed the Chagatai Khanate from its subservience to Kaidu and his sons, which had lasted since 1271, and restored relations with the Yuan for the first time since the mid-thirteenth century. His work proved transitory: less than forty years later the eastern part of the khanate split off, and in the 1360s Timur reduced the western khans to puppets. Babur's memoirs trace the descent of his grandfather Yunas Khan from Duwa.
duy-tan: Duy Tân was born Nguyễn Phúc Vĩnh San on 19 September 1900, the 11th emperor of the Nguyễn dynasty. His father was the emperor Thành Thái, who opposed French rule. Because of that opposition and his erratic actions, which some speculate were feigned to shield his opposition from the French, Thành Thái was declared insane and exiled to Vũng Tàu in 1907. The French passed the throne to his son, who was only seven years old. They hoped that someone so young would be easily influenced and raised to be pro-French.

The prince was enthroned with the reign name Duy Tân, meaning friend of reform, but the French efforts to raise him to support them largely failed. As he grew older he noticed that, although he was treated as emperor, it was the colonial authorities who were obeyed. As a teenager he came under the influence of the mandarin Trần Cao Vân, who opposed the colonial administration, and they began to plan a secret rebellion with others.

In 1916, while France was preoccupied with World War I, Duy Tân was smuggled out of the Forbidden City with Trần Cao Vân to call on the people to rise against the French. The secret was revealed, France sent troops, and after only a few days they were betrayed and captured. Because of his age, Duy Tân was deposed and exiled rather than killed, while Trần Cao Vân and the other revolutionaries were beheaded.

Duy Tân was exiled to Réunion with his father and continued to favour national liberation for Vietnam. In the Second World War he resisted the Vichy regime, then joined the Free French Forces, rising from second lieutenant in December 1942 to lieutenant-colonel in September 1945. In late 1945 Charles de Gaulle spoke to him about returning to Vietnam as emperor, but he died in a plane crash in Central Africa on the way home. France posthumously made him a Companion of the Ordre de la Libération. In 1987 his remains were brought back to Vietnam to rest in the tomb of his grandfather, Emperor Dục Đức, and most cities in Vietnam have named major streets after him.
dvaita-vedanta: Dvaita Vedanta, originally called Tattvavada, meaning arguments from a realist viewpoint, is a sub-school of the Vedanta tradition of Hindu philosophy. It was systematised by the 13th-century philosopher-saint Madhvacharya as a dualistic interpretation of the Vedas. Dvaita is a Sanskrit word meaning duality. Madhvacharya divides reality by independence and dependence: the one independent reality is Vishnu, identified as Brahman and Supreme God, and the dependent reality is everything else. Believers hold that Vishnu is almighty, eternal, all-knowing and compassionate, a personal God endowed with attributes. Sannyasis of the tradition belong to the ēkadaṇḍi order.

The school teaches five eternal and real differences: between souls and God, between matter and God, between one soul and another, between matter and souls, and between kinds of matter. The world is called prapañca for this reason. Individual souls (jivas) are eternal and infinite in number, and are reflections of the divine, never identical with it, even after liberation. Madhva also taught three classes of souls: those qualified for liberation, those subject to eternal rebirth, and those condemned to eternal hell. This concept of eternal damnation differed significantly from traditional Hindu belief.

Liberation (moksha) is the realisation that all finite reality depends on the Supreme. It comes by the grace of God together with the soul's own effort, through righteous living, study of scripture, devotion and direct vision of God. Madhva placed great importance on a guru's guidance. He held that the devas are souls rewarded for good deeds, so that only Vishnu is to be worshipped.

Dvaita philosophers challenge the Advaita view of Adi Shankara, in which Brahman and the soul are identical, arguing among other things that if ignorance belongs to Brahman, it must be real. They also reject the qualified non-dualism of Ramanuja's Vishishtadvaita as an inconsistent middle ground, although Madhva accepted Ramanuja's affirmation of a real world and a personal God. Vallabhacharya's Shuddhadvaita shares its devotional orientation, but Dvaita rejects its identification of the world with the divine.

Scholars Kulandran and Kraemer judge that the historical influence of Dvaita Vedanta has been salutary but not extensive. According to B. N. K. Sharma, its ideas most influenced the Chaitanya school of Bengal Vaishnavism and Assam, and Madhva's theology influenced later thinkers such as Nimbarka, Vallabha and Chaitanya Mahaprabhu.
dwight-d-eisenhower: Eisenhower was born David Dwight Eisenhower in Denison, Texas, on 14 October 1890, the third of seven sons of Ida Stover and David Jacob Eisenhower. His mother soon reversed his forenames to avoid two Davids in the family. All the boys were nicknamed Ike, and by the Second World War only Dwight still was. He graduated from West Point in 1915. In the First World War his request for an overseas assignment was denied, and he commanded a unit that trained tank crews at Camp Colt, his first command; he never saw combat.

He was promoted to brigadier general on 3 October 1941. In November 1942 he was appointed commander of the Allied forces in the North African theatre, in the campaign designated Operation Torch. In December 1943 President Roosevelt decided that he, not Marshall, would be Supreme Allied Commander in Europe, and he planned and carried out the Normandy assault of June 1944, Operation Overlord. After the German surrender he was military governor of the American-occupied zone of Germany, and he ordered camera crews to document the Nazi concentration camps for the Nuremberg Trials. He then served as Army Chief of Staff, president of Columbia University from 1948, and first supreme commander of NATO.

He entered the 1952 presidential race as a Republican, in part to block Senator Robert A. Taft, who opposed NATO, and won that election and the 1956 election, 457 to 73 in the electoral vote, against Adlai Stevenson II. As president he gave the Atoms for Peace speech to the United Nations on 8 December 1953, and in 1956 he signed the bill authorising the Interstate Highway System. After the Soviet launch of Sputnik he led the American response, which included NASA. Alaska and Hawaii were admitted as states in 1959. He died on 28 March 1969, aged 78.

His New Look policy relied on nuclear deterrence, building a stockpile of nuclear weapons and delivery systems to deter threats and save money by cutting expensive Army combat units. In his first State of the Union address in February 1953 he said he would use the authority of the presidency to end segregation in the District of Columbia and the Armed Forces, and when the services resisted he used government control of military spending to force the change. In his farewell address he warned of the dangers of massive military spending, which he called the military–industrial complex.
dying-gaul: The Dying Gaul, also called the Dying Galatian, is a marble semi-recumbent statue copied from a lost Greek sculpture of the Hellenistic period, thought to have been bronze. The original may have been commissioned between 230 and 220 BCE by Attalus I of Pergamon to celebrate his victory over the Galatians, the Celtic people of parts of Anatolia, and its sculptor is believed to have been Epigonus, a court sculptor of the Attalid dynasty. The marble in Rome is thought to date from the 1st or 2nd century CE and, according to an analysis of the stone, is white Docimian marble from Afyon, probably from a Roman imperial quarry. Scholars still disagree about the dating of the copies and about how exact they are.

The statue was first recorded in a 1623 inventory of the Ludovisi family collections, and probably came from the site of the Gardens of Sallust, where Cardinal Ludovico Ludovisi built his villa. It was restored in 1623, apparently by Ippolito Buzzi with the young Gian Lorenzo Bernini.

Napoleon's forces took it in 1797 under the Treaty of Tolentino, and it was displayed in Paris until it was repatriated in October 1815 through the intervention of Antonio Canova. It returned to the Capitoline Museum in 1816. It had been placed there in 1733. Until the 20th century it was usually called the Dying Gladiator. Ennio Quirino Visconti first identified the figure as a barbarian from his neck torc, matted hair and moustache, and in the mid-19th century it was identified as a Gaul or Galatian.

The statue suggests both the defeat of the Celts and a memorial to their bravery as worthy adversaries. Its nakedness agrees with ancient accounts of Celtic fighting; Polybius describes the Gaesatae at the Battle of Telamon in 225 BCE as fighting naked, and it may also give the figure heroic dignity. H. W. Janson reads its message as that they knew how to die, barbarians though they were.

In the 17th and 18th centuries its pathos won great admiration; it was a must-see on the Grand Tour and Byron commemorated it in Childe Harold's Pilgrimage. François Perrier engraved it in 1638, and a plaster cast was made for Philip IV of Spain in 1650. Michel Monnier carved a marble copy for Louis XIV that remains at Versailles.
dynamis-bosporan-queen: Dynamis, whose name means the powerful one and who bore the epithet Philoromaios, friend of Rome, was of Iranian and Greek Macedonian descent, the daughter of Pharnaces II and his Sarmatian wife, with an older brother Darius and a younger brother Arsaces. When Pharnaces invaded Roman Anatolia in 47 BCE he left Asander in charge of the Bosporan Kingdom, and Asander rebelled. According to Appian, before his battle with Julius Caesar Pharnaces offered Dynamis to Caesar in marriage. After Pharnaces died fighting Asander, Asander married Dynamis, probably to make his rule legitimate.

Caesar allowed Mithridates of Pergamon to conquer the Bosporus, and Asander and Dynamis went into exile, sheltered, according to the scholar Mayor, by her mother's Sarmatian tribe. Asander later overthrew Mithridates, and his coins named her Queen Dynamis. On his death she was entrusted with the regency, and a solitary stater shows her ruling alone in 17/16 BCE. She then married Scribonius, who claimed descent from Mithridates VI; when Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa sent Polemon I of Pontus against him, the Bosporans killed Scribonius, resisted Polemon, and surrendered only when Agrippa prepared a campaign. Polemon married Dynamis with the sanction of Augustus.

The marriage lasted little more than a year, and Polemon then married Pythodorida. Dynamis reappears on coins and inscriptions from 8 BCE, apparently ruling alone; gold staters with the heads of Augustus and Agrippa carry a monogram that Mommsen read as her name. She dedicated statues to Augustus at Phanagoria and Panticapaeum and to Livia, and Phanagoria was renamed Agrippia.

Ancient writers say almost nothing about her, and her later reign rests on coins and inscriptions. Rostovtzeff argued that she took refuge with Sarmatian tribes, married Aspurgos as a fourth husband and helped bring about the death of Polemon, but Rose holds that the evidence does not support this. Rostovtzeff saw her reign as the end of Bosporan autonomy, a ruler in the name of Augustus; Kersley instead sees Augustus as having kept and enhanced the authority of a female ruler. She appears to have ruled until 7-8 CE.
dynamite: Alfred Nobel's father, Immanuel Nobel, was an industrialist, engineer and inventor who built bridges and buildings in Stockholm. His construction work led him to look for ways of blasting rock that were more effective than black powder. At 17 Alfred was sent abroad for two years and in France studied under the chemist Théophile-Jules Pelouze, who cautioned him against using nitroglycerin as a commercial explosive because it was so sensitive to shock. Nobel invented the detonator, or blasting cap, which allowed a controlled explosion to be set off from a distance, and in 1863 he made his first successful detonation of pure nitroglycerin. On 3 September 1864 his brother Emil and several others were killed in an explosion at the factory at Heleneborg.

Despite the blasting cap, nitroglycerin was too unstable for commercial use. Nobel tried to combine it with a substance that would make it safe to handle without lessening its force. Mixtures with cement, coal and sawdust failed, but diatomaceous earth, which is fossilised algae, stabilised it. He obtained patents in England on 7 May 1867 and in Sweden on 19 October 1867. Dynamite is usually sold as cardboard cylinders about 200 mm long and 32 mm across, and is rated by its weight strength, the share of nitroglycerin it contains, usually from 20 to 60 per cent. It weeps nitroglycerin over time.

Dynamite rapidly gained wide use as a safer alternative to black powder and nitroglycerin. Nobel controlled his patents tightly and shut down unlicensed makers, though a few American businessmen avoided the patent by using other absorbents such as resin. In the United States it was first made by the Giant Powder Company of San Francisco. For several decades from the 1940s the largest producer in the world was the Union of South Africa, where De Beers established a factory at Somerset West in 1902 to supply the gold mines of the Witwatersrand.

Dynamite has never been popular in warfare, because it degenerates quickly under severe conditions and can be set off by fire or a stray bullet. The German armed forces adopted TNT as a shell filling in 1902.
dzibanche: The city lies 130 kilometres north-east of Chetumal, a short distance inland from the Bacalar Lagoon, on raised ground surrounded by a bajo, a seasonal swamp with fertile soils. Its ancient name was Kaanu'l, place of snakes, from which the ruling dynasty took its name. The modern name means writing on wood and was given after Thomas Gann rediscovered the site in 1927 and found carved wooden lintels in the Temple of the Lintels. With its farmland the city covers over 60 square kilometres, in four groups, the Main Group, Tutil, Lamay and Kinichná, joined by sacbe causeways that also lead to the city of Ichkabal.

Settlement began around 300 BCE. Between the late 4th and early 5th centuries the Kaanu'l dynasty began a military expansion through conquest and alliance, subordinating nearby sites such as El Resbalón, Los Alacranes, Pol Box and Dzibantunich and allying with Naranjo and Caracol. The hieroglyphic stairway holds the earliest known use of the Kaan emblem glyph, dated to 495 CE. The expansion brought conflict with Tikal, which Dzibanche defeated in 562.

After part of the lineage moved its seat to Calakmul, the branch that stayed went on building and winning victories over nearby sites. Dzibanche was among the last Maya cities to carve a dated hieroglyphic text, in 909, and was abandoned around the 11th century.

The Main Group, the royal core, is laid out around the Gann, Xibalba and Pom plazas. The Temple of the Owl holds a tomb of about 400 CE with the remains of a high-ranking woman, named after a vessel with an owl-shaped lid; the Temple of the Cormorants, the largest pyramid, holds the tomb of the ruler Sky Witness, who reigned from 572 to 598. The Temple of the Captives shows bound prisoners taken by Yuknoom Chʼeen I. The 35-metre K'inich Na' pyramid stands about 2 kilometres north of the core.
dzud: A zud, or dzud, is a periodic disaster in the steppe, semi-desert and desert regions of Mongolia and Central Asia, including Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan, in which large numbers of livestock die, mainly from starvation because particularly severe conditions stop them grazing. In winter it may be caused by an impenetrable ice crust and in summer by drought. Mongolian herders recognise several kinds.

A tsagaan or white zud follows heavy snowfall that covers the grass. A khar or black zud comes from a lack of snow, which leaves both animals and people without water, and mostly affects the Gobi. A tumur or iron zud occurs when a short thaw is followed by freezing, so that the snow melts and refreezes into an ice cover. A huiten or cold zud occurs when very low temperatures and strong winds last for several days. A havsarsan zud combines at least two of these.
In Kazakhstan a proverb says that the djut has seven relatives, naming seven severe conditions, among them summer drought, early winter, deep snow, winter rains, an ice crust and a blizzard.

Traditional protection includes drying and storing cut grass in summer to feed the animals, and stacking blocks of dried sheep and goat dung, called argal in Mongolia and kizyak in Central Asia, into walls that shelter the animals from wind and that can also be burnt as winter fuel. Herders move seasonally, wintering in valleys protected by mountains. Under the communist regime the state regulated herd sizes to prevent overgrazing. After the economy was deregulated in the 1990s and worldwide demand for cashmere rose, the number of goats grew greatly. Goats damage pasture by nibbling at the roots and with their hooves, which leads to desertification, and climate change has brought snowier winters and stronger droughts.

A zud can kill over a million head of livestock in a winter. A record loss of almost seven million in 1944 was later surpassed. Three zuds in a row in 1999-2000, 2000-2001 and 2001-2002 killed a combined 11 million animals. In the winter of 2009-2010 snow covered 80 percent of Mongolia, extreme cold lasted almost 50 days in Uvs, 9,000 families lost their entire herds and 33,000 more lost half, and by May 2010 the United Nations reported that eight million animals, about 17 percent of the country's livestock, had died. The zud of 2023-2024 killed 7.1 million animals by early June.

Herders who lose all their animals often move to cities, and Ulaanbaatar is ringed by settlements of wooden houses without roads, water or sewers, where displaced herders may find no work and sink into poverty, while others take dangerous illegal mining jobs.
dzungar-genocide: The Dzungar Khanate, a confederation of Tibetan Buddhist Oirat Mongol tribes that emerged in the early 17th century, was the last great nomadic empire in Asia. Its lands stretched from the western end of the Great Wall to present-day eastern Kazakhstan, and the Dzungars made their own gunpowder weapons and built a mixed farming and herding economy with mining and manufacture. After inconclusive wars from the 1680s, the Qianlong Emperor defeated them in 1755 with the help of the Dzungar leader Amursana and planned to divide the khanate among four khans. Amursana, who wanted to rule a united Dzungar nation, rebelled.

The enraged emperor ordered the eradication of the whole Dzungar nation and its name: in the translation of the historian Peter C. Perdue, he told his commanders to show no mercy and spare only the old and weak. He repeated the order many times, punishing the generals Hadaha and Agui for letting people escape and rewarding others, such as Tangkelu, for their part in the killing. Manchu, Han and Khalkha Mongol troops carried it out, supported by the Turkic oasis people of Altishahr, who had resented Dzungar rule; women and children were handed to Manchus and Mongol banners as slaves.

The Qing scholar Wei Yuan put the Dzungar population before the conquest at about 600,000 in 200,000 households, and wrote that about 40 percent of households died of smallpox, 20 percent fled to Russia or the Kazakhs, and 30 percent were killed by Manchu bannermen. Many survivors were seized in Kazakh raids or enslaved in the Tarim Basin. The historian Mark Levene called it arguably the eighteenth-century genocide par excellence.

The Qing named the conquered land Xinjiang and presented it as part of a multi-ethnic China, giving Chinese names to its towns, such as Dihua for Ürümqi in 1760. With northern Xinjiang emptied, the state settled Han, Hui, Uyghur, Sibe and Manchu colonists there; from 1760 to 1830, 155,000 Han Chinese settled on state farms in Dzungaria and Ürümqi. The Qing kept Han settlers out of the Uyghur oases of the south, but the promise of autonomy made to the Uyghurs was not honoured, and revolts in the Tarim Basin continued for about a hundred years. A small number of Oirat descendants still live around Bortala and Bayingholin.
dzungar-qing-wars: After the fall of the Yuan dynasty in 1368 the Mongols withdrew north and their state broke into khanates. By the 1650s the Dzungar Khanate, an Oirat state ruled by the Choros clan and centred in Dzungaria and western Mongolia, had become the leading power of the region and was often in conflict with the Khalkha Mongols of the east. Galdan Boshugtu Khan, who took the throne after his brother Sengge died in 1670, extended Dzungar rule as far as present-day eastern Kazakhstan and southern Siberia while keeping peace with the Qing.

When Galdan's brother Dorjijab was killed in a skirmish with Khalkha troops in 1687, Galdan invaded eastern Mongolia and destroyed several Khalkha tribes at Olgoi Nor in 1688, sending twenty thousand refugees south to Qing territory. The Treaty of Nerchinsk with Russia kept Galdan from finding Russian allies, and the Qing, fearing a united Mongol state under the Dzungars, turned against them.

In September 1690 a Qing army under Prince Fuquan met the Dzungars at Ulan Butung, where the Dzungars, outnumbered five to one, formed a camel wall, beat back two assaults and escaped. In 1691 the Khalkha rulers declared themselves Qing vassals at Dolon Nor. The Kangxi Emperor then prepared a great expedition, and in May 1696 a Qing army under Fiyanggu defeated Galdan at Jao Modo, where his wife, Queen Anu, was killed. Galdan died in 1697, by his own hand according to Mongolian accounts, or of disease according to the historian Peter C. Perdue.

Galdan's successor Tsewang Rabtan invaded Tibet in 1717 and killed Lha-bzang Khan, the last ruler of the Khoshut Khanate. A Qing expedition with Tibetan forces under Polhané Sönam Topgyé and Kangchennas drove the Dzungars out in 1720, beginning Qing rule in Tibet. Under the Yongzheng Emperor fighting resumed: a Qing army of 10,000 under Furdan was annihilated near the Khoton Lake in 1731, and a Khalkha ally of the Qing defeated the Dzungars near the Erdene Zuu Monastery in 1732. A treaty fixed the border in 1739.

In 1752 the Khoit-Oirat prince Amursana, defeated by his rival Dawachi, fled to the Qing court. The Qianlong Emperor backed him, and in 1755 the Manchu general Zhaohui forced Dawachi to surrender at Ili. Amursana, given only one of four equal khanships, then led most of the remaining Oirats in revolt. Zhaohui defeated him at Oroi-Jalatu and Khurungui, and Amursana fled to Russia, where he died. The wars brought Outer Mongolia, Tibet and Xinjiang into the Qing Empire until its fall in 1911–1912, and ended with the genocide of much of the Dzungar population.
dzungaria: Dzungaria, also called Northern Xinjiang or Beijiang, is the northern half of Xinjiang and covers about 777,000 square kilometres. The Altai Mountains bound it on the north and the Tian Shan on the south, and it borders Kazakhstan on the west and Mongolia on the east. Before the mid-18th century the name could cover a wider area, coterminous with the Oirat-led Dzungar Khanate. Its core is the triangular Dzungarian Basin, with the Gurbantünggüt Desert at its centre. The western corner of the basin is the Dzungarian Gate, a historically important gateway between Dzungaria and the Kazakh Steppe, and the northern corner is the valley of the upper Irtysh River.

The first inhabitants were Indo-European-speaking peoples such as the Tocharians in prehistory and the Jushi Kingdom in the first millennium BCE. The Han dynasty sent an explorer west along the northernmost Silk Road trackway, and in the latter half of the sixth century the Göktürk leader Istämi received Dzungaria as an inheritance from his father. Over the centuries the region was ruled or controlled, wholly or in part, by the Xiongnu, the Tang dynasty, the Mongol Empire and the Yuan dynasty, among others.

Travellers going west from China went either north of the Tian Shan through Dzungaria or south of it through the Tarim Basin. Trade usually took the south side and migrations the north, because the Tarim leads to the Ferghana Valley and Iran, while Dzungaria leads only to the open steppe.

The region takes its name from the Dzungar people, from the Mongolian zűn gar, meaning left hand, since the western Mongols, the Oirats, stood on the left when the Mongol Empire divided. Dzungar power reached its height in the second half of the 17th century, when Galdan Boshugtu Khan repeatedly intervened in the affairs of the Kazakhs, and its widest limit included Kashgar, Yarkand and Khotan. The Qing Empire destroyed the khanate about 1757–1759. At the time of the Qing conquest Dzungaria was inhabited chiefly by nomadic, steppe-dwelling Tibetan-Buddhist Dzungars. After what is called the Dzungar genocide the Qing repopulated the area with Han and Hui people, and in 1884 they unified Dzungaria and the Tarim Basin into one province, Xinjiang.

The main cities are Ürümqi, Yining and Karamay. Wheat, barley, oats and sugar beets are grown, irrigated with melted snow from the mountains, and cattle, sheep and horses are raised. The region has deposits of coal, gold and iron as well as large oil fields. The name has largely disappeared from the map, but survives in the Dzungarian Alatau and in the Djungarian hamster.
dzungars: The name comes from the Mongolian züün gar, left hand: the left and right hands formed the military and administrative divisions of the Oirats, and the Dzungars were one of the major tribes of the Four Oirat confederation. The confederation emerged in the early 17th century to fight the Altan Khan of the Khalkha, Tümen Zasagt Khan and later the Manchu for control of the Mongols. It rose in the Junggar Basin between the Altai Mountains and the Ili Valley and at first joined the Oöled, Dörbet and Khoid; parts of the Khoshut and Torghut were later forced into its army. Oral history makes the Oöled and Dörbet heirs of the Naimans of Genghis Khan's time.

At its height Dzungar territory reached from the western end of the Great Wall to present-day eastern Kazakhstan and from northern Kyrgyzstan to southern Siberia. The Dzungars made gunpowder weapons of their own, built up a mixed farming and herding economy with mines and workshops, and promoted the Oirat language through laws across their realm. Inconclusive wars with the Qing began in the 1680s. After the Qianlong Emperor's victory in 1755, the Dzungar leader Amursana rejected a plan to split the khanate among four khans and rebelled.

Qianlong then ordered the Dzungars wiped out. Qing bannermen and Khalkha Mongols killed the men and enslaved women and children. The Qing scholar Wei Yuan put the population before the fall at 600,000 and wrote that 40 percent of households died of smallpox, 30 percent were killed by the army and 20 percent fled to Russia or the Kazakhs. Historian Peter Perdue calls it an ethnic genocide carried out by a deliberate policy of massacre.

The emptied land was settled by Han Chinese, Hui, Uyghurs, Xibe, Manchu bannermen and Kazakhs, and the Qing founded cities such as Ürümqi and Yining; in 1759 they declared the former Dzungar lands absorbed into China. The survivors were called Oolods or Eleuths, a Qing euphemism for the hated name Dzungar. Groups were resettled in Bayankhongor, Hulunbuir and Khovd, and in 2010 some 15,520 people in Mongolia claimed Ööled ancestry.
